l-orfeo: Claudio Monteverdi was born in Cremona in 1567 and joined the court of Duke Vincenzo Gonzaga at Mantua as a viola player in 1590 or 1591. He rose to become master of music in 1601. The librettist, Alessandro Striggio, was a young lawyer and diplomat at the Gonzaga court and a member of the Accademia degli Invaghiti, Mantua's intellectual society, which was the chief outlet for its theatrical works.

Work on the libretto was under way in January 1607, when Francesco Gonzaga wrote asking his brother for a high-quality castrato for a 'play in music' being prepared for Carnival. By then Monteverdi had sixteen years of experience of stage music. The premiere was on 24 February 1607, a date established by two letters of 23 February, probably in a room of the apartments of the Duke's widowed sister, Margherita Gonzaga d'Este.

The action alternates between the fields of Thrace and the Underworld. La musica sings a prologue and introduces Orfeo, who celebrates his wedding to Euridice. A messenger brings news that Euridice has died of a snakebite while gathering flowers, and Orfeo resolves to bring her back. Speranza guides him to the gates of Hades, where the ferryman Caronte refuses him passage until Orfeo plays his lyre and lulls him to sleep.

Proserpina persuades her husband Plutone to release Euridice on condition that Orfeo not look back as he leads her out. Distracted by a noise offstage, he looks round and she vanishes. In the printed score Apollo then descends and takes Orfeo to the heavens, where he will see Euridice's likeness in the stars. Striggio's 1607 libretto instead had Orfeo threatened by a chorus of Bacchantes, and his fate left uncertain.

Monteverdi listed around 41 instruments in his score, using distinct groups to depict scenes: strings, harpsichords and recorders for the fields of Thrace, and heavy brass for the underworld. He published the score in 1609 and again in 1615, and after his death in 1643 the opera went unperformed for many years.

Robert Eitner published an abridged score in Berlin in 1881, and Vincent d'Indy's edition formed the basis of a concert performance at the Schola Cantorum on 25 February 1904 and of the first modern staged performance at the Théâtre Réjane, Paris, on 2 May 1911. The first recording was issued in 1939, and the 1969 recording by Nikolaus Harnoncourt and the Vienna Concentus Musicus was praised for making the music sound as Monteverdi imagined. The quatercentenary in 2007 was marked by performances around the world.
la-brabanconne: The title La Brabançonne refers to the Duchy of Brabant. According to legend, the anthem was written in September 1830, during the Belgian Revolution, by a young revolutionary called Jenneval, who read the lyrics at a meeting in the Aigle d'Or café. Jenneval was a Frenchman, Alexandre Dechet, an actor at the theatre where the revolution began in August 1830; he died in the war of independence.

François van Campenhout composed the music, based on the tune of a French song, L'Air des lanciers polonais, written by the French poet Eugène de Pradel. That tune was itself an adaptation of L'Air du magistrat irréprochable, found in a popular collection of drinking songs, La Clé du caveau. The anthem was first performed in September 1830.

The original text exists in two versions of 1830. The first, from August, addresses the Belgians as worthy children who should remain under arms, and appeals to Nassau, the House of Orange, to confirm their rights, using the image of the Orange graft that blooms on the tree of Liberty. It warns that if the cannon are turned on the people, the Orange will fall from the tree. The second version, of September, written after cannon had been fired, declares that grapeshot has shattered the Orange and ends with a lament for the dead.

The third version dates from 1860, when Belgium formally adopted the song and music as its national anthem. It tells of Belgians who, after centuries of slavery, have reconquered their name, rights and flag, and whose motto is the King, the Law, Liberty.

When Belgium adopted the anthem in 1860, the prime minister, Charles Rogier, edited out lyrics attacking the Dutch House of Orange, working from the version written by Louis Hymans. A ministerial circular of the Ministry of the Interior on 8 August 1921 decreed that only the fourth verse of Rogier's text should be considered official, in French, German and Dutch. An unofficial short version combining the words of the fourth verse in all three official languages is sung on Belgian National Day, 21 July. A monument of 1930 by the sculptor Charles Samuel in Brussels carries partial lyrics.
la-ceiba: La Ceiba lies on the southern edge of the Caribbean, forming part of the south-eastern boundary of the Gulf of Honduras. It is a municipality as well as the capital of the department of Atlántida. The city was named after a giant ceiba tree that grew near the old dock. It has a tropical monsoon climate, with an average annual rainfall of about 3,200 millimetres and a peak between October and February, when the trade winds are strongest. Pico Bonito, 2,435 metres high in the Nombre de Dios range, forms a backdrop to the city.

In 1872 Manuel Hernández built a small shack under the ceiba tree near the old docks. People then came from other parts of Honduras, especially the departments of Olancho and Santa Bárbara, and from around the world, drawn by work in the banana industry. La Ceiba was declared a municipality on 23 August 1877, when Marco Aurelio Soto was president of Honduras. Late in the 19th century North American banana companies, among them the Vaccaro Brothers' Standard Fruit Company of New Orleans, took an interest in the trade, and their work attracted national and foreign immigrant labourers.

The neighbourhood called Barrio Inglés was the first recognised in the city and was named for its many English-speaking residents. The main thoroughfare was then the present Avenida La República, where the Standard Fruit Company laid the railway that carried bananas from the plantations to ships at the port. The company was largely responsible for the early growth of the city. Banana and pineapple production formed the basis of the economy. Other enterprises followed, among them Banco Atlántida, founded in 1913 and described as the oldest bank in the country, and the brewing company Cervecería Hondureña, founded in 1918.

The first municipal building was made of wood and was burned in 1903 by people who wanted to destroy the records of private property ownership. It was set on fire again on 7 March 1914 during social unrest, and offices that had been moved were burned once more in 1924. Soon afterwards the present building was constructed on land donated by Manuel Mejía.

La Ceiba has an estimated population of 209,000. It is the second most important port of Honduras after Puerto Cortés, and its pier offers ferry services to the Bay Islands, including Roatán and Útila. Each year the city holds a carnival in honour of its patron saint, Isidore the Laborer, on the third or fourth Saturday of May. Pineapple is the major export, and the Cangrejal River and the Cuero y Salado wildlife refuge lie close by.
la-chaux-de-fonds: La Chaux-de-Fonds lies in the Jura Mountains at an altitude of 992 metres, a few kilometres south of the French border. Because of the altitude and the lack of water, with a porous sandstone beneath, the land is ill suited to farming, and the town grew through craft rather than agriculture. It is the fifth-largest city in French-speaking Switzerland and the most important centre of watchmaking in the area known as the Watch Valley.

People first lived in the region about 10,000 years ago, and the place is first mentioned in 1350. It lay under the lords of Valangin, and settlers came first from the Val-de-Ruz and later from the valleys of Le Locle and La Sagne. In 1531 only about 35 people lived there. Like the rest of the Valangin lands it adopted the Reformed faith by 1530, and by 1615 it had 355 inhabitants. Its position on the route between Neuchâtel, Franche-Comté and the Bishopric of Basel made it an important crossroads, and the community grew during the Thirty Years' War.

Lace-making and watchmaking developed in the 18th century, and the watchmaker Pierre Jaquet-Droz, best known for his automata, was prominent in this period. A fire devastated the town in 1794, and Charles-Henri Junod designed the new town in 1835 on a grid plan, with the Avenue Léopold Robert as its central avenue. The grid survives beside the narrow, winding streets of the eastern section, which the fire spared.

In the 1870s American firms began to make watches on an industrial scale, and the traditional Swiss model of individual craftsmen entered a crisis. Modernisation took hold from the 1880s. The Ditesheim brothers, who moved to the town in 1876, founded one of the first modern factories; the firm was renamed Movado in 1905. Jewish families owned about 30 per cent of the town's roughly 180 medium-sized family businesses in 1912. During the First World War the watch companies received many armament orders, for example for precision fuses for artillery shells.

La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle were jointly given UNESCO World Heritage status in 2009 as two mono-industrial towns whose planning reflects the needs of watchmaking artisans. Karl Marx had already called La Chaux-de-Fonds a huge factory town in 1867. It is the birthplace of the architect Le Corbusier, the poet Blaise Cendrars and the car maker Louis Chevrolet, and it is home to the International Museum of Watchmaking.
la-guaira: La Guaira was founded in 1577 as an outlet for nearby Caracas, which the Spanish had founded in 1567. The city has almost no land on which to expand, lying beside the Caribbean Sea. About 12 miles off the coast lies La Guaira Bank, an underwater ridge about 12 miles long and 4 miles wide, rising from depths of around 260 metres. Westerly currents meet it and bring nutrients to the surface, attracting whales, porpoises, seabirds, tuna, sharks and marlin.

The port became important during the 18th century. Attacked by buccaneers and by English, Dutch and French fleets, it was turned into a fortified, walled city. In the War of Jenkins' Ear the Royal Navy attacked it for the first time, and in March 1743 an English squadron of 19 ships under Admiral Charles Knowles failed to take it: coastal batteries led by Gabriel de Zuloaga, José de Iturriaga and Don Mateo Gual drove it off.

The Royal Gipuzkoan Company of Caracas held a trading monopoly over La Guaira and Puerto Cabello and was instrumental in developing large-scale cocoa production in the coastal valleys. In 1797 the crew of the English frigate HMS Hermione mutinied and delivered the ship to the Spanish authorities at La Guaira.

The great earthquake of 26 March 1812 badly damaged the town, and in the same year privateers of the United States and the United Kingdom fought a small naval battle off the port. In December 1822 an unusual hurricane struck, and at least 28 ships and about 100 lives were lost. In 1998 the state of La Guaira, then named Vargas, was created from parts of the former Federal District of Caracas, and the city became its capital. The town and port were badly damaged by the floods and mudslides of December 1999. The city's baseball team, the Tiburones de La Guaira, has played in the Venezuelan professional league since 1962.
la-mancha: La Mancha is a natural region and comarca in the autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha, covering parts of the provinces of Albacete, Ciudad Real, Cuenca and Toledo. Authors give its area as anywhere from 15,000 to 30,000 square kilometres, and its boundaries are imprecise. It is a vast plain at an average altitude of 600 to 700 metres, formed by Miocene sediments of limestone and marl, and it lies across the basins of the Tagus, Guadiana, Guadalquivir and Júcar rivers. The climate is continental Mediterranean, with harsh winters, hot summers and annual rainfall of 300 to 400 millimetres. Its name is often thought to be Arabic, from a word for "high plateau", though other derivations have been proposed.

Paleolithic remains are plentiful, especially along the Guadiana and its tributaries. After the Roman Empire declined in the fifth century, the Vandals and Alans passed through, followed by the Visigoths, who made Toledo their capital in 569; vast areas stayed depopulated. After the Arab conquest of 711 the region remained sparsely populated under Muslim rule, though Calatrava, founded by the Umayyads, Cuenca and Alcaraz grew, the last two as centres of the textile industry. The Arabs contributed advanced irrigation techniques and introduced Merino sheep.

Toledo became a hub of the Revolt of the Comuneros of 1520, which ended in defeat in 1522; in 1523 Pope Adrian VI attached the masterships of the military orders of Santiago and Calatrava to the Spanish Crown. The Peninsular War of 1808 to 1813 devastated the region, and the Superior Junta of La Mancha, formed against the Afrancesado administration, published a gazette in 1811 and 1812. The prefectures made in 1810, with Manzanares as capital, did not outlast the return of Ferdinand VII in 1814.

La Mancha has traditionally been agrarian, with dryland cereals, grapes and olives and transhumant sheep. Its vineyards are the largest in the world by area, and the La Mancha wine denomination covers 190,980 hectares. Saffron has its own protected designation. Wetlands such as the Tablas de Daimiel National Park and the Lagunas de Ruidera belong to the Mancha Húmeda, a UNESCO biosphere reserve. The region is the setting of Miguel de Cervantes's novel Don Quixote, published in 1605 and 1615, whose windmills and characters have become symbols of La Mancha.
la-marseillaise: On 25 April 1792 Baron Philippe Friedrich Dietrich, the mayor of Strasbourg and Worshipful Master of the local Masonic lodge, asked his guest Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle to compose a song that would rally soldiers from all over to defend their threatened homeland. That evening Rouget de Lisle wrote the Chant de guerre pour l'Armée du Rhin, War Song for the Army of the Rhine. Dietrich was executed the next year during the Reign of Terror. The lyrics reflect the invasion of France by foreign armies from Prussia and Austria that was under way, and Strasbourg itself was attacked a few days later. As most Alsatians did not speak French, a German version was published in Colmar in October 1792.

The melody soon became a rallying call of the Revolution. It was adopted as La Marseillaise after volunteers from Marseille, the fédérés, sang it in the streets by the end of May 1792. A young volunteer from Montpellier, François Mireur, had sung it at a patriotic gathering in Marseille, and the troops took it up as the marching song of the National Guard of Marseille. The fédérés entered Paris on 30 July 1792. The invading forces were repulsed after their defeat at the Battle of Valmy.

The Convention accepted it as the national anthem in a decree of 14 July 1795, France's first anthem. It lost this status under Napoleon I and was banned outright by Louis XVIII and Charles X, being reinstated only briefly after the July Revolution of 1830. Napoleon III's government brought it back during the Franco-Prussian War. In the 19th and early 20th centuries it was recognised as the anthem of the international revolutionary movement, and the Paris Commune adopted it in 1871 with new lyrics. It was reinstated as France's national anthem in 1879 and has remained so since.

Several antecedents have been suggested for the melody, among them a work by the Italian violinist Giovanni Battista Viotti, though it seems to have been published after the song, in 1795, and pieces by Mozart and by Jean Baptiste Lucien Grison. Hector Berlioz arranged it for soprano, chorus and orchestra about 1830, and Franz Liszt wrote a piano transcription. Robert Schumann quoted it in 1839 in a work for piano, although singing it was then forbidden in Austria as likely to cause public disorder, and Tchaikovsky quotes it in his 1812 Overture. Protesters used it in the Korean March First Movement in 1919, and Julián Felipe incorporated elements of it in the piece that became the Filipino national anthem.
la-massana: La Massana, originally La Maçana, lies in the north-west of the Principality of Andorra, and its name derives from the Latin mattianam, a variety of apple. The parish covers 65 square kilometres and adjoins the parishes of Ordino, Encamp, Escaldes-Engordany and Andorra la Vella, and also France and Spain. Its other settlements include Pal, Arinsal, Anyós, Erts, Sispony, L'Aldosa, Escàs, Xixerella, Mas de Ribafeta and Pui. The town of La Massana stands at an average elevation of 1,240 metres.

The parish is extremely mountainous. Coma Pedrosa, at 2,942 metres the highest point in Andorra, rises in the north-west and has panoramic views of the Pyrenees; it is the site of the Coma Pedrosa Nature Reserve and usually keeps some snow in summer. The next-highest peaks are Medacorba, Sanfonts, Pla de l'Estany and Racofred. There are four lakes, Forcats, Montmantell, Estany Negre and Les Truites, and three main rivers: the Valira del Nord, a 14-kilometre tributary of the Gran Valira which begins at the Llac de Tristaina, the Pal and the Montaner. Above the tree line, at about 2,100 to 2,400 metres, the climate is alpine; the valleys are milder.

Tourism is the main industry. The ski resort of Vallnord, formed by the Arinsal and Pal sectors, has 89 km of runs between 2,600 and 1,550 metres, and summer visitors hike, climb and cycle in the mountains. The 262 hectares of farmland, 14 per cent of Andorra's agricultural land, grow tobacco, potatoes and other vegetables and cereals, and the rough pastures on the higher slopes keep dairy cattle and horses for trekking.

There are two museums, the Casa Rull Ethnographic Museum in Sispony and Farga Rossell, a forge built in the mid-19th century that demonstrates iron working. The parish celebrates the festa patronale on 17 November, the festa major on 15 August, the Rosary fete on the second Sunday of July, and a fiesta at the end of June or beginning of July that marks the consecration of the livestock and pastures. A gondola lift links the town to Vallnord throughout the year; there are no railways or airports in Andorra.
la-pampa-province: La Pampa is a sparsely populated province in the Pampas in the centre of Argentina. It borders San Luis, Córdoba, Buenos Aires, Río Negro, Neuquén and Mendoza, and is larger than Austria, Taiwan, Ireland or Greece. Only two major rivers cross it, the Colorado, on the border with Río Negro, and the Salado, whose level has been dropping as its tributaries in Mendoza are diverted for irrigation.

The centre and east are a plain tilted gently towards the east, with a calcrete crust and cut by valleys running north-east to south-west. Some of these hold very large fossil inland dunes, and they now lie between the dry and humid Pampas. The province is mostly flat but has mountains such as the Sierra de Lihuel Calel, made largely of ignimbrite, a volcanic rock. The climate is temperate in the east and semi-arid in the west, and most rain falls in summer.

Hernando Arias de Saavedra was the first European explorer to reach the area, in 1604, and Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera explored it in 1662. Spanish colonists did not establish permanent settlements until the 18th century. Resistance by the local indigenous people prevented much expansion until the government of Juan Manuel de Rosas, and it ended only with Julio Roca's conquest of the desert in the 19th century. The territory was then divided among the officers, who built the first Argentine settlements.

The Territorio Nacional de La Pampa Central was created in 1884, with about 25,000 inhabitants and with territory that included the Río Negro Province and parts of other surrounding provinces. By 1915 it had 110,000 residents, a sign of the movement of settlers into the area. In 1952 the province's constitution was written and it was renamed after Eva Perón. In 1955, after the government changed and the Peróns went into exile, La Pampa and Chaco, which had been named for Juan Perón, took back their original names.

Cattle ranching is the most important agricultural activity and takes place across the province, while the more fertile north-east grows wheat, sunflower, maize and other cereals. The province also has oil and gas wells and deposits of sodium chloride, sodium sulfate and copper. Its capital is Santa Rosa, and it is divided into 22 departments. Visitors go to Lihué Calel National Park and the Parque Luro Provincial Reserve.
la-paz: La Paz lies in west-central Bolivia, 68 kilometres southeast of Lake Titicaca, in a canyon cut by the Choqueyapu River, in a bowl-like depression surrounded by the high mountains of the Altiplano. Overlooking the city is the triple-peaked Illimani, always snow-covered. At about 3,650 metres above sea level it is the highest administrative capital in the world, with a subtropical highland climate of rainy summers and dry winters.

The area had been the site of an Inca city on a major trading route. Spanish conquistadors entered it in 1535 but did not find La Paz until 1548. Pedro de la Gasca commanded Alonso de Mendoza to found a city to commemorate the end of the civil wars in Peru, and it was founded on 20 October 1548 as Nuestra Señora de La Paz, 'Our Lady of Peace', with Juan de Vargas as first mayor. The site first chosen was at the settlement of Laja, and a few days later the town was moved to the more clement valley of Chuquiago.

The city saw numerous revolts. In 1781 the indigenous leader Túpac Katari besieged it for six months before he was defeated. On 16 July 1809 Pedro Domingo Murillo began a revolution for independence, which marked the beginning of the Spanish American Wars of Independence. After the republican victory at Ayacucho in 1825 the city's full name was changed to La Paz de Ayacucho.

La Paz is the seat of government of Bolivia, with 755,732 residents in 2024, and a metropolitan area, including El Alto, of about 2.2 million. The presidential palace, the Palacio Quemado, and the legislature stand there, while Sucre, the constitutional capital, keeps the judicial power. The Plaza Murillo, the San Francisco Church, the Metropolitan Cathedral and Jaén Street preserve its colonial heritage. The Alasitas fair, held each year from 24 January, is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
la-paz-baja-california-sur: La Paz lies on the Bay of La Paz on the Baja California peninsula, near the Sierra de la Laguna, which has more than 100 endemic plants. It has a hot desert climate with little rain, and in summer the Coromuel winds blow at night from the Pacific over the peninsula into the bay. Its census population was 250,141 in 2020, nearly a third of the state's population.

The first European known to have landed in Baja California was Fortun Ximenez. In 1533 Hernan Cortes sent two ships to explore the Pacific. On the Concepcion, Ximenez led a revolt in which the captain, Diego de Becerra, was killed, then sailed to the bay of La Paz, believing it an island. The Spaniards saw the large pearls the local people extracted from oysters in the bay, plundered them and raped the women. The violence led to a confrontation in which Ximenez and some of his companions died.

Cortes led a third expedition himself and on 3 May 1535 reached the bay he named Bahia de la Santa Cruz, where he took possession and planned a colony. The transport ships bringing supplies were lost in a storm, and Cortes left to find food. Francisco de Ulloa was left in command, but complaints from relatives of the colonists led the viceroy to order the colony abandoned. An enemy of Cortes then gave the territory the name California, drawn from a novel of the time, perhaps to insult him.

The city was founded in 1720. Between 1768 and 1803 Franciscan missionaries established political and religious jurisdiction over Baja California Sur, shaping settlement and relations with Indigenous people. In the mid-19th century the American filibuster William Walker made La Paz the capital of his short-lived venture, which collapsed through lack of US support and pressure from the Mexican government to retake the region.

La Paz is the capital and largest city of the Mexican state of Baja California Sur. Its economy rests on tourism, especially eco-tourism around the Isla Espiritu Santo group, as well as fishing, agriculture and silver mining. It is home to several marine biology institutes, among them CIBNOR and CICIMAR. The Regional Museum of Anthropology and History, opened in 1981, shows fossils, archaeology and replicas of rock paintings. John Steinbeck visited in 1940 and described the town in The Pearl.
la-petite-pierre: The castle of Lützelstein was built by Count Hugo, a son of Hugh, Count of Blieskastel. In 1223 the Bishop of Strasbourg laid claim to it, but the count defended it successfully. After Count Friedrich died without a male heir, the county became the subject of a long inheritance dispute between his uncle, Frederick Burkhard, and his sister, who was married to John of Leiningen. John and the sons of Burkhard both died within a short time and without heirs, and in 1462 the whole county passed to the Electoral Palatinate.

In the partition of the Wittelsbach lands in 1533 the county went to Palatinate-Zweibrücken. Wolfgang, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken, gave it to his uncle Ruprecht, Count Palatine of Veldenz. Ruprecht's successor George John I tried to make his Alsatian lands the centre of his state and founded the city of Pfalzburg in 1570, settling it with Protestant refugees from the Duchy of Lorraine. The scheme proved too costly, and in 1583 he had to sell the city and half of the County of Lützelstein to Lorraine.

After the death of George John I, Anna Maria of Sweden ruled the county as regent. When Palatinate-Veldenz was divided in 1598, Lützelstein went to John Augustus, Count Palatine of Lützelstein. He died without issue in 1611 and was succeeded by his younger brother George John II of Guttenberg, who renamed the united state Palatinate-Lützelstein-Guttenberg. When George John II died in 1654 with no surviving children, the territory fell back to Palatinate-Veldenz, and after Leopold Louis, Count Palatine of Veldenz, died without issue it returned to Palatinate-Zweibrücken in 1694.

Palatine rule after 1680 was only nominal, because France occupied the place. After the Treaty of Ryswick, Zweibrücken held Lützelstein as a French fief, but the Kingdom of France ruled it in fact. Marshal Vauban expanded its fortress. It was enlarged again in 1815 and partly demolished by the Germans in 1872. The town was formally annexed by France together with Palatinate-Zweibrücken and belonged to the Bas-Rhin department in 1801; since then it has shared the fate of Alsace.

La Petite-Pierre is a commune in the Bas-Rhin department of the Grand Est region, in Alsace. Its name means little rock. The upper part of the town is built as a fortified town around the château, also called the Château de Lützelstein, which houses the headquarters of the Northern Vosges Regional Nature Park. The town has a church begun in the fifteenth century, parts of which remain, and its surroundings are marked with walking trails kept by a local division of the Club Vosgien.
la-plata: La Plata lies in the north-east of Buenos Aires Province, 9 kilometres inland from the southern shore of the Río de la Plata estuary. It is the provincial capital and its largest city. Its neighbours include Ensenada and Berisso to the north-east, and the district covers 893 square kilometres. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and cool winters.

La Plata was planned and developed to serve as the provincial capital after the city of Buenos Aires was federalised. Governor Dardo Rocha was put in charge of creating it, and he hired the urban planner Pedro Benoit, who designed a layout based on a rationalist conception of urban centres. The city was officially founded on 19 November 1882. Many of its public buildings were built at the time of the founding, following an international call for proposals, and its construction was documented in photographs by Tomás Bradley Sutton.

The plan is a square with a central park and two main diagonal avenues, numbered 73 and 74, which cross the city and meet at Plaza Moreno. Other than the diagonals, the streets run on a numbered rectangular grid, and the design is repeated in blocks of six by six, with a small park or square at every sixth block. For this La Plata is nicknamed the city of diagonals, and for its many linden trees the city of lindens. At the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1889 the new city received gold awards, and Jules Verne handed the prize to Rocha.

In the 20th century the oil company Yacimientos Petrolíferos Fiscales founded the La Plata distillery under Enrique Mosconi, during Alvear's presidency of 1922 to 1928. Juan Domingo Perón and Eva Duarte married in the city on 10 December 1945. Between 1952 and 1955 the city was renamed Ciudad Eva Perón.

Plaza Moreno has the neo-Gothic cathedral, the largest church in Argentina, on one side and the town hall opposite. Other landmarks are the Museum of Natural Sciences, the Provincial Legislature, the Teatro Argentino, rebuilt after a fire of 1977, and the Curutchet House, one of two buildings by Le Corbusier in the Americas. The municipal cemetery, designed by Benoit and opened in 1886, holds vaults in neoclassical, Neo-Gothic, Art Nouveau and Egyptian revival styles. The National University of La Plata is one of the best-known universities in Argentina.
la-rioja: La Rioja covers part of the Ebro valley in the north and the Iberian Range in the south. The Ebro runs through the community for 120 km, and seven rivers flow towards it from the mountains, so that the region is sometimes called the Zone of the Seven Valleys. The name Rioja is generally taken to come from the river Oja, though other derivations have been proposed. It is first attested in 1099, in the Miranda de Ebro charter.

In Roman times the territory was inhabited by the Berones, Autrigones and Vascones. After the Muslim invasion of 711 it fell into Al Andalus. Most of it was reconquered in 923 by Sancho I of Pamplona, acting with the Kingdom of León and the Counts of Castile. La Rioja briefly formed the independent Kingdom of Viguera from 970 to about 1005, when it became part of the Kingdom of Pamplona. Sancho Garcés moved the capital of Pamplona to Nájera, and after the independence of Castile in 1035 the two kingdoms fought for La Rioja. In 1076, after the murder of Sancho IV, Navarre was divided between Castile and Aragon, Castile obtaining La Rioja.

The Navarrese under García Ramírez and his son Sancho VI fought Castile for its recovery from 1134, and the region was awarded to Castile in a judgement by Henry II of England and annexed in 1177. Its importance lay partly in the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, which crossed the Ebro at Logroño. In 1833 a province of Logroño was formed.

In 1980 the province changed its name to La Rioja, and after the adoption of the Estatuto de San Millán in 1982 it was constituted as a single-province autonomous community. Its capital and largest city is Logroño. It is organised into 174 municipalities and borders the Basque Country, Navarre, Aragón and Castile and León. The region is well known for its wines under the Denominación de Origen Calificada Rioja.
la-rochelle: La Rochelle is a seaport on the Bay of Biscay and the capital of the Charente-Maritime department. Since the Middle Ages its harbour has opened onto a protected strait, the Pertuis d'Antioche, and the city has been regarded as a gateway to the ocean. Its western position saved days of sailing time and favoured fishing and trade across the Atlantic, even though it lies at no river mouth. The name was first recorded in 961 as Rupella, a Latin diminutive meaning little rock.

The Romans developed salt production along this coast, and villas and salt ponds of the period have been found. The harbour was established after Duke Guillaume X of Aquitaine defeated Isambert de Châtelaillon in 1130 and destroyed Châtelaillon's harbour. The city came under Plantagenet rule after Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet in 1152, and it was the Knights Templar's largest base on the Atlantic. It traded with England, the Low Countries and Spain until Louis VIII captured it in 1224. It returned to the English in 1360 after the Treaty of Brétigny, and expelled them in June 1372.

La Rochelle adopted Calvinism during the Renaissance, and from 1568 declared itself an independent Reformed Republic on the model of Geneva. It sheltered Sea Beggars raiding Spanish shipping. After the St Bartholomew's Day massacre it endured a siege in 1572–1573, ended by the Peace of La Rochelle of 1573, which limited Protestant worship to Montauban, Nîmes and La Rochelle. Revolts against Louis XIII followed in 1622 and 1625. In the siege of 1627–1628 Cardinal Richelieu blockaded the city for 14 months despite an English expedition under the Duke of Buckingham; it surrendered and lost its mayor and its privileges. Louis XIV expelled 300 Huguenot families in November 1661.

The port prospered afterwards in trade with New France and the Antilles. Its shipowners took part in the triangular trade, dealing in enslaved people from Africa, sugar from the West Indies and Canadian furs. From La Rochelle the Carignan-Salières Regiment sailed for New France in 1665.

La Rochelle had 78,535 inhabitants in 2021 and is the most populous commune of its department. A bridge 2.9 kilometres long, completed on 19 May 1988, links it to the Île de Ré. It keeps a rich historical fabric, including the Saint-Nicholas tower, and has three ports for fishing, trade and yachting.
la-scala: The previous theatre, the Teatro Regio Ducale, was destroyed by fire on 25 February 1776 after a carnival gala. Ninety wealthy Milanese who owned boxes in it asked Archduke Ferdinand of Austria-Este for a new theatre. The neoclassical architect Giuseppe Piermarini produced a first design, which Count Firmian, the governor of Austrian Lombardy, rejected. A second plan was accepted in 1776 by Empress Maria Theresa. The church of Santa Maria della Scala was deconsecrated and demolished to make room, and the new house took its name from it.

The theatre was inaugurated on 3 August 1778 as the Nuovo Regio Ducale Teatro alla Scala, with the premiere of Antonio Salieri's Europa riconosciuta. It had six tiers of boxes and above them the loggione, two galleries. The building costs were covered by the sale of boxes, which their owners decorated lavishly, impressing observers such as Stendhal. La Scala soon became the preeminent meeting place of noble and wealthy Milanese. The main floor had no chairs and spectators stood, the orchestra was in full sight because no pit had yet been built, and the foyer served as a casino.

The house hosted the first productions of operas by Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti, Verdi and Puccini, including Norma in 1831, Nabucco in 1842, Otello in 1887 and Turandot in 1926. Verdi for several years refused to let his work be played there after a disagreement over Giovanna d'Arco in 1845, saying the orchestra had corrupted his music, but he conducted his Requiem there on 25 May 1874.

The original structure was renovated in 1907 and given its current layout with 1,987 seats. Bombing severely damaged the house in 1943, during the Second World War. It was rebuilt and reopened on 11 May 1946 with a concert conducted by Arturo Toscanini and a soprano solo by Renata Tebaldi. The Filarmonica della Scala orchestra was established in 1982. A major renovation by the architect Mario Botta, which preservationists feared would lose historic details, kept the theatre closed from January 2002 to December 2004, when it reopened with Salieri's Europa riconosciuta.

The season opens each year on 7 December, the feast of Saint Ambrose, patron saint of Milan. The loggioni, regular occupants of the galleries, are known as the most critical aficionados, giving artists who fail what the tradition calls a baptism of fire.
la-seu-durgell: The town lies at the confluence of the Segre and the Gran Valira, on a plain about 7 km long and 691 metres above sea level, surrounded by high mountains such as the Cadí range. The plain, called the plana de la Seu, was formed by the Segre. The town stands at one of the major crossroads of the Catalan Pyrenees, where the roads to Andorra, Cerdanya and the lower Segre meet, and this has given it a distinct role in the county of Urgell. Above the Valira rise the remains of two great fortresses, the Ciutadella and the castle of Ciutat in Castellciutat.

An Iberian settlement, Arse-durgui, stood on the hill of Castellciutat, then called Puiolo Urgelli. A city, the civitas Orgellia or ciutat d'Urgell, grew up there, and the name Castellciutat comes from it. The name Urgell is pre-Roman, and the linguist Joan Coromines linked it to the presence of water. Shortly after the destruction of the former Orgellia a new neighbourhood arose, which became the home of the Diocese of Urgell. Its name, vicus Sedes Urgelli, from the Latin sedes, seat, shows that it was the episcopal see of the Bishop of Urgell.

Over time Sedes Urgelli grew in importance and lost the word vicus, while civitas Orgellia lost its second word and was known simply as Ciutat until the eighteenth century. Castell was then added because of an ancient castle that had been the home of the Counts of Urgell. Urgellet and Andorra together were originally the County of Urgell, with its capital at La Seu d'Urgell, before the county expanded to the south. The church of Sant Miquel, beside the cloister, is the only building left of the cathedral complex built by Saint Ermengol, which dates from 1035.

La Seu d'Urgell is in the Alt Urgell county of Catalonia, Spain, and has 13,009 inhabitants. It is the head of its judicial district and the seat of the Bishop of Urgell, one of the co-princes of Andorra. The cathedral of Santa Maria and the Diocese of Urgell Museum, which houses the Urgell Beatus illuminated manuscript, stand in the old town. The Segre Olympic Park, built for the 1992 Barcelona Olympic Games, staged the canoe slalom, and the town also held the world championships in the sport in 1999, 2009 and 2019. The Fira de Sant Ermengol, held in October, is described as the oldest in Spain.
la-soufriere-saint-vincent: La Soufrière is an active stratovolcano on the island of Saint Vincent, in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. It is the highest peak on the island and the highest point in the country, and it is the island's youngest and northernmost volcano, with a crater lake. When it is quiet, visitors can climb a hiking trail through rainforest to the crater rim.

A site of 4,991 hectares around the mountain is an Important Bird Area designated by BirdLife International, because it supports significant populations of birds including the Saint Vincent amazon, the Saint Vincent tanager and the lesser Antillean swift.

The volcano has had five explosive eruptions in the recorded period, in 1718, 1812, 1902, 1979 and 2021. A painting by J. M. W. Turner of the eruption of 30 April 1812 belongs to the Victoria Gallery and Museum of the University of Liverpool.

The eruption of 6 May 1902 came just hours before that of Mount Pelée on Martinique, which killed 29,000 people. On Saint Vincent a further 600 people were injured or burned and some 4,000 were left homeless. The death zone lay mainly within the habitat of the Island Caribs, an indigenous people of the Lesser Antilles, and this last large remnant of Carib culture was destroyed as a result. By 1907 the volcano was considered inactive and the crater lake had re-formed. A minor event in 1971 altered the structure of the crater lake.

The eruption of 13 April 1979 caused no confirmed casualties, because advance warning allowed thousands of residents to evacuate to nearby beaches. Its ash plume reached Barbados, 160 km to the east. A newspaper reported that two infants died during the evacuation of some 1,500 people, but the report was not confirmed.

Seismic activity increased in December 2020, and on 27 December an effusive eruption began to form a new lava dome inside the summit crater. By 22 March 2021 the dome was 105 metres tall, 243 metres wide and 921 metres long. On 8 April, after a sustained rise in volcanic and seismic activity, a red alert was declared and an evacuation order issued.

An explosive eruption at 8:41 in the morning on 9 April 2021 sent an ash plume to about 8,000 metres, and by then some 16,000 people had left the area. Explosions continued over the following days, ash reached Barbados, and the island suffered power cuts and cut water supplies, while its airspace was closed. The final explosion came on 22 April. The eruption was rated VEI-4, comparable in size to that of 1979. Saint Lucia, Grenada, Antigua and Barbados agreed to take evacuees, and cruise ships carried residents to neighbouring islands. The World Bank announced US$20 million in long-term funding on 13 April.
la-tene-culture: The La Tène culture succeeded the Hallstatt culture without any definite cultural break. The transition across Central Europe was gradual and is mainly detected through elite artefacts in the La Tène style, which first appear on the western edge of the old Hallstatt region. There is no agreement on the precise region where the culture first developed, but a broad consensus places its centre north of the Alps, between the valleys of the Marne and Moselle and the nearby Rhineland.

An elite grave group of the early 5th century BCE excavated at Glauberg in Hesse in 1994 lay in a region once thought peripheral. The culture took shape under considerable Mediterranean influence from the Greeks, the Etruscans and the Golasecca culture, though its art did not depend on them.

Its bearers were the people known to Greek and Roman writers as Keltoi and Galli, though archaeologists have repeatedly concluded that language, material culture and political affiliation do not necessarily run parallel. Society was hierarchical, with nobles, Druids, merchants, artisans and farmers, and tribes were usually ruled by kings. Julius Caesar describes three main classes: knights, Druids and commoners. Women could attain high rank, and some of the richest graves in central Europe are those of women. Slavery also existed.

Settlements began as open villages under hill forts. Walled towns called oppida appeared in the 2nd century BCE, with areas of up to hundreds of hectares and massive ramparts, and more than 180 are known from France to Hungary. They served as centres of craft, commerce, politics and religion. Coinage began in the late 4th century BCE after contact with Greek states and the employment of Celtic mercenaries, and iron production grew vastly, with 200 types of iron tools in use by the 2nd century BCE.
Noric steel was sought by the Roman military in the 1st century BCE. The art is marked by curving decoration in metalwork, on torcs, fibulae, helmets and shields, often laid out with compasses.

The type site lies on the northern shore of Lake Neuchâtel. After a drought lowered the lake by about 2 metres in 1857, Hansli Kopp, searching for antiquities for Colonel Frédéric Schwab, found rows of wooden piles and collected about forty iron swords. Ferdinand Keller interpreted the remains in 1863 as a Celtic village built on piles, while the geologist Eduard Desor saw an armoury on platforms, later destroyed by enemy action.

Another reading, which accounts for swords that had never been sharpened, takes it as a place of ritual deposits. Otto Tischler divided the culture into early, middle and late stages in 1885, and the period is now mostly divided in four, following Paul Reinecke.
la-turbie: La Turbie is a commune in the Alpes-Maritimes department of south-eastern France, bordering the Principality of Monaco. It can be reached from Cap-d'Ail on the coast or by the Grand Corniche. A limestone outcrop above the village is called the Tête de Chien, or head of dog, a folk etymology from its former name Testa de camp, meaning head of a military camp. The commune once had wider boundaries and included the territory of Beausoleil, formerly Haut-Monte-Carlo, and of Cap-d'Ail, which was separated at the beginning of the 20th century. Only the old main town, around the remaining structure of the Roman trophy, forms the present commune.

In Roman times La Turbie lay on the Via Julia Augusta and was known for the Trophy of Augustus, also called the Trophée des Alpes, which Augustus made to celebrate his victory over the Ligurian tribes of the mountains, who had attacked merchants on the Roman trade routes. Much of the village is built partly of old stones taken from the ruins of the monument.

In the Middle Ages the village, then called Turbia, was mainly under the rule of the Republic of Genoa, and Dante wrote in the Divina Commedia that Turbia was the western limit of Italian Liguria. It belonged at times to Savoy and at times to the Principality of Monaco, from which its people took the Monegasque dialect, although the local Ligurian speech kept some features of the Niçois dialect of nearby Nice. That local dialect is nearly extinct, mainly since the inclusion of the Sardinian County of Nice in France in 1860.

La Turbie is regarded as the cradle of automobile mountain races. On 31 January 1897 the last stage of the Marseilles-Nice race was a 17-kilometre hillclimb between Nice and La Turbie, won by André Michelin in a steam-powered De Dion at an average of 31.8 kilometres an hour. The driver Wilhelm Bauer was killed there on 30 March 1900, the first driver killed in a hillclimb event, and the use of the course was banned after a second death in 1903, until the ban was lifted in 1909. From 1968 to 1995 nearly the same route formed the last stage of the cycle race Paris-Nice.

La Turbie is a commune of the Alpes-Maritimes that borders the Principality of Monaco. The Trophy of Augustus, also called the Trophée des Alpes, stands within the town and remains its best-known monument, and many of the village buildings are made from stones taken from its ruins. AS Monaco has had its training ground in an old quarry at La Turbie since 1981.
laayoune: Laayoune stands south of the dry river Saguia el-Hamra, where the old lower town built by Spanish colonists lies. Its name is the French and Spanish form of the Hassaniya Arabic name Layoun, which may mean the springs, a reference to the oases that supply the town with water. The climate is a hot desert one, moderated by the Canary Current, with an average annual temperature just over 21 °C.

The Spanish captain Antonio de Oro is thought to have founded the modern city in 1938 as a small military outpost. The site was chosen for its water and for its strategic position, and its place on the banks of the Saguia el-Hamra allowed good communication with the harbours of Tarfaya and Boujdour. From 1958 it was the administrative capital of the Spanish Sahara, governed by the Governor General of Spanish West Africa.

The discovery of large phosphate deposits at Bou Craa brought a burst of economic growth. On 17 June 1970 the town was the scene of the Zemla Intifada, which ended in a massacre; the dead are put at between two and eleven, with hundreds injured. After the Spanish withdrew, Laayoune and much of the rest of Western Sahara came under Moroccan control. Many Moroccans have since moved to the city and now outnumber the indigenous Sahrawis, who have gradually given up their traditional nomadic lifestyle.

Laayoune is the largest city of Western Sahara, with a population of 262,791 in 2024. It is the capital of the Laâyoune-Sakia El Hamra region administered by Morocco and the de jure capital of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, and the territory remains under the supervision of the UN mission MINURSO. The city is a hub for fishing and phosphate mining, has a desalination plant, and is served by Hassan I Airport. The St. Francis of Assisi Cathedral, built in the Spanish period, is still in use.
labourd: Labourd extends from the Pyrenees to the river Adour along the Bay of Biscay. Gipuzkoa and Navarre lie to the south, Lower Navarre to the east, and the Landes to the north. The province covers almost 900 square kilometres and is the most populous of the three French Basque provinces. Its main town is Bayonne, but until the Revolution its capital was Ustaritz, 13 kilometres away, where local Basque leaders assembled. Other important towns are Biarritz, Anglet, Hendaye, Ciboure, Saint-Jean-de-Luz and Hasparren. Its people speak Basque, in the Lapurdian dialect, and the Gascon language also has a long tradition there, notably along the Adour.

In ancient times Labourd was inhabited by the Tarbelli, an Aquitanian tribe whose fortified town of Lapurdum became Bayonne and gave the region its name. In the Middle Ages it formed part of the Duchy of Vasconia, later called Gascony. Many authorities say Duke Sancho VI of Gascony ceded it to King Sancho III of Navarre around 1023, but the story has no basis in contemporary documents.

Richard the Lionheart ruled it directly between 1169 and 1199 and gave Bayonne a charter in about 1174 or 1175. His marriage to Berengaria of Navarre in 1191 settled the border: Lower Navarre was annexed to Navarre while Labourd and Soule stayed in Angevin Aquitaine. In 1193 the legitimate viscounts, who had their seat at Ustaritz, sold their rights, and Ustaritz was the capital until the province was suppressed in 1790.

Labourd passed into French hands in 1451, just before the end of the Hundred Years' War, and was largely self-ruled as an autonomous French province until the Revolution. A major witch hunt led by the judge Pierre de Lancre, after feuds between merchants and nobility, ended with some 70 supposed sorginak burned at the stake. In 1793-1794, during the War of the Pyrenees, the Convention's repression brought mass deportation to the Landes, seizure of land, and the deaths of an estimated 1,600 civilians. France suppressed the provinces in 1790 and joined Labourd with Béarn in the département of Basses-Pyrénées.

Labourd's coast played an important part in the early European exploitation of the Atlantic. Labourdin whalers gave the viscount the oil of the first animal they caught as early as 1059, and Basque whaling in Newfoundland and Labrador began in the 1530s. The rudder is first mentioned as steering in the Navarrese or the Bayonne fashion, and the development may have been specifically Labourdine.

After Navarre lost San Sebastián and Hondarribia to Castile in 1200, a treaty made Bayonne the port of Navarre for nearly three centuries. Traditional buildings have low roofs, half-timbering and red, white and green paint; the Villa Arnaga at Cambo-les-Bains, home of Edmond Rostand, is now a museum.
labrador: Labrador is the mainland part of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. It makes up 71 per cent of the province's area and is separated from the island of Newfoundland by the Strait of Belle Isle. Its shape is roughly triangular, and it covers the easternmost section of the Canadian Shield, a region of thin soil and abundant mineral resources. Its western border with Quebec follows the drainage divide of the Labrador Peninsula, so that land draining into the Atlantic belongs to Labrador and land draining into Hudson Bay to Quebec. The Torngat Mountains in the north hold Mount Caubvick, the highest point in the province. Its indigenous peoples include the Inuit of Nunatsiavut and NunatuKavut and the Innu of Nitassinan.

Norsemen were probably the first Europeans to sight the coast, around 1000 CE, and called the area Markland. The name Labrador comes from the Portuguese explorer João Fernandes Lavrador. In 1542 Basque mariners came ashore on the Strait of Belle Isle and set up a whaling station at what is now Red Bay, where the whaling ship San Juan sank in 1565 and was raised in 1978. The Moravian Brethren came to the coast in 1760 to minister to the Inuit and founded Nain, Okak, Hebron, Hopedale and Makkovik.

Labrador was part of New France until the Seven Years' War. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 transferred it to the British, who ruled it as part of the Province of Quebec and from 1791 as part of Lower Canada. In 1809 the British imperial government detached it from Lower Canada and gave it to the Newfoundland Colony. Because the inland boundary had never been precisely stated, the dispute with Canada was referred to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, whose decision of 1927 set the boundary mostly along the coastal watershed. Newfoundland joined Canada in 1949.

In October 1943 a German U-boat crew installed an automated weather station near Cape Chidley, the only known armed German military operation on the North American mainland during the war. Canada built a major air force base at Goose Bay during the Second World War.

Iron ore deposits found in western Labrador and adjacent Quebec in the first half of the 20th century gave rise to the towns of Labrador City and Wabush. In the 1960s the Churchill River was diverted at Churchill Falls, flooding the area now called the Smallwood Reservoir and supplying a hydroelectric station. The Inuit self-government region of Nunatsiavut was created in 2005. Red Bay is regarded as one of the best-preserved examples of a 16th-century Basque whaling station.
labyrinth: Labyrinth is a word of pre-Greek origin whose derivation is uncertain. Maximillian Mayer suggested in 1892 that it came from labrys, a Lydian word for a double-bladed axe, and Arthur Evans took this to mean the house of the double axe. That link lost ground after the deciphering of Linear B in the 1950s, when a Mycenaean Greek form, da-pu₂-ri-to, appeared. It may be related to the Minoan word du-pu₂-re, found in Linear A on libation tablets and connected with Mount Dikte and Mount Ida, both associated with caverns.

Evans believed the complexity of the palace at Knossos, with its bull motifs and carved labrys signs, showed it to be the Labyrinth of Daedalus. On the strength of a passage in the Iliad, it has also been suggested that the palace held a dancing-ground made for Ariadne by Daedalus. In the 2000s the geographer Nicholas Howarth called Evans's view something to be treated sceptically. His team found that the Skotino cave was natural, and another candidate is a series of partly human-made tunnels at Gortyn.
Herodotus applied the word to a building complex in Egypt near the City of Crocodiles, which he thought surpassed the pyramids. Its remains were found at Hawara in the Faiyum by Flinders Petrie.

As a pattern, the single-path seven-course Classical design appears on Cretan coins from about 430 BCE, even though the myth clearly describes a branching maze in which the Minotaur was trapped. Depictions from the Roman era to the Renaissance are almost always of this single-path kind, and many scholars now use labyrinth for it and maze for a branching puzzle.

Romans made many decorative labyrinths in mosaic, often with the Minotaur at the centre. Medieval examples followed, and the Chartres pattern, the commonest, appears in manuscripts as early as the 9th century. The great pavement labyrinths of Chartres, Reims and Amiens date from the twelfth to fourteenth centuries. Some 500 or more labyrinths of stone were also laid out in Scandinavia, often named Troy Town, perhaps to trap malevolent trolls or winds for fishing communities.

Similar designs appear in other cultures, among them the Tohono O'odham, whose pattern features I'itoi, the Man in the Maze. From the late 20th century labyrinths have been revived, and about 6,000 are registered with the Worldwide Labyrinth Locator.
lachlan-macquarie: Lachlan Macquarie was born on 31 January 1762 on the island of Ulva off the coast of the Isle of Mull. His father was a carpenter and miller and his mother Margaret the sister of Murdoch Maclaine, laird of Lochbuie. He joined the British Army in 1776 and served in the American War of Independence, in India, and in Egypt in 1801, where he was Deputy Adjutant-General of a British-Indian force sent against the French. He returned to Britain in 1803 with a fortune of £20,000, and in 1807 travelled overland from India through Persia and Russia.

Appointed Governor of New South Wales in 1809, Macquarie arrived at Sydney Cove on 28 December with his own regiment, the 73rd. The government had chosen an army officer to win over the New South Wales Corps, whose officers had mutinied against and imprisoned William Bligh in the Rum Rebellion. He planned the street layout of central Sydney, built Macquarie Street, and created Hyde Park as the first public park. He promoted marriage and church attendance, and appointed emancipists to office: Francis Greenway became colonial architect and William Redfern colonial surgeon.

In 1813 he authorised the crossing of the Blue Mountains by Gregory Blaxland, William Wentworth and William Lawson, and in 1815 he ordered the founding of Bathurst, the first inland British settlement. He called for Aboriginal people to be treated with kindness, yet his orders led to the Appin Massacre of Gundungurra and Dharawal people. His championing of emancipists and heavy public spending aroused opposition in the colony and in London, and in 1819 Earl Bathurst sent John Bigge to inquire into the colony.

Macquarie returned to Scotland and died in London in 1824 while defending himself against Bigge's charges. His reputation grew after his death, especially among emancipists and their descendants. Many regard him as the most enlightened of the early governors, and he formally adopted the name Australia for the continent, first using it in an official despatch in 1817. Many places and institutions, among them Macquarie University, Lake Macquarie and the Macquarie River, are named after him. A 2012 statue in Sydney's Hyde Park has drawn criticism over his punitive expeditions against Indigenous people.
ladenburg: Ladenburg lies on the right bank of the Neckar, on the river's alluvial cone, about 10 kilometres from both Heidelberg and Mannheim. The Kandelbach flows into the Neckar south of the built-up area. The first settlement took place at some point between 3000 and 200 BCE, and the place began as a Celtic settlement called Lokudunom, meaning sea castle. In 200 BCE the Celtic centre of the region was moved there from the Heiligenberg near Heidelberg.

In 40 CE the Romans settled Suebian peasant militia, called the Suebi Nicrenses, and in 74 they founded an auxiliary fort with a camp village, the core of the later town. In 98 Emperor Trajan made Lopodunum a civitas and the capital of the Civitas Ulpia Sueborum Nicrensium. Around 220 it had a forum with a market basilica, temples, a theatre, baths and a town wall. With a walled area of about 32 hectares it was the largest Roman town in what is now Baden-Württemberg. Alamanni apparently destroyed it around 260. Valentinian I retook it in 369 and built a late antique harbour fortification, and Roman rule ended about the middle of the fifth century.

The Merovingians built a royal court there in 496, and in 628 the Frankish king Dagobert I gave the town and region to the diocese of Worms. In 1385 rule over Ladenburg was divided between Worms and the Palatinate after a bloody feud. In 1400 the citizens of Worms expelled their bishop, and Ladenburg became the bishop's seat. Under Bishop Johann III von Dalberg, from 1455 to 1503, it had its fullest flourishing. The Thirty Years' War brought partial destruction in 1622, and in 1705 Ladenburg fell wholly to the Electoral Palatinate. After Napoleon Bonaparte rearranged the political map of Europe it passed to Baden, and in 1849 the Neckar bridge was fiercely contested during the Baden Revolution.

The old town keeps half-timbered houses from the late Middle Ages, and St. Gallus Church has a south tower built in 1412 by Bishop Johann II von Fleckenstein. Carl Benz, inventor of the automobile, lived in Ladenburg from 1906 until his death in 1929, as did his wife Bertha, and the Bertha Benz Memorial Route passes through the town. An automobile museum bearing his name occupies the former factory buildings of C. Benz Söhne. Ladenburg marked the 1900th anniversary of its Roman city rank in 1998.
ladislaus-i-of-hungary: Ladislaus was the second son of the future King Béla I of Hungary and Richeza (or Adelaide), a daughter of King Mieszko II Lambert of Poland. He and his elder brother Géza were born in Poland, where Béla had settled after being banished, and the family returned to Hungary around 1048. After Béla's death in 1063, the brothers acknowledged their cousin Solomon as king in a treaty of 20 January 1064, in exchange for their father's duchy, a third of the kingdom. Relations turned tense in the early 1070s, and Ladislaus and Géza defeated Solomon at the Battle of Mogyoród on 14 March 1074. Géza became king, with Ladislaus as his chief adviser.

Géza died on 25 April 1077, and because his sons were minors, his supporters proclaimed Ladislaus king. Solomon resisted with the help of Henry IV of Germany, abdicated in 1081 but plotted to regain the crown, and was imprisoned. In 1085 Ladislaus canonised the first Hungarian saints, among them King Stephen I and Duke Emeric, and freed Solomon during the ceremony. His laws, issued after an assembly at Pannonhalma, were severe measures to protect property: thieves were to be hanged, and lesser offenders blinded or sold as slaves.

When the Croatian nobility divided after the deaths of King Demetrius Zvonimir and his successor, Ladislaus intervened at the request of his sister Helen, Zvonimir's widow, and invaded in 1091. A local nobleman, Petar Snačić, was crowned king and fought on in the Gvozd Mountains, so the conquest was incomplete. Ladislaus founded a diocese at Zagreb, and the popes, who claimed Croatia as a fief, found him unwilling to accept their claim. He died on 29 July 1095, near the Hungarian-Bohemian border, naming his nephew Álmos as successor.

After his victories over the Pechenegs and Cumans, the nomads of the Pontic steppes did not invade Hungary until the Mongol invasion of 1241. His conquest of Croatia began the association of the two kingdoms that lasted until 1918. Pope Celestine III canonised him on 27 June 1192, and a pilgrimage to his shrine at Várad became a customary rite for a newly crowned king. Legends present him as a pious knight-king, and the best known tells of his fight with a Cuman warrior who had abducted a Hungarian girl.
ladislaus-iv-of-hungary: Ladislaus was born on 5 August 1262, the elder son of Stephen, son of Béla IV of Hungary, and Stephen's wife Elizabeth the Cuman, the daughter of a chieftain of the pagan Cumans who had settled in Hungary. In 1269 his father allied with King Charles I of Sicily, and Ladislaus, aged seven, was engaged to Charles's daughter Elizabeth, whom he married in 1270.
In the summer of 1272 Joachim Gutkeled, the ban of Slavonia, kidnapped the boy and held him at Koprivnica. Stephen V besieged the fortress but fell ill and died on 6 August 1272.

Archbishop Philip Türje crowned Ladislaus at Székesfehérvár about 3 September 1272. In theory his mother ruled as regent, but baronial parties, chiefly the Abas, Csáks, Kőszegis and Gutkeleds, fought one another for power. An assembly of prelates, barons, noblemen and Cumans declared Ladislaus of age in May 1277. He allied with Rudolf I of Germany against Ottokar, and his forces played a decisive part in Rudolf's victory in the Battle on the Marchfeld on 26 August 1278, in which Ottokar was killed.

Ladislaus could not restore royal power. The papal legate Philip, bishop of Fermo, arrived in early 1279 and demanded that the Cumans give up their pagan customs and live in houses. They refused, and Ladislaus, himself half Cuman, sided with them, so the legate excommunicated him and placed Hungary under interdict. In January 1280 the Cumans imprisoned the legate at the king's demand, and Finta Aba captured Ladislaus; both were freed within two months, though many Cumans chose to leave Hungary.

In January 1285 the Mongols of the Golden Horde under Khans Talabuga and Nogai invaded and devastated the country east of the Danube; local forces resisted, and they withdrew after two months. Many subjects accused the king of inciting them. He imprisoned his wife Isabella in 1286, lived among Cuman mistresses and, according to Archbishop Lodomer of Esztergom, who excommunicated him, threatened to destroy the clergy with Tartar swords.

Ladislaus spent his last years wandering the country while prelates and barons ruled independently. In 1290 the Kőszegis offered the crown to Andrew the Venetian, who was captured and handed to Albert. Pope Nicholas IV planned to proclaim a crusade against Ladislaus, but three Cumans, Arbuz, Törtel and Kemence, assassinated him at the castle of Körösszeg on 10 July 1290. The pope ordered an inquiry into whether the king had died as a Catholic Christian; its result is unknown.
ladislaus-of-naples: Ladislaus was born in Naples on 15 February 1377, the son of Charles III of Naples and Margaret of Durazzo, both of the Capetian House of Anjou. His parents had lived at the court of King Louis I of Hungary and named him after King Saint Ladislaus I of Hungary. He became king at the age of nine under his mother's regency, after his father was assassinated while pursuing a claim to the Hungarian throne. Pope Urban VI, who had assigned the throne to Louis II of Anjou, refused to recognise him and called a crusade against him in 1387. Naples was occupied by an Angevin army, and mother and son took refuge in the fortress of Gaeta. In 1389 Pope Boniface IX recognised Ladislaus.

In 1390 Louis II invaded and a war began that lasted nine years. Ladislaus confined him to the city of Naples and the Terra d'Otranto, and in 1399 he regained the city with the support of powerful barons. He also tried to restore Angevin rule in Hungary and Croatia against King Sigismund of Luxembourg. After a treaty with Venice he landed at Zara on 19 July 1403, and on 5 August the archbishop of Esztergom, János Kanizsai, crowned him king of Hungary and Croatia. His authority never extended beyond Dalmatia and little beyond Zara, and he returned to Apulia. In 1409 he sold his rights over Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats.

Ladislaus then turned to central Italy. He murdered or had murdered several members of the Sanseverino family, and in 1408 captured Ostia and entered Rome. His expansion brought a war with Florence, whose condottiere Braccio da Montone defeated him in Tuscany. Antipope Alexander V excommunicated him and called Louis II back, but in 1410 Louis's fleet was intercepted and partly destroyed off the Tuscan coast, and Ladislaus took his treasure. A peace on 14 June 1412 left Ladislaus invested with the Neapolitan crown. In June 1413 his troops sacked Rome, and Florence signed a treaty recognising his conquest of the Papal States.

Ladislaus fell ill in July 1414 and returned to Naples, where he died on 6 August 1414. Rumours of poisoning remain unproven, and an infection is thought more likely. He is buried in the church of San Giovanni a Carbonara. He married three times, and none of the marriages produced children, though he had at least two illegitimate children. He was the last male of the Capetian House of Anjou and was succeeded by his sister Joanna II of Naples.
ladysmith-kwazulu-natal: Ladysmith lies on the banks of the Klip River, 'stone river', on the foothills of the Drakensberg, 230 kilometres north-west of Durban and 365 kilometres south-east of Johannesburg. It is the seat of the Alfred Duma Local Municipality and the Uthukela District Municipality, and was officially renamed uMnambithi in March 2024.

The centre of the town and much of its residential area lie within the river's flood basin, and flooding has troubled it since its founding: 29 serious floods occurred in the 110 years to 1997, when the Qedusizi Dam was completed. The worst in 30 years came in 1996 and caused R500 million in damages and the evacuation of 400 families.

In 1847 a number of Boers created the Republic of Klip River in the area, which the British annexed the same year. In June 1850 the place was proclaimed a township called Windsor. On 11 October 1850 it was renamed Ladysmith after Juana María de los Dolores de León Smith, the Spanish wife of Sir Harry Smith, governor of the Cape Colony and high commissioner from 1847 to 1852. A fort built in 1860 protected the villagers from the Zulu.

In the Second Boer War, Lieutenant-General Sir George White made Ladysmith his base for defending Natal. After battles beginning on 29 October 1899 the British fell back to the town, and the Boers surrounded it. The siege lasted 118 days, from 2 November 1899 to 28 February 1900. Three attempts by General Sir Redvers Buller to relieve it ended in Boer victories at Colenso, Spion Kop and Vaal Krantz.

On 6 January 1900 Commandant-General Piet Joubert tried to take the town at the battle of Platrand, or Wagon Hill. Buller broke the siege on 28 February 1900 by close cooperation between infantry and artillery. Winston Churchill, a war correspondent for The Morning Post, was present at the relief, and Mohandas Gandhi, with the stretcher-bearer corps he had set up, took part in actions around Ladysmith. The town of Ladysmith on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, was named in honour of the relief.

Food processing, textiles and tyre production are important industries. Many of the Boer War battlefields around the town are preserved as memorial sites. The Siege Museum, built in 1884 as a marketplace and opened as a museum in 1995, holds about 60,000 documents on the siege and the war. Two British howitzers from the siege stand before the Town Hall, which Boer artillery damaged. On Wagon Hill the Burgher Memorial of 1979 honours 781 Boer fighters killed in Natal. Ladysmith is the home town of Joseph Shabalala, founder of the group Ladysmith Black Mambazo.
lae: Lae lies near the delta of the Markham River on the northern coast of Huon Gulf and is the capital of Morobe Province. It stands at the start of the Highlands Highway, the main land transport corridor between the Highlands Region and the coast. In German it was called Preußen-Reede and later Lehe. The city lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire in the Ramu-Markham Fault Zone, where tectonic plates converge at up to 50 millimetres a year, and the Ramu-Markham zone has produced large thrust earthquakes, among them one of magnitude 6.4 in April 1999. Its tropical rainforest climate brings about 4,500 millimetres of rain a year.

Lucas divides the history of Lae into four periods: the mission phase from 1886 to 1920, the gold phase from 1926 until the Second World War, the timber and agricultural phase until 1965, and the industrial boom from 1965, with the opening of the Highlands Highway. On 12 July 1886 the German missionary Johann Flierl sailed to Simbang and arrived at Lae shortly afterwards. After the First World War Eastern New Guinea came under Australian control, and in 1921 the gold prospector Cecil John Levien became District Officer of Morobe.

In 1927 he arranged for an airstrip at Lae to serve the gold mines around Wau. Lae was declared a town on 31 March 1931 and became the prototype for New Guinean towns built around airstrips, with cargo flown from Lae to the Wau goldfields.

In July 1937 the American aviator Amelia Earhart was last seen flying out of Lae on her way back to the United States. After volcanic eruptions at Rabaul that year it was decided to move the capital of the Territory of New Guinea to Lae, but the war prevented it.

Japan occupied the town on 8 March 1942, and Lae, Rabaul and Salamaua became its major bases in New Guinea. The Battle of the Bismarck Sea in March 1943 was fought over a Japanese attempt to reinforce Lae by sea. After weeks of fierce fighting in the Salamaua–Lae campaign the town fell to the Allies on 16 September. It was proclaimed a city in 1972, and its postwar growth was tied to the highlands, whose coffee and tea needed a port and then a road.

Lae is the industrial hub of Papua New Guinea and its largest cargo port. The Papua New Guinea University of Technology stands 8 kilometres outside the city. Lae War Cemetery, established in 1944, holds the remains of over 2,800 soldiers, many of whom died in the Salamaua–Lae campaign, and is the resting place of two Victoria Cross recipients. The city is nicknamed the Garden City.
lagash: Lagash, modern al-Hiba in Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq, lay northwest of the junction of the Euphrates and Tigris and east of Uruk. The Lagash state incorporated three cities: Lagash itself; Girsu (modern Telloh), about 25 kilometres to the northwest, the religious centre with its main temple, the E-ninnu, dedicated to the god Ningirsu; and Nina (Tell Zurghul), which marked the state's southern limit.

Significant occupation began early in the 3rd millennium BCE, in the Early Dynastic I period (c. 2900–2600 BCE), and peaked at about 500 hectares in Early Dynastic III (c. 2500–2334 BCE), the age of the First Dynasty of Lagash. Ur-Nanshe left inscriptions mostly about temple building and claimed to have conquered Umma. His grandson Eannatum made Lagash a major power across much of Mesopotamia, though many of the realms he conquered often revolted.

A long border dispute with Umma over the fertile Guʾedena plain is told on the Stele of the Vultures, dated about 2450 BCE, which shows one of the earliest organised battles known, with Lagash's army advancing in a dense phalanx. The last ruler of the dynasty, Urukagina, known for judicial, social and economic reforms, was defeated by Lugalzagesi.

About 2300 BCE Sargon of Akkad laid waste the land from Lagash to the sea, and Lagash passed under the Akkadian Empire. His son Rimush faced revolts and reconquered Lagash among other cities; for Ur and Lagash he recorded 8,049 killed, 5,460 captured and enslaved and 5,985 expelled and annihilated. After Akkad fell, a Second Dynasty (c. 2260 – c. 2023 BCE) won full independence, and under Gudea Lagash entered a period of riches and power. Thousands of inscriptions and many statues survive from his reign, among them the Gudea cylinders, which hold the longest known text in Sumerian.

Nam-mahani, the last ruler of the dynasty, was defeated by Ur-Nammu, first ruler of the Ur III empire, whose law code names him as slain; statues of Nam-mahani and his wife were beheaded. Under Ur, Lagash, Girsu and Nigin formed the largest and most prosperous province, and the Grand Vizier, the second highest official of the empire, lived there.

The site is one of the largest archaeological sites in the region, about 3.5 kilometres from north to south and 1.5 from east to west. Robert Koldewey excavated it for six weeks in 1887, Thorkild Jacobsen and Fuad Safar identified it as Lagash in 1953, and a team from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and New York University worked there for five seasons between 1968 and 1976. After the Old Babylonian period it was largely deserted until a Seleucid fortress was built in the 2nd century BCE.
lagny-sur-marne: From 644 Lagny-sur-Marne was the site of Lagny Abbey, a monastery founded that year. After the Normans destroyed it, it was refounded about 990. The state seized the monastery at the French Revolution, and since 1842 its buildings have housed the offices of the municipality. The Hôtel de Ville, established in the buildings of the former abbey, was completed in 1765. The town was also one of the hosts of the Champagne fairs in the 12th and 13th centuries. In 1846 Lagny annexed the commune of Saint-Denis-du-Port.

During the Middle Ages Lagny was one of the most popular places for tourneys in northern France. A notable tournament was held there in November 1179 by Louis VII of France in honour of the coronation of his son. In 1170 the young knight Baldwin of Bethune and his lifelong friend William Marshal had been at the court of Henry the Young King, and at the great international tournament of Lagny in 1180 Baldwin was a knight banneret leading the Flemish team, while William headed the English team.

The commune lies in the Seine-et-Marne department of Île-de-France, 26.1 km from the centre of Paris, about 25 minutes by train from the Gare de l'Est. It was officially called simply Lagny until 1971, and is part of the Val de Bussy sector of the new town of Marne-la-Vallée. Its inhabitants are called Latignaciens or Laniaques. The railway station, Lagny–Thorigny, stands across the Marne from the town centre in the neighbouring commune of Thorigny-sur-Marne. Lagny has been twinned with Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts in Quebec since 1969, and also with Alnwick in Northumberland.
laguna-de-bay: Laguna de Bay lies in the heart of Luzon, between the province of Laguna to the south and Rizal to the north, with Metropolitan Manila to the north-west. It is a shallow freshwater lake with a surface area of about 911 square kilometres, a shoreline of 220 kilometres and an average depth of 2.8 metres. It is shaped like a crow's foot, with two peninsulas jutting from the northern shore into the volcanic Laguna Caldera, which is believed to have formed in two major eruptions, about a million years ago and 27,000 to 29,000 years ago. Talim, the largest and most populated island, lies in the middle.

It is considered the third largest inland body of water in Southeast Asia, after Tonle Sap in Cambodia and Lake Toba in Sumatra, and its surface area is given variously as 911 to 949 square kilometres. The lake is fed by 21 major tributaries, among them the Pagsanjan River, which supplies 35% of its water, and its excess water is discharged through the Pasig River.

The name means the lagoon of the town of Bay, the former provincial capital of Laguna, whose name is believed to come from the Tagalog bahayan, settlement. The province was named after the lake. In the pre-Hispanic era the lake was known as Puliran Kasumuran, in the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of about 900 CE, and later as Pulilan in a Tagalog vocabulary of 1613. Bay Island, off the coast of Bay, is associated with the precolonial crocodile-deity myths of that town.

The lake has served as a navigation lane for passenger boats since the Spanish colonial era. The Laguna Lake Development Authority was created by Republic Act 4850 in 1966, and its charter was strengthened in 1975 and 1983 to include environmental protection and jurisdiction over the surface waters of the lake basin. In 1986 the Manggahan Floodway was built to divert peak flows of the Marikina River into the lake, which serves as a temporary reservoir.

The lake is a multipurpose resource, used for fishing, aquaculture, transport, irrigation, power generation and flood management, and it is one of the main sources of freshwater fish in the Philippines. Its shores are densely settled, and population growth, industrial development and the escape of non-native fish from aquaculture, among them the janitor fish and the Thai catfish, have put pressure on its water. The lake has shaped local culture, from folk medicine to the bamboo cured in its waters for nipa huts. Some experts suggest that the legend of Mariang Makiling began with the Lady of Laguna de Bay.
laguna-province: Settlement in the area goes back to prehistoric times.
