The written history of the province and of the Southern Tagalog region dates from about 900 CE, the time of the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, the oldest known written document found in the Philippines. It records the release of its subject from a debt to the Lord of Pailah, Jayadewa. The province was formerly called La Laguna, after the lake Laguna de Bay, which took its own name from the town of Bay, the first provincial capital. Captain Juan de Salcedo conquered it for Spain in 1571 with a band of one hundred Spanish-Mexican soldiers.

Laguna was one of eight provinces that rose against Spanish rule in the Philippine Revolution. Its leaders included Paciano Rizal in Calamba, Severino Taiño in Pagsanjan and Agueda Kahabagan in Calauan. At the Battle of Sambat the Katipuneros took Pagsanjan but were driven out by forces under Basilio Augustín. In the Philippine-American War, generals Juan Cailles and Paciano Rizal led the defence. Filipino forces won the Battle of Mabitac, but American forces under Henry W. Lawton won at Santa Cruz, Pagsanjan and Paete and secured the province.

Under the Japanese occupation Laguna was a centre of resistance. In June 1942 Marking's Guerrillas raided the Cine Lumban to free 115 American prisoners of war. Only one was rescued, and the Japanese executed ten prisoners in reprisal. The International Rice Research Institute was established at Los Baños in 1960. When martial law was declared in September 1972, many of Laguna's citizens were arrested, and some were tortured or disappeared.

Laguna lies in the Calabarzon region of Luzon, south-east of Metro Manila, and covers 1,917.85 square kilometres on the southern shore of Laguna de Bay. Its capital is Santa Cruz, which has been the seat of government since 1858, after Bay and Pagsanjan. Its largest city is San Pablo. It has 24 municipalities and 6 cities, and the 2024 census counted 3,687,345 people. Almost all speak Tagalog, and the Roman Catholic Church is the largest religion.

José Rizal, the national hero, was born in Calamba. The province is known for the wood carvings of Paete, the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, Pagsanjan Falls and the University of the Philippines Los Baños.
lahaina: Lahaina lies on the north-west coast of Maui. It was originally called Lele in Hawaiian and was known for its breadfruit trees; the name Lahaina is generally explained as a combination of the words for sun and cruel, with several other proposed meanings. The town lies in the rain shadow of the West Maui Mountains and is one of the driest places in Hawaii. According to Hawaiian tradition, the first ruler of western Maui was Haho, and the line that followed him produced later rulers, among them Piʻilani, the first to rule the whole island.

In 1738 Lahaina and most of West Maui saw a series of battles between rival chiefs of the royal family and their allies from Hawaii Island and Oʻahu. When George Vancouver visited in 1793, he described a village among breadfruit and coconut groves whose people were impoverished by long wars. From 1802 to 1803 Kamehameha I stationed his fleet of war canoes there. American Protestant missionaries set up the first mission station on Maui at Lahaina in 1823, and in 1831 they founded Lahainaluna Seminary, where Hawaiian students, among them the historian David Malo, were taught religion and crafts. Its press issued the first newspaper in the Hawaiian language in 1834, and teachers and students helped translate the Bible into Hawaiian.

In the 19th century Lahaina was an important stop for whalers, who came for fresh water, fruit and vegetables. Conflict with the missionaries sometimes led to riots, and in 1827 the British whaler John Palmer shelled the town. Governor Hoapili built the Old Lahaina Fort in 1831. Kamehameha III lived in a royal compound on the island of Mokuʻula from 1837 to 1845, and on 8 October 1840 he proclaimed the first Hawaiian constitution at Luaʻehu in Lahaina. In 1845 he moved the capital to Honolulu, which was growing in commercial importance. A fire on 1 January 1919 destroyed more than thirty buildings and led to the creation of the Maui Fire Department.

Lahaina is a census-designated place in Maui County, with a population of 12,702 at the 2020 census. Its historic district, centred on Front Street, held 60 historic sites, among them the Old Lahaina Courthouse, the fort and the Baldwin House. A banyan tree planted in 1873 to mark the 50th anniversary of the missionaries' arrival became the largest in the United States. Wildfires in August 2023 destroyed about 80 per cent of the town.
lahaul: Lahaul lies in the west of Lahaul and Spiti district, with Keylong as its main town, geologically in the Himalayas and on the Tibetan Plateau. It is connected to Manali in the south through the Rohtang Pass. It has three valleys: the Chandra Valley, locally Rangloi, after the Chandra River; the Bhaga Valley, locally Ghar, after the Bhaga River; and the Chandra-Bhaga Valley, locally Pattan and further on the Chenab Valley, where the two rivers meet at Tandi. The Kunzum Pass, at 4,551 metres, connects it to Spiti in the east. Lahaul receives much more rainfall than Spiti.

The harsh conditions allow only scattered tufts of hardy grasses and shrubs to grow even below 4 km, and glacier lines are usually at about 5 km. Farmers grow potatoes, cabbages and green peas as cash crops.

Lahaul was under the influence of the kingdom of Ladakh until the early 17th century, though the rulers of Chamba and Kullu also vied for control. In the 17th century it came under the Rajas of Kullu, particularly Biddhi Singh (r. 1672 to 1688) and Man Singh (r. 1688 to 1719). Dogra forces captured it in the early 19th century, and after the Anglo-Sikh War of 1845-46 it came under the British Raj as a waziri of the Kullu sub-division of the Kangra district of Punjab.

Three hereditary jagir districts, Kolong, Gumrang and Gondhla, each headed by a Thakur, had pre-dated British rule, and the British made the Thakur of Kolong wazir of all Lahaul, a magistrate, police officer, jailer, revenue collector and forest officer in one. The last of the line was Thakur Pratap Chand, by the 1930s. The wazir's powers were reduced from 1941, and Lahaul and Spiti were joined as a district in 1960; in 1966 it became part of Himachal Pradesh.

Trade was an important occupation beside agriculture and pastoralism. A major Central Asian route through Lahaul linked the plains of Punjab and the Kullu valley with Ladakh and Yarkand, and Patseo, near Darcha, held an important annual wool mart in the colonial period. Moravian missionaries, among them Heinrich August Jäschke, ran a mission at Keylong from 1853 to 1940. They won few converts but introduced potatoes, turnips, lettuce, spinach and cauliflower, as well as knitting and newspapers.

The 2011 census gave Lahaul and Spiti district a population of 31,564, all rural. The Lahaulis are generally of Tibetan and Indo-Aryan descent, and the language of both Lahauli and Spiti Bhots is Bhoti, a Tibetic language. The family is the basic unit of kinship, headed by the senior male, the Yunda, and polyandry, once widely practised, has been dying out. Historic sites include the monastery and fort at Gondhla, the Triloknath temple, Khangsar palace and the Mrikula Devi temple.
lahijan: Lahijan is a city near the Caspian Sea in the Central District of Lahijan County in Gilan province, of which it is the capital. It stands on the northern slope of the Alborz Mountains at an altitude of 94 metres, west of Langarud and east of Astaneh-ye Ashrafiyeh, and its foundations rest on sediments laid down by the rivers of Gilan, among them the Sefid-Rud. It has a humid Hyrcanian climate with warmer winters and cooler summers than most of Gilan. The city had 19,877 inhabitants at the census of 1956 and 101,073 in 2016, making it the third largest city in the province after Rasht and Bandar-e Anzali.

Before Iran's present provincial divisions the Sefid-Rud divided Gilan into east and west, and Lahijan became capital of the eastern part, called Biehpish. The region has long been a centre of silk production. Tradition attributes the city's foundation to Lahij ebne Saam. The Mongol ruler Oljaito conquered it in 705 AH, and Amir Teimoor attacked the region. Plague broke out in 703 and a fire in 850, and the Russian army occupied Lahijan in June 1725. It was also one of the main bases of the Jungle Movement.

Lahijan was the first place in Iran to grow tea. Prince Mohammad Mirza, known as Kashef-ol-Saltaneh, who was born in Lahijan and served as the first mayor of Tehran and as ambassador to British-ruled India, posed as a French labourer to learn the secrets of tea production and brought about 3,000 saplings from the Kangra region of northern India, using his diplomatic immunity to avoid scrutiny. A first attempt with imported Indian seed in 1882 had failed. The first modern tea factory opened in 1934, and the Gilan hills came to hold about 107 factories and 32,000 hectares of tea. Kashef's mausoleum in Lahijan is part of the Iran National Tea Museum.

Lahijan blends traditional and modern architecture and is a tourist destination in northern Iran. Its sights include the Lahijan Pool, a reservoir of 17 hectares with an island that tradition says Shah Abbas I meant for a palace and the tomb of Sheikh Zahed Gilani, grandmaster of the Zahediyeh Sufi Order. Lahijan is known for the kulucheh, a filled cookie, and for its Ashura ceremonies, in which long reed trumpets called karna are played in villages such as Mashk, Lasht and Rudbeneh.
lahn: The Lahn is about 245 km long, of which 23 km lie in North Rhine-Westphalia, 165.6 km in Hesse and 57 km in Rhineland-Palatinate. It rises at the Lahnhof, near Netphen, in the south-eastern Rothaargebirge at 600 m, on the divide between the Rhine and Weser. It first runs north-east and east, then turns south at the Wetschaft and flows through the Marburg-Gießen valley and the Gießen Basin.

Below Wetzlar it narrows into the Weilburg valley, where the town of Weilburg lies in a loop of the river crossed by a boat tunnel unique in Germany. After the Limburg Basin it enters the lower valley, cut more than 200 m deep into the Slate Mountains, and joins the Rhine at Lahnstein. Its longest tributaries are the Ohm and the Dill.

The valley was settled in the Stone Age, and a settlement of the Linear Pottery culture about 7,000 years old has been found at Dalheim near Wetzlar. The Roman fort at Bad Ems stood where the Limes crossed the Lahn, and the Waldgirmes Forum, found in the 1990s, was a Roman town that changed the understanding of Roman activity east of the Rhine.

In the Migration Period the Alamanni settled the lower valley and were later ousted by the Franks. The origin of the name is uncertain; it may be pre-Germanic. By the early 14th century the staple right of Diez points to considerable shipping, and by the end of the 19th century over 300 castles, fortresses and fortified churches had been built along the river.

Navigation was improved in stages, from John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg's towpath of 1559 to works by the Duchy of Nassau from 1808 and an agreement between Nassau and Prussia in 1816 to make the river passable to Gießen. Iron ore mining around Weilburg raised the number of vessels counted at Runkel from 278 in 1827 to 464 in 1833, and Prussia wanted the ore for the Ruhr. Locks and the Weilburg ship tunnel were built by the 1840s. The Lahntal railway, built in 1857 to 1863, gradually drew freight away. Freight shipping ended in 1981.

The Lahn is used only by recreational boats. Gravel mining in the valleys at Marburg and Gießen from 1960 to 1996 left lakes and one of the largest nature reserves in Hesse, the Lahnau Nature Preserve. A cycle path runs the length of the valley, and wine is grown at Obernhof and Weinähr. Limburg Cathedral stands on an outcrop of Devonian limestone known as Lahn marble.
lahore: Lahore lies in the northeastern part of Pakistan, in central-eastern Punjab, with the Ravi River flowing on its northern side. It has a hot semi-arid climate, bordering on humid subtropical, in which June temperatures routinely exceed 45 °C and the monsoon rains arrive in late June. Its historic core is the Walled City in the northern part of the modern city, which was built piecemeal, with small cul-de-sacs, rather than to a geometric plan.

Early Muslim historians recorded the city's name in several forms, among them Luhawar, Lūhār and Rahwar, and no definitive record of its early history exists. The site has been inhabited for over two millennia, and Lahore rose to prominence in the late 10th century. Sultan Mahmud conquered it between 1020 and 1027 for the Ghaznavid Empire, and the governor Malik Ayaz rebuilt and repopulated the devastated city, erecting walls and a masonry fort in 1037–1040. It later served as a capital of several states, including the Delhi Sultanate.

Babur captured and sacked Lahore in 1525. Sher Shah Suri seized it in 1540, and Humayun reconquered it in February 1555. Mughal rule brought the most prosperous era of its history, and the city holds more Mughal-era monuments than Delhi or Agra. It was the capital under Akbar. In the 18th century Ahmad Shah Durrani occupied it in 1748 and invaded again in 1751, 1752 and 1757. The Bhangi Misl, a Sikh state, took it in 1767, and it later became the capital of the Sikh Kingdom of Lahore. Hazuri Bagh was built in 1818 under Ranjit Singh.

The East India Company seized control in February 1846 from the declining Sikh state, and the Punjab was annexed in 1849. At partition in 1947 the city's future was fiercely contested before the Boundary Commission; the 1941 census gave it a population of 671,659, 64.5 per cent Muslim. Partition weakened its economy, and Karachi rather than Lahore became the capital of Pakistan.

Lahore is the capital of the Pakistani province of Punjab and the country's second-largest city. It is a UNESCO City of Literature and a centre of Pakistan's publishing and of qawwali music. The Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981. Other landmarks include the Badshahi and Wazir Khan mosques and the Tomb of Jahangir. Punjabi is the most widely spoken first language.
lajos-kossuth: Lajos Kossuth was born on 19 September 1802 at Monok, in Zemplén county, the eldest of five children in a Lutheran family of the lower nobility with Slovak origins. His father, László, held a small estate and worked as a lawyer. The family moved to Olaszliszka in 1803 and to Sátoraljaújhely in 1808. Kossuth entered national politics as deputy to Count Hunyady at the Diet of Hungary, which met in Pressburg. His marriage to Meszlényi, a Catholic, took place on the day of his release from prison, and neither would convert. The mixed marriage caused a scandal and shaped his later defence of such unions.

In January 1841 Kossuth became editor of the Pesti Hírlap. Authorities expected censorship to blunt him, but his editorials on the economy, social injustice and the legal inequality of the common people combined into a coherent reform programme, and the paper reached the then immense circulation of 7,000 copies. He differed with Count Széchenyi, who wanted reform slowly and carefully to avoid Habsburg intervention and favoured a limited suffrage, while Kossuth saw rights as unitary and pointed to universal suffrage.

On 3 March 1848, after news of the revolution in Paris, he demanded parliamentary government for Hungary. On 7 December 1848 the Diet refused to acknowledge Franz Joseph I as king and called the nation to arms. From then until the revolution collapsed Kossuth, as elected regent-president, was Hungary's ruler. After defeat he crossed into Ottoman territory, where the authorities refused to surrender him to Austria. He was feted in England in 1851 and arrived in New York on 6 December 1851, giving over 600 speeches in the United States. He then lived in London for eight years, working with exiles such as Giuseppe Mazzini.

In 1861 Kossuth moved to Turin. On the day before the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 he published the open letter called the Cassandra letter, which condemned the settlement and Ferenc Deák and predicted that Hungary would fall with the Habsburgs. He remained committed to full independence and never returned to Hungary. In 1890 he lost his Hungarian citizenship under the law of 1879, having said he would rather be a man without a country than swear an oath to the Habsburgs.

Kossuth died in Turin on 20 March 1894. His body was taken to Pest, where Mór Jókai delivered the funeral oration. The Party of Independence and '48, formed in 1884, regarded him as its spiritual leader, and his son Ferenc Kossuth became Minister for Trade in 1906. The square before the Hungarian Parliament Building in Budapest bears his name.
lake-albano: Lake Albano, also called Lago di Castel Gandolfo, is a small volcanic crater lake in the Alban Hills of Lazio, at the foot of Monte Cavo, 20 km south-east of Rome. It is about 170 m deep, the deepest lake in Lazio, and measures 3.5 km by 2.3 km. It was formed by the overlapping union of two volcanic craters, as the ridge in its centre, rising 70 m, shows. In Roman times it was known as Albanus Lacus and lay not far from the ancient city of Alba Longa.

Plutarch reports that in 406 BCE the lake surged over the surrounding hills although no rain fell and no tributaries fed it. The flood destroyed fields and vineyards before pouring into the sea. It is thought to have been a limnic eruption, in which volcanic gases trapped in sediment on the lake bed built up and were suddenly released.

During the wars between Rome and Veii a discharge tunnel was cut through the crater walls to control flooding, a gigantic work given the modest means of the time, said to have been built by 30,000 men. It is 1,350 m long and runs 128 m below the surface. Livy says the Oracle of Delphi prompted the work, declaring that Rome could beat Veii only when the lake's waters were channelled and used for irrigation. In 393 BCE the lake rose again without rain, and a haruspex of Veii recited a prophecy that Veii would be impregnable while the waters stayed high. Georges Dumézil saw the story as a festival myth giving significance to an exceptional event.

Castel Gandolfo, which overlooks the lake, is the site of the Papal Palace. The lake hosted the canoeing and rowing events of the 1960 Summer Olympic Games in Rome, and the lane marking system developed for them is commonly called the Albano buoy system.
lake-atitlan: Lake Atitlán lies in the Sololá Department in the Guatemalan Highlands, about 50 km west-northwest of Antigua. Its name means between the waters and comes from Nahuatl. It is about 18 km by 8 km, with a surface area of 130.1 square kilometres and a maximum depth of about 340 metres, which makes it the deepest lake in Central America. It is endorheic, fed by two rivers and not draining to the sea. The basin fills a caldera formed by a supervolcanic eruption about 79,500 years ago, known as Los Chocoyos, which spread ash over some 6,000,000 square kilometres. Three volcanoes, Atitlán, San Pedro and Tolimán, have since grown on the southern side. Atitlán has erupted most recently, in 1853.

Maya communities have lived around the lake for a long time. Samabaj, a site about 55 feet below the present surface, appears to date from at least the pre-Classic period and has the remains of several groups of buildings, among them large structures thought to have been a city centre. During the Spanish conquest the Kaqchikel at first allied with the invaders against their historic enemies, the Tz'utujil and K'iche', but were themselves conquered when they refused to pay tribute.

The lake became a national park in 1955. In 1958 the black bass was introduced, at the suggestion of Pan American World Airways, to attract anglers. It eliminated more than two thirds of the native fish and contributed to the extinction of the Atitlán grebe. In the Guatemalan Civil War, from 1960 to 1996, the lake was the scene of human rights abuses as the government pursued a scorched earth policy against indigenous people assumed to support the guerrillas. The missionary Stanley Rother was killed in the church at Santiago Atitlán in 1981, and in 1990 soldiers fired on a protest march, killing 11 unarmed civilians. Hurricane Stan in October 2005 buried the village of Panabaj in a landslide.

The communities around the lake are rooted in living Maya heritage, kept chiefly by the Tz'utujil and Kaqchikel, with traditional dress and textiles. Santiago Atitlán, the largest, is noted for the worship of Maximón, an image that fuses Maya deities, Catholic saints and conquistador legends and is moved between the houses of a religious brotherhood each year. Panajachel is dominated by visitors. No road circles the lake, and some villages can be reached only by boat. The area grows coffee, avocados, corn and onions. Alexander von Humboldt called it the most beautiful lake in the world.
lake-baikal: Lake Baikal lies in southern Siberia between Irkutsk Oblast to the north-west and the Republic of Buryatia to the south-east. It sits in a rift valley formed by the Baikal Rift Zone, where the Earth's crust is slowly pulling apart. The lake is 636 km long and 79 km wide, and its maximum depth is 1,642 metres. The rift is young and active, widening about 4 mm a year, and the area is seismically active. The lake has three basins, North, Central and South, drains into the Angara, and is among the clearest in the world. Its surface freezes from early January to early May or June.

The Baikal area has a long history of human habitation. At Mal'ta, some 160 km north-west of the lake, the remains of a young male known as Mal'ta Boy point to the Mal'ta–Buret' culture about 24,000 years ago. The Kurykans gave the lake a name that translates as much water; the Buryats later called it Baygal nuur, the natural lake. It lay in the former northern territory of the Xiongnu confederation and is one site of the Han–Xiongnu War, and Han records called it the North Sea, one of the semi-mythical Four Seas. It was under the Tang dynasty's Anbei Protectorate from 647 to 682.

Little was known to Europeans about the lake until Russia expanded into the area in the 1600s. The Baykalsk Pulp and Paper Mill, built in 1966 directly on the shore, discharged waste into the lake; Soviet scientists protested against it, and it closed in November 2008.

Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world, estimated at 25 to 30 million years old, and holds more than 1,000 plant species and 2,500 animal species, many of them found nowhere else, among them the Baikal seal, or nerpa. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1996. Buryat peoples live on its eastern side, where they raise goats, camels, cattle, sheep and horses.
lake-balaton: Lake Balaton is a freshwater rift lake in the Transdanubian region of Hungary. The Zala River provides the largest inflow of water, and the canalized Sió is the only outflow. The average depth is 3.2 metres. The lake affects the local climate, bringing about 5 to 7 centimetres more precipitation than most of Hungary and less extreme temperatures, and it freezes over in winter. The mountainous northern shore is a wine region, and the Mediterranean-like climate and volcanic soil have made the region notable for wine since the Roman period. The flat southern shore is known for its resort towns.

The Romans called the lake Pelso. The modern name is Indo-European in origin and derives from the Slavic word for mud or swamp. In January 846 the Slavic prince Pribina began to build a fortress and several churches near Zalavár, among forests and swamps along the Zala. His castle was the capital of the Lower Pannonian Principality, known as Blatnohrad or Moosburg, meaning Swamp Fortress, and served as a bulwark against both the Bulgarians and the Moravians.

The lake has long been important both tactically and culturally, and many folk tales surround it. During the Ottoman wars it helped defend Royal Hungary, and battles were fought there. Balatonfüred and Hévíz have long been resort centres for the Hungarian aristocracy. Only in the late 19th century did the middle class begin to visit, when landowners ruined by phylloxera in their vineyards began building summer homes to rent out.

Railways built in 1861 and 1909 increased tourism, and by the turn of the 20th century Hungarian biologists, geologists and hydrologists were researching the lake. The country's first biological research institute was built on its shore in 1927.

The last major German offensive of World War II, Operation Spring Awakening, took place in the region between 6 and 16 March 1945. Sepp Dietrich's Sixth Panzer Army and the Hungarian Third Army attacked, and the Red Army won. During the 1960s and 1970s government efforts made Balaton a major destination: overnight guests in July rose from 700,000 in 1965 to two million in 1975, many on subsidised trade union holidays. It also drew East Germans and other Eastern Bloc residents, and West Germans could visit, so that families separated by the Berlin Wall could meet there until 1989.

Balaton is the largest lake in Central Europe and one of the region's foremost tourist destinations. The major resorts are Siófok, Keszthely and Balatonfüred, and the Tihany Peninsula is a historical district. Keszthely has the Festetics Palace, and Badacsony is a volcanic mountain and wine-growing region.
lake-biwa: Lake Biwa lies entirely within Shiga Prefecture in west-central Honshu and has an area of about 670 square kilometres. It is of tectonic origin and dates to at least 4 million years ago, in the mid-Pliocene, which makes it one of the oldest lakes in the world; it is estimated to be the 13th oldest. Small rivers drain into it from the surrounding mountains, and its main outlet, the Seta, becomes the Uji and then, joined by the Katsura and Kizu, the Yodo River, which flows into the Seto Inland Sea at Osaka Bay. Because the lake lies close to Kyoto, the historical capital, it appears often in Japanese literature, particularly in poetry and in accounts of battles.

The name Biwa-ko was established in the Edo period. It is generally believed to come from the lake's resemblance in shape to the biwa, a stringed instrument. In the 14th century Kōsō, a learned monk of Enryaku-ji, wrote that the lake is the Pure Land of the goddess Benzaiten, who lives on Chikubu Island and favours the biwa. The lake was formerly called Aumi, the Freshwater Sea, a word whose present pronunciation, Ōmi, survives in the name of Ōmi Province.

The submerged shell midden at Awazu, near Ōtsu at the southern end of the lake, is an important site of the Jōmon period and goes back to the beginning of the Initial Jōmon, about 9300 BCE. Its Middle Jōmon layer, dated 3520 to 2470 BCE, held abundant horse chestnuts, about 40 per cent of the estimated diet, which indicates that the people had mastered a processing technology to remove their harmful tannic acid. Ishiyama-dera is another lake site, dating to the Early Jōmon. The Lake Biwa Canal, built in the late 1890s and expanded in the Taishō era, played a crucial part in the revival of Kyoto's industrial life after its steep decline following the transfer of the capital to Tokyo.

The lake serves as a reservoir for Kyoto and Ōtsu and provides drinking water for about 15 million people in the Kansai region. It is a breeding ground for freshwater fish, including trout, and for the pearl culture industry. Naturalists have documented more than 1,000 species and subspecies in the lake, about sixty of them endemic, including 46 native fish species and subspecies and 38 freshwater snails, 19 of them endemic. It was designated a Ramsar wetland in 1993. A law to prevent eutrophication, which followed a citizens' campaign known as the Soap Movement, was first enforced on 1 July 1982, now called Lake Biwa Day.
lake-bolsena: Lake Bolsena lies in the northern part of the province of Viterbo, called Alto Lazio or Tuscia. It is the largest volcanic lake in Europe. Roman records indicate that the Vulsini volcano was active as recently as 104 BCE, and it has been dormant since. The lake formed when a circular area collapsed after the magma chamber that fed the volcanic district was depleted, and the two islands in the south were formed by underwater eruptions following that collapse. It has an oval shape, with its long axis running north to south, and a roughly conical bed. The Marta River is its only outlet and flows to the Tyrrhenian Sea near Lido di Tarquinia.

The Romans called the lake Lacus Volsinii, adapting the Etruscan name Velzna, that of the last Etruscan city to hold out against Rome, whose people were moved after 264 BCE; its original site has not been securely identified. A modernised Roman consular road, the Via Cassia, runs along one side. One third of the lake was donated to the Church by the noble Alberici family of Orvieto, who were honoured with a ceremony three times a year performed by the Bishop of Orvieto.

The island of Bisentina, the largest at 17 hectares, gave refuge from Saracen raids in the 9th century. About 1250 it passed to the lord of Bisenzio, who burned it after disputes with its inhabitants. Urban IV reconquered it in 1261, and in 1333 Louis IV of Bavaria destroyed it. It belonged to the Farnese family from 1400 and was visited by many popes. Its monuments include a church with a cupola by Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola and a small temple of Saint Catherine by Antonio da Sangallo. On Martana, it is said, the Ostrogothic queen Amalasuntha was assassinated, which Justinian I used as a reason for war.

The watershed had 22,000 permanent residents in 2004 and 35,000 in summer. Eight comuni stand on the shore: Bolsena, Montefiascone, Marta, Capodimonte, Valentano, Gradoli, Grotte di Castro and San Lorenzo Nuovo, which was moved from an older site further down the slope to escape malaria from marshes on the northern shore. Etruscan antiquities remain at the old site. Orvieto lies about 14 kilometres to the north-east. Each shore comune has a stretch of beach, and the surroundings hold camping and farm-stay establishments.
lake-chad: Lake Chad is a shallow freshwater lake without an outlet to the sea, with a catchment area of more than 1,000,000 square kilometres. It is divided by a shallow sill called the Great Barrier into a deeper southern part and a shallower northern part. Its main source of water is the Chari River, which with the Logone supplies about 95 per cent of the inflow; the Yobe supplies less than 2.5 per cent. Water seeps underground toward the Bodélé Depression, about 480 km to the north-east, which takes away most of the salt and keeps the lake fresh. Levels vary strongly with the seasons, and in the 19th century the lake still covered about 28,000 square kilometres.

For most of the Quaternary the basin held abundant water. The lake known as Mega-Chad once covered about 400,000 square kilometres and drained to the Benue River. In the wetter period that followed, lakeside fishing settlements appeared; a pottery culture called Gajiganna emerged by 1800 BCE, and permanent villages were established south of the lake by 500 BCE, including those of the Sao civilization. By the 5th century CE camels carried trans-Saharan trade, and after the Arab conquests of the 7th and 8th centuries the basin was increasingly linked to Muslim lands.

Around 900 CE the Kanem people unified nomadic tribes and founded the Kanem Empire north-east of the lake. They were Islamized and settled at Njimi in the 11th century, and the empire reached its peak in the 13th. Its vassal Bornu rose as Kanem declined, and the centre of power moved there around 1400. In the later 16th century Bornu imported firearms from the Ottoman Empire. It declined in the 18th century and lost its western region to the Sokoto Caliphate in the early 19th. By the second decade of the 20th century Britain, France and Germany held the lake region, drawing boundaries that largely remain.

Lake Chad lies where Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon meet. It shrank sharply between 1960 and 1990, from about 25,000 square kilometres in 1960 to about 2,000 in 1980, because of drought and the diversion of water. The Lake Chad Basin Commission, established on 22 May 1964, manages the lake and its water, with headquarters at N'Djamena. More than 70 ethnic groups live around it, relying on fishing, farming and herding, and natron has long been dug on its north-eastern shore.
lake-champlain: Lake Champlain is 107 miles (172 km) long and covers about 514 square miles, with a shoreline of 587 miles and a maximum depth of 400 feet. It lies in the Champlain Valley between the Green Mountains of Vermont and the Adirondack Mountains of New York, and the Richelieu River carries its water north into the St Lawrence at Sorel-Tracy, Quebec. Its basin extends south as far as Lake George. The valley is the northernmost part of the Great Appalachian Valley, and the Chazy Reef on Isle La Motte is an Ordovician coral reef formation. The lake holds roughly 80 islands, three of which, South Hero, North Hero and Isle La Motte, make up most of Grand Isle County, Vermont.

The lake has long been a border between indigenous nations, standing at the frontier of Abenaki and Mohawk territories. The Abenaki name, Pitawbagok, means middle lake or lake in between, and the Mohawk name, Kaniatarakwà:ronte, means a bulged lake. It was an important eastern gateway to the lands of the Iroquois Confederacy. The French explorer Samuel de Champlain encountered it in 1609, and in the same year he recorded a monster in the lake, the origin of the later legend of Champ. New France granted concessions along the shore to French settlers and built forts to defend the waterways.

In colonial times the lake was the easiest passage between the Saint Lawrence and Hudson valleys, by boat in summer and by sledge on the ice, since overland roads were unpaved and often muddy. Its ports of Burlington, Plattsburgh and Port Henry had commercial and military importance in the 18th and 19th centuries. On 11 September 1814 British and American forces fought the Battle of Lake Champlain, or Plattsburgh, which ended the last British invasion of the northern states and denied the British leverage for demands before the Treaty of Ghent. The Champlain Canal, opened on 9 September 1823, joined the lake to the Hudson River and the Erie Canal, and the Chambly Canal has bypassed rapids on the Richelieu since 1843.

The lake lies mostly between New York and Vermont and extends north into Quebec. Burlington, Vermont, is the largest city on its shore, followed by Plattsburgh, New York, and South Burlington. Fort Ticonderoga stands towards the south. Because it links the St Lawrence and the Hudson, it is sometimes called the Sixth Great Lake. In 1989 UNESCO designated the area around it the Champlain-Adirondack Biosphere Reserve.
lake-como: Lake Como has an area of 146 square kilometres, making it the third-largest lake in Italy after Lake Garda and Lake Maggiore, and it is more than 400 metres deep. Its Y shape resulted from the movement of the ancient Adda glacier, which was diverted by the mountainous terrain and carved three branches. It lies at the southern end of the Alps, about 45 kilometres north of Milan. The Adda enters near Colico at the northern end and leaves as the only major outflow from the southeastern branch, which leaves the southwestern branch a cul-de-sac. For this reason the city of Como was historically more prone to flooding than Lecco.

The first significant settlement, Comum, emerged in the Iron Age within the Golasecca culture. In 196 BCE a Roman army under Claudius Marcellus conquered the area from the Celtic Comenses. The Romans built the Via Regina, linking the lake, which they called Larius, to the Rhaetian region and serving as a trade route between the Po and Rhine valleys. In 59 BCE Julius Caesar re-established the town on its present lakeside site as Novum Comum. Pliny the Younger described the lake in his letters as a haven for study, hunting and fishing.

In the Middle Ages the lake remained strategically vital for access to the Alpine passes. Como became an independent commune around 1000 and fought Milan, and its defensive towers were built under Frederick Barbarossa between 1158 and 1162. Power later passed to the Visconti and Sforza families of Milan. In 1859, after Garibaldi's victory over the Austrians at San Fermo, the lake became part of the new Kingdom of Italy. Silk made the region prosperous in the 19th and 20th centuries, and wealthy Milanese families built villas as summer retreats, among them Villa Olmo, Villa Serbelloni and Villa Carlotta.

Lake Como is known for its villas and gardens, a tradition that goes back to the Roman estates of Pliny the Younger and was revived in the Renaissance. The Sacro Monte di Ossuccio, with fifteen Baroque chapels built between 1635 and 1710, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Silk weaving remains a leading industry around Como, and tourism is a major part of the local economy.
lake-constance: Lake Constance consists of three bodies of water on the Rhine at the northern foot of the Alps: the Upper Lake, or Obersee, the Lower Lake, or Untersee, and the connecting stretch of the Rhine called the Seerhein. The Alpine Rhine enters from the south and the High Rhine leaves westward. The lake is 63 kilometres long, nearly 14 kilometres wide at most, covers about 536 square kilometres and lies 395 metres above sea level; its maximum depth, 252 metres, is in the middle of the Upper Lake. Its shoreline of 273 kilometres runs through Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and the exact location of the borders within the lake has never been settled between the three states.

The largest island is Reichenau in the Lower Lake. Lindau and Mainau lie in the Upper Lake, and the large peninsula of Bodanrück separates the two lakes. The largest towns on the Upper Lake are Constance, Friedrichshafen, Bregenz, Lindau, Überlingen and Kreuzlingen.

The lake was formed by the Rhine Glacier during the Quaternary glaciation. About 10,000 years ago, after the last glacial period, the Obersee and Untersee still formed one lake. Hunters and gatherers of the Mesolithic frequented the area without settling, and the first lasting settlements, pile dwellings and wetland villages, date from the middle and late Neolithic. A pile-dwelling village at Unteruhldingen has been reconstructed as an open-air museum. In 2015 a 20-kilometre line of about 170 man-made underwater stone mounds, dated to the Neolithic or early Bronze Age, was found near Bottighofen and Romanshorn.

The Roman geographer Pomponius Mela, around 43 CE, called the upper lake Lacus Venetus and the lower Lacus Acronius. Around 75 CE Pliny the Elder named both Lacus Raetiae Brigantinus after the main Roman town on the lake, Brigantium, later Bregenz, a name linked to the Celtic Brigantii. In English and the Romance languages the lake is named after the city of Constance, from the Roman emperor Constantius II, while the German name Bodensee derives from the village of Bodman.

The abbey island of Reichenau is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its three early medieval churches, and is also known for intensive cultivation of fruit and vegetables. The lake supplies municipal waterworks around its shores and the Bodensee-Wasserversorgung. The Alpine Rhine and the Seerhein do not mix greatly with the lake's water but flow through it on courses that change little.
lake-edward: Lake Edward, locally Rwitanzigye or Rweru, is one of the smaller African Great Lakes. It lies in the Albertine Rift, the western branch of the East African Rift, with its northern shore a few kilometres south of the equator. At an elevation of 920 metres it is 77 kilometres long and 40 kilometres wide at its maximum points, and covers 2,325 square kilometres. About two thirds of its waters are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and one third in Uganda. The Nyamugasani, Ishasha, Rutshuru, Ntungwe and Rwindi rivers feed it, and Lake George empties into it by the Kazinga Channel.

The western escarpment of the Rift Valley towers up to 2,000 metres above the western shore, while the southern and eastern shores are flat lava plains. The Semliki River carries its water north into Lake Albert, whence it joins the White Nile.

The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley first saw the lake in 1888, during the Emin Pasha Relief Expedition, and it was named in honour of Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, son of Queen Victoria and later King Edward VII. In 1973 Uganda and Zaire renamed it Lake Idi Amin, after the Ugandan ruler; it recovered its former name after his overthrow in 1979.

The region shows much evidence of volcanic activity over the last 5,000 years. The Katwe-Kikorongo and Bunyaruguru volcanic fields, with extensive cones and craters, lie either side of the Kazinga Channel on the north-western shore. It is thought that Lakes George and Edward were once one larger lake, divided by lava from these fields, with the Kazinga Channel as the remnant of the union. Stanley visited the crater lake of Katwe in 1889 and noted its depression, its salinity and a nearby sulphurous spring, but did not connect them to volcanism; the volcanic origin of the area was first reported by G. F. Scott Elliot in 1894.

The lake lies wholly within Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Queen Elizabeth National Park in Uganda, and has little settlement on its shores. Ishango in the north holds a park ranger training facility; the main Congolese settlement in the south is Vitshumbi, and the Ugandan settlements are Mweya and Katwe. Lake Katwe is the chief producer of salt for Uganda. Its fish include Bagrus docmak, two species of Oreochromis tilapia and over 50 haplochromine species, and fishing is important to local residents.
lake-erhai: Erhai is an alpine fault lake in Dali City, Dali Prefecture, Yunnan. It lies 1,972 metres above sea level and measures 40 kilometres from north to south and roughly 7 to 8 kilometres from east to west, with an area of 250 square kilometres, a circumference of 116 kilometres and an average depth of 11 metres. It forms the backdrop to all of Dali City and sandwiches Dali Town against the Cang Mountain. The Miju and Mici rivers feed it from the north, the Bolou River from the east and smaller streams from the Cang Mountains in the west. The Yangbi River in the south is its outlet and eventually flows into the Lancang River, the upper Mekong.

In ancient times the lake was known as Yeyuze or Kunming Lake. During the Han to Tang periods a people called the Kunming Yi lived in the neighbouring region, which explains the second name. According to Bai scholars, Yeyu comes from the Bai language and means lower water. The modern name is said by Fang Guoyu to derive from a variant character, and the character for er does not mean ear. The lake was once a royal deer ranch for the Nanzhao Kingdom.

The lake is an important food source for the Bai people, who are known for fishing with trained cormorants that catch fish and return them to fishmongers; rings round the birds' necks stop them from swallowing the catch. Visitors can hike the lakeshore and reach islands such as Guanyin Ge, Jinsuo Island, Nanzhao Folklore Island and Xiaoputuo Island. Erhai is one of three major Yunnan lakes with many endemic species. Of 23 fish species and subspecies known there, eight are endemic, and most of these have not been recorded in decades and are likely extinct. More than ten introduced fish species now live in the lake.
lake-garda: Lake Garda lies between Brescia and Milan to the west and Verona and Venice to the east, cutting into the edge of the Italian Alps, and its shore is divided between the provinces of Brescia, Verona and Trentino. It is about 52 kilometres long and 16 kilometres wide, and its shape is typical of a moraine valley formed under a glacier.

The Sarca is its main tributary, and the Mincio, at Peschiera, its only outlet. In Roman times the lake was called Benacus, and some revered it as a god. The modern name derives from the town of Garda and from a Germanic word meaning place of guard, a trace of the Lombards. The mild climate supports olives, lemons and cypresses.

The strongest evidence of prehistoric settlement dates to the Bronze Age, when stilt houses stood in the lower lake. Romanisation took place mostly in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. In 268 CE a Roman army under the future emperor Claudius Gothicus won a decisive battle over the Alamanni at the lake. The Roman presence is attested by villas, including the Grottoes of Catullus.

Under the Lombards the area was divided among the duchies of Brescia, Verona and Trento. In the 13th century the Scaliger family subdued the eastern shore, built the castles of Sirmione, Malcesine and Riva, and completed a fortified line called the Serraglio in 1355. Venice gained the eastern shore in 1405 and the western shore in 1426, and the 34 lake municipalities received ample autonomy.

In 1438 a fleet of six galleys and twenty-five ships was hauled over Monte Baldo by 2,000 oxen. After 1815 the lake belonged to Austria, in the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. In 1943 the Italian Social Republic placed its ministries at Salò, Desenzano and other lake towns, and Mussolini's headquarters at Gargnano; Salò became its capital.

Around the lake lie 26 comuni, of which Desenzano del Garda is the most populated. The economy depends largely on tourism, which developed from the end of the 19th century, beginning with Gardone Riviera, where the poet Gabriele D'Annunzio built the Vittoriale degli Italiani, now a museum. Gardaland is the biggest Italian theme park, and Riva, Torbole and Campione are known for the winds that attract sailors and windsurfers. The rare carpione, a salmonid fish, is found only in the lake.
lake-geneva: Lake Geneva is one of the largest lakes in Western Europe and the largest on the course of the Rhône. Sixty per cent of its surface belongs to Switzerland, in the cantons of Vaud, Geneva and Valais, and forty per cent to France, in Haute-Savoie. It is crescent-shaped, with a northern shore of 95 km and a southern shore of 72 km, and is divided into the Haut Lac in the east, the Grand Lac, the largest and deepest basin, and the Petit Lac in the south-west.

Its maximum depth, between Évian-les-Bains and Lausanne, is 310 metres. The Rhône enters it between Villeneuve and Le Bouveret and leaves at Geneva, where the Seujet Dam controls the average surface height of 372 metres. The shore between Nyon and Lausanne is called La Côte, and the vineyard slopes between Lausanne and Vevey are Lavaux.

The name lacus Lemannus was in use in the time of Julius Caesar, from a Greek phrase meaning the port's lake. Medieval Latin called it Lacus Lausonius, and Old French Lac de Lausanne; after the rise of Geneva it became Lac de Genève, though Le Léman remains the usual name in French.

According to Gregory of Tours and Marius Aventicensis, a tsunami swept along the lake in 563, destroying the fort of Tauredunum and other settlements and killing many people in Geneva. Simulations indicate that a landslide near the Rhône delta caused a wave eight metres high that reached Geneva within 70 minutes. In 888 the area was part of the new Kingdom of Burgundy, which was absorbed into the Holy Roman Empire in 1033.

In 1827 the first measurement of the speed of sound in fresh water was made on the lake by the French mathematician Jacques Charles François Sturm and a Swiss physicist, using two moored boats and exploding gunpowder. Edmund Ludlow, who had signed the death warrant of Charles I, was granted protection at Vevey in 1662 and lived there until his death in 1692. Mary and Percy Shelley and Lord Byron holidayed beside the lake and wrote ghost stories, one of which became the basis of the novel Frankenstein. Empress Elisabeth of Austria was stabbed to death on the quay at Geneva in September 1898.

Geneva, Lausanne, Thonon-les-Bains and Montreux are the main towns on its shores. The beauty of the shores has long been admired: the northern bank falls in gentle vine-covered slopes set with villages and castles, while the southern mountains of Savoy and Valais are more rugged. The cold north-easterly wind called the bise can bring severe icing in winter. Yacht racing is popular, and the Tour du Lac rowing event, around the whole lake over 160 km, is the longest non-stop rowing regatta in the world.
lake-huron: Lake Huron is shared on the north and east by the Canadian province of Ontario and on the south and west by the American state of Michigan. Hydrologically it is the eastern part of Lake Michigan–Huron, having the same surface elevation as Lake Michigan, to which it is joined by the wide and deep Straits of Mackinac. The main inlet is the St. Marys River from Lake Superior, and the main outlet is the St. Clair River, toward Lake Erie. It is split into five basins, including Georgian Bay, Saginaw Bay and the North Channel, and Manitoulin Island, the largest freshwater island on Earth, separates the North Channel and Georgian Bay from the main basin.

Its surface lies 176 metres above sea level, and it is about 332 kilometres long. With its 30,000 islands it has the longest shoreline of any Great Lake. Like the others, it was formed by melting ice as the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, over a low depression once crossed by the now-buried Laurentian and Huronian Rivers.

About 9,000 years ago, when the water was approximately 100 metres below today's level, the Alpena-Amberley Ridge was exposed as a land bridge used as a migration route by large herds of caribou. Since 2008 archaeologists have found at least 60 stone constructions along the submerged ridge, thought to have been hunting blinds of Paleo-Indians. A 2013 underwater discovery confirmed that a trade network brought obsidian from Oregon almost ten thousand years ago.

On the eve of European contact, a town on or near the lake held more than one hundred large structures and between 4,000 and 6,000 people. The French, the first European visitors, often called the lake La Mer Douce, the fresh-water sea. A map of 1656 by Nicolas Sanson names it Karegnondi, a Wyandot word variously translated as Freshwater Sea, Lake of the Hurons, or simply lake, and early maps generally labelled it Lac des Hurons.

More than a thousand wrecks have been recorded in the lake. Le Griffon, built in 1679 and sailed by Robert Cavalier, Sieur de la Salle, is purportedly the first European vessel on the Great Lakes and the first lost. Sent back with a cargo of pelts in late November 1679, she was never seen again, and two wrecks claimed to be hers remain unverified.

The largest city on the lake is Sarnia, with Bay City, Port Huron and Alpena on the American side and Owen Sound, Collingwood and Parry Sound on Georgian Bay. Thunder Bay National Marine Sanctuary, established in 2000, protects 116 of the recorded wrecks.
lake-kivu: Lake Kivu lies in the Albertine Rift, the western branch of the East African Rift, on the border between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda. It is about 42 kilometres long and 50 kilometres at its widest, with a surface at 1,460 metres above sea level. Its maximum depth is 475 metres. The lake bed lies on a rift valley that is slowly being pulled apart, which causes volcanic activity in the area. About 58 percent of its waters lie within the borders of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Settlements on its shore include Bukavu, Kabare, Kalehe, Sake and Goma on the Congolese side and Gisenyi, Kibuye and Cyangugu in Rwanda.

In the past Lake Kivu drained north and contributed to the White Nile. About 13,000 to 9,000 years ago volcanic activity blocked its outlet to the Nile watershed and raised mountains, including the Virungas, between Lake Kivu and Lake Edward. The water was then forced south down the Ruzizi River. This in turn raised the level of Lake Tanganyika, which overflowed down the Lukuga River.

Researchers have found evidence around the lake of massive local extinctions about every thousand years, presumably caused by outgassing events. Its fish fauna is relatively poor, with 28 described species. In late 1959 the Belgian agronomist Alphonse Collart introduced the Lake Tanganyika sardine to fill an empty niche, since no fish fed on plankton in the open water. The sardine has since gained substantial economic and nutritional importance for people on the shore.

Lake Kivu is meromictic: a freshwater surface layer becomes more saline with depth. With Lake Nyos and Lake Monoun in Cameroon it is one of three lakes known to undergo limnic eruptions, in which the overturn of deep layers releases dissolved carbon dioxide. Its bottom also holds methane, estimated at 65 cubic kilometres, produced by microbial reduction of volcanic carbon dioxide, and about two million people live in the lake basin. The Swahili word mazuku, evil wind, names the outgassing of methane and carbon dioxide that kills people and animals. Methane has been drawn from the lake for a brewery at Gisenyi and for electricity generation in Rwanda.
lake-kyoga: Lake Kyoga, whose name in Runyoro means the place of bathing, covers about 1,720 square kilometres at an elevation of 1,033 metres. The Victoria Nile flows through it on its way from Lake Victoria to Lake Albert, and the main inflow from Lake Victoria is regulated by the Nalubaale Power Station at Jinja. Another source of water is the Mount Elgon region on the border between Uganda and Kenya. The lake belongs to the African Great Lakes system but is not itself counted as a great lake. Its extensions include Lake Kwania, Lake Bisina, Lake Bugondo and Lake Opeta.

The lake is very shallow. It reaches a depth of about 5.7 metres, and most of it is less than 4 metres deep. Water lilies cover the areas under 3 metres, and much of the swampy shoreline is covered with papyrus and with water hyacinth, an invasive plant. Papyrus also forms floating islands that drift between small permanent islands, and extensive wetlands fed by streams and rivers surround the lakes. Nile crocodiles are numerous.

There are at least 60 haplochromine cichlid species, many of them endemic and closely related to those of Lake Victoria. As in Lake Victoria, the introduced Nile perch has decimated them and some species are extinct. Less than 50 haplochromine species survive in the main lake, where Nile perch is common, while smaller satellite lakes without Nile perch keep at least 50 or 60 each. Fishing in the system has shifted from many native species to mainly the Lake Victoria sardine, the Nile perch and the introduced Nile tilapia, and in 2006 only 4 per cent of catches were haplochromine cichlids.
lake-ladoga: Lake Ladoga is the largest lake entirely in Europe and the second largest in Russia after Lake Baikal. It has an average surface area of 17,891 square kilometres, a length of 219 km from north to south and an average depth of 47 m, reaching 230 m in the north-west. About 660 islands, with a total area of about 435 square kilometres, lie mostly in the north-west, among them the Valaam archipelago, Kilpola and Konevets. The lake drains through the Neva River into the Gulf of Finland and is part of the Volga–Baltic Waterway. Its main tributaries are the Svir from Lake Onega, the Volkhov from Lake Ilmen and the Vuoksi from Lake Saimaa.

The name Ladoga seems first to have belonged to a river, then a city, then the lake. It comes from Old Norse Aldeigja or Aldoga, borrowed by Slavs as Ладога, and archaeology shows that Scandinavians arrived in the early 750s, a couple of decades before the Slavs. In the Middle Ages the lake was a vital part of the trade route from the Varangians to the Eastern Roman Empire, with the Norse emporium at Staraya Ladoga defending the mouth of the Volkhov from the 8th century. The area was disputed between the Novgorod Republic and Sweden, and in the early 14th century the fortresses of Korela and Oreshek were established on its banks.

By the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617 Russia ceded the northern and western coast to Sweden, and it returned to Russia in 1721 under the Treaty of Nystad. In the 18th century the Ladoga Canal was built to bypass the lake, whose winds and storms had destroyed hundreds of cargo ships.

The Valaam Monastery, on the largest island, was abandoned between 1611 and 1715, restored in the 18th century and evacuated to Finland during the Winter War in 1940. During the Siege of Leningrad (1941–44) the lake provided the only access to the city, as part of the eastern shore remained in Soviet hands, and supplies came by trucks over the ice on the winter roads called the Road of Life and by boat in summer.

The northern shore, Ladoga Karelia with the town of Sortavala, is part of the Republic of Karelia, and the western shore, the Karelian Isthmus, belongs to Leningrad Oblast. Both are in north-western Russia. The lake was shared between Finland and Russia from around 1812 until 1940, and after the Winter War it became an internal basin of the Soviet Union. It is home to the Ladoga seal, an endemic subspecies of the ringed seal, and to forty-eight forms of fish.
lake-lucerne: Lake Lucerne is the fourth largest lake in Switzerland. It has an irregular shape, with sharp bends and four arms, and covers 114 km2 at an elevation of 434 m, with a maximum depth of 214 m. The Reuss enters it at Flüelen, in the part called the Urnersee, and leaves it at Lucerne; the Muota, the Engelberger Aa and the Sarner Aa also flow in. Much of the shoreline rises steeply into mountains up to 1,500 m above the lake, among them the Rigi and Pilatus. Its level was stabilised between 1859 and 1860, when a needle dam was built in the Reuss at Lucerne; before that the lake was liable to flooding along its shore.

The lake formed at the end of the last ice age from the meltwater of the Reuss Glacier, which melted between 20,000 and 15,000 BCE. Archaeologists surveying the lake bed between 2019 and 2021 found the remains of a Bronze Age village with artefacts from around 1000 BCE, which showed that the area was settled 2,000 years earlier than historians had thought. The lake was a transport axis at least since the opening of the Gotthard Pass in 1230, and it was the only connection along that route until 1863. A mail coach road across the pass opened in 1830 with its northern end at Flüelen, and the first steamer, the Stadt Luzern, began service in 1837.

Before the 16th century the whole lake was called the Luzerner See, as it still is in English. The name Vierwaldstättersee, the lake of the four forested settlements, is first used in the 16th century. Since the 14th century the Waldstätte had been the confederate allies Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, and the notion of four, with the addition of the canton of Lucerne, is first recorded in the 1450s. The meadow of the Rütli, on the shore of the Urnersee, is the traditional site of the founding of the Swiss Confederation.

Many of the oldest communities of Switzerland lie along the shore, among them Küssnacht, Weggis, Vitznau, Gersau, Brunnen, Altdorf and Buochs. Steamers and other passenger boats still ply between the villages and towns, and the lake remains a popular destination for visitors. The Vitznau-Rigi Railway, opened in 1871, was the first rack railway in Europe, and in 1889 a cog railway was built from Alpnachstad up Pilatus. The 35 km Swiss Path around the Urnersee was built in 1991 for the country's 700th anniversary. Ludwig Rellstab's description of moonlight on the lake in 1832 gave Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata its name.
lake-malaren: Mälaren covers 1,140 square kilometres and reaches a depth of 64 metres at most, though it is low-lying and mostly shallow. It lies in Svealand, bounded by the provinces of Uppland, Södermanland and Västmanland, and spans 120 kilometres from east to west. It drains to the Baltic Sea through Norrström and Söderström in Stockholm and through the artificial Södertälje Canal. Its easternmost bay, Riddarfjärden, lies in central Stockholm. The largest islands are Selaön and Svartsjölandet. The name comes from the Old Norse mælir, meaning gravel, recorded in the 1320s; the lake was earlier called Lǫgrinn, The Lake.

After the last ice age the land rose as the weight of the ice was removed, and this uplift, which continues today at about a centimetre a year or less, reshaped the Mälaren basin. In the Viking Age the lake was still a bay of the Baltic Sea, and seagoing vessels could sail far into the interior of Sweden. The Viking Age settlements of Birka on the island of Björkö and Hovgården on neighbouring Adelsö stood by the trade routes through the Södertälje Canal.

By about 1200 the canal and the mouth of Riddarfjärden had become so shallow that ships had to unload near the entrances, and the bay gradually became a lake. The decline of Birka and the founding of Stockholm at the choke point of Riddarfjärden were partly due to this rebound.

In Norse mythology, as told in the thirteenth-century Prose Edda, the goddess Gefjon created the lake when she tricked the Swedish king Gylfi and dragged land into the sea, where it became the island of Zealand. Since modern maps fit this better with Lake Vänern, the myth may originally have concerned that lake. From the mid-17th century expeditions tried to chart the lake, which was strategically and economically important. In 1687 King Charles XI commissioned Carl Gripenhielm to map it. His map, completed in 1689 and framed by 96 small gouache paintings of towns, castles and mansions, stayed valid until a more accurate map by Jacob Nordencreutz in 1739.

Birka and Hovgården have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993, as has Drottningholm Palace on the island of Lovön. The barrow of Björn Ironside stands on the island of Munsö. Stockholm is sometimes called Mälardrottningen, the Lake Mälar Queen, in Swedish literature, and the area around the lake hosted the cycling events at the 1912 Summer Olympics.
lake-malawi: Lake Malawi is between 560 and 580 kilometres long and about 75 kilometres wide at its widest point, with a surface area of about 29,600 square kilometres. Its deepest point, in a depression in the north-central part, is 706 metres, while the southern half is shallower. The Shire River drains it at the south into the Zambezi. It is a meromictic lake, which means its water layers do not mix.

The lake lies in a valley formed by the opening of the East African Rift, where the African plate is being split. It was long estimated to be 1 to 2 million years old, but more recent evidence points to a considerably older lake, whose basin began to form about 8.6 million years ago. Its levels have varied dramatically, from almost 600 metres below the present level to 10 to 20 metres above it, and at times the lake nearly dried out. Between 1390 and 1860 it may have stood 120 to 150 metres below its present level.

The Portuguese trader Candido José da Costa Cardoso was the first European to visit the lake, in 1846. David Livingstone reached it in 1859 and named it Lake Nyasa. He also called it the Lake of Stars, after the lights of fishermen's lanterns on the water, and the Lake of Storms, after the violent gales that sweep it.

On 16 August 1914 the lake saw a brief naval battle of the First World War. The British gunboat Gwendolen found the German Empire's only gunboat on the lake, the Hermann von Wissmann, in a bay near Sphinxhaven and disabled it with a single cannon shot from about 1,800 metres. The Times hailed it as the first naval victory of the war for the British Empire.

The lake's borders rest on colonial agreements. In 1954 a British and Portuguese agreement made the middle of the lake the boundary with Mozambique, except for Chizumulu and Likoma islands, now part of Malawi. Between Malawi and Tanzania both sides cite the Heligoland Treaty of 1890, and Tanzania protested officially in 1967.

The lake is known as Lake Malawi, Lake Nyasa in Tanzania and Lago Niassa in Mozambique. It is home to more species of fish than any other lake, including at least 700 species of cichlid. Part of it is included in Lake Malawi National Park at the southern end, and the portion in Mozambique was declared a reserve in 2011.
lake-manasarovar: Lake Manasarovar, also called Mapam Yumtso, lies near Mount Kailash in Burang County, Ngari Prefecture, at 4,586 metres, close to the western trijunction of China, India and Nepal. It is one of the highest freshwater lakes in Asia, set among mostly saline lakes on the Tibetan Plateau. Roughly round, it covers 320 square kilometres, has a circumference of 88 kilometres and a maximum depth of 100 metres. It overflows into the salt-water lake of Rakshastal through the Ganga Chhu channel, and the sources of the Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra and Karnali rivers lie in the region.

In Hindu literature the lake is named in the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, though no early Vedic text mentions it explicitly. In the Ramayana, Vishvamitra tells Rama that Brahma created the lake out of his consciousness, hence the name Manas Sarovar, and that the river Sarayu flowed from it past Ayodhya. Mount Kailash, on its banks, is held to be the abode of Shiva. Buddhists identify Kailash with Mount Meru, and tradition says Maya bathed in the lake before the Buddha was conceived.

For the Bon people the region was the centre of the ancient empire of Zhang Zhung, and Tonpa Shenrab, the founder of Bon, is said to have bathed in the lake. Vajrayana Buddhists believe that Milarepa (c. 1052 – c. 1135) held a contest with Naro Böncham, a follower of Bon, on its shore. Jains connect the area with Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara, who attained nirvana on Ashtapad Mountain.

Modern texts call the lake among the most sacred sites of several religions, yet early literature never explicitly names it as a pilgrimage site, and until the 1930s there is no evidence of temples or pilgrim facilities there. According to Luciano Petech, Tibetan records show the region regarded as sacred geography by the late 12th century, and the 13th-century Mahanirvana Tantra gives its first chapter to Kailash and Manasarovar. Pilgrimage grew in the 1930s. China permitted it after occupying Tibet in 1950–51, but access from India was restricted after 1959 and the borders were closed after the Sino-Indian War of 1962; pilgrimage from India resumed in 1981.

Pilgrims trek to the lake and make the kora, a circuit of the 53-kilometre path round Mount Kailash, clockwise for Hindus, Buddhists and Jains and counterclockwise for followers of Bon. Bathing in the lake is believed to cleanse sins. Stupas, flag poles, monasteries and praying stations stand on its banks, though many structures were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976.
lake-maracaibo: Lake Maracaibo lies in north-western Venezuela between the states of Zulia, Trujillo and Mérida. Its present hydrology may classify it better as an estuary or semi-enclosed bay connected to the Gulf of Venezuela by a narrow strait. With a surface area of 13,512 square kilometres it would be the largest lake in South America if counted as one, and it is said to be one of the oldest lakes on Earth, formed some 36 million years ago when faults collapsed as the Andes rose in the late Eocene.
It is about 210 kilometres long and 121 wide, and many rivers feed it, the largest being the Catatumbo. Above its southern part occur the almost silent flashes known as Catatumbo lightning.

The Añú people who lived on its banks call it Coquivacoa, and the Wayuu, Caquetíos and Quiriquires also lived in the area. When Amerigo Vespucci and the fleet of Alonso de Ojeda sailed there on 24 August 1499, the stilt houses of the Añú reminded Vespucci of Venice, and he named the region Veneziola, or Little Venice, from which the name Venezuela comes. Spain made two attempts to settle around the lake, in 1529 and 1569, but the city of Maracaibo was successfully founded only in 1574.

The privateer Henry Morgan raided settlements on the lake in the spring of 1669 and defeated a Spanish squadron sent to intercept him. On 24 July 1823 Venezuela won the Battle of Lake Maracaibo during its War of Independence.

The first Spaniards used tar seeping from the lake to caulk ships. The Maracaibo oil field was discovered in 1914, the first well was built in 1917, and large-scale exploitation began in 1922. Dredging in the 1930s deepened the lake's mouth from about 4 to 8 metres, and a breakwater finished in 1957 allowed ocean-going tankers to enter, which turned the northern part from fresh water to brackish.

The lake and the Catatumbo River are main routes for goods in the region, and the city of Maracaibo, capital of Zulia State, is an oil port and a transshipment centre for coffee from the Andes. Fishing families live in traditional stilt houses on the water. The General Rafael Urdaneta Bridge, 8,678 metres long, crosses the strait and was completed in 1962, at its inauguration the longest cable-stayed concrete bridge in the world.
lake-mweru: Lake Mweru lies on the border between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo and makes up 110 km of the length of the Congo, between its Luapula and Luvua segments. Mweru means lake in a number of Bantu languages. It is fed mainly by the Luapula, which enters through swamps from the south, and by the Kalungwishi, and drained at the north by the Luvua.

It is a rift valley lake, about 118 km long and 45 km wide on average, at an elevation of 917 m. It is shallow in the south and reaches 27 m in the north. Its level varies by only 1.7 m a year, because the Bangweulu Swamps absorb the annual flood and the Luvua flows swiftly.

Arab and Swahili traders in ivory, copper and slaves knew the lake and used Kilwa Island as a base. Their route ran from Zanzibar to Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika, then to Mweru and the Lunda, Luba, Yeke or Kazembe kingdoms, so that Mweru lay on a transcontinental trade route. Portuguese traders visited Kazembe between 1796 and 1831 but left no account of the lake. David Livingstone, who called it Moero, is credited with its discovery during his travels of 1867 and the following year; his reports of the slave trade helped rally opposition to it, though slave trading there lasted into the 1890s.

Wars between the Yeke king Msiri and neighbouring chiefs unsettled the area between 1870 and 1891. The Stairs Expedition of 1892 killed Msiri and took Katanga for King Leopold II of Belgium. The western shore became part of the Belgian Congo and the eastern shore part of Northern Rhodesia, where a British boma was set up at Chiengi in 1891. The Scottish missionary Dan Crawford founded the first mission station on the lake, at Luanza, in 1892. Zambia has 58 per cent of the lake's waters and the Democratic Republic of the Congo 42 per cent.

Many fishing villages, some of them seasonal camps, dot the shores. The main towns are Nchelenge, Kashikishi and Chiengi in Zambia and Kilwa, Lukonzolwa and Pweto in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The lake has long been noted for longfin tilapia, traditionally dried in the sun, and for catfish and tigerfish. Commercial fishing was pioneered in the first half of the 20th century by Greek fishermen from the Dodecanese islands who settled at Kasenga.
lake-nasser: Lake Nasser is one of the largest man-made lakes in the world. It is named after Gamal Abdel Nasser, the second president of Egypt. Strictly the name applies only to the larger part of the lake, which lies in Egyptian territory and makes up 83 percent of the total; the Sudanese prefer to call their smaller part Lake Nubia. The lake is about 16 km across at its widest point, near the Tropic of Cancer, covers 5,250 square kilometres and holds some 132 cubic kilometres of water. When the water is high enough the overflow empties westward into the Toshka Lakes.

Before the lake, the land it covers was a significant part of Nubia, home to several pharaohs of Egypt and to empires such as that of Kush. Construction of the Aswan High Dam began in 1960 at the wish of Nasser and was finished in 1970; President Anwar Sadat inaugurated the dam and lake in 1971. The dam replaced the insufficient Aswan Low Dam of 1902, and its aims were a more stable water supply, more agricultural production and electricity for Egypt. Sudan opposed the project beforehand because it would flood land in the north of the country where many Nubians lived and would have to be resettled.

Tens of thousands of Nubians were forced to leave their homes, and although some settled on the new shores, their original homes were lost. The flooding of the region also prompted the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia, led by UNESCO. The temples of Kalabsha, Wadi es-Sebua and Amada were saved and moved, and the temples at Abu Simbel were taken apart and rebuilt safely above the lake. Others, such as the fortress of Buhen, could not be rescued and lie under the water.

The lake gives Egypt irrigation water through the year in place of the seasonal floods of the Nile, and the country's arable land increased by about 30 percent. Damming the Nile has cut the supply of nutrients that the floods once brought downstream, so farmers use mineral fertilisers. The lake has 52 species of fish, among them tilapia, which make up most of the catch, and the Nile perch. The Aswan High Dam produces about 2.1 gigawatts of hydroelectricity. Cruises and the relocated monuments, above all Abu Simbel, draw visitors.
lake-neuchatel: Lake Neuchâtel lies mainly in Romandy, the French-speaking part of Switzerland, at the foot of the Jura mountains on the Swiss Plateau. It is shared by the cantons of Neuchâtel, Vaud, Fribourg and Bern and forms part of the Three Lakes Region with Lake Biel/Bienne and Lake Morat/Murten. It has a surface of 218.3 square kilometres, is 38.3 km long and 8.2 km at its widest, lies 429 metres above sea level and is at most 152 metres deep. It holds about 14.0 cubic kilometres of water and is the largest lake entirely within Switzerland, since Lake Geneva and Lake Constance are shared with neighbouring countries.

The lake is fed by the Orbe, the Arnon, the Areuse, the Seyon and the Menthue and by the Broye canal, and the Thielle canal drains it into Lake Biel. Since the Jura water correction of the 19th and 20th centuries, it has served with Lake Morat as a compensation basin for the waters of the Aare flowing into Lake Biel. The extinct deepwater trout Salvelinus neocomensis once lived in it.

Prehistoric people frequented the lake, as remains at Auvernier and in the Laténium archaeological museum show; bones of brown bear and Eurasian beaver were found there. Megalithic monuments line the shore, including the alignment of Clendy and the menhirs of Gorgier, Grandson, Saint-Aubin-Sauges and Vauroux. A Celtic settlement on pile-dwellings at La Tène gave its name to the second Iron Age. Mont Vully, a fortified area of about 50 hectares built around 120 BCE, controlled the lakes of Morat and Neuchâtel while the La Tène area stayed almost unoccupied. Yverdon, then Eburodunum, was settled from the 4th century BCE, fortified in 80 BCE, and became a vicus in the first centuries CE.

The first written mention of the lake dates from 998 CE, as the laci everdunensis, the lake of Yverdon, near which the priory of Bevaix was founded. That name dominated through the Middle Ages, and the name Lake Neuchâtel appears from the 15th century and became dominant in the 19th, with the lowering of the lake's level and the Vaudois railway, which reduced the importance of the Port of Yverdon.

Settlements on the north-western shore run from Yverdon-les-Bains through Grandson, Concise and Bevaix to Neuchâtel and Marin-Epagnier, and those on the south-eastern shore include Estavayer-le-Lac, Cudrefin and Gampelen. Neuchâtel became a popular tourist destination in the Belle Époque for its climate and its panoramic views of the Alps, and the lake's shore has seen significant economic development since the regional motorway network was completed.
lake-nicaragua: Lake Nicaragua, also called Cocibolca or Granada, is a freshwater lake of tectonic origin with an area of 8,264 square kilometres. It lies 32.7 metres above sea level and reaches a depth of 26 metres. Nicaraguans know it as Lago Cocibolca or Mar Dulce, literally the Sweet Sea, since agua dulce is Spanish for freshwater. It is slightly smaller than Lake Titicaca and is the nation's largest source of freshwater.

The lake receives the intermittent Tipitapa River when Lake Managua stands high, and drains by the San Juan River eastwards to the Caribbean Sea. Together these waters form the largest international drainage basin in Central America. Easterly winds raise sizeable waves, and the lake has a reputation for periodically powerful storms. It holds the volcanic islands of Ometepe and Zapatera and the Solentiname archipelago.

Because the San Juan River runs to the Caribbean, the city of Granada on the north-western shore was historically an Atlantic port, although both the city and the lake lie closer to the Pacific. The Pacific can be seen from the mountains of Ometepe, the largest island. The lake has a history of Caribbean pirates, who assaulted Granada on three occasions.

During the California Gold Rush of the late 1840s, the trip up the San Juan River, through the lake and across a short overland stretch was one of the two preferred routes between the Atlantic and the Pacific, the other crossing Panama. Before the Panama Canal was built, a stagecoach line owned by Cornelius Vanderbilt's Accessory Transit Company linked the lake with the Pacific across the low hills of the Isthmus of Rivas.

Plans for an interoceanic Nicaragua Canal along this route were made, but the Panama Canal was built instead. In the Bryan–Chamorro Treaty of 1916 the United States secured all rights to a canal along the route; the United States and Nicaragua rescinded the treaty by mutual agreement in 1970.

Boats remain the only way to reach the Solentiname archipelago. The lake holds sawfish, tarpon and sharks. Scientists first took the sharks for an endemic species, the Lake Nicaragua shark, but in 1961 it was identified with the widespread bull shark. They were presumed to be trapped, until the late 1960s, when it was found that they can leap up the rapids of the San Juan River almost like salmon. Bull sharks tagged in the lake have since been caught in the open ocean, some completing the journey in as little as seven days.
lake-ohrid: Lake Ohrid lies in a tectonic basin on the mountainous border between the south-west of North Macedonia and eastern Albania. It is the deepest lake in the Balkans, with a maximum depth of 288 metres, and covers 358 square kilometres. It is 30.4 kilometres long and 14.8 kilometres wide; 64 per cent of the shore and 69 per cent of the surface lie in North Macedonia and the rest in Albania. Together with Lake Prespa it belongs to a chain of grabens known as the Dessaret group. The oldest lake sediments are Pliocene, possibly 3 to 5 million years old. Ohrid survives through its depth, continuing subsidence and inflows from Lake Prespa that carry little sediment.

The prehistoric pile-dwelling near Lin, at Pogradec in Albania, is the oldest of its kind in Europe, according to specialists at the University of Bern. The settlement is over 8,500 years old, and it developed agriculture 8,000 to 9,000 years ago, playing a part in spreading farming across Europe.
