It predates similar Swiss sites by more than 2,000 years. Archaeologists have excavated the remains.

The lake lay close to the Via Egnatia, a main highway of the Roman Empire running from Durrës on the Albanian coast to Constantinople. Religious monuments such as the Black Madonna south-west of Struga stand beside the traces of later wars, such as the fortifications of the Macedonian Front across Mount Galičica. The strongest earthquake measured in the area struck on 18 February 1911, with a magnitude of 6.6, and destroyed houses without loss of life.

The towns on the shore are Ohrid and Struga in North Macedonia and Pogradec in Albania. The Macedonian side of the lake was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, and in 1980 the site was extended to the cultural and historic area of Ohrid, making it a mixed natural and cultural site. The Albanian side was added in 2019. The lake has more than 200 endemic species, including the Ohrid trout complex, and almost 80 per cent of its mollusc species are endemic. The Macedonian and Albanian parts are each an Important Bird Area, and the lakeshore wetlands shelter hundreds of thousands of wintering water birds.
lake-okeechobee: Lake Okeechobee covers about 1,900 square kilometres and is exceptionally shallow for its size, with an average depth of about 2.7 metres. Its name comes from the Hitchiti words oki, water, and chubi, big. The Kissimmee River, which enters from the north, is its largest source, providing more than 60 per cent of its inflow. The lake sits in a shallow trough that also underlies the Kissimmee River valley and the Everglades. Until about 6,000 years ago the trough was dry land, and as sea level and the water table rose, wetlands built up peat that eventually formed a natural dam along the southern edge until the lake overflowed into the Everglades.

Occupation of the area around the lake probably began about 1000 BCE with the Belle Glade culture, which lasted until about 1700 CE and left many large mounds and other earthworks. In the 16th century Hernando de Escalante Fontaneda reported a lake in southern Florida called Mayaimi, meaning big water, and said that towns around it were subject to the Calusa of the southwest coast. In the early 19th century the lake was known as Mayacco Lake or Lake Mayaca, after the Mayaca people who had moved near it in the early 18th century. The Battle of Lake Okeechobee was fought on its northern shore in 1837 during the Seminole Wars.

Florida's legislature created the Everglades Drainage District in 1905 and 1907 to lower the lake and drain the Everglades, and canals were completed by 1917. A levee 47 miles long was begun around the southern side in 1921. On 26 September 1926 the Great Miami Hurricane collapsed the levee on the western side and killed approximately 300 people in the Moore Haven area. The levee was being raised when the 1928 Okeechobee hurricane reached the lake on 17 September 1928, pushing its level to 29.6 feet above sea level and overtopping the levee. The Red Cross reported 1,836 deaths, a figure revised in 2003 to at least 2,500.

After President Herbert Hoover visited the area, the United States Army Corps of Engineers designed channels, gates and nearly 140 miles of levees, creating the Herbert Hoover Dike. The Okeechobee Waterway, completed in 1937, crossed the lake with two dredged channels. After two hurricanes in 1947 flooded parts of southern Florida for months, the Corps began the Central and South Florida Flood Control Project in 1948.

The lake is the largest freshwater lake in Florida and the headwaters of the Everglades. Its water is divided among five counties, Glades, Okeechobee, Martin, Palm Beach and Hendry, which meet at one point near its centre. Its uses include flood control, navigation, water supply and recreation, and the dike carries the Lake Okeechobee Scenic Trail, part of the Florida National Scenic Trail.
lake-peipus: Lake Peipus is the largest trans-boundary lake in Europe and the fifth-largest lake in Europe, after Lake Ladoga, Lake Onega, Lake Vänern and Lake Saimaa. It covers 3,555 square kilometres and has an average depth of 7.1 metres, the deepest point being about 15 metres. It consists of three parts: the northern Lake Peipus proper, which holds 73 per cent of the area, the southern Lake Pskov, and the sound called Warm Lake that connects them. About 30 rivers and streams flow into it, the largest being the Velikaya and the Emajõgi, and it drains into the Gulf of Finland through the Narva River.

The origin of the name Peipus is uncertain. The Russian name, Chudskoye ozero, means Chud Lake; the ethnonym Chud referred to various Finnic peoples in what is now Estonia, Karelia and north-western Russia. The lake is a remnant of a larger body of water left by the last glaciation, the Weichselian, which ended about 12,000 years ago. It freezes from late November or December and thaws in April or early May.

On 5 April 1242 the frozen southern part of the lake was the site of the Battle on the Ice, also called the Battle of Lake Peipus, in which Novgorod troops led by Alexander Nevsky defeated an army of crusading knights. The battle was unusual in being mostly fought on the frozen surface of the lake.

The largest city on the lake, Pskov, stands on the Velikaya River about 10 kilometres from the shore. It is one of the oldest cities in Russia, known since at least 903 from a record in the Primary Chronicle of the Laurentian Codex. It kept a certain independence while dominated by its neighbours Novgorod, Lithuania and Muscovy, and was eventually incorporated into the Russian state. Its monuments include the Mirozhsky Monastery, founded in 1156 and holding frescoes of the 14th to 17th centuries, and the Pskov Kremlin, of the 14th to 17th centuries.

Gdov was founded in 1431 as a fortress and became a city in 1780. Kallaste, on the Estonian shore, was founded in the 18th century by Old Believers who had fled from the Novgorod area, and it still has a Russian Orthodox Old-Rite church.

The lake is used for fishing, navigation and recreation. Its shallow shores are lined with marshes that flood in spring, and its 29 islands include Kolpina, Piirissaar and Kamenka. It is a stopover for migrating swans, geese and ducks, among them Bewick's swan.
lake-poyang: Poyang Lake lies within Jiujiang Prefecture in Jiangxi Province. It is fed by the Gan, Xin and Xiu rivers and flows northward into the Yangtze through a channel. In a normal year its area averages 3,500 square kilometres, but it fluctuates dramatically between the wet and dry seasons. It provides a habitat for half a million migratory birds, and in winter it is home to many Siberian cranes, as much as 90 per cent of the world's population of this critically endangered species.

The lake was historically also called Pengli Lake, though the two are not the same. Before the Han dynasty the Yangtze followed a more northerly course through what is now Longgan Lake, and the area of Poyang Lake was a plain along the Gan River, with the Pengli Marsh at the river's lower reaches. Around 400 CE the Yangtze switched to a more southerly course, causing the Gan to back up and form the lake.

It flooded Poyang County, from which it takes its name, and Haihun County, forcing a mass migration to Wucheng Township, in what is now Yongxiu County. This gave rise to the Chinese idiom that drowning Haihun County gave rise to Wucheng Township. Poyang itself was named for Po County of the Qin dynasty, which took its name from the city of Poyi in the state of Chu.

The lake reached its largest extent during the Tang dynasty, when its area reached 6,000 square kilometres. In 1363 it was the scene of the Battle of Lake Poyang, which is claimed to be the largest naval battle in history.

The lake's area has been decreasing overall in recent years, and in early 2012 drought, sand quarrying and the storing of water at the Three Gorges Dam lowered it to about 200 square kilometres. A fishing ban has been in place since 2002. The finless porpoise, known locally as the jiangzhu, lives in the lake and in Dongting Lake, and its numbers have fallen.
lake-prespa: Lake Prespa lies at the tripoint of North Macedonia, Albania and Greece, at an elevation of 853 metres, and the two lakes are the highest tectonic lakes in the Balkans. The Great Prespa Lake covers 259 square kilometres, of which 176.3 belong to North Macedonia, 46.3 to Albania and 36.4 to Greece. The Little Prespa Lake to the south covers 46.8 square kilometres, mostly in Greece, with its westernmost tip of 4.3 in Albania. A 4-kilometre isthmus, 500 metres wide, on Greek territory separates them. It carries an embankment and a road to the village of Psarades, and a short canal links the lakes at its western side.

The Great Prespa sits in limestone country about 150 metres above Lake Ohrid, which lies about 10 kilometres to the west. Its only outlets are underground channels in the karst, which emerge as springs feeding streams that run into Lake Ohrid.

In Classical times the region formed part of ancient Lynkestis, and the lakes were called Little and Great Brygeis. In the 10th century Tsar Samuel built a fortress and a church of St Achillius on the island of Agios Achillios in the Small Prespa Lake, on the Greek side. The largest island of the Great Prespa, Golem Grad in North Macedonia, and Mal Grad in Albania, the site of a ruined 14th-century monastery of St Peter, are both uninhabited today.

The Greek part of the region was for many years underpopulated and militarily sensitive, and outsiders needed special permission to visit. It saw fierce fighting during the Greek Civil War, and much of the local population then emigrated to escape poverty and political strife. In the 1970s the Albanian communist regime diverted the Devoll River, which fed the Little Prespa, to irrigate farmland around Korçë, which contributed to the shrinking of the lake's surface. On 17 June 2018 the Prespa Agreement, renaming the Republic of Macedonia as North Macedonia, was signed at Psarades.

The area holds three national parks: Galičica National Park in North Macedonia and Prespa National Park in both Albania and Greece. The largest town of the region is Resen in North Macedonia. In 2014 the Ohrid-Prespa Transboundary Biosphere Reserve between Albania and North Macedonia was added to UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves, and the area was declared a Transnational Park in 2000. Of the 11 native fish species of the lake, nine are endemic.
lake-sevan: Lake Sevan lies in Gegharkunik Province, one of the largest freshwater alpine lakes in Eurasia and, with Lake Van and Lake Urmia, one of the three great seas of historic Armenia. It is the only one of the three within the present-day Republic of Armenia. Twenty-eight rivers and streams feed it, and the Hrazdan River drains about 10 per cent of the incoming water while the remaining 90 per cent evaporates. Tectonic movement in the early Quaternary formed a Palaeo-Sevan ten times larger than the present lake; the current lake formed some 25 to 30 thousand years ago.

In Medieval Armenia, Sevan was the name of the lake's major island and its monastery. The early medieval name was the Sea of Gegham, and in classical antiquity it was called Lychnitis. A scholarly explanation derives Sevan from the Urartian word suinia, usually translated as lake, which is attested on an 8th-century BCE inscription of King Rusa I at Odzaberd, on the southern shore.

Chardin, writing in 1673, noted the extraordinary sweetness of the water, a monastery on a small island in the middle whose prior was an archbishop, and nine sorts of fish. The naturalist Friedrich Parrot, who climbed Mount Ararat in 1829, wrote that all Armenians held the lake sacred on account of the old religious houses on its shores.

In the 19th century Sevan was seen as a major potential water resource, its height above the fertile Ararat plain attracting engineers. In a booklet of 1910 the Armenian engineer Sukias Manasserian proposed using its water for irrigation and hydroelectric power by draining the lake by 50 metres. The Soviet authorities adopted the proposal in the 1930s under Joseph Stalin, and work began in 1933. A tunnel was bored about 40 metres under the lake's surface. Finished in 1949, it let the level fall by more than one metre a year, supplying irrigation and the Sevan–Hrazdan Cascade of six hydroelectric stations on the Hrazdan.

By 2002 the level had dropped by 19.88 metres and the volume had fallen by 43.8 per cent, from 58.5 to 32.9 cubic kilometres. Before this the lake covered 1,416 square kilometres; it now covers 1,242. The fall left Sevan Island a peninsula, the site of the medieval monastery of Sevanavank. The lake provides some 90 per cent of Armenia's fish and 80 per cent of its crayfish catch.
lake-skadar: Lake Skadar lies on the border of Albania and Montenegro and is the largest lake in Southern Europe. Its surface area varies seasonally between 370 and 530 square kilometres, and it is about 44 km long, extending from the north-west to the south-east. About 65 per cent of the surface belongs to Montenegro and about 35 per cent to Albania.

It is a karst lake and a cryptodepression, filled mainly by the river Morača, which supplies about 62 per cent of its water. The Buna River, 41 km long, drains it into the Adriatic Sea, and the Drin River links it with Lake Ohrid. More than 200 karst springs, many beneath the surface, also feed it.

The southern and southwestern shores are rocky, barren and steep, while the north has a large inundated area whose boundaries change with the water level. Small islands include Beška, with two churches, and Grmožur, a former fortress and prison.

Geologists think the basin is of tectonic origin, formed by folding and faulting during the Cenozoic. In the Miocene and Pliocene the sea covered the Zeta Plain as far as Podgorica, and the connection of the lake with the sea was interrupted during the younger Pliocene. The origin of its waters is of particular interest to biologists, since they may have provided its first species and the basis of its present high degree of endemism. In the Second World War the steamboat Skanderbeg was sunk by partisans in 1942 near the mouth of Rijeka Crnojevića, and its wreck lies well preserved 11 metres below the surface.

The Montenegrin part of the lake and its surroundings became a national park in 1983, the Albanian part is a managed nature reserve, and the lake was added to the Ramsar list of wetlands of international importance in 1996. It is one of the largest bird reserves in Europe, with 270 bird species, among them some of the last pelicans in Europe. Of its 34 native fish species, seven are endemic. About 31 per cent of its freshwater snails are endemic, and the lake is a centre of the evolution of the snail genus Bithynia.
lake-starnberg: Lake Starnberg lies in southern Bavaria, 25 kilometres south-west of Munich, in a glacial hollow created by ice age glaciers from the Alps. It extends 19.45 kilometres from north to south and is 3 to 5 kilometres wide. It has a single small island, the Roseninsel, and a single outlet, the Würm river. Its main inflow is a small river, the Steinbach or Ostersee-Ach, which runs through a chain of small lakes to the south. Bronze fish-hooks and a dugout dating to the 9th or 8th century BCE have been found at the lake, and some professional fishers still continue a family tradition.

The earliest surviving mention of the lake, as Uuirmseo, is in a document of 818 referring to Holzhausen, now part of Münsing. The name became Wirmsee, already recorded under the Holy Roman Emperor Louis the Bavarian (1314–1347), and was taken from the river Wirm, now spelt Würm. In the late 19th century a railway connection between Munich and Starnberg made the lake an accessible excursion from the city, and it came increasingly to be called Lake Starnberg; the name Würmsee was officially changed in 1962. Passenger ferries and excursion ships have operated on the lake since 1851.

Because of its ties to the Wittelsbach royal family the lake is also called Fürstensee, the Prince's Lake. On the Roseninsel stands a royal villa of Ludwig II. The small town of Berg is known as the place where King Ludwig II of Bavaria was found dead in the lake in 1886.

The lake and its surroundings lie in three Bavarian districts, and the lake belongs to the state. It is a popular recreation area for Munich and has been protected as a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention since 1976. A path of about 49 kilometres allows walkers and cyclists to go round it, although much of the shore is private. Among the settlements on its shores are Starnberg, Berg, Münsing, Seeshaupt, Bernried, Tutzing, Feldafing and Pöcking. The lake is mentioned in T. S. Eliot's poem The Waste Land.
lake-tana: Lake Tana lies in the Amhara Region of the north-western Ethiopian Highlands, at an elevation of 1,788 metres. It is about 84 kilometres long and 66 kilometres wide, with a maximum depth of 15 metres, and its surface area ranges from 3,000 to 3,500 square kilometres depending on season and rainfall. Volcanic activity blocked the flow of the inflowing rivers in the early Pleistocene, about 5 million years ago, and the lake was originally much larger. Seven large permanent rivers and 40 small seasonal ones feed it, the main ones being the Gilgel Abay, Megech, Gumara and Rib.

The lake discharges into the Blue Nile, whose flow to the Blue Nile Falls (Tis Abbai) is controlled by a weir. Its level rises and falls by 2 to 2.5 metres in a year, peaking in September and October, and the surrounding plains often flood.

The lake's islands hold monasteries that keep the remains of ancient Ethiopian emperors and the treasures of Ethiopian Christianity. The monasteries are believed to have been built in the Middle Ages over earlier religious sites. They include the fourteenth-century Debre Maryam and the eighteenth-century Narga Selassie. Yekuno Amlak is buried in the monastery of St. Stephen on Daga Island, where the tombs of Dawit I, Zara Yaqob, Za Dengel and Fasilides also lie. Tana Qirqos is said to have housed the Ark of the Covenant before it was moved to Axum, and tradition holds that Frumentius, who introduced Christianity to Ethiopia, is buried there.

Travellers counted the islands differently as the lake level changed. The Portuguese missionary Manuel de Almeida, in the early 17th century, reported 21 islands, seven or eight with monasteries. James Bruce in 1771 heard of 45 inhabited islands but thought the true number nearer eleven. Anton Stecker examined the lake in 1881 and counted 44, and a 20th-century geographer named 37, of which he believed 19 have or had monasteries or churches. The lake has fallen about 1.8 metres in 400 years. Before their emigration to Israel, the Beta Israel lived around the lake, where the only Jewish monasteries in the world stood.

The area around the lake has long been associated with the Gondar and Begemder region. Gorgora on the northern shore and the Zege Peninsula, site of the Azwa Maryam monastery, are historic religious centres, and a ferry links Bahir Dar with Gorgora via Dek and lakeshore villages. Its fisheries, based on Labeobarbus barbs, Nile tilapia and sharptooth catfish, are a major local industry.
lake-tanganyika: Lake Tanganyika is an African Great Lake and the world's longest freshwater lake. It is the second largest freshwater lake by volume and the second deepest, after Lake Baikal. It extends 676 km north to south, covers 32,000 square kilometres and has a mean depth of 572 m and a maximum depth of 1,471 m. It lies in the Albertine Rift and is shared among Tanzania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi and Zambia. It is one of only twenty lakes more than a million years old.

The one major outflow, the Lukuga River, runs into the Congo system, and in the past the lake has rarely had an outflow to the sea. Its deeper waters hold no oxygen, which limits fish to the upper layers. It has at least 250 endemic species of cichlid fishes and supports a major fishery.

In the mid-19th century Swahili Arab traders from Zanzibar established a caravan route from Bagamoyo through Tabora to Ujiji on the lake. They brought sailing dhows and traded in slaves, ivory, guns and cotton, and Tippu Tip established a state west of the lake. The British explorers Richard Burton and John Speke, searching for the source of the Nile, were the first known Westerners to reach it, in 1858. David Livingstone visited it several times in 1866-73 and met Henry Morton Stanley at Ujiji in 1871. Britain, Germany and King Leopold of Belgium established colonies on the lake in the late 19th century and in the early 20th ended the slave trade.

During the First World War the Germans, with the ship Graf Goetzen, held complete control of the lake early on. Lieutenant Commander Geoffrey Spicer-Simson of the Royal Navy brought two armed motor boats, HMS Mimi and HMS Toutou, from England by rail, road and river to Albertville, now Kalemie. In December 1915 they captured the gunboat Kingani, and the Hedwig was sunk in February 1916. The Goetzen was scuttled on 26 July 1916, raised in 1924 and renamed MV Liemba.
lake-texcoco: Lake Texcoco was a natural saline lake in the Valley of Mexico, a closed basin in the southern highlands of the central altiplano at an average elevation of 2,236 metres. It lay across the southern half of the basin and was the largest of a chain of five major lakes, the others being Xaltocan, Zumpango, Chalco and Xochimilco. It was the lowest-lying of them, so that water ultimately drained towards it. Fresh water came from the springs of Chalco and Xochimilco, while thermal springs at Zumpango, Xaltocan and Texcoco itself supplied saline water. After the rainy season the lakes were often joined as one body of water, and in dry winters they separated.

The lake reached its maximum extent about 11,000 years ago, at about 5,670 square kilometres and over 150 metres deep, and shrank as the climate warmed. The remains of seven Columbian mammoths found there suggest human presence. Agriculture began around the lake about 7,000 years ago, and by 1250 BCE the Tlatilco culture had more complex settlements. Cuicuilco was the major power in the valley until the Xitle volcano destroyed it around 30 CE. After the fall of Teotihuacan city-states such as Azcapotzalco, Tlacopan and Culhuacán coexisted for centuries, remembered in Aztec chronicles as a golden age. By 1300 the Tepanec of Azcapotzalco had begun to dominate.

According to tradition the Mexica wandered for a hundred years before reaching the valley. Tenochtitlan was founded on an islet in the western part of the lake in 1325, and the Aztecs enlarged it into an artificial island using a method like that of chinampas. They built dams to separate salt water from the fresh water of the streams and to control the lake's level. The ruler Ahuitzotl's aqueduct to bring fresh water failed, and a flood struck the city in 1502.

Cortés destroyed the dams in his siege of 1521 and they were never rebuilt, so the new Mexico City suffered floods, including those of 1604 and 1607 and one in 1629 that covered most of the city for five years. Enrico Martínez directed a drain, and the lake was eventually drained by channels and a tunnel to the Pánuco River. The Drenaje Profundo, a deep drainage system of tunnels, was completed in 1967. The basin is now almost completely occupied by Mexico City. The name Texcoco Lake now refers only to an area of salt marshes about 4 km east of the city. The axolotl and other native species have become endangered or extinct.
lake-trasimeno: Lake Trasimeno covers 128 square kilometres in the province of Perugia, on the border between Umbria and Tuscany. Only two minor streams flow directly into it and none flows out, and its level changes considerably with rainfall and with the seasonal demands of the towns, villages and farms on its shore. It is shallow, muddy and rich in fish such as pike, carp and tench, with an average depth of about 5 metres.

The lake has no natural outlet above ground. The Romans dug an artificial drainage tunnel in the San Savino area, which was restored in the Renaissance, and a modern canal, the Emissario del Trasimeno, was built in 1898. The shallow water favoured malarial mosquitoes, and a proposal to drain the lake was rejected; the channel near San Feliciano, built at the end of the 19th century, evened out the level changes and eased the malaria.

The lake environment dates back to the Middle Pleistocene, and in prehistoric times the lake extended almost to Perugia, which is why it was historically known as the Lake of Perugia. Trasimene is also the name of a mythological figure, joined to Agilla, a nymph born in Agello, a hill that was formerly an island in the lake. The first civilisation in the area was that of the Etruscans, and three of their main cities, Perugia, Chiusi and Cortona, lie within 20 kilometres of the lake. Little physical evidence of Etruscan or Roman settlement remains, but Castiglione del Lago has Roman ruins and main streets laid out like a chessboard in the Roman style.

The Battle of Lake Trasimene took place on the northern shore in June 217 BCE, during the Second Punic War. Its exact location is unknown because the lake then extended further north; it was fought in the territory of Tuoro sul Trasimeno, near the hills overlooking the lake. Place names near Cortona recall it: Ossaia, from the Italian for ossuary, and Sanguineto, probably meaning a bloody place.

A natural park was established over the whole lake surface and its shores in 1995, and a 50-kilometre bicycle path around the lake opened in 2003. Half the lake is ringed by hills rich in olives, and the western shore near Tuscany has vineyards and fruit and vegetable growing. Castiglione del Lago has the longest shore, as it stands on the only significant peninsula, which may once have been an island joined to the shore by the Romans. The lake has 19 fish species, 15 of them introduced, and goldfish, introduced in 1988, are now the commonest.
lake-urmia: Lake Urmia is an endorheic salt lake in the Iranian region of Azerbaijan, near the Armenian border and south of the Caspian Sea. At its fullest extent it was the largest lake in West Asia, with a surface area of about 6,000 square kilometres, a length of 140 kilometres, a width of 70 kilometres and a maximum depth of 20 metres. It is fed by 13 permanent rivers and many small springs, and almost half its inflow comes from the Zarrineh and Simineh rivers. It has no outflow, and water is lost only by evaporation. Its salt content once reached roughly four times that of seawater.

The name has been explained in several ways. Richard Nelson Frye proposed an Urartian origin, while T. Burrow linked it to Indo-Iranian words for wave. A more likely derivation is from Neo-Aramaic, ur for city and mia for water, after the nearby city of Urmia. The Old Persian name was Chichast, meaning glittering, after the mineral particles in the water. The Greeks called it Spauta, and the traditional Armenian name, Kaputan tsov, means blue sea.

Yanik Tepe on the east shore has been settled since about 6000 BCE, and a large group of sites south of the lake includes Dalma Tepe, Teppe Hasanlu, Geoy Tepe and Hajji Firuz Tepe. The Se Girdan kurgans on the south shore have been redated to the second half of the 4th millennium BCE. Assyrian records of the reign of Shalmaneser III (858 to 824 BCE) are among the early mentions of the lake. They name Parsuwaš, the Persians, and Matai, the Medes, in its area. Shahi Island, the largest of its islands, is the burial place of Hulagu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, and of his son Abaqa, who were buried in a castle above cliffs on the shore.

In the last five hundred years the area has been home to Azerbaijanis, Kurds, Persians, Assyrians and Armenians. The Assyrians of Urmia speak Northeastern Neo-Aramaic dialects and belong to the East Syriac churches and to Protestantism. The lake and its roughly 102 former islands are protected as a national park, and it is both a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and a Ramsar site. A causeway and the Urmia Lake Bridge, completed in 2008, now divide it into northern and southern halves. Through drought, the damming of its rivers and the pumping of groundwater, the lake had shrunk to about a tenth of its former size by late 2017.
lake-van: Lake Van lies in eastern Anatolia, in the provinces of Van and Bitlis, in the Armenian highlands, at 1,640 metres above sea level. It covers 3,755 square kilometres and is 119 kilometres across at its widest. Its average depth is 171 metres. The water is strongly alkaline and rich in sodium carbonate, and its salinity usually keeps it from freezing. The lake has no outlet. A volcanic eruption blocked its original outlet in prehistoric times, and the lake is primarily tectonic, formed more than 600,000 years ago by the subsidence of a block of crust along faults. The stratovolcano Mount Süphan stands on the northern shore, and the dormant volcano Mount Nemrut close to the western tip.

The lake was the centre of the kingdom of Urartu from about 1000 BCE, afterwards of the Satrapy of Armenia, the Kingdom of Greater Armenia and the Armenian Kingdom of Vaspurakan. Tushpa, the capital of Urartu, stood near the shore, on the site of what became the castle of medieval Van. Assyrian sources called the lake the Upper Sea of Nairi, with Lake Urmia the Lower Sea. Greek-speaking Byzantines called it Thospitis limne.

In the 11th century the lake lay on the border between the Eastern Roman Empire and the Seljuk Empire. Emperor Romanus IV Diogenes was defeated and captured at the Battle of Manzikert, north of the lake, on 26 August 1071. Alp Arslan divided the conquered lands among his Turcoman generals, and gave the region around the lake to Sökmen el-Kutbî, who made Ahlat his capital. The Shah-Armens, also called Sökmenler, ruled the area from 1085 to 1192 and were succeeded by the Ayyubid dynasty. The Ilkhanate Mongols later took the region, and it passed between the Ottoman Empire and Safavid Iran until Sultan Selim I took control for good.

The lake is the largest in Turkey. Its shores are surrounded by fruit orchards and grain fields, and the region is known for the Van cat breed. On Akdamar Island stands the 10th-century Cathedral of the Holy Cross, the royal church of the kingdom of Vaspurakan, and the other three main islands also have Armenian religious buildings. The Ahlatshahs left a large number of headstones near Ahlat, tentatively listed for World Heritage status. A train ferry crosses the lake between Tatvan and Van. According to legend a monster lives in it, but there is no evidence of one.
lake-vanern: Vänern covers 5,655 square kilometres and its surface lies 44 metres above sea level. Its maximum depth is 106 metres and its average depth 27 metres, so the lake floor is above sea level on average, although the deepest part of the basin lies 62 metres below it.

The lake is divided between the provinces of Västergötland, Dalsland and Värmland, on the border between Götaland and Svealand. The main inflow is the Klarälven, which enters near Karlstad on the northern shore and rises in Trøndelag in Norway. Other tributaries include the Gullspångsälven, Byälven and Norsälven. The Göta älv drains the lake to the south-west towards Gothenburg and the Kattegat.

The lake reached its present form after the Quaternary glaciation, about 10,000 years ago. When the ice melted, water covered the whole width of Sweden. Once post-glacial rebound outpaced the rise in sea level, Vänern became part of the Ancylus Lake that occupied the Baltic basin, joined to it by a strait at Degerfors in Värmland. Further uplift cut it off from the Baltic, and the amphipod Monoporeia affinis, a species not normally found in freshwater lakes, survives in it as a result of that old connection.

The Icelandic mythographer Snorri Sturluson told in the Prose Edda how the woman Gefjon, whom the Swedish king Gylfi had promised as much land as four oxen could plough, uprooted the land and dragged it into the sea, where it became the island of Zealand. He placed the story at Mälaren, but since the inlets of the lake match the headlands of Zealand much better at Vänern, the tale was probably first told of Vänern. The Battle on the Ice of Lake Vänern, recorded in the Norse sagas and referred to in the Old English poem Beowulf, was fought in the 6th century.

The Göta Canal, built in the 19th century, links the Göta älv waterway with Lake Vättern and the east coast. The lake's level is regulated by the Vargön Hydroelectric Power Station. Towns around its shores, among them Lidköping (chartered in 1446), Mariestad (1583), Karlstad (1584), Kristinehamn (1642), Åmål (1643) and Vänersborg (1644), have supported themselves for centuries by fishing and easy transport. The Djurö archipelago in the middle of the lake is a national park.
lake-vattern: Vättern is the second-largest lake in Sweden, after Vänern, and the sixth-largest in Europe. It is a long, finger-shaped body of fresh water in south-central Sweden, south-east of Vänern. The lake is relatively deep, holding about half as much water as Vänern despite having only about a third of its surface area. Its surface area is about 1,912 square kilometres, its average depth 41 metres and its deepest point, south of the island of Visingsö, 128 metres. Its name is closely related to the Swedish word vatten, water. It lies in Götaland and is bounded by the provinces of Västergötland, Närke, Östergötland and Småland. Towns on its shores include Jönköping, Vadstena, Hjo, Askersund, Karlsborg and Motala, where the lake drains into Motala ström.

Vättern formed by tectonics as a graben 700 to 800 million years ago, in the Neoproterozoic, unlike many smaller lakes of southern Sweden, which came from glacial stripping. The present-day lake began as an independent body of water left by the receding Scandinavian glacier around 10,000 years ago, and for a time was a minor bay of the Baltic ice lake. Most of its relict species, like the Arctic char, date from that time. About 8000 years ago the uneven land rise of Scandinavia lifted Vättern above the Ancylus Lake and the two became distinct. Since 1832 the lake has also had a downstream connection through the Göta Canal to Vänern and the Kattegat.

Catholic tradition holds that Saint Catherine of Vadstena performed a miracle involving three people in peril on the lake ice. Thomas Nashe mentioned the lake, as Lake Vether, in Terrors of the Night, published in 1594, although he mistakenly placed it in Iceland. On the night of 19 November 1918 the steamer Per Brahe sank in bad weather on the lake, and the artist John Bauer, his wife Ester and their three-year-old son Bengt drowned.

Many municipalities in the area draw their drinking water directly from the lake, which needs very little treatment. Vättern is noted for fishing, serving people in the nearby districts, and is known for its Vättern char. The annual cycling race Vätternrundan covers 300 kilometres around the shores. About 62 per cent of the drainage basin is covered with forest and 26.7 per cent is used for agriculture.
lake-victoria: Lake Victoria is one of the African Great Lakes. It covers about 59,947 square kilometres and is the world's largest tropical lake and the second-largest fresh water lake by surface area after Lake Superior. It lies in a shallow depression, with an average depth of 40 metres and a maximum of about 80 metres, and its catchment area covers 169,858 square kilometres. Tanzania holds 49 per cent of the lake, Uganda 45 per cent and Kenya 6 per cent.

The lake receives 80 per cent of its water from direct rainfall, the rest from rivers and streams, the largest of which is the Kagera River on the western shore. Its only outflow is the Nile River near Jinja, Uganda. One account puts the lake's age at about 400,000 years: it formed as westward-flowing rivers were backed up when a block of the Earth's crust tilted along the Great Rift Valley. Its shores are home to haplochromine cichlids, of which more than 500 species are almost all found nowhere else.

The first recorded information about the lake comes from Arab traders who travelled the inland routes in search of gold, ivory, other goods and slaves. Many African peoples lived in the catchment area. The explorer John Hanning Speke, travelling with Richard Francis Burton, was the first European to see it, reaching its southern shore in 1858. He named it after Queen Victoria and believed he had found the source of the Nile.

Burton, who was recovering from illness at Kazeh, near present-day Tabora, rejected the claim as unproven. A very public quarrel followed, which provoked debate among scientists and drew other explorers to confirm or refute Speke's view. In 1952 engineers acting for the government of colonial Uganda blasted out the natural rock weir at Jinja, which had controlled the outflow for at least 12,000 years, and replaced it with a barrage. Uganda later added the Kiira Hydroelectric Power Station, completed in 2002.

The lake supports Africa's largest inland fishery. Nile perch and several tilapias were introduced in the 1950s, and the Nile perch in particular is blamed for the extinction of many native cichlids; the loss has been called the most dramatic example of human-caused extinctions within an ecosystem. Kisumu, Kampala, Entebbe, Jinja, Mwanza and Bukoba are among the towns and cities on or near the shore. Ferries have been an important means of transport between Uganda, Tanzania and Kenya since the 1900s, and the main ports are Kisumu, Mwanza, Bukoba, Entebbe, Port Bell and Jinja.
lake-zug: Lake Zug lies between Lake Lucerne and Lake Zurich and stretches for 14 kilometres between Arth and the Cham-Zug bay. The Lorze, its main feeder river, empties into the lake at its northern extremity, and about a kilometre further west leaves it to flow towards the Reuss. A second river, the Rigiaa, feeds only a marginal amount at the southern end. About 10 square kilometres at the southern end lie in the canton of Schwyz, and the canton of Lucerne claims about 2 square kilometres north of Immensee.

Towards the south-western end the Rigi descends steeply to the water's edge, and its summit, at 1,798 metres, is the highest point of the lake's drainage basin. Part of the eastern shore forms a narrow level band at the foot of the Rossberg, 1,583 metres high, and the Zugerberg. The northern shores are nearly level, and on the western shore the wooded promontory of Buonas, with its old and new castles, projects into the water. The principal place on the lake is the town of Zug, and the shore settlements include Arth, Cham, Immensee, Risch and Walchwil.

The first steamer was placed on the lake in 1852. In the early 20th century a railway that was formerly part of the St. Gotthard main route ran along the eastern shore past Walchwil to Arth, which was connected at first by a steam tramway with the Arth-Goldau station. Another line runs from Arth along the western shore to Immensee, where it turns south-west to Lucerne. From Immensee a further railway leads to Cham, 5 kilometres west of Zug. Three railways thus follow the shore, connecting Zürich, Zug, Lucerne and the St. Gotthard line.

Many fish, including pike and carp of considerable weights, are taken in the lake, which is known for an endemic kind of trout called Rolheli locally. Because the lake is poorly fed, pollution would cause lasting damage, and a great part of the fauna of its deep parts has already been lost. Public transport on the water is run by the Zugersee Schifffahrt.
lake-zurich: Lake Zürich is a glacial lake formed by the Rhine-Linth glacier. Its main tributary, the Linth, rises in the glaciers of the Glarus Alps. The Linth originally flowed directly into the lake, but the Escher canal, completed in 1811, diverted it into Lake Walen, from which the straightened Linth Canal, completed in 1816, carries its waters to the east end of the lake near Schmerikon. Until the early 16th century another lake, Lake Tuggen, lay upstream. Water leaves the lake at its north-western end and passes through the city of Zürich as the Limmat, a tributary of the Aare.

Nine prehistoric pile dwellings stand on the lakeshore in the cantons of Schwyz, St. Gallen and Zürich, among them Freienbach-Hurden Rosshorn, Meilen-Rorenhaab and Zürich-Enge Alpenquai. They are part of the 56 prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps that form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Because the lake has grown over time, the original piles now lie 4 to 7 metres below the water level of 406 metres. In Kempraten, in what is now Rapperswil-Jona, there was a Roman vicus named Centum Prata, and Turicum was another settlement, in Zürich.

The island of Ufenau, west of the Seedamm, is where Ulrich von Hutten took refuge in 1523 and died. The freezing of the lake, called Seegfrörni in Swiss German, is a rare event. It is recorded in 1223, 1259 and 1262, and often in later centuries, among them 1435, 1573, 1684, 1830, 1880 and 1929, with 1963 the last time.

The lake is divided between the cantons of Zürich, St. Gallen and Schwyz. The Seedamm, an artificial causeway carrying a railway and a road from Rapperswil to Pfäffikon, crosses the narrowest point at the Hurden peninsula and divides the Obersee, the Upper Lake in the east, from the lower lake. Zürich, at the north-western end, is the largest city on the lake and Hurden the least populous settlement. Along the shores lie towns such as Rapperswil, whose medieval castle houses the Polish museum, and Stäfa, Wädenswil, Meilen and Horgen. Apart from the Quaibrücke in Zürich and the Seedamm there are no bridges across the lake, and a car ferry links Horgen and Meilen.
lakota-people: The Lakota speak Lakȟótiyapi, the westernmost of three closely related Siouan languages, and are one of the three prominent divisions of the Sioux, with the Eastern and Western Dakota. Siouan speakers originated in the central Mississippi Valley, and their movement north-west was triggered in part by the collapse of the Mississippian cultures and Cahokia from the twelfth century. The Lakota, the westernmost of the Seven Council Fires, pushed farthest. Their own tradition holds that the people emerged from Wind Cave in the Black Hills. Their winter counts, pictorial calendars painted on hides, record that White Buffalo Calf Woman gave them the sacred pipe, which remains central to their religion.

Conflicts with the Anishinaabe and Cree pushed the Lakota onto the northern Great Plains in the seventeenth century. After adopting horse culture around 1730 they crossed the Missouri River and by the 1770s were established in the Black Hills. Their first official contact with the United States came in September 1804, when the Lewis and Clark Expedition met Sicangu leaders near the Bad River; a council turned tense when warriors seized a boat's cable, and Black Buffalo ended the standoff by releasing it.

The 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty recognised Lakota sovereignty over much of the central Plains. The 1868 treaty, which ended Red Cloud's War, closed the Black Hills to white settlement, but the discovery of gold there in 1874 made this meaningless within two years. In the Great Sioux War, Lakota and Cheyenne under Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull destroyed Custer's column at the Little Bighorn on 25 June 1876. A reinforced army ended resistance by 1877. After Sitting Bull was killed at Standing Rock, the 7th Cavalry killed more than 250 Lakota men, women and children at Wounded Knee in 1890.

There are seven Lakota bands: the Sičháŋǧu or Brulé, Oglála, Itázipčho, Húŋkpapȟa, Mnikȟówožu, Sihásapa and Oóhenuŋpa. Today the Lakota live mainly on five reservations in South Dakota, Pine Ridge, Rosebud, Lower Brule, Cheyenne River and Standing Rock, each governed by an elected tribal council. In 1980 the United States Supreme Court awarded the Sioux nations $122 million for the taking of the Black Hills; the tribes refused the money, since accepting it would end their claim to the land.
lakshadweep: Lakshadweep is an archipelago of 36 islands and islets, with 12 atolls, three reefs and five submerged banks, lying 220 to 440 km off the Malabar Coast. Only ten are inhabited, and the total land area is about 32.62 square kilometres. There are three subgroups: the Amindivi Islands in the north, the Laccadive Islands, and the atoll of Minicoy south of the Nine Degree Channel. The name means one hundred thousand islands in Malayalam and Sanskrit, and Laccadive appears to be its anglicised form. The islands lie at the northern end of the Chagos-Lakshadweep Ridge.

Archaeological evidence from Kalpeni shows settlement from at least 1500 BCE. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea mentions the islands as a source of turtle shell, and the geographer Ptolemy names some of them, including Kavaratti, Agatti, Amini and Minicoy. Finds from Kadamath and Androth show trade with the Roman Empire from the 2nd century CE. Tamil Sangam literature says the Cheras ruled the region. Local tradition credits Cheraman Perumal, the last Chera king of Kerala, with the first settlement, though no historical evidence supports it, and holds that Islam came with Ubaidullah in 661 CE.

Later the islands passed to the Pallavas, the Kadambas and the Cholas, and Rajendra Chola I captured the region in 1018-19. In the late 15th century the Portuguese took control to obtain coir; the islanders revolted and expelled them in 1545. Most islands then came to the Arakkal family of Kannur, while the Amindivi Islands came under Tipu Sultan of Mysore. The Arakkal family held the rest in return for an annual tribute to the British, who later took over the administration, citing unpaid taxes. After Indian independence in 1947 the islands became a union territory in 1956 and were renamed Lakshadweep on 1 November 1973.

Lakshadweep is administered as a single district, with Kavaratti as its capital since 1964. English is the official language. Jeseri, a dialect of Malayalam, is widely spoken, and Mahl, a dialect of Dhivehi, on Minicoy. The 2011 census counted 64,473 people, about 96.6 per cent of them Muslim, and most are descended from migrants from the Malabar coast. The earliest settlers were probably Hindus, as the social stratification and matrilineal kinship suggest. Fishing, coconut growing and tourism are the main occupations.
lakshmi: Lakshmi, also called Shri, does not appear as a fully personified goddess in the earliest Vedic texts. There the word shri names a set of auspicious qualities: radiance, beauty, abundance, power and majesty. The Rigveda, dated to about 1500 BCE, mentions Shri around 130 times, always in connection with prosperity, health, fortune and radiance, and uses the name Lakshmi once, for a mark of auspicious fortune. Scholars such as Mandakranta Bose and David Kinsley see in her the gradual personification of ideals of well-being and sovereignty, a pattern found in other Indo-European traditions. Some scholars propose that Shri and Lakshmi were originally different goddesses who merged into one figure.

In the Vajasaneyi Samhita of the Yajurveda, Shri and Lakshmi are named as the two wives of Vishnu. Her importance grew in the late epic period, around 400 CE, when she became closely tied to Vishnu as his consort. In the epics Sita is regarded as an incarnation of Lakshmi, as are Rukmini in the tradition of Krishna and, in the Critical Edition of the Mahabharata, Draupadi.

Lakshmi is revered as the goddess of fortune, wealth, prosperity, beauty, fertility and sovereignty, and with Parvati and Sarasvati she forms the Tridevi. In Vaishnavism she is Vishnu's consort and his divine energy, and in Sri Vaishnavism devotion to her is held to be essential for reaching him. In Shaktism she is the prosperity aspect of the supreme goddess.

Indian art shows her as an elegantly dressed golden woman seated or standing on a lotus, holding a lotus. Her four arms stand for the four aims of human life: dharma, artha, kama and moksha. She is often shown with two elephants pouring water over her, the Gaja Lakshmi form, which symbolises fertility and royal authority. According to the Ramayana, she rose from the Ocean of Milk when the gods and demons churned it to obtain the nectar of immortality, holding a lotus, and is therefore also called Padma.

Many Hindus worship Lakshmi at Deepavali, the festival of lights held in autumn, when they light lamps in and outside the home and offer family prayers to her. Other days sacred to her include Lakshmi Panchami in the first week of the Hindu new year, Sharad Purnima and the Lakshmi Puja of Navaratri. Her image is among those most often found at archaeological sites: terracotta figurines from the 3rd century BCE come from Vaisali, Sravasti and Kausambi, and she appears on coins of Azes II, Azilises and the Shunga king Jyesthamitra. She is also honoured in Jainism, and in Chinese Buddhism as Gongdetian, the goddess of fortune and prosperity.
lal-bahadur-shastri: Lal Bahadur Shastri was born on 2 October 1904 at the home of his maternal grandparents in Mughalsarai. His family had no links to the independence movement, but a teacher at Harish Chandra High School, Nishkameshwar Prasad Mishra, inspired in him an interest in the freedom struggle. In January 1921, he attended a meeting in Benares addressed by Mahatma Gandhi. Answering Gandhi's call to students to leave government schools, he withdrew from school the next day and joined the Congress as a volunteer in the non-cooperation movement. He was jailed but released as a minor.

In 1928 Shastri became an active member of the Indian National Congress at Gandhi's call and was imprisoned for two and a half years. After the Quit India speech of 8 August 1942 he directed activists for a week from Jawaharlal Nehru's home, Anand Bhavan. In all he spent nearly nine years in British prisons. After independence he became Minister of Police and Transport in Uttar Pradesh under Govind Ballabh Pant, and as Transport Minister was the first to appoint women conductors.

In 1951 he became General Secretary of the All-India Congress Committee and organised the party's successes in the general elections of 1952, 1957 and 1962. Nehru called him to the centre as Minister of Railways and Transport on 13 May 1952. After the Ariyalur train accident of 1956 he offered his resignation again, taking political and moral responsibility, and it was accepted; he left office on 7 December 1956. He later served as Minister of Commerce and Industry in 1959 and as Minister of Home Affairs in 1961.

Nehru died in office on 27 May 1964, and Congress president K. Kamaraj was instrumental in making Shastri prime minister on 9 June. In 1965 he created the National Dairy Development Board for the White Revolution, and he promoted the Green Revolution, which raised grain production in Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

After skirmishes in the Kutch in August 1965 came the war with Pakistan, during which his slogan Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan became popular. He signed the Tashkent Declaration on 10 January 1966 and died the next day. Many of his supporters and relatives have refused to believe the circumstances of his death and have alleged foul play. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously, and the Vijay Ghat memorial in Delhi commemorates him.
lalibela: Lalibela is a town in the Lasta district of the Amhara Region of Ethiopia, about 2,500 metres above sea level. It is known for its rock-cut monolithic churches, designed in contrast to the earlier monolithic churches in Ethiopia, and for some Christians it is one of Ethiopia's holiest cities and a centre of pilgrimage. The rock-hewn churches were declared a World Heritage Site in 1978. The town was traditionally known as Roha, and its name appeared in a European publication on the Fra Mauro map, made in Venice in 1457-59, as Lalabeda.

The churches date from the 7th to the 13th centuries, and most are thought to have been built during the reign of the Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela, who ruled from about 1181 to 1221. According to local tradition he was guided by Jesus on a tour of Jerusalem before his accession and told to build a second Jerusalem in Ethiopia. The layout and names of the major buildings are widely accepted, especially by local clergy, as a symbolic representation of Jerusalem, which has led some experts to date the present church construction to the years after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187.

The dating is disputed. David Roden Buxton assumed that the carving extended into the 14th century. David Phillipson has proposed that the churches of Merkorios, Gabriel-Rufael and Danagel were first carved between 600 and 800, in the days of the Kingdom of Aksum, as fortifications or palace structures. Excavations have yielded pottery and animal remains dating to 900-1100, indicating that the site was largely a secular settlement before King Lalibela turned it into a religious centre.

The Portuguese priest Francisco Álvares visited in the 1520s and wrote that he feared he would not be believed if he described the buildings further. According to the Futuh al-Habasha, Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi burned one of the churches during his invasion of Ethiopia, though Richard Pankhurst noted that the Royal Chronicles, which record his laying waste to the district in 1531, say nothing of it. During the Second Italo-Ethiopian War Haile Selassie made a pilgrimage to the churches before returning to his capital in April 1936.

UNESCO identifies 11 churches in four groups. The Northern Group includes Biete Medhane Alem and Biete Maryam, possibly the oldest, and the Western Group the Church of Saint George, thought the most finely executed and best preserved. The churches show significant Aksumite influence, such as framed doors and windows that seem to mimic the stelae of Aksum, as well as some Syrian and Coptic influence in details. Pilgrims gather for the festivals of Genna on 7 January and Timkat on 19 January.
lalitpur-nepal: Lalitpur stands on the elevated ground of the Kathmandu Valley, at an altitude of 1,350 metres, on the south side of the Bagmati River, which separates it from the city of Kathmandu to the north and west. The Karmanasa Khola forms its eastern boundary. The city was built on thin layers of clay and gravel in the central part of a dried ancient lake known as the Nagdaha. In the Newar language it is called Yala, and in Sanskrit Patan.

Tradition holds that King Varadeva founded the city in 290 CE, though local legends trace its origins earlier still. The Mauryan emperor Ashoka is said to have visited around 249 BCE and to have raised four stupas at the cardinal points of the city, which are still taken as markers of its early Buddhist heritage. During the Licchavi period, from about 400 to 750 CE, Patan became a centre of trade and religion, and inscriptions and stone sculptures point to a thriving urban culture.

The city flourished under the Malla kings, who ruled between the 12th and 18th centuries and made it a showpiece of Newar architecture and planning. Patan Durbar Square was developed in this era, with the Krishna Mandir, built in 1637 by King Siddhi Narsingh Malla, the Hiranya Varna Mahavihar, Sundari Chowk and Mul Chowk. Metalwork, wood carving and stone sculpture were exported across Asia, and Hindu and Buddhist practice coexisted and often merged in festivals and iconography. In periods of political instability a council of noble officials, the Six Pradhans, governed the city.

In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah annexed Lalitpur during the unification of Nepal. Unlike the conquests of Kathmandu and Bhaktapur, that of Patan was reportedly peaceful, but it was followed by economic decline and the loss of autonomy, as the Shah rulers centralised power in Kathmandu and dissolved the royal court. Under the Rana regime (1846–1951) modernisation was limited, and families went on practising traditional crafts.

Patan Durbar Square is one of the seven monument zones that make up the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site; an earthquake on 25 April 2015 heavily damaged it. Other landmarks include the Golden Temple and the Mahabouddha Temple, modelled on the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya. Newars form the largest ethnic group, and the population is mostly Hindu with a large Buddhist minority. After the People's Movement of 1990 the city gained local governance rights, and in 2017 it was declared a metropolitan city of 29 wards.
lambarene: Lambaréné is a town and the capital of Moyen-Ogooué in Gabon, 75 kilometres south of the equator. It lies in the Central African Rainforest on the Ogooué River, which divides it into three districts: Rive Gauche, Ile Lambaréné and Rive Droite. The Albert Schweitzer Hospital stands on Rive Droite. Most people live in the district of Isaac on Rive Gauche, which has the airport. The climate is tropical savanna, with an average temperature of 27 °C, a rainy season from October to June with a short dry spell in December and January, and a long dry season from July to September.

Today the town is inhabited mainly by Bantu groups such as the Fang, Bapounou, Eshira and Myéné, who displaced the Pygmies to the east and north of Gabon. The Italo-French explorer and later colonial governor of French Equatorial Africa, Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, lived in Lambaréné on several occasions. The anthropologist and priest André Raponda Walker worked nearby. In 1913 the Franco-German theologian, musician and physician Albert Schweitzer, who later won the Nobel Peace Prize, founded his hospital in the town and supervised it.

The main economic activity is fishing, and a new port was under construction at the time of the 2013 census, which counted 38,775 inhabitants. The Hôpital Albert Schweitzer has departments of internal medicine, surgery and paediatrics, a maternity clinic and a dentistry clinic, and since 1981 a Medical Research Unit that concentrates on malaria research. Rose Francine Rogombé, who served as interim president of Gabon after the death of Omar Bongo, was born in Lambaréné.
lambert-of-italy: Lambert, born around 880 at San Rufino, was the son of Guy III of Spoleto and Ageltrude. He was crowned king in May 891 at Pavia and joint emperor with his father on 30 April 892 at Ravenna, by a reluctant Pope Formosus. In 893 Formosus asked Arnulf of Carinthia to free Italy, and Arnulf's forces, joined by Berengar of Friuli, defeated Guy. Guy died in late 894, and Lambert became sole king and emperor and duke of Spoleto and Camerino, under the regency of his mother. Arnulf's second campaign took Rome by force on 21 February 896, where Formosus crowned him and declared Lambert deposed. Arnulf then suffered a stroke and withdrew, and Formosus died in the same year, leaving Lambert in power.

Lambert then held Italy with his supporters. He retook Pavia and in 896 agreed with Berengar to divide the kingdom: Berengar kept the land between the Adda and the Po and Lambert the rest. The chronicler Liutprand of Cremona later remarked that the Italians always suffered under two monarchs. In 897 Lambert and Ageltrude persuaded Pope Stephen VI to put the corpse of Formosus on trial in the Cadaver Synod. In January 898 Pope John IX rehabilitated Formosus against their will.

In February 898 Lambert convened a diet at Ravenna where seventy bishops confirmed the pact of 891, declared Arnulf's coronation invalid, confirmed his imperial title and reaffirmed the Constitutio Romana of Lothair I, which required the emperor's presence at papal elections. He continued his father's policy of renovatio regni Francorum, the renewal of the Frankish kingdom, and was the last ruler to issue capitularies in the Carolingian manner. In 898 he legislated against using the services owed by arimanni to create benefices for vassals, and the Lex Romana Utinensis was composed at his court.

He defeated the rebellious Adalbert of Tuscany at Borgo San Donnino in 898 and took him prisoner to Pavia. Returning to Marengo, where he had been hunting, he was killed on 15 October 898. Liutprand, the main source, is reserved about whether he was assassinated or fell from his horse. He was buried in Piacenza. Liutprand remembered him as an elegant youth and a stern man. After his death the kingdom was contested by several candidates, and within days Berengar had taken Pavia.
lamian-war: After his victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Philip II of Macedon forced the Greeks into the League of Corinth, but resentment remained high. Thebes revolted in 335 BCE and was razed by Alexander, and the Spartan king Agis III led another war of liberation that Antipater defeated at Megalopolis. Alexander's Exiles' Decree of 324 BCE, read at the Olympic Games on 4 August before a crowd of 20,000 exiles, ordered all Greek states to allow exiles home.

It forced Athens to give up the island of Samos, which Athenian settlers had held since 365 BCE, and the Aetolian League to leave Oiniadai. When news of Alexander's death reached Greece in June 323 BCE, most mainland states revolted and founded the Hellenic League, recalling the alliance of the Persian Wars with Macedonia now cast as the invader. Athens had been preparing for war; it began probably in early September.

The Athenian Leosthenes, who had gathered about 8,000 of Alexander's discharged mercenaries at Cape Taenarum, became general of the Greeks, defeated a Boeotian and Macedonian force near Plataea and held Thermopylae with about 30,000 men. Antipater, advancing with 13,000 phalangites and 600 cavalry, lost his cavalry when the Thessalian cavalry deserted him and withdrew into Lamia, where he was besieged through the winter.

Leosthenes was killed in a sortie. Leonnatus arrived from Phrygia in early spring 322 BCE and was killed in a cavalry battle, but the Greeks lifted the siege to fight him, and Antipater escaped. He joined Craterus, who had come from Cilicia, and their combined army defeated the Greeks at Crannon on 6 August 322 BCE, with about 500 Greek dead against 130 Macedonian.

At sea, Cleitus the White arrived with 240 ships and defeated the Athenian admiral Euetion off the Echinades. Athens had more than 410 warships but could crew only about 200, and in late summer 322 BCE its overextended navy was soundly beaten off Amorgos.

Antipater refused to negotiate for the whole alliance and took the cities one by one. Athens had to accept a Macedonian garrison in Munychia, taken on 18 September 322 BCE, and to surrender its anti-Macedonian leaders. Hypereides was murdered at Kleonai on 6 October and Demosthenes took his own life a week later. Citizenship was restricted to those with property worth over 2,000 drachmas, reducing the citizen body from 21,000 to 9,000, and Athens lost Oropus and Samos.

Antipater was called back to Asia by the Wars of the Diadochi before he could defeat the Aetolian League, which survived and became an important Hellenistic state. Athens never again played a leading role in Greek affairs. The main source, Diodorus, drew on the pro-Macedonian Hieronymus of Cardia, who is thought to have renamed the Hellenic War the Lamian War.
lamu-old-town: Lamu is a small town on Lamu Island, part of the Lamu Archipelago of Kenya, reached by crossing a sea channel from Mokowe Jetty, the end of the road that runs 341 kilometres north-east from Mombasa. The original name was Amu, which Arabs rendered Al-Amu; the Portuguese called it Lamon and applied the name to the whole island. The town is believed to have been established in 1370 and is Kenya's oldest continually inhabited town, one of the original Swahili settlements along the East African coast. It was first attested in writing by the Arab traveller Abu-al-Mahasini, who met a judge from Lamu visiting Mecca in 1441.

In 1506 a Portuguese fleet under Tristão da Cunha sent a ship to blockade Lamu, and its king had to agree to pay an annual tribute and 600 meticals at once. Portugal held a monopoly of shipping along the East African coast and taxed exports. In the 1580s, prompted by Turkish raids, Lamu led a rebellion against the Portuguese, and in 1652 Oman helped it resist their control.

From the late seventeenth to the early nineteenth century Lamu was an Omani protectorate, and this is regarded as its golden age. It was governed as a republic by a council of elders called the Yumbe, and became a centre of poetry, politics, arts, crafts and trade, with many buildings in a distinct classical style. The poet Mwana Kupona, author of Advice on the Wifely Duty, had a higher status there than convention elsewhere in Kenya allowed.

In 1812 a coalition Pate-Mazrui army landed at Shela and was violently repulsed in the Battle of Shela; Lamu then asked Oman for a Busaidi garrison at its new fort. Fumo Madi ibn Abi Bakr, sultan of Pate, began the fort and died in 1809, and it was finished by the early 1820s.

The town came under the political influence of the sultan of Zanzibar in the mid-nineteenth century, and a German post office operated there from 22 November 1888 to 3 March 1891. In 1890 Lamu came under British rule under the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty. Its economy rested on the slave trade until abolition in 1907, and the Uganda Railroad, begun at Mombasa in 1901, further hampered it.

Lamu Old Town was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2001 as the oldest and best-preserved Swahili settlement in East Africa. Most of its people are Muslim, and it has 23 mosques; the island has no motorised vehicles, and about 3,000 donkeys do the carrying. The Maulidi Festival celebrates the birth of the Prophet Muhammad.
lanai: Lānaʻi is separated from Molokaʻi by the Kalohi Channel to the north and from Maui by the Auʻau Channel to the east. Its land area is 364 square kilometres, and its highest point, the inactive volcano Mount Lānaʻihale, rises to 1,026 metres. Traditionally the island was administered in 13 ahupuaʻa, grouped into two districts, kona (leeward) and koʻolau (windward). Its only settlement of note is Lānaʻi City, and the 2020 census counted 3,367 residents on the island.

Lānaʻi has been under the control of nearby Maui since before recorded history, and its first inhabitants may have arrived as late as the 15th century. They probably came from Maui and Molokaʻi, settled fishing villages along the coast and then spread into the interior, where they grew taro in the volcanic soil. When George Vancouver passed in 1792 he ignored the island because it seemed to have neither inhabitants nor villages. A legend tells of a Maui prince, Kauluāʻau, banished there for his pranks, who drove away the ghosts and goblins said to haunt it.

A farmer from China, Wong Tse Chun, produced a small amount of sugar there in 1802. In 1854 members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints took a lease at Pālāwai, and Walter M. Gibson, who arrived in 1862, bought the land in his own name and by the 1870s held most of the island, which he used for ranching. The population had fallen to 200 by 1890. Charles Gay planted the first pineapple there in 1921, when the population was about 150, and a year later James Dole, president of the Hawaiian Pineapple Company, bought the island and turned much of it into the world's largest pineapple plantation. Dole ended its pineapple operations in 1992.

Lānaʻi is sometimes called the Pineapple Island, after its plantation past. It joined Maui County at statehood in 1959. It has one school serving all grades and no traffic lights, and most attractions outside the town can be reached only by dirt roads. The Hotel Lanai was built in 1923 by Dole as a lodge for plantation executives and was the island's only hotel until 1990.
lancashire: Lancashire is a ceremonial county in North West England covering 3,079 square kilometres, bordered by Cumbria to the north, Yorkshire to the east and the Irish Sea to the west. The west contains flat coastal plains, including the Fylde, while the east is upland, with the West Pennine Moors in the south-east and the Forest of Bowland in the north-east. The rivers Lune, Wyre and Ribble flow west into the Irish Sea. The largest settlement is the city of Preston, and the county also holds Blackburn, Burnley, Lancaster and the seaside resort of Blackpool.

In Roman times the area belonged to the territory of the Brigantes, and towns including Manchester, Lancaster and Ribchester grew around Roman forts. After the Roman withdrawal in 410 CE the north probably formed part of the Brythonic kingdom of Rheged. In the mid-8th century the land north of the Ribble was incorporated into the Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of Northumbria and the land to the south into Mercia, both of which later became parts of England.

The county was established in 1182 and was divided into the hundreds of Amounderness, Blackburn, Leyland, Lonsdale, Salford and West Derby. In the Domesday Book of 1086 much of what became Lancashire had been treated as part of Yorkshire and Cheshire. Until the early modern period it was a comparatively poor backwater, although in 1351 it became a palatine with a semi-independent judicial system. The Red Rose of Lancaster, the county's flower, recalls the House of Lancaster in the Wars of the Roses.

Lancashire was one of the homes of modern industrialisation, above all in textiles. It had a long history of supplying wool to weavers and had many cottager weavers by the 18th century, and increased imports of cotton needing processing triggered innovation. John Kay, Richard Arkwright, Samuel Crompton and James Hargreaves were all from Lancashire. Until 1974 the county included Liverpool, a major port, and Manchester, which with its surrounding towns dominated textile manufacture. The Lancashire coalfield was also exploited, and canals including the Leeds and Liverpool Canal and the Bridgewater Canal formed part of the industrial network.

Since 1974 Liverpool and Manchester have lain outside the county. The Duchy of Lancaster, the private estate of the sovereign, still exercises the Crown's right in the County Palatine of Lancaster, whose boundaries remain the historic ones. Lancaster Castle, Lancaster Cathedral, Blackburn Cathedral and Hoghton Tower are among its notable buildings, and Lancashire hotpot, a lamb casserole, is a dish that originated there.
lancaster-pennsylvania: Lancaster lies in the Piedmont region of Pennsylvania, slightly north of the Conestoga River, a left tributary of the Susquehanna River. It is the seat of Lancaster County and a hub of Pennsylvania Dutch Country, about 95 kilometres west of Philadelphia. The city covers about 19 square kilometres. Its neighbourhoods include Cabbage Hill, named for the cabbage patches kept there by ethnic Germans.

Settled in the 1720s, Lancaster is one of the oldest inland cities in the United States. It was first called Hickory Town and was renamed after the English city of Lancaster by a local man, John Wright; its symbol, the red rose, comes from the House of Lancaster. The site lay within William Penn's charter of 1681 and was laid out by James Hamilton in 1734. It became a borough in 1742 and a city in 1818.

Lancaster was the capital of Pennsylvania from 1799 to 1812, with the state government at the Court House, built in 1784 and demolished in 1852; the site is now the Soldiers and Sailors Monument at Penn Square. In 1812 the capital moved to Harrisburg. In 2011 the city council recognised 27 September as Capital Day, marking Lancaster's one day as capital of the United States in 1777. Lancaster is also credited with the first Conestoga wagon, used widely for migration before the railroad, and the first Pennsylvania Rifle, made by Martin Meylin in the 1700s. The Hamilton Watch Company released the first battery-powered watch there in 1957. James Buchanan, the 15th president of the United States, is among the city's notable people.

At the 2020 census Lancaster had 58,039 inhabitants. Central Market, built in 1889, is the oldest continuously run farmers' market in the United States. Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church, built in 1879, aided freedmen moving north after the Civil War, and its congregation had earlier used a former church as a station on the Underground Railroad. The Fulton Opera House is one of the oldest working theatres in the country, and Franklin and Marshall College is based in the city.
lanciano: Lanciano stands on hills about 10 kilometres from the Adriatic Sea, at an elevation of about 265 metres. Archaeological findings show that the area was settled from the 5th millennium BCE. A tradition holds that the city was founded in 1181 BCE by Solimus, a Trojan refugee who came to Italy with Aeneas; the account is legend.

Under the Frentani the city was probably within the influence of Greater Greece. After the end of the Samnite Wars, in which the Frentani were allied with the Romans, it obtained the status of municipium. It was probably a flourishing commercial site on an old trade route connecting Pescara to Apulia. During the fall of the Western Roman Empire it was sacked by the Goths and then destroyed during the Lombard invasion, around 571. The Byzantines conquered it in 610 and allowed trade to restart, and in the late 8th century the Franks took it.

In 1060 the Normans made it a centre of the unified Kingdom of Sicily. By 1340 it was the largest city in Abruzzo, with 6,500 inhabitants and industries in ceramics, wool, silk, goldwork and ironwork. Frederick II and his son Manfred granted it important privileges and a substantial administrative autonomy. Spanish rule after the Italian Wars and the shift of commerce after the discovery of America impoverished the city, which became a baronial possession in 1640.

Lanciano took the side of the Neapolitan Republic of 1799 and rose against the Bourbon kings in 1848, 1849 and 1853. In 1860 it voted to join the new Kingdom of Italy. It was an active centre of the Resistance during the German occupation, and on 6 October 1943 Italian citizens attacked German soldiers.

Lanciano is a comune in the province of Chieti. Its Cathedral of Santa Maria del Ponte, built on bridgework along a precipice, dates from 1619 and holds an 8th-century Byzantine statue of the Madonna. The church of San Francesco, of 1258, was built over a 7th-century temple, and San Biagio, of the 11th century, is the oldest church of the city.
land-of-punt: The Egyptians wrote the name as pwnt, and the land produced and exported gold, aromatic resins, blackwood, ebony, ivory and wild animals. They also called it Ta netjer, the Land of the God, a name that places it among the regions of the sun god, in the direction of the sunrise to the east of Egypt. Its location is debated. A majority of scholars place it in the Horn of Africa or in African lands south-east of Egypt, since the products shown in Hatshepsut's reliefs were abundant there and less common or absent in Arabia.

Ian Shaw wrote in 2003 that a strong argument had been made for southern Sudan or the Eritrean region of Ethiopia, where plants and animals most closely match those in the Egyptian reliefs. Isotope analysis of mummified baboons in 2010 and in 2020 pointed to an area stretching across Eritrea, Ethiopia and north-western Somalia. Dimitri Meeks disagrees and argues from inscriptions that only the Arabian Peninsula satisfies all the Egyptian indications, which place Punt both north and south-east of the Nile Valley. Some scholars have proposed Sri Lanka, but that identification is now considered unconfirmed.

The earliest recorded Egyptian expedition to Punt was organised by Pharaoh Sahure of the Fifth Dynasty, although gold from Punt was in Egypt as early as the time of Khufu of the Fourth Dynasty. Further expeditions followed in the Sixth, Eleventh, Twelfth and Eighteenth dynasties. Under Mentuhotep III an officer named Hannu organised voyages, and in the Twelfth Dynasty the trade was the subject of the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor.

Hatshepsut of the Eighteenth Dynasty built a Red Sea fleet, and the best-known expedition to Punt sailed in the ninth year of her reign. Reliefs in her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri show a five-ship voyage led by Chancellor Nehsi and describe Punt as ruled by King Parahu and Queen Ati. The Puntites traded incense, ebony and short-horned cattle, and also gold, ivory and animal skins from other African lands.

In 2005 the archaeologist Kathryn Bard found remains of Egyptian seagoing vessels and inscribed stelae at Mersa/Wadi Gawasis, the Egyptian port for the voyages. Thutmose III and Amenhotep III continued the trade, which lasted into the start of the 20th dynasty, when Papyrus Harris I records an expedition's return in the reign of Ramesses III. After the New Kingdom Punt became in later tradition a fabulous land of myths and legends.
landau: Landau in der Pfalz is an autonomous town surrounded by the Südliche Weinstraße district of southern Rhineland-Palatinate. It lies east of the Palatinate Forest, on the German Wine Route, among vineyards and wine-growing villages, and wine-making continues to be an important industry. It has been a university town since 1990. The districts of Arzheim, Dammheim, Godramstein, Mörlheim, Mörzheim, Nussdorf, Queichheim and Wollmesheim belong to it.

Landau was first mentioned as a settlement in 1106 and was held by the counts of Leiningen-Dagsburg-Landeck. King Rudolf I of Germany granted it a charter in 1274 and declared it a Free Imperial Town in 1291. Prince-Bishop Emich of Speyer, a major landowner in the district, seized the town in 1324, and it regained its ancient rights only in 1511, from Maximilian I. An Augustinian monastery was founded there in 1276.

After the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 control of Landau was ceded to France, with certain ill-defined reservations, and the town was part of France from 1680 to 1815. Vauban, Louis XIV's military architect, gave it its modern fortifications in 1688-1699, making the little town, of about 5,000 inhabitants in 1789, one of Europe's strongest citadels.

It underwent four sieges in the War of the Spanish Succession. The French lost it in 1702, regained it in 1703 after the Battle of Speyerbach, lost it again in a siege that ended on 23 November 1704, and recaptured it in a final siege from 6 June to 20 August 1713 under Marshal Villars. During the 1704 siege King Joseph I arrived from Vienna in a newly developed convertible carriage, which became popular and was named the landau.

Landau remained French after Napoleon's Hundred Days and was granted to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1815, becoming the seat of one of the thirteen Bezirksämter of the Bavarian Rheinkreis, later renamed Pfalz. The political cartoonist Thomas Nast was born there in 1840. After World War II it was an important barracks town for the French occupation.

The large main square, the Rathausplatz, is dominated by the town hall and the market hall, the Altes Kaufhaus. The Protestant Collegiate Church, begun in the 14th century and completed in the mid-16th, is one of the oldest buildings. The Festhalle, in Art Nouveau style, dates from 1905-1907. The former fortifications gave way in the 19th century to a ring road around the old town.
landnamabok: Landnámabók, often shortened to Landnáma, is a medieval Icelandic written work that describes in considerable detail the settlement of Iceland by the Norse. The initial settlement largely took place during the Viking Age, between 870 and 930, but the book mentions descendants well after the settlement period, at least into the 11th century.
