Ari Þorgilsson may have written the earliest version, in addition to his shorter Íslendingabók; early versions may also have been based on genealogies that Ari says he left out of Íslendingabók. Some have suggested a single author, while others believe it was put together when people met at assemblies.

The book is divided into five parts and 102 chapters. The first part tells of how the island was found and of the first settlers. The later parts count settlers quarter by quarter, beginning with the west and ending with the south. For each settler it says where they settled and gives a brief genealogy of their descendants, sometimes with short anecdotes. More than 3,000 people and 1,400 settlements are described, and 435 people, men and women, are listed as the initial settlers, most of them in the northern and south-western parts of the island.

Five versions survive. Three were written in the Middle Ages: Sturlubók, thought to date from between 1275 and 1280 and attributed to Sturla Þórðarson; a version in the early 14th-century Hauksbók, which Haukr Erlendsson says he based on Sturlubók and a lost 13th-century Styrmisbók; and Melabók, written about 1300, of which two sheets survive. The other two, Skarðsárbók and Þórðarbók, were compiled in the 17th century from medieval material.

Landnámabók remains an invaluable source for the history and genealogy of the Icelandic people, and one of the main sources on the heathen religion of the settlers. According to Sveinbjörn Rafnsson, Sturlubók and Hauksbók tend to overemphasise Christianity, and Melabók does so less. An epilogue to Þórðarbók justifies the study of Icelandic history as a defence against foreign accusations of descent from slaves or rogues.

Historians debate how far the account is historical. Gunnar Karlsson notes that the story of Hrafna-Flóki resembles the biblical account of Noah and his ravens, and the earliest surviving versions were written after the Christianization of Iceland. Helgi Þorláksson holds that the story of Ingólfr Arnarson's settlement seems accurate and agrees with other sources.
lands-of-the-crown-of-saint-stephen: The Lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen were the Hungarian territories of Austria-Hungary, and the name referred to the historic coronation crown of Hungary, which had symbolic importance to the Kingdom of Hungary. The informal name Transleithania means the region beyond the Leitha River, from an Austrian point of view. The Leitha had been the historical border between Hungary and the German lands since a peace between Géza and Henry, later Emperor Henry II, in 996. After the Compromise of 1867 Transleithania consisted of the Kingdom of Hungary, including the former Principality of Transylvania, the self-governed Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia and the free port of Rijeka. Its capital was Budapest, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was governed jointly with Cisleithania.

The Compromise gave the Hungarian government more control of its domestic affairs than it had held since the Battle of Mohács. Emperor Franz Joseph I ruled as Apostolic King of Hungary. A prime minister and cabinet answered to the Diet of Hungary, elected by a narrow franchise, while foreign affairs, defence and finance were common ministries. At Franz Joseph's insistence Hungary and Croatia reached a similar settlement in 1868, the Nagodba, which defined this half of the monarchy as a state union of the Kingdom of Hungary and the Triune Kingdom of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia. Croatia kept its Sabor, although in practice its autonomy was limited, since the Croatian Ban was nominated by the Hungarian prime minister.

The Nationalities Law of 1868 defined Hungary as a single Hungarian nation with equal rights for nationalities, except in language. Slovaks, Romanians and Serbs wanted more autonomy, and later governments pursued Magyarization. Kálmán Tisza's Liberal Party governed from 1875. Hungary's population rose from 13 million to 20 million between 1850 and 1910, and the share of Hungarians working in industry doubled between 1890 and 1910, while the peasantry suffered in the depression of the 1880s and 1890s and emigrated in growing numbers.

Transleithania had no flag of its own. Under the Nagodba the symbols of both Hungary and Croatia had to be used in joint affairs. The First World War led to the disintegration of Austria-Hungary, which ended on 16 November 1918. A series of governments, including a communist regime, then took power in Budapest.
landshut: Landshut lies in the Alpine foothills, about 70 kilometres from both Munich and Regensburg. The River Isar runs through the city and splits in two in the centre, leaving the Mühleninsel between its arms. The Hofberg, where Trausnitz Castle stands, is the highest point in the city area, at 505 metres above sea level.

A settlement grew around Trausnitz Castle after its foundation in 1204. Landshut was a Wittelsbach residence by 1231, and in 1255, when the duchy of Bavaria was divided in two, it became the capital of Lower Bavaria. Duke Henry XVI was the first of the three 'rich dukes' who ruled Bavaria-Landshut in the 15th century. In 1475 the wedding of Duke George with the Polish princess Jadwiga Jagiellon was held in the town with one of the most splendid festivals of the Middle Ages. After his death and the Landshut War of Succession, Bavaria-Landshut was reunited with Bavaria-Munich.

Between 1537 and 1543 Louis X, Duke of Bavaria, built the Landshut Residence after a visit to Italy. It was the first Renaissance palace constructed north of the Alps and was modelled on the Palazzo Te in Mantua. William V, Duke of Bavaria, rebuilt Trausnitz Castle from a Gothic fortification into a Renaissance complex while he lived in Landshut as crown prince for ten years until 1579. The town then lost most of its importance until the University of Ingolstadt was moved there in 1800; in 1826 the university was transferred to Munich.

Swedish forces took and plundered the city three times in the Thirty Years' War, in 1632, 1634 and 1648. Napoleon won the Battle of Landshut in 1809 against an Austrian army, as part of the War of the Fifth Coalition. In the Second World War a subcamp of the Dachau concentration camp, supplying slave labour for local industry, stood in the city, which was taken by American troops on 29 April 1945.

Landshut has a population of more than 75,000 and is the largest city in Lower Bavaria, as well as the seat of the surrounding district. Its historic centre is mostly Gothic, with Trausnitz Castle, the Church of Saint Martin, the Churches of St. Jodok and Holy Spirit, the Town Hall and the Ländtor, the only surviving gate of the medieval fortification. The Renaissance courtyard of Trausnitz and the ducal Residence stand beside Baroque churches. The Landshuter Hochzeit, held every four years, commemorates the marriage of 1475.
landsknecht: The word Landsknecht first appeared in German about 1470 for troops in the army of Charles, Duke of Burgundy. In the Burgundian Wars the Swiss pikemen, called Reisläufer, repeatedly defeated Charles and eventually killed him. Archduke Maximilian, who became co-ruler of the Burgundian lands in 1477 by marrying Mary of Burgundy, was greatly influenced by the Swiss victories. He wanted a permanent force like the Swiss, while the French held a monopoly on hiring Reisläufer. He began raising the first Landsknecht units in 1486, with 6,000 to 8,000 mercenaries, and one unit was trained with Swiss instructors at Bruges in 1487 as the Black Guard.

In 1488 Maximilian formed the Swabian League army of 12,000 infantry and 1,200 cavalry, regarded as the first Landsknecht army raised in Germany. In 1490 the Landsknechte helped drive the Hungarians out of Austria, but they refused to serve after sacking Stuhlweissenburg, citing lack of pay. At Marignano in 1515 they performed well against the Reisläufer. Under Charles V of Habsburg, with captains such as Georg von Frundsberg, they took part in the victory at Pavia in 1525, where Francis I was captured.

The Sack of Rome in 1527 was carried out by mutinous, unpaid imperial troops, among them 14,000 Landsknechte under Frundsberg. After his death their reputation declined from the 1560s, and in the French Wars of Religion their bravery and discipline were criticised. The Spanish tercios gained a higher reputation, and increasing indiscipline led to their replacement by the Kaiserlicher Fussknecht, a system less reliant on mercenaries.

The Landsknechte were often recruited from South Germany, from a society with growing population and unemployment. Dispossessed craftsmen and peasants served beside burghers, aristocrats and runaway serfs. Their libertine and often brutal way of life was countered by officers who dismounted to fight beside their men and by harsh discipline, including capital punishment. A regiment of about 4,000 men was raised by a lord's letter patent, the Bestallungsbrief, which named the colonel and set out the unit's structure, pay and Articles of War.

The regiment held ten Fähnlein, each of 400 men including 100 veterans, divided into Rotten of ten ordinary Landsknechte or six Doppelsöldner, the double-pay men who formed the front line with the Zweihänder and arquebus. A spokesman for the men, the Gemeinweibel, was elected monthly.
langres: Langres is a commune in north-eastern France, a subprefecture of the department of Haute-Marne in the region of Grand Est. The town was built on a limestone promontory of the same name. It was the capital of the Romanized Gallic tribe known as the Lingones, and was called Andematunnum, then Lingones, and now Langres. Its climate is influenced by both oceanic and humid continental patterns, with cold, snowy winters.

The stronghold was first occupied by the Lingones. The Romans later fortified it, at a strategic crossroads of twelve Roman roads. The Triumphal Gate of the first century and the many objects in its museums are remains of its Gallo-Roman history. After the period of invasions the town prospered in the Middle Ages, partly through the growing political influence of its bishops. The diocese covered Champagne, the Duchy of Burgundy and Franche-Comté, and the bishops obtained the right to coin money in the ninth century and to name the city's military governor in 927. The Bishop of Langres was a duke and peer of France.

The troubled 14th and 15th centuries led the town to strengthen its defences, and it entered a period of royal tutelage. The Renaissance brought a return of prosperity and the construction of many civil, religious and military buildings that still stand. A "Vauban" citadel was added in the 19th century.

The historic town centre is surrounded by defensive walls with a dozen towers and seven gates. The cathedral of Saint-Mammès, dedicated to Mammes of Caesarea, a martyr of the 3rd century, dates from the late 12th century. The town gives its name to an AOC-protected soft cow's milk cheese with a washed rind. It was long known for its cutlery industry, and Didier Diderot, father of the encyclopedist Denis, was a cutler. Denis Diderot was born in Langres in 1713, and a museum, the Denis Diderot House of Enlightenment, opened there in 2013 in a private mansion of the 16th and 18th centuries.
langston-hughes: Langston Hughes was born in Joplin, Missouri, on 1 February 1901, though in his autobiography he gave 1902. Like many African Americans he was of mixed ancestry: both his paternal great-grandmothers were enslaved Africans and both paternal great-grandfathers white slave owners in Kentucky. His maternal grandmother, Mary Patterson, was one of the first women to attend Oberlin College. Her first husband, Lewis Sheridan Leary, was fatally wounded in John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry in 1859, and her second, Charles Henry Langston, was an abolitionist.

Hughes had a poor relationship with his father. After high school in 1920 he lived with him in Mexico, and they agreed that Hughes would study engineering if he could attend Columbia University. He enrolled in September 1921 but dropped out in 1922, having met racial prejudice and being drawn more to Harlem than to his studies. He eventually graduated from Lincoln University.

Hughes's poem The Negro Speaks of Rivers appeared in 1921 in The Crisis, the magazine of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, and became his signature poem. It was collected in his first book, The Weary Blues, published in 1926. His work was influential during the Harlem Renaissance, alongside Zora Neale Hurston, Wallace Thurman, Claude McKay and Countee Cullen, with whom he worked on the short-lived magazine Fire!!

Hughes and his contemporaries tried to depict the real lives of Black people in the lower social and economic strata. His essay The Negro Artist and the Racial Mountain, published in The Nation in 1926, is regarded as their manifesto. In the 1930s his political writing often engaged with left-wing and Communist-aligned ideas. In 1932 he travelled to the Soviet Union for a proposed film on Black life in the United States, which was abandoned, and in 1937 he went to Spain as a correspondent during the Spanish Civil War. From 1942 to 1962 he wrote a weekly column for The Chicago Defender.

Hughes died in New York City on 22 May 1967, aged 66, from complications following abdominal surgery related to prostate cancer. His ashes are interred beneath a floor medallion in the foyer of the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture in Harlem, a cosmogram titled Rivers. His house at 20 East 127th Street became a New York City landmark in 1981 and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982.
languedoc: The province of Languedoc covered about 42,700 square kilometres in the central part of southern France, roughly between the river Rhône, the border with Provence, and the Garonne, the border with Gascony. It extended north to the Cévennes and the Massif Central, where Auvergne began. Historically the region was the County of Toulouse, which at times also took in Quercy, Rouergue, Agenais, Gévaudan, Velay, part of Vivarais and even the northern half of Provence. After the French conquest the county was dismantled, and its central part came to be called Languedoc.

The Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis fell to the Visigothic Kingdom, which held it from the 5th to the 8th centuries. The Emirate of Córdoba occupied it briefly between 719 and 759, and Pepin the Short incorporated it into the Kingdom of the Franks in 759 after the Siege of Narbonne. After the decline of the Carolingian Empire, political rule fragmented into small territorial divisions. The name Languedoc first described a cultural region that was not necessarily politically unified.

The Albigensian Crusade (1208–1229) set out to end what the Catholic Church considered the Cathar heresy, and it let the Capetian dynasty extend its influence south of the Loire. The Trencavel lands, the viscounties of Albi, Carcassona, Besièrs, Agde and Nîmes, joined the royal domain in 1224. The County of Toulouse followed in 1271. Smaller enclaves were absorbed up to the early 16th century, among them Montpellier in 1349 and the Viscounty of Narbonne in 1507. The Estates of Languedoc first met in 1346, and in 1542 the province was divided into two généralités, Toulouse for Haut-Languedoc and Montpellier for Bas-Languedoc.

Under the Ancien Régime Toulouse, seat of the Parlement founded in the middle of the 15th century, was often called the capital, while the monarchy favoured Montpellier, where the intendant resided and the Estates met from the 18th century. The province was one of the few in France that kept the right to decide on taxation. Most of its territory now lies in the region of Occitanie, formed in 2016, and the rest in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes. The historic cities of Carcassonne, Toulouse and Montpellier, the Roman arenas of Nîmes, medieval abbeys, the ruined Cathar castles of the Corbières and the Canal du Midi, built for the wheat trade, survive from its past.
lanse-aux-meadows: The site lies near St. Anthony on the northernmost tip of the island of Newfoundland. The name is a French-English one that can be translated as Grassland Bay, though how the village acquired it is debated. It may be a corruption of the French L'Anse aux Méduses, Jellyfish Cove, or derive from L'Anse à la Médée, Medea Cove, as an 1862 French naval chart marks it. Five Indigenous groups occupied the place before the Norse, the oldest about 6,000 years ago, but none at the same time as the Norse. The most prominent were the Dorset people, who were there about 300 years before them.

Carbon dating gives the Norse settlement a range of 990 to 1050 CE, with a mean of 1014, and a 2021 study of three tree-ring samples, using the atmospheric carbon-14 anomaly of 993, pinpointed 1021 as a date of Norse activity. The remains of eight buildings, of sod over a wooden frame, were found, with over 800 Norse objects. 6 metres and had several rooms.

Others were workshops: an iron smithy with a forge and slag, a carpentry workshop and a boat repair area with worn rivets. A spindle and a needle suggest that women as well as men lived there, and butternuts, which do not grow naturally north of New Brunswick, show that the Norse travelled farther south.

How long the site was used is uncertain. John Steinberg suggests occupation at least sporadically for perhaps 20 years, while a 2019 study allows activity for as long as a century. Eleanor Barraclough suggests a temporary boat repair base rather than a permanent settlement, noting that there are no burials, farming remains or animal pens, which suggests an orderly abandonment. The dwellings could hold 30 to 160 people, far fewer than the roughly 2,500 then living in Greenland.

In 1960 George Decker, a resident of the hamlet, led the Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad to grassy mounds the locals called the old Indian camp. Helge Ingstad and the archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad led excavations from 1961 to 1968 and identified a Norse settlement by comparison with sites in Greenland and Iceland from around 1000 CE. Parks Canada later ordered further excavations, under Bengt Schonbach in 1973 to 1975 and Birgitta Wallace in 1976. The site became a National Historic Site of Canada in November 1968 and a World Heritage Site in 1978.

It is the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland. Whether it is Leifsbudir or Hóp, settlements of Vinland named in the Saga of the Greenlanders and the Saga of Erik the Red, has been claimed, but Stuart C. Brown found Ingstad's attempt to show it was Leifsbudir wholly unconvincing.
lanzhou: Lanzhou lies at 1,600 metres above sea level on the southern bank of the Yellow River, which flows through it from west to east, in a narrow and curved valley hemmed in by mountains, among them the Qilian Ranges. It is the geographical centre of China's land territory. The climate is semi-arid, with hot summers and cold, very dry winters, and annual rainfall of about 309 millimetres falls almost entirely between May and October. The city is a key transport hub, linking areas further west by rail to the eastern half of the country.

The area was originally the territory of the ancient Western Qiang and became part of the State of Qin in the 6th century BCE. In 81 BCE, under the Han dynasty, it was taken from the Huns' Huyandi Chanyu and made the seat of Jincheng commandery. It was a major link on the ancient Northern Silk Road and an important crossing of the Yellow River, and the Great Wall was extended as far as Yumen to protect it; parts of the wall still stand in the built-up area. From the 5th to the 11th century the region of present-day Gansu was a centre of Buddhist study.

Lanzhou became the seat of a prefecture of that name under the Sui dynasty and kept the name under the Tang. In 763 the area was overrun by the Tibetan Empire and in 843 the Tang reclaimed it. It later passed to the Western Xia, was absorbed by the Song in 1081, fell to the Jin after 1127 and came into the possession of the Mongol Empire after 1235. Under the Ming it was reduced to a county, and reestablished as a political unit in 1477. It took its current name in 1656 under the Qing, and became the capital when Gansu was made a separate province in 1666.

Lanzhou is the capital and largest city of Gansu and the third largest city in north-western China after Xi'an and Ürümqi. During the Second Sino-Japanese War it was the terminus of the 3,200 km Chinese–Soviet highway that carried Soviet supplies, and it was heavily bombed by Japanese aircraft. On 20 August 1949 the First Field Army of the People's Liberation Army under Peng Dehuai began the Battle of Lanzhou and entered the city by 26 August. It is a centre for heavy and petrochemical industry and for research and education, with institutions including Lanzhou University.
lao-peoples-revolutionary-party: The forerunner of the party was the Indochinese Communist Party, which Ho Chi Minh established in February 1930 to organise a coordinated fighting force against French domination of Indochina, in cooperation with the Communist International. Though it claimed to be Indochinese, it was dominated by Vietnamese and had no Cambodian or Laotian members before its formal dissolution on 11 November 1945, when the Indochinese National Democratic Revolution was proclaimed.

In 1946 the underground party began a drive to recruit Laotian cadres. Kaysone Phomvihane, half Vietnamese, was recruited in 1946-47 while a student at the University of Hanoi, but by February 1951 only 81 of its 2,091 members were Lao. The Lao People's Revolutionary Party was established on 22 March 1955 by former members of the Indochinese party.

The party led the insurgency against the Royal Lao Government and supported North Vietnamese forces in the Vietnam War. The insurgency ended with the party securing power in 1975. Kaysone Phomvihane was general secretary from 1955 until his death in 1992, yet he was unknown to most citizens in the party's first years in power, when it kept its secretive ways. Voices of the movement before 1975, such as the Lao Patriotic Front chairman Souphanouvong, were set aside, and independent news organisations were closed or forced into the Lao Front for National Construction, a mass organisation controlled by the party. By 1980 ten percent of the population had left the country.

The party aimed to abolish the capitalist mode of production and build a planned economy on the Soviet model. In December 1975 it decided to skip the capitalist phase on the way to socialism, while judging that Laos was too underdeveloped for immediate socialist construction. It collectivised agriculture from 1978. In the 1980s, influenced by market reforms in China and Vietnam, it privatised state companies and legalised private property. By the 1990s it held that the state would use state capitalism to build the material base of socialism.

The party's organisation follows democratic centralism, conceived by Lenin: lower organs obey higher ones and internal factions are banned. Its highest body is the National Congress, which meets every five years and elects the Central Committee. The committee elects the Politburo, the Secretariat and the General Secretary, the highest party officer. Article 3 of the constitution guarantees its monopoly on state power. It follows Marxism-Leninism and Kaysone Phomvihane Thought, and holds that there is no ideological reason for other parties to exist. Its youth league, the Lao People's Revolutionary Youth Union, was established in 1983, and it keeps close relations with the Communist Party of Vietnam.
laocoon-and-his-sons: The group stands just over 2 metres high, with nearly life-sized figures of the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons Antiphantes and Thymbraeus. Pliny the Elder, who saw it in the palace of Emperor Titus, ascribed it to three sculptors from Rhodes, Agesander, Athenodoros and Polydorus, but gave neither a date nor a patron.

Its style is that of the Hellenistic Pergamene baroque of around 200 BCE, but it is not known whether it is an original or a copy of an earlier bronze. Proposed dates range from 200 BCE to the 70s CE, and a date under the Julio-Claudian emperors, 27 BCE to 68 CE, is now preferred. It was probably made for the home of a wealthy Roman, possibly one of the imperial family.

The story comes from the Greek Epic Cycle and is not in Homer. Sophocles wrote a tragedy about it, now lost, and the accounts vary. In Virgil's Aeneid Laocoön, a priest of Poseidon, is killed with both sons after striking the Trojan Horse with a spear. In Sophocles he was a priest of Apollo who had married, and the serpents killed only his sons. In some versions he was punished for wrongdoing, in others for being right. The agony is conveyed through contorted faces and straining bodies, and has been called the prototypical icon of human agony in Western art.

The group was unearthed in February 1506 in the vineyard of Felice De Fredis on the Oppian Hill. Pope Julius II sent for Michelangelo and the architect Giuliano da Sangallo, whose son Francesco later recalled that his father identified it at once as the Laocoön Pliny mentions. Julius acquired it on 23 March and by August it stood in a niche in the Belvedere Garden at the Vatican, the date from which the Vatican Museums count their history.

The right arm of Laocoön was missing, and artists debated how to restore it. Michelangelo suggested it was bent back, but later restorers, among them Giovanni Antonio Montorsoli in 1532, set it outstretched. In 1905 Ludwig Pollak found a marble arm fragment in a builder's yard in Rome, and in 1957 the Vatican decided it belonged to the group and replaced the arm with it, bent as Michelangelo had proposed. The find strongly affected Italian art. Michelangelo drew on it for his Rebellious Slave and Dying Slave, and Raphael used Laocoön's face for Homer in his Parnassus. Gotthold Ephraim Lessing's essay Laocoon later used the group to compare the limits of painting and poetry.
laodicea-on-the-lycus: Laodicea on the Lycus was built on the site of an earlier settlement, above the Lycus river near its confluence with the Maeander. Antiochus II Theos founded it between 261 and 253 BCE in honour of his wife Laodice. According to Pliny the Elder it was first called Diospolis, "City of Zeus", and afterwards Rhoas. In 213 BCE Antiochus the Great defeated Achaeus, who had declared himself king of the region, and transported 2,000 Jewish families from Babylonia to Phrygia. After the Romans defeated the Seleucids at Magnesia in 190 BCE, the Treaty of Apamea gave western Asia Minor to Pergamon, whose territory was bequeathed to Rome in 133 BCE.

Laodicea received the title of free city, suffered in the Mithridatic Wars and recovered. Under the first emperors it was among the most flourishing commercial cities of Asia Minor, with large money transactions and an extensive trade in black wool. It was the chief city of a Roman conventus of 24 cities, and Cicero records holding assizes there about 50 BCE. An earthquake in the reign of Nero, in 60 CE, destroyed it, but its inhabitants declined imperial help and rebuilt it themselves. Byzantine writers mention it often under the Komnenian emperors: John II Komnenos took it from the Seljuks in 1119, Manuel I Komnenos fortified it in 1160, and the Seljuks sacked it in 1161. It was destroyed in the Turkish and Mongol invasions.

With a large Jewish community, Laodicea early became a seat of Christianity and a bishopric. The Epistle to the Colossians asks that its letter be read publicly at Laodicea and that another letter, to the Laodiceans, be read at Colossae. The city is one of the seven churches of Asia in the Book of Revelation. When Phrygia was divided, Laodicea became the metropolis of Phrygia Pacatiana; the last bishop is recorded in 1450, and the see is now titular.

Since 2002 Pamukkale University has excavated and restored the site, which was placed on Turkey's Tentative List of World Heritage Sites in 2013. The remains include a stadium, baths, temples, a gymnasium, two theatres and a bouleuterion. The west theatre, built in the Hellenistic period, held 8,000 spectators and was restored in 2022. The water supply used an inverted siphon of stone pipes to cross a valley. A marble block found in 2015 carries a water law of 114 CE, fining those who polluted water or damaged channels. A statue of the emperor Trajan was unearthed in 2019.
laos: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, bordered by Myanmar and China to the north-west, Vietnam to the east, Cambodia to the south-east and Thailand to the west and south-west. Its forested landscape is mostly mountains, the highest being Phou Bia at 2,818 metres. The Mekong forms part of the western boundary with Thailand, the Annamite Range makes up most of the eastern border, and there are two major plateaus, the Xiangkhoang in the north and the Bolaven in the south. The climate is mostly tropical savanna, with a rainy season from May to October.

A skull at least 46,000 years old found in Tam Pa Ling Cave in the Annamite Mountains was the oldest modern human fossil in Southeast Asia at the time of its recovery in 2009. An agricultural society developed during the 4th millennium BCE, bronze artefacts appeared around 1500 BCE and iron tools by 700 BCE. Tai-speaking groups migrated south-west from Guangxi into present-day Laos and Thailand between the 8th and 10th centuries.

Prince Fa Ngum founded the kingdom of Lan Xang, meaning a million elephants, in the 14th century. Leading 10,000 Khmer troops, he conquered principalities in the Mekong basin and captured Vientiane, and he made Theravada Buddhism the state religion. Ministers forced him into exile in 1373. Photisarath moved the capital from Luang Prabang to Vientiane in 1520 to counter the threat of a Burmese invasion, and Setthathirath, who became king in 1548, commissioned That Luang. Sourigna Vongsa expanded the borders after 1637, and when he died without an heir the kingdom split in 1707 into Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak.

Anouvong, installed by the Siamese as vassal king of Vientiane, launched an unsuccessful rebellion against Siam in 1826 under Vietnamese pressure; Vientiane was ransacked and he died a captive in Bangkok. The three kingdoms were unified under French rule in 1893 as part of French Indochina. Laos regained full independence in 1953 as a constitutional monarchy under Sisavang Vong. A civil war from 1959 to 1975 pitted the communist Pathet Lao against the Royal Lao Armed Forces, backed by the United States, and ended with the founding of the Lao People's Democratic Republic in 1975.

Laos is a unitary communist state led by the Lao People's Revolutionary Party. More than half the population is ethnic Lao, and 66 per cent were Theravada Buddhist in 2010. The country has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Luang Prabang, Vat Phou and the Plain of Jars.
lapita-pottery: Lapita pottery was typically low-fired earthenware, tempered with shells or sand and decorated with a toothed stamp. Its makers used a variety of materials and techniques, depending on what was available. It has been suggested that the designs were transferred to clay from less durable materials such as bark cloth, mats or tattoos, or the other way round. Besides decorated ware the Lapita made undecorated beakers, cooking pots and bowls. In 2003 a cemetery was discovered at Teouma on Efate Island in Vanuatu, with 25 graves containing burial jars and 36 skeletons, all headless: the skulls had been removed after burial and replaced with rings made from cone shells. Carbon dating of the shells places the cemetery's use around 1000 BCE.

The Lapita people are believed to have come from the northern Philippines, and their pottery resembles pottery from the Nagsabaran site on Luzon more than any found elsewhere. In 2011 Peter Bellwood proposed that migrants moved east from the northern Philippines into the Mariana Islands and then south into the Bismarcks, possibly with others taking different routes. On the Bismarck Archipelago the Lapita complex appears suddenly, as a fully developed horizon with no earlier stages, which suggests that a migrating population brought it.

The orthodox view, the Triple-I model of intrusion, innovation and integration, holds that Austronesian peoples moved into Near Oceania, developed new technologies there and merged with the existing populations. In 2016 DNA from four Lapita skeletons found in Vanuatu and Tonga showed descent from inhabitants of Taiwan and the northern Philippines.

Artifacts with Lapita designs later than 1,200 BCE have been found in the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia, and Lapita pottery styles from around 1000 BCE in Fiji and Western Polynesia. In Western Polynesia the pottery became less decorative and simpler over time.

The first recorded discovery was in 1909, when the Sacred Heart missionary Otto Meyer found potsherds on Watom Island exposed by a tropical storm. In 1920 William C. McKern unearthed over 1,500 potsherds on Tongatapu, and the connection between the two finds was made in 1940 with pottery from the Ile des Pins. In 1952 Edward W. Gifford and Richard Shutler Jr. excavated in New Caledonia. Archaeologists misheard a word of the local Haveke language, xapeta'a, meaning to dig a hole, and coined the name Lapita. More than 200 Lapita sites have since been found, ranging over 4,000 km from the Bismarck Archipelago to Fiji and Tonga, with Samoa as the eastern limit.
lapland-finland: Lapland is the largest and northernmost region of Finland, with an area of 100,367 square kilometres. It borders Sweden, Norway and Russia, and its borders follow the rivers Tana, Muonio and Torne. Its landscape runs from vast mires and forests in the south to fells in the north, and the highest point in Finland, 1,324 metres on Halti, lies on its border. The Arctic Circle crosses the region, so the midnight sun, the polar night and the northern lights can be seen there. Winters last about seven months. The lower course of the Tornio was the last part of Finland to be deglaciated, about 10,100 years ago.

From 1634 to 1809 Lapland was split between two counties of the Swedish Realm: the northern and western areas belonged to Västerbotten County, and the southern areas to Ostrobothnia County. In 1809 the northern and western areas were transferred to Oulu County, and Lapland Province was separated from Oulu Province in 1938.

During the Interim Peace and the start of the Continuation War the Finnish government allowed the German army to station itself in Lapland. After Finland made a separate peace with the Soviet Union in 1944, the Soviet Union demanded that Finland expel the Germans. In the resulting Lapland War almost the whole civilian population was evacuated, and the Germans used scorched earth tactics before withdrawing to Norway. Between 40 and 47 per cent of the dwellings in Lapland were destroyed, along with 417 kilometres of railway and 675 bridges, and ninety per cent of Rovaniemi was burned to the ground.

After the war the municipality of Petsamo and part of Salla were ceded to the Soviet Union, and the following decades brought rebuilding, industrialisation and fast economic growth, with large hydroelectric plants and mines. In the late 20th century the population began to decline in most of the region.

Lapland has 21 municipalities, which cooperate in a regional council, and Rovaniemi is its regional centre. It is by far the most sparsely populated part of Finland, with about 3 per cent of the country's people. The Sámi homeland, formed by the northernmost municipalities, lies within it, and Northern Sámi, Inari Sámi and Skolt Sámi are spoken there.
lapland-war: Germany and Finland had been at war with the Soviet Union since 1941, and the German 20th Mountain Army was stationed in Lapland. As early as mid-1943 the German high command planned for the possibility of a separate Finnish peace, intending to pull back northward to shield the nickel mines near Petsamo. On 9 April 1944 the withdrawal plan was named Operation Birke.

After a Soviet offensive in southern Finland in the summer of 1944 and a change of leadership in August, Finland negotiated a separate peace. The Moscow Armistice required it to break relations with Germany and to expel or disarm German troops remaining after 15 September. The Soviet Union also demanded that most of the Finnish forces be demobilised.

At first both sides tried to keep the evacuation smooth, and by 15 September a secret agreement let the Germans use Finnish transport and destroy roads and bridges behind them. Under Soviet pressure and the threat of occupation, the Finnish III Corps under Lieutenant General Hjalmar Siilasvuo opened fire on a German rearguard near Pudasjärvi on 28 September. Finnish ships landed troops at Tornio from 30 September; the battle there lasted into October.

The Germans adopted a delaying strategy of destroying and mining roads and bridges. On 13 October Generaloberst Lothar Rendulic's army ordered everything that could be used by an enemy destroyed in northern Finland. Rovaniemi burned on 14 October after the Germans destroyed government buildings and a train loaded with ammunition exploded. Fighting effectively ended in early November, and the last German soldiers left Finland on 27 April 1945.

The 20th Mountain Army withdrew most of its more than 200,000 men with their supplies. Finnish losses were 774 killed, 262 missing and about 2,904 wounded; Germany lost about 1,000 dead and 2,000 wounded, and 1,300 German prisoners were handed to the Soviet Union.

Lapland was devastated: about 14,900 buildings, some 40 to 46 percent of its property, 470 km of railway, 9,500 km of road and 675 bridges were destroyed. Reconstruction lasted until the early 1950s, and the railway network was not working again until 1957. No peace agreement was ever signed with Germany; in 1954 the Finnish government noted that the war had ended.
lapulapu: Very little is reliably known about Lapulapu. The only primary source that names him is the account of Antonio Pigafetta, who recorded the name as Çilapulapu and noted two datus of Mactan, Zula and Lapulapu. The historian Resil B. Mojares observes that no European who left a record of Magellan's voyage saw him or heard him speak. Cebuano oral tradition holds that his father was a datu named Mangal. The Aginid, a book published in 1952 by Jovito Abellana, makes him a settler from Borneo, but most Filipino historians regard it as a hoax or as imaginative fiction. The evidence points to a Visayan follower of the indigenous anito beliefs, not a Muslim, as some later traditions claim.

When Ferdinand Magellan reached the Philippines in Spanish service, Zula gave tribute to the Spanish king, but Lapulapu refused. On 27 April 1521 Magellan came to Mactan with about 60 Spaniards and boats of warriors from Rajah Humabon of Cebu. Rocks and reefs kept his ships off shore, so Magellan and 49 heavily armoured men waded in, telling Humabon's warriors to stay in their boats. According to Pigafetta, they faced about 1,500 warriors. Magellan was wounded in the leg by a poisoned arrow, was recognised as the captain and was overwhelmed and killed.

The historian William Henry Scott suggests that Magellan wrongly assumed that Humabon, as king of Cebu, ruled Mactan too, when Visayan societies were loose federations of chiefdoms. Mactan's position let its chiefs intercept ships entering Cebu's harbour, so Lapulapu may have been the more powerful. Humabon was married to Lapulapu's niece. The battle left the expedition with too few men to crew three ships, and it abandoned the Concepción. Spanish expansion into the archipelago was delayed until the expedition of Miguel López de Legazpi in 1565.

Lapulapu is regarded, retroactively, as the first Filipino hero. A shrine was built on Mactan in 1969, the town of Opon became Lapu-Lapu City, and his face appeared on the 1-centavo coin from 1967 to 1994. In 2021 an executive order fixed the spelling Lapulapu, without a hyphen, following Pigafetta's original. Local legend says he never died but was turned into stone and still guards the sea of Mactan.
larache: Larache stands on the south bank of the Loukkos River, where it meets the Atlantic, roughly 80 kilometres southwest of Tangier. It has a compact medina beside the river and a larger new town, laid out by the Spanish colonial administration after 1911, which stretches southwards over the coastal plateau. The climate is Mediterranean, with hot summers and wet, cool winters. Across the river to the north lies Lixus, an ancient city developed by the Phoenicians over an earlier Bronze Age settlement.

Lixus later passed from Carthaginian domination to the Kingdom of Mauretania and reached its height under King Juba II. Some Greek writers placed the mythical garden of the Hesperides and a sanctuary of Hercules there. Larache itself is not mentioned in Arabic sources until the 13th century. It was founded by the Idrisite Banu 'Arus, who called it al-'Ara'ish, trellis of grape vines, after the abundant vines. The Almohad caliph Ya'qub al-Mansur built a fortress there in the late 12th century, and the Spanish made a successful raid on the city in 1270.

In 1471 Portuguese settlers from Asilah and Tangier drove out the inhabitants, and the site stayed empty until the Saadi sultan Mohammed ash-Sheikh repopulated it and built a stronghold above the river. The Kasbah, built in 1491 by Moulay en Nasser, later became a pirate stronghold. The town passed to the Spanish in 1610, who used the port mainly as a trading stop and never really administered the town, and Moulay Ismail conquered it in 1689. A French fleet failed in the Larache expedition of 1765, and in 1829 Austrian ships bombarded the city as a punishment for Moroccan piracy. Spain occupied Larache in 1911 and held it until 1956.

Larache is one of the more important cities of the Tanger-Tetouan-Al Hoceima region, and its commune had 133,731 inhabitants in the 2024 census. Its landmarks include the Plaza de España, the old medina with its Kasbah, and Port Lixus. The writer Jean Genet, who lived there for several years and asked to be buried in the town, lies in its Spanish cemetery, as does the Spanish novelist Juan Goytisolo. Schools teach in Arabic, French and Spanish.
larino: Larino lies in the fertile valley of the Biferno River in Molise. The old town, seen from the mountains, is shaped like a bird's wing, and the new town, called Piano San Leonardo, is built on a mountainside. The place has been continuously inhabited for millennia. It was originally settled by the Dauni and Frentani tribes of southern Italy, and then came under the control of the Oscan civilisation.

The Romans defeated Hannibal at Larino in 217 BCE. The city was later incorporated into the Roman Empire, classified first as a municipium and then as a colonia, and added to the Secunda Regio, which was Apulia. Pompey the Great is said to have joined two of his legions encamped at Larinum when he and Julius Caesar fought for power. The city's name appears in the works of Livy and Pliny, and an important senatus consultum restricting public performances by members of the Roman upper classes was found nearby.
The Roman city lay along the main road to the south-east, which began on the coast at Histonium and ran from Larinum eastward to Sipontum, with a branch to Bovianum Vetus.

The modern city was built in the 14th century, after the old one, about 1.5 kilometres away, was destroyed in an earthquake having repeatedly been sacked by the Saracens. In 1656 a plague nearly wiped out the city, and its 373 survivors were prepared to abandon the settlement until Bishop Giuseppe Catalano persuaded them to stay. In the 1950s and 1960s the town faced a large exodus because of the extreme poverty of the Molise region, and a large community of Larinesi lives abroad.

The elliptical Roman amphitheatre was built in the 1st century CE by a prominent citizen of Larino who had made his fortune in Rome. Its arena could seat about 12,000 spectators, and the structure was built into a natural declivity in the terrain.

The cathedral, made a minor basilica in 1928, has a portal decorated with lions, gryphons and a Crucifixion lunette, surmounted by a Gothic rose window. Across from it stands the Galuppi Tower of 1312, which was part of the old town's defences and incorporates reused ancient stone. The Palazzo Ducale, now the seat of municipal government, was probably built as a Norman castle. The festival of San Pardo, held on 25 to 27 May, features carts decorated with hand-made flowers and drawn by white oxen.
larnaca: Larnaca stands on the south-eastern coast of Cyprus, on the ruins of the ancient city of Kition. The name comes from the Greek larnax, meaning coffer, box or chest, and by extension cinerary urn or sarcophagus. An informal explanation links it to the many sarcophagi found in the area. The state archaeologist Sophocles Hadjisavvas notes that a consul of the last quarter of the 19th century claimed to have explored more than 3,000 tombs there. The city is also called Skala, Greek for ladder, after its historic port. The Salt Lake near it fills with water in winter and is visited by flamingoes from November until the end of March.

Kition was first established as a city-kingdom in the 13th century BCE. New pottery and architecture between 1200 BCE and 1000 BCE are read as signs of political change and of the arrival of the Achaeans, the first Greek colonists, and Phoenicians settled the area about the same time. The Phoenicians rebuilt the city, which became a centre of Phoenician culture, and the remains include cyclopean walls, a complex of five temples and a naval port. In the first millennium BCE it was conquered by a series of powers: the Assyrian Empire, then Egypt, and then the Persian Achaemenid Empire.

The Athenian general Cimon died at sea in 450 BCE while supporting a revolt against Persian rule on Cyprus, and on his deathbed he urged his officers to hide his death from allies and Persians alike. Zeno of Citium, founder of the Stoic school, was born in Kition in 334 BCE and studied philosophy in Athens.

Strong earthquakes struck in 76 CE and the year after, and again in 322 and 342, which destroyed Kition, Salamis and Pafos. Kition's harbour silted up, probably as a result of earthquakes, deforestation and overgrazing, and the population moved to the seafront farther south. From 1571, in the Ottoman period, the commercial port stood at Skala, the shore south of Larnaca Castle.

Larnaca is the capital of the Larnaca District. Its landmarks include the Church of Saint Lazarus, Hala Sultan Tekke, the Kamares Aqueduct, also called the Bekir Pasha Aqueduct, Larnaca Castle and the Larnaca District Archaeological Museum. The seafront promenade, Finikoudes, is lined with palm trees, and a bust of Cimon stands on it. Larnaca International Airport, the busiest on the island, lies in the neighbouring village of Dromolaxia, and the city has a seaport and a marina.
larsa: Larsa was a city-state of ancient Sumer and the centre of the cult of the sun god Utu, whose temple was the E-babbar. Its site, now Tell as-Senkereh, lies about 25 km south-east of Uruk in Iraq's Dhi Qar Governorate, near the east bank of the Shatt-en-Nil canal. The city was linked in antiquity to the biblical Ellasar, and Berossos called it Larancha. It is thought to be the source of a number of tablets of Babylonian mathematics, among them Plimpton 322, which contains patterns of Pythagorean triples. Its remains cover about 200 hectares.

Larsa appears on proto-cuneiform lexical lists from the Uruk IV period, in the late 4th millennium BCE, and for most of its history it was chiefly a cult site of Utu. Eannatum of Lagash, around 2500–2400 BCE, annexed it, and his nephew Entemena cancelled the debts of its citizens. The Temple Hymns of Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad, mention it, and Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur recorded rebuilding the E-babbar.

After the Third Dynasty of Ur collapsed around 2004 BCE, Ishbi-Erra set up a government at Isin and recaptured Ur, Uruk and Lagash, to which Larsa was subject. An Amorite governor of Larsa, Gungunum, broke with Isin, founded an independent dynasty and captured Ur. Because Larsa was the main centre of trade through the Persian Gulf, Isin lost a profitable route. His successors Abisare and Sumuel cut Isin off from its canals. Larsa never held a large territory, but under Rim-Sin I it controlled about ten to fifteen other city-states, and Mashkan-shapir served as a second capital.

After Hammurabi of Babylon defeated Rim-Sin I, Larsa became a minor site. It remained active under the Neo-Babylonian, Achaemenid and Hellenistic rulers, the E-babbar burned in the 2nd century BCE, and the site was abandoned by the 1st century BCE.

William Loftus first excavated the site, in 1850 for less than a month, and recovered bricks of Nebuchadnezzar II that identified it as Larsa. Edgar James Banks found in 1905 that local people were looting it. André Parrot worked there in 1933, and an expedition led by J.-L. Huot dug for 13 seasons between 1976 and 1991, concentrating on the Neo-Babylonian E-babbar. Excavations resumed in 2019 and have traced a large system of internal canals and a port area.
las-anod: Las Anod is the administrative capital of the Sool region, lying in the Nugaal Valley along trade routes between Somaliland and Puntland. The city is almost surrounded by hills and has considerable water resources, which has drawn people from the generally arid regions around it. It has a hot arid climate with almost no rain except erratically in May and October. It is inhabited mainly by people of the Somali ethnic group, in particular the Dhulbahante sub-clan of the Harti Darod; the the UNFPA estimated the population of the district at 156,438 in 2014. Most of its goods arrive through the ports of Berbera and Bosaso.

On 31 July 1903 thirty British scouts fought for two hours with the advance scouts of a party of 128 followers of the Mullah, a few miles west of Heli Madu near Las Anod. In the British protectorate era the town was capital of the Nogal District, the forerunner of Sool. The United Somali Party was founded there to form a non-Isaaq axis, and from 1959 to 1961 it was the seat of Garad Ali's party. On 15 October 1969 Somali President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke was shot dead by one of his bodyguards while visiting the city, and on 21 October a bloodless military coup led by Major General Mohamed Siad Barre seized power.

The city is disputed between Puntland, whose claim rests on kinship between the Dhulbahante and the Majeerteen, and Somaliland, whose claim rests on the border of the former British Somaliland Protectorate. Somaliland forces took it from Puntland forces in the Battle of Las Anod in 2007. In December 2022 the assassination of a local politician led to confrontations in which 20 protesters died, and in February 2023 war broke out between Somaliland and Khatumo State forces. Somaliland blamed al-Shabaab, while Nicholas Delaunay of the International Crisis Group said no concrete evidence had been provided. By 23 February the United Nations reported more than 185,000 people displaced. On 25 August 2023 Khatumo State forces drove Somaliland's forces out of Las Anod.

Las Anod is the centre of political power of the Dhulbahante clan. Nugaal University, founded in 2004, was the first institution of higher learning established in the area, and its first four-year students graduated in September 2009. Ilays National University and Gollis University were established in 2015. The city was the capital of Khatumo State until 2017, and its notable natives include the runner Abdi Bile.
las-medulas: Las Médulas lies near the town of Ponferrada in the comarca of El Bierzo, in the province of León in Castile and León. It was the most important gold mine in the Roman Empire and the largest open-pit gold mine there. The area now in the Roman province of Hispania Tarraconensis was conquered by the emperor Augustus in 25 BCE. Before the conquest the indigenous inhabitants took gold from alluvial deposits, and large-scale production did not begin until the second half of the 1st century CE.

The landscape came from ruina montium, the wrecking of the mountains, a technique of hydraulic mining described by Pliny the Elder, who was a procurator in the region in 74 CE and may have written from direct observation. A mountain was undermined with large quantities of water, brought by interbasin transfer along at least seven long aqueducts that tapped streams in the La Cabrera district, where rainfall is relatively high. The same aqueducts washed the extensive alluvial gold deposits. Pliny also describes washing ore on riffle tables to collect the heavy gold particles. Open-cast work used fire-setting, building fires against the rock and quenching them with water, and the weakened rock was swept away by waves of water.

Pliny stated that 20,000 Roman pounds, or 6,560 kg, of gold were taken each year, and that the workings, which employed 60,000 free workers, produced 5 million Roman pounds in 250 years. He also wrote that galleries driven for long distances were worked by lamplight, and that miners did not see daylight for months, and that collapses crushed men at work. Aerial surveys using LIDAR in 2014 confirmed the wide extent of the Roman works. Ice cores from Greenland suggest that atmospheric lead from mining peaked in the Roman period and was not reached again until the Industrial Revolution, some 1,700 years later.

Parts of the aqueducts remain well preserved in steep places, and some have rock-cut inscriptions. Claude Domergue carried out the main early research, and since 1988 a group of the Spanish Council for Scientific Research has studied the area systematically, treating it as a cultural landscape. Las Médulas became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997, and the Las Médulas Foundation oversees the cultural park. The delegate of Thailand opposed the designation, because he considered the site the result of destructive human activity.
las-meninas: In 17th-century Spain painters rarely enjoyed high status, since painting was regarded as a craft rather than an art such as poetry or music. Velázquez nonetheless rose through the court of Philip IV and in February 1651 was appointed palace chamberlain, a post that brought status but left him few works in his last eight years, mostly portraits of the royal family. The king allowed him to include himself in Las Meninas although he resisted being portrayed in old age. In the early 1650s Philip gave Velázquez the main room of the late Balthasar Charles's quarters, then the palace museum, as a studio; the painting is set there, in the Royal Alcázar of Madrid.

The five-year-old Infanta Margaret Theresa, then the only surviving child of Philip IV and Mariana of Austria, stands in the centre foreground. Two ladies-in-waiting, or meninas, attend her: Doña Isabel de Velasco, who is about to curtsy, and Doña María Agustina Sarmiento de Sotomayor, who kneels to offer her a drink. To the right are the dwarfs Mari Bárbola and Nicolás Pertusato, who nudges a mastiff with his foot, and the chaperone Doña Marcela de Ulloa speaking to a bodyguard. Behind them Velázquez portrays himself at a large canvas, and a mirror at the back reflects the upper bodies of the king and queen.

Nine figures appear, eleven counting the reflections, yet they fill only the lower half of the canvas. Three figures, Velázquez, the infanta and Mari Bárbola, appear to look straight at the viewer. The mirror places the king and queen on the viewer's side of the picture, although some scholars have speculated that their image is a reflection of the painting Velázquez is working on. The painting has been cut down on both sides and was damaged in the 1734 fire that destroyed the Alcázar; the infanta's left cheek was almost entirely repainted afterward.

Early inventories called the painting La Familia, and it entered the Prado at its founding in 1819; the Prado catalogue first listed it as Las Meninas in 1843. Luca Giordano described it as the theology of painting, and in 1827 Sir Thomas Lawrence called it the true philosophy of the art. Michel Foucault opened The Order of Things with a long analysis of it. Svetlana Alpers reads it as Velázquez's claim that painting is a liberal rather than a mechanical art, a point that mattered because the rules of the Order of Santiago excluded those in mechanical occupations. Goya etched a print of it in 1778 and modelled Charles IV of Spain and His Family on it.
lashio: Lashio is the largest city and the capital of northern Shan State, about 200 kilometres north-east of Mandalay. It stands on a low mountain spur overlooking the valley of the Yaw River, and Loi Leng, the highest mountain of the Shan Hills, lies 45 kilometres to the south-east. The population is mostly Shan, Chinese and Bamar. It grew from about 5,000 in 1960 to 88,590 in 1983 and was estimated at about 131,000 in 2009. It is the home of Lashio University and several other colleges.

Before British rule Lashio was the centre of authority for the northern Shan States, but the Burmese post lay close to the Nam Yao, in an old Chinese fortified camp. The valley had been very populous until a rebellion started by the sawbwa of Hsenwi, about ten years before the British occupation, ruined it. British colonial rule in this part of the country began in 1887, and the railway from Mandalay reached Lashio in 1903. In 1900 the town had a European station with a court house, a military police post, a bazaar, and a native station where Shans, Burmans, Hindus and Muslims lived in separate quarters, with reserves for the temporary residences of the five sawbwas of the northern Shan States.

Lashio became important in the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Burma campaign of the Second World War as the Burmese terminus of the Burma Road. Japanese forces took it on 29 April 1942, and the Allies liberated it on 7 March 1945.

Lashio lies at the end of the Burma Road and at the terminus of the Mandalay–Lashio railway, and the Goteik viaduct, the highest bridge in Myanmar, is near it. It has a large Chinese population and since 2000 has been important for border trade with China. Landmarks include the Yan Tine Aung Pagoda, the Mansu Shan Monastery and a Chinese temple that many visit at Chinese New Year.

During Operation 1027 of the Myanmar civil war, the Ta'ang National Liberation Army and other rebel forces took towns around Lashio. After the ceasefire collapsed, the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and its allies attacked the city in the Battle of Lashio and took it in August 2024. A Chinese-brokered ceasefire was agreed on 20 January 2025, and in April 2025 officials of the State Administration Council returned to the city as the MNDAA withdrew, reinstating the council's administration by 21 April.
lastovo: Lastovo, also known as Lagosta, is an archipelago and municipality of 46 islands in Dubrovnik-Neretva County, with a land area of about 53 square kilometres. The main island is about 9.8 kilometres long and up to 5.8 kilometres wide, lying thirteen kilometres south of Korčula in the central Dalmatian archipelago, one of the most remote inhabited islands in the Adriatic. The town of Lastovo is built on the steep banks of a natural amphitheatre facing away from the sea, which is unusual among Adriatic islands. About 60 per cent of the island is forested, mostly with holm oaks and Aleppo pines.

Stephanus of Byzantium, drawing on the 4th-century BCE historian Theopompus, called the island Ladesta, a name with an Illyrian suffix. The Romans named it Augusta Insula and left villa rustica estates and water catchments known as lokve. In the Middle Ages the name became Lagusta or Lagosta, and the Slavic suffix gave Lastovo. About 950 Constantine VII Porphyrogenitos mentioned it as Lastobon. In 998 the Venetian Doge Pietro Orseolo II launched operations against Croatian and Neretvian pirates, which ended in 1000 with the destruction of the town. The inhabitants then built a new town on an inner hill, away from the coast.

In 1252 the islanders joined the Republic of Ragusa after it promised to honour their internal autonomy, an agreement codified in the Ragusa Statute of 1272. Lastovo's own Statute followed in 1310, with a council of 20 members holding office for life. In 1486 the council's authority passed to the Parliament of the Republic, and after rebellions in 1602 and 1652 the island lost its autonomy.

France took Ragusa in 1806 and abolished it in 1808, and Lastovo was included in the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy. The Royal Navy captured it in early 1813, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna awarded it to the Austrian Empire. Italy received Lagosta under the Rapallo agreement of 1920, and its peak population of about 2,000 was reached under Italian rule. Afterwards it was part of Yugoslavia and then of independent Croatia.

The municipality has 792 inhabitants, 94.7 per cent of them ethnic Croats. The island is noted for its Venetian Renaissance architecture of the 15th and 16th centuries and for many small churches. Its major cultural event is the Poklade carnival. In 2006 the Croatian Government designated the island and its archipelago a nature park.
laszlo-rajk: László Rajk was born on 8 March 1909 in Székelyudvarhely, the ninth of eleven children in a family of Transylvanian Saxons. He joined the Communist Party of Hungary at an early age, was expelled from his university for his political ideas, and became a building worker. In 1936 he went to the Spanish Civil War and became commissar of the Rakosi Battalion of the XIII International Brigade. He was interned in France until 1941, when he returned to Hungary and became Secretary of the party's underground Central Committee. Arrested by the Arrow Cross Party in December 1944, he was saved by the intercession of his brother Endre and released on 13 May 1945.

Rajk was appointed Minister of the Interior on 20 March 1946. In that post he organized the party's secret police, the ÁVH, and became directly responsible for it. Under the cover of struggle against fascism and reaction he prohibited and liquidated about 1,500 religious, nationalist and other groups and set up the first show trials. On 5 August 1948 he became Minister of Foreign Affairs. Mátyás Rákosi, who regarded him as a threat, had him arrested on 30 May 1949 on trumped-up charges.

Rajk was accused of being a Titoist spy and agent of western imperialism. He was tortured and promised acquittal if he took responsibility for the charges. At his trial in Budapest from 16 to 24 September 1949 he confessed to all of them, but the prosecution demanded the heaviest sentences. He, Tibor Szönyi and András Szalai were sentenced to death, and Rajk was executed on 15 October 1949. The trial opened Stalin's anti-Titoist drive. On 28 March 1956 he was rehabilitated, and on 6 October 1956 he was reburied before 100,000 mourners, a precursor to the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, which began on 23 October.
lata-mangeshkar: Lata Mangeshkar was born Hemalata Deenanath Mangeshkar on 28 September 1929 in Indore, then the capital of a princely state in British India. Her father, Deenanath Mangeshkar, was a Marathi and Konkani classical singer and theatre actor who took his surname from his ancestral village of Mangeshi in Goa. When Lata was 13, in 1942, her father died of heart disease. Master Vinayak, the owner of the Navyug Chitrapat film company and a close friend of the family, took care of them and helped her begin a career as a singer and actress. She disliked the acting that the industry first required of her.

During the 1950s she sang for most of the music directors of the period, among them Anil Biswas, Shankar Jaikishan, Naushad Ali and S. D. Burman. She recorded in Sinhala and Telugu in 1955, and she sang 185 songs in Bengali. Her song Pyar Kiya To Darna Kya from Mughal-e-Azam, composed by Naushad, in 1960 remains well known. On 27 January 1963, against the background of the Sino-Indian War, she sang the patriotic song Aye Mere Watan Ke Logo in the presence of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, which is said to have brought him to tears.

In the 1970s she recorded many songs with Laxmikant–Pyarelal and Rahul Dev Burman. She recorded in more than thirty-six Indian languages and a few foreign ones, mainly Hindustani, Bengali and Marathi. In 1974 she became the first Indian playback singer to perform at the Royal Albert Hall in London. She also composed for several Marathi films under the pseudonym Anand Ghan and produced four films. She recorded barefoot, as a mark of respect for the recording studio, which she considered a temple.

Mangeshkar received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1989 and the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in 2001, becoming the second singer to receive it. In 2009 France made her an officer of the Legion of Honour. She won four Filmfare Best Female Playback Awards, and in 1969 she gave up the Filmfare award in order to promote new talent. She died of multiple organ dysfunction on 6 February 2022, aged 92, after treatment for COVID-19 and pneumonia. Historians note that her soprano style became the industry standard, and that more traditional singers such as Shamshad Begum saw their work decline, a claim she consistently denied.
latakia: Latakia is the principal port city of Syria and the capital of the Latakia Governorate, on the Mediterranean coast. It stands on the Ras Ziyarah promontory, which has a long history of occupation: a Phoenician city called Ramitha was located there. Seleucus I Nicator named the Greek city Laodikeia on the Coast in honour of his mother, Laodice, and in Latin the name became Laodicea ad Mare. Strabo described it as a most beautifully built city with a good harbour, whose mountain slopes were covered with vines that supplied much of the wine drunk in Alexandria.

Pompey conquered the city, along with most of Syria, in the 1st century BCE, and Julius Caesar declared it a free polis. The emperor Septimius Severus rewarded it with the title of Metropolis in the 2nd century CE, exempted it from taxation, fortified it and for a few years made it the capital of Roman Syria. It fell to Muslim rule in the 7th century, when the general Ubadah ibn al-Samit attacked it during the conquest of Syria.

From 750 to 968 the city lost importance because it lay on the border between the Byzantine Empire and the Abbasid Caliphate. The Byzantines under John I Tzimiskes recaptured it in 970, but the Fatimids took it in 980. The Seljuks took it in 1086, and during the First Crusade Raymond of Saint-Gilles captured it in 1098. It was later ruled by the Ayyubids and the Mamluks, and came under the Ottomans after the Battle of Marj Dabiq in 1516.

Under the Ottomans it had only about 1,400 to 1,700 inhabitants in the 16th century. From the late 17th century the Ibn al-Matarji family ruled it, and the growth of the tobacco industry helped the town to develop rapidly in the 18th century. After the First World War the city was assigned to the French mandate of Syria and became the capital of the territory of the Alawites, the Alawite State, whose creation has often been interpreted as a divide and rule strategy against anti-colonial nationalism.

Little of the classical city survives, many of its buildings having been destroyed by earthquakes. A Roman triumphal arch with four entrances and the Colonnade of Bacchus remain, and the National Museum, in a 16th-century Ottoman caravanserai, holds inscribed tablets from Ugarit. The Port of Latakia, begun in 1950, is the main seaport of Syria.
late-bronze-age-collapse: The Late Bronze Age, from about 1550 to 1200 BCE, was marked by advanced civilizations with extensive trade networks. The Egyptians, Hittites, Mesopotamians and Mycenaeans built monumental architecture, worked metals and kept written records, and a flourishing trade in copper, timber, pottery and farm goods, together with diplomatic ties, deepened their interdependence. Most of these powers relied on a palace economy, in which wealth was concentrated in a central bureaucracy and then redistributed according to the ruler's wishes. This web of dependencies, together with the rigidity of the palace system, exposed the societies to the cascading effects of distant disturbances.

The German historian Arnold Hermann Ludwig Heeren first dated the collapse to about 1200 BCE. The Mycenaean palaces did not survive, and the palace economy of Greece and Anatolia gave way to small village cultures of the Greek Dark Ages. In Anatolia the Hittite Empire was already fragmenting under famine, plague and civil war, and its capital Hattusa was burned at an unknown date in this period, though it may in fact have been abandoned. Ugarit was destroyed, and Egypt faced attacks by Libyans and the Sea Peoples. Ramesses III defeated them, but the expense strained the Egyptian treasury, and the New Kingdom shrank considerably by the mid-twelfth century BCE.

Earlier historians believed that almost every city between Pylos and Gaza was violently destroyed. More recent research by Jesse Millek found that, of 148 sites said to have been destroyed around 1200 BCE, 94 were misdated, assumed on little evidence or never destroyed at all, and some scholars now see the collapse as more limited in scale than once thought. Assyria and Elam survived in weakened forms, and the Phoenician city-states gained autonomy as Egyptian and Assyrian power in West Asia declined.

Many causes have been proposed, among them drought, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, disease, invasions by the Sea Peoples, the spread of ironworking and changes in warfare that ended the dominance of chariots. None has won agreement, and the causes were probably several. Joseph Tainter's systems theory holds that rising complexity left societies unable to rebuild once they were seriously disrupted. Tree rings in Anatolia show a severe dry period from about 1198 to 1196 BCE.

Robert Drews called the collapse arguably the worst disaster in ancient history. Later Greek tradition remembered a lost golden age, and Hesiod set the Age of Heroes between the Bronze Age and the cruel Age of Iron. Slow changes in metallurgy then led to the Iron Age of the first millennium BCE across Europe, Asia and Africa.
late-middle-ages: The term refers to the last of three periods of the Middle Ages, after the early and High Middle Ages. Leonardo Bruni was the first historian to use this threefold division, in his History of the Florentine People of 1442, and Flavio Biondo used a similar framework in his Decades of History. The division became standard after the German historian Christoph Cellarius published his Universal History in 1683. Some historians, particularly in Italy, prefer not to speak of a late Middle Ages at all, and see the High Middle Ages passing straight into the Renaissance and the modern era.

Around 1300 to 1350 the Medieval Warm Period gave way to the Little Ice Age. The colder climate caused agricultural crises, the first known as the Great Famine of 1315–1317, and later came the plagues, above all the Black Death, for which estimates of the death rate range from one third to as much as sixty per cent. By about 1420 recurring plagues and famines may have reduced Europe's population to no more than a third of what it had been a century earlier, and it took 150 years to regain the level of 1300. Peasant uprisings such as the Jacquerie and the Peasants' Revolt, the Hundred Years' War between England and France and the Western Schism of 1378 to 1417 added to the strain.

Military practice changed. Battles such as Courtrai in 1302, Bannockburn in 1314 and Morgarten in 1315 showed that feudal cavalry had lost its advantage to well-equipped infantry, and the English longbow served them against the French. Cannons used as siege weapons altered the design of fortifications. In trade, Italy saw a commercial revolution in the late 13th and early 14th centuries, with new forms of partnership, insurance, bills of exchange and double-entry bookkeeping. The Hanseatic League peaked in the 14th century and declined in the fifteenth.

The century also brought progress in the arts and sciences. Humanism challenged scholasticism, the early 14th-century painter Giotto prefigured Renaissance art, and in 15th-century Florence patrons such as the Medici supported painters and sculptors. William of Ockham insisted that reason and faith be kept apart. The fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453 sent Byzantine scholars to the West, and printing spread learning. Ottoman expansion cut off trade with the East and drove Europeans to seek new routes, leading to Columbus's voyage to the Americas in 1492 and Vasco da Gama's to India in 1498. Many scholars therefore see the period as the end of the Middle Ages, though the division is somewhat artificial, since ancient learning was never entirely absent from European society.
later-zhou: The Later Zhou was a short-lived imperial dynasty and the last of the Five Dynasties that controlled most of northern China during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. It followed the Later Han, a regime ruled by Shatuo Turks, and was succeeded by the Northern Song. Its founder, Guo Wei, a Han Chinese, had been Assistant Military Commissioner at the Later Han court. After Liu Chengyou, a teenager, came to the Later Han throne in 948, Guo Wei led a successful coup and declared himself emperor of the new Later Zhou on New Year's Day in 951.

Guo Wei, posthumously Emperor Taizu, was the first Han Chinese ruler of northern China since 923. He is regarded as an able leader who attempted reforms to lighten the burdens of the peasantry, but he died of illness in 954 after three years. His adoptive son Chai Rong, also called Guo Rong and posthumously Emperor Shizong, came to the throne. His reign was effective, with victories over the Southern Tang in 956, though efforts to dislodge the Northern Han in the north proved ineffective. He died of illness on campaign in 959.

Shizong issued the Zhouyuan Tongbao cash coins from 955. They were cast from the bronze statues of 3,336 Buddhist temples, and citizens had to hand in their bronze utensils, mirrors excepted. He also sent a fleet of junks to Korea to trade silk for copper. When reproached, he is said to have remarked that the Buddha would not mind the sacrifice.

Guo Rong was succeeded by his seven-year-old son. Soon afterwards Zhao Kuangyin usurped the throne and declared himself emperor of the Great Song dynasty, which eventually reunited China and brought the southern states and the Northern Han under its control by 979. The Zhouyuan Tongbao coins later gained a reputation for magical powers because they were made from Buddhist statues, and charms modelled on them were said to cure malaria and help women in difficult labour.
lateran-treaty: During the unification of Italy in the mid-19th century the Papal States under Pope Pius IX resisted incorporation into the new nation. The Kingdom of Italy occupied Romagna in 1860, leaving the pope only Lazio, and annexed Latium, including Rome, in 1870. For the following sixty years relations between the papacy and the Italian government were hostile.

Under the Law of Guarantees of 1871 the Italian government offered Pius IX and his successors the use, but not sovereignty, of the Vatican and Lateran Palaces and a yearly income of 3,250,000 lire. The Holy See refused, on the grounds that the pope's spiritual jurisdiction required clear independence from any political power, and each pope thereafter considered himself a prisoner in the Vatican.

Negotiations began in 1926 between the Holy See and the fascist government led by Benito Mussolini. The agreements take their name from the Lateran Palace, where they were signed on 11 February 1929, and the Italian Parliament ratified them on 7 June 1929. They are often presented as three instruments: a treaty of 27 articles, a financial convention of three articles and a concordat of 45 articles.

The political treaty recognised the full sovereignty of the Holy See in Vatican City. The pope was pledged to perpetual neutrality in international relations and to abstention from mediation unless all parties requested it. In its first article Italy reaffirmed the principle of the 1848 constitution that the Catholic, Apostolic and Roman religion was the only religion of the state. The financial convention settled all claims of the Holy See arising from the loss of the Papal States, for a sum less than Italy had offered in 1871.

The Italian racial laws of 1938 prohibited marriages between Jews and non-Jews, including Catholics. The Vatican regarded this as a violation of the concordat, which specified that marriages performed by the Catholic Church would always be considered valid by civil authorities.

The constitution of the Italian Republic, adopted in 1948, states that relations between the state and the Catholic Church are regulated by the Lateran Treaties. In 1984 the concordat was significantly revised, and both sides declared that Catholicism as the sole religion of the Italian state was no longer in force. Vatican City remains a distinct sovereign entity.
latgale: Latgale, also called Latgalia, is one of the Historical Latvian Lands. It lies north of the Daugava River, has an area of 14,547 square kilometres and is landlocked, bordering Russia and Belarus. It is known as the land of lakes: Lake Rāzna is the largest in the region and Lake Drīdzis the deepest in Latvia. The largest city is Daugavpils, and Rēzekne is often called the heart of Latgale. The region has a large Russian population, many of them Old Believers, and Belarusian and Polish minorities.

The territory was first populated by the eastern Baltic Latgalian tribe. In the 10th to 12th centuries two principalities, Jersika and Atzele, existed there. Jersika allied with the Principality of Polotsk and Lithuanian dukes against the Bishopric of Livonia and was defeated in 1209; its remainder became a vassal state and in 1239, after the death of King Visvaldis, was absorbed into the territory of the Livonian Order. Livonian knights began the castle of Wolkenburg near Lake Rāzna in 1263, the oldest order stronghold in the region.

During the Livonian War Latgale passed to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, which was incorporated into the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569. Ivan IV of Russia annexed it in 1577 but gave up his claims in 1582. Most of the Duchy of Livonia went to the Swedish Empire in 1621, but Latgale stayed under Polish-Lithuanian rule as the Inflanty Voivodeship, which began the region as it is known today. The Latgalian language was influenced by Polish and developed apart from the Latvian of other regions. Russia annexed Latgale in 1772 after the First Partition of Poland.

Russification from 1865 included a ban on printing Latgalian in the Latin script, lifted in 1904. In January 1920 Latvian and Polish forces defeated the Soviet 15th Army at Daugavpils, and under the Latvian–Soviet Peace Treaty Latgale joined the Republic of Latvia. The Soviet Union occupied it in 1940 and Nazi Germany in 1941, and the Soviet Union again from 1944.

Latgale is predominantly Catholic, a legacy of Polish–Lithuanian rule, while the rest of Latvia is mostly Lutheran. The Basilica of the Assumption at Aglona, built in 1780, is one of the eight international shrines recognised by the Holy See and draws pilgrims each 15 August.
