Latgale has long been a centre of pottery, and works by Andrejs Paulāns and Polikarps Vilcāns won a gold medal at the 1937 Paris Exhibition.
lathe: The lathe is an ancient tool. There is tenuous evidence for a turned artefact at a Mycenaean Greek site as early as the 13th or 14th century BCE, but clear evidence begins in the 6th century BCE. In China, during the Warring States period, rotary lathes were used about 400 BCE to sharpen tools and weapons on an industrial scale. Pliny describes the use of a lathe for turning soft stone in his Natural History.

Precision metal-cutting lathes developed organically in the lead-up to the Industrial Revolution, with many inventors contributing, and they were critical to the manufacture of the mechanical inventions of that period. The literature makes many claims for the person who invented the precision lathe.

The most common design is the universal or parallel lathe, built on a bed, usually a horizontal beam, with a headstock holding the spindle and a tailstock that can be moved to suit the length of the work. A workpiece held between the two centres is supported at both ends and can take more force from the tool. Work held only at the headstock, on a faceplate or in a chuck, is called face work and must be cut more gently. Re-mounting the piece on a new axis allows eccentric turning, a technique used for camshafts and some chair legs.

Woodworking lathes are the oldest variety apart from the potter's wheel, and all others descend from them. The turner shapes the wood with hand-held tools resting on a tool-rest and then smooths it with sandpaper. In a metalworking lathe a hardened cutting tool fixed to a tool-post or turret is moved against the work by lead-screws, and the same machines cut threads. Thomas Blanchard's copying lathe, which reproduced a pattern, revolutionised gun stock making in the 1820s, and Andrey Nartov designed a copying lathe for ornamental turning, now in the Hermitage Museum, for making medals and guilloche patterns.

Other kinds serve other trades. Watchmakers' lathes turn parts such as balance staffs, and the original watchmaker's turns was a simple dead-centre lathe whose workpiece was rotated by a bow wrapped around it. Glass-working lathes turn a hollow vessel over a flame, and metal-spinning lathes press sheet metal over a mandrel. Immanuel Nobel invented the rotary lathe that peels logs into veneer, and recording lathes cut the grooves of wax cylinders and discs.
latifundium: The word comes from the Latin latus, spacious, and fundus, farm or estate. A latifundium was a great landed estate specialising in agriculture for sale: grain, olive oil or wine. Such estates were characteristic of Magna Graecia and Sicily, Egypt, north-west Africa and Hispania Baetica. They were the closest approximation to industrialised agriculture in antiquity, and their economics depended on slavery. Each included a villa rustica, often with a luxurious residence for the owner, and the work relied on a large number of slaves, sometimes kept in an ergastulum. They produced livestock, olive oil, grain, garum and wine for profit, although Rome still had to import grain, from Sicily and North Africa in the Republic and from Egypt under the Empire.

The basis of the latifundia in southern Italy and Hispania was the ager publicus, state-owned land confiscated from conquered peoples from the 3rd century BCE. As much as a third of the arable land of a new province was taken and leased out, at least in theory by competitive auction. From the early 1st century BCE agricultural colonies founded to reward army veterans created smaller holdings, which large landowners, mainly patricians, bought up in times of economic distress. Efforts to reverse this by agrarian laws were generally unsuccessful. Land organised in latifundia defined the Roman senatorial class, since it was their only socially acceptable source of wealth, and senators paid no land tax.

Larger estates achieved greater economies of scale, and owners reinvested their profits in neighbouring smaller farms, which could not compete, in an ancient precursor of agribusiness. Pliny the Elder (23 or 24 to 79 CE) was distressed to see only slaves working the land, not the sturdy farmers who had been the backbone of the Republic's army. He argued that the latifundia had ruined Italy and would ruin the provinces, and reported that six owners once held half the province of Africa, which may be rhetorical exaggeration.

Landless peasants moved to Rome and depended on state subsidies, though some became tenants. The system fell into crisis between the 1st and 2nd centuries as conquests slowed and the supply of slaves dwindled. Latifundia dominated Sicily from medieval times until land reform of 1950 to 1962, and the Portuguese and Spanish borrowed the word for large colonial grants such as fazendas and haciendas.
latin: Latin is a classical language of the Italic branch of the Indo-European languages, originally spoken by the Latins in Latium, the lower Tiber area around Rome. Through the expansion of the Roman Republic it became the dominant language of the Italian Peninsula and then of the Roman Empire. The earliest known form, Old Latin, was spoken from the Roman Kingdom, traditionally founded in 753 BCE, through the later Republic until 75 BCE. It is attested in inscriptions and in some of the earliest surviving literary works, such as the comedies of Plautus and Terence. The Latin alphabet was devised from the Etruscan alphabet, which was drawn from the Greek, and the writing changed from a right-to-left or boustrophedon script to a strictly left-to-right one.

From about 75 BCE to 200 CE a new Classical Latin arose, a conscious creation of the orators, poets, historians and other literate men who wrote the great works of classical literature, which were taught in grammar and rhetoric schools. Beside it stood the informal registers called Vulgar Latin, a term Cicero's sermo vulgi renders as the speech of the masses, found in Plautus and in fragments of everyday speech. Late Latin is the literary form from the 3rd century CE onward.

Latin grammar is highly fusional: nouns and adjectives belong to one of five declensions and have seven cases, and verbs are inflected for person, number, tense, voice, mood and aspect. Word order is relatively free because inflections show the connections between words. After the fall of Tarentum in 272 BCE the Romans began Hellenising, borrowing Greek words and adding the letters Y and Z to the alphabet. Classical Latin had no punctuation, letter case or word spacing, and ancient numbers were written only with letters.

Between the 6th and 9th centuries natural change in the vernacular Latin of different regions evolved into distinct Romance languages, among them Italian, French, Portuguese, Spanish, Romanian, Catalan, Romansh and Sardinian. Although often called a dead language, Latin did not undergo language death as formally defined. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it remained the common language of international communication, science and scholarship in Europe into the early 19th century.

Medieval Latin served as a working and literary language across Western and Catholic Europe from the 9th century to the Renaissance, which then developed Renaissance Latin, the basis of Neo-Latin. It was taught to be written and spoken at least until the late seventeenth century. Latin roots appear in the technical vocabulary of theology, the sciences, medicine and law. About 270,000 Latin inscriptions are known, and Ecclesiastical Latin remains the official language of the Holy See.
latin-america: Latin America is defined by culture rather than geography: it is the part of the Americas where Spanish or Portuguese is the national language, with a common culture and tradition, and where the dominant religion is Roman Catholic. It therefore includes countries from both North and South America, most of Central America, South America and the Caribbean. English-speaking and Dutch-speaking countries such as Belize, Guyana and Suriname are not counted, because they speak Germanic languages. Hispanic America is the narrower term for the Spanish-speaking nations, and Ibero-America the broader one. Most of the region lies in the Neotropical realm, which holds more tropical rainforest than any other, including the Amazon.

Before Europeans arrived in the late 15th and early 16th centuries the region was home to many indigenous peoples, including the Olmec, Maya, Muisca, Aztecs and Inca. The kingdoms of Spain and Portugal established colonies, imposed Roman Catholicism and their languages, and brought African slaves as labourers. The Spanish Crown allowed only Christians to emigrate to the New World, and until independence trade was regulated by the Casa de Contratación in Seville. The term Latin America was first used in 1856 at a conference in Paris, where the Chilean politician Francisco Bilbao used it for countries sharing a cultural and linguistic heritage, and it gained prominence in the 1860s under Napoleon III, whose government sought to justify French intervention in the Second Mexican Empire.

In the early 19th century nearly all of Spanish America won independence by armed struggle, the exceptions being Cuba and Puerto Rico. Brazil became a monarchy separate from Portugal and a republic in the late 19th century. Independence did not end black slavery, and it brought political and economic instability. As regional caudillos rose, leaders shifted from aristocracy toward republicanism. Great Britain and the United States exercised considerable power in the economic sphere while the new nations kept political sovereignty, a situation described as neo-colonialism. Puerto Rico passed to the United States after the Spanish-American War of 1898.

Spanish is spoken as a first language by about 60 per cent of the population and Portuguese by about 30 per cent, mostly in Brazil, the largest and most populous country. About 10 per cent speak other languages such as Quechua, Mayan languages, Guaraní, Aymara and Nahuatl. Most people are Christians, mostly Roman Catholics, and the population descends from indigenous peoples, Europeans, Africans and Asians. Indigenous languages left loanwords in Spanish and Portuguese such as pampa, taco and cacique, and the Maya, Aztecs and Inca are among the indigenous civilizations whose legacies remain strong.
latium: Latium was originally a small triangle of fertile volcanic soil, called Old Latium, on the left bank of the Tiber, extending north to the River Anio and south-east to the Pontine Marshes and the Circeian promontory. The right bank was held by the Etruscan city of Veii. The earliest Latium was the country of the Latini, whose recognised centre was the dormant volcano of Mons Albanus, the Alban Mount, 20 kilometres south-east of Rome. On its second-highest peak, Monte Cavo, stood a temple to Jupiter Latiaris where the Latins held state functions. The name is most likely derived from the Latin latus, wide, expressing the idea of flat land in contrast to the Sabine high country.

The region had settled agricultural populations from the early Bronze Age. By the 10th century BCE archaeology records numerous villages whose people grew spelt, barley, grapes, olives, apples and figs. Etruscan cultural and political influence grew from about the 8th century BCE, but the Etruscans could not assert hegemony over small, autonomous Latin city-states. Alba Longa, on the Alban range, was regarded as the primitive seat of the Latin stock and the mother city of Rome. Tusculum, Tibur, Praeneste, Gabii, Lavinium and Laurentum were other ancient Latin centres.

The Latin League tied the communities together by religion and descent. Its ritual was the Latin festival, at which an ox was sacrificed to Jupiter Latiaris on the Alban Mount, and thirty villages were originally entitled to take part. Alba Longa held religious primacy but never political power. Rome soon acquired the presidency, and Alba Longa was destroyed in the mid-7th century BCE. According to Livy it was razed, except for its temples, by King Tullus. Rome's generous grant of citizenship to outsiders, even former slaves, gave it more manpower than any other Latin city. Rome later defeated Veii and the Italic neighbours, and the name Latium came to cover the area south of Rome too, as Latium adiectum, as far as Casinum.

Augustus made Latium, with Campagna, Region I of Italy. After the Gothic War of 535–554 the Roman Duchy came to the Byzantine emperor, and the bishop of Rome later took over the region. The papacy returned control of Latium in 1353–1367 after the period at Avignon, and from the middle of the 16th century it was administered as part of the Papal States. It became part of the Kingdom of Italy after the capture of Rome on 20 September 1870.

The modern Italian region of Lazio, called Latium in Latin, is somewhat larger than ancient Latium, including a large area of ancient southern Etruria and Sabina. It contains the national capital, Rome, and holds many works of art and architecture. It gained a significant level of autonomy after a constitutional reform in 2001.
latvian-riflemen: By April 1915, with the German army advancing into Latvian territory, deputies in the State Duma led by Jānis Goldmanis called on Tsar Nicholas II to form all-Latvian battalions, arguing that Latvians knew the area and that nationalist feeling among them was more anti-German than anti-Russian. The Russian Stavka under Mikhail Alekseev approved, and on 19 July 1915 the tsar authorised the Latvian Riflemen. Volunteers applied from 12 August at Riga; three battalions were formed instead of the two planned. They were the first Latvian military units with Latvian commanders, and many of their first men were refugees from Courland and workers from evacuated Riga factories. Many veterans of the armed groups of the 1905 Revolution joined.

From 1915 to 1917 the riflemen fought along the Daugava river; from 1916 conscription filled eight combat regiments and one reserve regiment, about 40,000 men in all. In the Christmas Battles of December 1916 and January 1917 they broke the German line, but the attack was not followed through. The Russian army lost over 26,000 soldiers, among them 9,000 riflemen, about a third of their number, which bred resentment of the generals and the tsar and support for the Bolsheviks.

After the February Revolution, from May 1917 large parts of the regiments transferred loyalty to the Bolsheviks. The Latvian Riflemen Division under Jukums Vācietis became the first regular division of the Red Army, took part in suppressing the Left SR uprising in Moscow and the Yaroslavl uprising in 1918, and fought the Czechoslovak Legion and the White generals Denikin, Yudenich and Wrangel. In September 1918 Vācietis became the first commander-in-chief of the Red Army.

In Latvia the Army of Soviet Latvia, built on the division, held most of the country by the end of January 1919 but was defeated by the Baltic Landeswehr, German Freikorps, the Latvian and Estonian armies and a joint Polish and Latvian campaign in Latgale. After the 1920 peace treaty the division was dissolved and 11,395 former riflemen returned to Latvia. Others stayed in Russia and rose in the Red Army, the Communist Party and the Cheka; many were later executed in the NKVD's Latvian Operation during the Great Purge. A smaller group of officers sided with the anti-Bolshevik forces. The riflemen remain a subject of Latvian art, including Aleksandrs Čaks's poems Mūžības skartie and Aleksandrs Grīns's novel Blizzard of Souls.
latvian-war-of-independence: On 18 November 1918 the People's Council of Latvia proclaimed the Republic of Latvia and created a provisional government headed by Kārlis Ulmanis. Soviet Russia invaded in early December. Much of the invading army consisted of Red Latvian Riflemen, and the offensive met little resistance: Alūksne fell on 7 December, Daugavpils on 9 December and Cēsis on 23 December, and the Red Army captured Riga on 3 January 1919. A Latvian Socialist Soviet Republic was proclaimed on 13 January, backed by Soviet Russia. By the end of January the provisional government and the remaining German units had retreated to Liepāja.

On 15 January 1919 the independent battalion under Oskars Kalpaks stopped the Soviet advance at Lielauce, a battle important for Latvian morale. German and Latvian forces counterattacked from 3 March and recaptured Tukums and Jelgava. On 16 April the Baltic nobility staged a coup in Liepāja and set up a puppet government under Andrievs Niedra, and the provisional government took refuge aboard the steamship Saratov under British protection. On 22 May the Baltic Landeswehr and the Iron Division recaptured Riga, and between 174 and 5,000 people suspected of supporting the Bolsheviks were shot, according to differing estimates. The Landeswehr then advanced on Cēsis, but on 23 June 1919 the Estonian 3rd Division, with a Latvian regiment, defeated it.

An armistice imposed by the Allies on 3 July restored the Ulmanis government. The Iron Division stayed, however, and passed over 14,000 men to the West Russian Volunteer Army of Pavel Bermondt-Avalov. On 8 October it attacked Riga and took the left bank of the Daugava. Latvian forces, helped by Estonian armoured trains and the British and French navies, counterattacked on 10–11 November, and by early December the Bermontians were out of Latvia.

In January 1920 Latvian and Polish forces attacked the Bolsheviks in Latgale and took Daugavpils, and the Soviet Latvian government dissolved itself on 13 January. A cease-fire with Soviet Russia followed on 1 February, peace talks began on 16 April and the Latvian-Soviet Riga Peace Treaty was signed on 11 August 1920. The date of the victory in Riga, 11 November, has since been marked as Lāčplēsis Day. The war has been treated in the novel Blizzard of Souls and in films.
latvians: Latvians are a Baltic ethnic group and nation native to Latvia and the surrounding Baltic region. They are occasionally called Letts, especially in older writing. Archaeologists date the first human inhabitants of the lands of present-day Latvia to about 9000 BCE, hunters who arrived almost immediately after the end of the last ice age, and an ancient culture there to about 3000 BCE. The Roman author Tacitus remarked on the Aestii, thought to be inhabitants of the Baltic lands.

A Balto-Finnic-speaking tribe, the Livs, settled on the northern coast. Germanic settlers took their name for the natives from the Livs, called all the natives Letts and their land Lettland, and named their colony Livonia or Livland. The Latin form Livonia came to cover the whole territory of present-day Latvia and southern Estonia. Latvians and Lithuanians are the only surviving members of the Baltic branch of the Indo-European family.

The Latvian peoples remained relatively undisturbed until the Teutonic Order, acting on papal decrees to spread Christianity in pagan lands, colonised Kurzeme (Courland) from the first half of the 13th century. The Order's attempts to Christianize the population are said to have failed, and it later redeployed southward to the region of East Prussia. In the late 18th century a small but vibrant Herrnhutist movement played a significant part in the development of Latvian literary culture before it was absorbed into the mainstream Lutheran church.

Latvian culture has been somewhat influenced by Germanic, Scandinavian and Russian traditions, and Latvians kept considerable contact and trade with their neighbours. The Baltic ethnic religion was followed before the Christian Teutonic Order arrived, and Latvians still celebrate traditional feasts such as Jāņi. Dievturība is a modern revival of the ethnic religion practised before Christianization in the 13th century. Most Christian Latvians belong to the Evangelical Lutheran Church, although the Roman Catholic Church predominates in Latgale and Alsunga Municipality, and a small minority are Latvian Orthodox.

The Latvian language has been recorded since at least the 16th century and had developed into a distinct language by the 9th century. The nearly extinct Livonian language, of the Baltic-Finnic branch of the Uralic family, is protected by law, as is Latgalian, treated as a historical variation of Latvian.
lau-islands: The Lau Islands, also called the Lau Group or the Eastern Group, lie in the southern Pacific just east of the Koro Sea. About thirty of the islands and islets are inhabited. The group has a land area of 487 square kilometres and had a population of 10,683 at the census of 2007. Most of the northern islands are high and of volcanic origin, while those of the south are mostly low carbonate islands.

The islands lie between Melanesian Fiji and Polynesian Tonga and are a meeting point of the two cultural spheres. The south-east trade winds made it easy to sail from Tonga to Fiji and much harder to return. The culture of the islands became more Fijian than Polynesian from around 500 BCE, but Tongan influence remains in names, language, food and architecture: Lauan houses tend to have rounded ends, as in Tonga, where most Fijian houses are square-ended.

The British explorer James Cook reached Vatoa in 1774, and by 1820, when the Ono Group was sighted by Europeans, Lau was the most thoroughly mapped part of Fiji. The first missionaries arrived at Lakeba in 1830 but were expelled.

Political unity came late. The islands formed three territories. Northern Lau, as far south as Tuvuca, was under the overlordship of Taveuni and paid tribute to the Tui Cakau, paramount chief of Cakaudrove. Southern Lau, from Ono-i-Lau north to Cicia, was the traditional chiefdom of the Tui Nayau. The Moala Islands were closer to Bau Island and Lomaiviti. Around 1855 Enele Ma'afu, with the help of the Tui Nayau's army, conquered the region and set up a single administration, with Lomaloma on Vanua Balavu as his capital. The Tui Nayau gave him the title Tui Lau, King of Lau.

The title Tui Lau was vacant after the death of Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna in 1958. In 1963 the Vuanirewa clan bestowed it on Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara, who was also installed as Tui Nayau after his father, Ratu Tevita Uluilakeba II, died in 1966, so that the two titles came into personal union in 1969.

Lauan villages remain very traditional, and the islanders are known for wood carving and masi painting. Cricket, not rugby or football, is the most popular team sport, and Lauan players dominate Fiji's national cricket team. In July 2014 Tonga's lands minister, Lord Maʻafu Tukuiʻaulahi, proposed that Tonga give the disputed Minerva Reefs to Fiji in exchange for the Lau Group; the proposal had not then been discussed with the Lau Provincial Council.
lausanne: Lausanne is a hilly city on the shores of Lake Geneva, about halfway between the Jura Mountains and the Alps, and it faces the French town of Évian-les-Bains across the water. It is built on the southern slope of the Swiss Plateau, with a difference in elevation of about 500 metres between the lakeshore at Ouchy and its northern edge. The city looks out over the lake and the Swiss and Savoyan Alps. Geneva, the nearest major city, lies 51.7 kilometres to the south-west.

The Romans built a military camp, which they called Lousanna, at the site of a Celtic settlement near the lake, where Vidy and Ouchy are situated. On the hill above stood a fort called Lausodunon or Lousodunon. By the 2nd century CE the place was known as vikanor[um] Lousonnensium, and by 400 as civitas Lausanna. The town later grew up at the foot of the cathedral of Notre Dame.

Forces from the canton of Bern invaded in 1536, and Bern ruled Lausanne until 1798. The Bernese stripped the cathedral of its Roman Catholic furnishings and removed a number of its treasures, including its hanging tapestries, which were never returned despite repeated requests from the city. The period brought mixed fortunes, but trade grew, municipal wealth increased and so did landownership, and influential patrician families rose, among them the Loys, the Seigneux, the de Praroman and the de Saussure.

On 24 July 1923 the Treaty of Lausanne, which established the modern Turkish Republic, was signed at the Beau-Rivage Palace. Lausanne hosted the Swiss National Exhibition in 1964. From the 1950s to the 1970s many Italians, Spaniards and Portuguese settled there, mostly in the industrial suburb of Renens.

Lausanne is the capital and largest city of the French-speaking canton of Vaud, with a municipal population of about 150,000. The Federal Supreme Court of Switzerland convenes there, although the city is not the nation's capital. It has been recognised as the Olympic Capital since 1994, and it hosts the International Olympic Committee, the Court of Arbitration for Sport and some 55 international sport associations. Its 28-station metro makes it the smallest city in the world with a rapid transit system.

Since the Reformation the city was mostly Protestant until the late 20th century, when immigration from largely Catholic countries made Catholics the largest group. The whole old city is listed in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the cathedral, restored by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, and Saint-Maire Castle are among its main monuments. Its universities include the University of Lausanne and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne.
lauterecken: Lauterecken lies in the North Palatine Uplands, in a hollow at the mouth of the Lauter, where it flows into the Glan, and at the mouth of the Grumbach, which also empties into the Glan. The town stands at some 170 metres above sea level, with hills on either side of the dales reaching about 300 metres, and lies roughly 20 km north-east of Kusel and 25 km north-west of Kaiserslautern. Its municipal area measures 893 hectares, of which 307 are wooded. The dense settlement of the inner town on its slope goes back to the medieval fortifications, and the old centre was crossed by the Obere Gasse with its marketplace, now part of Hauptstraße.

Settlement here goes back to about 5000 BCE, with New Stone Age tools, a Bronze Age hoard from the Schäferberg and Iron Age finds. The Romans occupied the area for more than three centuries, and after they withdrew the Franks advanced into it. After Clovis I was baptised, Christianization spread from missionary centres such as Hornbach Monastery, Remigiusberg Monastery at Kusel and Disibodenberg. The Counts of Veldenz, whose lands came through the Frankish Bishopric of Veldenz, held the estate of St. Medard am Glan, with Lauterecken and Odenbach.

Count Palatine Ludwig II introduced the Reformation into the Duchy of Palatinate Zweibrücken, and the townsfolk had to convert to Lutheranism. After his death in 1532 his brother Ruprecht became regent for the underage Wolfgang, who later gave him his own county palatine, made up of the Ämter of Veldenz and Lauterecken. Ruprecht raised Lauterecken to a residence town and commissioned a large palatial castle. He died in 1544, leaving a young son, Georg Johannes I of Veldenz-Lauterecken, who fell into financial trouble and became entangled in a lawsuit before the Reichskammergericht that outlasted him.

In 1566 he added the County of Lützelstein in Alsace and later moved his residence there. In Louis XIV's wars of conquest the Chambers of Reunion demanded the union of Lauterecken with France, since it was still a landhold of the Bishopric of Verdun. The last Count Palatine, Leopold Ludwig, opposed the demand and had to leave until the French occupation ended.

Lauterecken is the seat of the Verbandsgemeinde Lauterecken-Wolfstein and a state-recognised tourism resort, nicknamed Veldenzstadt after the comital family. Its listed buildings include the Catholic parish church of Saint Francis Xavier, built from 1848 to 1853, the Protestant parish church of 1865 and 1866 in the Gothic Revival style, and a Blücher memorial of 1936. Its calendar includes a spring market in May, a Folk Festival in August, an autumn market in October and a Christmas market in December.
lavaux: Lavaux is a region in the canton of Vaud, in the district of Lavaux-Oron. It consists of 830 hectares of terraced vineyards that stretch for about 30 km along the south-facing northern shore of Lake Geneva. The main wine grape grown here is the Chasselas. The terraced vineyards date back to the 11th century, when the land was under the rule of Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries. Many hikes are possible through the vineyards, including a trail called the Terrasses de Lavaux, which runs from Saint-Saphorin to Lutry.

In the late 20th century the vineyards became the subject of popular votes in Vaud. In 1977 the voters of the canton accepted, with 55 per cent, a popular initiative called Save Lavaux, and in 1979 a law was made to protect the region, the Loi sur le plan de protection de Lavaux. Under cantonal law the vineyards are protected from development.

When the new cantonal constitution came into force in 2003 it did not contain the clause protecting Lavaux. A second Save Lavaux initiative, launched to restore it, was accepted in 2005 by 81 per cent of voters. A third, launched in 2009 by Franz Weber to reduce the opportunities for new construction, was rejected on 19 May 2014 by 68 per cent of voters, while the counter-proposal of the Council of State of Vaud, which strengthened the protection less strictly, was accepted by the same share.

Since July 2007 Lavaux has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site under the formal name Lavaux, Vineyard Terraces. The region also appears in popular culture: Prince named a song Lavaux on his album 20Ten, released in 2010, and in 2011 the Swiss Post issued three special stamps for it.
lavr-kornilov: Lavr Georgiyevich Kornilov was born on 30 August 1870 (18 August in the old calendar) in Ust-Kamenogorsk. Accounts of his ancestry differ: one story makes him a Don Cossack Kalmyk adopted by his mother's brother, while his sister wrote that he had not been adopted and that their mother was of Polish and Altai Oirot descent. He entered military school in Omsk in 1885 and the Mikhailovsky Artillery School in St. Petersburg in 1889, and in 1892 was assigned to the Turkestan Military District, where he led exploration missions in Eastern Turkestan, Afghanistan and Persia and learned several Central Asian languages.

After graduating from the General Staff Academy in 1897 Kornilov returned to Turkestan as a military intelligence officer. In the Russo-Japanese War he fought at Sandepu and Mukden and received the Order of St. George, and from 1907 to 1911 he was military attaché in China. In the First World War he commanded the 48th Infantry Division, was captured by the Austrians in April 1915 when his division was cut off, and escaped in July 1916.

After the abdication of Tsar Nicholas II he commanded the Petrograd Military District from March 1917, and on 8 March placed the Empress Alexandra and her children under house arrest. He then took the Eighth Army, whose success in the Kerensky Offensive took 10,000 prisoners before a retreat, and on 24 July took the southern front. A week later he replaced Aleksei Brusilov as supreme commander. Believing the Petrograd Soviet responsible for the army's breakdown, he ordered an assault on it after ambiguous exchanges with Alexander Kerensky. The Petrograd Soviet gathered workers and soldiers against him, the coup failed and he was arrested.

Kornilov escaped from the Bykhov jail on 19 November 1917, helped by guards loyal to him, and reached the Don region, where with General Mikhail Alekseev he became military commander of the anti-Bolshevik Volunteer Army. He is reported to have promised that the greater the terror, the greater the victories, and bands of his officers killed more than 500 people in the village of Lezhanka.

On 24 February 1918 he led the army on the Ice March towards the Kuban and laid siege to Yekaterinodar on 10 April. A Soviet shell hit his headquarters and killed him on 13 April 1918. Bolshevik troops later dug up his coffin and burned his remains. His legacy is contested: some see a patriot defending Russia's unity, others a reactionary who deepened the country's chaos.
lavrentiy-beria: Lavrentiy Pavlovich Beria was born on 29 March 1899 (17 March in the old style) at Merkheuli, near Sukhumi, in the Russian Empire, into a Georgian Orthodox family of the Mingrelian group. His father was a landowner. He attended a technical school in Sukhumi and later claimed to have joined the Bolsheviks in March 1917 while a student at the Baku Polytechnicum. In 1920 he enlisted in the Cheka and rose quickly through its ranks. After the Red Army invaded the Menshevik-controlled Democratic Republic of Georgia and the Georgian SSR was formed, he was deputy chairman of the Georgian OGPU from 1922 to 1924. He then led the repression of a Georgian nationalist uprising in 1924, after which up to 10,000 people were executed.

Beria met Joseph Stalin in the summer of 1931, when Stalin rested at Tsqaltubo and Beria took charge of his security. In August 1938 Stalin brought him to Moscow as deputy head of the NKVD, and in November he succeeded Nikolai Yezhov as its head. Under Yezhov the NKVD had carried out the Great Purge, which imprisoned or executed possibly over a million people. Beria's appointment brought a relative easing: over 100,000 people were released from the camps and the government admitted some excesses, which it blamed entirely on Yezhov. Arrests, torture and executions continued, and Yezhov was executed in 1940.

After the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, Beria organised the Katyn massacre of 22,000 Polish officers and intelligentsia. After the occupation of the Baltic states and parts of Romania in 1940 he oversaw the deportation of hundreds of thousands of people to remote areas or Gulag camps. He expanded the system of forced labour and set millions of Gulag prisoners to wartime production. In 1943 and 1944 he oversaw the mass deportation of millions of members of ethnic minorities from the Caucasus, which many scholars describe as ethnic cleansing or genocide. From 1945 he oversaw the Soviet atomic bomb project, whose first nuclear test took place in 1949. At his trial it became known that he had committed numerous rapes.

After Stalin's death in March 1953, Beria became First Deputy Premier and head of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and formed a triumvirate with Georgy Malenkov and Vyacheslav Molotov. He released the victims of the Doctors' Plot, announced an amnesty that freed 1,200,000 of the Gulag's 2,750,000 inmates, and returned the Gulag to the Ministry of Justice. His rivals, led by Nikita Khrushchev, feared his ambition. On 26 June 1953 he was arrested at a meeting of the Presidium, with the help of Marshal Georgy Zhukov and armed officers. He was tried for treason and other offences and executed on 23 December 1953, and many of his associates were later executed too.
layla-and-majnun: The story belongs first to Arabic tradition. It concerns the 7th-century poet Qays ibn al-Mulawwah and Layla al-Amiriyah, and it originates in Najd, in present-day Saudi Arabia, where the two are traditionally associated with Al-Aflaj and with a town named after Layla. Arabic records place Qays's birth around 645 and his death around 688, in the reign of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik. Before Nizami the legend circulated in short anecdotes, recorded in the Kitab al-Aghani and in Ibn Qutaybah's Al-Shi'r wa-l-Shu'ara', which are loosely connected and show little plot development. Nizami gathered both secular and mystical sources and drew on Udhrite love poetry, which is marked by longing for a beloved who cannot be had.

In the older account Qays and Layla fell in love when young. He composed poems naming her often, and his obsession led his tribe, the Banu Amir, to call him Majnun, meaning crazy. Her father refused his request, since it would be a scandal for Layla to marry a man thought unbalanced, and she was forcibly married to a rich merchant of the Thaqif tribe, Ward al-Thaqafi. Majnun left the camp and wandered the desert, reciting poetry to himself, while his family left food for him. Layla is generally said to have moved north with her husband, fallen ill and died. Majnun was later found dead near her grave, where he had carved three verses on a rock.

In Nizami's version the lovers meet at school, but a family feud keeps them apart and Layla's family arranges her marriage to another man. The love is called virgin love, because the lovers never marry.

Nizami's poem, composed in 1188 as the third part of his Khamsa, carried the theme from Arabic into Persian, Turkish and Indic languages. Imitations followed, among them Amir Khusrow Dehlavi's Majnun o Leyli, completed in 1299, and Jami's version of 1484, which runs to 3,860 couplets. Fuzuli's poem in Azerbaijani, written in 1535, became widely known in Ottoman Turkey and India. The scholar Hekmat listed forty Persian and thirteen Turkish versions. Mystics told many stories of Majnun to illustrate concepts such as fanaa, annihilation, and in Sufi writing the name Layla stands for the Beloved.

Sir William Jones published Hatefi's version in Calcutta in 1788, and Isaac D'Israeli translated the poem into English early in the 19th century. In 1908 the Azerbaijani composer Uzeyir Hajibeyov based the first opera of the Islamic world, Leyli and Majnun, on Fuzuli's work.
laz-people: The Laz speak Laz, a language of the South Caucasian family that also includes Mingrelian, Svan and Georgian. Modern theories hold that the Colchian tribes were direct ancestors of the Laz and Mingrelians, and that the Lazuri-speaking ancestors came from the north-east, around Abkhazia, and settled their present homeland in antiquity. The Kingdom of Colchis formed in the 13th century BCE, covering modern western Georgia and the north-eastern Turkish provinces of Trabzon, Rize and Artvin, and it was rich in gold, wax, hemp and honey. Classical authors record the Laz name only later. By the mid-third century CE the Lazi dominated most of Colchis and founded the kingdom of Lazica.

Related Tzanni, living in Tzanica between Byzantine territory and Lazica, were subdued and Christianized under Justinian I. From 542 to 562 Lazica was a scene of the rivalry between the Eastern Roman and Sassanid empires, in the Lazic War, in which 1,000 Tzanni auxiliaries fought. In 780 the kingdom of Abkhazia took over Lazica by dynastic succession, and the Tzanni then lived under nominal Byzantine rule in the theme of Chaldia, based at Trebizond. After the Byzantine collapse in 1204 the Empire of Trebizond was founded on the south-eastern Black Sea coast with a large Kartvelian-speaking population. Its eastern part had an autonomous coastal theme of Greater Lazia. Its rural areas seem to have been predominantly Laz, though Greek in higher culture.

The Ottomans conquered the Laz lands in 1547 and organised them as the Lazistan sanjak of the eyalet of Trabzon. Through the 17th century the Laz gradually converted to Islam, and in many districts native Laz derebeys, or valley-lords, held real authority and paid nothing to the sultan. Sultan Mahmud II tried to break their power after 1829. The Laz derebeys under Tahir Ağa Tuzcuoğlu of Rize rose in revolt in 1832, were put down by spring 1834, and their power was broken. After the Russian conquest of Batumi in 1878 about 40,000 Laz had settled in the Ottoman Empire by 1882. The Lazistan sanjak lasted until 1923 and the name was officially banned in 1926.

Lazistan is a series of narrow, rugged valleys running north from the Pontic Alps. Its economy rested on hazelnuts, farming with some difficulty in the steep mountains, and stock, orchards and bees, with smelting and the cutting of timber for shipbuilding. The Laz are good sailors. Their folk literature was passed on orally, and Turkish and Georgian serve as the main literary languages. Their folk dances, the horon, are related to the Khorumi of the Ajarians, and their instruments include the guda bagpipe, the kemenche fiddle, the zurna and the doli drum. The festival Kolkhoba is held at Sarpi in late August or early September.
lazar-of-serbia: Lazar Hrebeljanović was born about 1329 in the Fortress of Prilepac, near the mining town of Novo Brdo. His family were hereditary lords of Prilepac. His father Pribac was a logothete, or chancellor, at the court of Stefan Dušan, who ruled as king of Serbia from 1331 to 1346 and as emperor from 1346 to 1355. Lazar became a stavilac at Dušan's court, an office with a role in the ceremony at the royal table. Around 1353 he married Princess Milica Nemanjić. Dušan died in 1355 and was succeeded by his son Stefan Uroš V, and separatism spread as powerful nobles asserted more independence.

Lazar left the court of Tsar Uroš in 1363 or 1365, aged about 35, and began his career as a regional lord, though his activity between 1363 and 1371 is poorly documented. The Mrnjavčević brothers, Vukašin and Jovan Uglješa, had become the most powerful nobles. A Ragusan document of 22 April 1371 calls him Comes Lazarus and says he held Rudnik. His state, called Moravian Serbia by historians, covered the basins of the Great, West and South Morava rivers. Between 1374 and 1379 the Serbian Church recognised him as Lord of Serbs and Podunavlje.

He sought to revive the Serbian Empire with himself at its head and claimed to be the direct successor of the Nemanjić dynasty, which died out in 1371. The Serbian Orthodox Church supported this, but the nobility did not accept him as supreme ruler. Although he is often called Tsar Lazar, he held only the title of prince. He was killed at the Battle of Kosovo in June 1389 while leading a Christian army against the Ottomans under Sultan Murad I, a battle that ended with no clear victor and heavy losses on both sides.

His widow Milica ruled as regent for their adolescent son Stefan Lazarević and in 1390 accepted Ottoman suzerainty in exchange for a military alliance, to protect the weakened state from Hungary. Lazar was first buried in Priština and in 1390 or 1391 his relics were moved to Ravanica Monastery, which he had built. He was probably canonised then and is venerated as a martyr, with his feast day on 15 June, and was the first lay person recognised as a saint after the Nemanjić rulers. In epic poetry the night before the battle he chose a heavenly kingdom over an earthly one. Monks took his relics north in 1690 during the Great Serb Migration.
lazare-hoche: Lazare Hoche was born on 24 June 1768 at Montreuil, now part of Versailles, the son of a groom at the royal hunting grounds. His mother died when he was two, and an aunt who sold fruit mostly raised him, while his maternal uncle, the parish priest of Saint-Germain-en-Laye, educated him and made him a choirboy. In October 1784 he enlisted as a fusilier in the French Guards Regiment. He was a corporal by May 1789 and joined the National Guard that September. During the October Days he was among the guardsmen who escorted Louis XVI and his family out of the Palace of Versailles.

Commissioned in 1792, Hoche served at Thionville and Namur and at Neerwinden in March 1793. After defending Dunkirk he was promoted to general of division in October 1793 and given command of the Army of the Moselle. On 22 December he won at Froeschwiller, and on 26 December 1793 he drove Wurmser's Austrians from Alsace at the Second Battle of Wissembourg. In March 1794 he was arrested on charges of treason brought by Pichegru and was held until 4 August, after the fall of Robespierre.

Given command in the west, Hoche defeated the Armée des Émigrés, which the Royal Navy had landed, at Fort Penthièvre on 21 July 1795, and by 1796 his mobile columns had brought about the capture of the rebel leaders Stofflet and Charette. He then led the expedition to Ireland, which sailed from Brest with between 12,000 and 25,000 troops on 15 December 1796. A gale separated his frigate from the rest, and the fleet dispersed after a failed landing attempt at Bantry Bay. On the Rhine he defeated the Austrians at Neuwied on 18 April 1797 and in July became Minister of War, but he resigned within a month.

On 2 September 1797 Hoche took command of the Army of the Rhine and Moselle. His health failed quickly, and he died of consumption at Wetzlar on 19 September, aged 29. The belief spread that he had been poisoned, but the suspicion seems unfounded. He was buried next to his friend François Marceau at Fort Petersberg in Koblenz, and a funeral procession was held on the Champ de Mars in Paris on 1 October. In 1919 the French Army in the Rhineland reburied his remains in the Monument General Hoche at Weißenthurm.

The Irish revolutionary Wolfe Tone recorded Hoche's view that guillotining a man gets rid of one individual but makes all his friends enemies of the government for ever. Statues of Hoche stand at Versailles, in the Louvre and at Quiberon.
lazaro-cardenas: Lázaro Cárdenas was born on 21 May 1895 in Jiquilpan, Michoacán, one of eight children in a lower-middle-class family of Purépecha ancestry; his father owned a billiard hall. After his father's death in 1911 he supported his mother and seven younger siblings, working as a tax collector, a printer's devil and a jail keeper. He joined the Mexican Revolution after Victoriano Huerta overthrew Francisco Madero in 1913, serving under Álvaro Obregón, then Pancho Villa, and after 1915 under Plutarco Elías Calles. He became a brigadier general at 25 and later governor of Michoacán. Calles chose him as presidential candidate in 1934, and nobody expected him to be anything but loyal to Calles.

Cárdenas was inaugurated on 1 December 1934, cut his salary in half and turned Chapultepec Castle into the National Museum of History. Calles expected to keep ruling behind the presidency, but Cárdenas out-maneuvered him and forced him into exile. He restructured the ruling party, renamed the Party of the Mexican Revolution in 1938, on the sectoral representation of peasants, labour unions and the army; bringing the army in was meant to reduce its power to stage coups. Using Article 27 of the constitution, he redistributed some 180,000 square kilometres of hacienda land to peasants and created ejidos, with major expropriations in La Laguna and Yucatán. He promoted the Confederation of Mexican Workers, and created a Department of Indigenous Affairs in 1936.

In 1936 the oil workers' union, with 18,000 members, forced the foreign-owned oil companies to sign a first collective bargaining agreement. When the companies refused to pay the wages that the Council of Conciliation and Arbitration and, on 1 March 1938, the Supreme Court upheld, Cárdenas nationalized Mexico's petroleum reserves and expropriated the companies' equipment on 18 March 1938. He also supported the Spanish Republic in the Spanish Civil War and offered exile to as many as 20,000-40,000 Spanish refugees; the Casa de España became the Colegio de México in October 1940.

Cárdenas endorsed the moderate Manuel Ávila Camacho as his successor and gave up power in December 1940, an achievement later writers stress. He was the first post-revolutionary president to serve a full six-year term. Commentators have called him the most constructive radical of the Revolution and also an authoritarian populist. He later served as Secretary of National Defence and died on 19 October 1970.
lazio: Lazio borders Tuscany, Umbria and Marche to the north, Abruzzo and Molise to the east, Campania to the south and the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west. The region is mainly hilly and mountainous, with plains along the coast and the Tiber valley. The Roman Campagna, a vast alluvial plain, surrounds Rome, and in the south the Agro Pontino was once a swampy and malarial area that was reclaimed over the centuries. Volcanic groups such as the Volsini, Cimini and Sabatini hold lakes in their old craters, among them Bolsena, Vico and Bracciano.

Latium was the region of the Latins, whose city-state became Rome. In remote antiquity it covered only a small part of the present region, between the lower Tiber, the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Monti Sabini and the Pontine Marshes. The land the Latins held later extended into the territory of the Samnites, the Marsi, the Hernici, the Aequi, the Aurunci and the Volsci, and was divided into Latium Vetus, Old Latium, and Latium adiectum, the added lands. The Tiber separated it from Etruria.

After the Gothic conquest of Italy at the end of the fifth century, the region belonged to the Ostrogothic Kingdom. Following the Gothic War of 535 to 554 it became the property of the Eastern Emperor as the Duchy of Rome. The Donation of Sutri in 728 gave the Pope his first territory in the region beyond the Duchy of Rome. Secular lords and the popes struggled for power until the middle of the 16th century, and the lords gained strength while the papacy resided at Avignon from 1309 to 1377. From the middle of the 16th century the papacy unified Lazio politically with the Papal States.

Lazio returned to the Papal States in October 1799 after the short-lived Roman Republic, was annexed to the French Empire in 1809, and returned to the Pope in 1815. On 20 September 1870 Rome was captured, and Lazio was incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy. In 1927 the province of Rieti joined it.

Lazio is one of the 20 administrative regions of Italy, with Rome as its capital and as the capital of Italy. It is the second most populated region, with more than five million inhabitants. Among its sights are the Roman Castles around the Alban Hills, the archaeological park of Ostia Antica, the port of ancient Rome, and the abbeys of Monte Cassino and Farfa.
le-corbusier: Charles-Édouard Jeanneret was born on 6 October 1887 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, in the canton of Neuchâtel in French-speaking Switzerland. His father was an artisan who enamelled boxes and watches, and his mother taught piano. His ancestors included Belgians with the surname Lecorbésier, which inspired the pseudonym Le Corbusier. He acquired French nationality in 1930.

In 1905, with two other students and under the supervision of their teacher René Chapallaz, he designed and built his first house, the Villa Fallet, a large chalet in the local alpine style. He first discovered reinforced concrete while working in the office of Auguste Perret in Paris, and in December 1914 he began a serious study of it as a building material.

Le Corbusier moved to Paris definitively in 1917 and began an architectural practice with his cousin Pierre Jeanneret. In 1918 he met the painter Amédée Ozenfant, and together they rejected Cubism and founded the movement Purism. Their journal L'Esprit Nouveau carried his polemical articles, which he collected in 1923 as his first and most influential book, Towards an Architecture. His book The Decorative Art of Today (1925) attacked the idea of decorative art itself.

In 1927 he published, with Pierre Jeanneret, the Five Points of a Modern Architecture, which include raising the building on reinforced concrete pilotis and replacing the sloping roof with a roof terrace. He put them into practice most dramatically in the Villa Savoye, built from 1928 to 1931. In 1926 his project for the League of Nations headquarters in Geneva appeared to be the jury's first choice among 337 entries, but the commission went instead to five neoclassical architects. He was a founding member of the Congrès Internationaux d'Architecture Moderne in 1928 and prepared the master plan for Chandigarh in India.

Le Corbusier died of a heart attack while swimming at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin on 27 August 1965. In 1959 a campaign had saved the Villa Savoye from demolition by having it declared a historic monument, the first such distinction for a work by a living architect. In 2016 seventeen of his projects in seven countries were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list. He remains a controversial figure: his ties with fascism, antisemitism and Benito Mussolini continue to be debated, and some of his urban planning ideas have been criticised for their indifference to existing cultural sites.
le-duan: Lê Duẩn was born Lê Văn Nhuận in Bích La village in Quảng Trị Province, into a poor family with five children. He worked as a clerk for the Vietnam Railway Company in Hanoi in the 1920s, where he met communist activists and taught himself Marxism. He joined the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League in 1928 and cofounded the Indochina Communist Party in 1930.

He was imprisoned in 1931 and released six years later, rose in the party, and joined its Central Committee at the second national congress. Arrested again in 1939 for fomenting an uprising, he was freed after the August Revolution of 1945 and became a trusted associate of Hồ Chí Minh. During the First Indochina War he headed the party's Central Office of South Vietnam from 1951 to 1954.

After the Geneva Accords of 1954 divided Vietnam, Lê Duẩn reorganised the Việt Minh fighters of the south, of whom 5,000 to 10,000 stayed there as a base for future insurgency. His thesis The Road to the South called for reunification, and he was informally chosen as First Secretary by Hồ in 1959 and elected to the post at the third national congress in 1960. At that congress Lê Duẩn called for a southern people's front, and the Viet Cong was established on 20 December 1960.

As Hồ's health failed, Lê Duẩn took on more of the daily decisions, and after Hồ died on 2 September 1969 he was first among equals in a leadership that pledged to remain collective. He was more militant than Hồ and wanted, in his own words, final victory. In 1976, after the fall of South Vietnam, he became General Secretary of the Communist Party of the unified country. The fourth national congress that year set a goal of completing socialist transformation within twenty years, but Vietnam moved from one economic crisis to another.

In 1978 he and Phạm Văn Đồng signed a 25-year treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union. Vietnam invaded Cambodia in December 1978, bringing down the Khmer Rouge on 7 January 1979, and China then invaded northern Vietnam in a short, inconclusive war.

Lê Duẩn was in poor health at the fifth national congress, where he and Lê Đức Thọ filled the leading bodies with their own supporters. He died in Hanoi on 10 July 1986 and was succeeded at first by Trường Chinh. He held that nation and socialism were one, and his idea of the collective mastery of the people, a statist and managerial one, was written into the 1980 constitution.
le-locle: Le Locle lies in the Jura Mountains a few kilometres from La Chaux-de-Fonds, on the Swiss side of the Col des Roches gorge that forms the border with France. The altitude is around 1,000 metres, and the porous limestone beneath leaves the land short of water and ill-suited to farming. The earliest traces of settlement are a Mesolithic shelter at the Col des Roches, discovered in 1926, which held the oldest pottery found in the canton of Neuchâtel. The town is first mentioned in 1332.

In 1150 the valley was granted to the abbey of Fontaine-André, and in 1360 John II of Aarberg received Le Locle as a fief from Count Louis of Neuchâtel. Colonists cleared the wooded mountainside and later received the status of free peasants, and in 1372 they were given a charter codifying their rights. In 1476 the town made a defensive alliance with Bern. It converted to the Protestant faith in 1536. In 1707 the Principality of Neuchâtel passed to the King of Prussia, restored to him in 1814, and a year later it joined the Swiss Confederation as its only monarchy. The peaceful Neuchâtel Revolution began in Le Locle, and on 28 February 1848 the republic's flag was raised there.

Fires struck the town in 1683, 1765 and 1833, and it was rebuilt in the second quarter of the 19th century. Watchmaking was brought to Le Locle by Daniel Jeanrichard, a self-taught watchmaker who encouraged farmers to make watch components for him during the long winters. Around 77 watchmakers worked in the Le Locle region in 1750 and over 800 by 1800, and the trade began to replace agriculture and lace making. Hundreds of exiles who had fled to Besançon in 1793 returned with skilled watchmakers and a republican attitude. Le Locle was known in the 19th century for pocket and marine chronometers, and its first factories were built in the last quarter of that century.

Tissot, Zenith, Ulysse Nardin, Universal Genève and Doxa all trace their roots to Le Locle. The Musée d'Horlogerie, in Monts Castle, documents the trade. Together with La Chaux-de-Fonds, the town was recognised by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2009 for its watchmaking town planning: parallel strips where housing and workshops mingle, an example of a mono-industrial town that moved from cottage industry to factory production. Underground mills in the Col des Roches, restored, can be visited.
le-mans: Claudius Ptolemy is the first to mention the Roman city of Vindinium, the capital of the Aulerci. It was also known as Civitas Cenomanorum, the city of the Cenomani, and the Romans seized it in 47 BCE; it lay in the province of Gallia Lugdunensis. A 3rd-century amphitheatre is still visible. During the crisis of the 3rd century the baths were demolished and workers were mobilised to build defensive walls, and the ancient wall around Le Mans is one of the most complete circuits of Gallo-Roman city walls to survive. As French replaced late Vulgar Latin, Cenomanus became Celmins, and the first syllable was taken for the French word for this and replaced by le.

As the principal city of Maine, Le Mans was the stage in the 11th century for struggles between the counts of Anjou and the dukes of Normandy. In 1069 the citizens of Maine revolted and expelled the Normans, and Hugh V was proclaimed count of Maine. Geoffrey V of Anjou married Matilda of England in the cathedral, and their son Henry II Plantagenet, king of England, was born in the town. In the 13th century the city came under the French crown, and in the Hundred Years' War it was invaded by England.

Le Mans stands on the Sarthe River where it meets the Huisne, and is the capital of the Sarthe department and the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese. Industry grew in the 19th century with railways, motor vehicles, textiles and tobacco. On 8 August 1908 Wilbur Wright began public demonstrations of the aeroplane that he had built with his brother Orville at the Hunaudières racecourse near the city. It was liberated on 8 August 1944 by the U.S. 79th and 90th Infantry Divisions. Its old town, the Cité Plantagenêt, is well preserved, and the Cathédrale St-Julien honours Julian, the city's first bishop. Since 1923 it has hosted the 24 Hours of Le Mans, the world's oldest active endurance sports car race.
le-puy-en-velay: Le Puy-en-Velay was a major bishopric by the early period of medieval France, and its foundation is largely tradition. A priest named George is said to have founded its church, but the church historian Louis Duchesne held that this legend is not earlier than the 11th century. A document of 1004 calls the settlement the city called Vetula in the country of the Vellavii, a name that Ruessium began to take in the 4th century. A bishop Evodius attended the Council of Valence in 374. Before the 10th century only six bishops are known with certainty, the first being Scutarius, dated by an inscription to the end of the 4th century.

Local tradition says that Bishop Evodius, called Vosy, moved the see from Ruessium to Anicium and built a church of Our Lady on the pinnacle of Mont Anis, where a megalithic dolmen stood. It was said to heal those who touched it. Pilgrims were early visitors, and in the Middle Ages Le Puy was the most popular destination in France. Charlemagne came in 772 and 800. In 1254 Louis IX gave the cathedral an ebony image of the Virgin, one of the Black Virgins of France. In the early 1180s peasants led by a carpenter named Durandus formed a sworn association, the Capuciati, which briefly challenged seigneurial dominance.

Le Puy-en-Velay is the prefecture of the Haute-Loire department, near the river Loire. The Cathédrale Notre-Dame du Puy dates chiefly from the first half of the 12th century, and its facade of white sandstone and black volcanic breccia is reached by sixty steps. The cathedral has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998 as part of the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France, and the Chemin du Puy is one of the principal French starting points of that pilgrimage. The town holds a jubilee when the feast of the Annunciation falls on Good Friday, the first in 1065, and it is known for its green lentils and for lace-making.
le-quesnoy: Le Quesnoy is a small town in the east of the Nord department, once part of the province of French Hainaut and known for fortifications of the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries. It did not change much during the Industrial Revolution: iron and steel works did not take hold, as they did at neighbouring Valenciennes and Maubeuge, and a canal planned from the Sambre to the Scheldt was abandoned because the forest of Mormal gave too little water. Shoemaking was a major trade until at least 1945, and a chemical works and a dairy opened on the outskirts after the war.

The region was occupied by the Nerviens in Caesar's time, and Roman pottery was found near the Fauroeulx gate in 1933. A medieval chronicler, Jacques de Guise, claimed that a knight named Aymond, count of Faumars and the Ardennes, founded the place around the year 800, a story that rests on his word alone. In 1466 the town was the seat of a district under a provost in the County of Hainaut. Several counts of Hainaut died there, among them Margaret II and William III.

The French royal army under Turenne took the town in 1654, at the end of the Fronde, and it became officially French in 1659 under the Treaty of the Pyrenees. Vauban, then very young, modified and reinforced its five bastions into eight, and the Royal bastion in the north and the Gard bastion in the south show his work most clearly.

The works were soon outdated: imperial troops took the town in six days in 1712. It was the chief town of its district from 1790 to 1795, was retaken from the Austrians in July 1794 after a siege in heavy rain, and was occupied by Russian troops for three years after the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with many marriages between officers and local women.

German troops took the town on 23 August 1914 and occupied it for four years. Its mayor, Achille Carlier, was sentenced in 1915 to five years of hard labour for hiding wounded French and British soldiers, and was released in June 1916. In May 1940 a small force including a battalion of Moroccan Tirailleurs held it against the 5th Panzer Division for four days. The ramparts remain the town's chief monument, and the belfry of the town hall, first built in 1583, was destroyed in 1794, 1918 and 1940. Two giant figures, Pierre Bimberlot and Maori, are kept in the town hall, and the New Zealand soldiers who freed the town in 1918 formed an entertainment troupe called the digger pierrots.
league-of-nations: Immanuel Kant's Perpetual Peace of 1795 had outlined the idea of a league of nations, and the Concert of Europe after the Napoleonic Wars was an early attempt at collective security. Schemes for an international organisation gained public support in the First World War. The British political scientist Goldsworthy Lowes Dickinson coined the term League of Nations in 1914. At the Paris Peace Conference in 1919 Woodrow Wilson, Cecil and Smuts all put forward drafts, and the delegates approved the creation of the League on 25 January 1919. The Covenant was signed on 28 April 1919 as Part I of the Treaty of Versailles and took effect on 10 January 1920.

The League lacked an armed force and depended on the victorious Allied Powers to enforce its resolutions and sanctions, which they were often reluctant to do. The League had 42 founding members in November 1920 and 58 at its largest, between 28 September 1934 and 23 February 1935. The United States never joined, and Germany and Japan left in 1933. The Soviet Union joined only in 1934 and was expelled in 1939 after invading Finland. Italy left in 1937. In 1921 it fixed Albania's frontiers as those of 1913, with three minor changes that favoured Yugoslavia.

The League supervised the mandates, which took in the former German colonies and Arabic-speaking Ottoman provinces. Fourteen mandate territories were divided among seven mandatory powers: the United Kingdom, South Africa, France, Belgium, New Zealand, Australia and Japan. During the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, Benito Mussolini answered the League's accusations by saying that it was very well when sparrows shout but no good when eagles fall out. The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 showed that it had failed its main purpose, and it was largely inactive until it ceased operations on 18 April 1946.

The League had several wings and agencies: the Permanent Court of International Justice, the International Labour Organization, the Health Organisation, the Mandates Commission, the Slavery Commission. Three of them passed to the United Nations after the Second World War: the Labour Organization, the Court, as the International Court of Justice, and the Health Organisation, as the World Health Organization. Scholars now generally hold that although the League failed to secure world peace, it extended the rule of law, strengthened collective security and gave a voice to smaller nations. Its mandate system also put colonial powers under international observation.
league-of-nations-mandate: The mandate system was set up under Article 22 of the Covenant of the League of Nations, signed on 28 June 1919 and in force from 10 January 1920. It applied to territories that, after the war, were no longer ruled by their former sovereigns but whose peoples were not considered able to stand by themselves under the strenuous conditions of the modern world. Woodrow Wilson and Jan Smuts both pushed for it: Smuts wanted the colonial powers to annex such territories, and Wilson wanted trusteeship, so the system was a compromise. Its two governing principles were non-annexation and administration as a sacred trust of civilisation for the benefit of the native people.

Germany's overseas colonies, together with the Free City of Danzig, the Memel Territory and the Saar Basin, were taken from it by the Treaty of Versailles, and the Allies allotted the colonies on 7 May 1919. The Ottoman territories were allotted at the San Remo conference in 1920.

The mandates fell into three classes by the level of development ascribed to their peoples. Class A mandates were former Ottoman lands: Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan went to the British Empire, and Lebanon and Syria to France. Class B mandates were former German colonies in West and Central Africa, where the mandatory power had to guarantee freedom of conscience and religion. Class C mandates, among them South West Africa and the South Pacific islands, could be administered as integral parts of the mandatory's own territory. They were created largely at the urging of Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, which wanted to annex the German colonies they had occupied.

In every case the mandatory power was forbidden to build fortifications or raise an army in the territory, and it had to send an annual report to the Permanent Mandates Commission. The historian Susan Pedersen judges that colonial administration in the mandates did not differ substantially from that elsewhere. The Commission had too little executive power to intervene, and no deadlines for independence were set.

When the League was dissolved after the Second World War, all but one of the mandated territories became United Nations trust territories. Japan lost its mandate over the South Pacific islands, which became a strategic trust territory under United States administration. South Africa proposed to annex South West Africa, which the UN General Assembly rejected, and the territory became independent as Namibia in 1990. Nearly all the former mandates had become sovereign states by 1990.
leather: Leather is a strong, flexible and durable material obtained from the tanning, or chemical treatment, of animal skins and hides to prevent decay. It most commonly comes from cattle, sheep, goats, horses and other equine animals, buffalo, pigs, ostriches, and aquatic animals such as seals and alligators. The difference between raw and tanned hides is that raw hides dry into a hard, inflexible material that putrefies when wetted again, while tanned material dries flexible and does not rot. Leather making has been practised for more than 7,000 years, and the finished material is used for clothing, footwear, handbags, furniture, tools and sports equipment, and lasts for decades.

Vegetable tanning, with tannins extracted from vegetable matter such as tree bark prepared in bark mills, is the oldest known method. The leather is supple and light brown, and the colour tan takes its name from undyed vegetable-tanned leather. Soaked and dried, it shrinks and hardens, a property used in traditional shoemaking, and boiled leather, hardened in boiling water or wax, was occasionally used as armour and for book binding. Brain tanning uses emulsified oils, often from the brains of deer, cattle and buffalo, and gives buckskin, known for its softness. Alum leather is not tanned but tawed, with aluminium salts mixed with flour and egg yolk, and reverts to rawhide if soaked long enough.

Chrome tanning, with chromium sulfate and other chromium salts, was developed in the latter half of the 19th century as tanneries wanted to speed the process and make leather more waterproof. It takes about a day and became the most common method in modern use. Leather is made in three main stages: preparation of the hide by soaking, hair removal, liming and similar steps, tanning, and crusting, which thins, lubricates and often colours it. Some leathers are then finished by oiling, polishing or embossing. Full-grain leather keeps the whole outer layer of the hide and develops a patina in use, and is usually considered the highest quality.
lebanese-civil-war: Lebanon became independent on 22 November 1943, and its political system divided offices by community: the president was to be a Maronite, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker of parliament a Shia Muslim. The country was relatively calm in the 1960s. After King Hussein evicted the Palestinian armed groups from Jordan in the events of 1970 known as Black September, they relocated their fighting strength to Lebanon, where some 400,000 Palestinian refugees already lived in camps. They created what was called a state within the state, which strained Lebanon's fragile sectarian balance.

The war began on 13 April 1975, when unidentified gunmen fired on a church in Ain el-Rummaneh, a Christian suburb of East Beirut, killing four people, and Phalangists then killed 30 Palestinians travelling in a bus. The two main alliances were the Lebanese Front of nationalist Maronites and the pro-Palestinian Lebanese National Movement. Syria moved troops into Lebanon in 1976 at the request of President Suleiman Frangieh. Beirut was divided along the Green Line, with the Palestinian and Muslim militias in the west and the Christians in the east. As central authority broke down, parties set up cantons of their own, such as the Phalangist territory known as Marounistan.

Israel invaded in March 1978, in Operation Litani, and the United Nations created UNIFIL. Israel invaded again in June 1982, and between 16 and 18 September 1982 Phalangists allied with Israel killed civilians at the Sabra and Shatila camps in numbers estimated between 460 and 3,500. A multinational force of US Marines and French, Italian and British units was deployed. Iran helped to found Hezbollah in the Bekaa Valley from 1982. Later fighting included the Mountain War of 1983, the War of the Camps from 1985 and the clashes between Amal and Hezbollah in 1988.

In October 1989 Lebanese parliamentarians meeting at Taif, in Saudi Arabia, agreed a national reconciliation accord, after a committee of the Arab League had formulated solutions. They ratified it on 4 November and elected René Mouawad as president the next day. General Michel Aoun in East Beirut refused to accept it, and the Lebanese Forces under Samir Geagea clashed with him in 1990. In March 1991 parliament passed an amnesty for political crimes, and in May the militias, except Hezbollah, were dissolved.

The war displaced about 900,000 people, a fifth of the pre-war population, and perhaps a quarter of a million emigrated permanently. Thousands of land mines remained, and the victims of kidnapping and of wartime disappearance number in the tens of thousands. The Taif accord gave Syria a large role in Lebanese affairs.
lebanon: Lebanon lies in the Levant between latitudes 33° and 35° N, bordered by Syria to the north and east, Israel to the south and the Mediterranean Sea to the west. Its area is 10,452 square kilometres. The country has four physiographic regions: a narrow coastal plain, the Lebanon mountain range, the Beqaa Valley and the Anti-Lebanon Mountains. The Lebanon range peaks at 3,088 metres in Qurnat as Sawda', while the Beqaa, part of the Great Rift Valley system, is 180 kilometres long. The longest river, the Leontes, is 145 kilometres long and empties into the Mediterranean north of Tyre.

Byblos, among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, shows settlement earlier than 5000 BCE. Lebanon was part of northern Canaan and the homeland of the Phoenicians, whose most prominent cities were Byblos, Sidon and Tyre. The Phoenicians are credited with the oldest verified alphabet.

Foreign powers, beginning with the Neo-Assyrian Empire, imposed tribute; the cities passed to the Neo-Babylonian Empire and in 539 BCE to the Achaemenid Empire, and later to Alexander the Great after the siege of Tyre in 332 BCE. Pompey annexed Syria in 64 BCE. In the late 4th and early 5th century a hermit named Maron founded a monastic tradition whose followers, the Maronites, moved into the mountains.

After the seventh century the region came under Arab caliphates, then Crusader states, the Ayyubids and the Mamluks, and in the early 16th century Ottoman rule. The Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate was set up under Sultan Abdulmejid I as a home for Maronite Christians. France administered the Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon after the First World War and created Greater Lebanon in 1920; independence came by 1943. The Lebanese Civil War lasted from 1975 to 1990, and Syria occupied the country from 1976 to 2005 and Israel from 1982 to 2000.

The National Pact of 1943 apportions power among the religious groups: the president is a Maronite Christian, the prime minister a Sunni Muslim and the speaker of Parliament a Shi'a Muslim. The 128 seats of Parliament are divided equally between Christians and Muslims, a balance fixed by the Taif Agreement that ended the civil war. No official census has been held since 1932 because of the sensitivity of the confessional balance. More Lebanese, counting partial ancestry, live abroad than in the country, with the largest community in Brazil.
lebus: Lebus lies on a ridge on the west bank of the middle Oder, about 10 km north of Frankfurt (Oder), in the Märkisch-Oderland District. Since 1945 the river has marked the eastern German border with Poland. The town was the centre of the historical region known as Lubusz Land, which gives its name to the present-day Polish Lubusz Voivodeship. Settlement in the area has been traced back about 3,000 years, and the ridges gave natural defence and led to fortifications being built on them.

From about the 7th century the area was inhabited by Slavic Leubuzzi tribes, and their lands on both sides of the Oder became known as Terra Lebusana. The region was under Polish control by 966, under Duke Mieszko I and his son Bolesław I the Brave. Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg mentioned the settlement as a town in a chronicle written between 1012 and 1018, and 13th-century chronicles called Lebus the key to the Kingdom of Poland. The Diocese of Lebus was founded in 1124–25 under Duke Bolesław III Wrymouth, dedicated to Saint Adalbert of Prague, to convert the resistant Liutizi tribes.

Lubusz Land became part of the Duchy of Silesia in 1138, and in 1163 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa granted it as a fief to the Silesian Piasts. German colonisation proceeded through the 13th century, and Duke Henry the Bearded granted the citizens town privileges in 1226. In 1248–49 Duke Bolesław II Rogatka pledged town and land to the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg and Archbishop Wilbrand of Magdeburg. Brandenburg took control, and the town became a stop on trade routes from the Baltic coast to Italy. In 1373 troops of Emperor Charles IV destroyed the cathedral, and the seat of the bishopric moved to Fürstenwalde.

The people became Lutheran in the Reformation, and the bishopric was secularised in 1555 after the death of the last Catholic bishop, Georg von Blumenthal. Lebus has been part of Prussia since 1701. In the last stage of the World War II the town, including its medieval centre, was almost completely destroyed in the Battle of the Seelow Heights. The parish church was restored in 1954.
Lebus is the administrative seat of the Amt Lebus. Its coat of arms shows a wolf carrying a sheep in its mouth, and the Turmberg offers a view of the Oder valley.
lech-river: The Lech is a right tributary of the Danube, 255 kilometres long, with a drainage basin of 3,919 square kilometres. It rises from the lake Formarinsee in Vorarlberg at an altitude of 1,870 metres and flows north-north-east. Crossing the German border it forms the Lechfall, a waterfall 12 metres high, and then runs through a narrow gorge, the Lechschlucht.

At Füssen it leaves the Alps and enters the plains of the Allgäu in Bavaria, where it used to mark the boundary with Swabia. It passes through the Forggensee, a man-made lake drained in winter, and flows north through the Lechrain past Schongau, Landsberg, Augsburg, where it receives the Wertach, and Rain, before entering the Danube just below Donauwörth. Its torrential character and gravel beds make it unnavigable. Many hydroelectric power plants stand along it, and Neuschwanstein Castle, near Füssen, gives extensive views of its valley.

The name first appears in the Celtic tribal name Licates, in inscriptions of 8 or 7 BCE. In the 2nd century the river is called Likios or Likias, around 570 Licca, and in the 8th century Lecha and Lech. The name is compared with the Welsh llech, a stone slab, and the Breton lec'h, a gravestone, and is explained as meaning the stony.

Historic events were decided on its banks more than once. In 278 the Roman emperor Probus defeated a larger force of Burgundians and Vandals that had been raiding the province of Rhaetia. In August 955 Otto I defeated the Magyars at the Lechfeld, a stony plain between the Lech and the Wertach near Augsburg. In April 1632, at the Battle of Rain, Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden defeated Johan Tzerclaes, Count of Tilly, and mortally wounded him.
lectoure: Lectoure is a commune in the Gers department of the Occitanie region, on the right bank of the Gers, which flows north through the western part of the commune. The river Auroue forms part of its southeastern and northeastern borders. The town lies 32 kilometres north of Auch, the capital of the department, 30 kilometres south of Agen and about 76 kilometres northwest of Toulouse.
