Its name in Latin was Lactora and in Gascon Leitora.

Lectoure was a prehistoric oppidum and the capital of the Lactorates. Barbarian invasions forced its residents to raise the walls, and the town was a stronghold for centuries. In 1325 it became the capital of the Earldom of Armagnac, which was ruled by a powerful family descended from the ancient Dukes of Gascony, who held court at Lectoure.

In 1473 Cardinal Jean de Jouffroy besieged the town on behalf of Louis XI, and after its fall the whole population was put to the sword. In the same year the crown created the office of seneschal for the county of Armagnac, and the Seneschalcy of Armagnac was built in Lectoure. The office and building remained active until the French Revolution abolished it. In 1562 the town again suffered severely, this time at the hands of the Catholics under Blaise de Montluc.

The French Ministry of Culture has designated Lectoure a town of art and history since 1985. The former cathedral, built between the 12th and 16th centuries, is a national monument, and the town hall was built between 1676 and 1682 by Bishop Hugues de Bar. Lectoure lies on the Via Podiensis, one of the three major French routes of the Way of St James, between Miradoux and Marsolan. Among the people of Lectoure are Jean Lannes and the writer Pierre Charron.
lee-kuan-yew: Lee Kuan Yew was born Harry Lee Kuan Yew on 16 September 1923 in Singapore, then part of the Straits Settlements, the first child of Lee Chin Koon and Chua Jim Neo, both English-educated third-generation Peranakan Chinese. During the Japanese occupation he was among the Chinese men rounded up in the Sook Ching operation and left the screening site on the second day, later learning that the group of men was likely taken to the beach and executed. In 1946 he sailed for the United Kingdom, studied law at Cambridge, and returned to Singapore in 1950. In London he had met Goh Keng Swee and Toh Chin Chye, and after his return they formed a political party.

Lee co-founded the People's Action Party (PAP) in 1954, and after it won the 1959 election he became prime minister. He and his colleagues held that Singapore could survive only through merger with Malaya. On 16 September 1963 he proclaimed Singapore part of Malaysia, together with Sabah and Sarawak, and tensions with the federal government over industrialisation and taxes followed; Singapore became independent in 1965.

As prime minister of the new state he appointed Goh Keng Swee to build the armed forces, introduced conscription in 1967, addressed unemployment through manufacturing, and gave the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau greater powers. Critics have described his government as an illiberal democracy that restricted press freedom and public assembly, and from 1968 to 1981 Singapore was a de facto one-party state.
He stepped down on 28 November 1990 after seven election victories, handing the premiership to Goh Chok Tong, and remained in the Cabinet as Senior Minister until 2004 and Minister Mentor until 2011.

Lee died of pneumonia on 23 March 2015, aged 91. A week of national mourning was announced, during which approximately 1.7 million people paid their respects. In Singapore he is widely regarded as instrumental in the development of the economy, education system, public housing and healthcare, and the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore bears his name. He argued that communitarianism and limited human rights were necessary for rapid economic development, and he said that he had had to do some nasty things, locking fellows up without trial.
lee-teng-hui: Lee Teng-hui was born in 1923 in the farming community of Sanshi Village, near Tamsui, of Hakka descent. His father, a policeman, worked for the colonial Japanese government and owned land. In 1943 he passed the competitive entrance exam for Japan and enrolled in the Faculty of Agriculture at Kyoto Imperial University, where he was interested in Marxian economics, and he served in the Imperial Japanese Army in the war. Returning to Taiwan in March 1946, he enrolled at National Taiwan University, where he briefly joined the Chinese Communist Party twice, in 1946 and 1947, and withdrew each time. He graduated in 1949, took a master's degree at Iowa State University in 1953 and a doctorate in agricultural economics at Cornell University in 1968.

By 1970 Lee was a well-known agricultural economist at National Taiwan University and the Joint Commission on Rural Reconstruction. Through the KMT official Wang Tso-jung he met Chiang Ching-kuo, who was impressed by him, and Lee joined the Kuomintang in July 1970. When Chiang became premier in 1972 he made Lee, at 49, minister without portfolio responsible for agricultural development, his youngest cabinet minister. Lee was mayor of Taipei from 1978 and governor of Taiwan Province from 1981.

Chiang Ching-kuo died in January 1988, and Lee succeeded him as president. Within the party, figures of the Palace Faction, among them General Hau Pei-tsun and Soong Mei-ling, doubted his leadership, but with the help of James Soong, who urged that each day of delay was a day of disrespect to Ching-kuo, he became party chairman. At the 13th National Congress in July 1988 he named 31 Central Committee members, 16 of them benshengren, locally born Taiwanese, so that for the first time they held a majority. He ordered the release of General Sun Li-jen from 33 years of house arrest.

Lee was the first president born in Taiwan and the first to be directly elected, and the last to be indirectly elected. He supported the Taiwanese localization movement and sought greater international recognition for Taiwan. In 1999 the foreign ministry, under Lee, asserted that the whole of the South China Sea and the Spratly islands belonged to the Republic of China. He left office in 2000.

After leaving office Lee supported the pro-independence Taiwan Solidarity Union, and was expelled from the KMT on 21 September 2001 after endorsing its candidates. He supported changing the name of the country to the Republic of Taiwan and kept warm ties with Japan. He was a Presbyterian and was baptised in 1961. Lee died in Taipei on 30 July 2020. Supporters called him Mr. Democracy and the father of Taiwan's democracy, while Kuomintang figures held him responsible for breaking up the party-state system.
leeuwarden: Leeuwarden lies centrally in Friesland, on ground that was once an estuary called the Middelzee. Its name came into use for Nijehove, the most important of three villages, with Oldehove and Hoek, which merged in the early 9th century; a form Villa Lintarwrde is recorded around 825. The second part, warden, means an artificial dwelling hill, or terp. The first part is uncertain. Modern Dutch leeuw means lion, which matches the city's arms, but some scholars derive it from words meaning sheltered from the wind or waterway, giving the sense of a sheltered landing place.

The oldest remains of houses, found near the Oldehove, date from the 2nd century CE. The place has been continuously inhabited since the 10th century, is first referred to as a population centre in German sources of 1285, and received city privileges in 1435. Along the Middelzee it was an active centre of maritime trade until the waterway silted up in the 13th century. The 15th century was marked by the struggle of two Frisian factions, the Vetkopers and the Schieringers. Bastions and a moat were built between 1481 and 1494, and the fortifications were pulled down in the first half of the 19th century.

From 1580 to 1752 a provincial mint struck the coins of Friesland. The last stadtholder to live in the Stadhouderlijk Hof was William IV, Prince of Orange, in 1747. A Jewish community, first mentioned in 1645, bought land for a cemetery in 1679 and peaked at 1,236 people in 1860. The city was occupied by German forces from 1940 to 1945 and was freed on 15 April 1945 when the Royal Canadian Dragoons advanced into it against orders. On 16 November 1951, in the incident called Kneppelfreed, police used batons against protesters for the Frisian language at the courthouse; an inquiry then recommended legal status for Frisian.

Leeuwarden is the capital of the province of Friesland and its main economic hub. The Oldehove, a leaning unfinished church tower, is a symbol of the city, and the Grote or Jacobijnerkerk is its oldest building. The city was the birthplace of Mata Hari, M. C. Escher and Saskia van Uylenburg, wife of Rembrandt. It has been a European Capital of Culture and a UNESCO City of Literature, and is the start and finish of the Elfstedentocht, a 200 km skating race over Frisian waterways.
leeward-islands: The Leeward Islands lie in the Lesser Antilles, where the northeastern Caribbean Sea meets the western North Atlantic. They begin with the Virgin Islands, east of Puerto Rico, and extend southeast. Most were formed by volcanoes in the Lesser Antilles subduction zone, and some are still active; the highest point is La Grande Soufrière in Guadeloupe, at 1,467 metres.

The name comes from the age of sail. Leeward means downwind, and the trade winds blow chiefly from the southeast, so a ship from the Gulf of Guinea would meet Dominica and Martinique first, the islands most to windward. Early Spanish explorers called Puerto Rico and the islands to its west Sotavento, and the islands south and east of it Islas de Barlovento. The British later named Antigua, Montserrat and the islands to the north the Leeward Islands, whereas in Dutch, French and Spanish the whole chain is still called the windward islands.

The Caribs, after whom the Caribbean is named, are believed to have migrated from the Orinoco River area of Venezuela about 1200 CE. In the century before Columbus arrived in 1492 they mostly displaced the Maipurean-speaking Taínos, by warfare, extermination and assimilation. The islands were among the first parts of the Americas to fall under the Spanish Empire, and many of their names date from Columbus's second voyage: Montserrat was named for the Monastery of Montserrat in Catalonia.

The Leeward Islands became a British colony in 1671, with William Stapleton as its first governor. The settler population changed sharply. In 1660 there were about 8,000 white settlers and about 2,000 enslaved Africans; in 1678 there were 10,408 settlers and 8,449 enslaved people; and by 1708 the settlers numbered 7,311 and the enslaved an estimated 23,500. The colony was dissolved as a federation in 1816, when the islands were ruled individually, and re-established in 1833.
leeward-islands-society-islands: The Leeward Islands, in French Îles Sous-le-Vent, 'Under-the-Wind Islands', are the western part of the Society Islands in French Polynesia. They lie south of the Line Islands, east of the Cook Islands and north of the Austral Islands, and cover about 404 square kilometres. The eastern islands are mainly volcanic: Bora Bora, Huahine, Maupiti, Tupai, Raiatea, the largest, and Tahaʻa. The westernmost are the three atolls of Manuae, Motu One and Maupihaa. The islands are mountainous and formed of trachyte, dolerite and basalt, with raised coral beds high up the slopes. Volcanic activity ceased so long ago that erosion has almost obliterated the craters.

The first European to reach the archipelago was James Cook, on 12 April 1769, during an expedition to observe the transit of Venus; he visited twice more. It is a common misconception that he named the islands after the Royal Society. Cook recorded in his journal that he called them the Society Islands because they lie close to one another.

France declared a protectorate over Tahiti in 1840. In 1847 the British and French signed the Jarnac Convention, and in 1888, eight years after the Windward Islands, the Leeward Islands became a French colony. Native resistance movements and conflicts followed the annexation, known as the Leewards War, and they continued until 1897.

The archipelago is one of the five administrative subdivisions of French Polynesia, with Uturoa on Raiatea as its capital. Its population is over 36,000. Six of its seven communes formed a community of communes, Havaʻi, in 2012; Bora Bora stayed outside it. The economy rests on tourism, and the main agricultural products are copra, sugar, rum, mother-of-pearl and vanilla. Bora Bora is also known for its World War II-era United States naval base.
legatus: The rank of legate existed as early as the Samnite Wars, but it was not standardised until 190 BCE, to manage the larger armies that the Second Punic War had forced Rome to raise. A legate of a Republican army was essentially a supreme military tribune, drawn from the senatorial class, who acted as second-in-command to the magistrate in charge. The Senate assigned him, usually after consulting the commander, so as to pair men who could work together and to avoid clashes like that of the consuls Varro and Paulus at Cannae. Scipio Africanus served in this way as adviser to his brother Lucius in the Roman-Seleucid War.

After the army changes of the late Republic in the 1st century BCE, the legate as a single second-in-command disappeared. Several legati were assigned to every army, each commanding a legion as legatus legionis, and Julius Caesar used them widely in the Gallic Wars. The post was lucrative, since legates received large shares of the spoils, and it could attract distinguished men: Lucius Julius Caesar served as a legate under his cousin Gaius Julius Caesar. The legatus pro praetore, an ex-consul, governed a province with a praetor's powers. A legate was entitled to twelve lictors, and a legatus legionis could order capital punishment.

From Augustus onwards the emperor gave the title legatus legionis to the senior commanders of legions, except in Egypt and Mesopotamia, where equestrian prefects commanded them. A legatus Augusti pro praetore of senatorial rank held supreme command in a province, and in a province with one legion he commanded it directly. Augustus set a maximum term of two years, but later emperors extended it to three or four. Gallienus removed senatorial legates from the army and chose commanders from the equestrian order.

A legatus legionis was the principal commander of his legion and handed operational duties to his staff: the tribunus laticlavius, the praefectus castrorum, the tribunus angusticlavii and the primus pilus. In the field he could be recognised by an elaborate Attic helmet, a muscled or plumed cuirass, a scarlet cloak and a sash tied at the waist. The title legatus was also used for an ambassador appointed by the Senate for a mission, a legatio, to a foreign nation, and for ambassadors who came to Rome. The idea survives in the diplomatic legation.
legio-xii-fulminata: The legion was levied by Julius Caesar in 58 BCE and accompanied him through the Gallic Wars until 49 BCE. It fought in the battle against the Nervians and probably at the Siege of Alesia, and was at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE, when Caesar defeated Pompey. After the civil war it was named Victrix; in 43 BCE it was enlisted by Lepidus and Mark Antony, who led it, renamed XII Antiqua, on his campaign against the Parthian Empire. In the later part of the reign of Augustus it served in Syria, camped at Raphana.

In 62 CE the Twelfth joined Legio IV Scythica under Lucius Caesennius Paetus and both were defeated by the Parthians and Armenians at the battle of Rhandeia; after their surrender the legions were shamed and withdrawn from that theatre. In 66, sent with detachments of two other legions to restore Roman authority in Jerusalem, it was ambushed by Eleazar ben Simon at the Battle of Beth Horon during the withdrawal of Cestius Gallus and lost its eagle. It fought well in the later part of the First Jewish–Roman War and supported Vespasian's bid for the throne, after which it was posted to Melitene with Legio XVI Flavia Firma.

In 75 Vespasian sent it to the Caucasus to support the allied kingdoms of Iberia and Albania. It was probably in Armenia for Trajan's campaign of 114, and in 134 helped the governor Arrian defeat the Alans. Under Marcus Aurelius it campaigned against the Quadi, where the sources report a rain and lightning storm, held to be miraculous, that saved one of its units; a belief that the emperor then forbade the persecution of Christians seems to rest on a forgery. Its loyalty during the revolt of Avidius Cassius in 175 earned the title Certa Constans, surely constant.

After the death of Pertinax in 193 the legion backed Pescennius Niger against Septimius Severus, and when the frontier was moved from the Euphrates to the Tigris it stayed in reserve, possibly as a punishment. The country around Melitene was among the first where Christianity spread, and Polyeuctes, a martyr under Valerian, was a soldier of the Twelfth. In the 3rd century it was under the command of Odaenathus of Palmyra, yet also received the title Galliena from Emperor Gallienus. Records then become scarce. The Notitia Dignitatum still lists it guarding the Euphrates at Melitene at the beginning of the 5th century.
legnica: Legnica lies in the central part of Lower Silesia, on the Kaczawa River and the Czarna Woda. It is first mentioned in chronicles of 1004, although settlement there dates to the 7th century. Tacitus and Ptolemy record the ancient Lugii in the area. Slavic Lechitic tribes moved in during the 8th century, and tree-ring dating shows that under Mieszko I a new fortified settlement was built in the early Piast style.

After the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138 began the feudal fragmentation of Poland, Legnica came under Bolesław IV the Curly, who made it an important residence. On 9 April 1241, in the first Mongol invasion of Poland, the Mongols defeated the Christian army of Duke Henry II the Pious at Legnickie Pole near the city and killed him. From 1248 Legnica was the seat of a duchy of its own. A parish school set up at the church of St. Peter in 1258 was probably the first of its kind in Poland.

At the beginning of the 14th century the city had nearly 16,000 residents and was one of the most important in Central Europe, but a great fire of its wooden buildings halted its growth for decades. The duchy became a vassal of the Kingdom of Bohemia while ruled by Piast dukes, and the Reformation was introduced there as early as 1522. After the death of King Louis II at Mohács in 1526 it became a fief of the Habsburg monarchy. When the last Piast duke died, the duchy passed to direct Habsburg rule. In 1742 Liegnitz became Prussian, and it was part of the German Empire from 1871.

After World War II, following the Potsdam Conference in 1945, the city was transferred to Poland, and most of its German population fled or was expelled. It was repopulated with Poles and the name Legnica was adopted. From 1945 the headquarters of the Soviet Northern Group of Forces stood in the city, much of which was divided into Polish and Soviet areas; the last Soviet units left in 1993. The Diocese of Legnica was established in 1992. Among its landmarks are the Piast Castle, one of the largest in Poland, and the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, a Gothic church built from 1327.
leh: Leh stands on the bank of the Indus River at an altitude of about 3,500 metres, in a landscape dominated by mountains, with peaks such as Nanga Sago rising well above 5,500 metres. It has a cold desert climate with long, cold winters from late November to early March and very little rain. At this elevation only one crop a year can be grown. The main crop is grim, a naked barley from which tsampa, the staple food of Ladakh, is made, and the water for farming comes from the Indus.

Leh was for centuries an important stopover on trade routes along the Indus Valley between Tibet, Kashmir, India and China. The main goods carried were salt, grain, pashm or cashmere wool, charas from the Tarim Basin, indigo, silk yarn and Banaras brocade. Routes converged on it from all four directions, and summer and winter routes ran from Leh to Yarkand via the Karakoram Pass. The journey generally took nearly a month.

Little is known of the region's history before the end of the 10th century, when the Tibetan prince Skyid lde nyima gon, a grandson of the anti-Buddhist king Langdarma, founded the kingdom of Ladakh. King Tashi Namgyal, who ruled in the last quarter of the 16th century, built the first recorded royal residence, a fort on the peak above the town, now ruined.

Leh Palace, nine storeys high, was built by King Sengge Namgyal (1612–1642), apparently between 1631 and the king's death. In the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal war of 1679–1684 the Nawab of Kashmir helped King Delegs Namgyal, and among his demands was a large Sunni mosque in Leh, which mixes Muslim and Tibetan architecture. The palace was abandoned when Kashmiri forces besieged it in the mid-19th century, and the royal family moved to Stok Palace across the Indus.

Leh is the largest city and a joint capital of Ladakh. Its people are of Ladakhi ethnicity and speak Ladakhi, a Tibetic language. Buddhism is the largest religion, followed by Hinduism, Islam and Sikhism, and Buddhists and Muslims have lived there together since early in the Namgyal dynasty. Monuments include Leh Palace, Namgyal Tsemo Gompa, the Shanti Stupa and the Jama Masjid. The old town was added to the World Monuments Fund's list of the 100 most endangered sites.
leica-camera: The company traces its origins to 1849, when Carl Kellner founded the Optical Institute in Wetzlar. He made glasses and telescopes that scientists prized for their quality and precision. Kellner died at the age of 29 on 13 May 1855, and Friedrich Belthle took over the firm. Ernst Leitz, who had studied mechanics, began work there in 1864 and became a partner a year later. When Belthle died in 1869 Leitz took over and renamed the company Ernst Leitz-Optische Werke-Wetzlar. It at first made only microscopes, adding binoculars in 1907 and cinema projectors in 1910.

Oskar Barnack, head of development at Leitz and an amateur photographer, began work on the camera in 1914. Because of poor health he no longer wished to carry the heavy plate cameras then in use. His prototype, known as the Ur-Leica, began Leica's camera production, though marketing started only in the mid-1920s. It was the first practical camera to use standard 35 mm cinema film, which it transported horizontally, enlarging the frame to 24 by 36 millimetres instead of the 18 by 24 of cinema cameras. The name Leica comes from the first three letters of Leitz and the first two of camera.

A rangefinder was added to the Leica II in 1932, and the Leica III of 1933 offered a shutter speed of 1/1000 second. Variants of the III were the best sellers into the late 1950s. The Leica M3 of 1954 introduced the M mount and a combined rangefinder and viewfinder. In 1986 the business was divided into Leica GmbH for cameras and binoculars, Leica Microsystems and Leica Geosystems. In 2004 the Salzburg entrepreneur Andreas Kaufmann entered the camera company, which was struggling with a 17 per cent fall in turnover, and led it back to profit by 2010.

Leica cameras are associated with street photography, especially in the later twentieth century, and were used by Henri Cartier-Bresson and Sebastião Salgado. The company awards the Leica Oskar Barnack Award for documentary photography and has given the Leica Hall of Fame Award since 2011. In 2022 a prototype of the 0-series, number 105, once owned by Barnack, was sold at auction in Wetzlar for 14.4 million euros.
leicester: Leicester stands on the River Soar, about 90 miles north-north-west of London, and is the county town of Leicestershire. Its name comes from Old English. It is first recorded in Latinised form in the early ninth century, appears as Ligera ceastre in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 924 and as Ledecestre in the Domesday Book of 1086.

The Iron Age settlement that the Romans met seems to have developed in the 2nd or 1st century BCE, with roundhouses along the east bank of the Soar and control of a ford. The tribe that held the area were the Corieltauvians. The Romans arrived around 47 CE, and from about 50 the settlement near a bridge on the Fosse Way developed as the tribal capital under the name Ratae Corieltauvorum. In the 2nd century it received a forum and a bathhouse, whose remains can be seen at the Jewry Wall.

After the Roman withdrawal the town seems to have been continuously occupied, with a much reduced population, and its memory was kept as Cair Lerion in the History of the Britons. It was occupied by the Middle Angles and then administered by Mercia, and it became a bishopric in 679 or 680. The see lasted until the 9th century, when Danish Vikings captured the town, and the settlement became one of the Five Burghs of the Danelaw. Leicester became a bishopric again only in 1927, when the parish church of St Martin became its cathedral.

After the Norman Conquest the town came under the Beaumont and De Montfort earls, notably Simon de Montfort, and after his death in 1265 it passed to the House of Lancaster, for whom Leicester Castle was a stronghold and, from 1399, a royal residence. Parliaments met there in 1318, 1414 and 1450. In the Early Modern era Puritanism flourished and the town supported the Parliamentarian cause in the Civil War. In the Victorian age it became known for hosiery and shoe manufacturing, and it gained city status in 1919.

Leicester is the largest city in the East Midlands, with a population of 383,116. Since the middle of the 20th century immigration from countries of the British Commonwealth has made it ethnically diverse. King Richard III spent his last days in the town before his death at the Battle of Bosworth and was buried there in August 1485; he was reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015, after his remains were found nearby in the foundations of the lost Greyfriars chapel.
leicestershire: Leicestershire is a ceremonial county in the East Midlands of England, bordered by Derbyshire, Nottinghamshire and Lincolnshire to the north, Rutland to the east, Northamptonshire to the south-east, Warwickshire to the south-west and Staffordshire to the west. It covers 2,156 square kilometres and is generally lowland, with small rolling hills. The River Soar bisects it from south to north, flowing through Leicester and Loughborough before it joins the Trent at the county boundary. West of the river lies Charnwood Forest, an upland area that contains Bardon Hill, the county's highest point at 278 metres.

The county has prehistoric earthworks, and Leicester was a Roman settlement. The Angles settled the region in the 6th century and it became part of the Kingdom of Mercia. The Domesday Book of 1086 records four wapentakes in the territory: Guthlaxton, Framland, Goscote and Gartree. The county name is first recorded in 1087 as Lægrecastrescir. The wapentakes later became hundreds, with Goscote divided into West and East Goscote and Sparkenhoe added.

The county has had a relatively settled history, but it was the site of the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485, which established the Tudor dynasty's position as monarchs of England. Its farming was long based on livestock. Robert Bakewell of Dishley, near Loughborough (1725 to 1795), was a pioneer of selective breeding, and his Leicester Longwool sheep were prized by farmers across the British Empire.

Knitwear, hosiery and footwear were the traditional industries of Leicester and the county, and the sheep on the county's coat of arms recognises this. Manufacturing began with hand knitting in the Middle Ages and was fully industrialised by the end of the 19th century. During the Industrial Revolution the Leicestershire coalfield in the north and west was worked, and the Coalville mines operated from the 1820s until 1986. Bellfounding has been carried on at Loughborough since the 14th century; in 1881 John Taylor and Company cast Great Paul for St Paul's Cathedral in London, the largest bell in Britain.

Leicester, at the centre of the county, is by far its largest settlement. Other towns include Loughborough, Melton Mowbray, Hinckley, Market Harborough and Coalville. Local government is divided between the county council with seven district councils and the separate city council of Leicester. The county is known for Stilton and Red Leicester cheeses and for Melton Mowbray pork pies. Among its places of interest are the Bosworth battlefield, Bradgate Park, Belvoir Castle and the Iron Age hill fort at Burrough Hill.
leiden: Leiden lies on the Oude Rijn, about 20 km from The Hague and about 40 km from Amsterdam. The settlement grew on an artificial hill, today called the Burcht van Leiden, at the meeting of the Oude and Nieuwe Rijn, and was called Leithon, a name from a Germanic word for canal. The city has long been wrongly linked with the Roman outpost Lugdunum Batavorum; that fort lay nearer Katwijk, and the Roman settlement near Leiden was called Matilo.

In 1420, during the Hook and Cod wars, Duke John III of Bavaria besieged Leiden for two months, and the city surrendered on 17 August. In the late 15th century its broadcloth weaving was very important, and a printing and publishing trade grew up beside it. The Elzevir family, founded in the city by Lodewijk Elzevir, ran the largest bookshop and printing works until 1712.

The city sided with the Dutch Revolt in 1572. The Spanish besieged it from May to October 1574 and the siege was lifted by cutting the dikes, which let ships bring food. When silver ran out, paper taken from prayer books was stamped with coin dies as money. Leiden lost about a third of its 15,000 people, yet reached 45,000 in 1622, with refugees from Flanders giving the textile industry new strength. The decline of cloth from the late 17th century cut the population to 30,000 between 1796 and 1811. On 12 January 1807 a boat carrying 17,400 kg of gunpowder blew up in the city, killing 151 people and destroying some 220 homes; the site became the Van der Werff park in 1886.

Leiden University, the oldest in the Netherlands, was founded in 1575, and the end of the siege is still marked each year on 3 October. Discoveries made there include Snell's law, the Leyden jar of 1746 and the first liquefaction of helium by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1908. Johan Rudolf Thorbecke wrote the Dutch Constitution at his house in the city in April 1848. Because of the long economic decline, much of the 16th- and 17th-century centre survives, the second largest such town centre in the Netherlands. The municipality had 127,046 inhabitants in 2023.
leif-erikson: Leif was the son of Erik the Red and his wife Thjodhild, and the grandson of Thorvald Ásvaldsson, who was banished from Norway for manslaughter. His birthplace is not given in the sagas, but he was probably born in Iceland, perhaps in the Haukadalur valley, where his mother's family was based and where Erik built the farmstead Eiríksstaðir around 970. Erik was later banished from Iceland and sailed west to Greenland, where he founded the first permanent settlement in 986. Leif grew up on the family estate of Brattahlíð in the Eastern Settlement. He had two brothers, Thorstein and Thorvald, and a sister, Freydís, and he called a thrall named Tyrker his foster father.

Two sagas thought to have been written around 1200, the Saga of Erik the Red and the Saga of the Greenlanders, give detailed but sometimes conflicting accounts of the voyages to Vinland. They are generally regarded as works of literature, and scholars debate how far they are accurate. In the first, Leif was blown off course on the way from Norway to Greenland, having been converted to Christianity at the court of King Olaf Tryggvason, and found wild grapes, self-sown wheat and maple trees.

In the second, he bought the ship of Bjarni Herjólfsson, who had earlier sighted unknown coasts, and sailed with thirty-five men to Helluland, Markland and then a fertile land he named Vinland, where his party built a settlement called Leifsbudir. He returned to Greenland with a cargo of grapes and timber, and he never went back to Vinland.

The site of L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, found in the early 1960s by Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad, has been suggested as Leifsbudir. Carbon dating puts it at 990 to 1050, and tree-ring analysis at 1021. Later evidence suggests Vinland may have been the area around the Gulf of St. Lawrence, with L'Anse aux Meadows a ship repair station and waypoint.

Erik died shortly after 1000, and Leif became paramount chief in Greenland. He is last mentioned alive in 1018, in the Saga of St. Olaf, and by 1025 his son Thorkell held the chieftaincy; the sagas do not tell of his death. Leif is in all likelihood a historical figure, but other details of his life are debated, and some scholars think Freydís and Tyrker are fictional, as may be his missionary commission. His expedition encouraged other Norsemen to follow, though no Norse settlement in North America was permanent.
leine: The Leine, called Lagina in Old Saxon, is a river in Thuringia and Lower Saxony, a left-bank tributary of the Aller and so of the Weser, 281 km long. Its source lies close to the town of Leinefelde in Thuringia. About 40 km downriver it enters Lower Saxony and runs northwards. The important towns along its course, from upstream to downstream, are Göttingen, Einbeck, Freden, Alfeld and Gronau, before the river enters Hanover, the largest city on its banks. Some 40 km north of Hanover, near Schwarmstedt, it joins the Aller, and the water reaches the North Sea by way of the Weser.

In the past the Leine served as an important barge transport route before the railways, as far upriver as Göttingen. Today only its northern, lower reaches can be navigated, and only by the smallest commercial carriers. At Göttingen at least one point of the river is partly diverted into a canal that runs more or less parallel to it.

Industry has left the river somewhat polluted, so its water is not used for drinking, but the pollution has never been severe enough to prevent fish from living in it. Like many West German rivers, it has become cleaner since the 1960s with the introduction of environmental controls. Sport fishing is enjoyed from small boats and along the banks, although yields are normally low. The river is rather minor and for most of its length quite narrow, with a small flow, which is why the novelist Tom Clancy's use of it in Red Storm Rising (1986) as a major obstacle to a Soviet advance has been called unrealistic: it would not be a significant barrier to an army.
leipzig: Leipzig lies in the Leipzig Bay, the southernmost part of the North German Plain, about 150 km south-west of Berlin. The White Elster is joined there by the Pleiße and the Parthe, and the three rivers form a broad delta-like landscape of swampy ground, known as the Leipziger Gewässerknoten. The Via Regia and the Via Imperii, two important medieval trade routes, crossed at the site, which marked the city's economic importance. The name is commonly held to derive from the Slavic word lipa, linden tree, which gave the city the poetic epithet Lindenstadt, though more recent research on the oldest forms of the name has questioned this.

Leipzig was first documented in 1015 in the chronicle of Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg as urbs Libzi, and received city and market privileges in 1165 from Otto the Rich. Its trade fair dates back to 1190 and is the oldest surviving trade fair in the world, which encouraged the growth of a merchant bourgeoisie. Between 1764 and 1945 the city was a centre of publishing. The Battle of the Nations of 1813 was the largest battle in Europe before the First World War, and the Monument to the Battle of the Nations marking its centenary was completed in 1913. Although over half of the Kingdom of Saxony was ceded to Prussia, Leipzig stayed with King Frederick Augustus I.

By 1907 the Leipziger Baumwollspinnerei, with over 240,000 spindles, was the largest cotton mill company on the continent. The population peaked at over 700,000 in 1930, fell to about 530,000 by 1989 and to 437,000 by 1998, mostly through outward migration and suburbanisation, and then rose again after the city area was almost doubled by the incorporation of surrounding towns in 1999.

Leipzig is the most populous city in the German state of Saxony, with about 620,000 inhabitants, and part of the Central German Metropolitan Region. It is a long-standing centre of music: the Thomanerchor was founded in 1212, the Gewandhaus Orchestra in 1743 and the Oper Leipzig in 1693, and Felix Mendelssohn established Germany's first musical conservatoire there in 1843. Richard Wagner was born in the city in 1813. The Leipzig Hauptbahnhof, opened in 1915, is the largest overhead railway station in Europe by built-up area. Leipzig is also the main seat of the German National Library.
leiria: Leiria lies in western Central Portugal, roughly halfway between Lisbon and Porto, 137 km from Lisbon and 70 km from Coimbra. Its historic centre spreads between the castle hill and the river Lis. The first evident inhabitants of the region were the Turduli Oppidani, a Celtic tribe akin to the Lusitanians, who settled about 7 km from the present city. The Romans later expanded that settlement under the name Collippo, and its stones were used in the Middle Ages to build much of Leiria. The name derives from leira, an area of small farming plots.

The Suebi occupied the area in 414 until the Romans forced them back to Galicia, and Leovigild incorporated it into the kingdom of the Visigoths in 585. Later the Moors held it until Afonso Henriques recaptured it in 1135 during the Reconquista. South of Leiria lay a no-man's land until Santarém and Lisbon were permanently retaken. In 1142 Afonso gave the town its first foral, a compilation of feudal rights, to encourage settlement. He and Sancho I rebuilt the walls against new incursions.

By the 12th century part of the population already lived outside the walls. The town became the setting of several cortes, the feudal parliaments of the kingdom. In the early 14th century King Denis restored the castle's keep, built a royal residence and lived in the town for long periods, and ordered the expansion of the Pinhal de Leiria along the Atlantic coast, whose timber later helped build ships for the Portuguese voyages of the 15th and 16th centuries.

In the late 14th century John I built a royal palace within the castle walls. Manuel I gave Leiria a new foral in 1510, and in 1545 it became a city and the see of a diocese. Its later history is one of relative decay: French troops attacked it in 1808, and a great fire in 1811 was caused by Napoleonic troops retreating from the Lines of Torres Vedras.

Leiria is the second largest city of Portugal's Central Region after Coimbra, with a municipal population of about 128,640 in 2021. It is the seat of its own district and of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Leiria-Fátima. The castle is used for cultural events, and the city has a polytechnic institute. The writer Eça de Queiroz set his first novel, O Crime do Padre Amaro (1875), there.
leith: Leith lies on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth at the mouth of the Water of Leith, and is home to the Port of Leith. Its name may be Brittonic, from *lejth meaning 'damp, moist', or it may come from Celtic words meaning 'grey'. The earliest documentary reference is the royal charter of 1128 authorising Holyrood Abbey, which calls it Inverlet. Late twentieth-century excavations at the Shore found medieval wharf edges from the 12th century. After centuries under Edinburgh's control, Leith became a separate burgh in 1833.

Mary of Guelders, bride of James II, arrived at Leith on 18 May 1449. The Earl of Hertford burned the town in 1543 on the orders of Henry VIII, after the Scottish Parliament rejected the Treaty of Greenwich. In 1560 the regent Mary of Guise ruled Scotland from Leith while her daughter Mary, Queen of Scots remained in France. When Scottish Protestant lords, reinforced by troops and artillery sent from England, attacked the large French garrison, she shut herself in Edinburgh Castle, where she died in June 1560.

The Siege of Leith ended with the French departure under the Treaty of Leith. In 1645 plague killed over half the population of the southern district, and a mass grave of 81 bodies was found in 2016. On 14 August 1779 John Paul Jones sailed intending to take Leith and hold it for ransom, but a gale on 16 September kept him at the mouth of the Firth of Forth. The scare led to Leith Fort, designed by James Craig and built in 1780.

The first wet dock in Scotland opened on 20 May 1806, and the Tally Toor, a martello tower, was built in 1809 to guard the harbour. Leith was the scene of the dockers' strike of 1913. It merged with Edinburgh on 1 November 1920, although its people had voted 26,810 to 4,340 against; its population was then 80,000, one fifth of the enlarged city's, in about 5% of its area.

Leith was long Scotland's leader in glass and soap. The Leith Glassworks, dating from 1746, produced about a million wine bottles a week around 1770, and the Leith pattern bottle is the form now standard in the wine industry. The Anchor Soapworks, set up about 1680, used whale oil.

After decades of industrial decline, Leith began to recover in the late 1980s, with new housing and restaurants at the Shore. The Royal Yacht Britannia is berthed at Ocean Terminal. Leith Links is associated with the early rules of golf, first formulated at Leith in 1744, and with horse races held on Leith Sands until 1816. Hibernian Football Club is based in Leith.
leitha: The Leitha is a right tributary of the Danube in Austria and Hungary, with a basin of 2,138 square kilometres. It rises in Lower Austria where its two headstreams meet: the Schwarza, which drains the Schneeberg, Rax and Schneealpe ranges of the Northern Limestone Alps, and the Pitten. Parts of its course form the border between Lower Austria and Burgenland. East of Nickelsdorf it passes into Hungary and flows into the Moson arm of the Danube near Mosonmagyaróvár. Large amounts of Schwarza water are diverted to the Wiener Neustadt Canal and to supply Vienna with drinking water, and in places the river bed is almost dry.

The river was first mentioned as the Lithaha in an 833 deed of Louis the German, in the Carolingian Avar March. Its name probably comes from a Pannonian word for mud. After the Magyar horsemen were defeated by King Otto I at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955, the forces of the Bavarian duke Henry the Wrangler gradually reconquered the lands up to the Leitha, where about 976 the March of Austria was established under the Babenberg margrave Leopold I. Around the turn to the second millennium the Hungarian frontier ran along the river, and from 1156 it formed the eastern border of the Duchy of Austria, with fortresses at Wiener Neustadt, Bruck and Hainburg.

The last Babenberg duke, Frederick II of Austria, was killed in 1246 in the Battle of the Leitha River against King Béla IV of Hungary. A deed of King Sigismund in 1411 confirmed the border when his daughter Elizabeth married the Habsburg duke Albert II of Austria.

After the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 the Viennese called Hungary Transleithania, beyond the Leitha, and the Austrian lands Cisleithania, on this side of it. These names reflected the Austrian view, since Vienna lay on this side. The river did not form the whole border: Galicia and Bukovina, part of Cisleithania, lay north-east of Hungary, and the Morava separated Cisleithanian Moravia from Upper Hungary. After the First World War the Treaty of Trianon gave Austria the West Hungarian territory of Burgenland, and the river became an internal Austrian border.
leizhou-peninsula: The Leizhou Peninsula, also romanized Luichow, lies in the southernmost part of Guangdong province, on the south-western side of the city of Zhanjiang. It covers about 8,500 square kilometres and is the third largest peninsula in China. The Gulf of Tonkin lies to its west, and the Qiongzhou Strait, 30 kilometres wide, separates it from Hainan Island to the south. Its largest city by population and area is Zhanjiang.

Basalt terraces make up 43 per cent of the peninsula's area, marine terraces 27 per cent and alluvial plains 17 per cent. The land is dotted with dormant volcanoes, beaches and low-lying plains. Two separate volcanic fields lie here: a Pleistocene to Holocene field at the northern end, west of Zhanjiang, and the northern end of the Qionglei volcanic field, which runs across the strait into northern Hainan. The volcanoes derive from the stretching and thinning of the lithosphere connected with the creation of the South China Sea basin. Two Pleistocene basaltic stratovolcanoes, Yingfengling and Tianyang, stand 15 kilometres apart in the centre of the peninsula.

The climate is humid subtropical, shaped by continental north-eastern monsoons and by maritime south-eastern and south-western monsoons. Typhoons occur occasionally, from both the Pacific Ocean and the South China Sea. Annual precipitation is 1,400 to 1,700 millimetres.

Trade was once welcome at the cities of the peninsula. In the 19th century the area was a hotbed of piracy, and pirates such as Zheng Yi were based there. Whales of several species, among them North Pacific right whales, western gray whales, humpback whales and blue whales, were once known to come to the waters around the peninsula in winter and spring to calve, and harbours such as Wailuo were ideal habitats for them. They were heavily hunted and wiped out in these regions by Japanese whalers, who set up whaling stations at various sites along the Chinese and Korean coasts, including on Hainan and at Daya Bay.

Hepu National Sanctuary of Dugongs was created west of the peninsula to protect endangered marine mammals, and dugongs still occur there in small numbers. Leizhou Bay and nearby waters form part of a sanctuary for the Chinese white dolphin, which holds the second largest population in the country. Bryde's whales, minke whales and whale sharks still occur in adjacent waters, including those off Hainan Island and in the Gulf of Tonkin.
lemgo: Lemgo lies between the Teutoburg Forest and the Weser Uplands, 25 km east of Bielefeld and 70 km west of Hannover. It was founded at the crossroads of two merchant routes and is the oldest town in the former principality of Lippe. Its historic centre survived the Second World War completely undestroyed, so that the overall urban character, with its testimonies from the Renaissance, was preserved.

Bernhard II, Lord of Lippe, founded the town in 1190. Lemgo became a member of the Hanseatic League, the medieval trading association of free or autonomous cities. During the Reformation the town adopted Lutheranism in 1522, whereas elsewhere in Lippe its spread was hampered until 1533 by the opposition of the Catholic ruling counts. In 1605 Simon VI, Count of Lippe, adopted Calvinism and demanded that Lemgo's citizens convert too, using the principle of cuius regio, eius religio.
The town defied the edict, which led to the Revolt of Lemgo, and the dispute was settled by the Peace of Röhrentrup in 1617, granting Lemgo the right to determine its faith independently.

On 15 October 1638, during the 30 Years War, a combined army of Palatine and Swedish troops besieged the town, but the siege was lifted when a hostile army approached; the Battle of Vlotho took place two days later. Lippe's Lutheran minority, living mostly in Lemgo, joined the Reformed Church of Lippe only in 1882. The town also had a dark side in this period.

Johann Cothmann, the mayor in the seventeenth century, is said to have used the fear of witchcraft to clear his political opponents out of the field, and had several dozen citizens, women and men, killed. From 1947 until 1993 British infantry battalions were stationed in the town.

Lemgo has about 45,000 inhabitants and is part of the OWL region, an important centre of mechanical engineering and industrial electronics. The Hexenbürgermeisterhaus of 1571, with a Weser Renaissance facade, takes its name from Cothmann. The town hall combines a 13th-century hall, a Gothic middle part of about 1480 to 1490 and Weser Renaissance additions, and Brake Castle, first mentioned in 1306, was extended in 1587 as the residence of the counts of Lippe. The artist Karl Junker's Junkerhaus dates from 1891, and the naturalist Engelbert Kaempfer was born in Lemgo.
lemkos: The name Lemko comes from the word lem, meaning only, and was probably first a nickname for people who used it in the borderlands between the Lemko and Boyko regions. It was first printed in 1834, in Yosyp Levytsky's grammar of the Ruthenian language in Galicia, but entered wider use as a name for themselves only in the early 20th century; before that Lemkos called themselves Rusyns or Rusnaks.

Their origin is probably diverse. They and other Carpatho-Rusyns are considered descendants of the medieval White Croats, affected by the migration of Rusyn-influenced Slovaks and by Vlach and Romanian migrations of the 14th and 15th centuries. Their homeland, the Lemko Region, ran until 1945 from the Poprad River in the west to the valley of the Oslawa in the east, largely in present-day Poland.

Lemkos became part of the Austrian province of Galicia in 1772. In 1914 the Austro-Hungarian authorities created the Thalerhof internment camp for Lemkos suspected of spying for Russia, and 1,767 people died there during the war. After the First World War the Lemko-Rusyn Republic, with a Russophile orientation, declared independence in the west of Galicia, and the Komancza Republic, Ukrainophilic in orientation, was founded. The Lemko-Rusyn Republic was incorporated into Poland in 1920. In 1926 the Lemkos of the village of Tylawa converted en masse to Orthodoxy after a conflict with their Greek Catholic priest, and many villages followed.

About 130,000 to 140,000 Lemkos lived in the Polish part of the Lemko Region in 1939. After the Second World War about 90,000 were resettled in the Soviet Union and later about 35,000 in Poland's western lands in Operation Vistula, a counter-insurgency operation against the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. Some 5,000 families returned to their home region in 1957 and 1958. In Poland's 2021 census 13,607 people identified as Lemkos.

Lemkos were traditionally farmers, ox grazers and sheep herders in a largely deforested part of the Carpathians. Originally Orthodox, they entered the Union of Brest with the Roman Catholic Church in the 17th century, and most are today Eastern rite or Byzantine-rite Catholics, with a substantial number in the Eastern Orthodox Church. Their wooden churches place the highest cupola at the entrance, with the roof sloping toward the sanctuary.

Their speech is variously described as a language of its own, a dialect of Ukrainian or a dialect of Rusyn. An open-air museum of Lemko culture opened at Zyndranowa in 1968, and a Lemko festival is held annually in Zdynia.
lemnos: Lemnos lies in the Aegean Sea halfway between Mount Athos and the western coast of Turkey. It is mostly flat, with a rocky and mountainous north-west whose highest point, Mount Skopia, rises to 430 metres. Its chief towns are Myrina, also called Kastro, on the west coast, and Moudros on a large central bay. For the ancient Greeks the island was sacred to Hephaestus, who according to the Iliad fell there when Zeus hurled him from Olympus.

The oldest human settlement yet found in the Aegean islands, at Ouriakos, has stone tools of the 12th millennium BCE. Homer names the early inhabitants Sintians, Thucydides Tyrrhenians, and a 6th-century stele preserves a trace of the Lemnian language. After Miltiades the Younger took the island in 510 BCE it was an Athenian possession until the Macedonian empire absorbed it, and by 450 BCE it was an Athenian cleruchy. Greece became a Roman province in 146 BCE.

As a Byzantine province Lemnos suffered Saracen raids in the 10th century and Seljuk raids in the 11th. After the Fourth Crusade it was held as a fief by the Navigajoso family until the Byzantines reconquered it in 1278. After the loss of Asia Minor in the 1320s it was a granary of Constantinople. Dorino I Gattilusio acquired it shortly before the fall of Constantinople in 1453, and in 1456 the Greek population submitted to Sultan Mehmed II.

The Venetians seized the island in 1464 and again in 1656, but it returned to Ottoman control each time. Russian forces besieged Kastro in 1770 and withdrew when the Ottoman fleet attacked them in Mudros Bay. Greek forces captured Lemnos on 8 October 1912, during the First Balkan War. In 1915 the Allies used Moudros harbour as a base for the Gallipoli campaign, and the Armistice of Mudros was signed there in October 1918. The Germans occupied the island on 25 April 1941 and it was liberated in October 1944.

Lemnos is a Greek municipality in the North Aegean region, with Myrina as its seat, and at 477.583 square kilometres the eighth-largest island of Greece. Its main crops are wheat, barley and sesame, and it is known for the cheese Kalathaki Limnou.
lenape: The name Lenni Lenape combines two autonyms, Lenni, meaning genuine or original, and Lenape, meaning real person or original person, and some Lenape prefer simply Lenape. The name Delaware came from the English colonists, who named the river after Lord De La Warr, first governor of the Province of Virginia, and applied it to the people who lived there. When Europeans first met them, the Lenape were a loose association of closely related peoples who spoke similar languages and shared family bonds in Lenapehoking, their country, which spanned what is now eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Lower New York Bay and eastern Delaware.

The first recorded contact was in 1524, when Giovanni da Verrazzano's ship entered Lower New York Bay and local people came out in canoes. After the Dutch set up Fort Nassau in the 1620s, the Lenape restricted Dutch settlement until the 1660s to no further than Pavonia on the Hudson. Dutch and Lenape relations centred on trade. Europeans often tried to contract for land with chiefs, mistaking Lenape culture for that of neighbours such as the Haudenosaunee, whereas in Lenape society clan and family controlled property, and kinship terms meant different things to each side. William Penn first met the Lenape in 1682.

After Penn's death in 1718 his heirs and their agents sought ways to sell Lenape land, which led to the Walking Purchase. In the 1730s colonial administrators produced a draft deed dating to the 1680s, which the Penns presented as legitimate, but Lenape leaders in the lower Delaware refused to accept it. In the last decades of the 18th century settlers and the American Revolutionary War displaced most Lenape north and west, and in the 1860s the federal government moved most of those still in the east to Indian Territory. Groups that fled to what is now Ontario remain there.

The Lenape never formed a political unity. A person identified first with family, clan and village, then with neighbouring villages, then with speakers of the same dialect and finally with those whose languages were mutually understood, including the Nanticoke. The Unami and Munsee languages belong to the Eastern Algonquian group and are largely mutually intelligible.

Women grew the Three Sisters, maize, beans and squash, while men hunted and fished, and the Lenape used fire to manage land. Dutch settlers and Swedes admired their clothing, such as women's skirts painted or decorated with porcupine quills. Federally recognised Lenape communities today are in Oklahoma and Wisconsin, and three First Nations in Ontario are recognised by Canada.
lend-lease: In the 1930s the United States Congress adopted several Neutrality Acts, motivated by non-interventionism after its costly involvement in the First World War, making it illegal for Americans to sell or transport arms to warring nations. In 1939 Roosevelt wanted more flexibility to help contain Axis aggression, and Congress passed the Neutrality Act of 1939, which allowed cash-and-carry purchases. After the Fall of France in June 1940 the British Commonwealth and Empire were the only forces fighting Germany and Italy, and by 1941 Britain had liquidated much of its overseas holdings and its gold reserves were becoming depleted.

Roosevelt knew that the change to Allied support had to be gradual, given isolationist feeling. A Gallup poll in early February 1941 found 54% of Americans in favour of aid to Britain without qualifications. Opposition was strongest among isolationist Republicans, who feared the measure would be the longest single step toward involvement in the war. The House of Representatives voted 260 to 165 on 8 February 1941, largely along party lines, and the Lend-Lease Act was signed on 11 March 1941. Roosevelt compared it to lending a garden hose to a neighbour whose house is on fire; Senator Robert Taft replied that lending war equipment is like lending chewing gum.

Over 1941 to 1945 the United States supplied food, oil and materiel worth $50.1 billion, or 17 per cent of its war expenditure: $31.4 billion went to the United Kingdom, $11.3 billion to the Soviet Union, $3.2 billion to France, $1.6 billion to China and $2.6 billion to other Allies. Roosevelt's aide Harry Hopkins held effective control of the programme. Reverse Lend-Lease to the United States, such as rent on bases, totalled $7.8 billion, mostly from Britain and the Commonwealth.

The programme was gradually wound down after the victory in Europe, and Congress voted in April 1945 that it should not serve post-war purposes. It ended after Japan surrendered. Little equipment was returned except a few unarmed transport ships, and surplus military goods had no peacetime value. Supplies that arrived after the cut-off were sold to Britain at a large discount for £1.075 billion on long-term loans, which Britain finished repaying on 29 December 2006. The Soviet Union repaid $722 million in 1972, and the remainder of its debt was written off.

Lend-Lease ended American neutrality as enshrined in the 1930s and marked a decisive step toward open support for the Allies. Its precise significance for Allied victory is debated. Even after 1943, its logistical supplies, including motor vehicles and railroad equipment, remained of enormous assistance.
lennart-meri: Lennart Georg Meri was born in Tallinn on 29 March 1929, the son of the diplomat and later Shakespeare translator Georg Meri and an Estonian Swedish mother, Alice-Brigitta Engmann. The family left Estonia early and he studied abroad, in nine schools and four languages; his warmest memories were of the Lycée Janson de Sailly in Paris. The Soviet Union invaded and occupied Estonia in June 1940, and in 1941 the family was deported to Siberia.

At twelve he worked as a lumberman, potato peeler and rafter to support them. In exile he became interested in the other Finno-Ugric languages around him, a kinship that remained a lifelong theme. After returning to Estonia he graduated from the University of Tartu in 1953.

Barred from working as a historian, Meri became a dramatist at the Vanemuine theatre and then a radio-play producer. His first book followed a trip to the Tian Shan Mountains and the Kara Kum Desert in 1958. His film The Winds of the Milky Way was banned in the Soviet Union but won a silver medal at the New York Film Festival. His best-known work, Hõbevalge (1976), reconstructs the history of Estonia and the Baltic Sea region and discusses the legend of Ultima Thule; its reconstruction is largely refuted by modern geneticists.

He founded the Estonian Institute in 1988 and was a founding member of the Estonian Popular Front. He was the first Estonian to publicise abroad the protests against Soviet phosphorite mining, which grew into the Singing Revolution.

After the multi-party election of 1990 he became foreign minister, building the ministry from nothing, and in 1992 helped to found the Council of the Baltic Sea States. After a short period as ambassador to Finland, he was sworn in as the second president of Estonia on 6 October 1992, the first since the breakup of the Soviet Union. Arnold Rüütel led the popular vote with 42 per cent to his 29, but the newly elected Riigikogu decided the election. He was re-elected on 20 September 1996 and served until 2001. In a speech at Hamburg on 25 February 1994 he spoke against the Karaganov Doctrine.

Diagnosed with a brain tumour in mid-2005, Meri died in Tallinn on 14 March 2006. Arvo Pärt wrote Für Lennart for his funeral, held on 26 March 2006, and he was buried at Forest Cemetery in Pirita. Tallinn Airport was renamed Lennart Meri Tallinn International Airport in 2009. His successor, Arnold Rüütel, said that in nine years as head of state Meri had both restored the presidency and built up the Republic of Estonia.
lennart-torstensson: Lennart Torstensson was born on 17 August 1603 at Forstena manor in Västergötland. His parents, Märta Nilsdotter Posse and Torsten Lennartsson, fled into exile in the year of his birth because his father had confessed loyalty to the deposed King Sigismund, and relatives raised the boy. At fifteen he became a page to the young King Gustavus Adolphus and was allowed to observe the campaign in Livonia. He served in the Prussian campaigns of 1628 and 1629. In 1633 he married Baroness Beata De la Gardie, and their son Anders Torstenson became a Privy Councillor.

In 1629 Torstensson took charge of the Swedish artillery, which contributed greatly to the victories of Breitenfeld and Lech. He was taken prisoner at Alte Veste and held for nearly a year at Ingolstadt, and illness contracted there forced him back to Sweden in 1641. After Johan Banér died in May 1641 he returned to Germany as commander of the Swedish forces, Governor General of Pomerania and Field Marshal. In 1642 he marched through Brandenburg and Silesia into Moravia and, returning through Saxony, crushed the imperial army at the second Battle of Breitenfeld on 23 October 1642. In 1643 he was recalled to invade Denmark in the Torstenson War.

In January 1645 he broke into Bohemia, and the destruction of the imperial army at the Battle of Jankau on 6 March 1645 opened the road to Vienna. He reached Korneuburg in April, but his exhausted army lost 8,000 men in a failed siege of Brünn from 3 May to 23 August, and in September he retreated. Crippled by gout, he gave up his command to Carl Gustaf Wrangel on 23 December 1645.

Torstensson was made a count in 1647 and governed the western provinces of Sweden from 1648 to 1651. He died in Stockholm on 7 April 1651 and was buried in the Riddarholm Church. His movements were remarkably rapid, and he often had to lead the army in a litter because his infirmities would not let him ride. He was often considered the most scientific artillery officer and most successful engineer in the Swedish army, and helped develop more mobile artillery on the battlefield.
leo-africanus: Most of what is known about Leo Africanus comes from autobiographical notes in his own work. He was born al-Hasan, son of Muhammad, around 1494, and his name in full was al-Ḥasan ibn Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Wazzān al-Fāsī. He grew up in Fez, where he studied at the University of al-Qarawiyyin. As a young man he accompanied an uncle on a diplomatic mission that reached Timbuktu, then part of the Songhai Empire, about 1510. In 1517, returning from a mission to Constantinople for the Sultan of Fez, he was at the port of Rosetta during the Ottoman conquest of Egypt, and he went on through Cairo and Aswan to Arabia, where he probably made the pilgrimage to Mecca.

In 1518, on his way back to Tunis, he was captured by Spanish corsairs and imprisoned on Rhodes, the headquarters of the Knights Hospitaller. When his captors realised his intelligence and importance, he was moved to the Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome and presented to Pope Leo X, who freed him and gave him a pension. He was baptized in St Peter's in 1520 as Johannes Leo de Medicis; in Arabic he translated this as Yuhanna al-Asad al-Gharnati, John the Lion of Granada. It is likely the pope wanted a collaborator who could give information on North Africa, as he feared Turkish forces might invade Sicily and southern Italy.

After Leo X died in 1521 and the new pope, Adrian VI, was suspicious of a Muslim at court, he left Rome and travelled in Italy for three or four years. At Bologna he wrote an Arabic-Hebrew-Latin medical vocabulary for the Jewish physician Jacob Mantino and an Arabic grammar. He returned to Rome in 1526 under Clement VII, and by his own account finished his book on African geography that year.

His Cosmographia et geographia de Affrica was published by Giovanni Battista Ramusio in Italian in 1550 as the Description of Africa. It was reprinted five times, appeared in French and Latin in 1556 and in English in 1600; the Latin text, from which the English was made, held many errors. Among European scholars it was regarded as the most authoritative treatise on the subject until modern European exploration. He also wrote an Arabic translation of the Epistles of St Paul and a biographical encyclopedia of Islamic and Jewish scholars.

It is possible that he did not visit all the places he describes. Pekka Masonen has argued that belief in his further travels rests on modern misreadings of the book as an itinerary. His later life is uncertain: one theory has him in Rome until about 1550, another that he returned to Tunis and to Islam, and a third that he went to Morocco after 1535.
leo-i-king-of-armenia: Leo was born in 1150, the younger son of Stephen, third son of Leo I, lord of Armenian Cilicia, and of Rita, a daughter of Sempad, Lord of Barbaron. His father was murdered on 7 February 1165 on his way to a banquet given by the Byzantine governor of Cilicia, Andronicus Euphorbenus. Leo and his elder brother Roupen then lived with their uncle Mleh I, who had made many enemies by his cruelties and was assassinated by his own soldiers in Sis in 1175. The nobles elected Roupen III as ruler. Roupen was taken prisoner by Bohemond III, and in 1187 Leo became ruler.

In 1187 Leo fought a war against Aleppo and Damascus and forced the allied forces to retreat. This drew away part of the forces facing the crusaders just as Saladin began his decisive battle against the Latin state of Jerusalem. Vahram of Edessa's Rhymed Chronicle records that he enlarged his principality, conquered Isauria, reached Iconium, took Heraclea and gave it up for a large ransom, nearly took Caesarea, and ringed Cilicia with forts and castles. He led his forces alongside the armies of the Third Crusade and gave the crusaders provisions, guides and pack animals. He was crowned in the Hagia Sophia at Tarsus, the traditional coronation place of Cilician monarchs, on 6 January 1198 or 1199.

Leo married Isabelle in 1188 or 1189 and divorced her in 1206, and married Sibylla of Cyprus around 1210. His heir was his daughter Isabella, born around 1216. Smbat Sparapet's Chronicle describes his anger when told of the unfaithfulness of the lady of Antioch, whom he had as a wife. Feeling his end near, he appointed the baron Atan regent and guardian of his daughter, and died on 2 May 1219. He was buried in the church of Agner, and part of his body was taken to Sis. Smbat describes him as wise, skilled on horseback and brave in battle.
leo-iii-the-isaurian: Leo was born about 685 at Germanikeia, in the north of Syria, with the name Konon, and spoke Arabic as his native language. Theophanes the Confessor called him Saracen-minded, though there is little evidence that Islam influenced him. Most modern scholars reject the nickname the Isaurian as a misnomer, perhaps arising when authors mistook his home town for Germanicopolis in Isauria. Under Justinian II he was sent on a mission to Alania and Lazica; Emperor Anastasius II later made him commander of the Anatolic Theme.

He then joined Artabasdos, commander of the Armeniac Theme, in a plot against Emperor Theodosius III, ostensibly in support of Anastasius. In 717 he marched on Constantinople, forced Theodosius to abdicate, and was crowned by Patriarch Germanus I at the Hagia Sophia on 25 March.

Leo at once faced the second Arab siege of Constantinople, which began in August 717. Umayyad forces of 80,000 to 150,000 men and a large fleet had come to seize the city. Preparations begun under Anastasius II, Leo's resistance, Greek fire and Bulgarian reinforcements wore the invaders down, and they abandoned the siege in August 718 after twelve months. He then reorganised the administration, put down a rebellion in Sicily and executed the deposed Anastasius II, who tried to retake the throne. He invited Slavic settlers into depopulated districts, restored the army, and allied with the Khazars and Georgians. Raids continued until a major invading force was destroyed at the Battle of Akroinon in 740.

After enforcing the baptism of Jews and Montanists in 722, Leo issued edicts against the veneration of images between 726 and 729. Patriarch Germanus resigned in 730 rather than accept iconoclasm. Popes Gregory II and Gregory III opposed it, and Leo transferred bishoprics of southern Italy and Illyricum from Rome to Constantinople. Some historians, notably Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon, doubt that Leo's policy involved mass persecution or destruction of images. His Ekloge, a revision of Justinian's code published in 741, replaced the death penalty with mutilation in many cases. In 721 he introduced the silver miliaresion.

Leo died of dropsy on 18 June 741 and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles. His son Constantine V succeeded him. The surviving sources were mostly written by iconodule clergy hostile to him; modern historians describe his reign as a period of violence that saved the Empire from destruction amid extensive reform.
leo-iv-the-khazar: Leo was born on 25 January 750, the son of Emperor Constantine V and his first wife, Tzitzak, who took the Christian name Eirene. Because his mother was a Khazar, he was given the epithet the Khazar. He was made co-emperor in 751 while still an infant, and in 769 he was married to Irene of Athens. Constantine V died while campaigning against the Bulgarian Empire, and Leo became senior emperor on 14 September 775.

Leo was already suffering from tuberculosis, which, together with the infancy of his son Constantine VI, encouraged his half-brothers, the caesares Nikephoros and Christopher, to hope for the throne. In 776 Leo raised Constantine to caesar and declared him his successor. The two brothers were soon found plotting against him. Although public opinion favoured their execution, Leo pardoned them, and exiled several other plotters to Cherson. Khan Telerig of Bulgaria took refuge in Constantinople in 776 and 777, was baptised in Leo's presence and married a relation of the empress Irene.

Caliph al-Mahdi of the Abbasids invaded the Byzantine Empire in 776, with himself present. The Byzantines replied in 778 with an invasion of Syria by the armies of several themes. Michael Lachanodrakon, commander of the Thracesian Theme, besieged Germanikeia for a time, then lifted the siege and raided the countryside, deporting many Jacobite Christians to Thrace. The Abbasids attacked him during the raid and were decisively defeated by several Byzantine armies, whose generals were given a triumphal entry into Constantinople. In 779 Leo repelled an Abbasid attack on Asia Minor. Leo died on 8 September 780 of a violent fever linked to his tuberculosis. His nine-year-old son became emperor as Constantine VI, with Irene acting as regent.
leo-tolstoy: Tolstoy was born on 9 September 1828 (28 August in the Old Style calendar) at Yasnaya Polyana, a family estate 12 kilometres southwest of Tula. He was the fourth of five children of Count Nikolai Ilyich Tolstoy, a veteran of the Patriotic War of 1812, and Princess Mariya Volkonskaya. His mother died when he was two and his father when he was nine, and relatives brought up the children. In 1844 he began studying law and oriental languages at Kazan University, where teachers described him as unable and unwilling to learn. He left before finishing and led a lax and leisurely life in Moscow, Tula and Saint Petersburg.

After running up heavy gambling debts, Tolstoy went to the Caucasus with his older brother in 1851 and joined the army. His first novel, Childhood, a fictional account of his own youth, was published in 1852. He served as an artillery officer in the Crimean War and was in Sevastopol during the 11-month siege of 1854–55. Appalled by the number of deaths, he left the army after the war.

Two trips around Europe, in 1857 and 1860–61, converted him from a dissolute society author to a non-violent and spiritual anarchist. In Paris in 1857 he witnessed a public execution, which marked the rest of his life. On 23 September 1862 he married Sophia Andreevna Behrs, sixteen years his junior; they had 13 children, eight of whom survived childhood. She acted as his secretary and editor while he composed War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

His autobiographical trilogy Childhood, Boyhood and Youth (1852–1856) tells of a rich landowner's son who slowly realises the gap between himself and his peasants. Anna Karenina tells parallel stories of an adulterous woman trapped by the conventions of society and of a landowner much like Tolstoy who works alongside peasants. He drew characters in his own image, such as Pierre Bezukhov in War and Peace and Levin in Anna Karenina.

In the 1870s Tolstoy underwent a moral crisis and a spiritual awakening, set out in Confession (1882). A literal reading of Jesus's ethical teaching, centred on the Sermon on the Mount, made him a Christian anarchist and pacifist. His ideas on nonviolent resistance, in works such as The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1894), influenced Mahatma Gandhi, who corresponded with him. He died of pneumonia on 20 November 1910 at Astapovo railway station.
leo-vi-the-wise: Leo was born on 19 September 866 to the empress Eudokia Ingerina, who was both the mistress of Michael III and the wife of Basil I. Basil assassinated Michael in 867 and became emperor, associated Leo on the throne in 870, and made him heir in 879 on the death of his older half-brother Constantine. Father and son disliked each other, and Basil almost had Leo blinded when he was accused of conspiring against him. Basil died in a hunting accident on 29 August 886.

One of Leo's first acts was to rebury Michael III with great ceremony in the Church of the Holy Apostles, which fed the suspicion that Leo believed himself Michael's son. He relied on bureaucrats such as Stylianos Zaoutzes and the eunuch Samonas, and his attempts to control great families such as the Doukai led to the revolt of Andronikos Doukas in 906. In December 886 he dismissed Patriarch Photios and replaced him with his own 19-year-old brother Stephen.

His fortune in war was mixed. He provoked a war with Simeon I of Bulgaria in 894 and was defeated, then lost the Battle of Boulgarophygon in 896 and had to pay annual tribute. He won a victory over the Emirate of Tarsus in 900, but Taormina fell in 902, the renegade Leo of Tripolis sacked Thessalonica in 904, and an expedition to recover Crete failed in 911–912. The Rus' under Prince Oleg attacked Constantinople in 907, and a trade treaty was signed after a second attack in 911.

He married four times. His first three wives died by 901, leaving no surviving heir, and he took Zoe Karbonopsina as mistress, marrying her after she bore a son in 905, against the opposition of Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos, whom he replaced with Euthymios. He had the boy, Constantine, crowned co-emperor on 15 May 908. Leo died on 11 May 912 and was succeeded by his brother Alexander.

Leo wrote political orations, liturgical poems and theological treatises. His legal commission completed the codification begun under his father: the Basilika, in 60 books, arranged nearly all the laws of the Corpus Juris Civilis. His Novels then dealt with current problems and, with the Basilika, removed obsolete institutions such as the Curiae, the Senate and the Consulate from the law. The Book of the Eparch and the Kletorologion of Philotheos were issued under his name, and he is the author or sponsor of the Tactica, a treatise on military operations.
leo-von-klenze: Born Franz Karl Leopold Klenze, he studied architecture and public building finance in Berlin under Friedrich Gilly, and then worked as an apprentice in Paris to Charles Percier and Pierre François Léonard Fontaine. Between 1808 and 1813 he served as a court architect to Jérôme Bonaparte, King of Westphalia. He then moved to Bavaria and began work as court architect to Ludwig I in 1816.

Ludwig I's passion for Hellenism shaped Klenze's style. In Munich he designed the layout of the Königsplatz, a neoclassical square, and built the Monopteros temple in the Englischer Garten in 1836. Near Regensburg he built the Walhalla temple, named after Valhalla, between 1816 and 1842.

His museums drew wide attention. The Glyptothek was Ludwig I's museum for ancient sculpture, and the Alte Pinakothek, a painting gallery for the Wittelsbach collection, opened in 1836 in open parkland. Its functional logic and modernity were much admired, and it was acknowledged as the most advanced museum building in Europe. In 1836 the House of Commons invited Klenze to London, where he was interviewed on Bavarian cultural policy and explained the educational and political aims of the Munich museums, which were free to the public.

When Greece won its independence, Ludwig I's son Otto became its first king, and Klenze was invited to Athens to submit plans for rebuilding the city in the style of ancient Greece. He took part in excavations of ancient buildings there and submitted proposals for the restoration of the Acropolis. In 1838 Nicholas I of Russia commissioned him to design a building for the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg, built from 1839 to 1852.

Klenze was also an accomplished painter. He often depicted ancient buildings, and the pictures served as models for his own projects. In 1841 he sold Ludwig I a collection of 58 landscapes and genre paintings by contemporary German painters, which form the core of the Neue Pinakothek's collection. He died in 1864 and was buried in the Alter Südfriedhof in Munich.
leon-battista-alberti: Leon Battista Alberti was born in Genoa on 14 February 1404. His father, Lorenzo di Benedetto Alberti, was a wealthy Florentine who had been exiled from his own city and was allowed to return in 1428. Alberti was sent to boarding school in Padua and studied law at Bologna. In 1431 he travelled to Rome, took holy orders and entered the service of the papal court, where his study of ancient ruins stirred his interest in architecture.
By the age of twenty he had written a comedy, Philodoxius, that was passed off as a genuine classical work and later deceived the editor Aldus Manutius. He never married.

In 1435 Alberti began Della pittura, dedicated to Filippo Brunelleschi in its Italian version, which analysed perspective, composition and colour and has been called the first scientific study of perspective. He held that mathematics underlay the arts and defined beauty as the harmony of all parts in relation to one another. His De re aedificatoria, completed in 1452 on the basis of Vitruvius, was the first architectural treatise of the Renaissance, covering subjects from history and town planning to engineering and aesthetics. It was dedicated to Pope Nicholas V and not printed until 1485.

He wrote widely beyond the arts.
