I libri della famiglia, in the Tuscan dialect, discussed education, marriage and household management; Momus was a comedy about the gods; and he composed the first Italian grammar and a work on ciphers. He is credited with inventing the first polyalphabetic cipher, and David Kahn called him the father of Western cryptography.

From 1438 Alberti turned more to architecture, encouraged by Leonello d'Este of Ferrara. In 1446 he designed the façade of the Rucellai Palace in Florence, executed by Bernardo Rossellino, and in 1447 he became architectural adviser to Nicholas V. Sigismondo Malatesta commissioned him in 1450 to transform the Gothic church of San Francesco in Rimini into the Tempio Malatestiano, whose façade was left incomplete.

At Santa Maria Novella in Florence he designed the upper façade, bridging nave and aisles with two large scrolls that became a standard feature of later church façades. He also designed two churches in Mantua, San Sebastiano, which was never completed, and Sant'Andrea, which was finished after his death and is considered his most significant work. He interested himself in the look and design of buildings rather than their construction. He died in Rome on 25 April 1472, aged 68.
leon-blum: Léon Blum was born on 9 April 1872 in Paris into a moderately prosperous, assimilated Jewish family in the mercantile business. The family identified strongly with the republic, and as a child Blum attended the public funerals of Léon Gambetta in 1882 and Victor Hugo in 1885. He saw himself as both French and Jewish, and was more influenced by the rationalism of the Enlightenment than by Judaism.

Blum showed little interest in politics until the Dreyfus Affair, which had a traumatic effect on him as on many French Jews. In 1898 he helped the defence of Émile Zola as a jurist, and campaigning as a Dreyfusard brought him into contact with the socialist leader Jean Jaurès, whom he greatly admired. He joined the French Section of the Workers' International (SFIO) and became its main theoretician. He led the SFIO through the 1920s and 1930s, and on 6 April 1921, after the Communists took control of L'Humanité, he made Le Populaire the party's newspaper, as its editor.

The Popular Front won a sweeping victory in June 1936, taking 386 of 608 seats, and Blum became prime minister, the first socialist and first Jew to hold the office. The election brought a wave of strikes involving two million workers, and the Matignon Accords he negotiated gave workers the right to strike, collective bargaining, 12 days of paid annual leave and a 40-hour week. The government also nationalised the arms industries, and dissolved the far-right leagues. The Spanish Civil War divided his coalition, and he adopted non-intervention and resigned in June 1937; his second government lasted from March to April 1938.

In a speech of 1922 Blum said that the Bolshevik regime in Russia was not a dictatorship of the proletariat but a dictatorship over the proletariat, and contrasted the cruelty he saw at the heart of the Communist regime with the humanism he held to be the essence of socialism.

After the fall of France in 1940 he was arrested on 15 September 1940 on a charge of high treason by the Vichy government, held at the Château de Chazeron and then at Bourassol, and wrote his memoirs. He later testified for the prosecution at the trial of Pétain. He headed the provisional government from December 1946 to January 1947 and died on 30 March 1950.
leon-mba: Léon M'ba was born on 9 February 1902 in Libreville, a member of the Fang ethnic group. His father was a small business manager and village chief who had once worked as hairdresser to the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, and his mother, Louise Bendome, was a seamstress. He joined a seminary in 1909, then worked as a store manager, lumberjack and trader before entering the French colonial administration as a customs agent. His activism for Black Gabonese, particularly the Fang, worried his superiors, and in December 1922 he was sentenced to prison for giving a colleague falsified documents.

In the mid-1920s he was reconciled with the authorities and made chef de canton of Libreville's Fang neighbourhood. Accused of complicity in the murder of a woman near Libreville, he was sentenced in 1931 to three years in prison and ten years in exile in Oubangui-Chari. There he wrote an essay on the customary law of the Fang, published in 1938, which became the main reference on the subject. He was allowed to return to Gabon in 1946.

After his return M'ba founded the Gabonese Mixed Committee, was elected to the Territorial Assembly in 1952 and became mayor of Libreville in 1956. On 21 May 1957 he was appointed vice-president of the governor's council, the highest position then held by a native African in French Gabon. He became the first prime minister of Gabon in 1959. In the month before independence he signed fifteen cooperation agreements with France, covering national defence, technical cooperation, economic support and national stability, and on 17 August 1960 independence was proclaimed.

In February 1961 he was elected president as the only candidate, and a new constitution that month gave him full executive powers. A cult of personality developed around him, with songs in his praise and stamps and loincloths bearing his image. On 17 and 18 February 1964 about 150 soldiers arrested him and announced a coup; a provisional government was offered to Jean-Hilaire Aubame. M'ba was restored within days after French intervention under Charles de Gaulle, and Aubame was sentenced to ten years of hard labour and ten years of exile.

From 1965 the French looked for a successor to the ageing and sick president and chose Albert Bernard Bongo, whom M'ba appointed vice-president in November 1966. M'ba was re-elected on 19 March 1967 with 99.9 per cent of the vote. He died of cancer in Paris on 28 November 1967, and Bongo succeeded him the next day. Gabon's main airport, Leon M'ba International Airport, was later named for him.
leon-trotsky: Lev Davidovich Bronstein was born on 7 November 1879 in Yanovka, in Kherson Governorate of the Russian Empire, now part of Ukraine, the fifth child of a wealthy but illiterate Jewish farming family. His father intended him to become a mechanical engineer. In 1896 he moved to Nikolayev and became involved in revolutionary activity; at first a narodnik who opposed Marxism, he was converted by his future first wife, Aleksandra Sokolovskaya. He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1898 and was arrested and exiled to Siberia. After escaping in 1902 he went to London, joined Lenin and the other editors of Iskra, and took the name Trotsky. In the 1905 Revolution he was elected chairman of the Saint Petersburg Soviet.

After the February Revolution of 1917 he joined the Bolsheviks and became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet. He helped lead the October Revolution, then as People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs negotiated the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, by which Russia left the First World War. In March 1918 he became People's Commissar of Army and Navy Affairs, with full control of the Red Army. Other Bolshevik military leaders protested against his reliance on strict discipline and former imperial officers. He led the Red Army to victory in the civil war.

As Lenin's health failed, Stalin became General Secretary in 1922, and Zinoviev and Kamenev joined him in a triumvirate to stop Trotsky from succeeding Lenin. From 1923 Trotsky led the Left Opposition. He was expelled from the Politburo in 1926 and from the party in 1927, exiled to Alma Ata in 1928 and expelled from the Soviet Union to Turkey in February 1929. He later lived in France and Norway before settling in Mexico in 1937.

In exile Trotsky wrote against Stalinism, argued in The Revolution Betrayed that the Soviet Union had become a degenerated workers' state, and in 1938 founded the Fourth International. The Moscow show trial of August 1936 sentenced him to death in absentia, and an independent commission chaired by John Dewey found him not guilty of the charges. Ramón Mercader, a Stalinist agent, assassinated him in Mexico City, and he died on 21 August 1940. He was written out of official Soviet history and, unlike most of Stalin's rivals, was never rehabilitated by later Soviet leaders. His ideas inspired a school of Marxism known as Trotskyism.
leonard-bernstein: Leonard Bernstein was born Louis Bernstein on 25 August 1918 in Lawrence, Massachusetts, to Jewish immigrant parents. His father, Samuel Joseph Bernstein, came from an ultra-Orthodox shtetl in the Russian Empire, wanted to become a rabbi and left for the United States in 1908. His mother, Jennie, born in Russia, arrived in 1905 and worked in the woolen mills of Lawrence. In 1935 he enrolled at Harvard College, where he studied music with Edward Burlingame Hill and Walter Piston, and his senior thesis was titled The Absorption of Race Elements into American Music. At Harvard he led a performance of Marc Blitzstein's recently banned musical The Cradle Will Rock in 1939.

Bernstein moved to New York City, where he coached singers, taught piano and transcribed jazz and pop music under the pseudonym Lenny Amber. In 1943 his last-minute debut with the New York Philharmonic at Carnegie Hall, broadcast live across the country, made him widely known overnight. He soon became the first American-born, American-trained conductor to achieve international standing, at a time when conductors traditionally came from Europe. In the 1950s he wrote five new works for Broadway, composed the score for Elia Kazan's On the Waterfront in 1954 and was appointed music director of the New York Philharmonic, with which he toured the world.

He led the orchestra for eleven seasons and championed Gustav Mahler, Carl Nielsen, Jean Sibelius and Charles Ives. He conducted over 40 world premieres, among them the first performance of Ives's Symphony No. 2. His works include Candide, West Side Story, the Chichester Psalms of 1965 and the theatre piece Mass of 1971. His Jewish heritage is audible in the symphonies Jeremiah and Kaddish. On television he introduced millions of viewers to symphonic music, notably through the Young People's Concerts. In the 1980s he co-founded the Los Angeles Philharmonic Institute, the Schleswig-Holstein Musik Festival Orchestral Academy and the Pacific Music Festival.

Bernstein supported civil rights, protested against the Vietnam War, advocated nuclear disarmament and raised money for AIDS research. On Christmas Day 1989 he conducted Beethoven's Symphony No. 9 in Berlin to celebrate the fall of the Berlin Wall. He announced his retirement from conducting on 9 October 1990 and died five days later at the Dakota in New York, aged 72, of a heart attack brought on by a pleural tumour. He is buried at Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn, next to his wife Felicia Montealegre.
leonard-woolley: Charles Leonard Woolley was born on 17 April 1880 at Upper Clapton, in the modern London Borough of Hackney, the son of a clergyman. He was educated at St John's School, Leatherhead, and New College, Oxford, and was interested in excavation from a young age. In 1905 he became assistant at the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, and in 1906 Arthur Evans volunteered him to run the excavations at the Roman site of Corbridge, near Hadrian's Wall. He later admitted in his book Spadework that he had no idea how to make a survey or a ground-plan.

Woolley then worked in Nubia with David Randall-MacIver, between 1907 and 1911. In 1912 to 1914 he excavated the Hittite city of Carchemish in Syria, with T. E. Lawrence as his assistant. The two were apparently working for British Naval Intelligence, monitoring the building of Germany's Berlin to Baghdad railway. In the First World War Woolley worked on naval espionage from Alexandria. His requisitioned yacht Zaida sank off Alexandretta on 17 August 1916, after striking a French-laid mine, and he was held by Turkey as a prisoner of war for two years.

From 1922 he led a joint expedition of the British Museum and the University of Pennsylvania to Ur, which included his wife, the archaeologist Katharine Woolley. Among the finds in the royal cemetery were the Bull-Headed Lyre and the pair of Ram in a Thicket figurines. Queen Pu-abi's tomb was untouched by looters. Her body lay with two attendants who had been killed to serve her after death, and Woolley reconstructed her funeral from the objects. Agatha Christie, invited to a dig in Iraq in 1930, met her second husband, Max Mallowan, there.

Interested in links between the ancient Aegean and Mesopotamia, Woolley turned in 1936 to Al Mina in Syria, and excavated Tell Atchana in 1937 to 1939 and 1946 to 1949. His team found palaces, temples, houses and fortification walls in 17 levels, including the inscribed statue of Idrimi, a king of Alalakh in the early 15th century BCE. At Ur he identified a flood stratum, and was among the first to propose that the flood of the Book of Genesis was local.

He was knighted in 1935 and is regarded as one of the first modern archaeologists to excavate methodically, keeping careful records and using them to reconstruct ancient life. During the Second World War he served in the Monuments, Fine Arts and Archives Section of the Allied armies. His books include The Sumerians (1928) and Excavations at Ur (1954). He died in London on 20 February 1960.
leonardo-bruni: Leonardo Bruni, also called Leonardo Aretino, was born in Arezzo in Tuscany around 1370. He was the pupil of Coluccio Salutati, under whom he developed his idea of civic humanism, and he later succeeded him as Chancellor of Florence. From 1405 to 1414 he served as apostolic secretary to four popes. His years as chancellor, 1410 to 1411 and again from 1427 until his death, were plagued by warfare, and although he held one of the highest offices he was relatively powerless beside the Albizzi and Medici families. He died in Florence on 9 March 1444 and was succeeded by Carlo Marsuppini.

His most notable work is the History of the Florentine People in twelve books. Bruni was the earliest person to write with the three-period view of history: Antiquity, the Middle Ages and the Modern. His dates for the periods are not exactly those of modern historians, but he laid the groundwork for the division. The idea builds on Petrarch, who distinguished the classical period from later cultural decline, the tenebrae or darkness. Bruni argued that Italy had revived in recent centuries and so was entering a new age. Because that view is secular, he has been called the first modern historian.

He also wrote the New Cicero, a biography of the Roman statesman, and biographies in Italian of Dante and Petrarch, and he used the phrase studia humanitatis, from which the word humanists comes. He translated Greek philosophy and history into Latin, including Aristotle and Procopius, and his versions of Aristotle's Politics and Nicomachean Ethics circulated widely in manuscript and print. In the Panegyric to the City of Florence (c. 1401) he drew on Aelius Aristides to support his republican arguments. He is buried in a wall tomb by Bernardo Rossellino in Santa Croce, Florence.
leonardo-da-vinci: Leonardo di ser Piero da Vinci was born on 15 April 1452 in or close to the Tuscan hill town of Vinci, about 35 kilometres from Florence. He was born out of wedlock to Caterina di Meo Lippi, from the lower class, and Piero da Vinci, a Florentine legal notary and landowner. Where he was born is uncertain: a local oral tradition names Anchiano, a hamlet that would have offered privacy, though he may have been born in a house Ser Piero had in Florence.

Both parents married separately the year after his birth, and Leonardo eventually had 16 half-siblings, with whom he had very little contact. He was educated in Florence by Andrea del Verrocchio, under whom he studied anatomy and first gained attention for the Baptism of Christ, painted in conjunction with Verrocchio.

For the better part of four hundred years Leonardo's fame rested on his painting. The qualities of his work include innovative techniques for laying on paint, detailed knowledge of anatomy, light, botany and geology, an interest in how people show emotion in expression and gesture, and subtle gradation of tone. They come together in the Mona Lisa, the Last Supper and the Virgin of the Rocks. He also drew prolifically, producing the Vitruvian Man, a study of the proportions of the human body.

His studies in science and engineering were recorded in about 13,000 pages of notes and drawings that fuse art and natural philosophy. His approach was observational: he tried to understand a phenomenon by describing and depicting it in utmost detail. He lacked formal education in Latin and mathematics, though he taught himself Latin. Relatively few of his designs for flying machines and the like were feasible in his lifetime, and he did not publish his findings.

Leonardo spent his last three years in France at the invitation of Francis I, and was buried in the collegiate church of Saint Florentin at the Château d'Amboise on 12 August 1519. His notebooks passed to his pupil and heir Francesco Melzi, and after Melzi's death in 1570 they were gradually dispersed. Many historians regard Leonardo as the prime exemplar of the Renaissance man or universal genius. The church was demolished in 1802, and the location of his remains is disputed.
leonhard-euler: Leonhard Euler was born in Basel on 15 April 1707, the oldest of four children of Paul III Euler, a pastor of the Reformed Church, and Marguerite, née Brucker. Soon after his birth the family moved to Riehen, where his father became pastor and Euler spent most of his childhood. His father, who had taken courses from Jacob Bernoulli at the University of Basel, taught him mathematics. Around the age of eight he went to live with his maternal grandmother and enrolled at the Latin school in Basel, and he was also tutored privately by the theologian Johannes Burckhardt.

Daniel Bernoulli, who had entered the Imperial Russian Academy of Sciences in Saint Petersburg, recommended Euler for a post, and Euler arrived there in May 1727. He was soon promoted from the medical department to the mathematics department, lodged with Bernoulli, mastered Russian and worked as a medic in the Russian Navy. In June 1741, concerned about turmoil in Russia, he left for the Berlin Academy at the invitation of Frederick the Great of Prussia and lived in Berlin for 25 years. There he published the Introductio in analysin infinitorum in 1748 and the Institutiones calculi differentialis in 1755. In 1766 he accepted an invitation to return to Saint Petersburg after Catherine the Great came to the throne.

Euler married Katharina Gsell on 7 January 1734; of their 13 children, five survived childhood. After her death in 1773 he married her half-sister, Salome Abigail Gsell. He became almost blind in his right eye in 1738, and a cataract in his left was discovered in 1766 and left him almost totally blind. With the help of scribes his productivity in many areas increased; in 1775 he produced on average one mathematical paper a week.

His writings, collected as the Opera Omnia, include 866 publications and over 4,500 letters. Euler introduced or popularised much modern notation, including f(x) for a function, e for the base of the natural logarithm, the Greek letter sigma for summations and i for the imaginary unit, and he popularised the use of the Greek letter pi, which originated with the Welsh mathematician William Jones. In 1735 he solved the Basel problem, finding the sum of the reciprocals of the squares, posed by Pietro Mengoli in 1644.

His solution of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem, showing that no path crosses each bridge exactly once, is considered the first theorem of graph theory. He also found the formula relating the vertices, edges and faces of a convex polyhedron. Euler died in Saint Petersburg on 18 September 1783 of a brain haemorrhage, after discussing the newly discovered planet Uranus with Anders Johan Lexell. He was buried beside Katharina at the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery.
leonid-brezhnev: Leonid Ilyich Brezhnev was born on 19 December 1906 in Kamenskoye, in the Yekaterinoslav Governorate of the Russian Empire, now Kamianske in Ukraine, the son of a metalworker. His ethnicity was given as Ukrainian in some documents, including his passport, and as Russian in others. He joined the Communist youth league in 1923 and became a party member in 1929. After the German invasion in June 1941 he oversaw mobilisation and the evacuation of factories, then joined the Red Army as a commissar, serving under Nikita Khrushchev on the Southern Front. He ended the war as a major general.

After the war Brezhnev was first secretary of the Zaporizhzhia and then the Dnipropetrovsk regional party committees. In 1950 he was sent to Moldavia, where he completed the introduction of collective agriculture. In 1955 he became first secretary in Kazakhstan, where he oversaw the construction of the Baikonur Cosmodrome and the Virgin Lands campaign. He joined the Central Committee in 1952 and the Politburo by 1957. Brezhnev stayed outwardly loyal to Khrushchev but became involved in a 1963 plot to remove him. After Khrushchev fell in 1964 he governed at first in a triumvirate with Alexei Kosygin and Nikolai Podgorny.

Brezhnev reached decisions in the Politburo by consensus, restoring the semblance of collective leadership. His rule was associated with the doctrine of Developed Socialism, adopted by him in 1971 and written into the constitution in 1977. In 1968 he publicly denounced the Prague Spring as revisionist, though archives suggest he first sought a compromise before deciding to intervene. Repression and censorship increased compared with the Khrushchev Thaw, and the period became known as the Era of Stagnation, with corruption, fewer consumer goods and slower growth.

A personality cult grew while his health declined. He received over 100 medals and the rank of Marshal of the Soviet Union on his 70th birthday. After a heart attack in 1975 he deferred increasingly to Yuri Andropov, Andrei Gromyko and the defence minister. He died on 10 November 1982, and Andropov succeeded him.
leonid-kravchuk: Leonid Makarovych Kravchuk was born on 10 January 1934 in the village of Velykyi Zhytyn in Volhynia, into an ethnic Ukrainian peasant family. The village was then part of the Second Polish Republic and was annexed into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic after the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939. His parents worked under Polish landowners, and his father, who had served in the Polish Army, was killed in the Second World War.

Kravchuk joined the Communist Party of Ukraine in 1958 and worked in the party apparatus in Chernivtsi Oblast from 1960. He entered the party's Central Committee in 1970 and became head of its Department of Agitation and Propaganda in 1980, where he promoted ideological propaganda and fought what the party called Ukrainian bourgeois nationalism. He became second secretary on 23 June 1990. Between 1989 and 1991 he changed from a hardline propagandist against Ukrainian nationalism into a supporter of it, a shift that the scholar Alexander Motyl described as a metamorphosis.

He became Chairman of the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR in 1990, opposed the coup attempt of 1991 and led Ukraine to independence. A referendum in December 1991 confirmed it, and he was elected president. He was inaugurated on 5 December 1991, when the Rada also renounced the 1922 treaty creating the Soviet Union. Kravchuk said at the ceremony that the empire which had endured for 337 years no longer existed.

As president, Kravchuk relied on an informal coalition of national communists and moderate national democrats. He treated state-building as more important than economic reform, supported the creation of an independent Armed Forces of Ukraine, gave up Ukraine's nuclear arsenal and welcomed the enlargement of NATO. Economic reform was postponed, and gross domestic product contracted by 40% during his time in office.

Coal miners in the Donbas began striking on 2 September 1992. Kravchuk dissolved the Verkhovna Rada on 17 June 1993 and called snap parliamentary and presidential elections for 1994. He lost the presidency on 19 July 1994 to his former prime minister Leonid Kuchma. He then served as a People's Deputy from 1994 to 2006 and died on 10 May 2022, aged 88, the last surviving signatory of the Belovezha Accords.
leonidas-i: Leonidas was born about 540 BCE, the son of King Anaxandridas II, and was the 17th king of the Agiad dynasty, a Spartan royal house that claimed descent from Heracles. According to Herodotus, his mother was also his father's niece and had been childless so long that the ephors urged Anaxandridas to set her aside. He refused, and the ephors let him take a second wife, who bore Cleomenes. A year later the first wife bore Dorieus, and then Leonidas. Anaxandridas died about 524 BCE and Cleomenes succeeded him. Leonidas married Cleomenes's daughter Gorgo before coming to the throne.

Leonidas succeeded his half-brother Cleomenes I, who had been deposed on grounds of purported insanity and had fled into exile. He ruled jointly with Leotychidas II until his death in 480 BCE. When the Greeks resolved to resist the second Persian invasion in 481 BCE they chose him to lead their combined forces, probably for his ability as a military leader and not simply as a tribute to Sparta's strength. His son Pleistarchus succeeded him.

Sparta consulted the Oracle at Delphi, which is said to have prophesied that either the city would be wasted by Persian men or Lacedaemon would mourn a dead king of the line of Heracles. In August 480 BCE Leonidas marched to Thermopylae with 300 Spartans and their attendants, and Greeks from other cities joined him under his command. A Malian traitor, Ephialtes, led the Persian general Hydarnes by a mountain track to the rear of the Greeks. Leonidas sent most of the troops away and stayed with his 300 Spartans, 900 helots, 400 Thebans and 700 Thespians, who stayed of their own will. The Thebans surrendered and the rest were killed on 11 August. Xerxes ordered the head cut off and put on a stake.

A hero cult of Leonidas lasted in Sparta until the 2nd century CE, with annual contests called the Leonideia, which only Spartans could enter. They were held opposite the theatre at Sparta, where stood the tombs of Pausanias and Leonidas. A bronze statue was erected at Thermopylae in 1955 and another in Sparta in 1969.
leopold-i-holy-roman-emperor: Leopold was born in Vienna on 9 June 1640, the second son of Emperor Ferdinand III and Maria Anna of Spain. He had been selected for a career in the higher clergy, and the plan was dropped when his elder brother Ferdinand IV died in 1654 and he became heir. His clerical education and Jesuit influence marked him throughout his life: he was unusually knowledgeable for a monarch in theology and jurisprudence and embodied the pietas Austriaca of his house. In July 1658 he was elected emperor at Frankfurt against the wishes of Cardinal Mazarin of France, who had hoped to place the crown on a non-Habsburg prince.

In a war with the Ottoman Empire that began in 1663, Raimondo Montecuccoli won at Saint Gotthard in August 1664, and the Peace of Vasvár brought a twenty years' truce. French expansion, above all the seizure of Lorraine in 1670, drew him into the Franco-Dutch War, the Nine Years' War and the War of the Spanish Succession. In Hungary, unrest caused partly by his wish to crush Protestantism led to a rising that was put down in 1671, and the country was treated with great severity for some years. He also expelled the Jewish community of Vienna from the area across the Danube Canal, which was then renamed Leopoldstadt.

In 1683 an Ottoman army besieged Vienna from July to September while Leopold took refuge at Passau. On 12 September the allied army, joined by King John III Sobieski of Poland, routed the Ottoman Turks. Victories followed at Mohács in 1687 and Zenta in 1697, and in January 1699 the Treaty of Karlowitz gave the Habsburgs almost the whole of Hungary. In 1687 the Diet of Hungary admitted the right of the Habsburgs to succeed without election. In 1700 he granted the Elector of Brandenburg the title of King in Prussia. He died on 5 May 1705.

Leopold regarded himself as an absolute sovereign and was extremely tenacious of his rights. He was a staunch proponent of the Counter-Reformation. Short, thin and of sickly constitution, he was cold and reserved in public, with the prominent Habsburg jaw; a 1670 silver coin, which most collectors doubt was accurate, led to his nickname the Hogmouth. He had a taste and talent for music and composed several oratorios and suites of dances, and his sacred music, including a Requiem Mass for his first wife, is perhaps his most successful. He supported composers such as Antonio Bertali and Johann Kaspar Kerll.
leopold-i-margrave-of-austria: Leopold was born about 940, and his origins are not known. According to some sources his father Berthold was count in the Nordgau, north of Regensburg; a more recent theory makes him a younger son of Duke Arnulf of Bavaria. His ancestry remains disputed, though descent from the Popponids, the Elder House of Babenberg, is assumed. He is first mentioned in a document of Emperor Otto I of 13 February 962 as Liupo, count of the Bavarian Donaugau and of the Traungau, and a faithful follower of the Emperor.

After his victory over the Magyars at the Battle of Lechfeld in 955, Otto I re-established the Eastern March of Bavaria under Margrave Burkhard. Burkhard joined the uprising of Duke Henry II against Otto II and was deposed at the Imperial Diet of Regensburg in 976. By a charter of 21 July 976 Leopold was appointed margrave of the Eastern March, the core of the later Archduchy of Austria. The resettlement of the east was slow and centred on the fortress of Pöchlarn down the Danube. His margraviate at first coincided with the Wachau valley, bounded in the east by the Traisen.

With the Magyar threat much reduced, Leopold concentrated on securing his holdings against internal threats. In 984 he reduced the fortress at Melk, still held by supporters of the late margrave, and probably made it his residence, founding a monastery there for twelve secular priests. By 987 his boundary reached the Wienerwald, and by 991, jointly with the reinstated Duke Henry II, it reached the Fischa river.

In 994 Leopold went to Würzburg to mediate between his cousin Margrave Henry of Schweinfurt and Bishop Bernward, one of whose knights Henry had seized and blinded. At a tournament on 8 July he was hit in the eye by an arrow aimed at his cousin, and he died on 10 July 994. He was buried in Würzburg; his son Ernest I, Duke of Swabia, was buried beside him in 1015, and in the 13th century their remains were returned to Melk Abbey. The chronicler Thietmar wrote that no man was wiser in all his actions. Otto III at once gave his son Henry I the margraviate.

Leopold married Richardis, and they had eight children, among them Henry I, Adalbert, the third margrave, and Poppo, Archbishop of Trier. In 1976 the thousandth anniversary of his appointment was marked as a Thousand Years of Austria.
leopold-i-of-belgium: Leopold was born on 16 December 1790 at Ehrenburg Palace in Coburg, the youngest surviving son of Francis, Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld. His eldest brother, Ernest I, founded the dynasty of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha and was the father of Prince Albert. Leopold held Russian military rank from the age of six, fought against Napoleon, and in 1814 went to England with Emperor Alexander.

On 2 May 1816 he married Princess Charlotte of Wales, the only legitimate child of the Prince Regent. He became a British citizen and a Field Marshal and Knight of the Garter that year. The marriage was happy but ended after a year and a half, when Charlotte died after delivering a stillborn son. As uncle of Queen Victoria, Leopold arranged her marriage to his nephew Prince Albert. He refused the throne of an independent Greece, offered under the London Protocol of February 1830, believing it too precarious.

Rebels in the southern provinces of the United Netherlands rose against Dutch rule at the end of August 1830, and a National Congress drew up a constitution for a popular monarchy. It refused any candidate from the Dutch house of Orange-Nassau, and the Great Powers wanted a neutral candidate. Leopold, the British-backed candidate, had connections with royal houses and was tied to no power believed to have territorial ambitions in Belgium. He took the oath as King of the Belgians on 21 July 1831, commemorated annually as Belgian National Day.

On 2 August 1831 the Netherlands invaded, starting the Ten Days' Campaign. Leopold led a small force defending the outskirts of Brussels and appealed for help, and the arrival of a French army forced the Dutch to withdraw. By the Treaty of London of April 1839 the Netherlands recognised Belgian independence. In 1832 he married Louise of Orléans, daughter of Louis Philippe I. He favoured the Liberals over the Catholics, although he refused to give up his Lutheran faith, and he helped fund Belgium's first railway in 1835. In 1848 about 6,000 armed émigrés of the Belgian Legion were stopped at Quiévrain and Risquons-Tout.

For his part in European affairs Leopold was called the Nestor of Europe. He worked to repair Franco-British relations, arranging a meeting at the Château d'Eu in 1843 between Louis Philippe and Queen Victoria. He died on 10 December 1865 of dysentery, aged 74, and his son Leopold II succeeded him.
leopold-ii-grand-duke-of-tuscany: Leopold II was born in Florence, the son of Ferdinand III of Tuscany and Princess Luisa Maria Amelia Teresa of the Two Sicilies, who were double first cousins. As a child he accompanied his father in flight to Germany when the French occupied Tuscany, and the family returned to Florence after Napoleon's defeat in 1814. He married Maria Anna of Saxony in 1817 and, after her death in 1832, Maria Antonia of the Two Sicilies in 1833. His son Ferdinand by the second marriage later succeeded him.

Leopold succeeded his father on 18 June 1824 and for twenty years devoted himself to the internal development of the state. His was the mildest and least reactionary of the Italian despotisms of the day: although subject to Austrian influence, he refused to adopt Austrian methods of government, allowed the press a fair measure of liberty and let political exiles from other states live in Tuscany undisturbed. After riots in 1845 and 1846 he granted administrative reforms, formed a National Guard on 4 September 1847, and on 17 February 1848 granted a constitution written by Gino Capponi. Under popular pressure he sent regulars and volunteers to fight beside Piedmont in Lombardy, and they fought bravely but unsuccessfully at Curtatone and Montanara.

Unrest followed the failure of that campaign, and Livorno fell into something like civil war. Alarmed by republican agitation, Leopold left Florence for Gaeta, and a republic was proclaimed on 18 February 1849 with Francesco Domenico Guerrazzi as dictator. The municipal council then invited him back, and he returned on 28 July. The Austrians, whose intervention he had requested, occupied Lucca, Livorno and Florence. In April 1850 he made a treaty with Austria suspending the constitution and admitting an occupation force of 10,000 men, and he formally revoked the constitution in 1852. Guerrazzi and many others were condemned to long prison terms. By the time the Austrians left in 1855 his popularity was gone.

On 27 April 1859, as France and Piedmont made war on Austria, a bloodless revolution broke out in Florence, and the Grand Duke and his family left for Bologna. On 21 July he abdicated in favour of his son Ferdinand IV, who never reigned, and Tuscany was later incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy. He lived in exile in Austria and was elected mayor of Schlackenwerth. He moved to Rome in 1869 and died there on 29 January 1870. Historians have judged him well-meaning but weak, too bound by family ties and Habsburg tradition to become a real Liberal. He ordered the water tunnel La Botte under the Arno, completed in 1859, which allowed the drainage of Lake Bientina.
leopold-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Leopold was born in Vienna on 5 May 1747, his parents' third son, and was first meant for a clerical career. The deaths of two older brothers made him heir to Tuscany, a territory designated for the second-born son. He married Maria Luisa, daughter of King Charles III of Spain, in person on 5 August 1765, and on the death of his father, Francis I, on 18 August 1765 became Grand Duke of Tuscany. For five years he held little more than nominal authority under counsellors appointed by his mother, until in 1770 he went to Vienna to end the guardianship.

He then spent twenty years reforming his small state. He removed restrictions on industry and personal freedom left from the Medici period, introduced a rational system of taxation at lower rates and carried out public works such as the drainage of the Valdichiana. With no army, he put his whole revenue into improvement.

His church policy, which brought him into collision with the Pope, failed to secularise monastic property. On 30 November 1786, after capital executions had been blocked in practice (the last was in 1769), he promulgated the Leopoldine Code, which abolished the death penalty and banned torture. A law of 23 January 1774 on the insane was the first of its kind in Europe, and a constitution he supported was never put into effect.

Joseph II died on 20 February 1790, and Leopold left Florence on 3 March, leaving Tuscany to his younger son Ferdinand III. As emperor he made large concessions to the Estates his brother had offended, pacified the Hungarians and Bohemians, and marched troops into the Austrian Netherlands. On 9 May 1790 he issued a decree returning thousands of Bohemian serfs freed by Joseph to servitude. He met Frederick William II of Prussia at Reichenbach in July 1790, was crowned King of Hungary on 11 November 1790, and made a truce with the Ottoman Turks that led to the Treaty of Sistova in August 1791.

The French Revolution endangered his sister Marie Antoinette. After the royal family's flight to Varennes he issued the Padua Circular, and on 25 August 1791 he and the King of Prussia drew up the Declaration of Pillnitz; he hoped that intervention in France would not be required. Mozart's opera La clemenza di Tito was commissioned for his coronation as King of Bohemia in Prague on 6 September 1791. Leopold died of pneumonia in Vienna on 1 March 1792. He had sixteen children, and his eldest son succeeded him as Francis II.
leopold-iii-duke-of-austria: Leopold was born in Vienna on 1 November 1351, a younger son of Duke Albert II of Austria and a grandson of King Albert I of Germany. His mother, Joanna of Pfirt, was 51 when she gave him birth and died shortly afterwards. His eldest brother, Rudolf IV, called the Founder, took over the Habsburg dominions on their father's death, despite Albert II's rules for joint rule, and on 18 November 1364 issued his own house law, the Rudolfinische Hausordnung, declaring the hereditary lands a common possession of the brothers, with extra rights to the eldest. On 23 February 1365 Leopold married Viridis Visconti, second daughter of Bernabò Visconti, Lord of Milan, and they had four sons and three daughters.

After Rudolf died on 27 July 1365, Albert III and Leopold took over the Habsburg lands, Albert holding the additional rights as eldest. While Albert ruled, Leopold became a general leading Habsburg troops. In 1368 he defeated a Bavarian incursion into Tyrol, and by 1370 all of Tyrol was under Habsburg authority. In 1372 he broke with his brother over rights, prestige and income, and a peace treaty of 25 July 1373 gave him control of Tyrol, Further Austria and Carniola, with income split between the dukes.

By 1375 Leopold had inherited the former Gorizia possessions in the Windic March, White Carniola, Friuli and Istria, and the city of Feldkirch. When Albert went to Prussia in 1377, he was left in charge of all the Habsburg lands. On 7 July 1379 the brothers signed the Treaty of Neuberg, which made Leopold exclusive ruler of Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, Tyrol and the Further Austrian lands in Swabia. In 1382 he was granted Trieste as part of his payment for defeating Venice.

Leopold's further attempts to expand his position in Switzerland failed when he was killed at the Battle of Sempach on 9 July 1386. He was first buried at Königsfelden Monastery; his remains were moved to St Blaise Abbey in a ceremony on 14 November 1770 and finally to Saint Paul's Abbey in Carinthia. He was the head and progenitor of the Leopoldian line, and his eldest son William succeeded him. His other sons included Leopold IV, Ernest the Iron and Frederick IV.
leopold-sedar-senghor: Léopold Sédar Senghor was born on 9 October 1906 at Joal, about 110 kilometres south of Dakar. His father, Basile Diogoye Senghor, was a wealthy Serer peanut merchant, and his mother, Gnilane Ndiémé Bakhoum, was his father's third wife. In 1922 he entered a seminary in Dakar but was told that the religious life was not for him. A scholarship took him to France in 1928, where he studied at the Sorbonne and the Lycée Louis-le-Grand, gained the agrégation in French grammar in 1935 and taught at Tours and near Paris. In Paris he was among the African and diaspora students who devised the idea of négritude.

Senghor was drafted in 1939 as a private in the 3rd Colonial Infantry Regiment. The Germans captured him in June 1940, and he spent two years in camps, writing poems and learning enough German to read Goethe. Released in 1942 for medical reasons, he joined the resistance while teaching. After the war he became a deputy for Sénégal-Mauritanie in the French National Assembly. He argued for French citizenship for all French territories and for a federation in which each African territory governed its own affairs. In 1948 he founded the Bloc démocratique sénégalais with Mamadou Dia.

He formed the Mali Federation with Modibo Keita, and it failed in 1960. He was then elected first President of Senegal on 5 September 1960. In December 1962 he had his prime minister Mamadou Dia arrested on suspicion of plotting a coup, and Dia was held for twelve years. By 1966 Senegal was a one-party state; in 1976 Senghor allowed opposition parties, limited to three. He resigned at the end of 1980 in favour of Abdou Diouf, the first African head of state to retire voluntarily.

With Aimé Césaire and Léon Damas, Senghor created the concept of Négritude, which sought to honour distinctive African values and aesthetics, as a reaction against the dominance of French culture in the colonies. He held that sub-Saharan Africa and Europe belong to one cultural continuum and that the idea called for dialogue among cultures. His verse includes Chants d'ombre in 1945 and Éthiopiques in 1956, and his Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache of 1948 has an introduction by Jean-Paul Sartre. He developed an African socialism as an alternative to Marxism and kept close ties with France. He died at Verson, in Normandy, on 20 December 2001.
leopold-von-ranke: Leopold von Ranke was born on 21 December 1795 in Wiehe, then part of the Electorate of Saxony, into a family of Lutheran pastors and lawyers. He was educated partly at home and partly at the gymnasium at Schulpforta. In 1814 he entered Leipzig University, where he studied classics and Lutheran theology and became expert in philology and in translating ancient authors into German. Between 1817 and 1825 he taught classics at the Friedrichs Gymnasium in Frankfurt an der Oder. There his interest turned to history, partly from a wish to take part in a developing and more professional field and partly from a wish to find the hand of God in its workings.

In 1824 Ranke published Histories of the Latin and Teutonic Peoples from 1494 to 1514, which drew on memoirs, diaries, letters, government documents, diplomatic dispatches and eyewitness accounts. The minister of education was impressed, and from 1825 Ranke was a professor at the University of Berlin for nearly fifty years. He used the seminar system and taught students how to check the value of sources. He was the first historian to use the forty-seven volumes of Venetian diplomatic archives of the 16th and 17th centuries, and he sent students to other archives as they opened. In 1841 he was appointed Historiographer Royal to the Prussian court.

His Popes of Rome (1834 to 1836) coined the term Counter-Reformation. As a Protestant he was barred from the Vatican Secret Archive and worked from private papers in Rome and Venice. The papacy denounced the book as anti-Catholic, while many Protestants thought it not anti-Catholic enough; Lord Acton defended it as fair-minded. Later came the History of the Reformation in Germany (1854 to 1857), built on ninety-six volumes of ambassadors' correspondence, and a History of England (1859 to 1867, expanded 1870 to 1884).

Ranke held that "every age is next to God": each period is unique and must be understood in its own context, and history is no account of progress. He opposed Hegel's philosophy of history. His wish to show the past wie es eigentlich gewesen, "as it actually was", became a guiding principle for many historians, though its meaning is debated. E. H. Carr called his empiricism naive. He died in Berlin on 23 May 1886, aged 90; his world history, begun in 1880, had reached only the 12th century.
leopoldo-galtieri: Leopoldo Fortunato Galtieri Castelli was born on 15 July 1926 in Caseros, Buenos Aires Province, to working-class Italian Argentine parents. In 1943, at seventeen, he enrolled at the National Military Academy to study civil engineering and began his career in the engineering branch of the army. He graduated from the US Army School of the Americas in 1949 and in 1958 became a professor of engineering at the Senior War College. In 1975, after more than 25 years as a combat engineer, he took command of the army's engineering corps.

Galtieri enthusiastically supported the March 1976 coup that overthrew President Isabel Perón and began the National Reorganization Process. He became a major general in 1977 and commander-in-chief of the army in 1980. During the junta's rule Congress was suspended, trade unions, political parties and provincial governments were banned, and in the Dirty War between 9,000 and 30,000 people deemed left-wing subversives disappeared. In March 1981 he visited the United States, where the Reagan administration treated the regime as a bulwark against communism. He secured Argentine support for the Contra rebels in Nicaragua and in August sent advisers to organise the Nicaraguan Democratic Force.

On 22 December 1981 he became president, eleven days after ousting Roberto Eduardo Viola, who was removed because his regime could not reverse the economic crisis. His economy minister, Roberto Alemann, cut spending, froze salaries amid 130 per cent inflation and began selling state industries, and GDP fell by 5 per cent. His government allowed limited expression of dissent, and anti-junta demonstrations soon became common.

With his popularity low, he ordered the invasion of the Falkland Islands on 2 April 1982. It was at first popular, and patriotic demonstrations replaced the protests. Galtieri and most of his government mistakenly believed that the United Kingdom would not respond militarily. British forces retook Stanley on 14 June 1982, and the rest of the junta removed Galtieri on 17 June.

Arrested in late 1983 with other former junta members, he was charged in a military court with human rights violations and with mismanaging the Falklands War. He was cleared of the civil rights charges in December 1985 but in May 1986 was found guilty of mishandling the war and sentenced to twelve years in prison. The sentences were confirmed in November 1988, and in 1989 President Carlos Menem pardoned him and 39 other officers. In July 2002 new charges concerned kidnapped children and disappearances in the late 1970s, and he was placed under house arrest. He died of a heart attack in Buenos Aires on 12 January 2003, aged 76.
leos-janacek: Leoš Janáček was born in Hukvaldy, Moravia, then part of the Austrian Empire, on 3 July 1854, the son of the schoolmaster Jiří Janacek and Amálie Janáčková. His family had limited means, and his father wanted him to become a teacher but deferred to his evident musical ability. In 1865 he enrolled as a ward of the foundation of St Thomas's Abbey in Brno, where he sang in the choir under Pavel Křížkovský.

In 1874 he entered the Prague organ school, where he lived in poverty, practising on a keyboard drawn on his tabletop. A published criticism of the director's performance of a Gregorian mass led to his expulsion, but he was readmitted and graduated on 24 July 1875 with the best results in his class.

Back in Brno he taught music and from 1876 taught at the Teachers' Institute, where his pupil Zdenka Schulzová, the director's daughter, later became his wife. In 1881 he founded the organ school and directed it until 1919, when it became the Brno Conservatory.

From the early 1890s he led the folklorist activity of Moravia and Silesia, and he composed piano accompaniments for more than 150 folk songs. His first opera, Šárka, dates from 1887-1888. Around the turn of the century he began to combine his folk studies with his transcriptions of the speech melodies of spoken Czech, which gave his vocal lines their distinctive character.

His daughter Olga died in February 1903, and he dedicated the opera Jenůfa to her memory. It was performed in Brno in 1904, but Prague refused it for twelve years; Karel Kovařovic, whose opera he had sharply criticised in 1887, was director of the National Theatre. The revised Jenůfa was accepted there in 1916 and brought Janáček his first acclaim.

In 1917 he met Kamila Stösslová, who inspired the rest of his work, including Káťa Kabanová, The Cunning Little Vixen, the Sinfonietta and the Glagolitic Mass. Most of his output, and his best-known works, belong to the last decade of his life.

In August 1928 he caught a chill on an excursion to Štramberk, which developed into pneumonia, and he died on 12 August 1928 in Ostrava at the age of 74. A large public funeral included music from the last scene of The Cunning Little Vixen, and he was buried in the Circle of Honour at the Brno Central Cemetery. After his death the Australian conductor Charles Mackerras promoted his work on the world opera stage and restored some compositions to their original forms. Janáček is considered one of the most important Czech composers, with Antonín Dvořák and Bedřich Smetana.
lepontic-language: Lepontic is an extinct Alpine Celtic language known from inscriptions found in an area centred on Lugano in Switzerland and including the Lake Como and Lake Maggiore areas of Italy. It was spoken in parts of Rhaetia and Cisalpine Gaul. The name may derive from Proto-Celtic *leikʷontio-, which was also the basis of Lepontina and so of the modern Val Leventina. It is named after the Lepontii, who inhabited parts of ancient Rhaetia. The earliest inscriptions predate the 5th century BCE, with examples from Castelletto Ticino dated to the 6th century BCE and possibly from Sesto Calende as early as the 7th, and their authors are generally associated with the Golasecca culture.

About 140 inscriptions are written in the alphabet of Lugano, one of five main Northern Italic alphabets derived from the Etruscan alphabet. It has 18 letters and does not distinguish voiced from unvoiced stops, so P stands for b or p, T for t or d and K for g or k. Similar scripts wrote Rhaetic and Venetic, and the Germanic runic alphabets probably derive from a script of this group. The alphabet also appears on the coinage of other Alpine tribes, so grouping every text in it as one language is disputed.

Most inscriptions are funerary and often give only the name of the dead, with or without the word pala, stone. Others are dedications. The Prestino stone, dated on epigraphic and archaeological grounds to about 480 to 450 BCE, records a gift to a man named Plialethos. An inscription on a vase from Ornavasso, probably meaning Naxian wine for Latumaros and Sapsuta, contains the P-Celtic conjunctive particle -pe, the P-Celtic form of a Proto-Indo-European clitic.

Its classification has been debated. Until about 1970 it was usually regarded as a para-Celtic or pre-Celtic Western Indo-European language, possibly related to Ligurian. Lejeune argued in 1971 that it is Celtic, perhaps as divergent as Celtiberian yet distinct from Cisalpine Gaulish, a view that has since become standard. Others, such as Joseph F. Eska, treat it as an early form of Cisalpine Gaulish, and Schumacher has considered it a primary branch of Celtic, perhaps the first to diverge from Proto-Celtic. Lepontic was assimilated first by Gaulish, after Gallic tribes settled north of the River Po, and then by Latin, once the Roman Republic gained control of Cisalpine Gaul.
leptis-magna: Leptis Magna stood at the mouth of the Wadi Lebda on the Mediterranean coast. Its ruins lie within present-day Al-Khums, Libya, 130 km east of Tripoli. The Punic name was written lpq, and the Greeks called it Leptis Megale, Greater Leptis, to tell it from the Lesser Leptis nearer Carthage. As a Roman colony it was also known as Ulpia Traiana, after the emperor Trajan.

The Punic city was founded in the second half of the 7th century BCE. It appears to have been strong enough to repel an attempt by Dorieus to found a Greek colony nearby around 515 BCE. It came under Carthage and then, after the Punic Wars, under Rome, but stayed highly independent after about 111 BCE. By 46 BCE its olive oil production allowed it to pay Julius Caesar three million pounds of oil a year as tax. Under Tiberius it was formally incorporated into the province of Africa; it became a municipium in 64 or 65 CE and a colonia under Trajan.

Leptis reached its highest prominence from 193 CE as the home town of the emperor Septimius Severus, who built a new forum, a massive basilica and new docks, and visited with his family in 205. The city reached a population of about 100,000 and prospered through trans-Saharan trade in ivory, wild animals for the arena, gold dust, ebony and ostrich feathers. When trade collapsed in the Crisis of the 3rd Century its importance fell, and by the mid 4th century large parts were abandoned, before a tsunami in 365 devastated it.

The Vandals took Leptis in 439 and demolished its walls. Berber raiders sacked it in 523. Belisarius recaptured it for Justinian I ten years later, but it never recovered from Berber attacks. Around 647 it fell to the Arab conquest, when it was mostly abandoned except for a Byzantine garrison and fewer than 1,000 inhabitants. By the 10th century Al-Khums had absorbed it.

Abandoned, the city lay buried beneath sand dunes and was remarkably preserved. Italian archaeologists unearthed it in the 1920s, and one of the first buildings found, in 1925 and 1926, was the Arch of Septimius Severus. Its ruins are among the best-preserved Roman sites in the Mediterranean. Mosaics of the 1st or 2nd century, including a gladiator resting beside his slain opponent, were found in a Roman villa at Wadi Lebda and are displayed in the Leptis Magna Museum.
les-cayes: Les Cayes, often called Aux Cayes and in Haitian Creole Okay, is a commune and seaport in the Les Cayes Arrondissement in the Sud department of Haiti, with a population of 151,696. Isolated from the turmoil of Port-au-Prince, it is one of Haiti's major ports, exporting mostly coffee and sugarcane, with minor exports of bananas and timber. It is the world's largest supplier of vetiver, a perfume ingredient, of which it exports 250 tons a year.

The first European settlement in the south-west was Salvatierra de la Sabana, founded by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar in 1504; Vasco Núñez de Balboa, a co-founder, lived there for several years raising pigs before leaving hidden in a barrel on an expedition. The settlement was abandoned in 1540. The French colonial administration later founded Aux Cayes, named for its nearness to Île-à-Vache. Hurricanes destroyed the town in 1781 and 1788, and in July 1793 the whites of Les Cayes were massacred.

Simón Bolívar arrived in Les Cayes on 24 December 1815 and on 2 January 1816 was introduced to Alexandre Pétion, President of the Republic of Haiti. After Bolívar pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied, Pétion gave him money and military supplies. During the American occupation, planes bombed Les Cayes on 5 December 1919; the anthropologist Jean-Philippe Belleau called it possibly the first air attack on civilians. On 6 December 1929 U.S. Marines fired on about 1,500 Haitians protesting local economic conditions, killing 12 to 22 and wounding 51. The massacre provoked international outrage, and President Herbert Hoover called for an investigation of conditions in Haiti the next day.

Hurricane Matthew struck Les Cayes on 4 October 2016, and a magnitude 7.2 earthquake on 14 August 2021 near the city killed over 2,200 people and injured about 12,700, most of them in and around Les Cayes. The town draws visitors to Gelée Beach, the Botanical Garden at Bergeau and the nearby Île à Vache. It has an airport, Antoine-Simon Airport, and the public Hôpital Immaculée Conception. André Rigaud, the Haitian revolutionary leader, was born there on a plantation.
lesbos: Lesbos lies in the far east of the Aegean Sea, facing the Turkish coast across the Mytilini Strait, which is about 5.5 kilometres wide at its narrowest. It covers 1,633 square kilometres and has about 400 kilometres of coastline. In the late Palaeolithic and Mesolithic periods it was joined to the Anatolian mainland. The island is roughly triangular, deeply cut by the gulfs of Kalloni and Gera, and its chief town, Mytilene, stands on the south-east coast. The name may originally have meant forested.

People have lived on Lesbos since at least 3000 BCE, with large settlements at Thermi and Lisvori. Two Hittite texts of the Late Bronze Age mention Lazpa, a place usually identified with Lesbos, then apparently a dependent of the Seha River Land. Later Greek writers said that the Penthilidae of Thessaly founded Mytilene and ruled it until a revolt of 590 to 580 BCE led by Pittacus. Emigrants from Thessaly are believed to have brought the Aeolic dialect, which survives in the poems of Sappho. In classical times the cities of the island formed a pentapolis of Mytilene, Methymna, Antissa, Eresos and Pyrrha. Pyrrha was destroyed by an earthquake in 231 BCE, and the Roman Republic destroyed Antissa in 168 BCE.

In the Middle Ages the island belonged to the Byzantine Empire. The deposed empress Irene was exiled to Lesbos in 802 and died there. The Emirate of Crete raided it heavily in the late 9th century, and about 1089 to 1093 the Seljuk emir Tzachas briefly held it but could not take Methymna. The Gattilusi ruled it as tributary vassals of the Ottomans after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, until Mehmed II conquered it in September 1462.

Mehmed II moved richer inhabitants to Constantinople, brought Muslim settlers from Rumelia and Anatolia, and had the cathedral of Mytilene made into a mosque. The island, called Midilli, became a sanjak. Greek naval forces landed on 21 November 1912 during the First Balkan War, and the Ottoman commanders surrendered on 21 December.

Lesbos is part of Greece, a regional unit of the North Aegean region with its seat at Mytilene. Its economy rests mainly on olive oil, with fishing, soap and ouzo. The whole island is the Lesvos Geopark, a member of the European Geoparks Network since 2000, known for its geological heritage and a petrified forest. Its landmarks include the castles of Molyvos, Mytilene and Sigri and a Roman aqueduct at Moria.
lesser-poland: Lesser Poland, Małopolska in Polish and Polonia Minor in Latin, lies in southern and south-eastern Poland in the basin of the upper Vistula, with the Carpathian Mountains and the Tatra range in the south. Historically it consisted of the three voivodeships of Kraków, Sandomierz and Lublin, and covered almost 60,000 square kilometres, reaching from Bielsko-Biała in the south-west to Siedlce in the north-east. It is mostly hilly, and is noted for its powerful magnates and wealthy nobility. The name follows a Polish custom of calling the younger of two like places lesser: Greater Poland was the older cradle of the state, and Lesser Poland appeared in documents in 1493, in the Statutes of Piotrków.

In the early years of Polish statehood the south was inhabited by the West Slavic tribe of Vistulans, with centres at Kraków and Wiślica, while Lublin and Sandomierz were probably the land of the Lendians. Mieszko I annexed the land of the Vistulans in the late 10th century, and Cosmas of Prague wrote that he took Kraków by ruse and killed the Czechs found there. The Archdiocese of Kraków was created around the year 1000, and under Casimir I the Restorer Kraków became capital of Poland for the first time, around 1040.

In the 16th century Lesser Poland remained the country's most important province. No major conflicts took place on its soil, and it was the centre of the Polish Renaissance. The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was created there in 1569 by the Union of Lublin. The Partitions began early in the region: in 1772 Austria seized the south-western corner south of the Vistula, with Żywiec, Tarnów and Biecz, as part of the territory later called Galicia. In 1918 the whole of historical Lesser Poland became part of the restored Polish state.

Lesser Poland should not be confused with the modern Lesser Poland Voivodeship, created in 1998 with Kraków as its capital, which covers only a small south-western part of the historical region. The historical region is now divided among several voivodeships. Kraków is regarded as the cultural capital of Poland, and its Old Town was placed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1978. Kraków's Jagiellonian University, founded in 1364, is the oldest university in Poland, and the Jasna Góra Monastery in Częstochowa draws pilgrims every year.
lester-b-pearson: Lester Bowles Pearson was born on 23 April 1897 in Newtonbrook, now part of Toronto, the son of a Methodist minister. He entered Victoria College at the University of Toronto in 1913. In 1915 he joined the Canadian Army Medical Corps as a stretcher-bearer, served in Egypt and on the Salonika front, and later trained as a flying officer in the Royal Flying Corps, where an instructor gave him the nickname Mike. He studied at St John's College, Oxford, then taught history at Toronto, and in 1925 he married Maryon Moody.

In 1927 Pearson began a career in the Department of External Affairs. He became the second Canadian ambassador to the United States on 1 January 1945 and played a role in establishing both the United Nations and NATO. The Soviet Union vetoed him as secretary-general in 1953. Mackenzie King made him Secretary of State for External Affairs in 1948, and he held the post under Louis St. Laurent until 1957. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957 for responding to the Suez Crisis through the United Nations, working with Dag Hammarskjöld to create the United Nations Emergency Force.

He became Liberal leader in 1958, lost to John Diefenbaker in 1958 and 1962, and formed a minority government after the 1963 election, sworn in on 22 April. His government introduced the Canada Pension Plan and Canada Student Loans, adopted the Maple Leaf flag, set up royal commissions on bilingualism and on the status of women, and merged the three armed services into the Canadian Forces on 1 February 1968. It signed the Auto Pact in 1965 and introduced a points-based immigration system in 1967. Pearson declined American requests for combat troops in Vietnam.

Pearson announced his retirement on 14 December 1967, and Pierre Trudeau succeeded him. He chaired the Pearson Commission on International Development in 1968 and 1969, and the first volume of his memoirs appeared in 1972. He died at his home in Ottawa on 27 December 1972, after cancer spread to the liver, and is buried at Maclaren Cemetery in Wakefield, Quebec. Toronto Pearson International Airport and the Lester B. Pearson Building, headquarters of Global Affairs Canada, bear his name.
leto: Leto is attested in Mycenaean Greek through the forms Latios, meaning son of Leto or related to Leto, and Lato. The meaning of her name is uncertain. Older sources linked it to the Greek word lethe, oblivion, and so to the hidden one, while 20th-century sources derive it from the Lycian lada, wife, since her earliest cult was centred in Lycia. Other scholars have suggested a pre-Greek origin. From the fourth century onwards she was identified as the principal mother goddess of Anatolian Lycia. Her sanctuary, the Letoon near Xanthos, predated Hellenic influence and united the Lycian confederacy of city-states.

Leto is the daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe and the sister of Asteria. Hesiod describes her as always mild and the gentlest goddess on Olympus. She is unusual among the lovers of Zeus in being tormented by Hera, who ordered all lands to shun her and sent the serpent Python and the giant Tityos against her. Leto found Delos, which was not joined to the mainland or the ocean floor and so was not counted as land, and gave birth there.

The Homeric Hymn to Apollo is the oldest surviving account of her wandering. It is concerned with Apollo's birth and does not call the children twins; the first to do so was Pindar. Leto also appears in myths in which she punishes mortals who slight her. Lycian peasants who stirred the mud of a pond to keep her from drinking were turned into frogs, according to Ovid, and when Niobe boasted of having more children, Apollo and Artemis shot all of Niobe's sons and daughters dead. In the Trojan War Leto supported the Trojans.

Leto was usually worshipped together with her children rather than on her own account. On Delos, her chief centre of worship, she was represented in a temple by a shapeless wooden image. In Lycia she was intensely worshipped as a mother goddess. She had sanctuaries in Attica, Argos, Sparta, Mantineia and Delphi, and was also worshipped on Rhodes and Crete. At Phaistos on Crete she was held to have given birth to her children, and the city of Lato bore her name. Herodotus reported that in Egypt the goddess the Greeks recognised as Leto was worshipped in the form of the cobra goddess Wadjet.
leuk: Leuk, in French Loèche, is a municipality and the capital of the Leuk district in the canton of Valais. It lies above the right bank of the Rhône, between the Dala gorge and the Feschelbach, and is surrounded by vineyards. Because it controls access to the Gemmi Pass it had some importance from the time of Roman Raetia, and the Leukerbad thermal baths lie just to the north. Its two gorges and the Rhône formed natural fortifications. The municipality includes the village of Leuk-Stadt, the castle, Susten on the left bank, several hamlets and, since 1 January 2013, the mountain village of Erschmatt.

Leuk is first mentioned in 515 as villa de Leuca, and La Tène graves show that it was inhabited before the Roman era. In the 6th century it belonged to the demesne of Sigismund, King of Burgundy, who gave it to the Abbey of Saint-Maurice. In 1138 the town came under the Bishop of Sion, who encouraged its growth: Leuk received the right to its own weights and measures in 1209, a hospital in 1285 and a warehouse in 1310 on the old trade route between northern Italy and the markets of Champagne. The episcopal officials built the Bishop's Castle and the Viztumsturm.

Its borders saw several clashes. In 1296 troops loyal to the bishop defeated the upper Valais nobility, and in 1386 Leuk stopped Count Amadeus VII of Savoy by destroying the Dala bridge. During the Rarner war of 1415 invaders destroyed the Bishop's Castle and the Viztumsturm, and in 1541 Ulrich Ruffiner built the present Gothic town hall on the ruins of the tower. French troops burned the town in 1799 after the Battle of Pfyn. In the later 16th century the leading families leaned to Protestantism, but after the Valais Grand Council voted in 1604 to remain Catholic they returned to the old faith.

Leuk has 3,991 inhabitants, most of whom speak German. The Church of St Stephan, built in the Gothic style by Ulrich Ruffiner and consecrated in 1494, the town hall, the Dalaturm, the Ringacker Chapel and Zen-Ruffinen Castle are Swiss heritage sites of national significance, and the whole small town is in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites. The Leuk Castle Foundation, set up in 1999, restores the Bishop's Castle, one of whose towers received a glass cupola designed by Mario Botta. A satellite earth station has made Leuk a telecommunications centre.
leutkirch-im-allgau: Leutkirch im Allgäu is a former Free Imperial City in the south-east of Baden-Württemberg, Germany, on the border with Bavaria. It lies in the western Allgäu, in the district of Ravensburg and the administrative region of Tübingen, and the border with Austria and Lake Constance are about 40 km away. The name comes from Leutekirche, 'church of the people', the church now called Sankt Martin. The town grew from the merger of the villages of Ufhofen and Mittelhofen, and the first mention of its church is in a document of the Abbey of St. Gall from 766.

In 1293 King Adolf of Nassau granted Leutkirch the right to rule itself under the town code of Lindau, effectively making it a Free Imperial City. A bailiff appointed by the king still ruled it for a while, a town council is first mentioned in 1311, and from the 15th century an elected mayor chaired it. The main industry was the linen trade, and the weavers' guild once had 200 members. The town joined the Swabian League in 1488 and gained a seat and vote in it and in the Imperial Diet.

Leutkirch became officially Lutheran in 1546 and later joined the Schmalkaldic League. A dispute with the abbot of Weingarten Abbey over St. Martin's parish church ended in a compromise in 1562: the Catholics kept the parish church and the Protestants took the hospital church, expanded in 1589 and now called the Memorial Church. The town suffered heavily in the Thirty Years' War, and its population fell drastically. A baroque town hall was built in 1740. After the Peace of Westphalia it remained one of the smallest of the fifty Free Imperial Cities.

In the mediatisation of the early 1800s the town lost its independence. It was annexed to Bavaria and in 1810 became part of the Kingdom of Württemberg. The surrounding countryside, the Free Men of the Leutkircher Heath, was a Free Imperial Village territory and shared its fate.

Since the municipal reform of 1972 the urban area includes eight former municipalities, among them Diepoldshofen, Friesenhofen and Wuchzenhofen. The Museum im Bock shows the history of the town and its craftsmen. Schloss Zeil, a Renaissance castle begun in 1599 by Truchsess Froben von Waldburg-Zeil after he demolished the medieval castle, stands five kilometres away; he built its church and monastery first. The sculptor and painter Hans Multscher, about 1400–1467, was born in the town.
leuven: The earliest mention of Leuven, as Loven, dates from 891, when the Frankish king Arnulf of Carinthia defeated a Viking army there. According to a legend, the red and white arms of the city depict the blood-stained shores of the river Dyle after that battle. Near the stronghold of the dukes of Brabant, the city became the most important centre of trade in the duchy between the 11th and 14th centuries. Ordinary linen cloth was known in late-14th and 15th-century texts as lewyn, a sign of its importance in cloth manufacture.

The university, founded in 1425, opened a new golden age. The Town Hall, built between 1439 and 1463, and Saint Peter's Church were raised, and painters such as Dirk Bouts worked in the city. By about 1500 it was a major centre of art and learning, where humanists such as Erasmus worked. In 1517 Hieronymus van Busleyden founded the Collegium Trilingue, which taught Latin, Greek and Hebrew. Thomas More published his Utopia at Dirk Martens's printing house there in 1516. Persecution of Protestants and turmoil from the late 1560s drove many professors abroad, to the benefit of the University of Leiden.

German troops burned much of the town in August 1914, killing about 300 civilians. The university library was destroyed on 25 August 1914, with about 230,000 volumes, among them 750 medieval manuscripts. The outrage was worldwide. A new library, a gift from the American people, opened on 4 July 1928. In May 1940, during the German offensive, shelling set it on fire and nearly a million books were lost.

Leuven is the capital of the province of Flemish Brabant, about 25 kilometres east of Brussels. Its university, KU Leuven, is the oldest Catholic university still in existence and the largest in Belgium. Saint Peter's Church and the Great Beguinage are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Town Hall, with 236 statues added in the 19th century, and the Linen Hall, now the University Hall, stand among its medieval buildings. The city is the headquarters of the brewing group Anheuser-Busch InBev, whose Stella Artois beer is brewed there.
levant: The Levant is a subregion of West Asia along the eastern Mediterranean. In its narrowest sense, used in archaeology, it covers Cyprus and the lands bordering the Mediterranean, including Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Palestine, Israel and south Cilicia. In its widest historical sense it took in all the eastern Mediterranean, from Greece to Egypt and Cyrenaica. It has been described as the land bridge between Africa and Eurasia and as the crossroads of West Asia, the eastern Mediterranean and north-east Africa. Archaeologists following The Oxford Handbook of the Archaeology of the Levant set its limits at the Taurus Mountains in the north, the eastern deserts, Wadi al-Arish in Sinai and the sea, with the Litani River dividing north from south.

The word comes from the Italian levante, meaning rising, the sun rising in the east, and is broadly equivalent to the Arabic Mashriq. In the 13th and 14th centuries it described Italian maritime commerce in the lands east of Venice, including Greece, Anatolia, Syria-Palestine and Egypt, and later it narrowed to the Muslim lands of Syria-Palestine and Egypt. It appears in English in 1497. The English Levant Company was founded in 1581 to trade with the Ottoman Empire, and the French Compagnie du Levant in 1670. Levantine at first meant the European residents of the region and later its native and minority groups.

In early 19th-century travel writing the term sometimes took in Ottoman Mediterranean provinces and Greece. The French mandate over Syria and Lebanon, from 1920 to 1946, was called the Levant States. Scholars now use Levant for the history of the region because it lacks the political overtones of Syria-Palestine, and archaeologists seeking a neutral label that is neither biblical nor national speak of Levantine archaeology.

The region has long been home to Arabs, Jews, Kurds, Assyrians, Armenians and others. Most people speak Levantine Arabic, a variety descended from pre-Islamic Arabic dialects of Syria and Hejazi Arabic that keeps significant influence from Western Middle Aramaic. Islam arrived with the Muslim conquest of the 7th century, though a Muslim majority may only have been reached by the 13th century. As the birthplace of Christianity, the Levant has many Christian churches, and it is also home to Samaritans, Druze and Yazidis.
leviathan: Both the name and the figure of Leviathan continue the Ugaritic sea monster Lôtān, a servant of the sea god Yammu who was defeated by Hadad in the Baal Cycle. The Ugaritic account has gaps, but most scholars describe Lôtān as the fugitive serpent. His role seems to have been prefigured by the earlier serpent Têmtum, whose death at Hadad's hands is shown on Syrian seals of the 18th to 16th century BCE.

Sea serpents feature prominently in the mythology of the ancient Near East. Sumerian iconography of the 3rd millennium BCE shows the god Ninurta overcoming a seven-headed serpent, and the Babylonian creation myth tells how Marduk defeated the serpent goddess Tiamat and made the heavens and the earth from her body. The origin of the Hebrew word is disputed: Gesenius derived it from a root meaning to twine, giving a sense of twisted in folds, while others thought it a loanword.

Leviathan is mentioned six times in the Hebrew Bible. Job 41 describes it at length as a creature with impenetrable scales and fiery breath. Psalm 104 praises God for having made it, and Isaiah 27:1 calls it the tortuous serpent that God will kill at the end of time. The Book of Enoch places it in the watery abyss as a female monster, with the male land-monster Behemoth in the desert.

Later Jewish sources describe a dragon living over the sources of the deep. In the midrash God made a male and a female leviathan but killed the female and salted her flesh for the banquet of the righteous at the coming of the Messiah. The Talmud tells that its skin will cover the tent of that banquet, and the festival of Sukkot ends with a prayer to dwell in the sukkah of the skin of Leviathan.

Christian writers read Leviathan as an image of the devil. The Septuagint usually renders the word as dragon, and the seven-headed dragon of the Book of Revelation explicitly is the devil, though the Old Testament never says so. Peter Binsfeld classed Leviathan as the demon of envy, one of the seven Princes of Hell. In Gnostic cosmology Leviathan encircles the material world as a serpent biting its tail.

In 1651 Hobbes used Leviathan as a metaphor for the omnipotence of the state. The word has also come to mean any overwhelmingly powerful person or thing, and it was used for great whales, as in Herman Melville's Moby-Dick. In modern Hebrew it simply means whale.
levuka: Levuka lies on the eastern coast of Ovalau, an island in Lomaiviti Province in Fiji's Eastern Division. It is the largest of 24 settlements on the island and its economic centre. At the northern end of the town stands the traditional Fijian village of Levuka, whose chief bears the title Tui Levuka and is a direct descendant of the chief who welcomed the first European settlers; he is also known as Tamana na vavalagi, Father of the Europeans. At the southern end lies the village of Nasova, where Seru Epenisa Cakobau signed the Deed of Cession on 10 October 1874.

The modern town was founded around 1820 by European settlers and traders as the first modern town in the Fiji Islands. Its population was a mixed band of traders, missionaries, shipwrights, speculators and respectable businessmen. The US Exploring Expedition visited in 1840, and by the mid-nineteenth century Levuka was a commercial hub for the sea cucumber trade. Marist priests led by Father Jean-Baptiste Bréhéret founded a mission there in 1858, and Wesleyan missions were built at about the same time. By 1870 the town had more than 2,000 inhabitants.

When the Kingdom of Fiji was founded in 1871, Cakobau was crowned king at Levuka. After Fiji was annexed as a British colony in 1874, the town stayed the capital for some years.
