The administration was moved to Suva because the steep hills, some 600 metres high and many with cliffs, around Levuka left no room for expansion, although the move was made official only in 1882.

Levuka was the site of many of Fiji's firsts: its first bank, post office, school, hospital, town hall and municipal government. The Fiji Times was founded there in 1869, and Levuka Public School, opened in 1879, was the first public school in the country. The town's Royal Hotel was in existence by the early 1860s and is the oldest hotel in the South Pacific still operating.

Levuka's wooden architecture is highly vulnerable to fire, and several historic buildings, among them the Romanesque-revival Masonic lodge, have been burnt. Its role as a stopover port for ocean vessels ended in the 1950s. The Pacific Fishing Company was founded there in 1964, and its tuna cannery, opened in 1976 as a joint venture with the government, became the largest private employer on Ovalau. Levuka was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in June 2013 as an exceptional testimony to the late colonial port towns of the Pacific. Its town hall, built in 1898 for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, and the Sacred Heart Church survive.
lewes-delaware: Lewes is an incorporated city on the Delaware Bay in eastern Sussex County, Delaware. It lies on the Atlantic Coastal Plain, and the ocean and the bay moderate its weather, giving hot, humid summers and mild winters. Its area is about 4.3 square miles, of which nearly 15 percent is water. It is adjacent to Cape Henlopen State Park, and Cape Henlopen itself lies just to the east. Savannah, Second and Front Streets are its main streets. The town takes its name from Lewes in Sussex, England, which has the same seal.

Dutch settlers founded a whaling and trading post on 3 June 1631 and named it Zwaanendael, Swan Valley. It was the first European settlement in Delaware, and a local Lenape group killed all 32 settlers in 1632. In 1662 the city of Amsterdam granted land at the Hoernkills, around Cape Henlopen, to a group of Mennonites led by Pieter Cornelisz Plockhoy. Their settlement lasted from 1663 until 1664, when the English captured New Netherland and ordered it razed, leaving, it was reported, not even a nail. Maryland colonists burned a later settlement in December 1673.

In 1680 the village was reorganised under the authority of the Duke of York as New Deale. In 1682 King Charles II gave the Delaware colonies to William Penn, who renamed the county Sussex and the settlement Lewes. Lewes was the county seat until 1791, when the seat moved to Georgetown. On 6 and 7 April 1813, during the War of 1812, Royal Navy ships under HMS Poictiers bombarded the town without effect; a cannonball remains in the foundation of Cannonball House. Lewes was incorporated on 2 February 1818, and in 1941 Fort Miles was built on Cape Henlopen to defend Delaware Bay and Philadelphia.

Lewes had 3,303 inhabitants in the 2020 census and is one of the principal towns of Delaware's Cape Region, with neighbouring Rehoboth Beach. Its motto, the First Town in the First State, rests on its place as the earliest settlement in Delaware, the first state to ratify the Constitution. The Zwaanendael Museum has exhibits on Delaware's history, and the Lightship Overfalls is moored on the Lewes and Rehoboth Canal. The National Harbor of Refuge offshore holds the Delaware Breakwater East End Light. It is a popular resort town, and the University of Delaware has a campus there.
lewis-and-clark-expedition: President Thomas Jefferson commissioned the expedition shortly after the Louisiana Purchase of 1803. He wished to find the most direct and practicable water communication across the continent for commerce, to learn the resources of the new territory and to declare United States sovereignty over the Native American peoples along the Missouri. Alexander Mackenzie had reached the Pacific coast of British Columbia in 1793, and his account of 1801 told Jefferson of Britain's intent to control the fur trade of the Columbia River. Scientific work was a secondary aim.

Clark and about thirty others left Camp Dubois, Illinois, on 14 May 1804 and went up the Missouri River. Lewis joined them at St. Charles, Missouri. The Corps may have had as many as 45 members, among them York, a Black man enslaved by Clark. Sergeant Charles Floyd died on 20 August 1804, apparently of acute appendicitis, and was the only member to die.

The party crossed the Continental Divide near Lemhi Pass and reached the Columbia River. It sighted the Pacific Ocean on 7 November 1805. Short of food, the party voted on 24 November to move to the south side of the river, and both Sacagawea and York took part in the vote. There the men built Fort Clatsop and spent the winter. The return journey began on 23 March 1806 and ended at St. Louis on 23 September.

Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, joined the expedition with her husband, Toussaint Charbonneau, and gave birth to a son in February 1805. Scholars say she was not the guide but was important as an interpreter, and the sight of a woman with an infant helped to give the impression of a peaceful mission. The expedition relied on the help of two dozen Native American nations.

The Corps did not find a continuous waterway to the Pacific, but it located a trail from the upper Missouri to the Columbia. It drew about 140 maps and described more than 200 new plant and animal species. Its medals, flags and proclamations of sovereignty were legal steps toward claiming title to the land of each indigenous nation under the discovery doctrine. The maps allowed further exploration and settlement.

All the other members received double pay and land, but Clark refused to free York, who received nothing and was still enslaved ten years after the expedition. His later life is disputed. Lewis and Clark County in Montana and the Lewis and Clark River in Oregon are named after the two leaders.
lex-hortensia: In the annalistic tradition a plebeian named Hortensius was appointed dictator around 287 BCE to deal with a civil uprising, which led to the secession of the plebs to the Janiculum hill; they returned only after the law had been passed in the Centuriate Assembly. The annals put the uprising down to debt, with a call to arms against the Lucanians as the immediate occasion, since the patricians needed plebeian manpower for the war.

There is considerable reason to doubt this account, which Livy attributes to an urban rabble in the forum. Large masses of urban poor did not really exist in the middle Republic, and rural landowners controlled 29 of the voting blocs of the Plebeian Council, which never numbered more than 35. The more likely cause is the wish of rural plebeians to control the distribution of the public lands won in the Third Samnite War, though the extreme measures of the consuls suggest considerable unrest in the city as well. An organised movement was needed to pass such a law, and it was probably coordinated by the plebeian tribunes.

In the early Republic the resolutions of the Plebeian Council, the plebiscita, bound only plebeians, because only plebeians voted there. The lex Valeria-Horatia of 449 BCE allowed them to bind all Romans if the Senate ratified them, and the lex Publilia of 339 BCE moved the Senate's approval to before the vote. The Hortensian law removed the requirement altogether. A plebiscitum remained distinct in name from a lex but was now treated as if it were one; later all binding laws came to be called leges.

The law also restricted when votes could be held. They were no longer allowed on market days, when they could have interfered with business, which hindered rural plebeians from taking part, since those were the days when they would have been in the city.

The law secured theoretically equal political rights for patricians and plebeians. It established the pre-eminence of the Tribal Assembly and the Plebeian Council in legislation, so that in the late Republic the other assemblies passed mainly minor and procedural laws, and it made the plebeians and their tribunes important political players, which the earlier laws had failed to do.
lex-manilia: The war against Mithridates, commonly called the Third Mithridatic War, had been conducted by Lucius Licinius Lucullus. By the winter of 68–67 BCE he had driven Mithridates out of Pontus and invaded the Armenian empire of his ally Tigranes the Great. His advance stopped when his discontented troops mutinied under the leadership of Publius Clodius Pulcher; many of these Fimbrian legions had been in the East since the command of Gaius Flavius Fimbria in 86 BCE.

Mithridates and Tigranes took their chance. Mithridates invaded Pontus and Tigranes Cappadocia, and in the summer of 67 BCE Mithridates inflicted a crushing defeat on Roman forces under Lucullus's legate Triarius at the Battle of Zela. Lucullus was superseded by the consul of 67 BCE, Manius Acilius Glabrio, who, seeing the difficulty of the situation, lingered in Bithynia. By the end of that year Mithridates had recovered the whole of his former kingdom.

The law recalled the three commanders then in the East, Lucullus in Pontus, Glabrio in Bithynia and Quintus Marcius Rex in Cilicia, and transferred all their legions and the entire conduct of the eastern war to Pompey. He was already in the East, completing the command against the pirates given him by the lex Gabinia of 67 BCE.

That earlier law had been opposed by almost the whole Senate. The proposal of Manilius, by contrast, had the support of many senators and of several eminent former consuls, among them Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus, Gaius Scribonius Curio, Gaius Cassius Longinus Varus and Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus. Cicero was serving as praetor when he delivered his speech for it, which survives. Opposition was largely confined to Quintus Hortensius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus, whose arguments against giving Pompey the command Cicero answers at length.

The law was passed in the Comitia Tributa without the violence that had attended the proposal of Gabinius the year before. Pompey soon moved against Mithridates and Tigranes and had defeated both by the end of 65 BCE, though Mithridates was not killed until 63 BCE. Manilius himself was prosecuted twice after leaving office in December 66 BCE. On the first occasion Cicero defended him against a charge of extortion, and the case was dropped in January 65 BCE amid disturbances and violence. On the second he was condemned on a charge of maiestas and went into exile.
lezgins: The name Lezgin is very old. Strabo gives the Greek form Légai and the Latin Legae, with parallels in Armenian, Georgian, Arabic and Persian. Greek historians including Herodotus, Strabo and Pliny the Elder mention a people called Legoi in Caucasian Albania, and Arab writers of the 9th and 10th centuries mention a kingdom called Lakz in what is now southern Dagestan. Before the Russian Revolution the word Lezgin was applied to all the ethnic groups of Dagestan.

Tribes speaking Lezgic languages formed a union of 26 tribes within the state of Caucasian Albania in the 4th century BCE, and the state was incorporated into the Achaemenid Empire in 513 BCE. Rule passed from the Parthians to the Sassanid Persians in 252-253. The Lezgins were probably first introduced to Islam as early as the 8th century but remained primarily animist until the 15th, when Muslim influence grew. In the early 16th century the Safavids consolidated control over much of Dagestan.

In 1721 the Lezgin leader and Sunni cleric Haji Davud sacked Shamakhi, the provincial capital of Shirvan, an event that contributed to the decline of the Safavid Empire. He founded a short-lived Shirvan Khanate recognised by the Ottomans. Russia gained southern Dagestan by the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813 and consolidated its control by the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828. Many Lezgins fought beside the Avar Imam Shamil in the Great Caucasian War, until his defeat in 1859.

In 1918 the Lezgin population of the Kuba district resisted the forced establishment of Soviet rule by the Bolsheviks and their Dashnak allies. A punitive detachment burned 162 villages, 27 of them completely, and more than 16,000 civilians were killed in the district, among them 14,000 Lezgins.

Lezgin society is structured around djamaat, unions of clans, within which there are about 200 to 300 clans called syhils. Each syhil has its own village quarter and mountain, and a gathering of the male residents, the Kim, addresses important questions of village life. The society has traditionally been egalitarian. An unwritten code of honour, Lezgiwal, covers every sphere of life and implies moral behaviour, generosity and the will to safeguard the honour of women. The eagle, lek in Lezgian, is a common symbol and is linked to the value of freedom.

Lezgin belongs to the Lezgic branch of the Northeast Caucasian family and has three mutually intelligible dialects: Kurin, Akhti and Kuba. Some Lezgins celebrate the pre-Islamic festival Yaran Suvar. In the mountains they traditionally practised sheep and goat husbandry and crafts.
lezhe: Lezhë is a city in Albania, seat of Lezhë County and Lezhë Municipality, and is one of the country's oldest continuously inhabited cities, with roughly 2,400 years of recorded history. A settlement with fortifications stood on a 413-metre mountain, the Mal i Shëlbuemit, from at least the 8th century BCE, near the mouth of the Drin river. Swords found there are attributed to exchange with Mycenaean Greece in the early Mycenaean period. The later city was built on a lower hill of 172 metres, with ramparts facing the Drin valley and the coast, to guard the route inland and to give Illyrian ships a secure anchorage.

The earliest fortification walls of the proto-urban settlement are of typical Illyrian construction and date to the late 4th century BCE. The name Lissos is considered Greek, from a word meaning smooth rock. By the 3rd century BCE Lissus was one of the main cities of the Illyrian kingdom under the Ardiaean and Labeatan dynasties. In the peace treaty of 228 BCE the Illyrian queen Teuta promised Rome not to sail south of Lissus with more than two unarmed ships. In 211 BCE Philip V of Macedon captured its citadel, Acrolissus, and the city became the Macedonian outlet to the Adriatic, though it was later recovered by the Illyrians.

Under the Illyrian king Gentius, in the first half of the 2nd century BCE, Lissus minted coins for the ruler, and it was from Lissus that he organised his army against the Romans. Coins show that it kept a large degree of municipal autonomy under both Macedonian and Illyrian rule. It was later subjected to Rome and lay in the province of Epirus Nova. Slavic populations captured it in the early 590s, and Byzantine control was re-established in the early 9th century.

In the Middle Ages the town, known in Italian as Alessio, frequently changed masters until the Venetians took it in 1386. Because it was under Venetian control, Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg chose it in 1444 as a neutral place for a convention of Albanian lords to organise their common defence against the Ottoman Empire, the League of Lezhë. Skanderbeg was buried in the cathedral, dedicated to Saint Nicholas. The town fell to the Turks in 1478, and the cathedral was later used as the Selimie Mosque.

Excavations begun in 2004 around the ancient acropolis of Lissos and the Skanderbeg Memorial have revealed Hellenistic, Roman and early Byzantine buildings and tombs. The city lies near the port of Shëngjin on the national road between the Montenegrin border and Tirana.
lhasa: Lhasa lies at about 3,600 metres in the centre of the Tibetan Plateau, with surrounding mountains rising to 5,500 metres. Its name means place of gods in Tibetan. Ancient Tibetan documents call the place Rasa, goat's place, since it was a herding site, and it was renamed Lhasa when it became the capital and the Jokhang temple, housing a holy statue of the Buddha, was completed. Lhasa is first recorded as a name, for the area's temple of Jowo, in a treaty between China and Tibet of 822 CE. The Lhasa River, or Kyi Chu, a tributary of the Brahmaputra, runs through the southern part of the city.

By the mid-7th century Songtsen Gampo led the Tibetan Empire, which had risen in the Yarlung Tsangpo valley. After conquering the kingdom of Zhangzhung he moved the capital to Rasa, where in 637 he raised the first structures on the site of the later Potala Palace. He is said to have married Princess Bhrikuti of Nepal in 639 and Princess Wencheng of the Tang court two years later, and Bhrikuti is said to have converted him to Buddhism. In 641 he built the Jokhang and Ramoche temples to house two Buddha statues brought by the princesses. Lhasa suffered extensive damage in the reign of Langdarma in the 9th century, when its sacred sites were destroyed and the empire fragmented.

Lhasa has been the religious and administrative capital of Tibet since the mid-17th century. The Fifth Dalai Lama, Lobsang Gyatso, began building the Potala Palace in 1645, after an adviser pointed out that the site lay ideally between the Drepung and Sera monasteries and the old city.

Lhasa holds many culturally significant Tibetan Buddhist sites, including the Potala Palace, the Jokhang Temple, Sera Monastery and the Norbulingka palaces. The Potala, Jokhang and Norbulingka form part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Potala being inscribed in 1994. The palace was converted into a museum after the 14th Dalai Lama fled to India during the 1959 Tibetan uprising. Many important sites were damaged or destroyed, mostly but not solely during the Cultural Revolution of the 1960s, and many have been restored since the 1980s. In the first half of the 20th century, when nearly half of its population were monks, Western explorers such as Francis Younghusband and Heinrich Harrer made journeys to the city.
lhokseumawe: Lhokseumawe lies on the north-east coast of Sumatra, between Banda Aceh and Medan, at an average altitude of 13 metres above sea level. It is a semi-enclave within North Aceh Regency, which surrounds it on all landward sides. The name comes from the Acehnese words lhok, meaning deep, bay or ocean trench, and seumawe, the swirling water in the sea off Banda Sakti and its surroundings. Its position between the two larger cities has made it a distribution point for trade in Aceh. It has a tropical rainforest climate with moderate to heavy rainfall throughout the year.

The area is linked to the emergence of the kingdom of Samudera Pasai around the 13th century, which later came under the sovereignty of the Sultanate of Aceh. Aceh was established by Sultan Ali Mughayatsyah in 1511. After the Portuguese occupation of Malacca in 1511, many Islamic traders passing the Strait of Malacca shifted their trade to Banda Aceh, which increased the wealth of its rulers. In the 17th century, under Sultan Iskandar Muda, Aceh's influence extended over most of Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, and it allied itself with the Ottoman Empire and the Dutch East India Company against the Portuguese and the Johor Sultanate. Its military power then waned gradually.

Before the 20th century the area was ruled by uleebalang of Kutablang. Under Dutch rule, in the second decade of the 20th century, a small island of about 11 square kilometres, separated from the mainland by the Krueng Cunda River, was filled with government, military and railway buildings. Over time this developed into a town with a harbour, market, railway station and government offices. On 21 and 22 September 1953 Darul Islam forces attacked Lhokseumawe twice, and the Indonesian army repelled both attacks.

In 1956 the North Aceh Regency was formed with its capital at Lhokseumawe. The town was made a city by a regional regulation signed by President Suharto on 14 August 1986 and inaugurated on 31 August 1987, with an area of 181.06 square kilometres. Law No. 2 of 2001, dated 21 June 2001, established it as a separate municipality.

Lhokseumawe is the second largest city in Aceh province after Banda Aceh, with 188,713 people at the 2020 census. It is divided into four districts. Its transport includes motorised rickshaws known as becak motor and minibuses called labi-labi, and it has beaches, including Ujong Blang and Meuraksa, among its attractions.
li-hongzhang: Li Hongzhang was born on 15 February 1823 into a scholar-gentry family in a village north-east of Hefei, in Anhui Province. His father, Li Wen'an, held the jinshi degree. Li obtained the juren degree in 1844, began taking classes under Zeng Guofan, and in 1847 won the jinshi degree at the age of 24, which brought him into the Hanlin Academy. After the Taiping Rebellion began in January 1851, he was taken to Anhui in 1853 to help organise militias against the rebels, and was rewarded for recapturing two counties and Lu Prefecture.

In 1862 Li sailed to Shanghai with troops recruited at Zeng Guofan's order, where they were commissioned as the Huai Army. He equipped it with Western firearms and artillery, and within two years its strength rose from 6,000 to about 60–70,000 men. In 1863 and 1864 it recaptured Suzhou, Changzhou and other territories from the Taiping rebels. An incident over the surrender of rebel leaders at Suzhou soured his relationship with Charles George Gordon, who was said to have wanted to shoot him. He later helped suppress the Nian Rebellion.

From 1870 Li was Viceroy of Zhili and Beiyang Trade Minister, and until his death he shaped the Qing Empire's foreign policy to a large extent. He signed the Yantai Treaty with Sir Thomas Wade in 1876, arranged treaties with Peru and the French, and supported the Chinese Educational Mission to the United States. He also strengthened the army and navy, fortified Port Arthur and the Dagu forts, and founded the Tianjin Military Academy in 1885. China's defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895 undermined his political standing and the wider Self-Strengthening Movement.

Sent to negotiate with Japan, Li was shot in the left cheek on 24 March 1895 at Shimonoseki by an assassin, which led Japan to agree to a ceasefire. He signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki on 17 April 1895. In 1896 he attended the coronation of Nicholas II and toured Europe, Canada and the United States.

In 1901 Li was the principal Chinese negotiator with the powers that had captured Beijing, and on 7 September he signed the Boxer Protocol. He died of liver inflammation two months later in Beijing. His reputation remains disputed. His biographer William J. Hail praised him as always progressive, yet patient and conciliatory, while Liang Qichao's 1902 biography blamed him for China's woes. History textbooks in the People's Republic of China long called him a traitor, and a serious debate among mainland historians began only in the 1980s.
li-qingzhao: Li Qingzhao, art name Yi'an Jushi, was born in 1084 in Qi Prefecture, Jingdong East Circuit, in present-day Zhangqiu, Shandong. Her father, Li Gefei, was an academic professor and well-known essayist who belonged to a poetry and literary circle led by Su Shi, and her mother, also a poet, descended from the prime minister Wang Kung-ch'en. The family's large collection of books gave her a comprehensive education. As a teenager she began a career as a poet by writing two poems in the shi form to rhyme with a friend's poem. Her first ci poem, "A Dream Song", recalls her hometown before her marriage and was written at about 16 or 17.

Her poetry was already well known in elite circles by 1101, when, aged eighteen, she married Zhao Mingcheng. They shared a love of poetry, literature, calligraphy, painting and bronze and stone sculpture, and they collected inscriptions and books and wrote poems about bronze vessels of the Shang and Zhou dynasties. In the Jin–Song wars the Northern Song capital Kaifeng fell in 1127, fighting reached Shandong and their house was burned. The couple fled south of the Yangtze River with many possessions and lived for a year in Nanjing. Zhao died of typhoid fever in 1129 on the way to an official post, and Li never recovered.

She settled in Hangzhou, where the Song government had made its new capital, and kept working on her husband's Catalogue of Inscriptions on Metal and Stone, describing their married life and flight in an afterword to the work, which was published after his death. According to some contemporary accounts she was briefly married to a man named Zhang Ruzhou, who treated her badly, and she divorced him within months.

Only around a hundred of her poems are known to survive, mostly in the ci form, which follows musical patterns and allows personal feeling. A few shi poems survive, as do the afterword and a study of ci poetry. Her work falls into two parts, divided by her move south: early poems on a maiden's feelings, close to love poems, and later ones tied to the war with the Jurchens, marked by nostalgic memories of her husband and her hometown. She is credited with the first detailed critique of the metrics of Chinese poetry and was regarded as a master of the subtle and concise style. It is widely believed that she died around the age of 71, but no records of this remain.
li-si: Li Si came from Cai in the state of Chu and began as a minor functionary in the local administration. According to the Records of the Great Historian, he once saw that the rats in an outhouse were dirty and hungry while the rats in the barn were well fed, and he concluded that people's standing depends on the circumstances in which they find themselves. He decided on a career in politics, a common choice for scholars not of noble family during the Warring States period. After finishing his education with the Confucian thinker Xunzi, he left Chu, where he could not advance, and went to Qin, the most powerful state of the time.

In Qin Li Si became a guest of the chancellor Lü Buwei and spoke to King Ying Zheng, the future Qin Shi Huang. He argued that unifying China was impossible if the other six states united against Qin, and the king adopted his proposals, spending generously to attract intellectuals and sending out assassins to kill important scholars and politicians in other states. In 237 BCE a clique at court urged the king to expel all foreigners. Li Si, a native of Chu, wrote a memorial explaining the benefits of foreigners to Qin, and the king relented and promoted him.

Li Si persuaded the king that Han Fei, a member of the Han royal clan sent to Qin on diplomacy, could neither be sent back nor employed. Han Fei was imprisoned, and in 233 BCE Li Si convinced him to take poison.

After Qin Shi Huang became emperor, Li Si persuaded him to suppress intellectual dissent and wrote the edict of 213 BCE that ordered the destruction of historical records and literature, including key Confucian texts. It is commonly thought that 460 Confucian scholars were buried alive. He also promulgated the small seal script, already in use in Qin, as the imperial standard, proscribing variant glyphs, and he systematised standard measures and currency.

When Qin Shi Huang died away from the capital, Li Si and the chief eunuch Zhao Gao suppressed his choice of successor, Fusu, tricked Fusu into suicide and installed another prince, Qin Er Shi. Zhao Gao later turned on Li Si and charged him with treason. Li Si was tortured until he confessed, and in 208 BCE he was subjected to the Five Punishments and executed by waist chop at a public market, and his family was exterminated to the third degree.

According to Sima Qian, he told his son that he wished they could take their brown dog and chase the crafty hare through the eastern gate of Shang Cai. The translator John Knoblock considered him one of the two or three most important figures in Chinese history.
li-zicheng: Li Zicheng was born in 1606 as Li Hongji to an impoverished farming family in Shaanxi province. He was literate, though the source of his education is disputed, and in his youth worked on a farm, in a wine shop and at a blacksmith's. He joined the army at sixteen, left it, and entered the postal service in 1626. A weak, financially strained Ming government was struggling with environmental problems and disease. Accounts of how he became a rebel differ: one says he killed a superior over unpaid wages in 1629; another, by Zheng Lian, says he was jailed in a debt dispute in 1630 and freed by peasants; a third says he rebelled after being charged with stealing rations.

Li rose in the rebel armies of northern China, joining Gao Yingxiang, "the Dashing King", whose nickname and command he inherited. Ming commanders defeated him repeatedly; in 1638 Hong Chengchou destroyed his army and he escaped with 17 followers. From 1639 the Chongzhen Great Plague, famine and drought deepened discontent, and Li rebuilt a force of over 30,000. His slogans of dividing land equally and abolishing grain taxes won peasant support; some historians call him a Robin Hood-style figure. In 1641 his forces sacked the Shaolin Monastery. In 1642 the Kaifeng flood, caused by breaches in the Yellow River dikes by both sides, killed over 300,000 of the city's 378,000 residents. In November 1643 he defeated Sun Chuanting, who was killed, and took Xi'an.

Li had by 1643 taken Xiangyang and proclaimed himself king, and on 8 February he declared the Great Shun dynasty in Xi'an. In April 1644 he marched on Beijing with 300,000 troops and reached its suburbs on 23 April. The gates were opened from inside, and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself. Li proclaimed himself emperor, but on 27 May he was defeated at the Battle of Shanhai Pass by Prince Dorgon and Wu Sangui, and the Qing took Beijing on 6 June.

Qing armies under Ajige, Dodo and Shi Tingzhu forced Li out of Xi'an in February 1645. The circumstances of his death remain unclear. Most sources agree he died in 1645; one account says village guards killed him while he raided for provisions, and another that he became a monk and died in 1674. Qing historiography treated him as an illegitimate usurper and outlaw. His call to equalise land is seen as a proto-socialist aspiration of the peasantry, and Roland Mousnier compared his early band to the Écorcheurs of the Hundred Years' War.
liao-dynasty: The Liao state grew from the consolidation of power among the Khitans in the 8th century and their expansionist campaigns in the latter half of the 9th century. The Yila chieftain Abaoji, born in 872, became leader of the Khitans and proclaimed a Chinese-style dynastic state. The Khitans had elected their leaders since the time of the Dahe Confederation, and the new rulers drew on that inheritance: the Rebirth Ceremony, performed every 12 years, confirmed the emperor's right to rule.

The state was officially the Great Khitan State, renamed Great Liao by Abaoji's successor Emperor Taizong of Liao, changed back to Great Khitan in 983 under Emperor Shengzong of Liao, and restored as Great Liao in 1066 under Emperor Daozong of Liao.

The Liao conquered the Sixteen Prefectures, including present-day Beijing and part of Hebei, by fuelling a proxy war that led to the collapse of the Later Tang. After the Song dynasty replaced Later Zhou, Emperor Taizong of Song annexed Northern Han in 979 and then invaded Liao, but lost a pitched battle on the Gaoliang River and fled wounded in a donkey cart. Under Shengzong, who came to the throne aged 11, his mother Xiao Yanyan ruled as regent until her death in 1009 and commanded an army of her own.

The Liao attacked the Northern Song in 1004, and after heavy fighting both sides agreed the Chanyuan Treaty, which made them peers and began about 120 years of peace. The dynasty ended in 1125, when the Jurchen-led Jin captured Emperor Tianzuo of Liao. Yelü Dashi, a survivor of the house, led loyalists west and founded the Qara Khitai, or Western Liao, which ruled parts of Central Asia for almost a century before the Mongol Empire conquered it.

The Liao ran two governments in parallel: a Northern Administration for the Khitans and other nomadic peoples, and a Southern Administration for the settled Han population. At its height the state held what is now Shanxi, Hebei, Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang and Inner Mongolia, with much of Mongolia and northern parts of the Korean peninsula. Its peak population is estimated at 750,000 Khitans and two to three million Han Chinese.

Khitan women hunted and managed herds, finances and property while men were at war, and elite women such as Shulü Ping and Xiao Yanyan took part in military affairs. Religion combined Buddhism, Confucianism, Daoism and Khitan tribal belief, with imperial patronage mostly going to Buddhism. A complete Tripitaka was finished in 1075. The Khitans buried their elite dead in metal masks and woven-wire suits.
liao-river: The Liao River is the principal river of southern Northeast China and one of the seven main river systems of China. It runs for 1,345 kilometres and drains a basin of over 232,000 square kilometres, yet its mean discharge is small, about 500 cubic metres per second, around one-twentieth that of the Pearl River. Because much of its course crosses powdery loess, its sediment load is exceedingly high.

It is formed by two tributaries. The Xiliao River, the larger, comes from the west and lies entirely in Inner Mongolia; it is made by the Xar Moron and Laoha rivers and was historically also called the Huang River. The Dongliao River comes from the east and rises in western Jilin. They meet near the junction of Liaoning, Jilin and Inner Mongolia, and the river then flows south across the Northeast China Plain.

The river takes its name from the Liao region, an old name for southern Manchuria, from which Liaoning province, the Liaodong Peninsula and the Liao dynasty are also named. Today it divides Liaoning into Liaodong, east of the Liao, and Liaoxi, west of it. Historically, however, that boundary was not the river itself but a large wetland on the west bank of the lower river, the Liao Mire, which stretched from the Yiwulü Mountain to the river between Xinmin and Panshan.

Its tributaries carry older names. The Hun River was also called the Little Liao River and the Shen River, and the Shen gave its name to the city of Shenyang. The Taizi River, whose name means crown prince river, was also known as the Yan River and the Liang River. According to legend it was the last refuge of Crown Prince Dan of Yan, who fled the Qin conquest after the failed attempt to assassinate the King of Qin.

The low, soft-soiled delta had a long record of shifting channels and was at risk of storm surges, which threatened Yingkou at the mouth of the Daliao River. In 1958 an engineering project blocked the upper Wailiao River at Liujianfang and sent the flow into the Shuangtaizi River, renamed the Liao River in 2011. The Hun and Taizi rivers were thereby separated from the Liao and now form the independent Daliao River system, and the Liao has no distributaries.
liaodong: The Liaodong Peninsula lies in southern Liaoning province in north-east China, between the mouths of the Daliao River in the west and the Yalu River in the east. It lies on the northern shore of the Yellow Sea and divides Liaodong Bay, the largest of the three bays of the Bohai Sea, from Korea Bay.

The word Liaodong literally means the east of the Liao region. It first referred to the Warring States period Yan commandery of Liaodong, which stretched from the modern Liaoning-Jilin border to the Chongchon River on the Korean Peninsula; modern usage means the half of Liaoning east of the Liao and Daliao rivers.

The region was settled in prehistoric times and later came under Gojoseon, a kingdom that included the northern Korean Peninsula. In the late 4th century BCE the expanding State of Yan conquered it and set up the Liaodong Commandery. After Yan fell it passed to the short-lived Qin dynasty and then the Han. When the Han fragmented at the turn of the 3rd century it changed hands among the Gongsun clan, the nomadic Wuhuan and Cao Wei, before falling to the reunified Western Jin.

During the Sixteen Kingdoms period it was ruled by Former Yan, Former Qin, Later Yan and later Goguryeo, until the Tang reconquered it. After the defeat of Wu Zhou at the Battle of Tianmenling in 698, the new state of Balhae ruled it for two centuries. The Khitan Liao dynasty followed, then the Jin, Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties.

In 1876 Chinese officials told the Customs commissioner at Yingkou that 600,000 people had landed on the peninsula, refugees from the Northern Chinese Famine of 1876 to 1879. The movement is known as Chuang Guandong.

The peninsula was a main area of fighting in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894 to 1895, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki of 17 April 1895 ceded it to Japan. The Triple Intervention of Russia, France and Germany on 23 April 1895 rescinded the cession, and Russia then pressed the Qing to lease Liaodong and Lüshunkou, or Port Arthur, to its navy. The Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905, including the siege of Port Arthur, brought more fighting.

Under the Treaty of Portsmouth of 5 September 1905 the leased territory passed to Japan as the Kwantung Leased Territory. Since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 it has been under unified Chinese rule. It includes the whole of the city of Dalian and parts of Yingkou, Anshan and Dandong.
liaoning: Liaoning is named after the Liao River, which runs through the province. It divides into highlands in the west, dominated by the Nulu'erhu Mountains, a flat central basin drained by the Liao and Daliao rivers, and hills in the east, where the Changbai and Qianshan mountains extend into the sea as the Liaodong Peninsula. A narrow coastal strip, the Liaoxi Corridor, joins the Liao basin to the North China Plain and ends at the Shanhai Pass of the Great Wall. The Yalu River marks the border with North Korea. The province has also yielded important fossils, among them Sinosauropteryx, announced in 1996 as the first example of a feathered dinosaur.

Before the 3rd century BCE the Donghu, Gojoseon and Yemaek peoples inhabited the area, and about 300 BCE the state of Yan conquered it and set up two commanderies, Liaodong and Liaoxi. As the Han dynasty fell, the warlord Gongsun Du and his family kept a semi-independent state in Liaodong until Cao Wei defeated it in 238. Xianbei states of the Murong tribe then ruled, and in 436 Goguryeo took the Liaodong Peninsula; the Tang dynasty annexed the region during the Goguryeo–Tang War.

After the An Lushan Rebellion the Bohai expanded into Liaodong, and the region was later conquered by the Khitan Liao dynasty, then held by the Jurchen Jin dynasty. Genghis Khan conquered it in 1206, and it was incorporated into the Yuan dynasty. The Ming took control in 1371 and about 1442 began building the Liaodong Wall, mostly an earth dike with moats, against the Oriyanghan and later the Jianzhou Jurchens, who became known as the Manchu.

The Qing conquest brought heavy loss of population: many residents were killed or fled south of the Great Wall, and Ming forces themselves destroyed many cities. In 1661 the civil governor reported that east of the Liao River only Shenyang, Liaoyang and Haicheng were more than nearly empty. The province was set up as Fengtian in 1907, and key battles of the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, including Port Arthur and Mukden, were fought here. Zhang Zuolin and his son Zhang Xueliang ruled it in the Warlord Era; the name Liaoning was first adopted on 29 January 1929, and Japan invaded in 1931, when it became part of Manchukuo.

Liaoning is a province of north-eastern China with its capital at Shenyang, and the port of Dalian is among its main cities. The population is mostly Han Chinese, with Manchus, Mongols, Hui, Koreans and Xibe; it has the highest number and share of Manchus in China. The Mukden Palace, where the Qing emperors lived before conquering the rest of China, and three Qing imperial tombs are part of World Heritage Sites, as is the Goguryeo site of Wunu Mountain City.
liaoyang: Liaoyang lies in east-central Liaoning province on the Taizi River, about an hour by car south of the provincial capital Shenyang. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of north-east China, dating back to before the Warring States period, and the site of the city has not changed since.

Under the Yan state and the Qin and Han dynasties, the city, then called Xiangping, was the capital of Liaodong Commandery and the political centre of the Liaodong region. In the Three Kingdoms period it was the focus of Sima Yi's Liaodong campaign. From the 5th to the 7th centuries it lay on the northern edge of the kingdom of Goguryeo, and remains of the old Goguryeo cities of Yodong and Baegam can still be seen near it. A major battle between the Tang and Goguryeo was fought there in 645.

The city rose to prominence under the Liao dynasty, and several of its buildings date from that time. Under the Jurchen Jin dynasty it served as the eastern capital, called Dongjing. In the 17th century the Manchu people rose against the Ming, and Liaoyang was one of the first Ming cities to fall. Nurhaci, the new ruler of the Later Jin dynasty, made it his capital in 1621 under the name Dongjing and moved the tombs of several relatives there, where they can be seen at Dongjingling east of the city. As the Manchu expanded he moved the capital again, to Shenyang, in 1625, and Dongjing then faded in importance.

During the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 Russian troops camped in the city and burned the ancient Guangyou Temple. In 1904 the Battle of Liaoyang, a major battle of the Russo-Japanese War, was fought there. In 1908 the city was one of the centres of the Manchurian revival, a Protestant Christian revival that spread through Mukden and the surrounding countryside.

The White Pagoda, in Baita Park at the centre of the city, with additions from the Yuan dynasty, is among the surviving buildings of the Liao period. Beside it stands the Guangyou Temple, one of the oldest and largest temple complexes in the north-east, covering some 60,000 square metres. The first temple on the site dates to 1145, and the temple was rebuilt after its destruction in 1900. Remains of the old city walls can still be seen, and a small museum stands in the rebuilt south gate. The novelist Cao Xueqin, author of Dream of the Red Chamber, is counted among its notable residents.
liaquat-ali-khan: Liaquat Ali Khan was born on 1 October 1895 in Karnal, in Punjab Province, the second of four sons of a wealthy landowner of a Rajput family. His grandfather, Nawab Ahmad Ali, had supported the British during the uprising of 1857–1858 and was rewarded with honours and the remission of his rent. Liaquat was taught at home and in Karnal, instructed in the Qur'an and hadith, and later studied at Aligarh Muslim University and the University of Oxford. His biographer Muhammad Reza Kazimi notes that little is known of his early life, which has to be pieced together from mostly hagiographic writings.

He returned to India in 1923 and entered national politics. The Indian National Congress invited him to join, but after meeting Jawaharlal Nehru he refused and joined the Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah. He was elected to the legislative council of the United Provinces in 1926, became its deputy president in 1932 and in 1940 entered the Central Legislative Assembly. In 1933 he and his wife Begum Ra'ana met Jinnah in London and urged him to return to India. On 12 April 1936 Liaquat was named honorary general secretary of the League, an office he held until 1947.

After independence in 1947 he became the first prime minister of Pakistan, and also held the posts of foreign minister, defence minister and minister for frontier regions. His government faced the first war with India over Kashmir, rivalry from socialist and communist groups, and a growing dependence on United States aid. On 12 March 1949 the Constituent Assembly passed the Objectives Resolution, which he called the Magna Carta of Pakistan's constitutional history; the Law Minister, Jogendra Nath Mandal, argued against it. In 1950 he signed the Liaquat–Nehru Pact with Nehru to ease tension and protect religious minorities on both sides of the border. After Jinnah's death he did not take the office of governor-general, which went to Khawaja Nazimuddin.

On 16 October 1951 Liaquat was shot twice in the chest while addressing a gathering of 100,000 at the Company Bagh in Rawalpindi. Police shot the presumed killer, Said Akbar, an Afghan national, at once. Liaquat died after reaching hospital, and the motive has never been fully revealed. He was buried at the Mazar-e-Quaid in Karachi, and the park was renamed Liaquat Bagh. He is known as Quaid-e-Millat, Leader of the Nation, and Shaheed-e-Millat, Martyr of the Nation. His assassination was the first political murder of a civilian leader in Pakistan and remains unsolved.
liberal-party-of-australia: The party's immediate predecessor was the United Australia Party. Its ideological ancestry lay in the anti-Labor groupings of the first Commonwealth parliaments, the Free Trade Party, later the Anti-Socialist Party, and the Protectionist Party. These merged in 1909 as the Commonwealth Liberal Party under Prime Minister Alfred Deakin, in response to the growing electoral prominence of the Labor Party. After Labor's split in 1916 the Commonwealth Liberals merged in 1917 into the Nationalist Party with several Labor outcasts, among them Billy Hughes, who became its first leader. The Nationalists governed until 1929. Robert Menzies founded the Liberal Party in 1944 as the successor to the United Australia Party.

After a loss to Labor in the 1946 election, Menzies led the Liberals to victory in 1949, and the party stayed in office for a record 23 years, the longest unbroken run in federal government. Menzies kept his promises to end rationing of butter, tea and petrol and to give a five-shilling endowment for first-born children. His government concluded defence and trade treaties that moved Australia out of Britain's orbit, opened the country to multi-ethnic immigration and began legal reforms regarding Aboriginal Australians. Harold Holt replaced him in 1966 and won 82 seats to Labor's 41 that year, but disappeared in rough surf in December 1967 and was declared presumed dead on 19 December.

In the early 1990s John Howard and Andrew Peacock contended for supremacy, and under John Hewson in November 1991 the opposition issued the 650-page Fightback! policy document, which proposed a goods and services tax. Howard led the party to victory over Paul Keating in 1996, after 13 years in opposition, and with Peter Costello as treasurer and Alexander Downer as foreign minister governed until defeat by Kevin Rudd in 2007. Brendan Nelson then led the party in opposition, followed by Malcolm Turnbull in 2008 and Tony Abbott in 2009, who won the leadership by one vote.

The party is dominated by six autonomous state divisions, reflecting its original commitment to a federal system, and policy is made almost entirely by the parliamentary parties. It has always been diverse in policy, defining itself mainly as anti-Labor and anti-socialist and as supporting individual freedom and private enterprise. Menzies expected the middle class to be its main constituency. Its wings include the Federal Women's Committee and the Young Liberals. At state level it was long dominant in Victoria, where it held office without a break from 1955 to 1982 under Henry Bolte, Dick Hamer and Lindsay Thompson.
liberal-party-uk: The party grew from the Whigs, whose roots lie in the Parliamentarian side of the English Civil War, together with free-trade Peelites and reformist Radicals. The Whigs wanted to reduce the power of the Crown and increase that of Parliament, and the more idealistic among them came to support wider democracy for its own sake. Under Earl Grey they returned to power in 1830 and carried the First Reform Act in 1832. Nonconformist Protestants were a major voting bloc that largely won over the Whigs and Liberals, pressing for an end to church rates and religious tests.

William Gladstone, prime minister four times between 1868 and 1894, was so closely identified with Liberalism for thirty years that the two were synonymous, and his moral tone and appeal to working-class and lower-middle-class audiences marked the party.

Gladstone's support for Irish Home Rule deeply divided the party. After 1886 it lost most of the Whig peerage and the upper and upper-middle classes, while keeping nonconformists and the Celtic fringe. The Liberal Unionists split away in 1886. The Second Boer War divided it again between Liberal Imperialists and the Pro-Boers, among them David Lloyd George. Under Henry Campbell-Bannerman the party won a landslide in the 1906 general election with 397 MPs. Together with H. H. Asquith, prime minister from 1908 to 1916, it passed reforms that created a basic welfare state, influenced by the New Liberalism of L. T. Hobhouse and John A. Hobson, which held that the state should remove poverty and ignorance as obstacles to freedom.

The First World War called for conscription, censorship and state controls that Liberals had long opposed. Lloyd George replaced Asquith in 1916 at the head of a coalition increasingly dominated by Conservatives, and the split between their factions weakened the party. By 1924 it had 40 MPs and 18% of the vote, and Labour absorbed most of its former voters. A three-way split followed in 1931 over the National Government. By the 1950s it had won as few as six seats. A revival began under Jo Grimond, leader from 1956, and the Orpington by-election of 1962. In 1981 it formed the SDP–Liberal Alliance with the Social Democratic Party, which won over a quarter of the vote in 1983 but only 23 seats.

The Liberals and the SDP merged in 1988 as the Social and Liberal Democrats, renamed the Liberal Democrats the following year, and a splinter group reconstituted the Liberal Party in 1989. The party's thinkers included John Stuart Mill, John Maynard Keynes and William Beveridge. It was a coalition with no unified national policy, which made it liable to deep splits.
liberalism: Liberal, liberty and libertine all derive from the Latin liber, meaning free. One of the first recorded uses of liberal, in 1375, described the liberal arts as an education desirable for a free-born man. The political tradition is mostly modern and began in the 17th century, although some of its ideas had precursors in classical antiquity and Imperial China. During the English Civil War the Levellers called for freedom of religion, frequent parliaments and equality under the law.

Thomas Hobbes built the idea of a social contract on a hypothetical state of nature and concluded that only an absolute sovereign could guarantee security. John Locke, generally regarded as the father of modern liberalism, took over the state of nature and the contract but argued that government needs the continuing consent of the governed. When a monarch becomes a tyrant, he held, the people have a right to overthrow him, since the contract protects life, liberty and property as natural rights.

Liberalism rests on individual rights, liberty, consent of the governed, political equality, private property and equality before the law. Different liberals understand these principles differently, and scholars often describe its doctrines as containing separate and often contradictory streams of thought. Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) held that where prices and competition are left free of regulation, the pursuit of self-interest, directed by an invisible hand, maximises a society's wealth. Jean-Baptiste Say and John Stuart Mill carried economic liberalism further, in 1803 and 1848.

Sismondi's New Principles of Political Economy (1819) was the first comprehensive liberal critique of early capitalism. By the end of the 19th century poverty, unemployment and organised labour challenged classical liberalism, and social liberalism emerged. The word now varies by region. In Europe and Latin America it means a moderate form of classical liberalism, while in North America it refers almost exclusively to social liberalism.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688, which entrenched parliamentary sovereignty, has been called the first modern liberal revolution. The American Revolution of 1776, the Constitution of 1787 and the French Revolution of 1789 used liberal philosophy against royal sovereignty. In the 19th century liberal governments were established in Europe and South America, and liberal ideas influenced reform in the Ottoman Empire and the Middle East, including the Tanzimat and Al-Nahda.

Liberalism has had many critics. The Roman Catholic Church was among its earliest and most outspoken. Edmund Burke attacked the liberal faith in rationality and natural equality, and Karl Marx rejected liberal theory. Before 1920 its main opponents were communism, conservatism and socialism, and it then faced fascism and Marxism–Leninism. Liberal ideas spread further in the 20th century, and social liberalism became a key component in expanding the welfare state.
liberation-of-paris: After the Normandy landings of June 1944, the plans of the Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force under General Dwight D. Eisenhower did not include an immediate assault on Paris. Its planners saw the Rhine and the Ruhr as the decisive targets, wished to avoid street fighting and to spare the city bombardment, and did not want to feed more than two million civilians. General Charles de Gaulle argued that French sovereignty should be restored quickly. British and American commanders stipulated that a French formation leading into the city consist of white personnel. Nearly two-thirds of the Free French Army were African colonial troops, so General Philippe Leclerc's 2nd Armoured Division was reorganised, its Black African soldiers being transferred out.

Railway workers began a strike on 10 August 1944, and the Métro, the police and the postal workers joined within a week, cutting the city's gas and electricity. On 18 August the Resistance leaders called a general strike and a mobilisation. Open fighting began on 19 August, when police occupied the Préfecture de Police and Resistance units attacked German garrisons. The Swedish consul general, Raoul Nordling, brokered a truce with the military governor, Dietrich von Choltitz, but it was never fully observed. German engineers had mined the Seine bridges, and Hitler ordered maximum destruction on 23 August.

On 24 August Leclerc disobeyed his American superior and sent a vanguard ahead, the 9th Company of the Régiment de marche du Tchad, called La Nueve, of whose 160 men 146 were Spanish Republicans. Under Captain Raymond Dronne it reached the Hôtel de Ville at 9:22 in the evening. Choltitz surrendered at the Hôtel Meurice on 25 August, and de Gaulle spoke at the Hôtel de Ville the same day, describing Paris as liberated by itself with the help of the French armies. On 26 August de Gaulle led a procession down the Champs-Élysées, watched by an estimated two million people, and gunfire from snipers scattered the crowds near the Place de la Concorde.

An estimated 800 to 1,000 Resistance fighters were killed and 1,500 wounded. The uprising gave the Provisional Government under de Gaulle the authority to govern mainland France in place of the fallen Vichy regime, and he formed a government of national unanimity from Gaullists, socialists, Christian democrats and communists. Food became scarce, but Allied convoys, one of which entered on 29 August, ended the crisis within ten days.

The collapse of Vichy was followed by extrajudicial reprisals. Several dozen suspected collaborators were executed without trial, and women accused of sexual relations with Germans had their heads shaved and were paraded through the streets. Choltitz was held near London until 1947, and no charges were brought against him.
liberation-tigers-of-tamil-eelam: Measures such as the Sinhala Only Act and anti-Tamil riots gave rise to separatist ideas among many Tamil leaders. Velupillai Prabhakaran cited the anti-Tamil pogrom of 1958 as one of the factors that led him to militancy. In 1975 he assassinated the Mayor of Jaffna, Alfred Duraiappah, in revenge for the incident at the Tamil conference of 1974. The LTTE was founded on 5 May 1976 as the successor to the Tamil New Tigers, as a reaction to the Constitution of 1972, which made Buddhism the primary religion and Sinhala the national language.

After the Black July anti-Tamil pogrom of 1983, Tamil militant groups grew dramatically and a full-scale insurgency began, the start of the Sri Lankan civil war. By 1986 the LTTE was the dominant Tamil militant group. An Indian Peace Keeping Force sent under the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord of 1987 left in March 1990. A ceasefire that held from June 1989 to June 1990 broke down when the LTTE massacred 600 police officers in the Eastern Province. A Ceasefire Agreement was signed in March 2002, monitored by Nordic countries.

At its peak in 2000 the LTTE held 76 per cent of the landmass of the Northern and Eastern provinces. After the election of Mahinda Rajapaksa as president in 2005 the LTTE pulled out of peace talks, and by August 2006 full-scale war had resumed. Prabhakaran led the organisation from its start until his death in 2009. At least 100,000 people were killed in the civil war between 1983 and 2009, many of them Sri Lankan Tamils.

From a guerrilla force the LTTE grew to resemble a conventional army, with a navy, an airborne unit, an intelligence wing and a suicide attack unit, the Black Tigers. It assassinated political opponents, and a suicide bomber killed the Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi on 21 May 1991. It was accused of attacks on civilians, of recruiting children, and of expelling Sinhalese and Muslim inhabitants from areas under its control, which the Sri Lankan Defence Ministry and Human Rights Watch have described as ethnic cleansing.

In its territory the LTTE ran a de facto state with Kilinochchi as its administrative capital, providing courts, police, a bank and radio and television stations. It presented itself as a secular national liberation movement. Countries including India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, and the European Union, designated it a terrorist organisation.
liberum-veto: The liberum veto, Latin for "free veto", allowed any member of the Sejm to end the current session and nullify the legislation already passed at it by crying Sisto activitatem!, "I stop the activity!", or Nie pozwalam!, "I do not allow!". It rested on the premise that all Polish-Lithuanian noblemen were equal, so every measure had to pass unanimously. Each deputy represented a region and was elected at a local sejmik, to which he answered for the decisions of the Sejm; a majority decision against even one sejmik was seen as a violation of political equality. At first dissenting deputies were often persuaded to withdraw, and the rule struck down only individual laws, as in the Sejm of 1611.

From the mid-17th century an objection to any item automatically caused earlier adopted legislation to be rejected, since a Sejm's legislation formed a whole. It is commonly and wrongly believed that the Trakai deputy Władysław Siciński first broke a Sejm this way in 1652; he vetoed only the continuation of its deliberations beyond the statutory time limit, though he set a dangerous precedent. In 1669 the Kyiv deputy Adam Olizar disrupted the whole Sejm at Kraków, and in 1688 a Sejm was dissolved before its Marshal was even elected. Under John III Sobieski (1674-1696) half of the proceedings were scuttled, and the practice spread to the local sejmiks.

In the 18th century Russia and Prussia found the veto a useful tool for frustrating reform, bribing deputies to exercise it. Of about 150 Sejms held between 1573 and 1763, 53 passed no legislation, and by Jacek Jędruch's count 32 of these were broken by the liberum veto. Only 8 of the 18 sessions under Augustus II passed laws, and from 1734 to 1763 only one did. Confederated sejms, which worked under the rules of a confederation, were used to avoid it.

Reforms of 1764 to 1766 introduced majority voting for non-crucial items, including most economic and tax matters, and outlawed binding instructions from sejmiks, though conservatives backed by foreign powers defended the veto in the Cardinal Laws of 1768. The Constitution of 3 May 1791, adopted by a confederated sejm, abolished it and established majority rule, but a confederated sejm at Grodno in 1793, under duress from Russia and Prussia, ratified the Second Partition. Many historians hold that the veto was a major cause of the Commonwealth's decline; Piotr Stefan Wandycz called it the "sinister symbol of old Polish anarchy". Others, such as Dalibor Roháč, stress that it checked the monarch and belonged to the Golden Liberty.
library-of-alexandria: The library was part of a larger research institution, the Mouseion, dedicated to the Muses. Libraries were not new: Uruk kept an archive of written materials around 3400 BCE, and the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh was founded in the seventh century BCE. The idea for Alexandria may have been proposed to Ptolemy I Soter by Demetrius of Phalerum, an exiled Athenian statesman, but sources disagree about the founding, and the library itself was probably not built until the reign of his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus.

The Ptolemaic kings meant it to hold all knowledge. They sent royal agents with large sums to buy as many texts as possible, favouring older copies. According to Galen, books found on ships entering the port were copied by official scribes and the copies returned to their owners. How many scrolls it held at any time is unknown, with estimates from 40,000 to 700,000.

Scholars at the library belonged to no philosophical school, but they answered to the king. Zenodotus of Ephesus worked on the text of Homer, Callimachus wrote the Pinakes, sometimes called the first library catalogue, and Eratosthenes of Cyrene, the third head librarian, calculated the circumference of the Earth. A daughter library was set up in the Serapeum under Ptolemy III Euergetes.

The decline came by stages. In 145 BCE Ptolemy VIII Physcon expelled the scholars, and the head librarian Aristarchus of Samothrace went into exile in Cyprus. In 48 BCE a fire started during Caesar's siege of Alexandria spread near the docks. Seneca, quoting Livy, says it destroyed 40,000 scrolls, but Cassius Dio mentions only storehouses of books and Florus and Lucan only the fleet and some houses, so it is unclear how much was lost. Under Roman rule membership of the Mouseion came to be granted for distinction in government, the army or athletics, and it seems to have ceased by the 260s CE. The Serapeum was demolished in 391 CE under a decree of Bishop Theophilus.

By the end of the Hellenistic period almost every city in the eastern Mediterranean had a public library. Much of the library's material may have survived through the Imperial Library of Constantinople, the Academy of Gondishapur and the House of Wisdom, and was transmitted to Europe from the 12th century. The modern Bibliotheca Alexandrina, completed in 2002, commemorates it.
library-of-ashurbanipal: The library was assembled at Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, whose site lies within the city of Mosul in northern Iraq. Ashurbanipal, who reigned from 668 to 627 BCE, had a reputation as a tenacious military commander, but he was also literate and a passionate collector of texts. As an apprentice scribe he mastered both Akkadian and Sumerian. He wrote to cities and centres of learning across Mesopotamia, instructing them to send him copies of all the works written in the region, and he hired scholars and scribes to copy texts, mainly from Babylonian sources. He also used war loot to stock the library. His interest in divination texts may have come from a wish to gain rituals and incantations vital to maintaining his royal power.

The texts were written mainly in Akkadian in cuneiform, in Neo-Babylonian and Assyrian scripts. The tablets were separated by content and placed in different rooms, for government, history, law, astronomy, geography and so on, and they were identified by coloured marks, brief written descriptions or the incipit, the first few words of the text. Many carry a stamp saying they belonged to the king's palace. Besides divination texts, omens, incantations and hymns, the library held medical, mathematical, astronomical and literary works, and sign lists that scribes needed to read old inscriptions. It also held the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Enûma Eliš creation story and the myth of Adapa. A large share of the original library consisted of writing boards, which have been lost.

Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BCE by a coalition of Babylonians, Scythians and Medes. A fire in the palace is believed to have partly baked the clay tablets, which helped preserve them. Austen Henry Layard made the first discovery in late 1849 in the South-West Palace of King Sennacherib, and three years later his assistant Hormuzd Rassam found a similar library in the palace of Ashurbanipal. No record was made of the findings, and the tablets were soon mixed with each other and with tablets from other sites.

Most went to the British Museum, whose database counts 30,943 in the whole Nineveh collection. If fragments of the same text are deducted, the library probably held some 10,000 texts. The museum has catalogued and photographed the collection in a project begun in 2002.
libreville: Libreville stands on the northern bank of the Gabon Estuary, near the Gulf of Guinea, in the north-western province of Estuaire. The city covers 65 square kilometres, and the Komo River passes through it and empties into the ocean. It has a tropical monsoon climate, with a wet season of about nine months from September to May and a short dry season. Its districts include Glass, the first European settlement in Gabon, and Owendo to the south, where the port and the terminus of the Trans-Gabon Railway lie.

The Mpongwe people lived in the area before colonisation. In 1839 the French admiral Édouard Bouët-Willaumez negotiated a trade and protection treaty with the Mpongwe ruler Antchoué Komé Rapontcombo, known to the French as King Denis. American missionaries from New England established a mission at Baraka, on what is now Libreville, in 1842.

In 1846 the French navy, which was tasked with contributing to the British blockade of Africa, captured the Brazilian slave ship L'Elizia near Loango. Fifty-two of the freed captives were resettled on the site in 1849, and the settlement was called Libreville, French for Freetown. After the French Revolution of 1848 and the establishment of the Second Republic, the former slaves held an election to choose the leaders of the new village, and a former slave named Mountier was elected mayor. From its earliest years the town functioned mainly as a trading post. Libreville was the administrative capital of France's Congo-Gabon colony from 1888 until 1904, when the capital moved to Brazzaville, and it exported timber, rubber and cocoa from concessions in the interior.

At independence in 1960 it was a trading post and minor administrative centre with a population of 32,000. It has since grown rapidly. Offshore petroleum discovered in the 1970s financed an expansion of its administration and construction, and the city hosted the Organisation of African Unity summit in 1977. The Trans-Gabon Railway, opened in stages between 1978 and 1986, links Owendo with Franceville.

Libreville is the capital and largest city of Gabon and the seat of its government. It is the country's main commercial and administrative centre and its leading gateway for imports and exports through the port complex at Owendo. French is spoken there, and is becoming a native language for many residents. Landmarks include the Arboretum de Sibang, the Palais du bord de mer and the National Museum of Arts, Rites and Traditions of Gabon, and Omar Bongo University was founded in 1970.
libya: Libya extends over 1,759,540 km2 and has the longest coastline of any African country on the Mediterranean, at 1,770 kilometres. It comprises three historical regions, Tripolitania, Fezzan and Cyrenaica. The climate is mostly extremely dry and desertlike, with a milder Mediterranean climate in the north, and the oases of Ghadames and Kufra are the most important of those scattered through the country.

About 90% of the people live along the coast, in less than 10% of the area. The name Libya first appears as rbw in an inscription of Ramesses II, and the Great Karnak Inscription records a war in 1208 BCE between King Meryey of the Libu and the pharaoh Merneptah, who defeated him. Italian geographer Federico Minutilli brought the name back into use in 1903.

Neolithic peoples inhabited the coastal plain from about 8000 BCE. The Garamantes, based at Germa, are the earliest known tribe by name, and the Phoenicians were the first to establish trading posts. Greeks colonised the area around Barca in 630 BCE and founded Cyrene, and four more Greek cities followed within 200 years. Persian rule began in 525 BCE, Alexander the Great ended it in 331 BCE, and the east then passed to the Ptolemaic Kingdom. Rome annexed Cyrenaica in 74 BCE, and Tripolitania reached a golden age in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, when Leptis Magna, home of the Severan dynasty, was at its height.

Libya was an early centre of Christianity and the home of Pope Victor I. The Vandals mostly held the area after the fall of the Western Roman Empire until the 7th century, when invasions brought Islam. Ottoman rule began in 1551 and continued until Italy occupied Libya in 1911. Italian Libya existed as a unified colony from 1934 to 1943, and Libya became independent as a kingdom in 1951.

Muammar Gaddafi overthrew King Idris I in a bloodless coup in 1969 and ruled for 42 years until he was overthrown and killed in the 2011 civil war. Arabs account for 92% of the population and Berbers for 5%, and there are about 140 tribes and clans.
licata: Licata is a city and comune on the south coast of Sicily, at the mouth of the Salso River, which in antiquity was the Himera, about midway between Agrigento and Gela. It is a seaport that ships sulphur and asphalt, and sulphur refining made it a major European exporting centre. West of the port a series of pocket beaches is separated by wave-cut headlands as high as 40 metres. The ancient Greek city stood on the right bank of the river, protected by the headland now named Monte San Michele, beside a small natural harbour about 80 metres across that has since been infilled.

Phoenicians traded at the site between the 12th and 8th centuries BCE. At the end of the 7th century BCE settlers from Gela built a fortified station to guard the river mouth, and in the first half of the 6th century BCE Phalaris, tyrant of Agrigento, built an outpost.

In 311 BCE Agathocles was beaten by the Carthaginians at the Battle of the Himera River near the town, which then fell to them. The city was refounded in 282 BCE by Phintias, tyrant of Agrigentum, who razed Gela, resettled its people and named the new city for himself. It was laid out on a great scale, with walls, temples and an agora, but never rose to the importance of Gela; as late as the 1st century BCE, inscriptions and coins show that its inhabitants still called themselves Geloi.

In 256 BCE the Romans won the Battle of Cape Ecnomus nearby in the First Punic War and freed the city from the Carthaginians. Cicero describes it as a seaport with a considerable export trade in corn. The Arabs conquered Licata in 827, and the Normans took it on 25 July 1086. In 1270 it rebelled against Angevin rule in the Sicilian Vespers. Corsairs under Dragut sacked it in 1553, after which the walls were rebuilt. In the 1870s two bridges to the inland sulphur mines and five refineries brought economic expansion. Licata served as an Allied landing point in 1943 during the invasion of Sicily.

The Museo Civico displays archaeological finds from burial grounds dating from prehistoric times to the 3rd century BCE. Among the sights are the remains of the ancient Greek city on Monte Sant'Angelo, the necropolis of Monte Petrulla, the 17th-century Castel Sant'Angelo and the Palazzo di Città, designed by Ernesto Basile. John Hersey's novel A Bell for Adano took Licata as its model.
lichfield: Lichfield lies in the south-east of Staffordshire, between the high ground of Cannock Chase to the west and the valleys of the rivers Trent and Tame to the east, about 27 kilometres north of Birmingham. Two Roman roads, Watling Street and Ryknild Street, crossed about 3 kilometres to the south at Letocetum, a Romano-British village at Wall whose Brittonic name means grey wood. In the post-Roman period it became Luitcoyt, and the modern name of Lichfield has this origin. The earliest evidence of settlement is Mesolithic flints, and there are traces of Neolithic occupation on the sandstone ridge where the cathedral stands.

The early history of Lichfield is obscure. The first authentic record is in Bede's history, which calls it Licidfelth and says that Chad fixed the see of the Mercians there in 669. Wulfhere, the first Christian king of Mercia, gave land for a monastery, and the place became the seat of the Diocese of Lichfield, about 11 kilometres north-west of the Mercian kings' seat at Tamworth. In the 12th century Roger de Clinton fortified the Cathedral Close and laid out the town on the ladder-shaped street pattern that survives. The pilgrims who came to the shrine of Saint Chad brought wealth, and in the Middle Ages woollen cloth and leather were the main industries.

The Reformation ended the pilgrim traffic when Chad's shrine was destroyed in 1538, and the Franciscan Friary was dissolved the same year. Plague in 1593 killed over a third of the population. The bishop had authority over the city until Edward VI's charter of 1548; a charter of 1553 from Mary I gave it a sheriff and made it a county separate from Staffordshire until 1888. Lichfield flourished in the 18th century as a coaching city and a centre of intellectual activity, the home of Samuel Johnson, David Garrick, Erasmus Darwin and Anna Seward, which led Johnson to call it a city of philosophers. The railways, arriving in 1837, ended its role as a staging post, and the city stayed largely unchanged while Birmingham grew.

Lichfield Cathedral, begun in 1195 and completed by the Lady Chapel in the 1330s, is the only medieval cathedral in Europe with three spires. It replaced a Norman building begun in 1085, which had replaced one or possibly two Anglo-Saxon buildings of the seventh century. The city centre has over 230 listed buildings, many of them Georgian. The Samuel Johnson Birthplace Museum and Erasmus Darwin House commemorate its two best-known residents. The Staffordshire Hoard, the largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver metalwork, was found about 6 kilometres south-west of the city in 2009.
lichtensteig: Lichtensteig lies in the Toggenburg, the upper basin of the Thur, on the right bank of the river. It is downstream of Wattwil and upstream of Dietfurt, west of the Wasserfluh Pass. The ruins of Neu-Toggenburg castle stand on a rocky outcrop above the village. With only 2.8 square kilometres, it is the smallest municipality of Toggenburg by area, and its height ranges from 591 to 1,146 metres. It had 1,879 inhabitants in 2020, and most speak German.

The counts of Toggenburg founded Lichtensteig in the early 13th century, and it is first mentioned in 1228 as Liehtunsteige. A market is mentioned in 1374, and the right to hold markets was confirmed in 1400. A letter of privileges of the lords of Raron in 1439 confirms a council of twelve burghers and the joint appointment of judges by burghers and landlords; the mayor was appointed by the landlord from a list drawn up by the burghers. After the Abbey of St Gallen acquired the Toggenburg in 1468, Lichtensteig became the seat of the abbot's reeve, and in 1469 Abbot Ulrich Rösch confirmed its privileges.

The council declared for the Reformation in 1528. The church was used by both Reformed and Catholics, while schools were separated by confession until 1868, when a neo-Gothic church was built that both confessions still used until two new churches were built in 1967 and 1970. The town grew in importance as a market town in the 19th century with the textile home-working industry of the Toggenburg. In the early 20th century it had six yearly markets and a weekly livestock market. The railway reached it in 1870, and in 1874 the settlements of Blatten, Hof and Loretto were added to it.

The Old Town Council building at Hintergasse 22 is listed as a Swiss heritage site of national significance, and the whole village is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites. The clockmaker, instrument maker and mathematician Jost Bürgi was born in Lichtensteig in 1552. The municipal coat of arms, a letter L in gold on a field divided red and black, was adopted in 1946 from elements in use since the 16th century.
licinius: Licinius was born to a Dacian peasant family in Moesia Superior and became a close friend of the emperor Galerius, whom he accompanied on the Persian expedition in 298. In 307 Galerius sent him as an envoy to Italy to seek an agreement with the usurper Maxentius, and left him in charge of the eastern provinces. On 11 November 308 Galerius raised him to the rank of Augustus in the West, with command of the Balkan provinces of Illyricum, Thrace and Pannonia. In 310 he inflicted a severe defeat on the Sarmatians.

After Galerius died in May 311, Licinius agreed with Maximinus Daza to share the eastern provinces, with the Hellespont and Bosporus as the dividing line. After Constantine I defeated Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in October 312, Licinius and Constantine recognised each other as supreme emperors, Licinius in the East and Constantine in the West. In March 313 Licinius met Constantine at Milan and married his half-sister Flavia Julia Constantia. The marriage was the occasion for the jointly issued Edict of Milan, which reissued Galerius's edict of toleration and added the return of confiscated property to Christian congregations and exemption of the clergy from municipal duties.

Maximinus Daza took Byzantium and Heraclea while Licinius was away, but on 30 April 313 Licinius crushed his army at the Battle of Tzirallum, and Daza died in August. Licinius then hunted down and killed several relatives of the Tetrarchs, among them Daza's wife and two children and Diocletian's wife Prisca. A civil war with Constantine in 316 saw Licinius defeated at Cibalae on 8 October and again at Mardia, after which they were reconciled and Licinius had his co-emperor Valens killed.

Tension rose again in 321 when Constantine crossed the Danube in pursuit of raiders. In 324 Constantine defeated Licinius's fleet, then his army at Adrianople on 3 July, and finally Licinius at Chrysopolis on 18 September. Licinius was at first spared through the intervention of his wife and imprisoned at Thessalonica, but was later executed; Constantine accused him of trying to raise troops among the Goths, and had him hanged.

Constantine's propaganda portrayed Licinius as a supporter of paganism, which may be inaccurate: evidence suggests he was for a period a committed supporter of Christians, and he adopted Christian symbols for his armies.
