Eusebius of Caesarea, writing under Constantine, charges him with expelling Christians from the palace and ordering sacrifices. After his death his statues were thrown down and his laws abolished, an erasure now called damnatio memoriae.
lidice: Lidice lies in a flat agricultural landscape on the Prague Plateau, about 4 kilometres east of Kladno and 12 kilometres northwest of Prague. Its name derives from the personal name Lída and means the village of Lída's people. The first written mention dates from 1318. For centuries it was an agricultural village belonging to the Buštěhrad estate, and after industrialisation in the second half of the 19th century many inhabitants worked in the mines and steelworks of Kladno and Slaný.

Lidice was chosen as a target for reprisals after the assassination of Reinhard Heydrich because its residents were suspected of harbouring resistance partisans and were falsely linked with helping the team members of Operation Anthropoid. The village was destroyed on 10 June 1942 on the orders of Adolf Hitler and the acting Reichsprotektor Kurt Daluege. On that day 172 boys and men aged from 14 to 84 were shot. In all about 340 people from Lidice were murdered in the reprisal: 192 men, 60 women and 88 children. The village was set on fire and the remains of the buildings destroyed with explosives.

After the war only 153 women and 17 children returned. They were rehoused in a new village built overlooking the original site in 1947–1949, paid for by the Lidice Shall Live campaign, which Sir Barnett Stross started in north Staffordshire. Evidence of the massacre, including Nazi propaganda films, was shown at the Nuremberg Trials, with testimony from two surviving children who had been forcibly rehoused as part of Germanisation.

Lidice is a municipality in Kladno District with about 600 inhabitants. The Lidice Memorial, built in 1946–1962 by architects led by František Marek, occupies the original village and holds fragments of burnt buildings, the Memorial to the Child Victims of War, a cemetery and the Rose Garden. It is protected as a national cultural monument. Many neighbourhoods and streets elsewhere took the name Lidice in remembrance, and in 1943 Bohuslav Martinů wrote Memorial to Lidice.
lidzbark-warminski: Lidzbark Warmiński, in German Heilsberg, is a historical town in the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship of northern Poland and the capital of Lidzbark County. The Elma, a tributary of the Łyna, flows through it. It was once the capital of Warmia and formerly its largest town, a religious and cultural centre known as the Pearl of Warmia. For a long period it was under the control of the Warmian bishops, and it was also a major economic centre, giving up its importance only to the nearby city of Braniewo.

The town began as a settlement of the Old Prussians known as Lecbarg, until the Teutonic Knights conquered it in 1240 and named it Heilsberg. In 1306 it became the seat of the Bishopric of Warmia, and it received town privileges in 1309. The castle of the Warmian bishops was built in the 1350s and expanded in the following centuries. In 1440 the town joined the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation, at whose request King Casimir IV Jagiellon incorporated the region into the Kingdom of Poland in 1454. That led to the Thirteen Years' War, and in the Second Peace of Thorn (1466) the Teutonic Order gave up its claim.

Nicolaus Copernicus first visited the town at the turn of 1495 and 1496 and lived at the castle from 1503; he is believed to have written part of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium there. King Charles XII of Sweden resided in the town in the winter of 1703–04 during the Great Northern War. In the mid-18th century Prince-Bishop Adam Stanisław Grabowski found a manuscript of the Gesta principum Polonorum, the oldest medieval Polish chronicle, in the castle and had it printed for the first time.

Prussia annexed the region in the First Partition of Poland in 1772, ending the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia, though the last Prince-Bishop, Ignacy Krasicki, kept his seat in the town until 1795. Afterwards the town lost the cultural significance it has not regained. It was heavily damaged when the Red Army took it in 1945, and on 19 May 1945 sovereignty was transferred to Polish authorities.

The main landmark is the Gothic Castle of the Warmian Bishops, with its fortifications, towers and the Baroque Grabowski Palace. It houses a museum and is a Historic Monument of Poland. Other sights include the Gothic collegiate church of Saints Peter and Paul, the medieval town walls and High Gate, and the Krasicki Orangery.
liechtenstein-castle: Liechtenstein Castle (German: Burg Liechtenstein) lies on the edge of the Wienerwald, the Vienna Woods, in Lower Austria, on the border with Vienna. Its name means bright stone in German. It is the ancestral seat and place of origin of the House of Liechtenstein, the ruling family of the Principality of Liechtenstein.

Hugo von Liechtenstein, who died in 1156, built the castle around 1122-36 on a fief that he received from the Babenberg margraves of Austria. He had come to Austria in the knightly entourage of Diepold III, Margrave of Vohburg, who gave him Petronell-Carnuntum on the Danube as a fief. Petronell and Rohrau became his own property in 1142 and remained important Liechtenstein seats in the High Middle Ages.

The castle began with a tower but probably grew into a larger palace complex during the 12th century. It passed to the Stadeck family through the marriage of Dietmut of Liechtenstein, who died in 1308, to Leutold of Stadeck, who died in 1295. From the time of Albert IV, Duke of Austria, it was pledged to various families. The Ottomans destroyed it in the siege of Vienna in 1529 and again in the Battle of Vienna in 1683.

Johann I Joseph, Prince of Liechtenstein, bought back the ancestral seat and in 1820-21 built Schloss Liechtenstein below it, which is now a retirement home. Around the ruins he had a romantic landscape garden laid out with several artificial ruins. The architect Joseph Hardtmuth carried out the first restoration work between 1808 and 1816, but the castle remained a ruin until 1884, when Carl Gangolf Kayser rebuilt it for Johann II.

The castle hosts the Nestroy Theatre Festival each summer. It appeared in films including A Walk with Love and Death (1969) and The Three Musketeers (1993). It was renovated and given a new roof in 2008 and 2009, and it has been open to the public since spring 2010, with guided tours daily.
liepaja: Liepāja lies on the Baltic coast in south-western Latvia, on a coastal dune embankment 1.5 to 6.5 kilometres wide. A Trade Channel divides the city into Vecliepāja, the old town, to the south and Jaunliepāja to the north, and north of the Karosta Channel lies the former naval district of Karosta. The name comes from the Latvian liepa, linden. The older name Libau is believed to come from the river Līva, which once flowed through the town. The sea off Liepāja is almost ice-free in winter.

The first recorded mention of Līva village is in a treaty of 4 April 1253 between the bishop of Courland and the master of the Livonian Order. In 1263 the Teutonic Order established a town it called Libau, and Lithuanians sacked and burned the village in 1418. By 1520 the Līva had become too shallow for easy navigation. The town received city rights on 18 March 1625, and a Trade Channel dug in 1703 helped it grow. Peter I of Russia visited a house on Kungu Street in 1697 and Charles XII of Sweden another in 1700.

Courland passed to Russia in 1795, in the Third Partition of Poland, and the town grew rapidly in the 19th century. The architect Paul Max Bertschy, appointed in 1871, designed much of its historic centre. During the Crimean War a landing party of 110 men from two British warships captured the unfortified port on 17 May 1854 without a shot. The Russian naval complex of Karosta was built to the north.

German ships shelled the city in August 1914 and German troops occupied it on 7 May 1915. In the interwar years Liepāja was the second city of Latvia, though business drifted to Riga. The Soviet Union occupied Latvia in 1940, and a second mass deportation to Siberia from Liepāja took place on 25 to 29 March 1949. As a military port the city was closed to outsiders. The commercial port reopened in 1991 and the last Russian troops left in 1994.

Liepāja is the largest city of the Courland region and an important ice-free port. It has many Art Nouveau buildings, and Graudu Street is almost entirely in that style. Its symphony orchestra is the oldest in the Baltic states, and the Liepāja Theatre, founded in 1907, is the oldest Latvian professional theatre still in existence.
lier-belgium: Lier lies in the Belgian province of Antwerp. The city centre grew up around the river Nete and is surrounded by it. The municipality is made up of Lier proper and the village of Koningshooikt, which was joined to the town as a sub-municipality in 1977. Its Latin name is Lyra, and the origin of the name Lier is still debated: it most likely refers to the Nete and the muddy soils around it. There is scant record of the place before the 7th century. Saint Gummarus, its patron saint, was born in that century and died on 11 October 714.

In 1194 Lier was given oppidum status, and in 1212 it was granted municipal rights. The beguinage was founded in 1258; the last surviving beguine died in 1994, and in 1998 the beguinage was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Flemish Béguinages. In the 14th century, according to the story, Duke Jan II offered the city a choice between a university and a livestock market as a reward for joining his fight against Mechelen. Lier chose the market, and the university was founded at Leuven in 1425. The inhabitants are still nicknamed Schapekoppen, sheep heads.

In 1496 Philip the Handsome, son of Maximilian of Austria, married Joanna of Castile at Lier. Their son Charles V, born at Ghent in 1500, went on to rule both the Holy Roman Empire and the Spanish Empire. King Christian II of Denmark and his wife Isabella, a sister of Charles V, lived in Lier until 1523 after the Danish nobility expelled him. In 1860 the skeleton of a mammoth was found where the city hall now stands, the first found in western Europe.

In the First World War King Albert and his chiefs of staff were briefly headquartered in Lier before retreating to Temse. As part of the defences of Antwerp, the city suffered heavy German artillery fire, and most of its medieval-style buildings today, including the town hall and belfry, are replicas built soon after the war.

Lier had a population of 35,712 in 2018 across 49.70 square kilometres. Its landmarks include the Gothic St. Gummarus Church of the 14th century, the rococo town hall of the 18th century, the belfry, which is part of the Belfries of Belgium and France World Heritage Site, and the Zimmer Tower, whose astronomical clock was built in the 1930s by Louis Zimmer. The town is known for its beers, the Lierse vlaaikes cake and the bus maker Van Hool, and it was the home of the writer Felix Timmermans.
lighthouse-of-alexandria: Pharos was a small island on the western edge of the Nile Delta. Alexander the Great founded Alexandria on the opposite shore in 332 BCE, and the island was later joined to the city by a mole more than 1,200 metres long, the Heptastadion. Sailing to Alexandria was dangerous because the African coast there is flat and inconspicuous, with shallow shoals and submerged reefs. After Ptolemy I Soter declared himself king in 305 BCE he commissioned the lighthouse, and it was finished in the reign of his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus, after twelve years of work, at a cost of 800 talents of silver.

Strabo, who visited in the late first century BCE, reported that Sostratus of Cnidus had a dedication to the Saviour Gods inscribed in metal letters on the tower. Pliny the Elder wrote that Sostratus was the architect, though that conclusion is disputed.

Medieval Arab writers describe the tower consistently, giving heights between 103 and 118 metres on a square base 30 metres on a side. It rose in three tapering tiers: a square lower section around a central core, an octagonal middle section and a circular top. At the top a fire was lit at night, and a mirror reflected sunlight by day. Roman coins struck at Alexandria show a statue of Triton at each corner and a statue of Poseidon or Zeus on top.

The tower was built of large light-coloured blocks of limestone and granite. Its three-stage form is echoed in the minarets of early Egyptian mosques. Julius Caesar describes the Pharos in his Civil Wars, noting that whoever held it controlled access to the harbour, and that by seizing it in 48 BCE he secured his supplies.

Earthquakes cracked the tower in 796 and 951, and that of 956 collapsed its top 20 metres or so, after which a dome in the Islamic style replaced the fallen statue. The earthquake of 1303 was the most destructive. Ibn Battuta saw it ruined in 1326 and found it impossible to enter in 1349. In 1480 the sultan Qaitbay built a fort on the site from the fallen stone.

Underwater work began with Gaston Jondet in 1916. A UNESCO expedition led by Honor Frost confirmed the ruins in 1968, and in 1994 a French team led by Jean-Yves Empereur found granite blocks of 49 to 60 tonnes, sphinxes, obelisks and columns on the floor of the Eastern Harbour. By the end of 1995 more than 3,300 pieces had been catalogued.
liguria: Liguria is bordered by France to the west, Piedmont to the north, and Emilia-Romagna and Tuscany to the east, and rests on the Ligurian Sea. Its narrow strip of land is hemmed in by the sea, the Alps and the Apennines, and the watershed runs at an average height of about 1,000 metres. Its coast is the Italian Riviera, which runs from the French border near Ventimiglia east to Capo Corvo, at the end of the Gulf of La Spezia.

The name Liguria predates Latin and has no settled etymology. It comes from the ancient Ligures, whose territory was much larger than the present region: it took in all of north-west Italy south of the Po and part of south-eastern France. Human presence is very old: traces of huts built by nomadic hunters about 300,000 years ago have been found at Terra Amata, near Nice.

In the First Punic War the Ligurians were divided, some siding with Carthage and others, including the people of Stalia, later Genoa, with Rome. In 180 BCE the Romans deported 47,000 Ligures Apuani. Under Augustus the region became Regio IX Liguria, reaching from the coast to the Po. From the 4th to the 10th century it was held by Byzantines, Lombards under King Rothari about 641 and Franks about 774, and invaded by Saracen and Norman raiders. In the 10th century it was divided into three marches, and the coastal towns became city-states under Genoa's growing rule.

French influence ended in 1528, when Andrea Doria allied with the king of Spain and imposed an aristocratic government that gave the republic relative stability for about 250 years. After a short independence in 1814, the Congress of Vienna in 1815 annexed Liguria to the Kingdom of Sardinia. A Genoese uprising against the House of Savoy in 1821 was put down with great bloodshed. Giuseppe Mazzini, Mameli and Nino Bixio of the Risorgimento were born there, and Giuseppe Garibaldi began his Expedition of the Thousand on 5 May 1860 from a rock at Quarto, a quarter of Genoa.

Liguria is a region of Italy with its capital at Genoa and it is roughly coextensive with the former territory of the Republic of Genoa. It is the third smallest Italian region, yet one of the most densely populated. Agriculture is specialised in flowers, wine and olive oil, and the cliffside vineyards of the Cinque Terre produce white wines.
ligurian-republic: The Ligurian Republic, also called the Republic of Liguria, was a French client republic formed by Napoleon in June 1797. It consisted of the old Republic of Genoa, which covered most of the Ligurian region of north-west Italy, and the small imperial fiefs that the House of Savoy owned inside its territory. It followed a conflict in May 1797 between Genoese inhabitants and their wealthy rulers, after which Napoleon took Genoa and established his own order. Archbishop Giovanni Lercari showed his support of the French three days after the founding was announced. A first constitution was drawn up as a temporary document, and a replacement was promulgated on 22 December 1797, establishing a directorial republic, which a large majority approved in a plebiscite.

In June 1798 the republic's rulers led the people into war against the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia after exiles tried to raise an uprising, and French intervention led to the French occupation of Piedmont. In 1800 an Austrian army and a British fleet besieged the republic. The conflicts caused an estimated 30,000 casualties, and the French army had to be relied on for economic restoration. The directory was deposed on 7 December 1799 and replaced temporarily by a commission. The republic was briefly occupied by Austrian forces in 1800 before Napoleon returned with an army and retook it.

A new constitution of 1802, imposed by Napoleon, established institutions more like those of the Genoese Republic, with a doge named for a five-year term as president of a Senate. The republic kept the traditional Genoese flag, a red cross on white. In June 1805 its territory was annexed directly by the First French Empire as the departments of Apennins, Gênes and Montenotte.

After the fall of Napoleon the republic was briefly restored between 28 April and 28 July 1814. The Congress of Vienna awarded it to Piedmont-Sardinia, which annexed it on 3 January 1815, and its territories formed the new Duchy of Genoa within the Savoyard state.
lihula: Lihula is a small town in Lääneranna Parish, in western Estonia. Its castle, known in German as Leal, Leale or Lihhola, was first mentioned in 1211, but it appears that the site had been used as a fortress since the Iron Age. From 1211 the town was the see of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Leal, also known as the bishopric of Estonia. That diocese was suppressed as such in 1235, and the Diocese of Dorpat, a prince-bishopric, was established on the same territory; it lasted until 1558, when it fell victim to the Reformation.

In 1220 a Swedish army began to build a castle at Lihula but was defeated by Estonian forces on 8 August 1220, in the Battle of Lihula. In 1238 the bishop of Saare-Lääne, in German Ösel-Wiek, built a crusader fortress on the site in cooperation with the Teutonic Order. This attempt was more successful, and the castle became one of the bishop's residences. The Teutonic Order also used it as the centre of its commandry between 1241 and 1477.

In 1560 the estate was reportedly granted to the alderman Gerdt Bellingshausen by Duke Magnus of Holstein, and in the course of the Livonian War the castle was destroyed. A new manorial estate grew up beside the original site. In the 1630s it was recorded as the property of the Swedish general Åke Tott, and it stayed in the Tott family until 1684, after which it belonged to various aristocratic families. The present neoclassical manor house was built in the early 19th century.

The neoclassical manor house of the early 19th century stands next to the site of the destroyed castle. Lihula was long a seat of bishops and a stronghold fought over in the crusading period, and that history is the main reason it appears in accounts of medieval Estonia.
lika: Lika is a traditional region of Croatia, bounded by the Velebit mountain to the southwest and the Plješevica mountain to the northeast, by the Ogulin-Plaški basin to the north-west and by the Malovan pass to the south-east. It takes up about 12 percent of Croatia's land area. Most of it lies in Lika-Senj County, with parts in Karlovac and Zadar County. Its main towns, Gospić, Otočac and Gračac, lie in karst poljes along the rivers Lika and Gacka. The name is said to derive from an old Illyrian word for a body of water, and first appears in the tenth-century De Administrando Imperio, which says the Croatian ban ruled "Krbava, Lika and Gacka".

From the first millennium BCE the region was inhabited by the Iapodes, related to the Illyrians, who fought the Roman Empire in the 2nd century BCE and were finally conquered by Augustus in 34 BCE. The White Croats migrated there in the first half of the 7th century, and Lika became part of the Kingdom of Croatia in 925. In 1493 the Croatian army suffered a heavy defeat by the Ottomans at the Battle of Krbava Field near Udbina.

The Ottomans took Modruš in 1513 and Udbina in 1527, and many inhabitants left; for almost half a century Lika and Krbava remained largely uninhabited. After 1683, 30,000 Muslims moved towards Bosnia, and Ottoman rule mostly ended with the recapture of Udbina in 1689. Lika was incorporated into the Military Frontier, which was abolished on 15 July 1881.

In 1941 Lika became part of the Independent State of Croatia, whose Ustaše carried out massacres of Serbian civilians; an uprising began there on 27 July, and ZAVNOH held its founding session at Otočac in June 1943. In 1991 eastern Lika joined the Republic of Serbian Krajina, while the fiercest fighting was the Battle of Gospić in August and September 1991. The Croatian Army retook the region in Operation Storm in 1995.

Lika is a rural area of farming, livestock and wood processing, and the Plitvice Lakes National Park and Northern Velebit National Park draw visitors. Ikavian and Shtokavian dialects of Croatian are spoken in most of it, with Chakavian around Brinje. Local cuisine is built on lamb, dairy products, potatoes and maize, with dishes such as Lički lonac, a stew of mutton and vegetables.
lile-rousse: L'Île-Rousse is a commune in the Haute-Corse department of France, on the island of Corsica. It is built on a bay bounded to the north-west by rocky islets of red porphyry, which give the town its name, and to the south by a white sand beach. Its Corsican names are Lìsula and Isula Rossa, and as Italian was the administrative language of Corsica until 1848, the town was originally called Isola Rossa, meaning Red Island. With Saint-Florent and Tox, it is one of only three communes in the department to have a French name.

The area is said to have been inhabited between 5000 and 3000 BCE. Tradition holds that around 1000 BCE a small prosperous town called Agilla stood here, dependent on Tyre, and that after destruction by a Phoenician fleet it passed under Roman rule as Rubico Rocega, meaning red rock, until the 4th century CE. Threatened by pirates, the coast then went uninhabited for centuries except by fishermen and peasants living in the villages of Santa Reparata and Monticello. In the 17th century merchants from Santa-Reparata-di-Balagna set up shops to trade by sea with coastal villages.

Pasquale Paoli, who often came to the Balagne, decided to give Corsica a port in the north-west, to cut the sea traffic between Genoa and Calvi. He persuaded the Balagne government, sitting in Algajola, to authorise a fort protecting the port, known as the Scalu, on 10 December 1765, and the town grew from that decision. Its fortifications and houses developed from 1765 into the first half of the 19th century. After 1815 the town took a blazon with the royal fleur-de-lis of France, and for half a century it was run by elected Bonapartist officials.

The old town, laid out by Paoli, whom the town calls the Father of the Fatherland, has almost straight, paved streets running north to south and a market with twenty-one columns. Its streets carry names such as Pasquale Paoli, Napoleon and Louis Philippe. The parish church of the Immaculée Conception de Marie stands west of the main square, shaded by date palms planted in 1890, and the place Paoli has plane trees. The town is popular with tourists.
lili-marleen: Norbert Schultze set the poem to music in 1938, and Lale Andersen first recorded it in 1939 as Das Mädchen unter der Laterne, The Girl under the Lantern. In early 1942 she recorded it in English, in a translation by Norman Baillie-Stewart, a former British army officer working for German propaganda. Other English texts followed: Tommie Connor's Lily of the Lamplight in 1944, and a version by Theodore Stephanides, published in his memoir Climax in Crete in 1946. An Italian version by the lyricist Nino Rastelli, recorded in 1942 by Lina Termini, was probably the first to be released.

After German forces occupied Belgrade in 1941, Radio Belgrade became their station Soldatensender Belgrad, heard throughout Europe and the Mediterranean. A lieutenant working there collected second-hand records from the Reich radio station, among them Andersen's recording, which had sold about 700 copies. Karl-Heinz Reintgen, the officer in charge, began playing it, and for lack of other recordings the station played it frequently. It became popular with Axis and Allied troops alike. Fitzroy Maclean, in his memoir Eastern Approaches, recalled the husky, nostalgic voice that reached listeners in the Western Desert in early 1942, and later, with the Yugoslav Partisans, how they listened for it on Radio Belgrade each night at ten.

Allied soldiers adapted the tune, and in Italy sang The D-Day Dodgers, with words by Harry Pynn, once the Normandy invasion had begun in 1944. In 1944 the American Office of Strategic Services included the song in its Muzak Project, musical propaganda designed to demoralize enemy soldiers, for which Marlene Dietrich recorded it in German. Decca released her English version in 1945. Dietrich sang it for Allied troops and kept it in her concerts from 1953 to 1975.

Andersen received a gold disc for over a million sales. Perry Como's recording of 27 June 1944 reached number 13 on the American charts, and Connie Francis, Vera Lynn, Bing Crosby and many others recorded it. In 2005 Bear Family Records issued a 7-CD set with nearly 200 versions. The Soviet counterpropaganda officer Lev Kopelev wrote a parody to demoralize enemy soldiers, and Joseph Brodsky later wrote a Russian poem based on it. The Special Air Service, the Special Air Service Regiment and Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry adopted the tune as their regimental slow march. Humphrey Jennings made a 29-minute film about the song in 1944, and Rainer Werner Fassbinder's 1980 film Lili Marleen told the story of Lale Andersen and her version.
lili-uokalani: Liliʻuokalani was born on 2 September 1838 in Honolulu to Analea Keohokālole and Caesar Kapaʻakea. According to Hawaiian custom her long name recalled an event at her birth: the regent Elizabeth Kīnaʻu had an eye infection, and the words liliʻu, loloku, walania and kamakaʻeha mean smarting, tearful, a burning pain and sore eyes. She was hānai, informally adopted, at birth by Abner Pākī and Laura Kōnia and raised with their daughter Bernice Pauahi Bishop. She was educated at the Royal School, and King Kamehameha III proclaimed her and her siblings eligible for the throne. She married the American-born John Owen Dominis, later Governor of Oʻahu.

After her brother David Kalākaua became king in 1874 she was given the title of Princess, and in 1877 she was proclaimed heir apparent. As regent in 1881 she met the smallpox epidemic by closing the ports, halting passenger vessels from Oʻahu and quarantining the sick; there were 789 cases and 289 deaths.

Liliʻuokalani took the oath of office on 29 January 1891, nine days after her brother's death, as the first and only female monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom. She replaced the holdover cabinet and named her niece Kaʻiulani as her successor. Petitions from the two main political parties, Hui Kālaiʻāina and the National Reform Party, asked her to rewrite the Bayonet Constitution of 1887. She moved to do so, supported by two thirds of registered voters, but her cabinet withheld support.

Her opponents, led by Lorrin A. Thurston and William Owen Smith, formed the Committee of Safety, drawing support mainly from American and European businessmen in Hawaiʻi. On 17 January 1893 the monarchy was overthrown, a coup made possible by the landing of US Marines under John L. Stevens. A Provisional Government became the Republic of Hawaiʻi, whose aim was annexation to the United States. In January 1895 Robert W. Wilcox and Samuel Nowlein led an unsuccessful rebellion. Liliʻuokalani was arrested and held in a bedroom of ʻIolani Palace, and on 24 January 1895 she abdicated in return for the commutation of death sentences passed on six of her supporters. The United States annexed Hawaiʻi after the outbreak of the Spanish-American War.

She spent more than a decade seeking compensation from the United States for the seized Crown Lands, and her lawsuit of 1909 failed. In 1911 the Territory of Hawaii granted her a pension of $1,250 a month. She died at Washington Place on 11 November 1917. A devout Christian who played the organ and led the choir at Kawaiahaʻo Church, she was also a songwriter and the composer of Aloha ʻOe. She wrote her autobiography, Hawaiʻi's Story by Hawaiʻi's Queen (1898), during her imprisonment.
lille: Lille lies along the Deûle river in the northern part of France, within French Flanders and close to the border with Belgium. It is nicknamed in France the Capital of Flanders, and it belongs to the historical region of Romance Flanders. The commune covers only 35 square kilometres, but together with its suburbs it forms a conurbation of several cities, including Roubaix, Tourcoing and Villeneuve-d'Ascq. It also forms part of a cross-border grouping with the Belgian cities of Mouscron, Kortrijk, Tournai and Menin.

Excavations suggest the area was inhabited as early as 2000 BCE, in the districts now called Fives, Wazemmes and Vieux Lille. Its early inhabitants were Gauls such as the Menapians, the Morins, the Atrebates and the Nervians, followed by Germanic peoples including the Saxons, the Frisians and the Franks. A Battle of Lille was fought in 1054. From the 12th century the fame of the Lille cloth fair grew, and the city has been a merchant city since its origins and a manufacturing city since the 16th century.

As a garrison town, protected by its citadel, Lille was often besieged and belonged successively to the Kingdom of France, the Burgundian State, the Holy Roman Empire and the Spanish Netherlands. In 1792, during the aftermath of the French Revolution, Austrian forces besieged it for eight days; their artillery destroyed many houses and the main church, but the city, led by Mayor François André-Bonte, did not surrender. The Column of the Goddess, erected in 1842, commemorates the resistance.

The Industrial Revolution made Lille a great industrial capital, built mainly on textiles and mechanical industries. German forces occupied it on 13 October 1914 after a ten-day siege and heavy shelling that destroyed 882 apartment and office blocks and 1,500 houses. In July 1921 Albert Calmette and Camille Guérin announced at the Pasteur Institute in Lille the first anti-tuberculosis vaccine, known as BCG. In the Second World War the city was occupied again and was liberated in early September 1944 by a British force largely of tanks.

Lille is the capital of the Hauts-de-France region and the prefecture of the Nord department. Its old centre has 17th-century red brick town houses around the Grand'Place, and the belfry of its city hall is among the belfries inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites in July 2005. Other sights include the citadel, the cathedral and the Palais des Beaux-Arts. Charles de Gaulle was born there. The annual Braderie, held on the first weekend of September, is thought to date from the twelfth century. Lille opened the first automatic light metro line in the world in 1983, and Eurostar trains have served it since 1994.
lillebonne: Before the Roman conquest of Gaul the site was the capital of the Caletes, the tribe that gave its name to the Pays de Caux. It was destroyed by Julius Caesar in the Gallic Wars, and Augustus built the city of Juliobona there in the first century. It became an important centre from which Roman roads branched out in all directions, to Harfleur, Étretat, Dieppe, Évreux and Rouen. Close to the Seine, it served as an administrative, military and commercial city and lay on a great route between Britannia and the rest of the Roman Empire.

The city was completely destroyed in the middle of the second century and was ruined again in the barbarian invasions of 273, after which the theatre was turned into a fortress: its exits were blocked, wells were dug and baths were put up in the arena. In the Middle Ages the town walls were built from materials taken from the Roman theatre.

The remains of Roman baths and of a theatre that could hold 3,000 people have been brought to light. The Gallo-Roman amphitheatre was built in the first century and altered in the second so that it could serve as both an amphitheatre and a theatre; part of it is visible from the Félix Faur Square, and the foundations of its wings and backdrop lie beneath the square. Many Roman finds come from the town, among them a bronze statue of Apollo, now in the Louvre, and a mosaic of a deer hunt from a suburban villa, now in the museum at Rouen. The mosaic was made by T. Sen Filix from Pozzuoli, Italy, and Amor, his local apprentice.

Under William the Conqueror the town recovered some of its importance. He built a castle there, and a council at Lillebonne decided on the conquest of England. At an ecclesiastical council held there in 1080, William was confirmed in his ultimate authority over the Norman church. The park holds a cylindrical keep and other remains of the castle, rebuilt in the thirteenth century, and the church of Notre Dame keeps a Gothic portal and tower of the sixteenth century.

Lillebonne is a commune in the Seine-Maritime department in Normandy, 5.6 km north of the Seine and 39 km east of Le Havre. It lies in the valley of the river Bolbec at the foot of wooded hills. Its older industries were cotton-spinning and the making of calico, candles and starch, and petrochemistry is now the main industry of the area.
lim-river: The Lim is the longest right tributary of the Drina and belongs to the Black Sea drainage basin through the Drina, the Sava and the Danube. Its drainage basin covers 5,968 square kilometres, and the river is not navigable. It flows out of Lake Plav to the north under the name Lim, passing Andrijevica, Berane and Bijelo Polje before it enters Serbia between the villages of Dobrakovo and Gostun. Its two most important tributaries, the Uvac and the Mileševa, join it from the right in Serbia.

On the border between Montenegro and Serbia the river has carved a long gorge, the Kumanička klisura, between the mountains of Lisa and Ozren. It then runs through the northern part of the Sandžak, past Brodarevo, Prijepolje and Priboj. After Priboj it turns north-west and enters Bosnia and Herzegovina for a few kilometres, returns to Serbia, and crosses into Bosnia again at Rudo. It empties into the Drina near the village of Međeđa, and its lowest section is flooded by the Višegrad Reservoir.

Linguists including Franz Miklosich, Eqrem Çabej, Aleksandar Loma and Ivan Popović derive the name from the Albanian word lumë, meaning river. According to Loma, the name probably passed into South Slavic before the 10th or 12th century CE, depending on whether it was taken from lumë or from its dialect form lymë, and it was later passed back into Albanian. Popović holds that the name is not an ancient substrate but belongs to a pre-Slavic Albanian layer.

After the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1991 and 1992, the stretch of the Lim that enters and leaves Serbia and Bosnia left several Serbian villages physically cut off from the rest of the republic. The governments in Belgrade and Sarajevo proposed an exchange of territory, but no agreement was reached. On 4 April 2004 a bus carrying Bulgarian tourists, 34 students and 16 adults returning to Svishtov from Dubrovnik, plunged into the river near Gostun after the driver lost control on a bend. Twelve children died, and the 38 others were rescued with the help of local people.

The fertile valley of the river is called Polimlje, meaning the Lim valley, and is made up of several gorges and depressions. It is divided into three large parts, the Montenegrin, Stari Vlah and Bosnian. The region is important for fruit growing and stockbreeding, and its road and railways, notably the Belgrade-Bar railway, link Serbia with Montenegro and the Adriatic coast. Priboj is heavily industrialised, while Berane, Bijelo Polje and Prijepolje are smaller industrial centres. The Potpeć power station on the Lim and several stations on the Uvac produce electricity for Serbia.
lima: Lima lies in the valleys of the Chillón, Rímac and Lurín rivers, in the desert zone of Peru's central coast, overlooking the Pacific Ocean. The urban area covers about 800 square kilometres on mostly flat terrain, sloping gently from the shore into valleys and mountain slopes as high as 1,550 metres. The seaport and the international airport are in the neighbouring Constitutional Province of Callao, with which the city forms a contiguous urban area.

Before the Spanish founding in 1535 the three valleys were occupied by pre-Inca settlements grouped under the Lordship of Ichma, and the Maranga and Lima cultures took shape there. The sanctuary of Pachacámac, built between the third and fifteenth centuries by several civilisations, was the main pilgrimage site in Inca times. The Wari Empire conquered these cultures and built the ceremonial centre of Cajamarquilla. As Wari power declined, local cultures such as the Chancay regained autonomy, and in the fifteenth century the territory was absorbed into the Inca Empire.

The name probably comes from Limaq, meaning talker or speaker in the coastal Quechua of the area, the name of an oracle in the Rímac Valley that the Spanish destroyed and replaced with a church. The city was founded in 1535 as the City of Kings, because its foundation was decided on 6 January, the feast of the Epiphany. Francisco Pizarro built the first Government Palace, known as the House of Pizarro, that year.

Lima became the capital and most important city of the Viceroyalty of Peru, and the National University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, is the oldest continuously operating university in the New World. After José de San Martín reached the city in 1821 during the Peruvian War of Independence, it was granted the title of Heroic and Courageous City of the Free. It then became the capital of the Republic of Peru.

Lima is the capital and largest city of Peru and the seat of its three branches of government. The Historic Centre was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. It keeps colonial buildings such as the Basilica and Convent of San Francisco, the Metropolitan Cathedral and the Palacio de Torre Tagle. About a third of the country's people live in its metropolitan area.
limassol: Limassol lies on the southern coast of Cyprus, between the ancient city-kingdoms of Amathus and Kourion, both founded around 1100 BCE. Its name comes from the ancient Greek Nemessos, meaning one found in the middle, which probably refers to that position; it later became Lemesos. The historic centre is around the medieval Limassol Castle and the Old Port. Human activity in the area goes back to the Neolithic, around 7000 BCE. Ancient writers and geographers do not mention the founding of the town.

The town's history is bound up with the Third Crusade. Richard the Lionheart was travelling to the Holy Land when a storm brought the ship of his fiancée Berengaria and his sister Joan to Limassol. Isaac Komnenos, the renegade Byzantine governor of Cyprus, called the noblewomen ashore, intending to hold them for ransom. When they refused, he denied them fresh water, and they put out to sea. Richard took Isaac captive when he arrived, and the Anglo-Normans took over the island, ending the long Byzantine dominion of Cyprus. Richard married Berengaria on Cyprus, and the castle is the traditional site of the wedding, held in 1191.

Queen Catherine Cornaro sold Cyprus to Venice in 1489. The Venetians wanted chiefly to tax the island, and travellers of the 16th century remarked on the poor condition of the local people. The Ottomans took Limassol and its castle in 1538, and the Venetian governor, after retaking it, ordered it demolished to prevent its seizure, which was completed in 1567 and 1568. The Ottomans invaded Cyprus in 1570 and took Limassol in July without resistance. They built a new fort on the remains of the castle in 1590, whose cells were used as a prison until 1950.

The British took over the administration of Cyprus in 1878. Their first governor of Limassol, Colonel Warren, had the roads cleaned and repaired, docks built for loading ships anchored offshore and trees planted. Lanterns lit the centre from the 1880s, and electricity replaced them in 1912. After the 1974 Turkish invasion the Turkish Cypriot inhabitants moved north, and many Greek Cypriot refugees settled in the city.

Limassol is the second-largest urban area in Cyprus and its main port, a role that passed to it from Famagusta in 1974. Armenians live around the Sourp Kevork church, and the Laniteio Lyceum, founded in 1819 as the Greek School, is the oldest lyceum in the city. The ruins of Amathus, with its Temple of Aphrodite, lie about 11 kilometres to the east. Kolossi Castle, built by the Knights Hospitaller in the 13th century and rebuilt in 1454, stands about 11 kilometres to the west.
limbazi: Limbaži is a town in the Vidzeme region of northern Latvia, about 90 km north-east of Riga, with a population of 6,888. The name is believed to be a Latvianised form of the Livonian word Lembsel, meaning a wide isle in a forest swamp, and the German name Lemsahl comes from the same source. A folk etymology tells that in the 17th century a newly arrived Swedish minister heard the Latvian words limba and āži, meaning male goats, and took them for the name of the place.

In ancient times the site was a Livonian settlement called Lemisele, part of Metsepole. In the early 13th century Bishop Albert and the Teutonic knights destroyed the village while conquering Metsepole and built a castle, around which the new town of Lemsahl formed. Until the start of the 16th century seagoing vessels could reach it up the Svētupe, and ships from as far as Lübeck and Copenhagen came for honey, wax, lumber, grain and furs. The town joined the Hanseatic League, held an annual conference of barons from all over Livonia and at least three fairs a year, and served the Archbishops of Riga as a spring residence. Walled to protect both the archbishop and the market, it was second only to Riga in population.

By 1500 the Svētupe had become too shallow to navigate, trade moved elsewhere and a century of decline began. During the Livonian War the forces of Ivan the Terrible burned the town in 1558, the Swedes burned it in 1567 and the Russians again in 1575. In 1602 Swedes and Poles fought over it and demolished its fortifications and walls, and when the wars ended only three houses and a handful of residents remained. Under Swedish rule it was renamed Limbaži. A fire destroyed the town again in 1747, after which its present layout began to develop.

The town grew again in the 19th century, from 674 inhabitants in 1821 to about 2,000 by 1900, helped by the hat-maker A. Tīls, who opened the felt company Limbažu filcs in 1876. A railway to Riga opened in 1934. Germany occupied the town from 4 July 1941 until 26 September 1944, and in the Soviet period it became a factory town with a farm machinery works, the felt factory and a large dairy. The remains of the old town wall, the ruins of the Archbishop's castle, the Livonian hill-fort at Ķezberkalns and St John's Lutheran Church survive, and the composer Kārlis Baumanis, who wrote the Latvian national anthem, is buried there.
limerick: Limerick, in Irish Luimneach, lies at the head of the Shannon Estuary, where the river widens before it flows into the Atlantic Ocean. The name originally referred to the general area along the banks of the estuary, known as Loch Luimnigh. The historic core of the city stands on King's Island, which is bounded by the Shannon and the Abbey River. To the south lies the Golden Vale, an area of rich pastureland whose produce long supplied much of the city's industry.

The earliest settlement on King's Island was called Inis Sibhtonn. The island was also known as Inis an Ghaill Duibh, 'The Dark Foreigner's Island', and Viking sources record the name as Hlymrekr. Vikings made the place a maritime trading port, and its position on the Shannon gave it access to the midlands of Ireland and to the north and west. King John's Castle dates from 1210 and St Mary's Cathedral from 1168.

By the 18th century, with the opening of canals across Ireland, Limerick Port had become the premier commercial port on the western side of the country. The Grand Canal gave further access to Dublin and the east, and goods travelled regularly by water between Limerick and Dublin until river transport declined in the 20th century. In 1620 the English-born judge Luke Gernon, then living in the city, wrote that at his first sight of it he had been struck by its lofty buildings of marble, like the Colleges in Oxford.

In the first decade of the 20th century a small Jewish community in the city was the target of an economic boycott that lasted more than two years. Instigated in 1904 by a Redemptorist priest, Father John Creagh, it was accompanied by assaults, stone-throwing and intimidation, which caused many Jews to leave Limerick.

Limerick is the centre of the Mid-West region. Its institutions of higher education include the University of Limerick and Mary Immaculate College, and technical education there traces its beginning to the Limerick Athenaeum Society of 1852. The Treaty Stone, King John's Castle and the Hunt Museum are among its sights. The humorous five-line verse called a limerick has an obscure connection with the city; the earliest known use of the name for it is from 1880, in a newspaper of Saint John, New Brunswick.
limmat: The Limmat is a river in Switzerland that begins at the outfall of Lake Zurich, in the southern part of the city of Zurich, and flows north-west for a further 35 km until it reaches the Aare. The confluence lies north of the small town of Brugg, shortly after the mouth of the Reuss. The main towns downstream of Zurich are Dietikon, Wettingen and Baden. The river's main tributaries are the Linth, the Wägitaler Aa and the Jona, all of which enter via Lake Zurich, the Sihl in Zurich and the Reppisch in Dietikon.

The name is first recorded in the 8th century as Lindimacus. It is of Gaulish origin, from lindo, meaning lake, and magos, meaning plain, and was probably first the name of the plain formed by the Linth.

Historically the Limmat was an important navigation route. Voyages from Zurich to Koblenz are recorded in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In 1447 Emperor Frederick III granted Zurich the privilege of free navigation on the Limmat and on the Rhine. Because of the current, boats usually travelled downstream only, and the barges were sold on arrival. The traditional boat of the river is the weidling, a flat-bottomed vessel usually about 10 metres long.

Prehistoric pile dwellings stood on the marshy land between the Limmat and Lake Zurich, on small islands and peninsulas around what is now Sechseläutenplatz. The settlements at Alpenquai in Enge, Kleiner Hafner and Grosser Hafner lay at the outflow of the river, on piles that protected them from occasional flooding by the Linth and Jona. Alpenquai is one of the 56 Swiss sites of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps.

Like many Swiss rivers, the Limmat is intensively used for hydroelectric power: its fall along the 35 km of its course feeds no fewer than ten power stations. Today the river is navigable for much of its length by small craft only, and many of the power plants have boat lifts. The uppermost stretch through the centre of Zurich can take larger vessels, though low bridges limit them, and a boat service runs there from the Landesmuseum to Lake Zurich.
limoges: Little is known of settlement before the Romans. They founded the city around 10 BCE as Augustoritum, the second part of the name being Gaulish for ford, as part of Augustus's reorganisation of the province. The Roman city had an amphitheatre measuring 136 by 115 metres, a theatre, a forum, baths and several sanctuaries, and it had a Senate and a currency of its own. Saint Martial is said to have evangelised it around 250. In the late 3rd century, as Germanic invasions made life unsafe, the population withdrew to a site that was easier to fortify, the modern Puy Saint-Étienne.

From the 11th century the Abbey of St. Martial and its large library made Limoges an artistic centre, home to a school of medieval music composition. In the 13th century the town, ruled by its bishops, and the castle, with its abbey, stood as two fortified settlements, sometimes at odds. In 1370 Edward of Woodstock, the Black Prince, occupied the town and massacred some 300 residents. The two settlements were united in 1792, and during the French Revolution the population destroyed the abbey of St. Martial among other religious buildings.

Limoges is known for its crafts. Enamels from the city were exported throughout the Christian world from the 12th century, and the discovery of kaolin near Saint-Yrieix-la-Perche in the 18th century began its porcelain industry. Leather work also settled along the banks of the Vienne, and luxury shoes, gloves and bags are still made in Limoges and Saint-Junien. The city has a tradition of voting on the left and of workers' movements; the Confédération Générale du Travail, the first French confederation of workers, was created there in 1895, and strikes in 1905 led to barricades and the death of a young porcelain worker, Camille Vardelle.

The Gothic cathedral of Saint-Étienne was begun in 1273 and finished only in 1888. The crypt of Saint Martial, of the 10th century, was found in the 1960s during building work, and remains of the Gallo-Roman amphitheatre, one of the largest in ancient Gaul, survive. During the Second World War many Jews from Alsace were evacuated to the area, and Limoges was liberated on 21 August 1944 by the Resistance led by Colonel Georges Guingouin, without fighting. The city has held the label City of Art and History since 2008 and joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in 2017.
lin-biao: Lin Biao was born into a prosperous merchant family in Huanggang, Hubei, with the name Lin Yurong. His father's small handicrafts factory closed because of heavy taxes imposed by local militarists, and his father then worked as a purser on a river steamship. Lin moved to Shanghai in 1919 to continue his schooling but preferred student movements to formal study. In 1925 he took part in the May Thirtieth Movement and enrolled at the newly founded Whampoa Military Academy in Guangzhou, where he studied under Zhou Enlai and admired the academy's principal, Chiang Kai-shek.

After the split between the Kuomintang and the Communists, Lin served in the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 1927 and in 1928 joined Mao Zedong and Zhu De in the Jiangxi–Fujian Soviet, where he became one of Mao's closest supporters and commanded the First Army Group. In September 1937, as commander of the 115th Division of the 8th Route Army, he organised the ambush at Pingxingguan, one of the few early Chinese successes against Japan. In 1938 a sharpshooter of Yan Xishan's army wounded him in the head after he rode out alone in a captured Japanese uniform, and he suffered ill health for the rest of his life.

After 1945 Lin commanded the Communist forces in Manchuria, which were well equipped with captured Japanese material handed over by the Soviets. Having taken Manchuria, he commanded over a million soldiers in the Pingjin Campaign, and General Fu Zuoyi agreed on 22 January 1949 to surrender Beijing, which the People's Liberation Army occupied on 31 January. Lin then crossed the Yangtze in spring 1949 and by the end of the year had occupied all Kuomintang positions on the mainland, the last being Hainan. He was Vice Premier from 1954, a Vice Chairman of the party from 1958 and Minister of National Defense in 1959.

In 1966, after President Liu Shaoqi was denounced, Lin became the party's only Vice Chairman and Mao's designated successor, and in April 1969 the party constitution recorded his future succession. He died on 13 September 1971 when an aircraft carrying him and members of his family crashed near Öndörkhaan, Mongolia. The official Chinese account says he fled after a failed coup attempt, called Project 571; other accounts hold that he fled fearing an imminent purge, and some name his son Lin Liguo as the plan's originator. Everyone on board died. Within a month over 1,000 senior military officials were purged, and the incident ended the myth within the party that Mao had always been correct.
lincoln-england: Lincoln is a cathedral city and the county town of Lincolnshire. It lies on the River Witham, which widens into the natural lake of Brayford Pool and flows through the Lincoln Gap in an escarpment known as the Lincoln Cliff. The city is divided informally into an uphill zone, on Castle Hill, and a downhill zone beside the river. Its name probably comes from the Brythonic word lindon, the pool, which was Latinised as Lindum, with the title Colonia added when army veterans settled there.

Archaeologists discovered in 1972 the remains of an Iron Age settlement of round wooden dwellings, dated to the 1st century BCE, built by Brayford Pool at the foot of the hill. The Romans conquered this part of Britain in 48 CE and built a legionary fortress on the hill, overlooking the pool and the northern end of the Fosse Way. Germanic peoples settled Lincolnshire in the 5th and 6th centuries, and the Latin name shrank in Old English to Lindocolina and then Lincylene.

In 1141, during the Anarchy, Lincoln was the site of a battle between King Stephen and the forces of Empress Matilda, led by her half-brother Robert, Earl of Gloucester. After fierce fighting in the streets Stephen's forces were defeated and he was captured and taken to Bristol. The cathedral was built after the see moved from Dorchester-on-Thames, within a walled close facing the castle, and was completed in 1092. It was rebuilt after a fire, and the 1185 East Midlands earthquake damaged it. The rebuilt minster had a central spire reputedly 160 metres high, widely accepted to have succeeded the Great Pyramid as the tallest man-made structure in the world.

Historians disagree about whether the city's fortunes declined from the 14th century, or whether it stayed buoyant in trade and communications well into the 15th. In 1409 it became a county corporate, the County of the City of Lincoln. Its fortunes revived in the Georgian era with the Agricultural Revolution, and the reopening of the Foss Dyke canal in 1745 eased the import of coal and other raw materials.

Lincoln was an engineering centre. William Foster & Co. designed and built the first tanks there in the First World War, testing them on land that is now Tritton Road, and Ruston and Hornsby later made diesel engines and gas turbines. During the typhoid outbreak of 1904 and 1905, which killed 113 people, Dr Alexander Cruickshank Houston installed a chlorine disinfection system, an early use of chlorine to treat a water supply. The cathedral, the Norman castle and the medieval Bishop's Palace draw visitors, and the University of Lincoln is based in the city.
lincolnshire: Lincolnshire is a ceremonial county covering 6,959 square kilometres, the second largest in England. It is bordered by the Humber estuary to the north, the North Sea to the east and several other counties to the south and west. The south-east contains part of the Fens, a naturally marshy region drained for agriculture, and the south-west is an upland region. A wide vale runs north to south from the centre of the county, and to its east the chalk hills of the Lincolnshire Wolds rise in the north-east, with a coastal plain and the Lincolnshire Marsh beyond.

The west of the vale is marked by the Lincolnshire Edge, a long escarpment, and the River Trent forms part of the western border. The county's main towns are Lincoln, Grimsby, Scunthorpe, Boston and Grantham.

Before the Roman conquest most of Lincolnshire was inhabited by the Corieltauvi, whose language would have been Common Brittonic. In the Roman period Lincoln was a major settlement known as Lindum Colonia, from which its name derives. In the fifth century the area was settled by Angles, who established the Kingdom of Lindsey in the north of the region.

Lincoln became the centre of a diocese in 1072, and Lincoln Cathedral was built over the following centuries. The late Middle Ages were a prosperous period: wealth from the wool trade paid for grand wool churches such as St Botolph's Church in Boston. The county has been described as having a comparatively quiet history, since it was predominantly rural, not heavily industrialised and faced limited external threats.

The Local Government Act 1888 established county councils for each of the three parts of Lincolnshire, Lindsey, Holland and Kesteven, which came into effect on 1 April 1889. Lincoln became an independent county borough on the same date, and Grimsby followed in 1891. During the Second World War the flat landscape made the county an important base for the Royal Air Force, which built nearly seventy air bases there and gave Lincolnshire the nickname Bomber County.

Lincolnshire remains predominantly rural and a long-standing agricultural area, growing wheat, barley, sugar beet and oilseed rape, with potatoes, cabbages and onions in the rich soils of the south. Its people are sometimes nicknamed Yellowbellies, a term most often thought to derive from the yellow facings of the uniform of the 10th Regiment of Foot, later the Lincolnshire Regiment. The folk song The Lincolnshire Poacher, dating from around 1776, serves as the county's unofficial anthem.
linderhof-palace: Linderhof lies about 10 km west of the village of Ettal in south-west Bavaria and is the smallest of the three palaces of King Ludwig II of Bavaria. Ludwig knew the area from his youth, when he accompanied his father Maximilian II on hunting trips. On becoming king in 1864 he inherited a hunting lodge, the Königshäuschen, and in 1869 began enlarging it. In 1874 he decided to demolish it and rebuild it at its present place in the park, adding three new rooms and the staircase and cladding the wooden exterior in stone. The building follows the style of the second rococo. A total of 8,460,937 marks was spent on Linderhof between 1863 and 1886.

Linderhof was inspired by the palace of Louis XIV, whom Ludwig took as an idol, and its style follows the mid-18th-century rococo of Louis XV, being based more directly on the Petit Trianon. The sun is a motif of the decoration and stands for the French idea of absolutism, which Ludwig saw as the ideal of a God-given monarchy but which the constitution of Bavaria did not allow. The palace has a private atmosphere, with only four rooms of real function. The Hall of Mirrors was a drawing room where Ludwig read through the night.

The dining room has a table on a lifting platform, called Tischlein deck dich, so that he could dine without servants, although the table was laid for four, since he is said to have talked to imaginary guests such as Louis XV and Marie Antoinette. The bedroom, the largest chamber, faces north, which reflects his image of himself as a Night-King, since he turned night into day. It was completely rebuilt in 1884 and could not be finished before his death two years later.

The park, laid out by the Court Garden Director Carl von Effner, combines formal Renaissance and Baroque gardens with landscaped sections like an English garden. The Venus Grotto, built between 1875 and 1877 under the opera set designer August Dirigl, is an iron construction covered in canvas and cement, made as an illustration of the first act of Wagner's Tannhäuser. It had a lake, a waterfall and a wave machine, and in 1878 dynamos driven by a steam engine were installed by Johann Sigmund Schuckert to light it. Hunding's Hut was inspired by Wagner's Die Walküre. In 2025 the palace was designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO.
lindisfarne: Lindisfarne lies close to the border with Scotland. It measures 4.8 kilometres from east to west and 2.4 kilometres from north to south and covers about 400 hectares at high tide. At its nearest point it is 1.3 kilometres from the mainland. It can be reached at low tide by a modern causeway and by an ancient pilgrims' path across the sand and mudflats, both covered by water at high tide. About one vehicle each month is stranded on the causeway. The island is surrounded by the Lindisfarne National Nature Reserve, which protects its dunes and tidal habitats, and by 2016 some 330 bird species had been recorded there.

The north-east of England was little affected by Roman rule and was raided by Scots and Picts. The Anglian king Ida, who reigned from 547, began the settlement of the coast by sea and made Bamburgh his royal settlement. The Historia Brittonum tells how Urien, prince of Rheged, with a coalition of North Brittonic kingdoms, besieged the Angles of Theodric of Bernicia on the island for three days and nights, until internal quarrels led to the Britons' defeat. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 793 records the Old English name Lindisfarena, while the Historia Brittonum gives the Old Welsh name Medcaut.

Irish monks founded a monastery on the island, and it stood for roughly 900 years. Under Saints Aidan, Cuthbert, Eadfrith and Eadberht it was an important centre of Celtic Christianity. The monastery was destroyed during the Viking invasions and was re-established as a smaller priory after the Norman Conquest. Monastic records from the 14th to the 16th century show a well-established fishing economy that supplied the community and the mother house at Durham with fish, and the monks also ran a lime kiln. After Henry VIII suppressed the priory, his troops used its remains as a naval store, and Lindisfarne Castle was built in 1550 on the hill called Beblowe, partly with stone from the priory.

The parish church of St Mary the Virgin stands on the site of the wooden church of Aidan, and its chancel wall and arch survive from the Anglo-Saxon church. It was restored in 1860. St Cuthbert's Isle, or Hobthrush, a small islet reached on foot at low tide, is reputed to be where Cuthbert spent the beginning of his solitary life, and has the remains of a medieval chapel. At Green Shiel, on the north coast, excavation found the stone foundations of an early medieval farmstead dated to the 9th century. Holy Island parish had 151 residents at the 2021 census, and the island is the eastern end of the St Cuthbert's Way long-distance path.
lindisfarne-gospels: The Lindisfarne Gospels were produced in the monastery at Lindisfarne, off the coast of Northumberland, and are presumed to be the work of a monk named Eadfrith, who became bishop of Lindisfarne in 698 and died in 721. The book was made in honour of God and Saint Cuthbert, who died on 20 March 687, and some parts were left unfinished, so Eadfrith was probably still working on it when he died.

In the 10th century Aldred, a priest of the monastery at Chester-le-Street, recorded in a colophon four men who made the book: Eadfrith wrote it, Ethelwald, bishop of the Lindisfarne islanders, bound it, the anchorite Billfrith ornamented it, and Aldred himself glossed it. The work took about five to ten years and used roughly 150 calf skins for its 516 pages.

The manuscript contains the four Gospels in Latin. It opens with a carpet page in the form of a cross and a major initial page for the letter of Saint Jerome to Pope Damasus I, followed by sixteen pages of canon tables. A portrait of the Evangelist, a carpet page and a decorated initial page precede each Gospel. Following Bede, each Evangelist has his own symbol: Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the calf and John the eagle.

The art is Insular, combining Mediterranean, Anglo-Saxon and Celtic elements, with interlaced animals and birds, spirals and knotwork. Eadfrith made 90 of his own colours from six local minerals and vegetable extracts. The blue, long thought to be ultramarine from Afghanistan, was found by Raman microscopy in the 2000s to be indigo.

The Old English gloss that Aldred inserted between the lines about 250 years after the book was made is the oldest extant translation of the Gospels into English. Because of Viking raids the monastic community left Lindisfarne around 875, taking Cuthbert's body and its books, and settled at Chester-le-Street.

The original jewelled binding was lost, and a new one was made in 1852 by Smith, Nicholson and Co. for Bishop Edward Maltby. After the Dissolution of the Monasteries the book passed to Sir Robert Cotton in the early 17th century, and in 1753 it became part of the founding collections of the British Museum. It is now in the British Library. When it was displayed at Palace Green Library in Durham in 2013, nearly 100,000 visitors saw it.
linear-a: Linear A consists of over 300 signs, counting regional variants and signs that occur only once, with a core group of about 90 that occur with some frequency. It is a logosyllabic system: some signs stand for syllables, others for words or concepts, and signs could be combined as ligatures. Numerals follow a decimal system, with vertical dashes for units, horizontal dashes for tens, circles for hundreds and circles with rays for thousands, and special signs for fractions and weights. It was usually written left to right. Arthur Evans named it Linear because its characters are simple lines in clay, unlike the more pictographic Cretan hieroglyphs.

The corpus is small: roughly 1400 inscriptions, amounting to 7400 sign tokens. Roughly half were found at Hagia Triada in southern Crete, with others from Zakros, Khania, Phaistos, Knossos and Palaikastro, and a few at sites such as Mycenae, Argos and Miletus. Most tablets come from the Neopalatial Period. Seals and clay sealings served for inventory control and ownership. About 1000 stone libation tables have been recovered at 27 Cretan sites, 41 of them with Linear A inscriptions that follow a standard libation formula. Short marks also appear on pots and as mason's marks.

Linear A probably descends from Cretan hieroglyphic, though the two were used together for much of the Middle Minoan period. During the Late Minoan I period it became the chief Minoan script. Much of the surviving corpus comes from the final decades of Late Minoan IB, when fires that destroyed Minoan towns about 1450 BCE baked clay tablets that would otherwise have been reused. After the destructions the script was never again used for administration, and a new system using Linear B arose after a gap of 50 to 75 years.

No text has been deciphered since the script was rediscovered in 1900. Approximate sound values for most syllabic signs are inferred from Linear B, which was deciphered in the 1950s as Mycenaean Greek. Some sign sequences name places and people, for example the Linear A toponym read pa-i-to, matching Phaistos in Linear B. These values are widely accepted but not incontrovertible, and they yield words that cannot be interpreted.

The corpus is small, with about 6000 inscriptions available for Linear B, and the texts are brief and repetitive, mostly lists of a name, a logogram and a numeral. No bilingual inscription exists. The underlying language, called Minoan as a placeholder, appears not to be a close relative of any known language. Internal analysis suggests it was agglutinative; the word ku-ro, found at the end of tallied lists, means total. The standard compendium of inscriptions, GORILA, appeared between 1976 and 1985, and a project from 2020 aims to put all inscriptions online.
linear-b: Linear B is a syllabic script used to write Mycenaean Greek, the earliest attested form of the Greek language, and it predates the Greek alphabet by several centuries. It was adapted from the earlier Linear A, an undeciphered script perhaps used for the Minoan language. The oldest tablets are probably those from the Room of Chariot Tablets at Knossos, dating to the latter half of the 15th century BCE. The earliest inscription from the mainland is a clay tablet found at Iklaina, dated to between 1400 and 1350 BCE. The script disappeared with the fall of the Mycenaean civilisation, and the Greek Dark Ages that followed provide no conclusive evidence of writing.

The script has roughly 200 signs, of two kinds: about 87 syllabic signs with phonetic values and over 100 ideograms that stand for objects or commodities. The ideograms have no phonetic value and are never used as word signs within a sentence. They typically stand at the end of a line before a number and show what the number counts, and they also express units of measure. The syllabic signs are of the type vowel or consonant plus vowel, and lengths of vowels and accents are not marked. Each sign may stand for a variety of about 70 distinct combinations of sounds, so the transcription is an approximation.

Tablets are of two shapes: palm-leaf tablets, which typically record a single transaction, and larger page-shaped tablets, which summarise several. Some 6,058 inscriptions are known, including about 170 on vessels, chiefly stirrup jars found at Thebes, Mycenae, Tiryns and Khania. Writing was mostly confined to administration at palace sites. A relatively small number of scribes has been detected in the handwriting: 45 at Pylos and 66 at Knossos. The tablets record disbursements of goods such as wool, sheep and grain, often given to groups of religious people, and some deal with military matters. Fires that destroyed the palaces baked many tablets and so preserved them.

Arthur Evans was given a Cretan sealstone with writing in 1886 and found the script at Knossos in 1894. Early attempts at decipherment by Florence Stawell, F. G. Gordon and Bedřich Hrozný did not succeed. Alice Kober showed that the language was inflected, demonstrated the existence of three grammatical cases, and held that each sign stood for a syllable. Emmett L. Bennett Jr. devised the numbering of the signs still in use and showed that the Pylos tablets carried the same script as those of Knossos. Michael Ventris, an English architect and self-taught linguist, deciphered Linear B in 1952, building on Kober's research. It is the only Bronze Age Aegean script to have been deciphered.
lingam: The word lingam appears in the Upanishads and epic literature, where it means a mark, sign, emblem or characteristic, and the evidence or proof of Shiva and his power. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad says that Shiva, the Supreme Lord, has no linga, meaning that he is beyond any characteristic, including gender. The word also occurs in early Indian logic, where an inference rests on a sign, and in early Sanskrit medical texts, where it means a symptom.

The word is not found in the Rigveda or the other Vedas, though Rudra, a proto-Shiva, is. John Marshall and Ernest Mackay proposed that Harappan artefacts show yoni-linga worship in the Indus Valley civilisation, but Encyclopædia Britannica states that there is no evidence the people there worshipped such objects as lingams. One account traces the worship of the lingam to an Atharva Veda hymn to the sacrificial post, the Yupa-Stambha, which in time gave way to the Shiva-linga. The Gudimallam Lingam, still worshipped at Gudimallam, is mostly dated to the 3rd to 1st century BCE and carries a figure of Lakulisha on its front.

A lingam is usually a short cylindrical pillar of stone, metal, gem, wood or clay, often set in a disc-shaped base, the yoni, which carries away liquid offerings. Styles include the mukhalingam, carved with the face of Shiva, and lingams with 108 or 1,001 miniature lingas cut on the main one. Shaiva Agama texts describe how one should be made. Scholars such as Wendy Doniger view the lingam as developed from a phallic symbol, while Shaivas regard it as the outward symbol of formless reality, and with the yoni as the union of the feminine and masculine that recreates all existence. The Linga Purana says Shiva is signless, and that the universe is the manifested linga.

The lingam is typically the main image in Hindu temples of Shiva. Rituals include offerings of flowers, grass, rice, fruits, leaves and water and a milk bath, while priests chant hymns and devotees view the sanctum and walk clockwise around it. Pilgrimage sites include about 70 self-manifested natural lingams, the most significant at Kashi, followed by Prayaga, Naimisha and Gaya, and the ice lingam of Amarnath, which forms each winter in a cave.

Lingayats, a Shaivite tradition that arose in Karnataka around the 12th century, wear a miniature lingam, the istalinga, in a box on a necklace. Each day the devotee takes it out, offers puja and meditates on becoming one with the linga. After the Muslim conquests of the 11th century, several sultans of Delhi, often iconoclastic, ordered lingas destroyed, and in some places they were laid at mosque thresholds.
lingua-franca: The term comes from the Mediterranean Lingua Franca, also called Sabir, a pidgin used around the Levant and the eastern Mediterranean as the main language of commerce and diplomacy from the late Middle Ages to the 18th century, most notably in the Renaissance. It was a simplified speech based mainly on Italian in the east and Spanish in the west, with many loanwords from Greek, Slavic languages, Arabic and Turkish. Some scholars claim it was only poorly used Italian. Lingua means a language in Italian, and franca means Frankish, since in the late Byzantine Empire Franks was a term for all Western Europeans. The name is first recorded in English in the 1670s, with an earlier use in 1632.

A lingua franca is any language regularly used for communication between people who do not share a native language, whatever its history or structure. It may be a pidgin, a creole, or an established language learned as a second language, such as the colonial languages used between diverse communities in former colonies. Pidgins are rapidly developed and simplified combinations of languages with few or no native speakers, while creoles develop from pidgins into fully complex languages with native speakers. A vernacular is the native language of a geographical community, whereas a lingua franca is used beyond its original community, for trade, religion, politics or scholarship. International auxiliary languages such as Esperanto have not been widely adopted and are not described as lingua francas.

Since the 16th century, as European colonisation made pidgins widely known, the term has shifted from the name of one language to a general term for pidgins, creoles and other vehicular languages. Lingua francas have existed since antiquity. Akkadian served much of Western Asia until Aramaic replaced it, and Sanskrit was adopted in Southeast and Central Asia in the 1st millennium CE through monks, pilgrims and merchants. Literary Chinese was the written and diplomatic language of East Asia until the early 20th century. Koine Greek spread after the conquests of Alexander the Great, and Latin remained the language of science and scholarship in Europe until well into the 18th century.
linux: Unix was conceived in 1969 at AT&T's Bell Labs, first released in 1971 and rewritten in the C programming language by Dennis Ritchie in 1973, which made it easier to port. Because a 1956 antitrust case forbade AT&T to enter the computer business, it gave the source code to anyone who asked, and Unix spread through universities and businesses. In 1984, freed of that obligation, Bell Labs began selling it as a proprietary product users were not legally allowed to modify.

In response the GNU Project, started in 1983 by Richard Stallman, aimed to create a complete Unix-compatible system made entirely of free software. By the early 1990s many of its programs were finished, but its kernel, GNU Hurd, was stalled. Minix, released in 1987 for teaching, had a licence that kept it from being free software until April 2000, and the first entirely free Unix for personal computers, 386BSD, appeared only in 1992.

Linus Torvalds created the Linux kernel because GNU lacked a working one, and first released it on 17 September 1991. Like GNU and 386BSD it contained no Unix code, so it avoided legal problems with AT&T. It is distributed under the copyleft GNU General Public License, and anyone may use, modify and distribute the source code, commercially or not, which makes creating a new distribution easier than for macOS or Microsoft Windows.

A distribution packages the kernel with software developed by others, such as GNU and X.Org; Debian, Fedora and Ubuntu are examples. The Free Software Foundation recommends the name GNU/Linux, a usage that is controversial. Distributions became popular in the 1990s and made Unix technologies accessible to home users on personal computers, where before they had been confined to sophisticated workstations.

Originally written for x86 personal computers, the kernel has been ported to more platforms than any other operating system. Linux runs on all of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers, and Android uses a Linux-based kernel. Eric S. Raymond saw the revolutionary aspect of Linux as social: huge numbers of volunteers coordinated through the Internet, and quality was kept by releasing every week and gathering feedback from hundreds of users within days.
lipari: Lipari lies in a volcanic archipelago between Vesuvius and Etna, 30 kilometres from Sicily, and covers 89.72 square kilometres. Its highest point is Monte Chirica at 602 metres. The comune of Lipari includes six of the seven Aeolian Islands and belongs administratively to the Metropolitan City of Messina. The fortified acropolis rises above the main town, and the large archaeological museum covers the history of the islands from prehistoric to classical times.

In Neolithic times Lipari was, like Sardinia, one of the few centres of trade in obsidian, a volcanic glass prized for its sharp edges. People may have lived there as early as 5000 BCE, and local legend names a leader called Liparus, who came from Campania. In the early Bronze Age settlers of Aeolian origin came from Mycenaean Greece and used the islands as outposts to control trade through the strait of Messina. In the 13th century BCE Ausonian peoples from Campania arrived, and an Ausonian site was burned in the late 9th century BCE and apparently not rebuilt.

Greek colonists from Knidos reached Lipara around 580 BCE after their first attempt to settle in Sicily failed and their leader Pentathlos was killed. The colony fought the Etruscans successfully for control of the Tyrrhenian Sea, and the town grew from the rocky acropolis to the foot of its slopes and the Civita hill, with walls built in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. Carthaginian forces held it briefly in 394 BCE, and Agathokles took it by treachery in 304 BCE.

In the First Punic War Lipara was a Carthaginian naval base until it fell to Rome in 252–251 BCE. Under the Roman Empire it was a place of retreat and exile, valued for its thermal baths.
