In 839 Saracen raiders slaughtered much of the population and the island was eventually almost abandoned. The Normans repopulated it and reinstated its bishopric in 1131. In 1544 the Ottoman admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa ransacked Lipari and enslaved its entire population, some of whom were ransomed at Messina. Charles V then had Spanish subjects resettle the island and build, in 1556, the walls that still stand on the old acropolis.
lippe-river: The Lippe is a river in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, and a right tributary of the Rhine. It is 220.3 km long, with an elevation difference of 125 metres and a catchment area of 4.890 km². The source lies at the edge of the Teutoburg Forest in Bad Lippspringe, close to Paderborn. The river runs westward through Paderborn and Lippstadt, then along the northern edge of the Ruhr area, parallel to the Emscher and the Ruhr, and finally enters the Rhine at Wesel. Its towns include Wesel, Dorsten, Marl, Lünen and Haltern, and its cities Paderborn, Lippstadt and Hamm.

In Roman times the river, called Lupia, was a gateway to Germania, running from the Rhine to the region around Paderborn. It carried supplies, and many Roman camps stood along its banks. Over the last 200 years many have been identified, above all the camp at Haltern, likely the headquarters of the imperial prince Tiberius. The camps lay about a day's walk apart for the troops, almost 30 km. Those identified are Olfen, Xanten, Haltern, Oberaden, Holsterhausen, Anreppen and Beckinghausen. The Battle of the Lupia River was fought in 11 BCE between Nero Claudius Drusus and the Sicambri.

The Lippe was partly navigable from 1820, but not enough for the transport of industrial goods. The landscape changed with the Cologne-Minden trunk line of the 1840s, which linked Rhine cities with the Weser harbours and the Lippe town of Hamm, and supported the coal and steel industry of the northern Ruhr. Hard coal mining, begun in the middle of the 19th century in the Emscher area, spread north into the Lippe catchment, and from the 1860s mining subsidence and polluted drainage became problems. Hamm, Lünen, Haltern and Dorsten, small settlements, expanded with new mines from about 1900.

Industrial pollution led to the founding of water boards, the Sesekegenossenschaft in 1913 and the Lippeverband in 1926. The Datteln-Hamm Canal (1914) and the Wesel-Datteln Canal (1930) run parallel to the river, which is not navigable for mass transport, and exchange water with it. Upstream of Hamm the catchment is more rural, and downstream settlement and industry mark it. Water pollution played little part in public debate until the 1970s; environmental standards, above all from the EU, have since led to efforts to improve the river's condition.
lippstadt: Lippstadt lies in the valley of the river Lippe in North Rhine-Westphalia, about 60 kilometres east of Dortmund and 30 kilometres west of Paderborn. Its historic centre stands between several branches of the river. It is the largest town in the district of Soest. The town was founded by Bernhard II zur Lippe. In the early 13th century it had a population of 2,700 and four parish churches, and an Augustinian abbey is recorded there from 1281.

From 1400 the enclave and town of Lippstadt were a condominium shared by the county of Lippe and the counts of Cleves-Mark, who were succeeded by the Hohenzollerns of Brandenburg and Prussia. This arrangement lasted until the middle of the 19th century. Heinrich von Ahaus founded one of his communities for women of the Brethren of the Common Life there. In 1523 the town formed a defensive alliance with the neighbouring cities of Osnabrück, Dortmund, Soest and Münster.

Augustinians who had studied at the University of Wittenberg brought Martin Luther's teaching home, and in 1524 their prior Westermann preached Lutheran doctrines in Lippstadt. The town was among the first to embrace Lutheranism officially, though it resisted the rise of Calvinism in the rural areas of Westphalia. In 1821 a papal bull gave the Lippian parishes of Cappel, Lipperode and Lippstadt, formerly under the Archbishopric of Cologne, to the Bishopric of Paderborn. In 1851 the whole town, until then divided between the Kingdom of Prussia and Lippe, was added to the Prussian province of Westphalia.

In 1944 a women's subcamp of Buchenwald was set up in Lippstadt, and after World War II the town was the site of a displaced persons camp. On 1 April 1945 the US 2nd Armored Division met the 3rd Armored Division there, joining the US Ninth Army with the First Army, and seized the town against scattered resistance.

Lippstadt is the headquarters of the automotive supplier Hella and has a factory of the bearing maker Rothe Erde. Among its natives are the Jewish mathematician and historian David Gans (1541–1613), the Catholic Bible translator Kaspar Ulenberg (1549–1617) and the theologian Anton Praetorius (1560–1613), who opposed witchcraft trials and torture.
lisbon: Lisbon lies at the mouth of the Tagus River and is the westernmost capital of a mainland European country. Its sheltered harbour in the Tagus estuary was an ideal site for an early settlement, a secure place to unload and provision trading ships. The city occupies about 100 square kilometres, and its boundaries coincide with those of the municipality. The Monsanto Forest Park takes up 10% of it. The climate is Mediterranean, with mild, rainy winters and warm to hot, dry summers.

During the Neolithic period pre-Celtic tribes built megaliths, dolmens and menhirs, some of which survive on the edge of the city. Iron Age people occupied the site of the Castelo hill from the 8th to the 6th century BCE and traded with the Phoenicians, and a Phoenician trading post stood on the southern slope of the hill. The settlement traded with inland tribes, supplying metals, salt, salted fish and Lusitanian horses. Julius Caesar made it a municipium called Felicitas Julia, adding that term to the name Olisipo.

After the fall of the Roman Empire it was ruled by Germanic tribes from the 5th century, most notably the Visigoths, and was captured by the Moors in the 8th century. Afonso Henriques conquered it in 1147, and in 1255 it replaced Coimbra as capital of Portugal. The population was about 35,000 in 1300, 70,000 by 1500 and almost 200,000 in 1700.

Lisbon is the seat of the Portuguese government, the Assembly of the Republic and the Supreme Court of Justice. Its architecture includes Romanesque, Gothic, Manueline and Baroque buildings, and its museums include the National Museum of Ancient Art, the National Coach Museum and the Gulbenkian Museum. Yellow trams, introduced in 1901, still run on the hills of the central city.
lisht: Lisht, or el-Lisht, lies on the west bank of the Nile about 65 km south of Cairo. It is a necropolis of the Twelfth Dynasty, close to the city of Itj-tawy, from which the modern village presumably takes its name. Amenemhat I, the first king of the dynasty, moved the capital from Thebes to Itj-tawy, which was close to the mouth of the Fayyum and well placed to control the Two Lands of Upper and Lower Egypt. Another suggested motive was land reclamation to increase farming output. The ruins of Itj-tawy have never been conclusively identified.

Amenemhat I and his son Senusret I were buried here, and their pyramids would have been visible to travellers approaching Itj-tawy from the south. Amenemhat's pyramid was originally about 55 m tall but, through poor construction, quarrying and tomb robbery, now stands about 20 m high. It was built of unfired mudbrick and stones taken from earlier monuments, including those of Khufu, Khafre, Unas and Pepi II. This reuse is thought to symbolise the restoration of Egypt to its Old Kingdom glory.

Senusret I built his pyramid about a mile to the south. Its base was 105 m wide and it once reached 61.25 m. Its builders raised a core of coarse limestone blocks filled with mudbrick and debris, then faced it with heavy blocks and a smooth casing of white limestone from Tureh, a technique used for much of the Middle Kingdom. The complex is the best preserved of the period. Both pyramids were flooded by Nile seepage in their burial chambers, and the tomb of Senusret I was robbed soon after it was sealed.

Smaller pyramids of royal family members and many mastabas of high officials were built around the two pyramids during the Twelfth and Thirteenth Dynasties. After the dynasty fell, the necropolis was no longer guarded and looters came.

Gaston Maspero first excavated Lisht in 1882, and French teams worked there in 1884-85 and in 1894-95. The Egyptian Expedition of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, worked at the site from 1906, and the museum returned between 1984 and 1991. Dieter Arnold excavated at the pyramid of Senusret I from 1984 to 1987. The tomb of Senebtisi was found undisturbed and yielded a set of jewellery, and the coffins in the tomb of Sesenebnef carry the earliest versions of the Book of the Dead. Statues of Senusret I from the site are in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo and the Metropolitan Museum.
lisieux: Lisieux is a commune in the Calvados department of Normandy, in north-western France, and the capital of the Pays d'Auge. The town lies at the confluence of the river Touques and its tributaries the Orbiquet, Cirieux and Graindain. The surrounding country is typical Norman hedged farmland, mixing livestock farming, mostly of milk cows, with the cultivation of cider apples, from which cider, calvados and pommeau are made.

The Latin name Noviomagus Lexoviorum means Noviomagus of the Lexovii, and the Celtic Novio Magos meant new field or new market. Lisieux was the capital of the Lexovii. Caesar mentions a Gallic oppidum in his Commentaries on the Gallic War, which has been identified at le Castellier, three kilometres south-west of the town, but the Gallo-Roman city stood where Lisieux is now. In the 4th century the Germanic laeti, auxiliaries of the Roman army, settled there with their families.

Henry II of England was staying in Lisieux when he announced his plan to marry Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152, and the town remained powerful for several centuries. Plague, war and famine devastated it in the 14th century. Pierre Cauchon, the supreme judge at the trial of Joan of Arc, became bishop of Lisieux in 1432; he commissioned a side chapel of the cathedral, where he is buried. In 1590 Henri IV took the town without force after the garrison fled. Paul Cornu made the first helicopter flight in 1907. An Allied bombardment on 6 and 7 June 1944 killed 800 people, and Allied troops liberated the town on 23 August 1944.

Lisieux has been the seat of a Roman Catholic bishopric since the Middle Ages. The bishopric was abolished in 1801 and recreated in 1855 merged with Bayeux. Devotion to Thérèse of Lisieux, a Carmelite nun who died in 1897, was canonised in 1925 and was named a doctor of the church by Pope John Paul II in 1997, has made the town one of the main places of pilgrimage in France. The basilica built in her honour draws pilgrims. Lisieux Cathedral survived the bombing of 1944 and was built between 1160 and 1230 under Bishop Arnoul, one of the first Gothic buildings in Normandy.
litani-river: The Litani rises in the fertile Beqaa Valley, west of Baalbek, and empties into the Mediterranean north of Tyre. It exceeds 140 kilometres in length and has an average annual flow estimated at 0.92 cubic kilometres. Its basin covers 2,110 square kilometres, the largest watershed in Lebanon, about 20 per cent of the country, and includes the marshes of Kafr Zabad and the Aammiq wetlands, which host nearly 250 bird species on a migration route. After flowing south parallel to the Syrian border the river bends westward, and this lower stretch is called the Qasimiyeh. Along it lies one of the largest irrigated areas of the country, where farmers grow mainly citrus and bananas.

The river is called Leontes, 'lion river', in Greek and Latin sources, and in medieval times Līṭa. Its name is thought to come from the Semitic sea serpent Ltn, a seven-headed servant of the sea god Yam, and the oldest reference to the name is in Papyrus Anastasi I. In antiquity the river marked boundaries between civilisations, including the Phoenicians and later Hellenistic and Roman authorities. The region was important for trade and agriculture, and irrigation systems were developed there in Roman times.

About 10 kilometres north of Tyre the river was crossed by the Roman Leontes Bridge, now in ruins. In June 1941 British commandos and Australian troops attacked Vichy French forces at the river's mouth in what is called the Battle of the Litani River.

From the early 1950s the river was seen as a basis for Lebanon's infrastructure, and the Litani River Authority was set up in 1954 with World Bank funding. After a first failed attempt, the dam was completed in stages from 1962 to 1966 under Henry Naccache, who had been appointed in 1960, and was named the Albert Naccache Dam after his father. It is 60 metres high and 1,350 metres long and created Lake Qaraoun. The 16-kilometre Awwali tunnel, whose first drilling in 1958 failed because of the difficult soil, was finished with the help of French experts.

The works tap a drop of 850 metres between Lake Qaraoun and the Mediterranean, and the generators produce a maximum of 185 megawatts, the largest hydroelectric project in Lebanon. The upper flows are diverted through tunnels, ponds and plants and meet the sea several kilometres north of the river's original mouth, so that the upper basin is hydrologically separate from the lower reaches. The river irrigates thousands of hectares and about 31 per cent of the income within the basin comes from agriculture.
lithium-ion-battery: One of the earliest examples of research into lithium-ion batteries was a copper fluoride and lithium battery developed by NASA in 1965. The breakthrough toward the modern battery came in 1974, when the British chemist M. Stanley Whittingham first used titanium disulfide as a cathode material. Its layered structure takes in lithium ions without significant change to the crystal.

Exxon tried to commercialise the battery in the late 1970s but found the synthesis expensive and complex, since titanium disulfide is sensitive to moisture and gives off toxic hydrogen sulfide on contact with water. The cells were also prone to catch fire spontaneously because of the metallic lithium in them, and Exxon discontinued development. The later prototype of Akira Yoshino replaced lithium metal with a carbonaceous anode.

A lithium-ion cell has an anode, a cathode, a separator, a casing, an electrolyte and a pair of current collectors. The negative electrode is typically graphite and the positive electrode a metal oxide or phosphate, while the electrolyte is a lithium salt in an organic solvent and the separator keeps the electrodes from shorting. In discharge, lithium ions carry the current through the electrolyte from the negative to the positive electrode. In charging, an external voltage forces them back to the negative electrode, where they become embedded in the porous material in a process called intercalation. Cells have a nominal voltage of 3.6 or 3.7 volts.

Different cathode materials suit different uses. Handheld electronics mostly use lithium cobalt oxide with a graphite anode, which offers high energy density, while lithium iron phosphate and lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide may offer longer life and a higher discharge rate, and the latter is widely used in the electrification of transport.

Lithium-ion batteries generally have higher specific energy, energy density and efficiency, and a longer life, than other rechargeable types. In the three decades after they were first sold in 1991, their volumetric energy density increased threefold while their cost dropped tenfold. They have enabled portable consumer electronics, laptop computers, mobile phones and electric cars, and they are used for grid-scale energy storage and in military and aerospace applications.

They carry a risk of fire or explosion because they contain flammable electrolytes, and overcharging can cause an explosion. Mining lithium is water-intensive, often in arid regions, and cobalt can be a conflict mineral, which has encouraged work on lithium iron phosphate and on sodium-ion and iron-air batteries. The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised the development of the battery.
lithography: The name comes from the Ancient Greek words for stone and for writing. Traditionally the image was drawn with a greasy substance such as oil, fat or wax on a smooth, flat limestone plate. The stone was then treated with a mixture of weak acid and gum arabic, which made the parts not protected by grease more attracted to water. For printing, the stone was moistened; the water stayed only on the etched areas, making them more oil-repellent. An oil-based ink applied next stuck only to the original drawing and was transferred to a blank sheet of paper in a press. Unlike intaglio printing, it uses a flat plate.

Senefelder had experimented with multicolour lithography in the early 19th century, and in his book of 1819 he predicted that the process would eventually be perfected to reproduce paintings. Godefroy Engelmann's chromolithography of 1837 used a separate stone for each colour, and each sheet went through the press once for every stone. The difficulty was keeping the images in register. The method suited large areas of flat colour and produced the characteristic poster designs of its period.

Lithography, or printing from soft stone, largely took the place of engraving in the production of English commercial maps after about 1852. It was quick and cheap, and had been used to print British army maps during the Peninsular War. In modern commercial work the image is made on a flexible metal or plastic plate by a photographic process, and in offset lithography a rubber cylinder carries the ink from the plate to the paper. This keeps the paper dry and allows fully automated high-speed printing.

In the early 19th century lithography had only a limited effect on printmaking, because technical difficulties remained. Engelmann, who moved his press from Mulhouse to Paris in 1816, largely resolved them, and in the 1820s artists such as Delacroix and Géricault adopted the medium. Goya made his last series of prints, The Bulls of Bordeaux, in 1828, and Daumier's lithographs were published in newspapers. Jules Chéret, called the father of the modern poster, made colour lithography a success in the 1890s, and he inspired Toulouse-Lautrec. In 1960 June Wayne founded the Tamarind Lithography Workshop in Los Angeles to train master printers.
lithuania: Lithuania lies on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea, bordered by Latvia to the north, Belarus to the east and south, Poland to the south and the Russian semi-exclave of Kaliningrad Oblast to the southwest. It covers 65,300 square kilometres and has around 99 kilometres of sandy coastline, much of it sheltered by the Curonian sand peninsula. The warm-water port of Klaipėda lies at the mouth of the Curonian Lagoon.

The landscape was smoothed by the glaciers of the last ice age and combines moderate lowlands and highlands, with numerous lakes and wetlands. The highest point is Aukštojas Hill at 294 metres. A mixed forest zone covers over 33% of the country, and the Nemunas River carries international shipping.

The first people settled after the Last Glacial Period, in the 10th millennium BCE, as travelling hunters of the Kunda, Neman and Narva cultures. Indo-Europeans arrived in the 3rd to 2nd millennium BCE and mixed with the local population to form the Baltic tribes, who kept trade contacts through the Amber Road. From the 9th to the 11th centuries coastal Balts were raided by Vikings. The remoteness of the area accounts for its separate linguistic, cultural and religious identity, and traditional pagan customs were long preserved.

The first known record of the name Lietuva is a 1009 story of Saint Bruno in the Annals of Quedlinburg. In the 1230s Lithuanian lands were united for the first time by Mindaugas, who formed the Kingdom of Lithuania on 6 July 1253. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania was the largest country in Europe by the 14th century. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was dismantled by neighbouring countries between 1772 and 1795, and Russia annexed most of Lithuanian territory.

Lithuania declared independence in 1918, and on 11 March 1990 it became the first Soviet republic to proclaim the restoration of its independence. It has a semi-presidential system: the president is directly elected for five years, and the Seimas has 141 members elected to four-year terms. The euro replaced the litas on 1 January 2015.

The population is 2.9 million, and 82.6% of residents were ethnic Lithuanians in 2024, with Poles (6.3%) and Russians (5.0%) the largest minorities. Lithuanian is a Baltic language believed to be the linguistically most conservative living Indo-European tongue. The first grammar, Grammatica Litvanica, was published in Latin in 1653 by Danielius Kleinas.
lithuanians: Theories about the origin of the Lithuanians have been recorded since the 15th century, when Lithuanian nobles, like those of many European nations, sought a noble and ancient descent. The most influential was the Palemon theory, which held that Lithuanians descended from Roman patricians led by a nobleman named Palemon who fled Rome. Modern scholarship holds that the Lithuanians formed from eastern Baltic tribes.

The Lithuanian nation traces its origins to the Lithuanian tribe and the land called Litua in the Annals of Quedlinburg of 1009. In Rus chronicles of the 11th and 12th centuries it appears as Litva. Over the centuries, especially under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, neighbouring tribes consolidated into the Lithuanian nation, mainly as a defence against the Teutonic Order and the Eastern Slavs.

Historians date the formation of the Lithuanian state variously between the 11th and the mid-13th centuries. Mindaugas, Lithuania's only crowned king and its first baptised ruler, is generally considered its founder. The Lithuanians were the only branch of the Baltic peoples to create a state before the modern era. The Lithuanian Crusade ravaged the country in the late Middle Ages and ended only with the Treaty of Melno in 1422, so it persisted after the Christianization of Lithuania in 1387, when Europe's last pagan people were baptised. Samogitia was baptised in 1413.

The state reached its height under Vytautas the Great (r. 1392–1430), when it ruled the lands between the Baltic and the Black Sea. After the Union of Lublin in 1569 the Grand Duchy kept its independence within the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth until 1795.

Lithuanians distinguish five historic regional groups: the Aukštaičiai, Dzūkai, Žemaičiai or Samogitians, Suvalkiečiai and Lietuvininkai, the last virtually extinct. The Žemaičiai of the west speak a dialect so distinctive that it is sometimes considered a separate language. The Lietuvininkai lived in Lithuania Minor, in northern East Prussia, were mostly Lutheran, and published the first printed work in Lithuanian, Martynas Mažvydas's Catechism of 1547; most were expelled or fled after World War II.

Lithuanian is conservative in grammar and phonology, keeping archaic features otherwise found in ancient languages such as Vedic Sanskrit and Ancient Greek, and is an important source for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European. A ban on printing Lithuanian was lifted in 1904. Most Lithuanians belong to the Catholic Church. Traditional life was rural, with mixed farming and forest foraging. The summer solstice holiday Joninės has pagan origins.
little-entente: The first attempts to organise a mutual defence of the successor states of Austria-Hungary were made at the Paris Peace Conference of 1919. Its most ardent proponent was Edvard Beneš, foreign minister of Czechoslovakia from 1918 to 1935, who was regarded as its real founder. The obvious aim was to prevent a resurgence of Hungarian power and a Habsburg restoration, but Beneš also meant it to stop any European power from encroaching on the members' independence and to strengthen their voice in international deliberations.

A second reading looks to the balance of power after the First World War. France planned to contain German aggression through an arrangement with Germany's neighbours. Before the war Russia had served that purpose, but France was reluctant to establish normal ties with the Soviet Union, so it sought other states near Germany and strongly supported the new alliance.

The alliance rested on a series of treaties. Czechoslovakia and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes signed a defensive convention against unprovoked Hungarian attack at Belgrade on 14 August 1920, ratified on 10 February 1921. Czechoslovakia and Romania followed on 23 April 1921, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and Romania on 7 June 1921, and Czechoslovakia and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes again on 31 August 1922.

The alliance was tested in 1921, when Charles I of Austria returned to Hungary on 26 March to reclaim the throne and left on 1 April. He returned on 20 October with part of the army behind him. The members began to mobilise, other powers opposed him, and Hungary arrested him on 24 October and abrogated his sovereign rights on 10 November.

A treaty signed at Štrbské Pleso on 27 June 1930 required the foreign ministers to meet at least once a year. The Pact of Organisation, signed at Geneva on 16 February 1933, created a Permanent Council, a Secretariat and an Economic Council.

The resurgence of German power after 1933 gradually undermined French influence among the members. On 22 August 1938 France signed the Bled agreement, which revoked certain restrictions placed on Hungary by the Treaty of Trianon, and on 30 September the Munich Agreement granted Germany parts of Czechoslovakia. The alliance collapsed and never went into wartime operation. During World War II Romania, the Independent State of Croatia and the Slovak State formed a similar alliance to stop further Hungarian expansion.
little-ice-age: The Little Ice Age was a period of regional cooling, particularly pronounced in the North Atlantic region, and not a true ice age of global extent. The term was introduced into scientific literature by François E. Matthes in 1939. It has conventionally been defined as extending from the 16th to the 19th centuries, but some experts prefer a span from about 1300 to about 1850.

According to J. M. Lamb, it was already under way in the wider North Atlantic region in the 13th and 14th centuries, when pack ice and Greenland glaciers began advancing. Radiocarbon dates from beneath ice caps on Baffin Island and Iceland indicate that cold summers began abruptly between 1275 and 1300. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change judged that the timing and the areas affected suggested largely independent regional changes rather than a globally synchronous glaciation, and that hemispherically it was a modest cooling of the Northern Hemisphere of less than 1 degree.

In Central Europe winters were generally cold until the end of the 19th century, and cold winters were the norm in the 14th century, except for the 37 years between 1340 and 1377. The Central England temperature series, which begins in 1659, shows an increase in exceptionally cold winters, which coincided with the frost fairs on the Thames. Winters were not unremittingly cold: the coldest in the series was 1684, yet the fifth warmest came in 1686.

Elsewhere the effects varied. In the winter of 1780 New York Harbor froze, so that people could walk from Manhattan Island to Staten Island. In China, oranges that had been grown for centuries were abandoned in Jiangxi Province, and some scholars argue that droughts and famines caused by the Little Ice Age were one reason for the fall of the Ming dynasty.

Several causes have been proposed: cycles in the Earth's orbit, low solar activity, heightened volcanic activity, changes in ocean circulation, falls in human population and the inherent variability of the climate. William Ruddiman and others proposed that the Black Death, which may have killed 30 to 60 per cent of the European population, led to reforestation that drew carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Each Middle Eastern empire had a primary food-growing region, and the Ottomans had Egypt. In the Ottoman Empire the cooling shortened growing seasons and lowered yields, and led to changes in farming, higher food prices and social unrest.
little-zab: The Little Zab, or Lower Zab, is called al-Zāb al-Asfal in Arabic, Zêy Koya in Kurdish and Zāba Taḥtāya in Syriac. It joins the Tigris just south of Al Zab in Iraq. Estimates of its length range from 380 to 456 kilometres, and it drains about 22,000 square kilometres, 74% of it in Iraq. It is fed by rainfall and snowmelt, with peak discharge from February to May and low water from July to October. Because of its torrential nature, medieval Arab geographers described it, like the Great Zab, as demoniacally possessed. Annual precipitation falls from over 1,000 millimetres in the Iranian Zagros to under 200 at its confluence with the Tigris, and the tree line stands at about 1,800 metres.

Human occupation of the basin is attested for every period since the Middle Palaeolithic site of Barda Balka, where Late Acheulean stone tools were found. Jarmo, a tell east of Kirkuk, was a Neolithic village of farmers and herders, and the Ranya Plain was occupied from the Ubaid to the Ninevite V periods, from the middle of the 6th to the middle of the 3rd millennium BCE. The region enters history at the end of the 3rd millennium BCE, when Shulgi of the Ur III dynasty mentions Erbil as Urbilum.

In the early 2nd millennium BCE Shamshi-Adad of Upper Mesopotamia fought in the land of Qabra, probably on the lower Little Zab, and installed garrisons. Tablets from Tell Shemshara, ancient Shusharra, show the local governor becoming his vassal. In the 14th century BCE the region belonged to the kingdom of Mitanni, with archives at Nuzi and Tell al-Fakhar. The lower basin lay in the heartland of the Middle and Neo-Assyrian empires. After the Neo-Assyrian fall control passed to the Medes and, in 550 BCE, to the Achaemenid Empire. Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at the Battle of Gaugamela, and after Alexander's death in 323 BCE the area fell to his Seleucid successors.

Two dams regulate the river in Iraq: the Dukan Dam, built between 1957 and 1961 as an arch dam 116 metres high that stores water for irrigation and generates hydroelectric power, and the Dibis Dam, built between 1960 and 1965 for the Kirkuk Irrigation Project. Because Lake Dukan would submerge archaeological sites, surveys and rescue excavations were carried out, notably at Tell Shemshara and Tell Bazmusian. For a short distance the river forms the border between Iran and Iraq, and on its lower course it divides the governorates of Erbil, Sulaymaniyah and Kirkuk.
liu-bei: Liu Bei, courtesy name Xuande, was born in Zhuo County, in present-day Zhuozhou, Hebei. The Records of the Three Kingdoms makes him a descendant of Liu Sheng, ninth son of Emperor Jing of Han, but Pei Songzhi's fifth-century commentary, drawing on the Dianlüe, traces him to the Marquis of Linyi, so his line is uncertain. His father, Liu Hong, died young and Liu Bei grew up poor, selling shoes and woven straw mats with his mother. A tall mulberry tree beside the house was said to promise a noble descendant, and as a child he declared that he would ride in an emperor's feather-covered chariot.

In 184 the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out, and Liu Bei led followers including Guan Yu, Zhang Fei and Jian Yong to join the government forces under Colonel Zou Jing. He was gravely wounded in one fight and survived by feigning death. He was appointed Commandant of Anxi County, and after Emperor Ling died in 189 he joined the campaign against Dong Zhuo and then the warlord Gongsun Zan, who made him Chancellor of Pingyuan State.

In 194 he marched to the aid of Tao Qian when Cao Cao attacked Xu Province. He later sheltered with Liu Biao at Xinye after Cao Cao's victory over Yuan Shao at the Battle of Guandu, and on the advice of Lu Su he allied with Sun Quan against Cao Cao. In 211 Liu Zhang, Governor of Yi Province, invited him in against Zhang Lu, and Liu Bei went on to conquer the province. A dispute with Sun Quan over the commanderies of Jing Province followed. In 215 Cao Cao took Hanzhong, and Liu Bei's forces, with Zhang Fei in the Ba region, later won the territory around it.

In early winter 219 Sun Quan's forces under Lü Meng invaded Jing Province and executed Guan Yu. Cao Cao died in 220, and his son Cao Pi ended the Eastern Han dynasty and founded Cao Wei. In August 221 Liu Bei led an army against Sun Quan to avenge Guan Yu, leaving Zhuge Liang in charge in Chengdu. Zhang Fei was murdered by his subordinates early in the campaign. Lu Xun withdrew to Yiling and refused battle. Liu Bei died on 10 June 223.

The historian Chen Shou, once a subject of Shu, compared Liu Bei's magnanimity to Emperor Gaozu's but judged him no match for Cao Cao as a strategist. The 14th-century Romance of the Three Kingdoms portrays him as a benevolent, Confucian ruler, while his governance has been described as Confucian in appearance but Legalist in substance. Shoemakers in Chengdu worship him as their patron.
liu-shaoqi: Liu Shaoqi was born on 24 November 1898 in a mud-brick farmhouse at Tanzichong, in Ningxiang, Hunan Province, the youngest child of his generation in the family. From the age of eight he attended village private schools, studying the Classic of Poetry and the Zuo Zhuan as well as arithmetic. After his father's death in 1910 and his brother's accounts of the 1911 Revolution, he insisted that his sister cut off her queue to show a break with the Qing dynasty. In January 1916 he joined student marches against Yuan Shikai's restoration of the monarchy.

In 1922 Mao Zedong appointed him to the Hunan committee of the Chinese Communist Party, and that September he and Li Lisan led the Anyuan coal miners' and railway workers' strike, which ended in victory on 18 September. He took part in the Long March and supported Mao at the Zunyi Conference in January 1935. During the Second Sino-Japanese War he led party bureaus in northern and central China, and on 8 July 1939 delivered his best-known speech, On the Self-Cultivation of Communist Party Members. In the civil war he presided over the National Land Conference at Xibaipo, which adopted the Outline of the Land Law of China.

After the People's Republic was proclaimed on 1 October 1949 he became a vice chairman of the Central People's Government and in June 1950 head of the Central Land Reform Committee. In 1954 he presented the draft of the first Constitution and was elected chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress. On 27 April 1959 he was elected chairman of the People's Republic. Mao had named him as his successor, and after the Seven Thousand Cadres Conference of 1962 he pursued policies of economic reconstruction.

When the Cultural Revolution began in May 1966 Liu at first supported it, but his work teams in the universities were condemned by Mao, and at the eleventh plenum in August 1966 Mao called on the party to bombard the bourgeois headquarters. Lin Biao replaced Liu as second-in-command, and by 1967 he was under house arrest, labelled China's foremost capitalist roader and a traitor. Held in solitary confinement in Zhongnanhai, he was refused hospital care when gravely ill in 1968, and he died in prison on 12 November 1969 of complications from diabetes.

The fifth plenum of the 11th Central Committee rehabilitated him on 24 February 1980. A state memorial service followed on 17 May, with Deng Xiaoping delivering the eulogy, and as he had asked, his ashes were scattered in the Yellow Sea.
liutprand-king-of-the-lombards: Liutprand's early life was inauspicious. His father Ansprand was driven into exile among the Bavarians, his older brother Sigipert was blinded by King Aripert II, and his mother Theodarada and sister Aurona were mutilated. Liutprand was spared only because his youth made him seem harmless, and Paul the Deacon calls him adolescens. He was released from Aripert's custody and allowed to join his father. His reign followed the overthrow of Aripert II and officially began just before Ansprand's death.

Liutprand ruled for thirty-one years. He opened his reign by moving against the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna, destroying Classe, occupying forts around Bologna and Osimo and capturing Sutri, while keeping an alliance with the Franks. In 715 he married Guntrud, a young Agilolfing, which tied him to the Bavarians, whose duke Theodo I was among his chief allies. In 726 Emperor Leo III issued his first edict against icons, and Pope Gregory II refused to comply. Liutprand, who had refused bribes from the exarch Paul and presented himself as a liberator, took the moment to strike. In 727 he crossed the Po and took Bologna, Osimo, Rimini, Ancona and other cities of Emilia and the Pentapolis, though not Ravenna itself.

In 727 he also seized the fortress of Sutri on the Via Cassia. Gregory II sent him money and gifts for about four months, and in 728 Liutprand gave Sutri to the Papacy, laying his royal insignia before the pope in a ceremony at Camp Neronis. The historian Jan Hallenbeck suggests that he took it either to extort money from the papacy or as part of his offensive against Byzantine territory, or both. Later he allied with the exarch Eutychius, marched with him to the gates of Rome, and then submitted to the pope and reconciled the two. When Saracens invaded Sardinia, he had the relics of Augustine brought to Pavia.

After Gregory III's election in 731 relations soured, and the Lombards were expelled from Ravenna. After Gregory's death Liutprand again threatened Rome, and Pope Zachary secured a twenty-year peace and the return of four towns. Liutprand's laws, issued in fifteen sessions from 713 to 735, show more Roman influence than those of his predecessors. One statute required Lombard women who married Romans to obey Roman law, and after 774 the Franks borrowed many of their legal procedures.

The historian Chris Wickham calls Liutprand the most powerful Lombard king, with hegemonic power across the peninsula by his death in 744. None of his successors, among them Ratchis, Aistulf and Desiderius, ruled as long or controlled as much territory. Herwig Wolfram holds that Liutprand and his successors prepared the ground for a medieval Italian nation.
liutprand-of-cremona: Liutprand was born around 920 into a prominent Lombard family of Pavia. In 931 he entered the service of Hugh of Arles, King of Italy, as a page, was educated at the court, and became a deacon of the cathedral of Pavia. After Hugh died in 947, Liutprand became confidential secretary and eventually chancellor to Berengar II, marchese d'Ivrea, the de facto ruler of Italy. His father and stepfather had both been sent as ambassadors to Constantinople, in 927 and 942, and it was his stepfather who told him of Prince Igor's attack on the city in 941.

In 949 Berengar sent him on a goodwill mission to the court of Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, partly to learn Greek; he knew a surprising amount and was among the first Westerners to use Greek minuscule. He fell out with Berengar and took revenge in his Antapodosis, then joined Otto I, who had been crowned King of the Lombards in 951. When Otto deposed Berengar in 961, Liutprand became bishop of Cremona. At Otto's court he met Recemund, a Córdoban ambassador, who urged him to write a history, and in 963 he attended the Synod of Rome that deposed Pope John XII, writing the only connected narrative of it.

In 968 Otto sent him to Constantinople, to the court of Nicephorus Phocas, to ask for the hand of Anna Porphyrogenita for the younger Otto. The embassy was humiliating and futile; the title of emperor caused friction, aggravated by a letter from Pope John XIII addressing Nicephorus as "the emperor of the Greeks". Constanze Schummer has questioned how good a diplomat he was, and speculated that Otto never saw his full account.

The Antapodosis, in six books, covers events largely in Italy from 887 to 949, and the Historia Ottonis praises his patron for the years 960 to 964. The Relatio de legatione Constantinopolitana, on the embassy of 968 and 969, is perhaps the most graphic and lively writing to survive from the 10th century, and a document of rare value on Constantinople, though highly coloured by hostility. The Catholic Encyclopedia judged him a strong partisan who was frequently unfair to his adversaries. He probably died before 20 July 972, and certainly before 5 March 973.
liuvigild: Liuvigild was a Visigothic king of Hispania and Septimania, born about 519. When King Athanagild died in 567, his brother Liuva I was raised to the kingship at Narbonne, the last bastion of Visigothic rule in Gaul. In the second year of his reign Liuva made Liuvigild co-king and heir, with Hispania Citerior, the eastern part of Hispania, to rule directly. Both were Arian Christians, the dominant faith of the Visigothic rulers until 587. Liuvigild married first Theodosia, who bore two sons, Hermenegild and Reccared, and then Athanagild's widow Goiswintha.

The Visigoths were still a military aristocracy whose kings had to be ratified by the nobility, and the Visigoths and their Ibero-Roman subjects remained separated by religion and by distinct law codes.

Almost every year Liuvigild marched against the Byzantines, the Suebi, the Basques or domestic rivals. According to John of Biclaro, in 569 he subdued Zamora, Palencia and León from the Suebi; in 570 he laid waste Bastetania and Málaga; and he later took Medina Sidonia and Córdoba from the Byzantines. His brother Liuva died in 571 or 572, leaving him sole ruler, and he associated his sons Hermenegild and Reccared with himself, making them dukes over Toledo and Narbonne. He adopted Byzantine ceremony, including the title Flavius, the throne, crown, sceptre and purple mantle, and struck gold coins in his own name.

He revised the Code of Euric as the Codex Revisus and repealed old Roman prohibitions on intermarriage between Goths and Ibero-Romans, once punishable by death. He put down revolts among the Cantabri, in Córdoba and Asturia, and in Toledo and Évora, punishing the rebels severely, and the Suebian king Miro agreed to a treaty with tribute in 576. He took Orespeda in 577, founded Recopolis in Celtiberia, named for Reccared, and captured Mérida in 582.

In 579 Hermenegild converted to orthodox Christianity, persuaded by his Frankish wife Ingund and Leander, bishop of Seville, and Baetica revolted. Liuvigild offered theological compromises, took Seville and in 584 banished his son to Valencia, where he was murdered in 585. In 585 Liuvigild also conquered the Suebi, ending some forty years of their independence.

Liuvigild's last year was troubled by open war with the Franks along his northern borders. He ruled from Toledo, where he settled toward the end of his reign, which is why the Visigothic monarchy is sometimes called the Kingdom of Toledo. Gregory of Tours records that he fell ill in 586 and on his deathbed embraced the Catholic faith. The historian Chris Wickham calls his legislation the most Roman-influenced of any of the barbarian kingdoms. His son Reccared, who succeeded him, made Catholicism the official religion of the kingdom in 589.
livadeia: Livadeia lies 90 kilometres north-west of Athens, in mountainous country where farming is mostly confined to the valleys and has traditionally meant cotton, tobacco, cereals and livestock. In antiquity Lebadeia stood near the western frontier of Boeotia, between Mount Helicon and Chaeroneia, at the foot of a precipitous height on the banks of the Herkyna river.

According to Pausanias, the height was first occupied by the Homeric city of Mideia, whose people under the Athenian Lebadus moved into the plain and founded the city named after him. Lebadeia was at first insignificant and rose to importance through the oracle of Trophonius, consulted by Croesus and by Mardonius and still consulted in the time of Plutarch, when the other oracles in Boeotia had fallen silent. The town was nevertheless taken and plundered by Lysander and by Archelaus, the general of Mithridates VI of Pontus. In the war against Perseus of Macedon it took the side of the Romans.

When Pausanias visited in the 2nd century he recorded many temples, including the hero's temple in the grove of Trophonius with a statue by Praxiteles, and higher up the oracle itself. Those about to consult it first spent days in a chapel of the Good Daemon and of Good Fortune. The town declined in the Byzantine period, recovered in the Frankish period and in the 14th century came under the Catalan Company. Ottoman rule began in 1458, when privileges granted to residents encouraged industry and trade, and the town broke free in the Greek War of Independence in the 1820s.

Livadeia is the capital of the Boeotia regional unit. A notable portion of its inhabitants are Arvanites. Shallow grottos with niches at the springs of the Herkyna are said to mark the site of the oracle. On the hill above stands a small medieval castle, largely the work of the Catalan Company in the 14th century and one of only four Catalan castles in Greece. Farther west are the remains of a large temple of Zeus Basileus, perhaps begun in the 3rd century BCE but never completed.
liverpool: Liverpool lies on the eastern side of the Mersey Estuary, near the Irish Sea, about 286 kilometres north-west of London. It is built across a ridge of sandstone hills. The name comes from the Old English lifer, meaning thick or muddy water, and pōl, a pool or creek, and is first recorded around 1190 as Liuerpul. The reference was to a tidal creek, now filled in, into which two streams drained.

Liverpool was established as a borough in Lancashire in 1207. In the Middle Ages it grew from farmland into a small town of farmers, fishermen and tradesmen and a base for King John. A tidal creek called the Pool gave ships a natural harbour. Disease and its subordination to the nearby port of Chester kept its growth from advancing until the late 17th and early 18th centuries. The Old Dock, opened in 1715, was the world's first enclosed wet dock. In the late 17th century the port became heavily involved in the Atlantic slave trade, and it also imported cotton for the Lancashire textile mills and became a major departure point for emigrants to North America.

The 19th century brought global economic importance and a run of firsts: the first inter-city railway, the first non-combustible warehouse system at the Royal Albert Dock, built in 1846 under Jesse Hartley, transatlantic steamships and a pioneering elevated electric railway. Liverpool was granted city status in 1880 and in 1974 moved from Lancashire to the new county of Merseyside. In the 20th century its position as a seaport made it vulnerable in the two world wars, and economic depressions and the containerisation of shipping contributed to decline, which was largely reversed after it was selected as European Capital of Culture for 2008.

Liverpool is a port city and metropolitan borough in Merseyside, England, and the core of the Liverpool City Region, which has over 1.5 million people. It has over 2,500 listed buildings, among them Speke Hall, a Tudor manor house completed in 1598, and English Heritage has described it as England's finest Victorian city. The Royal Albert Dock now houses the Merseyside Maritime Museum, the International Slavery Museum and Tate Liverpool. It is the birthplace of the Beatles, and Liverpool Lime Street is the world's oldest still-operating main line railway station.
livingstone-zambia: Livingstone lies in Southern Province, 10 km north of the Zambezi River, close to the Victoria Falls, and has road and rail connections to the resort town of Victoria Falls in Zimbabwe on the opposite side of the falls. It had 177,393 inhabitants at the 2022 census. Before it was founded the largest village in the area was Mukuni, whose Baleya inhabitants were conquered in the 16th century by Chief Mukuni, who came from the Congo. The Batoka under Chief Musokotwane were the predominant people. In 1855 the Subiya-Kololo Chief Sekeletu showed David Livingstone the Victoria Falls.

In the 1890s Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company established British rule north of the Zambezi in a territory called North-Western Rhodesia. The main crossing of the river was at the Old Drift above the falls, where a colonial settlement grew and around 1897 became the first municipality in the country. Malaria led the Europeans to move to higher ground after 1900, and the new town was named Livingstone in honour of the explorer. In 1904 the railway reached the falls on the southern side. The city was founded in 1905, the company moved the territory's capital there in 1907, and in 1911 it merged the territory with North-Eastern Rhodesia as Northern Rhodesia.

Livingstone prospered as a gateway for trade between the north and south sides of the Zambezi and from farming and timber. After the capital moved to Lusaka in 1935, to be closer to the Copperbelt, industries in timber, hides, tobacco and cotton grew, and a hydroelectric plant took water from the Eastern Cataract of the falls. Colonial Livingstone took on the most British character of the towns of Northern Rhodesia and was segregated, with African townships such as Maramba in the east and south. Northern Rhodesia became Zambia in 1964, and Livingstone declined economically in the 1970s.

Tourism is the town's mainstay, and Livingstone is the main base for visiting the Victoria Falls. It is served by Harry Mwaanga Nkumbula International Airport and by the Zambia Railways main line, and the Mulobezi Railway links it to the timber industry in the west. Its museums include the Livingstone Museum, which holds archaeology, ethnography, history and memorabilia of David Livingstone, the Maramba Cultural Museum, the Railway Museum and the Victoria Falls Field Museum.
livius-andronicus: Livius Andronicus was born in Tarentum, in Magna Graecia. Little is known of his childhood, but he is believed to have been a highly educated Greek who was bought as a slave by Roman nobles. Andronicus is the Latin form of the Greek name Andronikos, and Livius is thought to be the family name of his patron, someone of the gens Livia. He began his career in servitude and was eventually freed. Jerome says he was given his liberty by Livius Salinator, whose children he taught. He started as an educator, and his Latin translations of Greek works, including Homer's Odyssey, were first meant as teaching aids for the school he founded.

His dates rest mainly on Cicero and Livy, and only two seem free of dispute. According to Cicero, his first performance at Rome took place in 240 BCE, the year before Ennius was born. Livy reports that in 207 BCE, after a series of evil portents, the pontiffs ordered three bands of nine maidens to sing through the city a hymn composed by Livius.

Livy states that Livius was the first to create a play with a plot. One story says that after straining his voice, he, who was also an actor, was the first to leave the singing to singers and to limit the actor to dialogue. His plays used the iambic senarius and the trochaic septenarius, with sung passages and spoken dialogue, and gave large parts to a solo chief actor, often himself. Whether he used a chorus is not known.

His Latin translation of the Odyssey, the Odyssia, was in Saturnian verse. Only parts of 46 scattered lines from 17 of the 24 books survive; in some lines he translates literally and in others more freely. Of his tragedies there remain fragments of Achilles, Aegisthus, Aiax Mastigophorus, Andromeda, Danae, Equus Troianus, Hermiona and Tereus, in all no more than about 60 fragments, which follow Greek models. Two comedies are certain, Gladiolus and Ludius, composed on the model of Greek New Comedy.

These comedies were called fabulae palliatae, after the Greek-style cloak, the pallium, worn by the actors, and later playwrights imitated the genre. The biographer Suetonius used the term half-Greek of Livius and Ennius, meaning their genre. Varro, Cicero and Horace regarded Livius as the originator of Latin literature, and he is the earliest Roman poet whose name is known.
livonia: Livonia, known in earlier records as Livland, is named after the historical Livonians, who lived on the shores of present-day Latvia. By the end of the 13th century the name was extended to most of present-day Estonia and Latvia, which the Livonian Brothers of the Sword had conquered in the Livonian Crusade. Its indigenous inhabitants were various Finnic tribes in the north and Baltic tribes in the south, and the descendants of the crusaders became the ruling class, eventually known as Baltic Germans. Bishop Albert of Buxhoeveden founded Riga in 1201.

Bishop Albert founded the military order of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1202, and Pope Innocent III sanctioned it in 1204. After the Lithuanians and Semigallians decimated the Order at the Battle of Saule in 1236, the survivors were incorporated in 1237 into the Teutonic Order as the Livonian Order, an autonomous branch with its own Master. Between 1237 and 1290 it conquered all of Courland, Livonia and Semigallia. After the Saint George's Night Uprising of 1343-1345, Denmark sold the Duchy of Estonia to the Teutonic Order in 1346, and medieval Livonia reached its largest extent.

The Livonian War of 1558-1583 ended this order. The Livonian Order suffered a decisive defeat by Muscovite troops at the Battle of Ergeme in 1560, and its last Master, Gotthard Kettler, secularised the Order, converted to Lutheranism and set up the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia for his family. In 1561 most of the rest fell to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and after 1569 Livonia was a joint domain of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

Sweden received roughly the former Duchy of Livonia after the Polish-Swedish War of 1621-1625. Swedish Livonia became a very important dominion: Riga was the second-largest Swedish city, and Livonia paid for one third of Sweden's war costs. Sweden lost it to the Russian Empire by the Capitulation of Estonia and Livonia in 1710 and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. Russia added Polish Livonia in 1772 in the Partitions of Poland.

Livonia remained within the Russian Empire until the end of World War I, when it was split between the newly independent states of Latvia and Estonia. The United Baltic Duchy proclaimed by the Baltic German nobility on 12 April 1918 was never recognised by any state and was dissolved at the German surrender in November 1918. The land has been divided between Latvia and Estonia ever since. The Livonian language is nearly extinct, and the unofficial anthem of the Livonians, Min izāmō, shares its melody with the Finnish and Estonian national anthems.
livonian-brothers-of-the-sword: The order, formally the Militia of Christ of Livonia, was a Catholic order of warrior monks, mostly from northern Germany. Albert, the third bishop of Riga, established it in 1202, and Pope Innocent III sanctioned it in 1204. Albert had realised that a standing army in Livonia would be more useful than crusaders who stayed a short time, since the rewards for secular knights were not enough to keep them. The brothers were to help convert the pagan Livonians, Latgalians and Selonians who lived along the trade routes eastward from the Gulf of Riga.

The Sword Brethren fought their first battle in 1205, ambushing Lithuanians returning with booty after the Semigallian duke Viesthard asked for help. They built a line of castles along the Daugava, and since they had superiority in heavy cavalry, the native peoples avoided pitched battles and most fighting consisted of raids. In 1211 they formed the core of an army that invaded southern Estonia and took Fellin after a siege. The next year they destroyed Saccalian resistance in a battle in which 2,000 Saccalians fell. They found that winter was the best season for war, when frozen swamps and rivers made movement easy, and by 1218 they had conquered southern Estonia. Courland was conquered and converted in 1230.

From the start the order tended to ignore its vassalage to the bishops. Master Wenno advanced north of the Daugava without Albert's leave and founded the castles of Segewold and Wenden. When he removed Wickbert, a man loyal to Albert, from Wenden, Wickbert fled to the bishop and killed Wenno with an axe. Estonia was divided between King Valdemar II of Denmark and Albert in 1222 in a settlement that displeased the order, which seized Danish land and rebuffed a papal legate. After Albert died in 1229 the legate Bernard of Aulne decided that the order should be suppressed, but the order defeated and captured him.

The order followed a rule adapted from the Knights Templar. Knights had to be of noble birth and take vows of obedience, poverty and celibacy, and the order also included soldiers, artisans and clerics. A general assembly of the knights chose a master, who served for life and chose a council and a military chief for each district castle. The first master was Wenno von Rohrbach, from 1204 to 1209, and the second, Volkwin Schenk von Winterstein, died in the Battle of Saule in 1236. The order kept one third of any new territory and the rest went to the bishop. After the defeat at Saule the survivors were absorbed in 1237 into the Teutonic Order as its Livonian branch.
livonian-crusade: The main source is the Livonian Chronicle of Henry, written around 1229 by Henry of Latvia at the urging of his lords, including his former teacher Albert, bishop of Riga, who is much praised in it. The historian James A. Brundage argued that Albert commissioned it to glorify his achievements. The earliest surviving papal letter on the crusade was issued by Pope Innocent III on 5 October 1199, allowing those who had vowed to go to the Holy Land to take part in the Livonian crusade instead.

Saint Meinhard of Segeberg arrived at Ikšķile in 1184 to convert the pagan Livonians and was consecrated bishop of Üxküll in 1186. His successor Berthold of Hanover arrived with crusaders in 1198 and was soon killed in battle.

Albert von Buxthoeven, consecrated bishop in 1199, arrived the next year with a large force and made Riga the seat of his bishopric in 1201. In 1202 he formed the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, partly to protect German trade. The Livonian leader Caupo of Turaida rebelled and was defeated in 1206, and in 1209 Albert captured Jersika, whose ruler Visvaldis had to submit his kingdom to the Archbishopric of Riga. From 1208 the crusaders attacked the Estonians, who were divided into counties led by elders. At the Battle of St. Matthew's Day on 21 September 1217 both Caupo and the Estonian leader Lembitu were killed, and the Estonians were crushingly defeated.

King Valdemar II of Denmark won the Battle of Lindanise in 1219, and northern Estonia fell to Danish control. In 1223 an Estonian uprising took every Christian stronghold except Tallinn, but by 1224 the crusaders had retaken the larger fortresses. Saaremaa accepted Christianity in 1227 and rose again several times. The northern Curonians made peace in 1230, and Courland was partitioned in 1266. The Semigallians won at Garoza in 1287, their last victory, but in 1290 they burned their last castle at Sidabrė and moved south.

On 2 February 1207 an ecclesiastical state called Terra Mariana was established as a principality of the Holy Roman Empire, which Innocent III proclaimed a subject of the Holy See in 1215. The legate William of Modena divided the conquered land into six feudal principalities: the archbishopric of Riga, the bishoprics of Courland, Dorpat and Ösel-Wiek, the lands of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, and the Danish Duchy of Estonia. After the defeat of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword at the Battle of Saule in 1236 the survivors merged in 1237 into the Teutonic Order as the Livonian Order. The conquerors held the country through a network of castles.
livonian-war: By the mid-16th century Old Livonia, in the territory of present-day Estonia and Latvia, was a prosperous but decentralised Livonian Confederation. It held the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, the prince-bishoprics of Dorpat and Ösel–Wiek, Courland, the Archbishopric of Riga and the city of Riga. The Reformation had split the Order since the 1520s, the Archbishop and the Order's Landmeister rivalled each other, and the country had weak defences. Its neighbours had their own aims: Sweden wanted Livonian ports and Denmark controlled the entrance to the Baltic.

Ivan IV took the Confederation's approach to Poland–Lithuania for protection under the Treaty of Pozvol as a casus belli, since a truce of 1554 had barred such an alliance. On 22 January 1558 he invaded Livonia.

Russian troops took Dorpat in May 1558 and Narva in July, and many fortresses surrendered without resistance. In 1559 Bishop Johann von Münchhausen sold the right to nominate the bishop of Ösel–Wiek to Frederick II of Denmark-Norway, who put his brother Magnus of Holstein there. In 1561 the nobles of Harrien–Wierland and Jerwen yielded to Sweden, forming the Duchy of Estonia, and Reval accepted Swedish rule. Poland–Lithuania was drawn in as well. From 1562 fighting slowed while Denmark and Sweden fought the Northern Seven Years' War, which ended in 1570 with the Treaty of Stettin. In 1565 Ivan began the oprichina, which left Russia in political chaos.

Russia took the lead again in the early 1570s, besieging Reval in 1570 and 1571 without success and sacking Weissenstein in 1573, where the occupiers roasted some of the Swedish garrison's leaders alive. The tide turned after Stephen Báthory became king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania in 1576. Between 1578 and 1581 his successes, including the Battle of Wenden and a long and difficult Siege of Pskov, pushed Russia back.

Under the 1582 Truce of Jam Zapolski, which ended the war between Russia and Poland–Lithuania, Russia gave up all its holdings in Livonia and Polotsk. In the Truce of Plussa, signed with Sweden on 10 August 1583, Russia gave up most of Ingria, leaving Narva and Ivangorod under Swedish control; Sweden also kept the Duchy of Estonia and most of northern Livonia.

Afterwards Báthory reduced the privileges granted to the Duchy of Livonia, Polish gradually replaced German as the administrative language, and the Jesuits and local clergy embraced the Counter-Reformation, although the population did not convert en masse.
livonians: The Livonians, or Livs, are one of the Finnic peoples indigenous to the Livonian Coast, in northwestern Latvia and southwestern Estonia, and they spoke Livonian, a Finnic language closely related to Estonian and Finnish. The date of their arrival is disputed. They claim to have lived in their homeland for over 5,000 years, while another view holds that Finnic tribes were pushed into the coastal regions by the Slav migrations of the sixth and seventh centuries CE. They called themselves rāndalist, coast dwellers, and lived mainly by fishing, with some farming. They controlled the trade route of the Daugava River and traded with Gotlanders, Russians and Finns and later with Germans, Swedes and Danes.

Missionaries followed the traders. In the 12th century Germans established a base at Uexküll, now Ikšķile. Bishop Meinhard died in 1196, and his successor Berthold of Hanover, who tried to convert the Livonians by force, was killed in 1198. Albert von Buxhövden then made the Livonian leaders at the mouth of the Daugava give him land, and building began in 1201; from this settlement grew the city of Riga. The Knights of the Sword defeated and converted the Livonians in a campaign of the Livonian Crusade, and in 1208 Pope Innocent III declared that all of them had been converted. They were then obliged to serve the Knights as infantry in wars against the Estonians and the Latvian tribes, which lasted until 1217.

The crusade devastated once prosperous Livonia, and Latvian tribes moved into the emptied regions from about 1220. War and the mingling of refugees led over the centuries to the complete assimilation of the Livonians of Livonia by the Latvians, and the last known speaker of the eastern dialect died in 1864.

On the tip of the Courland peninsula, the Livonian Coast, the Livonians survived because their sea-based fishing life was separated from the farming Latvians of the interior by dense forests and marshes. A revival in the interwar years, led by the Livonian Society founded in 1923, brought a choir, song festivals, a reader and a monthly magazine, and gave them the ethnic name līvõd. Livonian culture was repressed in the Soviet period, when many were deported to Siberia and the western villages of the coast were evacuated. After 1991 they were recognised as an indigenous minority, and in 1992 Latvia created the protected territory Līvõd rānda, covering twelve villages.
livorno: The origins of Livorno are controversial, although the place was inhabited from the Neolithic, as bones, copper and ceramic found in a cave between Ardenza and Montenero show. The Etruscan settlement was called Labro. Livorna is mentioned for the first time in 1017 as a small coastal village and port, with the remains of a Roman tower, under the rule of Lucca. A tower was built by Matilda of Tuscany in 1077, and the Republic of Pisa owned the place from 1103 and built a quadrangular fort, the Quadratura dei Pisani, to defend the port. Porto Pisano was destroyed after the Pisan fleet was crushingly defeated at the Battle of Meloria in 1284.

After the Medici, the ruling dynasty of Florence, arrived, the Fortezza Vecchia was built between 1518 and 1534 and voluntary resettlement of the population was encouraged, though Livorno remained a rather insignificant coastal fortress, with 1,562 residents by 1551. It became the seat of the crusading and corsairing Order of Saint Stephen after 1561, distinctive for its aggressive approach towards the Muslim world, and a major Mediterranean slave trade hub in the early modern period, rivalling Malta's, with a slave population that may have exceeded 25 per cent of its inhabitants. Designed as an ideal town in the Renaissance, it developed considerably from the second half of the 16th century, and its intense commercial activity was largely dominated by foreign traders.

At the end of the 17th century Livorno underwent a period of great urban planning and expansion, with a new fortress, town walls and a system of navigable canals through its neighbourhoods. The port of Pisa had silted up in the 13th century, so Livorno took over as the main port of Tuscany, the seat of consulates and shipping companies. Its population had risen to 32,534 by 1745. Its high status as a multiethnic, multicultural city lasted until the second half of the 19th century, when other cities surpassed it.

Livorno is a port city on the western coast of Tuscany, the capital of the Province of Livorno, with 152,451 inhabitants. Its people speak a variant of Tuscan known as a vernacolo, and the Jewish community once used bagitto, a Judæo-Italian dialect with Spanish and Portuguese words from Jews expelled from the Iberian peninsula in the late 15th century.
livy: Livy was born in Patavium, modern Padua, probably in 59 BCE. His city was then the second wealthiest on the Italian peninsula, and it was known for conservative values in morality and politics. His teenage years fell in the civil wars of the 40s BCE. When the governor Asinius Pollio tried to bring Patavium over to Mark Antony, the wealthy citizens refused money and arms and pledged their allegiance to the Senate. The wars probably kept Livy from a higher education in Rome. Pollio later mocked his Latin for its patavinity, the provincialisms of Patavium.

Livy probably went to Rome in the 30s BCE but never became a senator or held office. Mistakes in his work on military matters suggest that he never served in the army. He was educated in philosophy and rhetoric, and had the means to live independently. He knew the emperor Augustus and encouraged the future emperor Claudius to write history.

His history of Rome, Ab Urbe Condita, told the story of the city from the legends before its traditional founding in 753 BCE through the reign of Augustus. He began it when already past his youth, probably at 33, and worked on it until he left Rome for Padua in old age. Together with Polybius he is one of the main accounts of the Second Punic War. Because he wrote under Augustus, his history stresses the triumphs of Rome and embellishes Roman heroism, in order to support the new form of government. Since he mostly described events hundreds of years old, its historical value has been questioned, although many Romans came to believe his account.

Livy died at Patavium in 17 CE. The ancient evidence for his dates is a chronicle of Eusebius, in Jerome's Latin version, whose manuscripts disagree, so that no standard dates exist for him; one manuscript puts his birth in 57 BCE.

His history was in high demand from its publication. Later writers such as Eutropius, Florus and Orosius drew on it. In the Middle Ages readers used summaries, since copying the whole was costly, and manuscripts were lost. In the Renaissance large sums changed hands for Livian manuscripts, and Petrarch and Pope Nicholas V searched for the missing books. Niccolò Machiavelli presented his Discourses on Livy as a commentary on the history.
ljubljana: Ljubljana lies in the Ljubljana Basin in Central Slovenia, between the Alps and the Karst, along a trade route between the northern Adriatic Sea and the Danube region and north of the country's largest marsh. The city centre sits on the Ljubljanica river at 298 metres, and Ljubljana Castle stands on Castle Hill to the south. The city stretches over an alluvial plain, and earthquakes have repeatedly devastated it, notably in 1511 and 1895. It lies some 250 km east of Venice, 124 km west of Zagreb and 350 km south-west of Vienna. Its symbol is the Ljubljana Dragon, which appears on the tower of the castle, on the coat of arms and on the Dragon Bridge.

Around 2000 BCE people living in pile dwellings settled the Ljubljana Marsh. Its prehistoric pile dwellings and the oldest wooden wheel in the world are among the notable finds, and the remains have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since June 2011. The area later served as a transit point for the Illyrians, the Iapodes and, from the 3rd century BCE, a Celtic tribe, the Taurisci. Around 50 BCE the Romans built a military encampment that became a permanent settlement called Iulia Aemona, held by the Legio XV Apollinaris. It housed 5,000 to 6,000 inhabitants. The Huns destroyed it in 452 on Attila's orders, and later the Ostrogoths and Lombards did the same.

The city was first mentioned in the first half of the 12th century, and the German name Laibach is documented from 1144. It was the historical capital of Carniola, a Slovene-inhabited part of the Habsburg monarchy, and was under Habsburg rule from the Middle Ages until 1918. It was the capital of the Illyrian Provinces from 1809 to 1814. After the Second World War it became the capital of the Socialist Republic of Slovenia within Yugoslavia, and in 1991 the capital of independent Slovenia. In the 19th century tension between German and Slovene residents shaped even the city's sport, and the Ljubljana Sokol gymnastic club, founded in 1863 and succeeded in 1868, served Slovene cultural and political aims.

Ljubljana is the capital and largest city of Slovenia, with about 300,000 inhabitants, and its cultural, educational, economic and political centre. After the earthquake of 1511 it was rebuilt in the Baroque style on Italian, especially Venetian, models, and after that of 1895 in the Vienna Secession style. The architect Jože Plečnik shaped large parts of the inter-war city, and Tivoli City Park, laid out in 1813 during the French administration, was renovated by him between 1921 and 1939.
ljudevit-gaj: Ljudevit Gaj was born Ludwig Gay in Krapina, then in Varaždin County in the Kingdom of Croatia within the Austrian Empire, on 8 August 1809. His father Johann Gay was a German immigrant from the Kingdom of Hungary, and his mother Juliana, née Schmidt, was the daughter of a German immigrant who arrived in the 1770s. The family was originally of Burgundian Huguenot origin and had reached Hungary in the 16th or 17th century, becoming serfs and, over time, Germanised. He finished high school in Varaždin, Zagreb and Karlovac, studied philosophy in Vienna and Graz, graduating in 1828, and law in Budapest from 1829 to 1831.

Gaj began publishing early, and a 36-page booklet on the manors of his native district, written in German, appeared in 1826 as Die Schlösser bei Krapina. In Buda in 1830 he published the Concise Basis for a Croatian-Slavonic Orthography, the first common Croatian orthography book after the works of Ignjat Đurđević and Pavao Ritter Vitezović. It was printed in Croatian and German. Following Vitezović and Czech orthography, he assigned one letter of the Latin script to each sound, using diacritics and the digraphs lj and nj.

The book brought him nationwide fame. In 1834 he obtained from the royal government of the Habsburg monarchy the permission for a Croatian daily newspaper that Đuro Matija Šporer had failed to win fifteen years earlier. Novine Horvatske appeared on 6 January 1835, with the literary supplement Danicza horvatzka, slavonzka y dalmatinzka on 10 January. The newspaper was printed in the Kajkavian dialect to the end of that year, while the supplement used Shtokavian alongside Kajkavian. In early 1836 they were renamed Ilirske narodne novine and Danica ilirska, since historians of the time held that the Illyrians had been Slavs and the forefathers of the South Slavs. He also wrote poetry, and his best-known poem, Još Hrvatska ni propala, dates from 1833.

Gaj married Paulina Krizmanić in 1842, and they had five children. He died in Zagreb in 1872, aged 62, and is buried at Mirogoj Cemetery. His alphabet is the basis of the Latin script used for Serbo-Croatian. Following Vuk Karadžić's reform of Cyrillic, he gave the Latin script a one-to-one correlation with Cyrillic, and the Slovenian alphabet of the mid-1840s is a variation of his, lacking only ć and đ. In 2008 a total of 211 streets in Croatia bore his name.
lleida: Lleida stands in the Catalan Central Depression, on the Segre, the river the Romans called the Sicoris and the principal tributary of the Ebro. In Roman times the town stood on a rise on its right bank, above its meeting with the Cinca, and commanded the country between the two rivers and the great road from Tarraco to the north-west of Spain, which crossed the river there. Recorded settlement goes back to the Bronze Age.

In antiquity the city was the chief town of the Ilergetes, an Iberian people, whose king Indíbil, with Mandoni, king of the Ausetanes, defended it against Carthaginian and Roman invaders. Under Augustus it became a municipium named Ilerda, in the province of Hispania Tarraconensis. In 49 BCE Pompey's legates Afranius and Marcus Petreius made it the key of their defence against Caesar and held it with five legions, until Caesar's generalship forced their surrender. The city minted its own coins, and its stone bridge over the Sicoris was so sturdy that its foundations still carry a bridge. It had fallen into decay by the time of Ausonius but recovered in the Middle Ages.

After Visigothic and Muslim rule Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona conquered it in 1149. A Jewish quarter, called La Cuirassa, dates to the 11th century, and a ritual bath of the 9th century, one of the oldest in Europe, has been found. A university was founded in 1297 and was the oldest in the Crown of Aragon until Philip V moved it to Cervera in 1717. In the Reapers' War the city was occupied by French and rebel forces and was taken by the Spanish under Felipe da Silva in 1644.

In the Spanish Civil War Lleida was a key defence point for Barcelona. Its air raids of 1937 and 1938 were severe: on 2 November 1937 the Condor Legion attacks killed about 300 people, among them 48 children and several teachers at the Liceu Escolar. The city fell to Franco's forces in 1938.

Lleida is the capital of its province and of the Segrià county, and its people speak Catalan, in the north-western dialect, and Spanish. The Seu Vella, a cathedral built in Romanesque and Gothic styles on the hill above the town, was turned into a fortress in the 18th century. Near it stand the remains of the Suda palace, built under Muslim rule and later a residence of the counts of Barcelona and kings of Aragon. The modern University of Lleida has been active since 1991.
lliria: Beneath the modern town lie the ruins of one of the most important Iberian cities in Spain. Then known as Edeta, it was the administrative centre of Edetania, an extensive territory between the Júcar and the Palancia River. The city stood on the hilltop called Sant Miquel, which overlooks the present town. After Roman troops destroyed it in 76 BCE, Quintus Sertorius moved the city downhill to its current location.

Under the Romans Llíria was as important as Valencia or Sagunt. The town is rich in Roman finds, among them a large leisure complex with a temple, shops, pools and hot baths. Excavations have also uncovered one of the largest buried caches of coins found in Spain, popularly called the Treasure of Carrer Duc de Llíria, which totals some 6,000 silver denarii minted in the first and third centuries. A mosaic of the Twelve Labours of Hercules came from a Roman house at Can Porcar and is displayed at the National Archaeological Museum of Spain in Madrid. The town's own archaeological museum holds imagery from the mosaic's original setting and other Roman objects.

The first church in Llíria was built in 1238 by King James I of Aragon, after his victory over the Moors and the conquest of the Valencian region. The Church of the Blood stands on the site of a mosque and is a typical example of Valencian Gothic architecture; some remains of the mosque can still be seen. In 1919 it was gazetted as a National Monument, the first religious monument in the Valencian Community to receive that distinction.

Llíria is the capital of the Camp de Túria area in the province of Valencia, at an altitude of 164 metres. Its traditional economy is based on agriculture, with textiles, construction materials, plastics and furniture also important. It is the end of the Metrovalencia train system, and about 24,000 people lived there in 2022. Both Spanish and Valencian are spoken.

The town is called the musical capital of its region, and on 30 October 2019 UNESCO declared it a Creative City in the category of Music. Several thousand residents play instruments, and the town is known for two rival wind bands. The Banda Primitiva was formed by the Franciscan friar Antoni Albarracín Enguídanos in 1819, and the second band split from it in 1903 to form the Unió Musical. Its Holy Week processions, which carry lifelike sculptures of scenes from Jesus's arrest to his burial, date from medieval times, and the town also keeps the feast days of Saint Vincent and Saint Michael.
