llivia: Llívia lies in the comarca of Cerdanya, in the province of Girona, Catalonia. It is surrounded by the French département of Pyrénées-Orientales and is separated from the rest of Spain by a corridor about 1.6 km wide, which includes the French communes of Ur and Bourg-Madame. The Segre river, a tributary of the Ebro, flows through the town. It is named after Livia, the wife of Augustus and matriarch of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.

Before the arrival of Rome, Llívia was the site of an Iberian oppidum that commanded the region. Under Rome it was the capital of Cerdanya until Hix, now a commune of Bourg-Madame, replaced it. In 672, under the Visigoths, its citadel was held by the rebel Flavius Paulus against King Wamba. In 1479, during the Catalan Civil War, the castle was destroyed by the forces of Louis XI after fourteen months of siege.

The Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 ceded Roussillon, Conflent, Capcir, Vallespir and northern Cerdanya to France, but stipulated that only villages were to be ceded. Llívia, as the ancient capital of Cerdanya, counted as a town, and so remained Spanish; the Treaty of Llívia of 1660 confirmed this. The maps were inaccurate, and at first it was not obvious that the town would become an enclave. The borders were ratified in the Treaty of Bayonne in 1866. Under Francisco Franco's government, residents needed special passes to cross France to the rest of Spain, and in the 1980s a dispute over stop signs placed by French authorities on the connecting road saw protesters remove them overnight.

Llívia has 1,562 inhabitants. The road across the corridor is owned partly by France and partly by Spain, and since the Schengen Area was implemented in 1995 there have been no formal borders on it. The two countries share a hospital at nearby Puigcerdà. The town's municipal museum holds the Esteve Pharmacy, with a large display of albarelli, antique drugs and a collection of prescription books, and the ruins of Llívia castle still stand.
llotja-de-la-seda: Behind the present building stood an earlier one of the fourteenth century, called the Oil Exchange (Llotja de l'Oli in Valencian, Lonja del Aceite in Spanish), which was used for trade, including agricultural oils. In 1348 percale, a type of silk, was traded there. Valencia's commercial prosperity reached its peak in the fifteenth century and led to the construction of a new building. Its design was derived from a similar structure, the Lonja of Palma de Majorca, built by the architect Guillem Sagrera in 1448.

The Llotja is a late Valencian Gothic civil building made up of three parts, together with the Orange Garden, a walled courtyard. The main hall, the Sala de Contractació or Trading Hall, is a large and richly decorated space supported by twisted columns; it was the financial centre where merchants worked out contracts. The architect in charge, Pere Compte, built it in only fifteen years.

The side wing is the Pavilion of the Consulate, seat of the Consolat del Mar, the first maritime merchant tribunal formed in Spain. Its first two floors held the main rooms, and the second floor had a richly decorated ceiling; the rooms still have their original furnishings. The third part is the central tower, in which the tribunal occasionally imprisoned merchants for debt.

A blue band runs along all four walls of the Trading Hall and carries an inscription in golden letters. It begins by saying that the house was built in fifteen years, and it praises honest trade, which does not deceive with the tongue and does not lend money at interest. The Valencian scholar Joan Francesc Mira read it as showing that one did not need to be a Protestant or a foreigner to enter into good trade, and as an example of ethical principles joined to the economy.

Further building and decoration continued after the hall was finished, among them the Consolat del Mar, a Renaissance building attached to the Llotja. In the following centuries it served as a silk exchange. In 1996 UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site, describing it as a wholly exceptional example of a secular building in late Gothic style that illustrates the power and wealth of one of the great Mediterranean mercantile cities.
lluis-companys: Lluís Companys i Jover was born on 21 June 1882 at El Tarròs near Lleida, the second of ten children of peasants with aristocratic roots. He studied law at the University of Barcelona. After the military attacked Catalan newspapers in 1906 he helped create the coalition Solidaritat Catalana, and he was jailed fifteen times for his youth activities. With Francesc Layret he represented the left-wing labour faction of the Catalan Republican Party and became a Barcelona councillor in 1916. In 1922 he helped found the peasants' union Unió de Rabassaires, and in 1931 he became an executive member of the new Republican Left of Catalonia.

On 14 April 1931, after the party won Barcelona in the local elections, Companys entered the City Hall, was proclaimed mayor and proclaimed the Republic from the balcony. After Francesc Macià died on 25 December 1933, the Catalan Parliament elected him president of the Generalitat. His government passed laws for the popular classes, among them the Crop Contracts Law protecting tenant farmers. On 6 October 1934, opposed to the inclusion of the CEDA party in the Spanish government, he proclaimed the Catalan State within the Spanish Federal Republic. The army suppressed the uprising and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, but the Popular Front's victory in February 1936 brought a pardon.

When the Civil War began in July 1936 he sided with the Republic. Militias and parties such as the CNT, the FAI and the POUM held more power than the government in Barcelona, and Companys helped organise the Central Committee of Anti-Fascist Militias on 21 July. After the violent clashes of May 1937, control of public order passed to the Spanish government.

Companys crossed into France on 5 February 1939. The Gestapo, working with the Spanish police, arrested him at La Baule-les-Pins on 13 August 1940, and in early September he was handed over to Spain, where he was held for five weeks, interrogated and tortured. A military trial in Barcelona lasting less than an hour sentenced him to death for military rebellion, and he was shot at Montjuïc Castle on 15 October 1940, refusing a blindfold and shouting Per Catalunya. He is buried at Montjuïc Cemetery. In Catalonia he is regarded as a martyr of Catalan nationalism, while his memory remains divisive in Spain.
llywelyn-ap-gruffudd: Llywelyn was the second of the four sons of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, eldest son of Llywelyn ab Iorwerth, and Senana ferch Caradog. His brothers were Owain Goch ap Gruffudd, Dafydd ap Gruffydd and Rhodri ap Gruffudd. His father was kept prisoner by his uncle Dafydd ap Llywelyn and then held by Henry III of England, and died in 1244 from a fall while trying to escape from the Tower of London. War followed in 1245, and Llywelyn supported his uncle in the fighting.

By the Treaty of Woodstock of 1247, Llywelyn and Owain were restricted to Gwynedd west of the Conwy. In June 1255 Llywelyn defeated Owain and Dafydd at the Battle of Bryn Derwin and became sole ruler there. In 1256 he crossed the Conwy at the appeal of the people of the Perfeddwlad, who resented English rule, and an English army was defeated at the Battle of Cadfan in June 1257. By early 1258 he was using the title Prince of Wales.

In 1265 he allied with Simon de Montfort by the Treaty of Pipton. After Montfort's death he defeated Marcher armies, and Henry III recognised him as Prince of Wales in the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267, in return for 24,000 marks. He later stopped paying, and refused to attend Edward I at Chester in 1275. His marriage by proxy to Eleanor de Montfort in 1275 angered Edward, who had her ship seized. Edward declared him a rebel in 1276, and the Treaty of Aberconwy of 9 November 1277 confined him to Gwynedd west of the Conwy.

In 1282 Dafydd attacked the English at Hawarden Castle on Palm Sunday and revolt spread. Llywelyn felt obliged to support his brother. He rejected an offer of an English estate, saying he would not abandon the people his ancestors had protected. On 11 December 1282 he was killed while separated from his army. Two accounts of his death survive and differ in detail. His head was sent to Edward and displayed in London, and the place of his burial is uncertain, though tradition names Abbeycwmhir.

Dafydd was captured in June 1283 and executed at Shrewsbury. Edward removed the regalia of Gwynedd, including the Cross of Neith, which he paraded through London in 1285. Llywelyn's daughter Gwenllian was placed in Sempringham Priory and died in 1337.
lobamba: Lobamba lies in the western part of Eswatini, in the wooded Ezulwini Valley, called the Valley of Heaven, in the Hhohho district. It is 16 kilometres from Mbabane and between Ezulwini and Mahlanya, with the Lusushwana river as its nearest river. The climate is subtropical, with wet summers and dry winters. Most of the country's people are Swazi, and the official languages are Swazi and English.

Two places have been called Lobamba. The first, now known as Old Lobamba, was established in 1750 in the south of the country. The settlement described here was created by King Sobhuza II in the north-west. The British government took control of Eswatini in 1903, after the Boer Wars, and the country was ruled by a regent until Sobhuza II became its leader in 1921.

Eswatini became independent of the British government on 6 September 1968. The independence was announced at a cattle byre in Lobamba by Prince Makhosini, the country's first prime minister and a great-grandson of Sobhuza I. The country became a constitutional monarchy under Sobhuza II, who lived in the royal residence, or kraal, at Lobamba. The Embo State Palace there was built by the British to house him and his family, which included 600 children. The constitution now in force was signed by King Mswati III on 26 July 2005.

Lobamba is the legislative and traditional capital of Eswatini. The Parliament, which has two chambers, the Senate and the House of Assembly, sits there. Ludzidzini Royal Village is the residence of the queen mother and includes her Royal Kraal, dwelling clusters and a parade ground for ceremonies. The king lives at Lozitha Palace, about ten kilometres away, and visits the Royal Kraal for the Umhlanga dance and the Incwala ceremony.

Two ceremonies are held at Lobamba each year: the Reed Dance, in August and September, in honour of the queen mother, and the Incwala, in December and January, in honour of the king. Both include dancing, singing and traditional dress. The National Museum of Eswatini, built in 1972, stands next to the Parliament building and holds a memorial to Sobhuza II. The King Sobhuza II Memorial Park contains his mausoleum and three of his vintage cars, and the Somhlolo National Stadium is nearby.
lobau: Löbau, called Lubij in Upper Sorbian, lies in the east of Saxony in the historical region of Upper Lusatia. It stands between the slopes of the Löbauer Berg and the fertile hilly area of the Upper Lusatian Mountains, and it is the gateway to this volcanic mountainous area. The town is halfway between Bautzen, Görlitz and Zittau.

Löbau was first mentioned in 1221 as Oppidum Lubaw. From 1319 it was part of the Bohemian Crown. In 1346 it was a founding member of the Lusatian League, which consisted of six cities, Bautzen, Görlitz, Kamenz, Lubań, Löbau and Zittau, and which was disbanded in 1815. In 1469 the town, along with the league, recognised the rule of King Matthias Corvinus and passed to Hungary, and in 1490 it returned to the Bohemian Crown under Vladislaus II.

From 1635 Löbau was ruled by the Electors of Saxony, from 1697 also kings of Poland, and from 1871 it was part of the German Empire. After Germany's defeat in World War II it lay in East Germany until 1990. The league was revived in 1991, though it holds no political power and mostly acts as a tourism promotion board.

The King Frederick Augustus Tower is Löbau's main landmark. Built of cast iron in 1854 on the Löbauer Berg, it is 28 metres tall and has been called the biggest cast-iron tower in Europe. The Schminke House, by the architect Hans Scharoun, dates from the 1930s and is regarded as one of the most important works of organic and expressionist architecture. The town hall mixes several architectural styles, and the town is widely known for the piano manufacturing company August Förster.
locarno: Locarno lies at the north-eastern tip of Lake Maggiore, on the north-eastern part of the delta of the river Maggia, at the southern foot of the Swiss Alps. Across the river lies the town of Ascona. Locarno is the capital of its district, and its official language is Italian. It is known for the Locarno International Film Festival, held every August with open-air screenings on the Piazza Grande, and for the Locarno Treaties, a series of European territorial agreements negotiated there in October 1925.

Roman tombs found between 1946 and 1949 show that the Roman town lay between the vicus of Muralto and a cemetery in use from the end of the La Tène period to the middle of the 3rd century CE. The place is first mentioned in 807 as Leocarni, and a royal court there is first mentioned in 866. In the early Middle Ages the town was led by the capitanei, prominent noble families, first named in a document of 1164 in which the Emperor Frederick I granted it market rights.

The Visconti of Milan took one of the town's castles in 1342, and it became known as the Visconti Castle. In the early 16th century the Swiss Confederates occupied Locarno, and the twelve cantons took turns to appoint a governor with civil and criminal jurisdiction. They demolished much of the castle in 1531, leaving the core. Under the Confederates Locarno grew into a commercial centre on a road linking Lombardy with German-speaking Switzerland.

By 1535 a Protestant community existed in Locarno, owing its existence to Giovanni Beccaria and refugees from Milan and Piedmont. After a public debate on 8 May 1549, Locarno declared itself Catholic in 1550, but a large group kept to the Protestant faith. In 1554 the Diet of Baden gave the Protestants an ultimatum to renounce their faith or go into exile, and on 3 March 1555 more than 100 people left for Zürich. The Act of Mediation of 1803 created the Canton of Ticino with Locarno as an independent municipality.

The sanctuary of Madonna del Sasso above the town, founded after a vision of the Virgin Mary experienced by the Franciscan brother Bartolomeo d'Ivrea in the night of 14 and 15 August 1480, is the main goal of pilgrimage. The Castello Visconteo, which now houses the Archaeological Museum, is one of nine Swiss heritage sites of national significance in the town.
locarno-treaties: Under the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost 13 per cent of its European territory and 12 per cent of its population, chiefly to France and a restored Poland, and its territory west of the Rhine was occupied by Allied troops. Revising the treaty became an aim of German politicians of the Weimar Republic. The foreign minister, Gustav Stresemann, hoped to win the goodwill of the Allies by fulfilling its terms, and wanted peace with France, the recovery of land lost to Poland and an end to reparations and the occupation. France was chiefly concerned with security and had signed treaties with Poland, Czechoslovakia, Romania and Yugoslavia.

The push came when the Allies postponed their withdrawal from the Cologne region after finding violations of the disarmament provisions. In early 1925 Stresemann sent secret memorandums to Britain and France proposing a treaty by which the parties interested in the Rhine borders would settle their issues peacefully. Opposition at home was strong, especially to renouncing Alsace-Lorraine.

The delegates met at Locarno, Switzerland, from 5 to 16 October 1925, and there were seven agreements. In the main treaty of mutual guarantee, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Belgium and Italy guaranteed the inviolability of the German-Belgian and German-French borders fixed at Versailles and promised to observe the demilitarised zone of the Rhineland. Germany and France, and Germany and Belgium, promised not to go to war with each other, with three exceptions, and to settle disputes peacefully with the League of Nations Council involved.

Arbitration agreements with France and Belgium, and arbitration treaties with Poland and Czechoslovakia, set up procedures for settling disputes. The treaties with Poland and Czechoslovakia gave no guarantee of Germany's eastern borders. France also signed treaties of mutual assistance with Poland and Czechoslovakia. The treaties were formally signed in London on 1 December 1925.

The Reichstag approved the treaties in November 1925 by 291 votes to 174, which led to the fall of the Luther government. In Poland they were seen as a defeat, and Józef Piłsudski said that every honest Pole spits when he hears the word Locarno. British troops left the Cologne region in January 1926, and Germany joined the League of Nations with a permanent seat on the Council on 10 September 1926. The last occupying troops left the Rhineland in 1930. Austen Chamberlain received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1925, and Aristide Briand and Stresemann shared it in 1926.

Contemporaries spoke of the spirit of Locarno, but Hans Mommsen wrote that it concealed a tenacious struggle over national interests. The treaties went out of force in practice on 7 March 1936, when German troops entered the demilitarised Rhineland and the other signatories responded only with verbal condemnation.
lodi-dynasty: The Lodis were an Afghan or Turco-Afghan tribe, first settled between the Gomal River and the Sulaiman Mountains, who took part in the valuable horse trade between Turan and India. Bahlul's grandfather, Malik Bahram, was a horse merchant who entered the service of the governor of Multan under Firuz Shah Tughlaq. His son Sultan Shah received the iqta of Sirhind and the title of Islam Khan, and gathered a large following there. After Islam Khan's death in 1431 the Lodis split into camps, and Bahlul soon succeeded in uniting them.

Bahlul Khan Lodi took power in Delhi on 19 April 1451 and reigned until 1489, replacing the Sayyid dynasty. Most of his reign was spent fighting the Sharqi dynasty of the Jaunpur Sultanate, which he annexed, placing his eldest surviving son Barbak on its throne in 1486. His son Sikandar Khan Lodi (r. 1489–1517) refounded Agra as a Muslim city in 1504 and shifted the capital there from Delhi. He required his Pashtun nobles to submit their accounts to a state audit, and conquered and annexed Bihar from the Sharqis.

Ibrahim Khan Lodi (r. 1517–1526), Sikandar's eldest son, faced numerous rebellions, among them that of his brother Jalaluddin and of Pashtun nobles who backed the governor of Bihar. He arrested the nobles who opposed him.

Daulat Khan, the governor of Lahore, asked Babur, the Timurid ruler of Kabul, to invade, and Ibrahim's uncle Alam Khan also supported Babur. At Panipat in April 1526 Babur, with about 24,000 men armed with muskets and artillery, faced Ibrahim's army of about 100,000 men and 1,000 elephants, which had never fought against gunpowder weapons. Ibrahim died on the field with some 20,000 of his men. The remaining Lodi lands passed to the new Mughal Empire, though Ibrahim's brother Mahmud Lodi kept up resistance until the battle of Ghaghra in 1529.

Like earlier sultans, the Lodis styled themselves deputies of the Abbasid caliphs. They gave cash stipends and revenue-free lands to the Muslim ulama and Sufi shaikhs. Sikandar's policy was strict Sunni orthodoxy: he destroyed Hindu temples and, under pressure from the ulama, allowed the execution of a Brahman. Muslims paid zakat and non-Muslims jizya, though Hindu officers served in the revenue administration. The Lodis minted no gold or silver coins for lack of the metals, and taxes were often paid in grain. Lodi architecture made extensive use of domes, and Sikandar composed Persian poetry under the pen name Gulrukhi.
lodz: Łódź first appears in a written record of 1332, issued by Władysław the Hunchback, Duke of Łęczyca, which transferred the village of Łodzia to the Bishopric of Włocławek. King Władysław II Jagiełło granted it town rights in 1423. For centuries it was a small remote settlement among woodlands and marshes, privately held by the Kuyavian bishops, and its economy rested on agriculture until the 19th century. In 1793 it passed to Prussia, and in 1815 it joined Congress Poland.

In 1820 the Congress Kingdom designated Łódź for centrally planned industrial development. Rajmund Rembieliński headed a commission that created a new city centre around an octagonal square and then cotton mill colonies along a main street, Piotrkowska. Growth was rapid from 1850, with many Jewish and German migrants. The population rose from 13,000 in 1840 to over 500,000 in 1913. Władysław Reymont's novel The Promised Land documents the city's social inequalities.

Łódź became the capital of its voivodeship in 1919. German forces took the city in September 1939, and it was incorporated into Reichsgau Wartheland and renamed Litzmannstadt in April 1940. Its large Jewish minority was forced into the walled Litzmannstadt Ghetto and from there sent to concentration and extermination camps. Soviet forces liberated the city on 19 January 1945, and it temporarily took over the functions of the capital before Warsaw was rebuilt. The National Film School opened in 1948. After 1989 the textile industry collapsed and the city declined.

Łódź is a city in central Poland, 120 kilometres south-west of Warsaw and the capital of Łódź Voivodeship. Piotrkowska Street, a little over five kilometres long, is its main commercial street. Its industrial heritage and Polish Art Nouveau architecture attract visitors, and the National Film School trained directors such as Andrzej Wajda and Roman Polański. Muzeum Sztuki, founded in 1931, was the first museum in Europe dedicated to modern art. The city is now a hub for business services, and in 2017 it joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Film.
lofoten: Lofoten is an archipelago and traditional district in the county of Nordland, Norway, at the 68th and 69th parallels north. It has dramatic mountains and peaks, open sea, sheltered bays and beaches. Seen from the sea it looks like a closed wall some 100 kilometres long, which gives it the name Lofotveggen. The principal islands, running north to south, are Austvågøya, Gimsøya, Vestvågøya, Flakstadøya and Moskenesøya, with the small isolated islands of Værøy and Røst further south. The open Vestfjorden lies between the archipelago and the mainland. Its winters are extremely mild for its latitude, because the Norwegian Sea is warmed by the North Atlantic Current. The Moskstraumen, a system of tidal eddies in western Lofoten, is the root of the term maelstrom.

There is evidence of human settlement in Lofoten for at least 11,000 years. The earliest archaeological sites are only about 5,500 years old, at the transition from the early to the late Stone Age. Iron Age agriculture, livestock and significant habitation can be traced to about 250 BCE, and in the lowlands, especially on Vestvågøy, agriculture has had a large part since the Bronze Age. The town of Vågan, near today's Kabelvåg, is the first known town formation in northern Norway. It existed in the early Viking Age, perhaps earlier.

For more than a thousand years the islands have been the centre of great cod fisheries. The cod migrate south from the Barents Sea in winter and gather in Lofoten to spawn. For a long time Bergen was the hub for the export of cod to different parts of Europe, particularly when the Hanseatic League controlled the trade. The Lofotr Viking Museum near Borg on Vestvågøya has a reconstructed longhouse 83 metres long, the largest known, and Borg has many finds from the Iron Age and Viking Age. In March 1941 British commandos raided the islands in Operation Claymore.

Lofoten comprises the municipalities of Vågan, Vestvågøy, Flakstad, Moskenes, Værøy and Røst, and its towns are Svolvær and Leknes. The main islands are joined to each other and to the mainland by road bridges. The sea around the islands is rich in life, and the Røst Reef west of Røst is a deep-water coral reef. Lofoten has the largest seabird colony in mainland Europe, with puffins among the millions of birds. The highest mountain is Higravstinden, at 1,161 metres on Austvågøy. In Svolvær the sun stays above the horizon from 25 May to 17 July.
logarithm: The history of logarithms in seventeenth-century Europe saw the discovery of a new function that took analysis beyond the reach of algebraic methods. Before Napier's book of 1614 there were techniques of similar aim, such as prosthaphaeresis, which relies on trigonometric identities, and tables of progressions, which Jost Bürgi developed extensively around 1600. Napier coined the Middle Latin term logarithmus, literally 'ratio-number', from the Greek logos, proportion or ratio, and arithmos, number. The modern view comes from Leonhard Euler, who in the 18th century connected logarithms to the exponential function and introduced the letter e as the base of natural logarithms.

The logarithm of a number to a given base is the exponent the base must be raised to in order to give the number, so that the logarithm of 1000 to base 10 is 3. It is the inverse of exponentiation, as subtraction is of addition. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms of the factors, and that of a quotient the difference. Three bases are particularly common: 10, the number e, about 2.718, and 2. Base 10 suits calculation by hand, base e is widespread in mathematics because of its simple derivative, and base 2 is used in computer science and information theory.

Henry Briggs compiled the first table in 1617, with the common logarithms of all integers from 1 to 1000 to 14 digits. Because numbers differing by a factor of 10 have logarithms differing by whole numbers, a table needed only the fractional part, the mantissa; the whole part, the characteristic, came from counting digits. Pierre-Simon Laplace called logarithms an admirable artifice that doubled the life of the astronomer by reducing the labour of many months to a few days. Gunter's rule, a logarithmic scale, was invented soon after Napier's work, and William Oughtred made it into the slide rule by setting two such scales to move against each other. Logarithms also underlie the decibel, pH, and the measure of information in bits.
logrono: Logroño lies in the north of La Rioja, mainly on the right, southern bank of the Ebro, 384 metres above sea level. It has historically been a place of passage, and the Camino de Santiago runs through it. The name is of uncertain origin. It first appears as Lucronio in a document of 965, in which García Sánchez I of Pamplona gave the place to the Monastery of San Millán. The most widely accepted view is that it comes from an older Celtic word, Gronio or Gronno, meaning the ford or the pass, from the frequent crossing of the Ebro there.

The site was an old settlement, first of the Romans under the name Vareia, a commercial port founded near an older city of the Berones. From the 10th century the kings of Navarre and Castile disputed possession of Logroño, and it was finally annexed to Castile. In 1095 Alfonso VI of Castile granted the town a charter of rights that served as a model for other Spanish cities.

John II of Castile made Logroño a city on 7 February 1431, and on 20 July 1444 added the titles Very noble and Very loyal, which still appear on its seal, in recognition of its loyalty against John II of Aragon. Francis I of France granted it three fleurs-de-lis for its shield on 5 July 1523, for its resistance to the French siege of 1521, which is remembered at the festival of San Bernabé on 11 June. In 1609 and 1610 Logroño was the main seat of the Basque witch trials, part of the Spanish Inquisition. Isabella II gave it the title of Excellence on 6 December 1854 for its conduct during a cholera epidemic.

Logroño is the capital of the autonomous community of La Rioja and its commercial and financial centre. Its economy depends heavily on Rioja wine, and the city also makes wood, metal and textile products. Its sights include the Con-Catedral de Santa María de la Redonda and the churches of San Bartolomé and Santiago. A bridge at Mantible, built in the Roman era, was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural in 1983.
logting: The name means Law Thing, a law assembly, from the Old Norse lǫgþing. A ting has existed in the Faroes for over a millennium, and in the Viking era the Løgting was the highest authority on the islands, an alþing with both legislative and judicial authority and no executive power. The earliest sources place it on Tinganes, now the oldest neighbourhood of Tórshavn; Vikings liked to hold a ting in a neutral, uninhabited place. Its founding is not documented, but the Færeyinga saga mentions it as well established in an account of a mid-10th century dispute between the chieftains Havgrímur and Einar Suðuroyingur. It was an assembly of the best men, wealthier farmers in a kind of republic of about 4,000 people.

In 1274 King Magnus VI of Norway introduced the Norwegian Landslog, and the ting became an assembly of representatives of six local vártings with only judicial authority, its president, the Løgmaður, appointed by the king. The Faroes gained their first constitution on 24 June 1298, the Seyðabrævið, or Sheep Letter. Around 1380 they came with Norway under the Danish throne. The Løgting kept some influence until absolute monarchy was introduced under Frederick III in 1660, and it was abolished in 1816, its judicial work passing to other courts.

Denmark's free constitution of 1849 ended the islands' special status without consulting the Faroese, many of whom wished to see the Løgting reinstated. The Act of 23 March 1852 reconstituted it as an advisory body, which first met on Ólavsøka in 1852. It became the platform of the Faroese nationalist movement, whose chief demand was home rule with legislative powers. Its protocols have been in Faroese since 1927.

During the Second World War the United Kingdom occupied the Faroes on 12 April 1940, and the Løgting functioned as a legislative assembly. At a vote on 14 September 1946 the electorate chose between a Danish proposal of home rule and secession, and 161 more votes favoured secession. The Danish government contested the legality of the process, and the king dissolved the parliament. A later election gave parties favouring union with Denmark a majority of 2,000 votes, and the Home Rule Act came into force on 1 April 1948.

Both sides still argue over the 1946 result: some hold that a majority was a majority, others that so small a margin was too little for so weighty a decision. Under home rule the Løgting legislates in the matters taken over from Denmark, while defence and foreign policy lie outside it.
loire: The Loire is 1,006 kilometres long and drains 117,054 square kilometres, more than a fifth of France. It rises near Mont Gerbier de Jonc in the Cévennes, in the department of Ardèche, flows north through Nevers to Orléans, then west through Tours and Nantes to the Bay of Biscay at Saint-Nazaire. Its largest tributary is the Allier, at 410 km, followed by the Vienne, the Cher and the Indre. Its name comes from the Latin Liger, itself from a Gaulish word meaning silt or sediment. It gives its name to six departments, and it flows with few dams or locks, floods usually coming in February and March.

Studies of the region suggest that the early Loire flowed north and joined the Seine, until the lower Loire, flowing west, captured it and produced the present river. The Gauls used it as a trading route by 600 BCE, linking the metals of the Armorican Massif with Phoenicia and Greece by way of Lyon. The Romans developed Cenabum, which they named Aurelianis, and began Caesarodunum, now Tours. Christianity spread through the basin from the 3rd century. In 408 the Alans, under King Sangiban, crossed the river and settled along its middle course.

During the Hundred Years' War the Loire marked the border between the French and the English. Joan of Arc's relief of the siege of Orléans in 1429 was the turning point of the war. Under François I, who reigned from 1515 to 1547, the Italian Renaissance deeply influenced the valley's architecture. River traffic was long hindered by floods and droughts; in the 17th century Jean-Baptiste Colbert had stone retaining walls and quays built from Roanne to Nantes. Floods in 1707 were said to have drowned 50,000 people. In 1700 Nantes had more inland waterway craft than any other French port, but railways killed off the surviving traffic from the 1850s.

The middle stretch, about 280 km long, is known as the Garden of France and holds over a thousand châteaux, among them Amboise, Chambord, Chenonceau and Villandry, many begun as feudal strongholds. Count Foulques Nerra of Anjou built defensive keeps there between 987 and 1040. The stretch between the Pays de la Loire and Centre-Val de Loire regions was added to UNESCO's World Heritage list on 2 December 2000. Vineyards run from Muscadet near Nantes to Sancerre, and Anjou, Saumur, Chinon and Vouvray lie between.
loja-ecuador: Loja was definitively founded on 8 December 1548 by the Spanish captain Alonso de Mercadillo in the Cuxibamba valley, after an earlier site of the mid-1540s near La Toma in the Catamayo canyon proved unhealthy. Accounts say the move followed severe earthquake damage and outbreaks of malaria, and that the town took its name from Mercadillo's birthplace, Loja in Spain. About a century after its founding it was destroyed by an earthquake and rebuilt on its present site. In 1660 the city was consecrated to St. Sebastian to prevent destruction by earthquakes.

In the colonial period Loja stood on the royal road between Quito and Cuzco, was an administrative hub for the southern highlands and lay near the gold-mining district of Zaruma. From the late 16th century expeditions toward the eastern Andean slopes and the Amazon Basin were organised from Loja, most notably those associated with Juan de Salinas Loyola. Its coat of arms was granted by King Philip II of Spain in 1571.

Two dates mark the city's part in the independence era. Civic commemorations name 18 November 1820 as the political declaration of independence, while the formal Acta de Independencia was recorded on 17 February 1822. Simón Bolívar visited the city in 1822, in the campaigns connected with the consolidation of Gran Colombia. The National University of Loja was founded in 1859, and the Church of Santo Domingo, built in 1557, lost most of its Gothic facade in an earthquake in 1867, leaving only its twin spires. A small hydroelectric plant began operating in 1897 and the Loja Hydroelectric Plant was inaugurated in 1899, and the city is widely credited as the first in Ecuador to have electric lighting.

Loja is the capital of Loja Province, in the Cuxibamba valley in the south of Ecuador, at 2,060 metres above sea level, and has about 203,000 inhabitants. It is known as the Music and Cultural Capital of Ecuador. The cathedral, with 16th-century adobe in its fabric and a building dating from 1838, houses the Virgin of El Cisne for six months of the year; her statue is carried on the backs of the faithful to and from the town of El Cisne, 45 kilometres north. The city lies beside Podocarpus National Park, and the Pan-American Highway runs past it.
lok-sabha: A large part of the Indian subcontinent was under British rule from 1858 to 1947, and the office of Viceroy of India was created along with an Executive Council of high officials. The Indian Councils Act 1861 provided for a Legislative Council of members of the Executive Council and non-official members. The Act of 1892 established legislatures in each province of British India, and the Act of 1909 admitted some Indians to the councils. These acts raised the representation of Indians, but their power stayed limited and the electorate very small. The Government of India Act 1919 created the Central Legislative Assembly, for which Parliament House in New Delhi was built and opened in 1927.

The Lok Sabha is the lower house of the bicameral Parliament of India, whose upper house is the Rajya Sabha. Members are elected by adult universal suffrage under a first-past-the-post system, and hold their seats for five years unless the president dissolves the house earlier on the advice of the union council of ministers. It meets in the Parliament House in New Delhi.

The Constitution set its maximum size at 552 members. Between 1952 and 2020 the president also nominated two members of the Anglo-Indian community, a practice abolished by the 104th amendment in January 2020. About 131 seats are reserved for scheduled castes and scheduled tribes. The number of seats per state has been frozen since a constitutional amendment of 1976, using the population of the 1971 census. The house elects a Speaker and a Deputy Speaker from among its members.

The Lok Sabha holds powers that the Rajya Sabha lacks. The Constitution makes the council of ministers responsible only to the Lok Sabha, so a motion of no confidence can be passed only there, and if it succeeds the Prime Minister and the council of ministers resign collectively. Money bills may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can deliberate on them for up to 14 days.

Three sessions are held in a year: budget, monsoon and winter. The first hour of each sitting is Question Hour, when members question ministers on administration and policy. If the two houses enact conflicting legislation, a joint sitting is held, in which the Lok Sabha generally prevails because it has more than twice as many members as the Rajya Sabha.
lokoja: The area has been inhabited for hundreds of years by people of different ethnic groups, drawn in part by its nearness to the Niger and Benue rivers. Nupe groups from Gbara near Bida are believed to have been among the first to settle, on Mount Patti. The Kupa and Kakanda are said to have come downstream along the Niger, and Oworo people, a Yoruba subgroup, from Ile-Ife joined them later. The area became a centre of trade. Several peoples claim to have named the city: the Oworo give Ilu Oke Oja, the market town on the hill, the Hausa Loko Ja, a red corner, and the Nupe Patti Lukongi, the hill of doves.

The Nupe and Zazzau emirs historically appointed Hausa people as political leaders of the town, while the Nupe held the post of chief imam. The rulers, called Maigari, included Hamza, Dauda, Musa and Muhammadu Maikarfi. The British explorer Dr William Balfour Baikie arrived first in 1854 and again in 1857, and the present settlement was established by him in 1857 on the site of an earlier model farm built during the failed Niger expedition of 1841. The British installed Bukar, a convert to Islam, who was widely seen as a stooge of the British.

Lokoja was the capital of the British Northern Nigeria Protectorate and remained a convenient administrative town after the amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria in 1914. Sir Frederick Lugard, the first Governor-General, governed the new nation from Lokoja. Sites of this period include the spot where the Royal Niger Company flag was lowered in 1900 and the Bishop Crowther primary school, regarded as the first primary school in Northern Nigeria.

Lokoja is the capital of Kogi State, about 165 km south-west of Abuja, and a trade centre for agricultural products. Its people include the Oworo, Nupe, Bassa-Nge, Igala and Ebira, who live in separate quarters but are closely related socially and politically. The Maigari of Lokoja still rules with twelve sub-chiefs. Islam, Christianity and traditional religion are all practised.
lola-montez: Eliza Rosanna Gilbert was born into an Anglo-Irish family, the daughter of Ensign Edward Gilbert and Eliza Oliver. Her father's regiment took the family to India in 1823, where he died of cholera, and her mother soon married Lieutenant Patrick Craigie. The child was sent back to Britain to school in Montrose, Sunderland and Bath, and was known as a mischief-maker. In 1837, at sixteen, she eloped with Lieutenant Thomas James; they separated five years later in Calcutta, and she became a professional dancer under a stage name.

Her London debut in June 1843 as Lola Montez, the Spanish dancer, was spoiled when she was recognised as Mrs James, so she left for the continent, where she had success in Paris and Warsaw. She had a disappointing Paris debut in 1844 in Fromental Halévy's opera Le lazzarone, and moved in literary circles that included Franz Liszt, George Sand and Alexandre Dumas. In 1846 she arrived in Munich and became the mistress of King Ludwig I of Bavaria.

Ludwig made her Countess of Landsfeld and Baroness of Rosenthal on 25 August 1847 and gave her a large annuity. For more than a year she used her influence in favour of liberalism and against the Jesuits. The minister of state, Karl von Abel, was dismissed with his cabinet after objecting to her Bavarian nationality and title, and at her insistence the king closed the university. In March 1848, under revolutionary pressure, the university was reopened, Ludwig abdicated in favour of his son Maximilian II, and she fled.

She went to London, married George Trafford Heald, and had to flee a bigamy action because her divorce from James forbade remarriage. In 1851 she went to the United States, and in 1853 reached San Francisco, where she married the newspaperman Patrick Hull and settled at Grass Valley, California. There she gave dancing lessons to the young Lotta Crabtree. In 1855 she toured Australia, where her Spider Dance scandalised Melbourne, and at Ballarat in February 1856 she attacked the editor Henry Seekamp with a whip after a bad review.

Back in America she failed to revive her stage career but found a new one as a lecturer, speaking on topics such as the Wits and Women of Paris, and as a writer, publishing The Arts of Beauty. In her last years she worked among women trying to leave prostitution. She died in New York on 17 January 1861, though accounts differ on the cause and her age, and she is buried in Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn. Her story has inspired novels and several films, and some writers have seen her as a source for Irene Adler in Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes story A Scandal in Bohemia.
lombard-league: The Lombard League was an alliance of cities, supported by the popes, formed to counter the attempts of the Hohenstaufen Holy Roman emperors to establish direct administrative control over the cities of the Kingdom of Italy, which had governed themselves in practice for many decades. It succeeded the Veronese League, set up in 1164 by Verona, Padua, Vicenza and the Republic of Venice after Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa claimed direct control of Italy at the Diet of Roncaglia in 1158 and began replacing the podestà magistrates with his own commissioners. Pope Alexander III backed it, and the town of Alessandria was named in his honour.

According to tradition the League was formed after the oath of Pontida on 7 April 1167. Besides Verona, Padua, Vicenza and Venice it included cities such as Cremona, Mantua, Piacenza, Brescia, Genoa, Bologna, Milan and Parma, and even some lords. Though it was not a declared separatist movement, it openly challenged the emperor's claim to power. Frederick strove against the cities, especially Milan, which had been occupied and devastated in 1162, but he could no longer play them off against each other. At the Battle of Legnano on 29 May 1176 his army was defeated.
A six-year truce followed the Treaty of Venice of 1177, and in the Peace of Constance of 1183 the cities agreed to remain loyal to the empire while keeping local jurisdiction over their territories.

The League was renewed several times. Emperor Frederick II's efforts to gain greater power in Italy were aborted by the cities, which earned the League an imperial ban. He took Vicenza and won the Battle of Cortenuova in 1237, but rejected Milan's peace overtures and insisted on unconditional surrender, and in October 1238 he had to raise the siege of Brescia. Pope Gregory IX excommunicated him in 1239. In the Siege of Parma in 1248 his camp was taken and he lost the imperial treasure. The League was dissolved in 1250, when Frederick II died.

Besides being a military alliance, the League had a stable government of its own, the Rectores Lombardiae, or regents of Lombardy, and is considered one of the first examples of a confederation in Europe. A council of its members, the Universitas, consisted of representatives appointed by the member cities, and voted by majority on matters such as admitting new members and war or peace with the emperor. Its powers grew over the years to include regulation, taxation and justice. The League also abolished duties by creating a customs union.
lombards: Roman historians of the 1st and 2nd centuries mention the Lombards, or Langobardi, as one of the Suebian peoples and report them on the Lower Elbe in the early 1st century. Tacitus, writing about 100 CE, calls them a small people surrounded by the most powerful, who kept safe by daring the perils of war. A single mention in the Cosmographia of Julius Honorius is the only source for the 3rd and 4th centuries.

The standard explanation derives the name from Proto-Germanic words for long and beard. Three early medieval texts give mythical accounts of the migration, the oldest being the Origo Gentis Langobardorum. They say the people were first called Winnili and were ruled by the brothers Ibor and Aio, whose mother and adviser was Gambara.

The Lombards reappear in the late 5th century near the Danube. After Odoacer defeated the Rugii in 487 or 488 they occupied Rugiland. King Audoin settled them in Pannonia and defeated the Gepid leader Thurisind in 551 or 552, and his successor Alboin destroyed the Gepid kingdom in 567. Near Szólád, archaeologists have found burials of Lombard men and women together as families, which was unusual among Germanic peoples.

In the spring of 568 Alboin, fearing the Avars, led the Lombards into Italy, which the Gothic War had left depopulated and devastated. Saxons, Suebi, Sarmatians, Gepids, Bulgars and others joined them, and the invasion was almost unopposed. By late 569 they held all of northern Italy north of the Po except Pavia, which fell in 572. The kingdom reached its height under Liutprand in the 8th century. Charlemagne conquered it in 774, but Lombard nobles ruled the south into the 11th century, when the Normans conquered them.

Lombard kings can be traced to about 380, and government is thought to have begun as an assembly that chose chiefs and war leaders from a nobility. The Lombard language is extinct, unless Cimbrian and Mòcheno are surviving dialects. Only fragments survive in runic inscriptions and in words quoted in Latin texts. St Barbatus of Benevento recorded that some Lombards venerated a golden viper and a tree. In their nomadic phase they made portable arms and jewellery, and settlement and Christianity brought churches and frescoes.
lombardy: Lombardy lies in northern Italy between the Alps and the tributaries of the river Po. It is bordered by the Swiss cantons of Ticino and Grisons to the north, by Trentino-Alto Adige and Veneto to the east, Emilia-Romagna to the south and Piedmont to the west. About 47 per cent of its territory is plain, 41 per cent mountains and 12 per cent hills. The Po forms its southern border for about 210 kilometres,. The name comes from the Lombards, a Germanic people whose name derives from Late Latin Longobardus, perhaps meaning long beard.

The area has been settled since at least the second millennium BCE, and the rock drawings of the Camuni in Valcamonica are well preserved. In the centuries after the fall of the Western Empire it suffered destruction from a series of invasions. After 540 Pavia became the permanent capital of the Ostrogothic Kingdom. The last and most effective invasion was that of the Lombards, who migrated from the Carpathian basin in 568 in fear of the Avars. Their long-lasting reign, with its capital at Pavia, gave the region its name, and Pavia remained the capital of the kingdom of Italy until 1024.

From the late 11th century Lombardy broke into many small autonomous city-states, the medieval communes. In the 15th century the Duchy of Milan was one of the wealthiest states of the Renaissance, and Milan and Mantua were centres of Renaissance culture, with Leonardo da Vinci and Andrea Mantegna. Lombard merchants and bankers traded as far as northern Europe, and the word Lombard came to mean a banker, as in Lombard Street in London. After the Battle of Pavia the Duchy of Milan became a possession of the Habsburgs of Spain, while the east, including Bergamo and Brescia, was controlled by the Republic of Venice.

Austrian rule was restored in 1815 as the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. The region was an important centre of the Risorgimento, with the Five Days of Milan in March 1848 and the Ten Days of Brescia in 1849. Lombardy was annexed to the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia after the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859, in which it was the main theatre of battle, with fighting at Magenta and Solferino.
Lombardy is the most populous region of Italy, with about 10 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Milan. Eleven of Italy's 58 UNESCO World Heritage Sites are in Lombardy.
lombok: Lombok is an island in West Nusa Tenggara province, Indonesia, in the chain of the Lesser Sunda Islands. The Lombok Strait separates it from Bali to the west and the Alas Strait from Sumbawa to the east. It is roughly circular, with a tail, the Sekotong Peninsula, to the south-west, and about 70 kilometres across. The provincial capital and largest city is Mataram. The Lombok Strait marks the biogeographical division between the fauna of the Indomalayan realm and that of Australasia, known as the Wallace Line after Alfred Russel Wallace, who first commented on it. The name Lomboq is Sasak for straight, honest.

The Majapahit manuscript Nagarakretagama, of the 14th century, names Lombok Mirah as one of the islands under Majapahit suzerainty. Little is known of the island before the 17th century apart from the Babad Lombok, which records the Samalas eruption of 1257. Before that time it was made up of numerous competing and feuding petty states, each presided over by a Sasak prince. The neighbouring Balinese took advantage of this disunity and took control of western Lombok in the early 17th century. The Makassarese meanwhile invaded eastern Lombok from their colonies on Sumbawa.

The Dutch first visited Lombok in 1674. By 1750 the Balinese had taken over the whole island, but infighting split it into four feuding Balinese kingdoms. In 1838 the Mataram kingdom brought its rivals under control. In the east the Balinese held control from garrisoned forts. The village head became little more than a tax collector for the Balinese, villagers became a kind of serf, and the Sasak aristocracy lost much of its power and land.

About 85 percent of the inhabitants are Sasak, whose ancestors are thought to have migrated from Java in the first millennium BCE. Another 10 to 15 percent are Balinese. The Sasak are culturally and linguistically close to the Balinese but are mostly Muslim, unlike the Hindu Balinese. Before Islam arrived, Lombok had a long period of Hindu and Buddhist influence that came through Java. Traders from Sumbawa may have first brought Islam in the 17th century. The Babad Lombok tells how Sunan Prapen was sent on a military expedition to Lombok and Sumbawa to spread the new religion. Each year the festival Bau Nyale marks the catching of sea worms said in legend to be the Princess Mandalika.
lombok-strait: The Lombok Strait lies between the islands of Bali and Lombok in Indonesia and connects with the Indian Ocean. It is about 60 km long and about 40 km across at its northern opening. Its narrowest point is at the southern opening, about 20 km wide between Lombok and the island of Nusa Penida, which lies in the middle of the strait. The Gili Islands are on the Lombok side. The strait is at least 250 m deep, much deeper than the Strait of Malacca, and ships that draw too much water for Malacca, known as post-Malaccamax vessels, often use it instead.

The strait forms part of the Wallace Line, the biogeographical boundary named for Alfred Russel Wallace, who noted how abruptly the animals of Indomalaya give way to those of Australasia. When sea levels fell in the Pleistocene ice age, Bali, Java and Sumatra were joined to one another and to mainland Asia and shared its fauna. The deep water of the Lombok Strait kept Lombok and the Lesser Sunda archipelago isolated, and Australasian fauna colonised them instead.

The strait is also one of the main passages of the Indonesian Throughflow, which exchanges water between the Pacific and Indian oceans. Tides mix the water strongly around the Nusa Penida Sill, and the flow has two layers: the upper layer runs permanently southward, while the lower one reverses between south and north. A coral reef expedition in April 2001 found that the reef fauna of the strait was among the most diverse and richest in the world, and the longnosed spinner dolphin lives there in large numbers.
lome: Lomé lies on the Gulf of Guinea at the south-western corner of Togo, with its western edge along the border with Ghana, a few hundred metres from the city centre. Its name comes from Alomé, which in the Ewe language means "in the alo trees", a reference to the forest that stood there. Despite its latitude near the equator it has a tropical savanna climate, because it lies in the Dahomey Gap, with annual rainfall of 800 to 900 millimetres.

The city was founded by the Ewes and grew in the 19th century through German, British and African traders. British customs duties on alcohol and tobacco weighed heavily in the neighbouring Gold Coast, and Ewe traders from the Aflao and Keta area chose the nearby coast at Lomé to unload goods out of reach of customs officers. Growth began around 1880, and Hausa caravans from the cola routes joined European firms there. Togoland was created within the German colonial empire on 5 July 1884 by the Treaty of Togoville, signed by Gustav Nachtigal and King Mlapa III.

A road to Kpalimé was begun in 1892. A port opened in 1904 and made Lomé the only maritime contact point of Togo, ruining its rival Aného, and railways reached Aného in 1905, Kpalimé in 1907 and Atakpamé in 1909.

The population was 8,000 in 1914. German discriminatory patents and licences gradually pushed African traders out of import and export. In 1916 German companies were evicted and replaced by British and French firms. The French authorities created a council of notables in 1922, elective from 1925. In January 1923 a Lomé Women's Revolt forced the release of two arrested Duawo leaders, and a tax increase provoked riots in January 1933. The population grew from 30,000 in 1950 to 80,000 in 1960, the year of independence, and 200,000 in 1970.

Lomé is the capital and largest city of Togo, with an urban population of 837,437 and 2,188,376 residents in its metropolitan area at the 2022 census. Its port, with a free zone opened in 1968, handles much of the transit trade of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso. The Lomé Convention between the European Union and African, Caribbean and Pacific countries was first signed there on 28 February 1975, and the Lomé Peace Accord for Sierra Leone on 7 July 1999. The University of Lomé was founded in 1970. Colonial buildings include the Sacred Heart Cathedral in German neo-Gothic style, and the Akodesséwa district holds a fetish market.
lon-nol: Lon Nol was born in Prey Veng Province on 13 November 1913 to a family of mixed Khmer and Chinese descent. He was educated at the Lycée Chasseloup-Laubat in Saigon and at the Cambodian Royal Military Academy. He entered the French colonial civil service in 1937 as a magistrate and by 1946 was governor of Kratie Province. He joined the army in 1952 and fought the Viet Minh. After independence his nationalist Khmer Renovation party became part of the core of the Sangkum, the movement set up by Norodom Sihanouk for the elections of 1955.

He was appointed army chief of staff in 1955, commander-in-chief in 1960 and deputy prime minister in 1963. He became prime minister after the elections of 1966, and the following year troops savagely repressed the Samlaut Uprising in Battambang Province. Injured in a car crash in 1967, he withdrew for a time, then returned as prime minister in 1969 with Prince Sisowath Sirik Matak as his deputy.

On 12 March 1970 the two men closed the port of Sihanoukville to the North Vietnamese and demanded that all North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces leave Cambodia within 72 hours. Lon Nol at first refused to see Sihanouk deposed; on the night of 17 March Sirik Matak, with three army officers, compelled him at gunpoint to sign the necessary documents. Pro-Sihanouk demonstrations on 28 and 29 March were suppressed with several hundred deaths. The republic was declared on 9 October 1970. Sihanouk later claimed that the CIA had planned the coup, but there is no concrete evidence of its involvement.

The regime carried out mass killings of Vietnamese Cambodians. After a stroke in February 1971 Lon Nol's rule grew erratic and authoritarian: he made himself Marshal in April and suspended the National Assembly in October. By 1975 his government held little more than Phnom Penh and the temple of Preah Vihear.

He resigned on 1 April 1975, his name being first on a list of people the Khmer Rouge had vowed to execute, and went to Indonesia and then to Hawaii. In 1979 he settled in Fullerton, California, where he died of a heart condition on 17 November 1985. His brother Lon Non, a minister of the republic, was executed by the Khmer Rouge after the fall of Phnom Penh. Lon Nol called his ideology, a blend of nationalism and mysticism, Neo-Khmerism, and hoped to unite the Khmers of Cambodia with those of the Mekong Delta and Thailand.
londinium: Londinium stood on the north bank of the Thames, where the Romans held a bridgehead and a road nexus shortly after the Claudian invasion. It was centred on Cornhill and the River Walbrook and reached west to Ludgate Hill and east to Tower Hill. Unlike many cities of Roman Britain it was not placed on a native settlement. Before the conquest the area was lightly rolling open countryside, contested by the Catuvellauni to the west and the Trinovantes to the east. Of fifteen British routes in the Antonine Itinerary, seven ran to or from the city. Its name is of unknown origin and was probably based on a native Brittonic place name.

The earliest securely dated structure is a timber drain of 47 CE. The first town covered only about 1.4 square kilometres. Tacitus wrote that at the time of Boudica's revolt it was much frequented by merchants and trading vessels, though it lacked the name of colony. In 60 or 61 the Romans abandoned Londinium, which was razed. A large military fort was then built at Cornhill and the town was rebuilt as a planned town, recovering within about a decade. A port complex near London Bridge was quickly restored and expanded into the 3rd century, importing pottery, jewellery and wine.

By the 2nd century Londinium had perhaps 30,000 or 60,000 people. Hadrian visited in 122, and evidence of a large fire, dated to the 120s or 130s, has been found in many excavations. After about 150 the population may have fallen by as much as two-thirds. Between 190 and 225 the Romans built the London Wall, about 5 kilometres long and 6 metres high, and Saxon raiding from about 255 led to a riverside wall. In 296 the Frankish mercenaries of the usurper Allectus sacked the city and were slaughtered by Roman warships on the Thames. In the 5th century, with few troops left in Britain, the town declined drastically.

Many Roman ruins lie buried beneath London. Roman stretches of the wall can be seen near Tower Hill station, and a section of the river wall is visible inside the Tower of London. Parts of the amphitheatre are on display beneath the Guildhall Art Gallery. The London Mithraeum, dating from around 240, was rediscovered in 1954, and finds from the city are held in the Museum of London and the British Museum.
london: London stands on the River Thames in southeast England, at the head of a 50-mile (80 km) tidal estuary down to the North Sea. Its ancient core, the City of London, kept its medieval boundaries, while the City of Westminster to the west has been the site of the national government and parliament for centuries. Until 1889 the name London applied officially only to the City of London; since then it has also denoted the County of London and Greater London.

Since the 19th century the name has referred to the metropolis around the City, historically split among the counties of Middlesex, Essex, Surrey, Kent and Hertfordshire. Since 1965 it has largely comprised Greater London, governed by 33 local authorities and the Greater London Authority.

The first major settlement was founded by the Romans around 47 CE, about four years after their invasion of 43 CE. It lasted until about 61 CE, when the Iceni, led by Queen Boudica, stormed it and burnt it to the ground. The rebuilt Londinium prospered and superseded Colchester as the principal city of the Roman province of Britannia in 100. At its height in the 2nd century, Roman London had a population of about 60,000.

After Roman rule collapsed in the early 5th century the walled city was effectively abandoned. From about 500 an Anglo-Saxon settlement known as Lundenwic developed slightly west of the old Roman city, and by about 680 it had become a major port again. Repeated Viking assaults from the 820s brought decline. London grew rapidly in the 19th century and became the world's largest city at the time. It took over as a major financial centre shortly after 1795, when the Dutch Republic collapsed before the Napoleonic armies and many Amsterdam bankers moved there.

Greater London had a population of just over 9.8 million in 2025, and its wider metropolitan area about 15.4 million. In the 2021 census 40.6% of Londoners were foreign-born, and more than 300 languages are spoken in the city. It is governed by two tiers: the Greater London Authority, led by the mayor of London, and 32 borough councils with the City of London Corporation.

London has more than 50 universities and colleges. The London Underground is the world's oldest rapid transit system, and the Royal Observatory at Greenwich defines the Prime Meridian. In 2012 London became the first city to host the Summer Olympics three times, after 1908 and 1948.
long-island-sound: Long Island Sound is a marine sound and tidal estuary of the Atlantic Ocean. It lies chiefly between Connecticut to the north and Long Island in New York to the south, and from west to east it stretches 110 miles (180 km) from the East River and the Throgs Neck Bridge in New York City, along the North Shore of Long Island, to Block Island Sound. It forms part of the Intracoastal Waterway. It is 21 miles (34 km) across at its widest and varies in depth from 65 to 230 feet (20 to 70 m), a mix of fresh water from tributaries and salt water from the Atlantic.

Connecticut's major cities on the sound include Stamford, Norwalk, Bridgeport, New Haven and New London, and on the New York side lie Rye, Glen Cove, New Rochelle, Oyster Bay, Port Jefferson and parts of Queens and the Bronx. Rivers that empty into it include the Connecticut, Housatonic and Thames. The whole watershed held about 8.93 million people at the 2010 census.

About 18,000 years ago Connecticut, the Sound and much of Long Island lay under the Late Wisconsin Glacier, an ice sheet about 1,000 metres thick in its interior, when sea level was about 100 metres lower than today. The Sound formed when the terminal moraine that dammed glacial Lake Connecticut failed and sea water mixed with the lake's fresh water. Before colonisation an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 native people lived along its shores.

The first European to record its existence was the Dutch navigator Adriaen Block, who entered it from the East River in 1614. In colonial times it was known as the Devil's Belt, and the reefs across it as the Devil's Stepping Stones, which gave Stepping Stones Lighthouse its name.

As the Industrial Revolution grew, the Sound was used for manufacturing such as textiles and metal finishing, as well as fishing and oyster harvesting, and the growth brought pollution, including mercury discharged by the hatting industry in Danbury. From the 1950s and 1960s the federal government recognised the effects on water quality and health. After the Clean Water Act of 1972, the Environmental Protection Agency joined Connecticut and New York in 1985 to establish the Long Island Sound Study, with plans for restoration and clean-up.

Ferries link Long Island and Connecticut, notably the Bridgeport and Port Jefferson Ferry and the Cross Sound Ferry between Orient Point and New London, carrying vehicles and foot passengers. The Sound has long supported commercial and recreational fishing for oysters, lobsters, scallops, flounder, striped bass and bluefish. Underwater cables carry electricity beneath it, and bridges and a tunnel have been proposed over the years; no crossing has been built since the Throgs Neck Bridge in the early 1960s.
long-march: The Chinese Communist Party was founded in 1921 and at first worked with the nationalist Kuomintang. Chiang Kai-shek broke with it in April 1927, and the suppression of the party in Shanghai and other cities, together with failed urban uprisings, drove many supporters to rural strongholds such as the Jiangxi Soviet, which Mao Zedong organised. By 1930 the Red Army had set up the Chinese Soviet Republic around Ruijin, in Jiangxi and Fujian.

Under Zhou Enlai, the Comintern adviser Otto Braun and Bo Gu, the Red Army defeated four Nationalist attacks. The fifth campaign began in September 1933. Advised by the German Hans von Seeckt, Chiang's forces ringed Jiangxi with a fortified perimeter and besieged it. In July 1934 the party leadership forced Mao off the Politburo.

Bo, Braun and Zhou organised the evacuation in complete secrecy, and even senior leaders learned of the movements only at the last moment. Some 16,000 troops stayed behind as a rear guard. By the time the marchers crossed the Xiang River on 1 December 1934, after heavy losses in breaking Nationalist blockades, only 36,000 men remained. At Mao's suggestion the army turned from Hunan, where Chiang had set up defences, towards Guizhou.

The Zunyi Conference met from 15 to 17 January 1935. Bo Gu blamed the defeats on the enemy's superior numbers; Zhou Enlai blamed leadership decisions, himself among them; Zhang Wentian attacked Bo and Braun directly. The meeting reduced Soviet influence and strengthened Mao's position. Mao then avoided battle, crossing the Chishui River four times to escape encirclement before entering Yunnan, and the army later crossed the Jinsha River and took the Luding Bridge on 29 May.

In June and July 1935 the First Army met the Fourth Army under Zhang Guotao at Maogong. Zhang, who commanded superior forces, challenged the leadership of Zhou and Mao, and the two armies went separate ways. Mao's army, attacked on the way by forces of the Hui Ma clique, reached Shaanxi in October 1935 with about 8,000 survivors and joined the local Communists led by Liu Zhidan, Gao Gang and Xu Haidong. The Fourth Army was largely destroyed, and the Second Army under He Long completed its own march in October 1936.

The retreat cost the party most of its army but gave it the isolation to recover in the north, and the endurance of its survivors won it a good name among peasants. In 1935 Mao wrote that the Long March was a manifesto and a propaganda force. It marked the start of his rise to primacy and was featured heavily in his public image.
long-turkish-war: Skirmishes along the Habsburg–Ottoman border intensified from 1591, and in 1592 the Croatian fort of Bihać fell to the Ottomans. In the spring of 1593 Ottoman forces from the Eyalet of Bosnia besieged Sisak in Croatia, and the Christian forces won the Battle of Sisak on 22 June 1593, which ended the Hundred Years' Croatian–Ottoman War.

The Long Turkish War itself began on 29 July 1593, when an Ottoman army under Sinan Pasha opened a campaign against the Habsburg monarchy with the Siege of Veszprém. In Hungary the war is called the Fifteen Years' War, counted from the Ottoman campaign of 1591–1592 that took Bihać. The Ottomans aimed to seize Vienna, the Habsburgs to recover the central territories of the Kingdom of Hungary held by the Ottomans, and control of the Danube line and its fortresses was crucial.

The Reichstag convened in 1594, declared a legal state of Türkenkriege and voted a tax grant that it renewed four years later and again in 1603. In 1595 Pope Clement VIII organised an alliance, and Emperor Rudolf II and Sigismund Báthory of Transylvania signed a treaty of alliance in Prague; Aron Vodă of Moldavia and Michael the Brave of Wallachia joined later that year.

Christian forces under Karl von Mansfeld captured Esztergom and Visegrád in 1595 but did not besiege Buda. Michael the Brave took forts along the Lower Danube from autumn 1594, and after an Ottoman counter-offensive of 100,000 men took Bucharest and Târgoviște, he defeated the Ottomans at Târgoviște, Bucharest and Giurgiu in October 1595.

The Ottomans took Eger in 1596. At Mezőkeresztes, on 24–26 October 1596, a combined Habsburg–Transylvanian force of 45–50,000 men lost the battle after soldiers who thought they had won stopped fighting to plunder the Ottoman camp. The Habsburgs recaptured Győr and Komárom in 1598. In 1599 the Ottomans and their Tatar allies raided towns in the Nitra valley in Upper Hungary and took thousands of people into slavery.

The last phase of the war, from 1604 to 1606, was the uprising of Stephen Bocskai, who resisted Rudolf's prosecutions of noblemen. Declared Prince of Transylvania on 21 February 1605 and of Hungary on 17 April 1605, he concluded the Treaty of Vienna with Rudolf in 1606. The Peace of Zsitvatorok of 11 November 1606 brought meagre gains to the two main empires: the Ottomans won Eger and Kanizsa but gave the region of Vác, occupied since 1541, to Austria.

It confirmed that the Ottomans could not penetrate further into Habsburg territory and that Transylvania was beyond Habsburg power. Rudolf presented the war as a victory, but he ended it deep in debt, and once peace was made the Habsburgs turned on one another in the Brothers' Quarrel between Rudolf and his brother Matthias.
longmen-grottoes: The earliest history of the grottoes is traced to Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei, who moved his capital from Datong to Luoyang. Work went on in four phases between 493 and 1127. The first belongs to the Northern Wei (493 to 534). The second, from 524 to 626, saw slow development because of strife in the region. The third, from 626 to the mid-8th century, was the peak under the Tang. The fourth, from the later Tang into the Northern Song, saw decline.

Guyang-dong, credited to Xiaowen, was the first cave temple, built at the centre of the southern floor of the West Hill. Emperor Xuanwu followed with three more caves, the Three Binyang Caves, two in memory of his father and one of his mother, built over 24 years. More than 30 per cent of the caves date from the Northern Wei.

The grottoes lie 12 km south of Luoyang, on both banks of the Yi River between the hills of Xiangshan and Longmenshan. The area was once called Yique, the Gate of the Yi River, and the name Dragon's Gate comes from the two hills, which resemble gate towers. The images, many once painted, are carved on the cliffs and inside caves cut into the limestone along about a kilometre of the river. There are as many as 100,000 statues, from 25 mm to 17 m in height, nearly 2,500 stelae and inscriptions, and over sixty pagodas. Most of the work is on the western bank.

About 60 per cent of the caves date from the Tang. The Fengxian-si cave was completed in 675, and Emperor Gaozong and Empress Wu Zetian intensified the work while ruling from Luoyang. Guyang-dong has about 800 inscriptions, the most of any cave in China, and a central Sakyamuni with bodhisattvas on either side. Its figures are slim in the Northern Wei style, while Tang work is more complex and includes women and court figures.

The site was heavily vandalised after the fall of the Qing in 1912. Western collectors removed major pieces in the early 20th century, and two murals taken from the grottoes are reported to be in the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art. During the Second Sino-Japanese War Japanese forces looted the site, and many relics are now in Japanese museums. The Cultural Revolution destroyed the heads of many statues. The site was protected after 1949, a Longmen Relics Care Agency was set up in 1953, and the State Council declared it a national monument under special protection in 1961. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage List in 2000.
loom: The word loom comes from the Old English geloma, which meant a utensil, tool or machine of any kind. Weaving is done with two sets of threads that cross one another. The warp threads are stretched on the loom, and each thread of the weft is inserted so that it passes over and under them. The ends of the warp are fastened to two beams, which are held apart to keep the threads taut.

A loom must perform three principal motions. Shedding pulls part of the warp aside to form a shed, the space through which the shuttle carries the weft. Picking inserts the weft, and battening beats the newest weft against the fell, the edge of the cloth. Lifting the odd and even threads alternately gives a tabby weave, while more intricate sequences of sheds give weaves such as twill.

Looms vary with the weaver's way of life: nomadic weavers tend to use light, portable looms, and those in cramped city dwellings a tall upright loom. The backstrap loom is a simple loom with ancient roots, still used in Andean textiles and in Central, East and South Asia. One bar is fixed to an object and the other to the weaver by a strap, so the weaver leans back to tension the warp.

The warp-weighted loom is a vertical loom that may have originated in the Neolithic period. Hanging weights keep bundles of warp threads taut, and the finished cloth can be rolled round the top beam. The earliest evidence of a horizontal loom is a pottery dish from ancient Egypt dated to 4400 BCE. It shows a frame loom with treadles that lifted the warp threads, leaving the weaver's hands free to pass and beat the weft.

John Kay patented the flying shuttle in 1733. A weaver flicked a picking stick joined by cords to the ends of the shed, and the shuttle shot across, so that one weaver could weave far wider cloth than an arm's length at much greater speed. Dandy looms, patented in 1802, rolled up the finished cloth automatically. Handlooms remained the most cost-effective way to make some textiles for most of the 1800s, even as power looms developed.

The loom is a symbol of cosmic creation and of the structure on which individual destiny is woven. In the classical myth of Arachne, the goddess Athena changed her into a spider out of jealousy of her skill at weaving. In Maya civilisation the goddess Ixchel taught the first woman to weave.
lop-nur: Lop Nur lies in the Lop Depression on the eastern fringe of the Tarim Basin, between the Taklamakan and Kumtag deserts. The name comes from an Oirat Mongolic name meaning Lop Lake, where Lop is a place name of unknown origin. The Tarim River and the Shule River drain into the lake system, which is the last remnant of the post-glacial Tarim Lake, once more than 10,000 square kilometres in area. The lake has no outlet and depended on meltwater from the Tianshan, Kunlun and western Qilian mountains. It measured 3,100 square kilometres in 1928, but dams on the rivers feeding it have dried it up, leaving a salt crust 30 to 100 centimetres thick.

From about 1800 BCE until the 9th century the lake supported a Tocharian culture, and archaeologists have found buried settlements and several of the Tarim mummies along its old shore. The kingdom of Loulan, a civilisation of the Silk Road, drew on the waters of the Tarim River and Lop Nur from the second century BCE. It became a client state of the Chinese empire in 55 BCE and was renamed Shanshan, and it was abandoned some time in the seventh century. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian crossed the Lop Desert between 395 and 414, and Marco Polo later passed through it. Early Chinese texts called the lake Yan Ze, Salt Marsh, and held, mistakenly, that it joined the Yellow River by an underground channel.

The lake was known as the Wandering Lake in the early 20th century, because the Tarim River changed course and moved its terminal lake among the Lop Nur, Kara-Koshun and Taitema basins. Nikolay Przhevalsky found it at Kara-Koshun in 1867, and Sven Hedin, who visited in 1900 and 1901, suggested that such changes had caused Loulan to perish. Human intervention moved the lake back in 1921, but it dried out again by 1964.

China established the Lop Nur Nuclear Test Base on 16 October 1959, with Soviet help in choosing the site, and the first Chinese nuclear bomb was tested there on 16 October 1964. A full-scale thermonuclear weapon followed on 17 June 1967. Forty-five tests were conducted before 29 July 1996, when China held its last and announced a moratorium the next day.

Archaeological sites near the lake include the Bronze Age Xiaohe Cemetery, where more than thirty well-preserved mummies have been excavated, and Qäwrighul, whose graves date mostly from 2100 to 1500 BCE. At Miran, to the south-west, excavated Buddhist monasteries have murals and sculptures that show influences from India and Central Asia. A reserve protects the wild Bactrian camel, about half of whose remaining population lives on the former test base. Potash has been mined at the lake since the mid-1990s.
lope-de-vega: Lope de Vega was born in Madrid in November 1562, the son of Félix de Vega, an embroiderer, and Francisca Fernández Flores. His friend and biographer Pérez de Montalbán claimed that he was reading Spanish and Latin at the age of five, and Lope himself said that he wrote his first play at twelve, though these statements are probably exaggerations. He studied under the poet Vicente Espinel, at the Jesuit Colegio Imperial and at the University of Alcalá, but did not take a degree.

In 1583 he served in the Spanish Navy at the Battle of Ponta Delgada in the Azores. Attacks on a former lover, Elena Osorio, and her family led to a libel conviction and banishment from the court. He married Isabel de Alderete y Urbina on 10 May 1588 and sailed with the Armada weeks later on the ship San Juan, one of those that returned to Spain.

After the Armada Lope lived in Valencia, where he refined his technique of weaving two plots into one play. He then served noble households in Toledo and Alba de Tormes, where he wrote the pastoral novel La Arcadia. Isabel died in 1594.
