Back in Madrid from 1595, he married Juana de Guardo in 1598 and from 1607 was secretary to the Duke of Sessa. After the deaths of his son Carlos Félix and of Juana he was ordained a priest on 24 May 1614, and in 1627 he was admitted to the Order of Malta. He died of scarlet fever in Madrid on 27 August 1635.

Lope established the three-act comedia as the standard form of Spanish drama. In his Arte nuevo de hacer comedias (1609) he defended breaking the neoclassical unities, arguing that the public who paid for plays cared nothing for them. He drew on Spanish history, the Bible, mythology and daily life, and his best-known plays are of the cloak-and-dagger type, among them El perro del hortelano and El castigo sin venganza. Many were written quickly and to order.

By his own records he had composed 230 comedias by 1604, 800 by 1618 and 1,500 by 1632. Of 637 plays known by title, about 450 survive. His poetry includes the Rimas (1604), the religious Rimas sacras (1614) and Rimas humanas y divinas del licenciado Tomé de Burguillos (1634), which is considered his poetic masterpiece.
lorch-am-rhein: Lorch am Rhein is a small town in the Rheingau-Taunus-Kreis in Hesse, Germany, and belongs to the Rhine Gorge World Heritage Site. It lies about 10 km north of the bend of the Rhine near Rüdesheim, between Rüdesheim am Rhein and Sankt Goarshausen, and owes its setting to its position at the mouth of the Wisper and to its steep vineyards. Its municipal area runs into the wooded Wisper valley, and the Rheinsteig hiking trail follows the heights above it. The Rhine island and nature reserve called Lorcher Werth lies nearby.

The area was settled early by Celts, then by the Ubii and later the Mattiaci. The Romans advanced to the Taunus in the first century CE, followed by the Alamanni and, with the Migration Period, the Franks. The town's oldest documentary mention is from 1085, when Archbishop Wezilo recorded a donation to the cathedral chapter of Mainz that included a house and vineyards in Lorch. In the Middle Ages Lorch was the northern bastion of the Archbishopric of Mainz facing the Rheingau and, from the twelfth century, stood at the southern end of the Rheingauer Gebück, a border defence of stunted trees. A parish was first documented in 1254. There was warfare in Lorch in 1460, 1631 and 1794.

On 10 January 1919 the Free State of Bottleneck, a provisional state-like entity between the occupation zones after the First World War, was proclaimed with Lorch as its de facto capital, and many coats of arms of the microstate still recall the time. In the early 1960s the Bundeswehr came with its Flugabwehrregiment 5, and a new settlement, the Ranselberg, was built for soldiers and their families. The barracks in the Wisper valley were closed in 1993, and an industrial park of about twenty firms later rose on the former military land.

Winegrowing and tourism characterise the town. Its vineyards, among them the Schlossberg and the Kapellenberg, lie in the Rheingau region and are planted mainly with Riesling. The Gothic Catholic parish church of St Martin was completed in the fourteenth century over a Late Romanesque basilica, and its high altar by Hans from Worms was installed in 1483. The Hilchenhaus of the mid sixteenth century is known as the loveliest Renaissance building on the Middle Rhine. The town's noble family named itself von Lorch, and its best-known member, Johann Hilchen (1484 to 1548), was a knight and Imperial field marshal.
lord-byron: George Gordon Byron was born on 22 January 1788 in Holles Street, London. He was the only child of Captain John Byron and his second wife, Catherine Gordon, heiress of the Gight estate in Aberdeenshire. Born with a deformity of his right foot, he suffered from a limp that caused him lifelong misery, and he called himself le diable boîteux, the limping devil.

He attended Aberdeen Grammar School from 1795 and Harrow School from 1801 to 1805, an undistinguished student who nevertheless played in the first Eton v Harrow cricket match at Lord's in 1805. He later studied at Trinity College, Cambridge. His first volume of poems, Fugitive Pieces, written when he was 17, was recalled and burned on a friend's advice because of its amorous verses.

Byron took his seat in the House of Lords on 13 March 1809 and left London for the Continent that June. In his first speech to the Lords, on 27 February 1812, he opposed a death penalty for the Luddite frame breakers of Nottinghamshire. His affair with Lady Caroline Lamb, who called him mad, bad and dangerous to know, shocked the British public.

Under pressure from creditors after the break-up of his domestic life, he left England in 1816 and never returned. That summer he settled at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva with his physician John William Polidori, and befriended Percy Bysshe Shelley and Mary Godwin. Kept indoors by rain, the group devised tales: Mary Shelley began what became Frankenstein, and Polidori wrote The Vampyre, inspired by a fragment of Byron's. He then lived for seven years in Italy.

His major works include Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Manfred and Hebrew Melodies. Don Juan, a poem of 17 cantos, ranks among the most important long poems published in England since Paradise Lost. He was also a bitter opponent of Lord Elgin's removal of the Parthenon marbles and denounced it in The Curse of Minerva.

In Greece Byron joined the war of independence against the Ottoman Empire and took part of the rebel army under his command despite his lack of military experience. He fell ill on 15 February 1824, bloodletting weakened him, and after catching a cold in April he died of a fever at Missolonghi on 19 April. A month later his Memoirs were burned in the offices of his publisher, John Murray. Greeks revere him as a folk hero.
lords-resistance-army: The conflict has roots in the divisions of Uganda. The south and east are largely inhabited by Bantu speakers such as the Baganda, who worked closely with the British after the creation of the Protectorate of Uganda in 1894, while the Nilotic-speaking Acholi of the north supplied much of the manual labour and came to make up a majority of the army. In 1986 Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army won the Ugandan Bush War and took control of the country. Its operations in the north, such as Operation Simsim, involved burning, looting and killing.

In late 1987 a civilian movement led by Alice Auma arose, who presented herself as a prophet inspired by the Holy Spirit. Joseph Kony founded the Lord's Resistance Army in 1987 and preached a similar belief in protection from bullets, with a cross drawn in oil on the chest.

In March 2002 the Ugandan army launched Operation Iron Fist against LRA bases in southern Sudan, and the LRA retaliated by attacking refugee camps in northern Uganda and Eastern Equatoria, killing hundreds of civilians. In February 2004 an LRA unit attacked the Barlonyo camp for displaced people, killing over 300. In 2006 UNICEF estimated that the LRA had abducted at least 25,000 children. The International Criminal Court issued its first arrest warrants in 2005, against Kony, Vincent Otti, Okot Odhiambo, Raska Lukwiya and Dominic Ongwen, for crimes against humanity and war crimes.

Talks were held at Juba from 2006 to 2008, and a truce was signed on 26 August 2006 under which the LRA was to gather in Garamba National Park in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Between December 2008 and March 2009 the forces of Uganda, the Congo and South Sudan attacked the Garamba camps, and Kony was not captured. Revenge attacks by scattered LRA remnants killed over 1,000 people.

The group relied heavily on abducting children to fill its ranks, using them as combatants and porters, and was organised in independent squads of 10 or 20 soldiers. Its ideology is disputed among scholars: many describe it as largely a cult of personality around Kony, mixing Christianity and traditional spiritualism, and a report of 1997 found that it had no political programme the local population could understand. The conflict disrupted education and family life in Acholiland.
lorelei: The Lorelei is a steep slate rock 132 metres high on the right bank of the Rhine in the Rhine Gorge at Sankt Goarshausen, part of the Upper Middle Rhine Valley World Heritage Site. An amphitheatre of the 1930s stands on top of it. The place has been a site of river disasters since its first records in the 10th century, and the high number of shipwrecks and the loud echo in the passage gave rise to a varied mythology.

The name comes from the old German lureln, a Rhine dialect word for murmuring, and ley, rock, so that it means murmuring rock. Heavy currents and a small waterfall, still visible in the early 19th century, produced a murmur that the echo of the rock amplified. Other theories derive the name from the verb lauern, to lurk, which would make it lurking rock. After the German spelling reform of 1901 the letter y was changed to i in almost all German words.

The rock and its murmur inspired various tales, and an old legend placed dwarfs in caves in the rock. The woman of the rock is a literary creation. In 1801 Clemens Brentano composed the ballad Zu Bacharach am Rheine, in which the beautiful Lore Lay, betrayed by her sweetheart, is accused of bewitching men and causing their death. The bishop sends her to a nunnery rather than condemning her, but on the way she asks to climb the rock to see the Rhine once more. Thinking that she sees her love in the river, she falls to her death, and the rock keeps an echo of her name. Brentano took inspiration from Ovid and the myth of Echo.

In 1824 Heinrich Heine adapted the theme in his poem Die Lorelei, which describes a siren who sits on the cliff combing her golden hair and unwittingly distracts boatmen with her beauty and song, so that they crash on the rocks. Friedrich Silcher set it to music in 1837, and the art song became well known in German-speaking lands.

The Lorelei of the Heine and Silcher song passed into German popular culture and is commonly but mistakenly believed to come from an old folk tale. Franz Liszt also set the poem, as did dozens of other musicians. Joseph von Eichendorff's poem Waldesgespräch, from his novel of 1812, also features Loreley and was set by Robert Schumann in his Liederkreis. Under the Nazi regime Heine, who was born a Jew, was discredited as the author of the words in an effort to hide the Jewish contribution to German art. The French poet Guillaume Apollinaire took up the theme in La Loreley, which is cited in the third movement of Dmitri Shostakovich's Symphony No. 14.
lorenzo-de-medici: Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici was born on 1 January 1449. His grandfather Cosimo de' Medici was the first of the family to lead the Republic of Florence and run the Medici Bank at the same time, and his father Piero was a patron and collector of art. His mother, Lucrezia Tornabuoni, wrote sonnets and was a friend of the poets and philosophers of the Medici Academy. Lorenzo was tutored by the diplomat Gentile de' Becchi and the humanist Marsilio Ficino, and was trained in Greek by John Argyropoulos.

Lorenzo took a leading role in the state on the death of his father in 1469, at the age of 20. Like his grandfather and father, he ruled Florence indirectly, through surrogates in the city councils, by means of payoffs and strategic marriages. On 26 April 1478 a group led by Girolamo Riario, Francesco de' Pazzi and Francesco Salviati, archbishop of Pisa, attacked Lorenzo and his brother Giuliano in the Cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore. Giuliano was stabbed to death, while Lorenzo escaped with a minor neck wound. The populace put down the conspiracy brutally, lynching the archbishop and members of the Pazzi family.

Pope Sixtus IV, whose blessing Salviati had, excommunicated Lorenzo and the Florentine government and placed the city under interdict. He then allied with King Ferdinand I of Naples, whose son Alfonso invaded the republic. The war dragged on until Lorenzo travelled to Naples himself and was for several months the king's prisoner; diplomacy ended the crisis. Lorenzo later followed a policy of keeping peace between the northern Italian states and keeping France and the Holy Roman Empire out of Italy.

He helped artists including Botticelli, Verrocchio, Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo to secure commissions, and Michelangelo lived for three years with his family. He wrote poetry in Tuscan and expanded the Medici Library begun by Cosimo.

Several branches of the Medici Bank collapsed through bad loans during Lorenzo's lifetime. He died on the night of 8 April 1492 at the family villa of Careggi. His eldest son, Piero, known as the Unfortunate, squandered the inheritance and brought down Medici rule in Florence in 1494. His second son Giovanni, who became Pope Leo X, retook the city in 1512 with the help of a Spanish army.
lorenzo-valla: Valla was born in Rome around 1407, of a family from Piacenza; his father, Luciave della Valla, was a lawyer in the Papal Curia. He attended the classes of Leonardo Bruni and Giovanni Aurispa, from whom he learned Latin and Greek, and is thought otherwise to have been largely self-taught. He gave offence to Antonio Loschi by championing the rhetorician Quintilian in an early work. In 1431 he was ordained a priest and tried in vain to secure a post as apostolic secretary. He then went to Piacenza and Pavia, where he held a professorship of eloquence until his attack on the Latin style of the jurist Bartolus de Saxoferrato made his stay uncomfortable, after which he lectured in many cities.

From 1435 to 1445 Valla was employed at the court of Alfonso V of Aragon, who was in a territorial conflict with the Papal States under Pope Eugene IV. In 1439–1440 he wrote his essay on the Donation of Constantine, which claimed that Constantine I gave the Western Roman Empire to the Church in gratitude for a cure from leprosy by Pope Sylvester I. In 1444 he was put on trial before the Inquisition but was protected from imprisonment by Alfonso. Pope Nicholas V invited him to Rome in 1447, where he worked on his Repastinatio, became a papal scribe and in 1455 a papal secretary.

Valla argued that the Donation's internal evidence told against a 4th-century origin, since its vernacular style could be dated to the 8th century. He held that Constantine could not legally have given Sylvester such powers, that the absence of contemporary evidence made so great a change implausible, and that the text used the word satrap, which Romans would not have used, and switched tenses in poor Latin. In textual criticism he proposed emendations to Livy. In his study of Jerome's Vulgate he questioned the system of penance and indulgences, arguing that paenitentia rendered the Greek metanoia, better translated as repentance, and Erasmus praised the work.

His dialogue De Voluptate and his treatise on the elegances of Latin made his reputation in his lifetime. Richard Claverhouse Jebb said the latter marked the highest level yet reached in the critical study of Latin, and it was reprinted nearly sixty times between 1471 and 1536.

Valla died in Rome on 1 August 1457 and was buried beneath the bronze Lex de imperio Vespasiani behind the altar of Saint John Lateran. In 1576 Pope Gregory XIII, a staunch believer in the Donation, had his tomb and epitaph destroyed when he moved the bronze; a memorial to Valla stands in the Lateran today. Martin Luther thought highly of him, Robert Bellarmine called him Luther's precursor, and Erasmus wrote that for Latin grammar there was no better guide.
lorraine: Lorraine is the only French region to border three other countries: Belgium, Luxembourg and Germany. Most of it lies in the Paris Basin, a plateau cut by river valleys, with the sharper relief of the Vosges in the east. The Moselle, the Meurthe and the Meuse run through it. Its position at the crossroads of four nations made it a strategic asset, and its rulers intermarried with royal families across Europe. Two languages are traditionally native to the region, the Romance language Lorrain in the south-east and Lorraine Franconian in the north and west.

The Treaty of Prüm of 855 divided Middle Francia in three, and the northern third, Lotharingia, went to Lothair II. Its rulers were called dukes from 903 and could side nominally with the eastern or western Carolingian kingdoms. In 959 it was split into Upper and Lower Lorraine; the lower duchy was defunct by the end of the 12th century. Lorraine and Bar were joined in a personal union in 1480, made permanent in 1506. France annexed Metz, Verdun and Toul in 1552, which the Empire recognised only in 1648, and annexed Lorraine and Bar themselves in 1766.

In 1871 Germany took the area of the present department of Moselle as part of Alsace-Lorraine and favoured German in administration and schooling. The Treaty of Versailles returned it to France. Nazi Germany annexed it again during the Second World War, and the Cross of Lorraine became the symbol of the Free French Forces under Charles de Gaulle.

Lorraine was an administrative region of France from 1982 until January 2016, made up of Meurthe-et-Moselle, Meuse, Moselle and Vosges, and is now part of the region Grand Est. Nancy, the seat of the duchy for centuries, is the largest metropolitan area. The last iron ore mine closed in 1997 and the last coal mines of the Saar-Lorraine basin in 2004. The region gave its name to quiche Lorraine.
lorsch: Lorsch is a town in the Bergstraße district of Hesse, about 60 km south of Frankfurt. It lies in the Rhine rift about 5 km west of the Bergstraße and just west of the Odenwald, between Darmstadt to the north and Mannheim to the south, not far from the lower reaches of the Weschnitz. Its neighbours include Einhausen, Bensheim, Heppenheim, Lampertheim and Bürstadt.

The abbey was founded in 764 by the Frankish Count Cancor and his mother Williswinda, and Benedictines from Gorze Abbey near Metz settled it. It was one of the major centres of Carolingian art, and several Carolingian kings of Germany were buried there. A document of 885 calls it Lauressam, the source of the town's present name. In the Early and High Middle Ages it was a powerful imperial monastery, with holdings in the nearby Odenwald, on the Bergstraße, in Rhenish Hesse, and in Alsace and Lorraine.

In the civil war arising from the Investiture Controversy in the 11th century the abbey lost much of its holdings to the nobility. In the late 12th century an attempt was made to reorganise its administration with a record of its old deeds, the Lorsch codex. Even so, in 1232 Lorsch was awarded to the Archbishopric of Mainz and newly settled by Premonstratensians. Mainz and the Electorate of the Palatinate then disputed who should hold the vogt rights. Of the Carolingian abbey, parts of which have been unearthed, the gatehall from about 800 has been preserved.

Lorsch Abbey has been named a World Heritage Site by UNESCO, and the Königshalle, declared a site in 1991, appears in the town's coat of arms along with the red cross formerly borne by the abbey. The town has a museum centre with departments of monastic history, folklore and tobacco, and the open-air museum Lauresham. The town hall was built between 1714 and 1715. Lorsch lies on the Nibelungenbahn railway between Bensheim and Worms, and the Autobahn A 67 runs through its territory.
los-angeles: Most of the city lies in the Los Angeles Basin beside the Pacific Ocean, extending partly through the Santa Monica Mountains and north into the San Fernando Valley. The eastern end of the Santa Monica Mountains runs from Downtown to the Pacific and separates the basin from the valley. The city covers about 1,302 square kilometres in all, including 88 square kilometres of water, and extends 71 km from north to south and 47 km from east to west. Its highest point is Mount Lukens, at 1,547 metres, in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains.

The Los Angeles Basin and the San Fernando Valley were dominated by the Tongva, later also called the Gabrieleño. The historic centre of Tongva power was the settlement of Yaanga, a name translated as 'place of the poison oak', which became the site where the Spanish founded the pueblo. Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo claimed the area for Spain in 1542, and Gaspar de Portolà and the Franciscan missionary Juan Crespí reached the present site on 2 August 1769.

On 4 September 1781, 44 settlers known as Los Pobladores founded El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles, 'The Town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels'. The town became part of the First Mexican Empire in 1821. At the end of the Mexican–American War in 1848, Los Angeles and the rest of California passed to the United States under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, and the city was incorporated on 4 April 1850, five months before California became a state. Oil discovered in the 1890s brought rapid growth, and the Los Angeles Aqueduct, completed in 1913, brought water from Eastern California.

Los Angeles is the most populous city in California and the commercial, financial and cultural centre of Southern California, with 3,898,747 residents counted in the 2020 census. It is the county seat of Los Angeles County and a charter city governed by a mayor and a city council. Well over 200 languages are spoken there. The city hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984, and is one of the oldest and largest hubs of film and television production.
lothair-i: Lothair was born in 795 to Louis the Pious, then king of Aquitaine and the son of Charlemagne, and Ermengarde of Hesbaye. Little is known of his youth. After Charlemagne's death in 814 he was sent to govern Bavaria for his father, the new emperor. In 817 Louis drew up the Ordinatio Imperii, which designated Lothair as his principal heir and overlord of his younger brothers Pepin of Aquitaine and Louis the German, and he was crowned joint emperor at Aachen.

When Bernard of Italy died in 818, after plotting against Louis and being blinded, Italy was awarded to Lothair. He received the royal crown of Italy at Easter 823, 5 April, and was crowned emperor again by Pope Paschal I at Rome. In November 824 he promulgated the Constitutio Romana on relations between pope and emperor.

His stepmother Judith won his consent to a plan to secure a kingdom for her son Charles, who was given Alemannia in 829. Lothair soon changed his attitude and spent a decade in strife with his father over the division of the empire. In 830 all three brothers rebelled and deposed Louis, who was reinstated in 831 and deprived Lothair of the imperial title, giving Italy to Charles. A second rebellion in 833, instigated by Angilbert II, Archbishop of Milan, deposed Louis again in 834. Through the loyalty of the Lombards Lothair kept Italy and his imperial position.

When Louis was dying in 840 he sent the imperial insignia to Lothair, who claimed the whole empire. His brother Louis the German and half-brother Charles resisted and allied against him. At Fontenay-en-Puisaye on 25 June 841 Lothair was defeated and fled to Aachen.

Peace talks began, and in June 842 the brothers met on an island in the Saône. The Treaty of Verdun, signed in August 843, gave Lothair the imperial title, northern Italy and a long stretch of territory from the North Sea to the Mediterranean along the valleys of the Rhine and the Rhône, including Lorraine, Alsace, Burgundy and Provence. He soon ceded Italy to his eldest son Louis. In his new kingdom he made futile efforts to defend his lands from attacks by the Northmen and the Saracens.

In 855 Lothair fell seriously ill, renounced the throne, divided his lands among his three sons and entered the monastery of Prüm on 23 September. He died six days later and was buried there; his remains were found in 1860. By the Treaty of Prüm Louis II received Italy and the title of emperor, Lothair II received Lotharingia, and Charles received Provence. The struggles among the brothers led directly to the breakup of the empire assembled by Charlemagne and laid the foundation for the development of modern France and Germany.
lothair-ii: Lothair II's grandfather was Louis the Pious, and his father, Lothair I, was crowned co-emperor at Aachen in 817. When the dying Lothair I divided his realm, Louis II, the eldest son, held Italy and the imperial title, Lothair II received the territory between Frisia and the Alps, and Charles, still a child, received Lower Burgundy. Lothair I died on 19 September 855. His magnates brought the young king to the court of his uncle Louis the German at Frankfurt for confirmation, and he probably ceded Alsace in exchange, though Louis did not keep it permanently.

Lothair's position was insecure, and to establish himself he had to marry Teutberga, the daughter of Boso the Elder, which secured the support of her brother Hucbert. Lothair already had several children by his boyhood mistress Waldrada, and as Hucbert's usefulness declined he dismissed Teutberga in 857. In 858 she was subjected to a trial by ordeal, in which her champion took an object from boiling water, and when his hand was judged to be healing normally she was found not guilty and Lothair's magnates forced him to take her back. A council at Aachen in 862 allowed Lothair to marry Waldrada, and Teutberga appealed to Pope Nicholas I.

Lothair also acted as a mediator between his uncles, helping to negotiate peace between Louis the German and Charles the Bald by June 860. When his brother Charles of Provence died on 24 January 863, Lothair and Emperor Louis II partitioned Lower Burgundy, Lothair receiving the Lyonnais and the Viennois. Nicholas I then turned against him, excommunicated two of his archbishops and in 865 forced him to take Teutberga back; he excommunicated Waldrada in 866. Against the Northmen, Lothair chased a raiding party in 863 and in 867 won a victory over Rorik of Dorestad, a Viking leader in Frisia, with heavy casualties.

Nicholas died in 867, and his successor Adrian II was more flexible, allowing Teutberga to live apart from the king and lifting Waldrada's excommunication. Lothair travelled to Italy in the summer of 869 to meet Adrian, dined with him in the Lateran and gave him many gifts. On the way back a fever and an epidemic struck his party, and he died at Piacenza, on 7 August 869. Charles the Bald was crowned king at Metz on 9 September, but he had to partition Lotharingia with Louis the German in the Treaty of Meerssen. Lothair's son Hugh, born to Waldrada, later claimed the kingdom, took authority in part of Lotharingia in 879 and was blinded by 885.
lothair-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Lothair was the son of the Saxon count Gebhard of Supplinburg, who joined the Saxon rebellion against the Salian dynasty and died on 9 June 1075 at the Battle of Langensalza. Lothair was born shortly afterwards at Unterlüß, and little is known of his youth. In 1107 he married Richenza, daughter of Count Henry of Northeim and heiress of the Brunonids. Land purchases, inheritance and marriage alliances brought him the domains of the House of Billung and the Counts of Northeim, making him the wealthiest nobleman among the Saxons. He supported Henry V's rebellion against Henry IV, and was rewarded with the Duchy of Saxony when Duke Magnus of Billung died without an heir in 1106.

As duke, Lothair joined the opposition to Henry V and in 1115 commanded the rebellious Saxon forces that defeated the emperor at the Battle of Welfesholz. After Henry's death in 1125 the electors met at Mainz and passed over the Hohenstaufen candidate, Duke Frederick, who refused to accept free election. Lothair was elected King of Germany at over fifty years of age and without a male heir. His election marked a departure from hereditary succession, as the electors preferred a ruler of moderate powers after the Salian era. A war with the Hohenstaufens followed, and the Swabians and Franconians declared Frederick's brother Conrad anti-king. Lothair took Nuremberg and Speyer in 1129 and defeated the Hohenstaufens in 1135, when they were pardoned at Bamberg.

In 1130 a papal schism arose between Innocent II and Anacletus II. Bernard of Clairvaux persuaded Lothair to favour Innocent, who crowned him in the Lateran Basilica on 4 June 1133, since Anacletus held St Peter's. In the north and east he made Albert the Bear Margrave of Brandenburg in 1134 and Conrad of Wettin Margrave of Lusatia in 1136. His campaign against Roger II of Sicily in 1136 and 1137 captured Capua and Apulia.

Lothair died in December 1137 on the return journey at Breitenwang, having given his son-in-law Henry the Proud the Margraviate of Tuscany, the Duchy of Saxony and the imperial insignia. His bones were taken to the Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Paul at Königslutter, for which he had laid the cornerstone in 1135. His only surviving child, Gertrude, was married to Henry the Proud in 1127, and their son was Henry the Lion. After Lothair's death the Hohenstaufen Conrad was elected king as Conrad III and deprived Henry the Proud of all his territories, ending Lothair's plan for a Welf kingship.
lothian: Lothian lies in the Scottish Lowlands, between the southern shore of the Firth of Forth and the Lammermuir Hills and Moorfoot Hills. Its principal settlement is Edinburgh, the Scottish capital, and other significant towns include Livingston, Linlithgow, Bathgate, Queensferry, Dalkeith, Musselburgh, Prestonpans, North Berwick, Dunbar and Haddington. Historically the name referred to a province covering most of what is now south-eastern Scotland.

The origin of the name is debated. It perhaps comes from the British Lugudūniānā, meaning country of the fort of Lugus, a Celtic god. Alternatively it may come from a stream now called the Lothian Burn. A popular legend derives it from King Lot of Arthurian legend. The usual Latin form is Laudonia.

In the post-Roman period Lothian was dominated by speakers of Cumbric, a British language closely related to Welsh, and Welsh tradition counts it part of the Old North. Angles settled it at an early stage, and it formed part of the kingdom of Bernicia, which extended south into present-day Northumberland and Durham and later united with Deira as Northumbria. Place names show that English became firmly established here from the 6th century onwards. In the 7th century the region came under Bernicia's control, though the Angles' grip weakened after their defeat by the Picts at the Battle of Nechtansmere.

Roger of Wendover wrote that Edgar, King of the English, granted Lothian to Kenneth II, King of Scots, in 973, on condition that Kenneth attend the English court whenever the English king wore his crown. Medieval historians widely accept this as the point at which Lothian became part of Scotland. Control was still not settled, and the Scots took the region at the Battle of Carham in 1018, after which the River Tweed became the de facto Anglo-Scottish border. William the Conqueror invaded Lothian and crossed the Forth but could not conquer it.

The Northumbrian dialect of Old English, at first confined to Lothian and the Borders, spread across the Lowlands and became the Scots language. Lothian is one of the few areas of mainland Scotland where Gaelic never dominated, though some Gaelic place names there are attributed to a Gaelic-speaking landowning aristocracy living there for 150 to 200 years.

By 1305 the area was divided into three shires, Edinburgh, Haddington and Linlithgow, informally called Midlothian, East Lothian and West Lothian, hence the popular name the Lothians. They took those names in law in 1921, 1925 and 1947. A Lothian Regional Council, with four districts, governed the region from 1975 until 1996.
lotus-sutra: The Sanskrit title, Saddharma Puṇḍarīka Sūtra, means the Discourse on the White Lotus of the True Doctrine. The sutra is presented as a drama of mythological scenes, with the whole cosmos as its stage, and it speaks almost exclusively in images. In the opening chapter the Buddha, at a gathering on Vulture Peak, enters deep meditation and sends a ray of light from between his eyebrows across thousands of Buddha-fields. Mañjuśrī says that the Buddha is about to expound his ultimate teaching.

Two teachings have been most influential. The first is the One Vehicle, which holds that all Buddhist paths and practices are skilful means leading to Buddhahood. In chapter 2 the Buddha says that the three vehicles are only such means, and five thousand monks leave rather than hear it. The second is that all beings can become Buddhas, so that, in the sutra's words, of any who hear the dharma none will fail to attain Buddhahood. Even Devadatta, the great Buddhist villain, receives a prediction of Buddhahood. The sutra also teaches that the Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable and that he achieved Buddhahood innumerable ages ago, so that his apparent death was a skilful means.

Scholars generally hold that the text took shape in phases, with chapters 2 to 9 forming the earliest layer, followed by chapter 1 and further chapters. Its authors are unknown, but Donald Lopez judges them to have been highly educated Buddhist monks. Peter Alan Roberts suggests that it may have arisen among the Mahāsāṃghika school and been written in a Prakrit that was later turned into Sanskrit, a claim that remains contested. In India it was copied often and cited by writers such as Vasubandhu, Candrakīrti and Śāntideva. According to Paramārtha there were over fifty Indian commentaries, but only one survives, and only in Chinese.

Dharmarakṣa's team made the first Chinese translation in 286 at Chang'an. It was superseded in 406 by the seven-fascicle translation of Kumārajīva's team, which became the standard version in East Asia, although it lacks the Devadatta chapter present in the earlier one. The sutra is the main scripture on which the Chinese Tiantai school and its derivatives, the Japanese Tendai and Nichiren, the Korean Cheontae and the Vietnamese Thiên Thai schools were founded. By the 8th century in Japan the emperor had set up a network of nunneries in each province, the Temples for the Eradication of Sins through the Lotus.

It has shaped East Asian art and literature for over 1,400 years, and its scene of Shakyamuni and Prabhutaratna Buddhas seated together became a popular theme in Chinese Buddhist art. Matteo Ricci mentioned and denounced it in 1603. Eugène Burnouf completed a French translation in 1839, published in 1852.
lough-corrib: Lough Corrib, in Irish Loch Coirib, covers 176 km2, lies mostly in County Galway with a small area of its north-east corner in County Mayo, and is connected to the sea at Galway by the River Corrib. It is the largest lake in the Republic of Ireland and the second largest on the island after Lough Neagh. A smaller, shallower basin in the south is joined by a narrow channel to a larger, deeper basin in the north. It is reputed to have 365 islands, though a recent chartmaker counts 1,327. Placename lore derives its name from Oirbsen, another name for the sea god Manannán mac Lir.

The first canal on the island of Ireland, the Friar's Cut, was dug in the 12th century to let boats pass from the lake to the sea at Galway. The Annals of Inisfallen record that in 1027 Muiredach Ua Flaithbertaig besieged Cathal, son of Ruaidrí, on Inis Crema in the lake. In 1225 the Lord Justice caused Odo O'Flaherty to give up Kirk Castle to Odo O'Connor, King of Connaught, as assurance of his fidelity. Hen's Castle, on a rock between Maam and Doon, was the home of the pirate Gráinne O'Malley, who lived in the time of Elizabeth I.

On Inchagoil Island, midway between Cong and Oughterard, there is evidence of an early monastic settlement and two churches, one of the 12th century; Saint Brendan of Clonfert is also said to have spent time on an island in the lake. William Wilde, father of Oscar Wilde, wrote Lough Corrib, its Shores and Islands in 1867 and built a summerhouse called Moytura House on its banks.

Surveys since 2007 have found Bronze Age and Iron Age dugout canoes, among them the carved Annaghkeen Boat, 40 ft long, a well-preserved 10th-century vessel from Carrowmoreknock carrying three Viking battle axes, and a Victorian pleasure yacht. All historic wrecks are protected, which makes the lake of international importance for marine archaeology. Lough Corrib was designated a Ramsar site in June 1996 and is also a Special Area of Conservation. Cruises leave from Cong, Ashford Castle, Galway and Oughterard.
louis-alexandre-berthier: Berthier was born at Versailles on 20 November 1753, the eldest of five surviving children of Lieutenant-Colonel Jean-Baptiste Berthier of the Corps of Topographical Engineers. Two of his brothers, César and Victor-Léopold, became generals in the Napoleonic Wars. His father instructed him in the military art, and he entered the army as a lieutenant in 1772. From 1780 to 1783 he served as a staff officer under the Count of Rochambeau in the American Revolutionary War. In July 1789 he became chief of staff of the Versailles National Guard and protected the family of Louis XVI from popular violence.

In 1792 Berthier became a maréchal de camp and chief of staff to Marshal Nicolas Luckner. He met Napoleon Bonaparte in March 1796 and was at once made chief of staff of the Army of Italy. His power of work, accuracy and mastery of detail made him the ideal chief of staff, and he remained Napoleon's most valued assistant for the rest of his career. In 1798 he entered Italy, organised the Roman Republic and took Pope Pius VI prisoner. Berthier supervised the pope's removal to Valence, where he died after a hard journey.

Berthier joined Napoleon in Egypt, helped in the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and became Minister of War for a time. In 1800 a mission to Spain brought the retrocession of Louisiana to France, which led to the Louisiana Purchase. Napoleon made him a Marshal of the Empire in 1804. In 1806 Napoleon deposed the king of Prussia as ruler of Neuchâtel, and Berthier became its prince, though he never visited it. He received the title Prince of Wagram in 1809. In Russia in 1812 he advised against the advance on Moscow.

After Napoleon's first abdication Berthier retired to his estate at Grosbois and made peace with Louis XVIII. When Napoleon returned in March 1815 he withdrew to Bamberg in Bavaria, and on 1 June 1815 he died in a fall from a window of the Neue Residenz. The window sill stood 1.2 metres from the floor, so an accident seems unlikely. According to some accounts he was assassinated by members of a secret society, while others say he threw himself out, maddened at the sight of Russian troops marching to invade France. It remains unclear whether it was suicide or murder.

Berthier was not a great field commander, and the French army in Bavaria suffered reverses when he held temporary command in 1809. He was nevertheless known for his organising skill and his ability to carry out the emperor's directions to the smallest detail. Napoleon is quoted as saying that had Berthier been at Waterloo he would not have met that misfortune.
louis-armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised in New Orleans, to Mary Estelle Albert, known as Mayann, and William Armstrong, who abandoned the family soon after. He was raised by his grandmother until the age of five, grew up in poverty in a rough neighbourhood known as the Battlefield, and at six began attending the Fisk School for Boys, which accepted black children in the segregated school system. In the late 1910s he played in brass bands and on riverboats, travelling up and down the Mississippi with the band of Fate Marable, who insisted that his musicians learn to read music. In 1918 his mentor Joe King Oliver left Kid Ory's band for the north, and Armstrong replaced him.

In 1922 Armstrong moved to Chicago at Oliver's invitation and played second cornet in Oliver's Creole Jazz Band. In 1924 he went to New York to play with the Fletcher Henderson Orchestra, the top African-American band of the time, switching to the trumpet. He returned to Chicago in 1925, formed Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five, and recorded Potato Head Blues and Muggles. In 1929 his version of Ain't Misbehavin', sung in the revue Hot Chocolates, became his biggest-selling record.

In 1943 he settled permanently in Queens, New York, with his fourth wife, Lucille. By the 1950s he was an international icon, though young jazz musicians such as Charlie Parker and Miles Davis found his half-entertainer style outmoded. He made three records with Ella Fitzgerald, and his 1964 recording of Hello, Dolly! won a Grammy Award.

Armstrong was a foundational influence in jazz, shifting its focus from collective improvisation to solo performance, and he was also an influential singer, skilled at scat. His Melancholy Blues is on the Voyager Golden Record, sent into space. He rarely discussed racial issues in public, to the dismay of some black Americans. In 1957, shortly after the school desegregation conflict in Little Rock, Arkansas, he denounced Governor Orval Faubus and President Dwight D. Eisenhower in an interview and said he would cancel a State Department tour of the Soviet Union. The FBI kept a file on him, and the remarks drew praise from Jackie Robinson and Lena Horne and a ban of his records by a Mississippi radio station.
louis-auguste-blanqui: Louis-Auguste Blanqui was born on 8 February 1805 in Puget-Théniers, in south-east France. His father, Jean Dominique Blanqui, had been a Girondist deputy in the National Convention. At 13 he was sent to Paris to study, and he graduated from the Lycée Charlemagne with honours in 1824. In 1822 he witnessed the execution of the four sergeants of La Rochelle, which he later cited as the origin of his declaration of war upon all factions that represent the past. He joined the Carbonari in 1824 and was wounded in the protests of 1827 against Charles X, after which he moved from Bonapartism to Jacobin republicanism.

Blanqui joined the July Revolution of 1830 but was disillusioned when it replaced one monarchy with another. At his trial in 1832 he declared his profession to be proletarian. Influenced by Philippe Buonarroti, he turned to disciplined conspiracy, founding the Société des Familles in 1834 and later the Société des Saisons. On 12 May 1839 he led it in an insurrection in Paris that was crushed after two days. Arrested in January 1840 and sentenced to death, commuted to life in prison, he spent years at Mont-Saint-Michel.

Released shortly before the Revolution of 1848, he founded the Société républicaine centrale and demanded the red flag in place of the tricolor. He was arrested after the demonstration of 15 May that marched on the National Assembly and was not released for ten years. He acquired the nickname L'Enfermé, the Prisoner.

On 14 August 1870 he led an abortive rising at La Villette, and on 17 March 1871, on the eve of the Paris Commune, he was arrested and held in Brittany. The Commune offered to exchange all its hostages, including the Archbishop of Paris, for him alone, but Adolphe Thiers refused. He was freed in June 1879 and died of a stroke in Paris on 1 January 1881; a crowd of between one hundred thousand and two hundred thousand followed his funeral to Père Lachaise.

Blanqui separated the domain of nature, governed by immutable laws, from human affairs, which depend on will. He therefore rejected economic, religious and positivist determinism, a view often called political voluntarism. He held that poverty has ignorance as its main cause. In prison he wrote Eternity by the Stars in 1872. Karl Marx early called him the foremost leader of the French proletariat, but Friedrich Engels later made Blanquism a pejorative term for conspiratorial putschism, which shaped his reputation.
louis-barthou: Barthou was born on 25 August 1862 in Oloron-Sainte-Marie. He served as a deputy for his home constituency and was an authority on trade-union history and law. He held ministerial office on 13 occasions besides his premiership, and was Foreign Minister in 1917 and 1934. As a national hero of World War I and a recognised author, he was elected to the Académie française at the end of that war. He loved the arts and worked with their leaders to publicise their fields, and the arts community dubbed him the minister of poets.

Barthou was prime minister from 22 March to 9 December 1913. His time in office saw a law of June 1913 safeguarding women workers before and after childbirth and, in July, the introduction of allowances for families with children. As foreign minister in 1934 he tried to create an Eastern Pact of the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia and the Baltic states, with Germany in some proposals, resting on French guarantees of the Soviet Union's borders and Soviet guarantees of Nazi Germany's eastern borders. In September 1934 he obtained the Soviet Union's entry into the League of Nations.

After Germany's withdrawal from the League he began a rearmament programme that focused first on the Navy and the Air Force. He was the primary figure behind the Franco-Soviet Treaty of Mutual Assistance of 1935, which his successor Pierre Laval signed.

Barthou met King Alexander I of Yugoslavia during his state visit to Marseille in October 1934. On 9 October Vlado Chernozemski, a Bulgarian, shot the king, and another bullet struck Barthou in the arm and severed an artery; he died of blood loss within an hour. The plot had been planned in Rome in August 1934 by Ante Pavelić, head of the Croatian Ustaše. A ballistic report of 1935, made public only in 1974, found that Barthou had been hit by an 8 mm Modèle 1892 revolver round of a kind used by French police, so he was killed by the police response rather than by the assassin. He was given a state funeral four days later.
The two deaths led to the Convention for the Prevention and Punishment of Terrorism, concluded at Geneva on 16 November 1937, signed by 25 nations and ratified only by India.
louis-bonaparte: Louis was born in Ajaccio, Corsica, on 2 September 1778, the fifth surviving child and fourth surviving son of Carlo Buonaparte and Letizia Ramolino. Following his older brothers into the French Army, he benefited from Napoleon's patronage, served in the campaign in Egypt and Syria, and was a general by the age of 25, though he felt he had risen too high too fast. On 4 January 1802 he married Hortense de Beauharnais, daughter of Empress Joséphine, a match arranged by Napoleon. Hortense at first opposed it and the couple never got on.

On 5 June 1806 Napoleon replaced the Batavian Commonwealth with the Kingdom of Holland and placed Louis on its throne, intending little more than a French prefect. Louis tried instead to rule independently. He called himself Lodewijk I, declared himself Dutch, and learned Dutch, though allegedly so badly that at first he called himself the Konijn van 'Olland, the Rabbit of 'Olland, instead of the Koning van Holland. He required his court and ministers to speak only Dutch, and he changed capitals more than a dozen times, among them Amsterdam, The Hague and Utrecht.

He oversaw relief after two disasters, the explosion of a gunpowder ship in Leiden in 1807 and a flood in 1809, and was known as Louis the Good. Napoleon remarked that to call a king good meant he had failed in his rule. Their quarrel deepened when Napoleon wanted to cut the value of French loans from Dutch investors by two thirds and to draw Dutch troops for the invasion of Russia, which Louis refused. After the British landed 40,000 men in 1809 and French militia drove them off, Napoleon cited Louis's inability to defend Holland. Louis abdicated on 1 July 1810 in favour of his second son, Napoleon Louis, and Holland was incorporated into France by the Decree of Rambouillet on 9 July.

Louis took the title Count of Saint-Leu and found refuge in Graz, in Austria, between 1811 and 1813, where he wrote and composed poetry. King William I refused his requests to visit the Netherlands, but under William II he travelled there in 1840 under a false name and was cheered by a crowd outside his hotel. After the death of his brother Joseph in 1844 the Bonapartists saw him as the rightful emperor, although he did little to press the claim. He died of a stroke on 25 July 1846 in Livorno and was buried at Saint-Leu-la-Forêt. His youngest son, Louis-Napoléon, founded the Second French Empire in 1852 as Napoleon III.
louis-botha: Louis Botha was born on 27 September 1862. In 1884 he led Dinuzulu's Volunteers, a group of Boers who had supported Dinuzulu against Zibhebhu, and in 1897 he became a member of the Transvaal parliament for the district of Vryheid. In 1899 he joined the Krugersdorp Commando in the Second Boer War, fought under Lucas Meyer in northern Natal and then as a general, leading Boer forces at Colenso and Spion Kop. After the death of P. J. Joubert he became commander-in-chief of the Transvaal Boers and fought at Belfast-Dalmanutha.

After a battle on the Tugela River he granted General Buller a twenty-four-hour armistice to bury his dead. Winston Churchill wrote that Botha took him prisoner at the Battle of Chieveley on 15 November 1899. More recent research credits Field cornet Sarel Oosthuizen, and another account names the Italian Volunteer Legion under Camillo Ricchiardi. After the fall of Pretoria in June 1900, Botha led a guerrilla campaign with Koos de la Rey and Christiaan de Wet.

Botha represented the Boers at the peace negotiations of 1902 and signed the Treaty of Vereeniging. In 1904 he and Jan Smuts founded the Het Volk Party in the Transvaal Colony, which campaigned for self-government. After Het Volk won the elections of February 1907, Lord Selborne asked him to form a government, and he became prime minister on 4 March 1907. He took part in the National Convention that led to the South Africa Act 1909.

When South Africa became a dominion in 1910, Botha was its first prime minister. In 1911 he and Smuts formed the South African Party. Widely viewed as too conciliatory towards Britain, he faced revolts within his party and opposition from J. B. M. Hertzog's National Party. Like Hertzog, he advocated the preservation of black traditions, which ultimately led to segregation. After the First World War began he sent troops to take German South-West Africa, a move unpopular among Boers that provoked the Boer Revolt.

At Versailles on 1 June 1919 Botha said that the peace made at Vereeniging had been bitter but not unjust. He thought the terms of the Versailles Treaty too harsh on the Central Powers, yet signed it. He died of heart failure after an attack of Spanish influenza on 27 August 1919, aged 56, and was buried in Pretoria. Equestrian statues of him stand before the South African Parliament building and the Union Buildings, and the General Botha Regiment bears his name.
louis-eugene-cavaignac: Cavaignac was born in Paris on 15 October 1802, the second child of Jean-Baptiste Cavaignac, a Jacobin member of the National Convention who had voted for the execution of Louis XVI, and Julie-Marie de Corancez. His elder brother was the republican journalist Éléonore-Louis Godefroi Cavaignac. He entered the École Polytechnique in 1820 and served in the Morea expedition of 1828 and 1829, and in 1830 he was one of the first officers to join the July Revolution. In 1831 he was removed from active duty for his declared republicanism.

Recalled in 1832, Cavaignac was sent to Algeria with the Army of Africa and served there with distinction for the next sixteen years. He rose to colonel in 1841 and to maréchal de camp in 1844. After the February Revolution of 1848 he was made general of division and Governor General of Algeria. Elected to the National Assembly for Lot, he accepted the Ministry of War on 17 May 1848.

On 23 June the Executive Commission put him in charge of suppressing the workers' insurrection in eastern Paris known as the June Days. The Assembly gave him dictatorial powers on 24 June, and he relied on the regular army, using cannon against the barricades, until he crushed the rising at the Place de la Bastille; by 26 June it was over.

On 28 June Cavaignac gave up his dictatorial powers, and the Assembly confirmed him as Chief of the Executive Power. His government controlled the political clubs and banned eleven newspapers, among them Le Père Duchêne, but it also closed the national workshops in July and replaced them with direct relief and public works. In the presidential election of 10 and 11 December he won 19.5 per cent against 74 per cent for Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte. Advised to carry out a self coup, he refused, and he handed over power on 20 December. He was arrested at the coup of 2 December 1851 and died on 28 October 1857.
louis-grand-conde: Born in Paris, the son of Henri II de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, and Charlotte Marguerite de Montmorency, he was at once given the title of Duke of Enghien. His father was a first cousin once removed of Henri IV. He studied history, law and mathematics for six years at the Jesuits' school at Bourges and then entered the Royal Academy at Paris, and at seventeen he governed Burgundy in his father's absence. His father betrothed him to Claire-Clémence de Maillé-Brézé, a niece of Cardinal Richelieu, and compelled him to marry her at thirteen, though he loved Marthe du Vigean. The marriage was unhappy, and he later confined his wife at Châteauroux.

Enghien took part in the siege of Arras, won Richelieu's favour during the Cinq Mars plot, and fought at the siege of Perpignan in 1642. In 1643 he was appointed to command against the Spanish in northern France and at the Battle of Rocroi, opposed by Francisco de Melo and the tercios, he conceived and directed the decisive victory. In 1644 he took command of the army in Germany to assist Turenne, and he fought at the Battle of Freiburg and, in 1645, at Nördlingen, where he was seriously wounded. In 1646 he captured Dunkirk. He succeeded as Prince of Condé that year.

His wealth, rank and ability made Anne of Austria, regent for Louis XIV, and her minister Mazarin uneasy. He won the Battle of Lens in August 1648 and subdued the Parlement of Paris, but in January 1650 he was arrested and imprisoned at Vincennes. After his release he joined the revolt, was defeated by Turenne at the Battle of the Faubourg Saint Antoine in July 1652, and defected to Spain, whose forces he commanded until his defeat at the Battle of the Dunes in 1658. The Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 brought his pardon and the return of his titles, though not his power as an independent prince.

He then lived at the Château de Chantilly, where he gathered writers including Molière, Racine, Boileau, La Fontaine and Bossuet. In the War of Devolution he conquered Franche-Comté, and in 1672 he and Turenne were the principal French commanders against the Dutch. He fought his last great battle at Seneffe on 11 August 1674, where three horses were killed under him. After Turenne's death in 1675 he repelled an Imperial invasion on the Rhine.

Tormented by gout, Condé spent his last eleven years at Chantilly in religious exercises. He died at Fontainebleau in 1686 at the age of sixty-five, and Bossuet pronounced his elegy. His victory at Rocroi is still studied by students of military strategy.
louis-i-duke-of-orleans: Louis was born on 13 March 1372, the second son of King Charles V of France and Queen Joanna of Bourbon. He was Duke of Touraine from 1386 and became Duke of Orléans in 1392. In 1374 he was betrothed to Catherine, heir presumptive to the throne of Hungary, whose father, King Louis I of Hungary, planned to leave the couple his claim to the Crown of Naples and the County of Provence. Catherine's death in 1378 ended the negotiations.

A proxy marriage with her sister Mary took place in April 1385, after the Avignonian Antipope Clement VII annulled Mary's betrothal to Sigismund of Luxembourg. Hungarian noblemen who followed the Roman Pope Urban VI did not recognise it, and four months later Sigismund invaded Hungary and married Mary. In 1389 Louis married Valentina Visconti, daughter of Gian Galeazzo Visconti, Duke of Milan.

In 1392 his elder brother, Charles VI, suffered the first of a lifelong series of attacks of insanity. A regency council presided over by Queen Isabeau of Bavaria was formed in 1393, and Louis gained powerful influence. He disputed the regency and the guardianship of the royal children with Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, until Philip's death in 1404, and then with Philip's son John the Fearless.

Louis was the king's brother, but his reputation as a womanizer and a rumoured affair with the queen made him unpopular in Paris. The royal children were in turn kidnapped and recovered by both sides, until John was appointed by royal decree as guardian of the Dauphin and regent. Louis tried to sabotage John's rule, including by squandering money raised for the siege of Calais, and only the intervention of their uncle John, Duke of Berry, prevented civil war. He was also blamed for the Bal des Ardents of 1393, at which four dancers were burnt alive when a torch he held came too close to their costumes.

On 20 November 1407 the two dukes exchanged solemn vows of reconciliation. Three days later fifteen masked men led by Raoulet d'Anquetonville, a servant of the Duke of Burgundy, attacked Louis in the streets of Paris as he rode a mule. His hand was cut off and his skull split by an axe. John the Fearless admitted the killing, supported by the people of Paris and the University, and had the Sorbonne scholar Jean Petit justify it as tyrannicide.

The murder turned a feud within the royal family into civil war between Burgundy and the royal house, which divided France until the Treaty of Arras in 1435. Louis's son Charles I, Duke of Orléans, was the father of King Louis XII.
louis-i-of-hungary: Louis was born on 5 March 1326, the first child of Charles I of Hungary and Elizabeth of Poland to survive infancy. A 1338 treaty between his father and Casimir III of Poland, Louis's maternal uncle, confirmed his right to inherit Poland if Casimir died without a son. He learned French, German and Latin, and his religious zeal owed much to his mother. He was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 21 July 1342, five days after his father's death; Elizabeth acted as a sort of co-regent for decades.

Early in his reign Louis restored royal power in Croatia and launched a crusade against the Lithuanians. When his brother Andrew, husband of Queen Joanna I of Naples, was murdered at Aversa on 18 September 1345, Louis blamed the queen, and punishing her became the main aim of his foreign policy. He campaigned in the Kingdom of Naples between 1347 and 1350, occupied large territories and took the Neapolitan royal styles, but the Holy See never recognised his claim. His rule was unpopular in southern Italy because of his arbitrary acts and the atrocities of his mercenaries, and he withdrew in 1351.

At home he ruled with absolute power but confirmed the liberties of the nobility at the Diet of 1351, which also introduced an entail system and a uniform rent for peasants and confirmed the peasants' right to free movement. In the 1350s he fought Lithuanians, Serbia and the Golden Horde, forced Venice to renounce the Dalmatian towns in 1358, and tried to extend his suzerainty over Bosnia, Moldavia, Wallachia and parts of Bulgaria and Serbia, though his rule there was mostly nominal. His attempts to convert pagan and Orthodox subjects made him unpopular in the Balkans. He founded a university in Pécs in 1367, but it closed within two decades for lack of revenue.

Casimir III died on 5 November 1370, and Louis was crowned king of Poland at Kraków on 17 November. Having no sons, he issued the Privilege of Koszyce in 1374 to secure his daughters' right to succeed him, though his rule remained unpopular in Poland. At the start of the Western Schism he acknowledged Urban VI as pope and helped Charles of Durazzo take the throne of Naples. He died on 10 September 1382, after suffering from a skin disease. Hungarian historians long regarded him as the most powerful Hungarian monarch, ruling an empire whose shores were washed by three seas, though his authority in some of those lands was only nominal.
louis-ii-of-hungary: Louis was born prematurely in Buda on 1 July 1506, and the court doctors kept him alive by wrapping him in the warm carcasses of slaughtered animals as a primitive incubator. He was the only son of Vladislaus II Jagiellon and his third wife, Anne of Foix. His father had him crowned in his own lifetime to ensure the succession: as king of Hungary on 4 June 1508 in Székesfehérvár Basilica, and as king of Bohemia on 11 March 1509 in St Vitus Cathedral in Prague. In 1515 he married Mary of Austria, a granddaughter of Emperor Maximilian I, under the First Congress of Vienna, and his sister Anne married Mary's brother Ferdinand.

Louis became king of Hungary and Croatia on his father's death in 1516. For most of his reign he was the puppet of the magnates and was kept in such poverty that he often pawned his jewels for food and clothing. His guardians, Cardinal Tamás Bakócz and Count George of Brandenburg-Ansbach, neglected him and squandered the royal revenues. After Bakócz died the magnates István Báthory, John Zápolya and István Werbőczy fought each other and used the diets as their tools. In Bohemia he was known as Ludovicus the Child, and the first thaler coins were minted there in his reign.

By 1520 Hungary was in near anarchy. The king's household expenses took about a third of the national income, border guards went unpaid and fortresses fell into disrepair. Louis refused to pay the annual tribute to Sultan Suleiman I and kept the sultan's ambassador Behram Çavuş waiting for years. Belgrade and many castles in Serbia fell to the Ottomans, which left Hungary open to further conquest.

In 1526 Suleiman marched again, and Louis left Buda in mid-July. On 29 August 1526 he led a medieval army with few firearms against the Ottomans at the Battle of Mohács, where Ottoman cavalry surrounded the Hungarian army and cannon and Janissary musketeers broke the centre. Nearly the whole royal army was destroyed in about two hours. In the retreat the twenty-year-old king fell from his horse while climbing a ravine of the Csele stream and, weighed down by his armour, drowned. Ferdinand, as husband of Louis's sister Anna, claimed the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary, but most of the Hungarian magnates elected John Zápolya. A monument stands north of Mohács, near the site of his death. Soma Turcsányi built the original column in 1864.
louis-ii-of-italy: Louis was born in 825, the eldest son of the junior emperor Lothair I and Ermengarde of Tours. He grew up in the court of his grandfather Louis the Pious, who in 839 designated him king of Italy. After Louis the Pious died the next year the empire was partitioned between Lothair, Louis the German and Charles the Bald, and on 15 June 844 Pope Sergius II crowned Louis king and co-emperor at Rome. His first claim to imperial rights in the city was decisively rejected. In 850 Pope Leo IV crowned him joint emperor, and in 851 he married Engelberga and took on the independent government of Italy.

In 850 Louis marched into southern Italy and compelled the rival dukes of Benevento, Radelchis I and Siconulf, to make peace, splitting the Lombard duchy between Benevento and an independent Salerno. He became sole emperor on the death of his father in September 855. The Treaty of Prüm gave him no territory outside Italy, which aroused his discontent. In 864 he reached Rome with an army to support archbishops whom Pope Nicholas I had deposed over the divorce of his brother Lothair II, but fell ill and made peace with the pope.

Louis spent much of his reign against the Aghlabids who were ravaging southern Italy. In 866 he routed them but lacked a fleet, so in 869 he allied with the eastern emperor Basil I, who sent ships, and Bari, capital of the Emirate of Bari, fell in 871. Afterwards he quarrelled with Basil and defended his right to the title emperor of the Romans. In August 871 Adelchis, prince of Benevento, attacked him in his palace, robbed him and held him prisoner for a month, until new Aghlabid landings made Adelchis release him. Pope Adrian II crowned him a second time in May 872.

Louis won further successes against the Aghlabids, relieving the siege of Salerno and driving them from Capua, but could not punish Adelchis. He died near Ghedi, in the province of Brescia, on 12 August 875, naming his cousin Carloman, son of Louis the German, as his successor in Italy, and was buried in the Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio in Milan. He left two daughters, Gisela, abbess of San Salvador at Brescia, and Ermengard, who married Boso of Provence. The chronicler Andreas of Bergamo, the main source for his campaigns in the south, noted that after his death a great tribulation came to Italy.
louis-iv-holy-roman-emperor: Louis was born in Munich on 1 April 1282, the son of Louis II, Duke of Upper Bavaria and Count Palatine of the Rhine, and Matilda, daughter of King Rudolph I. He was raised at the court of Albert of Habsburg alongside Frederick the Fair, who later became his rival for the German throne. His father died in 1294, and Louis ruled Upper Bavaria with his elder brother Rudolf I. A dispute between the brothers over the inheritance broke out in 1310, ended by the Peace of Munich of 21 June 1313. On 14 October 1308 he had married Beatrice of Silesia.

The death of Emperor Henry VII in August 1313 began a 14-month election. John of Bohemia was at first favoured, but the archbishops of Mainz and Trier, fearing Habsburg strength, persuaded him to stand aside for Louis as a compromise. On 19 October 1314 four electors chose Frederick the Fair, and the next day five electors at Frankfurt chose Louis. The two claimants fought until Louis defeated Frederick at the Battle of Mühldorf in 1322. In the Treaty of Ulm of 7 January 1326 they agreed that Frederick would administer Germany as king of the Romans while Louis would be crowned emperor in Italy, a division of kingship that was never truly repeated. Frederick died on 13 January 1330.

Pope John XXII, who did not recognise imperial claims to the Kingdom of Italy, excommunicated Louis; Louis tried to depose him and install an anti-pope. He was king of Italy from 1327 and emperor from 1328. In 1340 he inherited Lower Bavaria and reunited the duchy. In 1342 he acquired Tyrol by voiding Margarete Maultasch's first marriage and marrying her to his son Louis V, and in 1345 he gave Hainaut, Holland, Zeeland and Friesland to his wife, Margaret II of Hainaut. These gains made the Luxembourgs his enemies.

In the summer of 1346 Charles IV of Luxembourg was elected rival king with the support of Pope Clement VI. Louis kept the support of the free cities, the knights and the Habsburg dukes, and resisted him. He died in October 1347 of a stroke suffered during a bear hunt at Puch near Fürstenfeldbruck, and is buried in the Frauenkirche in Munich. His sons backed Günther von Schwarzburg against Charles, then joined the Luxembourg party after Günther's death in 1349. He was the last Bavarian to be king of Germany until 1742. In his reign he granted privileges to cities, permitting the Frankfurt Trade Fair in 1330 and giving Lübeck the right to coin gold gulden in 1340.
louis-iv-of-france: Louis was the only son of King Charles the Simple and his second wife Eadgifu of Wessex, daughter of King Edward the Elder, and so descended from both Charlemagne and Alfred the Great. After Charles was dethroned and captured in 923, Eadgifu took the infant Louis to Wessex, which gave him the nickname d'Outremer, and he was raised at the courts of Edward and then of his uncle Æthelstan. He became heir to the western Carolingian line when his father died in captivity in 929. In 936, at fifteen, he was recalled by Hugh the Great, margrave of Neustria, to succeed the Robertian king Rudolph. Hugh's envoys invited him to come and take the head of the kingdom, and he received homage at Boulogne.

Archbishop Artald of Reims crowned Louis on 19 June 936, probably at Laon. He spoke neither Latin nor Old French and knew little of his kingdom. Hugh the Great, who had ruled in fact since 923, became his guardian, and Louis held few lands around the old Carolingian domains and some abbeys. He repeatedly confirmed Hugh's title of duke of the Franks, in 936, 943 and 954. In 939 Gilbert of Lotharingia rebelled against Otto I of East Francia and offered Louis the crown. Louis married Gilbert's widow Gerberga of Saxony without the consent of her brother Otto, who then invaded Lotharingia.

In 940 East Frankish forces took Reims and expelled Artald. After the deaths of William Longsword in 942 and Herbert II of Vermandois in 943, Louis entered Rouen and took the young Richard I into his keeping, and divided the lands of Herbert's sons. He was imprisoned in 945–946. Otto I and Conrad I of Burgundy invaded in 946, and the Synod of Ingelheim in June 948 sided with Louis and threatened Hugh with excommunication. In 949 Louis took Laon and in 950 he and Hugh reconciled. He held real authority only north of the Loire.

In late summer 954 Louis fell from his horse while trying to capture a wolf in the forest of Voas, on the road from Laon to Reims, and died of his injuries on 10 September. The chronicler Flodoard reports a fall and tuberculosis, while the canons of Reims read the wolf as a divine punishment for his seizure of Corbeny. He was buried at the Abbey of Saint-Remi, where his widow Gerberga promoted the dynasty's memory. His son Lothair was crowned on 12 November 954 with the approval of Hugh the Great, and the regency passed to Hugh and then to Gerberga's brother Bruno the Great, which marked Ottonian influence in France.
louis-ix-of-france: Louis was born on 25 April 1214 at Poissy, the son of the future Louis VIII and Blanche of Castile. His father died on 8 November 1226, and Louis was crowned at Reims Cathedral on 29 November, at the age of twelve. His mother Blanche ruled as regent during his minority and remained his trusted adviser until her death in November 1252. She confronted rebellious vassals and in 1229 ended the Albigensian Crusade by an agreement with Raymond VII of Toulouse. Louis's younger brother Charles I of Sicily was created count of Anjou.

As an adult Louis dealt with conflicts with powerful nobles such as Hugh X of Lusignan and Peter I of Brittany. England's Henry III sought to recover the Angevin lands on the Continent and was defeated at the Battle of Taillebourg. Louis added several provinces to the royal domain, including parts of Aquitaine, Maine and Provence. In 1258 the Treaty of Corbeil with James I of Aragon had Louis renounce French overlordship claims over Catalonia, while James gave up claims to Languedoc, Provence, Toulouse and other lands in southern France.

His legal reforms are regarded as his most lasting work. He allowed subjects to appeal judgments directly to the king, abolished trial by ordeal and combat, introduced the presumption of innocence in criminal cases, and created provosts and bailiffs to apply the new framework. Contemporaries chose him as arbiter in quarrels among European rulers. He also enforced Catholic orthodoxy strictly, with harsh laws against blasphemy, and ordered the Jewish population to wear a yellow badge; after the Disputation of Paris the Talmud was burned. Between 1239 and 1241 he acquired the crown of thorns and a fragment of the True Cross from Emperor Baldwin II, paying 135,000 livres to clear Baldwin's debt, and housed them in the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, consecrated on 26 April 1248.

In the Seventh Crusade, called in 1245, Louis landed in Egypt on 4 or 5 June 1249 and took Damietta, but the march on Cairo was slow and he was captured and ransomed. He then spent four years strengthening the Kingdom of Jerusalem at Acre, Caesarea and Jaffa, and sailed from Acre on 24 April 1254.

On 24 March 1267 Louis and his three sons took the cross again. He resolved to land at Tunis, and the crusaders landed at Carthage on 17 July 1270, where disease broke out in the camp. Louis died at Tunis of dysentery on 25 August 1270, and his son Philip III succeeded him. Pope Boniface VIII canonised him in 1297, and he is the only French king declared a saint. Admirers have long held him up as the model Christian monarch.
louis-mountbatten: Louis Mountbatten was born Prince Louis of Battenberg on 25 June 1900 at Frogmore House in Windsor, the youngest child and second son of Prince Louis of Battenberg and Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine. His maternal grandmother was Princess Alice, a daughter of Queen Victoria. His paternal grandparents had made a morganatic marriage, so he and his father bore the style Serene Highness rather than Royal Highness. His elder sister Princess Alice of Battenberg was the mother of Prince Philip. In 1917, when the royal family adopted the name Windsor, he became known as Lord Louis Mountbatten, until he was created a peer in 1946.

Posted as a midshipman to the battlecruiser HMS Lion in July 1916 at the age of 16, Mountbatten accompanied Edward, Prince of Wales, on tours of Australia in 1920 and of India and Japan in 1921. He married Edwina Ashley on 18 July 1922. In the Second World War he commanded the 5th Destroyer Flotilla from HMS Kelly, which was torpedoed by a German E-boat on the night of 9 to 10 May 1940. In August 1943 Churchill appointed him Supreme Allied Commander, South East Asia Command.

Clement Attlee advised the king to appoint him Viceroy of India on 20 February 1947, charging him with overseeing the transition to independence by 30 June 1948. His instructions were to avoid partition and preserve a united India, though he was allowed to adapt to changing circumstances. India and Pakistan became independent at midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947, and at Jawaharlal Nehru's request he became the first Governor-General of independent India. Later he served as First Sea Lord from April 1955 to July 1959, as Admiral of the Fleet from 22 October 1956, and as Chief of the Defence Staff until 1965.

In August 1979 Mountbatten was assassinated by the Provisional Irish Republican Army, when a bomb exploded aboard his fishing boat at Mullaghmore, County Sligo. His death prompted widespread condemnation and international mourning, and he received a ceremonial funeral at Westminster Abbey.

His career and reputation remain debated. Admirers point to his energy, charm and administrative ability; critics accuse him of vanity, self-promotion and flawed judgement, particularly over the partition of India and his wartime assessments in South East Asia. He was also a mentor to his great-nephew, the future King Charles III.
louis-nicolas-davout: Louis-Nicolas d'Avout was born on 10 May 1770 at Annoux in Burgundy, the eldest son of an impoverished minor noble family with a tradition of military service. He was educated at the military academy at Brienne-le-Château, which Napoleon also attended, and at the École Militaire in Paris, and in 1788 became a sous-lieutenant of cavalry. He embraced the Revolution, but was removed from the active list because of his noble birth. He served in the Rhine campaign of 1796 and accompanied General Louis Desaix on Napoleon Bonaparte's Egyptian expedition. Napoleon promoted him to general of division and arranged his marriage to Aimée Leclerc, sister-in-law of Napoleon's sister Pauline.

Davout was one of the original 18 Marshals of the Empire in 1804, the youngest and least experienced of them, which earned him the hostility of other generals. At Austerlitz his III Corps bore the brunt of the allied attack after a forced march of 48 hours. At Auerstädt in 1806 his single corps of 28,000 men defeated the main Prussian army of the Duke of Brunswick, which had more than 63,000, and the battle gave him the nickname Iron Marshal. He became governor-general of the Duchy of Warsaw in 1807, Duke of Auerstädt, and after Wagram Prince of Eckmühl. In Russia in 1812 he commanded the I Corps and led the rear guard in the retreat until Napoleon replaced him with Marshal Michel Ney.

In 1813 Davout took command at Hamburg, which he held through a long siege, surrendering only on the order of Louis XVIII after Napoleon's abdication. He expelled up to 25,000 of the city's poorest citizens into the winter, and many died of cold and starvation. He was a stern disciplinarian who forbade plundering on pain of death.

During the Hundred Days Davout was Minister of War, though Napoleon kept him in Paris rather than give him a field command. After Waterloo he directed the defence of Paris until the provisional government ordered him to negotiate. He was exiled and deprived of his titles, but they were restored in 1817 and he became a Peer of France in 1819. He died in Paris on 1 June 1823 and lies in the Père Lachaise Cemetery. Contemporaries counted him among the ablest of Napoleon's marshals.
louis-pasteur: Louis Pasteur was born on 27 December 1822 in Dole, Jura, France, to a Catholic family; his father, Jean-Joseph Pasteur, was a poor tanner. The family moved to Marnoz in 1826 and to Arbois in 1827. He was dyslexic and dysgraphic, and as a boy was an average student whose interests were fishing and sketching.

He studied at the Collège d'Arbois and, from 1839, the Collège Royal at Besançon, earning a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics at Dijon in 1842, but with a mediocre grade in chemistry. He passed the entrance test for the École Normale Supérieure with a high ranking in 1843 and in 1847 submitted two theses, one in chemistry and one in physics, while working as a graduate laboratory assistant for the chemist Antoine Jérôme Balard.

Pasteur became professor of chemistry at the University of Strasbourg in 1848. In 1854 he was named dean of the new faculty of sciences at the University of Lille, where he began his studies on fermentation. In 1857 he moved to Paris as director of scientific studies at the École Normale Supérieure, which he directed from 1858 to 1867, introducing reforms that raised its standards. His rigid decrees led to two student revolts, and when he threatened to expel any student caught smoking, 73 of the 80 students resigned.

He established the Pasteur Institute in 1887 and directed it for the rest of his life. He married Marie Laurent in 1849, and three of their five children died young. Pasteur died on 28 September 1895, and his body was interred in a vault beneath the institute.

In 1848 Pasteur resolved a problem about tartaric acid. The compound derived from living things rotated polarised light, while the chemically synthesised one did not. He found that crystals of tartrates in racemic mixtures were half right-handed and half left-handed, and he concluded that an asymmetric internal arrangement of the molecules was responsible. This was the first demonstration of molecular chirality and the first explanation of isomerism.

In 1856 a local wine manufacturer asked his advice, and Pasteur began research on fermentation. His experiments with sterilised flasks disproved spontaneous generation and won him the Alhumbert Prize in 1862. He supported the germ theory of disease, and he is best known for treating milk and wine to stop bacterial contamination, a process named pasteurization. In 1878 he told his family never to reveal his notebooks, and the historian Gerald Geison argued in 1995 that they showed misleading accounts of his discoveries, a view Max Perutz contested.
