louis-philippe-i: Louis Philippe was born on 6 October 1773 in the Palais-Royal in Paris, the eldest son of Louis Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, later known as Philippe Égalité. The Orléans cadet branch was distrusted by the elder Bourbon branch, and his father was exiled from court. From 1782 the Countess of Genlis tutored him and gave him a fondness for liberal thought. He joined the Jacobin Club, as his father supported.

As Duke of Chartres he commanded troops in the Revolutionary Wars and was a lieutenant general by the age of nineteen. After he was drawn into the treason of Dumouriez he fled in 1793, and his father was executed during the Reign of Terror. He lived under an assumed name in Switzerland, travelled to Scandinavia, Finland and the United States, and then settled in England. His exile lasted 21 years.

After Napoleon's abdication Louis Philippe returned to France during the Bourbon Restoration, and his resentment at the treatment of his family led him to side with the liberal opposition. In 1830 the July Revolution overthrew Charles X, who abdicated in favour of his grandson Henri and named Louis Philippe Lieutenant général du royaume. Louis Philippe did not announce the wish that Henri should succeed, and the Chamber of Deputies, aware of his liberal record and popularity, proclaimed him king.

He ruled in an unpretentious style, but his support came from the wealthy bourgeoisie. He was called the Citizen King and was at first much loved, but his government came to seem increasingly conservative. From 1840 to 1848 he followed conservative policies under the influence of François Guizot. He promoted friendship with the United Kingdom and colonial expansion, notably the conquest of Algeria, and he survived seven assassination attempts.

Economic conditions deteriorated in 1847. On 24 February 1848, during the Revolution, Louis Philippe abdicated in favour of his nine-year-old grandson Philippe and left Paris in disguise. He fled to England on a boat offered by the British consul at Le Havre. The Second Republic was proclaimed on 26 February. Louis Philippe lived in exile in the United Kingdom until his death on 26 August 1850. His supporters in France are known as Orléanists, and his grandchildren included Leopold II of Belgium and Empress Carlota of Mexico.
louis-riel: Louis Riel was born on 22 October 1844 at St-Boniface, near the fork of the Red and Seine rivers, the eldest of eleven children of a locally respected family. The Red River Settlement was administered by the Hudson's Bay Company and largely inhabited by Métis people of mixed First Nations and European descent. His father, Louis Riel Sr., had organised a group that supported Guillaume Sayer, a Métis tried for challenging the company's trade monopoly; Sayer's release effectively ended it. The Riels were noted for their devout Catholicism and strong family ties.

Tensions rose in 1869, when Anglophone Protestant settlers from Ontario arrived and the transfer of Rupert's Land to Canada was negotiated without the Métis. A survey party that came on 20 August laid out townships that cut across Métis river lots. The Métis National Committee declared a provisional government on 8 December, and Riel became its president on 27 December. During the resistance he had a Canadian nationalist, Thomas Scott, executed after a court martial. Delegates sent to Ottawa agreed with John A. Macdonald on language, religious and land rights, forming the basis of the Manitoba Act, but could not obtain a general amnesty. Riel fled to the United States and was elected three times to the House of Commons without taking his seat.

In 1884 the Métis leaders of Saskatchewan, including Gabriel Dumont, asked him to help with their grievances over land. He declared a Provisional Government of Saskatchewan at Batoche on 19 March 1885. The Battle of Duck Lake on 26 March began the North-West Rebellion, and troops brought quickly by the Canadian Pacific Railway defeated the Métis at Batoche.

His trial opened in Regina on 20 July 1885 before a jury of six Anglophone Protestants. Riel gave two long speeches and rejected his lawyers' plea of insanity. The jury found him guilty but recommended mercy, and he was sentenced to death. Appeals and petitions failed, and he was hanged on 16 November 1885 at Regina. His execution polarised Canada along ethno-religious lines, and French Canadians saw him as a heroic victim. Historians remain divided between portraits of him as a dangerous religious fanatic and as a charismatic defender of the Métis.
louis-the-blind: Louis was born around 880, the son of Boso, the usurper king of Provence, and Ermengard, a daughter of Emperor Louis II. When Boso died on 11 January 887 Louis was a child, and his mother, rather than proclaim him king herself, approached her relative Emperor Charles the Fat, declared Burgundy's submission to the Empire and received confirmation of the family estates. Charles adopted Louis and placed him under protection, but he was deposed in November 887 and died in January 888, and several other lords were proclaimed kings in 888, among them Rudolph I in Upper Burgundy, Odo I in West Francia and Berengar I in Italy.

Ermengard then sought the support of King Arnulf of East Francia and of Pope Stephen V for her son. His kingdom was smaller than his father's: it did not include Upper Burgundy, lost to Rudolph I, and was restricted to the environs of Vienne and Provençal regions. Local barons elected Ermengard regent, and in 894 Louis himself did homage to Arnulf. In 896 he fought the Saracens, pirates who had set up a base at Fraxinet and raided the coast of Provence.

In 900 various lords, including Adalbert II, Margrave of Tuscany, who suffered from Magyar raids and Berengar I's weak rule, invited Louis into Italy as grandson and heir of Louis II. He drove Berengar from Pavia and was crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy on 12 October 900. In 901 Pope Benedict IV crowned him emperor in Rome. He could not stem the Magyar incursions, the Italian nobles drifted back to Berengar, and in 902 Berengar defeated his armies and made him promise never to return.

In 905, urged on by nobles led by Adalbert I of Ivrea, he invaded again, took Pavia and then Verona with a small following. Berengar returned with Bavarian troops and entered Verona at night. Louis took refuge in the church of St Peter but was captured, and on 21 July 905 he was blinded for breaking his oath and forced to give up his Italian and imperial crowns.

Louis went back to Vienne and by 911 had put most royal powers in the hands of his cousin Hugh, count of Arles, who was made Margrave of Provence and Marquis of Vienne, moved the capital to Arles and married Louis's sister Willa. Louis lived on in obscurity and continued to style himself Roman emperor. He died on 5 June 928 and was succeeded by his brother-in-law. His sons included Charles-Constantine, later Count of Vienne, and Rudolph; whether he married the Byzantine princess Anna, to whom he was betrothed in 899, remains a matter of controversy.
louis-the-child: Louis was born in September or October 893 at Altötting in the Duchy of Bavaria. He was the only legitimate son of King Arnulf of Carinthia and his wife Ota, a member of the Conradine dynasty. He had at least two brothers: Zwentibold, his elder illegitimate half-brother, who ruled Lotharingia, and Ratold, who briefly ruled the Kingdom of Italy. He succeeded his father in East Francia and Zwentibold in Lotharingia.

Louis was crowned at Forchheim on 4 February 900, the earliest East Frankish royal coronation about which records exist. He was in weak health and often sick, and because of his youth the government was entirely in the hands of the nobles and bishops. The coronation was probably possible because there was little Louis could gain at the expense of the nobles. His most influential councillors were Hatto I and Solomon III, bishop of Constance. They saw to it that the court decided for the Conradines against the Babenbergers over the Duchy of Franconia, and they appointed Louis's nephew Conrad as duke. The Raffelstetten customs regulations of 903 were the first customs regulations in the East Frankish part of Europe.

In Lotharingia Louis kept a separate chancery under Archbishop Radbod of Trier. He appointed an East Frank, Gebhard, as duke, which alienated the Lotharingian nobles, who took no part in East Frankish assemblies.

The reign was dominated by Magyar raids. The Magyars ravaged Bavaria in 900, Carinthia in 901, Saxony in 906 and Alemannia in 909. In 904 Louis invited their leader Kurszán to negotiations but killed him and his delegation. In 907 the Magyars destroyed a Bavarian army at the Battle of Pressburg, killing Margrave Luitpold and many high nobles, and in 910 they defeated Louis's own army at the Battle of Augsburg.

Louis died at Frankfurt am Main on 20 or 24 September 911, aged seventeen or eighteen, in a state of despair and possibly of severe depression. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Emmeram in Regensburg, where his father also lay. His death ended the eastern branch of the Carolingian dynasty. In 911 the dukes of East Francia elected Conrad of Franconia as king, while the nobles of Lotharingia chose the Carolingian Charles the Simple, already king of West Francia.
louis-the-german: Louis was the third son of Louis the Pious and his first wife, Ermengarde of Hesbaye, and a grandson of Charlemagne. In 817 his father's Ordinatio Imperii made him king in Bavaria, with authority over Carantania, Bohemia and other dependent Slavs and Avars. He ruled from Regensburg, the old Bavarian capital, married Hemma in 827, and in 828 and 829 repelled Bulgarian invaders of Pannonia. When the emperor changed the succession in 829, Louis was drawn into the family wars; in 832 he invaded Alamannia, which his father had given to the young Charles, and was driven back and disinherited.

After his father's death in 840 Louis allied with Charles the Bald against Lothair I, defeating Lothair's commander at the battle of the Ries on 13 May 841 and, with Charles, Lothair and Pepin II of Aquitaine at Fontenoy on 25 June. The Annals of Fulda called Fontenoy the biggest bloodbath the Franks had known. By the Treaty of Verdun, concluded by 10 August 843, Louis received the lands east of the Rhine, with a district round Speyer, Worms and Mainz, including Bavaria, Thuringia, Franconia and Saxony. He crushed the Stellinga rising in Saxony in 842 and in 844 compelled the Obotrites to accept his authority, putting their prince Gozzmovil to death.

His invasion of West Francia in 858 collapsed through desertion and the loyalty of the Aquitanian bishops to Charles, and both kings swore to keep the peace at Koblenz on 7 June 860. The Treaty of Meerssen in 870 brought Lotharingia into his kingdom, and in 874 he reached a longer-term peace with the Moravians after decades of conflict. His later years were troubled by rebellions of his sons, and he divided his lands among them. His efforts to win the imperial title failed: Charles the Bald reached Rome first, in December 875.

Louis died of a stroke at his palace in Frankfurt on 28 August 876 and was buried the next day by his son Louis at Lorsch Abbey, though it cannot be determined with certainty that the body in the sarcophagus is his. His son Louis the Younger defeated Charles the Bald at Andernach on 8 October 876. Only 172 royal documents survive from his 59 years as king, and his rule shows a marked decline in written administration. He may be called the founder of the German kingdom. He was nicknamed the German only in the 18th century; West Frankish sources called him king of Germania, meaning the land east of the Rhine, and contemporaries gave him the epithet pius.
louis-the-pious: Louis was born in 778, the third son of Charlemagne and Hildegard, while his father was campaigning in the Pyrenees. He was crowned King of Aquitaine as a three-year-old child in 781 and sent there with regents and a court, since Charlemagne wished his sons to be raised in the lands they would rule. As king he was charged with defending the empire's southwestern frontier. After a siege of seven months, his army took Barcelona from the Emirate of Córdoba in 801. His brothers Pepin and Charles died in 810 and 811, and he was crowned co-emperor with his father at Aachen on 11 September 813.

Louis inherited the whole Carolingian Empire on his father's death in 814. He began by purging the court of those he considered morally dissolute, sent his unmarried half-sisters to nunneries and made the monk Benedict of Aniane the reformer of the Frankish church. In 817 he issued the decree known as the Ordinatio Imperii, which made his eldest son Lothair co-emperor and gave Aquitaine to Pepin and Bavaria to Louis the German, while declaring the empire undivided. It omitted his nephew Bernard of Italy, who plotted against him, surrendered and was blinded, dying after two days. In 833 Louis did penance for this at Attigny.

The birth of his son Charles, by his second wife Judith, led to civil wars that marked the last two decades of his reign, since the older sons refused to accept the changes he made in Charles's favour. In 830 Pepin and Louis the German captured him, but he was freed in 831.

In 833, on the plain of the Rothfeld, most of his army deserted him in what was called the Field of Lies. A synod deposed him in November 833 and made him do public penance, and he was restored in March 834. A third civil war began in 838 when Pepin died and Louis tried to give Aquitaine to Charles. On the frontiers he fought Slavs, Danes, Basques and Bretons, and Vikings sacked Utrecht and Antwerp in the 830s.

Louis died on 20 June 840 on an island in the Rhine near Ingelheim, in the arms of his half-brother Drogo. He pardoned his son Louis and proclaimed Lothair emperor. Fighting between the brothers continued until 843, when the Treaty of Verdun divided the empire into three sovereign realms. West Francia and East Francia became the kernels of modern France and Germany. He was buried in the Abbey of Saint-Arnould in Metz. His reign is generally compared unfavourably with his father's, although he faced different problems.
louis-the-stammerer: Louis was born on 1 November 846, the eldest son of Emperor Charles the Bald and Ermentrude of Orléans. He was physically weak. In 856, during peace negotiations between his father and Erispoe, duke of Brittany, he was betrothed to one of Erispoe's daughters, whose name is not known; the contract was broken in 857 after Erispoe was murdered.

Louis married twice. His first wife, Ansgarde of Burgundy, bore two sons, Louis III and Carloman II, who both became kings of West Francia, and daughters including Hildegarde and Gisela. His second wife was Adelaide of Paris, and their children included Ermentrude and a posthumous son, Charles the Simple, who became king of West Francia long after his elder half-brothers had died.

Louis became ruler of Aquitaine on the death of his younger brother Charles the Child. In 877 he succeeded his father as ruler of the whole of West Francia, including Lower Burgundy with Provence, but without Italy, so he did not become emperor. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, crowned him at Compiègne on 8 October 877, and Pope John VIII crowned him a second time at Troyes in August 878, while attending a council there. The pope may have offered him the imperial crown, which he declined.

Louis had relatively little impact on politics. A contemporary description calls him a simple and sweet man, a lover of peace, justice and religion. In 878 he gave the counties of Barcelona, Girona and Besalú to Wilfred the Hairy.

His last act was to march against invading Vikings, but he fell ill soon after setting out and died at Compiègne on 10 April 879, outliving his father by a year and a half. His realms were divided between his sons Carloman II and Louis III, while the powerful duke Boso of Provence tried to carve out a realm in Lower Burgundy. His epithet is first recorded in the chronicle of Regino of Prüm, who says he was called the Stammerer because he was somewhat impeded and slow in speech.
louis-the-younger: Louis the Younger, born between 830 and 835 and sometimes called Louis the Saxon or Louis III, was the second of three sons of King Louis the German and Queen Hemma, after Carloman and before Charles. In 854, at the invitation of Aquitainian nobles opposed to Charles the Bald and Pepin II, he led an army into Gaul to receive the Aquitainian crown and marched as far as Limoges before turning back.

He formed close ties with the nobles of East Francia, and in 865 he and his brother Charles rebelled against their father. They were reconciled that year, and the elder Louis divided the remaining territories between them: Louis received Saxony, Thuringia and Franconia. In 869 he married Liutgard, daughter of Liudolf, Duke of Saxony, at Aschaffenburg. She was politically ambitious and spurred him to pursue ambitious goals. The match increased tensions with his father, and he rebelled again in 871 and 873, reconciling each time.

On the death of Louis the German on 28 August 876, the three brothers succeeded under the earlier partition, Carloman taking Bavaria and the Pannonian March, Louis Franconia, Saxony and Thuringia, and Charles Alamannia. Louis buried his father at Lorsch, in his own territory, to stress his primacy, and kept his chief adviser, Liutbert, Archbishop of Mainz. On 8 October 876 at Andernach he defeated a much larger host of West Francia led by Charles the Bald, who had tried to annex the eastern parts of Lotharingia.

In 878 Louis and Louis the Stammerer promised each other to respect the succession of their sons by the Treaty of Fouron. When the Stammerer died in April 879, western nobles invited Louis the Younger to rule the western kingdom. He invaded as far as Verdun and retreated after the new kings ceded their part of Lotharingia, which the Treaty of Ribemont confirmed in February 880. Carloman, struck by a stroke in 879, named Louis his successor in Bavaria, which he held outright from 880.
From 879 Vikings raided deeply into the Frankish lands. In February 880 Louis defeated a Norse host at the Battle of Thimeon, near modern Charleroi, in which his illegitimate son Hugh was killed.

Louis fell sick in 881 and died at Frankfurt on 20 January 882, and was buried beside his father at Lorsch. With no heir, his territories passed to his brother Charles, who reunited the whole East Frankish kingdom.
louis-vi-of-france: Louis was born around 1081 in Paris, the son of Philip I of France and Bertha of Holland. He was knighted in 1098 by Guy I of Ponthieu, and by 1103 his father had associated him with the government of the kingdom. Abbot Suger of Saint Denis, his adviser and later his biographer, wrote that he tired early of hunting and boyish games and turned to arms. Louis married Lucienne de Rochefort in 1104; the marriage was annulled in 1107. In 1115 he married Adelaide of Maurienne, niece of Pope Callixtus II, who was politically active and appears on 45 royal charters of his reign. They had eight children.

Louis succeeded at the age of 26. His half-brother prevented him from reaching Rheims, so Daimbert, Archbishop of Sens, crowned him at Orléans on 3 August 1108. The kingdom was then a collection of feudal principalities, and beyond the Île-de-France the king had little authority over the great dukes and counts. Louis spent much of his reign campaigning against the lords whose castles, such as Le Puiset, Châteaufort and Montlhéry, lay around Paris. Clerical writers accused them of charging tolls, waylaying merchants and pilgrims and looting churches. Hugh of Le Puiset rebuilt his castle twice before Louis finally defeated him.

Louis also fought Henry I of England for twenty years over the strategic castle of Gisors. His forces were routed at the Battle of Bremule in August 1119, and peace followed in 1120 with Gisors left to Henry. In 1124 the Emperor Henry V, Henry I's son-in-law, planned an invasion towards Rheims, but France rallied to Louis, who carried the banner of Saint Denis, and the plan was dropped. After the murder of Charles the Good in 1127 Louis intervened in Flanders and had William Clito elected count, but the towns rebelled against Clito, and Louis had to confirm Thierry of Alsace instead.

On 9 April 1137 the dying William X, Duke of Aquitaine, made Louis guardian of his daughter and heiress Eleanor of Aquitaine. Louis married her to his heir, the future Louis VII, at Bordeaux on 25 July 1137, adding one of the most powerful duchies of France to the Capetian domains. He died of dysentery on 1 August 1137 and was buried in the Basilica of St Denis.

His weight had grown so great by his forties that campaigning became hard, which gave him the name the Fat. He was the first Capetian to issue ordinances applying to the whole kingdom, and the recognition of his authority led many in French society to see the king as their protector. The marriage in 1128 of the Empress Matilda to Geoffrey Plantagenet, Count of Anjou, created an alliance that later troubled his successor.
louis-vii-of-france: Louis was the second son of Louis VI of France and Adelaide of Maurienne, and was prepared for a career in the Church. After the accidental death of his older brother Philip in 1131 he unexpectedly became heir, and in October 1131 Pope Innocent II anointed and crowned him in Reims Cathedral. He spent much of his youth at Saint-Denis, where he formed a friendship with Abbot Suger. On 25 July 1137 he married Eleanor of Aquitaine, who had inherited the duchy of Aquitaine from Duke William X, and on 1 August 1137 his father died.

Louis came into violent conflict with Pope Innocent II over the vacant archbishopric of Bourges, rejecting the pope's nominee, and the pope laid an interdict on him. A war with Theobald II of Champagne followed, lasting from 1142 to 1144. In it the royal army assaulted and burned the town of Vitry-en-Perthois, and at least 1,500 people who had taken refuge in the church died in the flames. Condemned by the Church, Louis withdrew and resolved to atone by a crusade, which Bernard of Clairvaux promoted at Vézelay at Easter 1146.

Louis and Eleanor set out on the Second Crusade in June 1147. In Anatolia the French army was ambushed by Turks near Mount Cadmus. Louis reached Antioch in March 1148, where Eleanor urged him to help her uncle Raymond of Poitiers, but he went to Jerusalem instead. The siege of Damascus, undertaken with Conrad III and Baldwin III of Jerusalem, was abandoned after four days, and Louis reached Paris in November 1149. The Council of Beaugency declared the marriage invalid for kinship, and it was annulled on 21 March 1152. Eleanor married Henry, Count of Anjou, on 18 May 1152, bringing him Aquitaine.

Louis married Constance of Castile in 1154 and, after her death in 1160, Adela of Champagne five weeks later. He sheltered Thomas Becket from 1166. He tried to weaken Henry II by backing his rebellious sons, but a lack of resources and indecision undermined the effort.

His son Philip was born in 1165 and crowned at Reims in 1179, when Louis, already paralysed, could not attend. He died in Paris on 18 September 1180 and was buried at Barbeau Abbey, which he had founded; his remains were moved to Saint-Denis in 1817. His reign saw the founding of the University of Paris and the building of Notre-Dame de Paris.
louis-viii-of-france: Louis was born on 5 September 1187, the son of King Philip II Augustus and Isabella of Hainault. His mother died in 1190, and his father allowed him nominal control of the county of Artois to learn governance. On 23 May 1200 he married Blanche of Castile, daughter of King Alfonso VIII of Castile, after prolonged negotiations with her uncle John, King of England. In 1214 Philip faced an alliance that included John, and Louis was given command against John in Poitou. After losing Angers he forced John to retreat from the castle of Roche-au-Moine, while Philip won the Battle of Bouvines in the north.

In 1215 Louis, fulfilling his father's crusading vow, went against the Albigensians and favoured Simon de Montfort the Elder at Narbonne and Toulouse, ordering the walls of both to be pulled down. That year English barons rebelled against King John and offered the throne to Louis, whose wife descended from Henry II. He landed in Kent on 21 May 1216 and entered London unopposed, where he was proclaimed king though never crowned. The papal legate Guala Bicchieri excommunicated him on 29 May.

John's death in October 1216 led many barons to desert Louis for John's son, Henry III. Louis's army was beaten at the Battle of Lincoln on 20 May 1217 and his fleet at the Battle of Sandwich on 24 August. By the Treaty of Lambeth he pledged never to attack England again, English rebels were given an amnesty, he received 10,000 marks and his excommunication was lifted.

Louis succeeded his father on 14 July 1223 and was crowned at Reims on 6 August. On 1 November 1223 he issued an ordinance forbidding his officials to record debts owed to Jews, reversing his father's policy; the financial effect was so great that in 1225 he invited Lombard moneylenders to Paris. In 1224 he refused to renew the truce with England and took Poitou, La Rochelle and Saintonge, leaving the English kings only Gascony on the continent.

In 1226 he took the cross against the Albigensians and captured Béziers, Carcassonne, Beaucaire and Marseille. Avignon held out until 9 September, at heavy cost, and his weakened army did not attack Toulouse. He died of dysentery on 8 November 1226 at the Château de Montpensier. His son Louis IX succeeded him, and his younger sons received apanages, among them Artois, Anjou and Maine, and Poitou and Auvergne. He is buried at the Saint Denis Basilica.
louis-xi: Louis was born at Bourges on 3 July 1423, the son of King Charles VII and Marie of Anjou, when the English held northern France, including Paris. In 1429 he met Joan of Arc at Loches. His first marriage, in 1436, to Margaret, daughter of King James I of Scotland, was arranged for diplomatic reasons, and she died childless in 1445. In 1440 he took part in the Praguerie, an uprising that sought to make him regent in place of his father. It failed, and the king forgave him.

Sent from court in 1446, Louis ruled the Dauphiné almost as a king. In 1451 he married the eight-year-old Charlotte of Savoy without his father's consent. In 1456 Charles sent an army against him, and Louis fled to Burgundy, where Philip the Good sheltered him.

Louis became king on 22 July 1461 after hurrying to Reims to be crowned. He pursued his father's aim of limiting the dukes and barons, with greater success. He made the tax system more efficient, promoted men of humble birth such as Philippe de Commines, and travelled the kingdom founding fairs and regulating trade. In 1464 he set up a network of royal postal relays, which gave rise to his nickname the Universal Spider.

His main enemy was Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy. Charles joined the League of the Public Weal, led by Louis's brother Charles, Duke of Berry, and Louis fought an indecisive battle with it at Montlhéry. At Péronne in 1468 he was forced into a humiliating treaty, which he declared invalid once free. In 1475 he signed the Treaty of Picquigny with Edward IV of England, whose army left France for a large sum of money. The Swiss defeated Charles at Grandson and Murten in 1476, and he was killed at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477. The Treaty of Arras of 1482 returned the lands of the Duchy of Burgundy to the French crown.

Louis died on 30 August 1483 at the Château de Plessis-lez-Tours after years of illness. His son Charles VIII, aged thirteen, succeeded him, with his daughter Anne as regent. In 1480 he had inherited René of Anjou's claim to Naples, together with Provence, which opened the way for French involvement in Italy. Historians credit him with laying the foundations of a strong monarchy. He was secretive and few mourned him. Machiavelli criticised him for abolishing his own infantry in favour of Swiss mercenaries.
louis-xii-of-france: Louis of Orléans was born on 27 June 1462 at the Château de Blois, the son of Charles I, Duke of Orléans, who was almost seventy, and Marie of Cleves. He became Duke of Orléans at the age of three. King Louis XI distrusted the Orléanist link with the Burgundians and opposed the idea of an Orléanist ever reaching the throne. In 1476 he forced Louis, his second cousin, to marry his own disabled and supposedly sterile daughter Joan, hoping to extinguish the Orléans cadet branch of the House of Valois.

Louis rose against the regency of Anne of France in the Mad War of 1485 to 1488. Allied with Francis II, Duke of Brittany, he was defeated and captured at the Battle of Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier on 28 July 1488. Pardoned three years later, he joined King Charles VIII in Italy, leading the vanguards. At Fornovo on 6 July 1495 he was left in a weak position when Ludovico Sforza changed sides, and he came to hate Sforza.

All four children of Charles VIII and Anne of Brittany died in infancy. Louis, great-grandson of Charles V, was the senior claimant under the Salic Law, and he became king on 7 April 1498. Pope Alexander VI annulled his marriage with Joan in December 1498, and Louis married Anne of Brittany, which kept Brittany tied to the crown. He reformed the legal system and reduced taxes, paying for it by cutting the pensions of the nobility and of foreign princes. The Ordinance of Blois of 1499 codified French customary law, and the Ordinance of Lyon of 1510 tightened tax collection.

He claimed Milan through his grandmother Valentina Visconti. In 1501 he sent an army to Naples, which a secret treaty signed at Grenada on 11 November 1500 had divided between France and Spain, but he was forced to cede it to Spain in 1504. In the War of the League of Cambrai he defeated the Venetians at Agnadello on 14 May 1509, but Pope Julius II founded the Holy League against him, and the Swiss drove the French from Milan in 1513.

The Estates conferred on Louis the title Father of the People in 1506, the only time a French king received it. Historians often attribute his popularity to his tax policy. He died on 1 January 1515, after suffering from gout, without a male heir, and was buried at Saint Denis. Francis I, his cousin and son-in-law, succeeded him.
louis-xiii-of-france: Louis XIII was born at the Palace of Fontainebleau on 27 September 1601, the eldest child of Henry IV, the first Bourbon king of France, and his second wife Marie de' Medici. In 1619 the English ambassador Sir Edward Herbert remarked on his extreme stutter. He became king shortly before his ninth birthday, when Henry IV was assassinated, and his mother acted as regent. She kept the Edict of Nantes but remained in power for years after he came of age, relying on her favourite Concino Concini, who was widely disliked as a foreigner. In 1617 Louis, encouraged by Charles d'Albert, had Concini arrested; he was killed in the attempt on 24 April, and Marie was exiled to Blois.

Charles d'Albert, made Duke of Luynes, then dominated the court until he died of camp fever in December 1621, during a campaign against the Huguenot rebellion led by Henri, Duke of Rohan. Louis then ruled by council. The Treaty of Montpellier of October 1622 confirmed the Edict of Nantes while the Huguenots kept Montauban and La Rochelle. In 1624, after dismissing several ministers, he turned to Cardinal Richelieu, who shaped French policy for the next eighteen years.

Under Louis and Richelieu the crown ended the revolts of the nobility, destroyed the castles of defiant lords and denounced duelling and private armies. It took back the political and military privileges Henry IV had granted the Huguenots, leaving their religious freedoms, and Louis successfully led the siege of La Rochelle. France intervened against the Habsburgs in the Thirty Years' War. Louis built a navy and founded the Musketeers of the King's Guard in 1622. The king and the cardinal are remembered for establishing the Académie française. Under Richelieu's guidance New France grew westward along the Saint Lawrence from Quebec City to Montreal.

In 1615 Louis married Anne of Austria, daughter of Philip III of Spain. After four stillbirths she gave birth on 5 September 1638 to the future Louis XIV. Louis was unwell through the winter of 1642 to 1643, and historians think he suffered from extrapulmonary tuberculosis. He died in Paris on 14 May 1643, the 33rd anniversary of his father's death. He was also a lutenist, and in 1635 he composed the music, wrote the libretto and designed the costumes for the Ballet de la Merlaison. He appears with Anne and Richelieu in Alexandre Dumas's novel The Three Musketeers of 1844.
louis-xiv: Louis XIV was born on 5 September 1638 at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye to Louis XIII and Anne of Austria, who had been married for 23 years. He was named Louis Dieudonné, the God-given, and contemporaries regarded his birth as a miracle. When Louis XIII died in 1643, a regency council headed by Anne ruled for his four-year-old son, and Anne picked Cardinal Mazarin as chief minister. As the Thirty Years' War ended, a civil war known as the Fronde broke out in France. Louis was declared of age on 7 September 1651, and when Mazarin died in March 1661 he took the government into his own hands and declared that he would rule without a chief minister.

Believing in the divine right of kings, Louis compelled many nobles to live at his palace of Versailles, which pacified an aristocracy many of whom had joined the Fronde. His Great Ordinance of Civil Procedure of 1667, the Code Louis, imposed uniform civil procedure on a kingdom that had been a patchwork of legal systems, and later became the basis for the Napoleonic Code. In 1682 La Salle followed the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico and claimed its basin for Louis as Louisiane.

Warfare defined his foreign policy. The War of Devolution began in 1667 after the death of Philip IV of Spain, since Maria Theresa's Spanish dowry was never paid. The Nine Years' War, from 1688 to 1697, ended with the Peace of Ryswick, which left Louis permanent sovereignty over Alsace, including Strasbourg. In 1700 Charles II of Spain left his empire to Louis's grandson Philip, Duke of Anjou, and the War of the Spanish Succession followed, ending in the Peace of Utrecht in 1713. Louis also revoked the Edict of Nantes, which had given Huguenots political and religious freedom, and the persecution that followed virtually destroyed the French Protestant community.

Louis outlived most of his legitimate family: his son the Dauphin died of smallpox in 1711, his grandson the Duke of Burgundy of measles a year later, and Burgundy's elder son a few weeks after that. His heir on his deathbed was a five-year-old great-grandson. He died on 1 September 1715, leaving a powerful but war-weary kingdom in major debt. According to Philippe de Courcillon's journal he advised his heir not to follow his example of undertaking war too lightly. He patronised Molière, Racine, Lully and Le Brun, and the saying "I am the state" attributed to him is apocryphal.
louis-xv: Louis XV was born at Versailles on 15 February 1710, the third son of the Duke of Burgundy and Marie Adélaïde of Savoy, and was styled Duke of Anjou. His place in the succession seemed remote until disease cleared it: his grandfather the Grand Dauphin died of smallpox in 1711, and in February 1712 his mother and father died within six days of each other. His elder brother, the new Dauphin, died on 8-9 March after measles and bloodletting. His governess, Madame de Ventadour, hid the two-year-old from the doctors and saved him. Until his majority in 1723 the kingdom was ruled by his grand-uncle Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, as Regent.

Cardinal Fleury was chief minister from 1726 until his death in 1743, after which the king took sole control and governed without a prime minister. Louis kept out of the War of the Austrian Succession at first, saying on hearing of the death of Emperor Charles VI that he would stay with his hands in his pockets. Madame de Pompadour, his mistress from 1745, advised him for about twenty years and helped him choose and dismiss ministers. On 5 January 1757 Robert-François Damiens stabbed him at Versailles; the wound was slight, and Damiens was executed in March.

Under the Duke de Choiseul, who became minister in 1758, France made the Family Compact with Spain and brought Lorraine into the kingdom in 1766 and Corsica in 1768. The Seven Years' War drained the treasury, and the Parlements of several provinces resisted new taxes and the authority of the royal intendants. In 1764 Louis suppressed the Jesuit order in France. In 1770 he dismissed Choiseul and handed the government to a triumvirate led by René de Maupeou, who in 1771 removed the members of the Parlement of Paris from their posts.

Louis XV died on 10 May 1774, after a reign of almost 59 years, the second longest in French history. Historians generally criticise his reign, holding that incompetence and extravagance weakened France, depleted the treasury and discredited the absolute monarchy. A minority argue that he was popular in his lifetime and that his reputation was later blackened by revolutionary propaganda. His grandson and successor Louis XVI inherited a kingdom close to financial disaster and badly in need of political reform.
louis-xvi: Louis-Auguste was born at the Palace of Versailles on 23 August 1754 and given the title Duke of Berry. He was the second surviving son of Louis, the Dauphin, and Marie-Josèphe of Saxony, and became Dauphin himself when his father died in 1765. On 19 April 1770, at fifteen, he married the fourteen-year-old Archduchess Maria Antonia of Austria, the Marie Antoinette of history, a daughter of Empress Maria Theresa.

He came to the throne on 10 May 1774, aged nineteen, when the government was deeply in debt and resentment of despotic monarchy was growing. His grandfather Louis XV had been widely hated by the time of his death, and the monarchy had spent heavily on unsuccessful wars. The young king felt woefully unqualified to resolve the situation.

The first part of his reign was marked by attempts at reform in line with Enlightenment ideas, among them greater tolerance of non-Catholics and the abolition of the death penalty for deserters. The nobility reacted with hostility, and the parlements blocked the financial reforms of Turgot and Malesherbes, who were removed in 1776. Jacques Necker then borrowed abroad instead of raising taxes, and his Compte-rendu of 1781 led the public to think that the kingdom ran a modest surplus.

Louis supported the American colonists from 1776, first by sending supplies in secret, and in 1778 by a formal Treaty of Alliance and war with Britain. The ensuing debt and financial crisis contributed to the unpopularity of the ancien régime. The Estates General met in 1789, and the storming of the Bastille forced him to recognise the legislative authority of the National Assembly. On 5 October 1789 a mob from Paris marched on Versailles, and the royal family was taken to the Tuileries Palace in Paris.

On 21 June 1791 Louis tried to flee secretly with his family to the fortress town of Montmédy, where he hoped to join the émigrés and be protected by Austria. The attempt failed at Varennes and seemed to confirm that he hoped for foreign intervention, which undermined his legitimacy. Louis was arrested during the Insurrection of 10 August 1792. The monarchy was abolished on 21 September 1792, and he became Citizen Louis Capet.

The National Convention tried him, found him guilty of high treason and had him guillotined on 21 January 1793. His death ended more than a thousand years of continuous French monarchy. Both his sons died in childhood, and his only child to reach adulthood, Marie Thérèse, was exchanged for French prisoners of war and died childless in 1851.
louis-xviii: Louis Stanislas Xavier was born at Versailles on 17 November 1755, a younger son of Louis Ferdinand, Dauphin of France, and Maria Josepha of Saxony, and grandson of Louis XV. He was styled Count of Provence from birth. In 1771 he married Princess Maria Giuseppina of Savoy, known in France as Marie Joséphine; the marriage was childless. When his brother Louis Auguste became Louis XVI in 1774, Louis Stanislas, as the king's eldest brother, took the title Monsieur but was refused a seat on the royal council, which he later called a gap of twelve years in his political life.

At the start of the Revolution the Count of Provence favoured a firm stand against the Third Estate. Unlike his brother Charles, Comte d'Artois, he stayed at Versailles in July 1789. After he left France in 1791 he proclaimed himself regent from the Low Countries and, with the other princes in exile, planned an invasion. In August 1791 he endorsed the Declaration of Pillnitz, which was badly received in France. The National Convention abolished the monarchy on 21 September 1792. When his nephew Louis XVII died in prison in June 1795, he claimed the throne as Louis XVIII.

He lived in exile at Blankenburg in Brunswick, at Jelgava Palace in Courland from 1798, and from 1808 at Hartwell House in Buckinghamshire. After the Sixth Coalition defeated Napoleon he entered Paris on 3 May 1814 and moved into the Tuileries. He rejected the constitution the Senate offered him and promised another, the Charter of 1814, which made France a constitutional monarchy, unlike the absolutist Ancien Régime.

Napoleon landed near Cannes on 1 March 1815. Louis had not removed Bonapartist troops from the army, and the army outside Paris went over to Napoleon on 19 March, the day Louis left the capital for Lille and then Ghent. He returned with Wellington's troops after Napoleon's defeat. At Cambrai on 26 June he promised that those who had served Napoleon would not be persecuted, except the instigators. His return led to a second White Terror, and the following year he dissolved the unpopular parliament, the Chambre introuvable.

Louis XVIII's health failed in the spring of 1824, with obesity, gout and gangrene, and he died on 16 September 1824. He was succeeded by his brother, the Count of Artois, as Charles X. He was the last French monarch to die while still reigning. His reign saw the formation of the Quintuple Alliance and a military intervention in Spain.
louise-michel: Louise Michel was born on 29 May 1830 to Marianne Michel, a domestic worker, and Laurent Demahis. She was raised by her paternal grandparents, Charlotte and Charles-Étienne Demahis, in north-eastern France, and spent her childhood at the Château de Vroncourt with a liberal education. After her grandparents died she completed teacher training and worked in villages. She moved to Paris in 1856, and in 1865 she opened a school there that became known for its modern and progressive methods. She corresponded with Victor Hugo, published poetry and took part in the radical politics of Paris, where Auguste Blanqui, Jules Vallès and Théophile Ferré were among her associates. In 1869 she joined a feminist group that focused on improving girls' education.

During the Siege of Paris Michel joined the National Guard, and when the Paris Commune was declared she was elected head of the Montmartre Women's Vigilance Committee. She fought with the 61st Battalion of Montmartre and organised ambulance stations at the start of the Bloody Week of 21 to 28 May 1871. Ferré and Raoul Rigault persuaded her to abandon a plan to assassinate Adolphe Thiers. On 24 May, after Montmartre had fallen, she surrendered in order to save her mother from possible imprisonment.

On 8 August 1873, after twenty months in prison, she was put aboard the Virginie to be deported to New Caledonia. On the voyage she met Henri Rochefort, who became a lifelong friend, and Nathalie Lemel, whose influence led her to anarchism. She stayed in New Caledonia for seven years, befriended the Kanak people, took an interest in their legends and languages, taught them French and took their side in the revolt of 1878. In 1880 the amnesty for the Communards allowed her to return to Paris.

In March 1883 she led a demonstration of unemployed workers; 500 demonstrators pillaged three bakeries shouting Bread, work, or lead. She reputedly carried a black flag, the first recorded use of the anarchist black flag. She was sentenced to six years of solitary confinement and released in 1886. After a further arrest in 1890 she lived five years in London, where she ran an International Anarchist School for the children of political refugees. In 1895 she and Sébastien Faure founded the periodical Le Libertaire.

Michel died of pneumonia in Marseille in January 1905. More than 100,000 people attended her funeral in Paris, and she is buried at Levallois-Perret beside Ferré. She is regarded as a founder of anarcha-feminism and remains a prominent revolutionary figure in French memory, remembered in the names of streets, schools and parks.
louise-of-mecklenburg-strelitz: Louise was born on 10 March 1776 near Hanover, the fourth daughter of Duke Charles of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, a brother of Queen Charlotte, and of Princess Friederike of Hesse-Darmstadt. Her mother died in childbirth when Louise was six, and after the early death of her stepmother the children were placed in the care of their grandmother Princess Maria Louise at Darmstadt. A governess from Switzerland taught them French, in which Louise became fluent while neglecting German. She learned to love German literature, above all Schiller. In 1793 she met the Prussian crown prince Frederick William at Frankfurt, and he at once chose her as his wife. They were married on 24 December 1793.

The couple preferred to live at Paretz Palace, outside Potsdam, and had nine children who survived infancy, including the future Frederick William IV and the future William I. On 16 November 1797 her husband became King Frederick William III. Louise became a public figure in her own right, which was new in Prussian history, and the king consulted her on affairs of state. She supported his neutrality in the early years of the wars against revolutionary France but later became an open advocate of war.

After the Prussian disaster at Jena-Auerstedt in October 1806 the royal family fled to Memel. When Napoleon dictated the Peace of Tilsit in 1807, the king sent for Louise to beg for better terms. She met Napoleon at Tilsit, but he made no concessions. Napoleon had tried to destroy her reputation, but his charges only made her more beloved in Prussia. The terms imposed an indemnity of one hundred and twenty million francs, equal to the whole yearly budget of Prussia. Louise supported the reforms of Baron vom Stein and Karl August von Hardenberg, and she helped bring about Stein's reappointment.

Louise died on 19 July 1810, aged thirty-four, in her husband's arms while visiting her father at Strelitz. The cause was an unidentified illness, which her subjects attributed to the French occupation. She was buried at Charlottenburg Palace, where a mausoleum with a recumbent statue by Christian Daniel Rauch was built over her grave. Napoleon is reported to have said that the king had lost his best minister.

She was revered as the soul of national virtue. In 1814 her husband founded the Order of Louise as a counterpart to the Iron Cross, and a statue of her was erected in the Tiergarten in Berlin in 1880. In the 1920s conservative women founded the Queen Louise League, which the Nazis disbanded in 1934.
louisiana-purchase: France controlled Louisiana from 1682 until it ceded the territory to Spain in the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau of 1762. For the United States the main issue was free transit down the Mississippi. Pinckney's Treaty of 27 October 1795 gave American merchants the right of deposit at New Orleans, but Spain revoked it in 1798 and restored it only in 1801. Meanwhile, in 1800, Spain had ceded Louisiana back to France in the secret Third Treaty of San Ildefonso, in exchange for territories in Tuscany. When Napoleon sent General Charles Leclerc to Saint-Domingue in December 1801, American fears grew that French troops would then go to New Orleans.

President Thomas Jefferson, eager to gain New Orleans, sent Robert R. Livingston to Paris in 1801 and later tasked James Monroe and Livingston with buying the city. Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours helped by back-channel diplomacy and introduced the idea of a much larger purchase. The failed French effort to suppress the revolt in Saint-Domingue and the prospect of renewed war with the United Kingdom led Napoleon to consider selling. Negotiating with the French treasury minister François Barbé-Marbois, the American envoys quickly agreed to buy the whole territory once it was offered.

The price was 80 million francs, about 15 million dollars, down from an initial 100 million francs. Of this, the United States assumed up to 20 million francs of French debts owed to its citizens and paid 60 million francs in government bonds at 6 per cent interest, which the banking houses of Baring and Hope bought. The land nominally comprised 828,000 square miles, most of the Mississippi's drainage basin west of the river. France controlled only a small part of it, and most was inhabited by Native Americans, so the United States chiefly bought the pre-emptive right to obtain their lands by treaty or conquest. The non-native population was about 60,000, half of them enslaved Africans.

Jefferson considered a constitutional amendment but was persuaded otherwise by his cabinet. Federalists opposed the purchase over its cost and constitutionality, and feared the power of the new western states and of new slave-holding states; some Northern Federalists explored a separate northern confederacy. A House vote to deny the request failed by 59 to 57. New Orleans was handed to the United States on 20 December 1803, three weeks after Spain transferred the colony to France, and the territory was organised in 1804. Its boundaries were not defined and were disputed with Spain until the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819, and its northern edge was adjusted with Britain in 1818.
lourdes: Lourdes is a market town in the foothills of the Pyrenees, at an elevation of 420 metres, in the Hautes-Pyrénées department of southwestern France. The fast-flowing river Gave de Pau runs through it. Before the mid-19th century the town was best known for its fortified castle, which rises from a rocky escarpment at its centre. On a loop of the Gave stands an outcrop of rock called Massabielle, and on its northern side is a shallow natural grotto.

The area was inhabited in prehistoric times, and from the 1st century BCE there was a Roman oppidum on the site of the present fortress, with a temple dedicated to the gods of water that was replaced in the 5th century by an early Christian church. In the Middle Ages Lourdes was part of the County of Bigorre, and its fortress was at times the seat of counts. It was given to England by the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360, and the English held it until 1407. In 1607 it was incorporated into the Kingdom of France. The castle became a prison under Louis XV and again under Napoleon.

Until 1858 Lourdes was a sleepy country town of around 4,000 people with an infantry garrison in the castle. On 11 February 1858 the 14-year-old Bernadette Soubirous reported that a beautiful lady had appeared to her at the grotto of Massabielle. She reported eighteen apparitions in all, and the lady identified herself as the Immaculate Conception, a reference to the dogma defined four years earlier by Pope Pius IX. Her parish priest was convinced by this, since the girl knew nothing of the doctrine. Pilgrims were coming by the thousand by 1859, and a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes was set up at the site in 1864.

The Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes is one of the leading Catholic Marian shrines and a place of mass pilgrimage each year from March to October. Pilgrims bathe in and drink the water that wells from the grotto, which some Catholics believe has healing properties, and the Church has officially recognised a number of cures as miraculous. The rugby team FC Lourdes won the French championship eight times between 1948 and 1968.
louvre: The Louvre stands on the Right Bank of the Seine in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, next to the Tuileries Gardens. The museum occupies the Louvre Palace, which King Philip II began in the late 12th century to protect the city from attack from the west, since the Kingdom of England then still held Normandy. Remnants of the medieval fortress are visible in the basement.

As the city grew, the fortress lost its defensive function, and in 1546 Francis I converted it into the main residence of the French kings. In 1682 Louis XIV chose Versailles for his household, leaving the Louvre mainly as a place to display the royal collection, which from 1692 included ancient Greek and Roman sculptures. In 1699 the first of a series of salons of the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture was held there.

In May 1791 the National Constituent Assembly declared that the Louvre would be a place for bringing together monuments of all the sciences and arts. After Louis XVI was imprisoned on 10 August 1792 the royal collection became national property, and the museum opened on 10 August 1793 with 537 paintings, mostly royal and confiscated church property. In 1802 Napoleon appointed Vivant Denon its first director, and in 1803 it was renamed Musée Napoléon. The collection grew with the spoils of the Napoleonic wars, though many works were returned to their owners after 1815.

Napoleon III transformed the building and the museum, and between 1852 and 1870 it added 20,000 artefacts. On 23 May 1871 Communards set fire to the adjoining Tuileries Palace, and the fire spread to the museum's north-west wing, but firemen and museum staff saved it. In 1981 President François Mitterrand proposed the Grand Louvre plan, which moved the Finance Ministry out of the North Wing so that almost the whole building could serve the museum. I. M. Pei's design of 1984 added an underground entrance reached through a glass pyramid in the Cour Napoléon.

The Louvre is a national art museum owned by the French government. Its collection is divided into eight departments: Egyptian Antiquities; Near Eastern Antiquities; Greek, Etruscan and Roman Antiquities; Islamic Art; Sculpture; Decorative Arts; Paintings; and Prints and Drawings. Among its best-known works are the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace. The Near Eastern department dates from 1881 and grew from Paul-Émile Botta's 1843 expedition to Khorsabad, where he found the palace of Sargon II.
louvre-abu-dhabi: In 2005 the United Arab Emirates proposed to the French government a museum in the Emirates bearing the name of the Louvre. Talks began in June 2005, when a delegation from Abu Dhabi visited Paris, and formal negotiations started in the summer of 2006. In 2006 the Abu Dhabi authorities chose Jean Nouvel as architect, a choice first suggested by Thomas Krens of the Solomon R.

Guggenheim Foundation. The project was revealed by Le Monde in September 2006 and met controversy, including a petition by the curators Françoise Cachin, Jean Clair and Roland Recht. The agreement was signed on 6 March 2007 and ratified by the French Parliament on 9 October 2007.

Construction began on Saadiyat Island on 26 May 2009. The opening, first expected in 2012, was postponed, and the museum was inaugurated on 8 November 2017 by President Emmanuel Macron of France, Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. It opened to the public three days later. Before then the collection was shown in preview exhibitions: an exhibition at the Emirates Palace in 2009 presented the first 19 acquisitions, among them a Mamluk Quran, a Virgin and Child by Bellini and a Mondrian, and Birth of a Museum in 2013 showed 130 works.

Nouvel designed a dome of 7,850 aluminium stars in eight layers, meant to recall sunlight through date palm fronds, over a museum of 55 buildings, 23 of them galleries, with tidal pools in the galleries to suggest a museum in the sea. Two public works were commissioned for the opening: a limestone sculpture by Jenny Holzer engraved with texts in cuneiform, Arabic and French, and an installation by Giuseppe Penone.

The museum is overseen by the Abu Dhabi Department of Culture & Tourism and linked to France by the 2007 agreement, which was extended in 2023 for an additional payment of €165 million. A French company, Agence France-Muséums, was incorporated on 23 August 2007, with shareholders that include the Louvre and other French cultural institutions. Under the agreement Abu Dhabi pays €400 million for the use of the Louvre name, as well as sums for art loans, special exhibitions and management advice.

Critics in France, led by the art historian Didier Rykner, opposed the deal, and a petition against it was signed by 4,650 curators, archaeologists and art historians. Human Rights Watch reported the confiscation of workers' passports during construction, and Nouvel defended the workers' conditions as better than in some European countries. Others have criticised a European focus in the modern and contemporary collections.
low-countries: The Low Countries form the lower basin of the Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt delta. Regions without access to the sea tied themselves politically and economically to those with access, forming unions of ports and hinterland that reached as far as parts of the German Rhineland, so that hilly regions such as Luxembourg and southern Belgium are counted too. The name arose at the court of the Dukes of Burgundy, who spoke of les pays de par deçà, the lands over here, as opposed to their lands in Burgundy. It later evolved into Pays-Bas. In the 12th century the region's trading centres rivalled northern Italy as one of the most densely populated parts of Western Europe, with guilds and councils governing most cities.

In Roman times the region belonged to the provinces of Gallia Belgica and Germania Inferior, and Frankish tribes entered it in the 4th and 5th centuries. After Louis the Pious died, Middle Francia under Lothair I took in most of the region, apart from the County of Flanders, which lay in West Francia. Afterwards the rulers of West and East Francia both coveted it, and its fiefs owed sovereignty either to the Kingdom of France or to the Holy Roman Empire.

In the 14th and 15th centuries separate fiefs came under one family, the Valois Dukes of Burgundy, and at the height of Burgundian influence the region became a political, cultural and economic centre of Northern Europe, famed for Early Netherlandish painting in cities such as Bruges, Ghent and Brussels. In 1477 the Burgundian holdings passed through Mary of Burgundy to the Habsburgs. Charles V, who inherited them in 1506, joined them as the Seventeen Provinces by the Pragmatic Sanction of 1549.

The Habsburg policy of unification, with new bishoprics and laws against heresy, angered inhabitants who saw their provinces as distinct and helped to cause the Dutch Revolt. After the northern provinces declared independence from Spain in 1581, the ten southern provinces stayed under the Army of Flanders and were called the Spanish Netherlands. They passed to Austria in 1713 under the Treaty of Utrecht. The United Kingdom of the Netherlands united the region from 1815 to 1830, after which it divided into the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg.

The Low Countries consist today of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, the three Benelux countries, whose economic union grew from the London Customs Convention signed by their exiled governments in 1944. The term is sometimes extended to parts of northern France and the German regions of East Frisia, Guelders and Cleves.
lower-austria: Lower Austria occupies the north-eastern corner of Austria and has a land area of 19,186 square kilometres. It borders the Czech Republic and Slovakia along a frontier of 414 kilometres, and the Austrian states of Upper Austria, Styria and Burgenland, and it surrounds Vienna. Almost all of it is drained by the Danube; the only river that flows to the North Sea, by way of the Vltava and the Elbe, is the Lainsitz in the north of the Waldviertel.

The land is divided into four quarters. The Mostviertel lies above the Vienna Woods and rises to the foothills of the Limestone Alps, the Industrieviertel lies below them, the Weinviertel is a hilly region below the Manhartsberg, and the Waldviertel above it is mostly a granite plateau. The state is rich in karst caves, with 4,082 recorded.

Human settlement here is old. At Schletz, in the area of the Linear Pottery culture, more than 200 Neolithic people were killed in a massacre some 7,000 years ago. Klosterneuburg Abbey is one of the oldest abbeys in Austria. The names Lower Austria and Upper Austria derive from the earlier Austria below the Enns and Austria above the Enns, after the river Enns, and in the middle of the 13th century the land became known as the Principality below the Enns.

The Battle on the Marchfeld, fought on 26 August 1278, marked the beginning of the ascendancy of the House of Habsburg in Austria and Central Europe. During the Ottoman wars in Europe the region was repeatedly raided by Tatars and Ottoman Akinji, irregular mounted troops, and many people were taken into slavery. In 1809 it was the site of the Battles of Aspern and Wagram, fought between French troops under Napoleon and an Austrian army led by Archduke Charles. Before the Second World War Lower Austria had the largest number of Jews in the country.

Lower Austria is the largest of the nine states of Austria and has a population of about 1.7 million. Vienna became a separate state in 1921, and Sankt Pölten has been the capital since 1986. The state has 20 districts, four independent towns and 573 municipalities. The Wachau valley between Melk and Krems is known for its landscape, culture and wine.
lower-bavaria: Lower Bavaria, in German Niederbayern, is one of the seven administrative regions of Bavaria and lies in the east of the state. It consists of nine districts and 258 municipalities, three of them cities, and is divided into two planning regions, Landshut and Donau-Wald. It includes the Bavarian Forest, a well-known tourist destination, and the Lower Bavarian Upland.

The Duchy of Lower Bavaria was first created by the First Bavarian Partition in 1255 under Duke Henry, though it did not match the extent of the present region. After a reunification in 1340, Bavaria was divided again in 1349, and in 1353 Bavaria-Straubing and Bavaria-Landshut were created in Lower Bavaria. Bavaria was later reunited permanently. For administration the land was split into Rentämter, and Lower Bavaria consisted of the Rentamt Landshut and the Rentamt Straubing. Control of Lower Bavaria was one of the issues in the War of the Bavarian Succession.

After the Kingdom of Bavaria was founded in 1805, following the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, the state was reorganised, and in 1808 it was divided into 15 districts, called Kreise, modelled on the French departments and named after their main rivers. Territorial changes, including the loss of Tyrol and the addition of the Palatinate, reduced them to eight, one of which was the Unterdonaukreis, the Lower Danube District. In 1837 King Ludwig I of Bavaria renamed the Kreise after historical territories and tribes, and the Unterdonaukreis became Lower Bavaria, with its capital moved from Passau to Landshut.
Lower Bavaria and the Upper Palatinate were joined in one district in 1932 and separated again in 1954. The region was reshaped in 1972 when its rural districts were reorganised.

The main tourist attractions include the former ducal residences of Landshut and Straubing, the baroque episcopal city of Passau, and Kelheim with the Befreiungshalle and Weltenburg Abbey. Scenic attractions include the Danube, with its gorge at Weltenburg, and the Bavarian Forest with Mount Großer Arber.
lower-egypt: Lower Egypt is the northernmost part of Egypt, the fertile Nile Delta between Upper Egypt and the Mediterranean Sea. In ancient Egyptian it was called mehu, meaning north. Greeks and Romans called it Aegyptus Inferior, while Copts kept the old northern name, Tsakhet or Psanemhit, and divided it into regions: Niphaiat in the west, Tiarabia in the east, Nimeshshoti in the north-east and Bashmur in the north. After the Muslim conquest the middle of the Delta was called al-Rif, the countryside, and the eastern part al-Hawf, the edge.

The Nile reaches the sea through two principal channels, at Rashid in the west and Damietta in the east, and the delta is crossed by channels and canals. Its climate is milder than that of Upper Egypt, with less extreme temperatures and more rain. In antiquity it was divided into nomes.

By about 3600 BCE Neolithic societies along the Nile lived by raising crops and domesticating animals. Soon afterwards Egyptian society grew rapidly toward a more refined civilisation: a new pottery related to that of the Southern Levant appeared, copper came into wider use, and the Mesopotamian sun-dried brick and architectural principles such as the arch became popular. At the same time the societies and towns of Upper Egypt and those of the Delta each went through a process of unification, and warfare between the two kingdoms was frequent. King Narmer, reigning in Upper Egypt, defeated his enemies in the Delta and joined the two kingdoms under his rule.

Memphis was the capital of Lower Egypt. Its patron goddess was the cobra Wadjet, its crown was the Red Crown, Deshret, and its symbols were the papyrus and the bee. After unification Wadjet and Nekhbet, the vulture goddess of Upper Egypt, were shown together as the Two Ladies, protecting all Egyptians.

The Palermo Stone, a royal annal written in the mid Fifth Dynasty, records kings who reigned over Lower Egypt before Narmer; none is attested outside it. Other kings, Double Falcon and Crocodile, are known from finds in Sinai and Lower Egypt. On the Narmer Palette the figure struck down by Narmer is named Wash, but it is uncertain whether he was a real person or an allegory.
lower-franconia: After the founding of the Kingdom of Bavaria the state was entirely reorganised and in 1808 divided into 15 administrative regions, called Kreise in Bavaria. They were created in the fashion of the French departements, fairly even in size and population, and named after their main rivers. Territorial changes, such as the loss of Tyrol and the addition of the Palatinate, then reduced the number to eight. One of them was the Untermainkreis, the Lower Main District.

In 1837 King Ludwig I of Bavaria renamed the Kreise after historical territorial names and tribes of the area, with some border changes and swaps. The Untermainkreis became Lower Franconia and Aschaffenburg, and the city name was dropped in the middle of the 20th century. From 1933 the regional Nazi Gauleiter, Otto Hellmuth, who had renamed his party Gau Mainfranken, insisted on giving the government district the same name. He met resistance from Bavarian state authorities but succeeded, and the change took effect on 1 June 1938. After 1945 the name Unterfranken was restored. The municipal reform of June 1972 consolidated its 22 country districts into nine.

Lower Franconia is one of the seven districts of Bavaria and the north-western part of Franconia, which Lower, Middle and Upper Franconia together make up. It consists of nine country districts and three district-free cities, with 308 municipalities in all, and most of the Franconian wine region lies within it. Its coat of arms combines the Franconian Rake, the arms of the Duchy of Franconia, with the Rennfähnlein banner associated with Würzburg and a wheel symbolising the clerical state of Mainz.

The former episcopal residence cities of Würzburg, with Veitshöchheim, and Aschaffenburg are its main sights, along with the towns of Miltenberg, Amorbach and Werneck, the Mainschleife at Volkach, the Rhön with the spa town of Bad Kissingen, and the Spessart with Mespelbrunn Castle. Its institutes of higher education include the Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg, the University of Applied Sciences Würzburg-Schweinfurt and the Hochschule Aschaffenburg.
lower-lusatia: Lower Lusatia stretches from the southeast of the German state of Brandenburg to the southwest of Lubusz Voivodeship in Poland. It lies within the North European Plain and is characterised by extended pine forests, heathlands and meadows. The middle Spree River bounds it in the north, and between Lübben and Cottbus the Spree branches out into the Spreewald riparian forest. In the east the Bóbr river forms the border with Lower Silesia. A morainic ridge called the Grenzwall, densely forested in the Middle Ages, separates it from Upper Lusatia.

Until the late Middle Ages the region was known simply as Lusatia, and it gained the name Lower in the 15th century, when the land of Bautzen became Upper Lusatia. In the early 960s Count Gero I forced the Slavic Lusatians to pay tribute to Otto I. In 1002 the Polish duke Bolesław I the Brave captured their lands, which remained Polish under the Treaty of Bautzen of 1018 until Germans recaptured them in 1031. In 1136 Conrad the Great of the House of Wettin received the March of Lusatia, and in 1303 the Ascanian margraves of Brandenburg acquired it.

In 1367 Elector Otto V sold the region to Emperor Charles IV, who incorporated it into the Bohemian Crown. Brandenburg acquired the Lordship of Cottbus in 1455, and it remained an exclave. Under the Luxembourg, Jagiellon and, from 1526, Habsburg dynasties the great majority of the population turned Protestant. In the 1635 Peace of Prague Emperor Ferdinand II ceded the Lusatias to Elector John George I of Saxony, and the 1815 Congress of Vienna gave Lower Lusatia to Prussia. After 1945 the Oder–Neisse line placed the lands east of the Neisse in Poland, and the western part became part of East Germany.

Lower Lusatia is a settlement area of the West Slavic Sorbs, whose endangered Lower Sorbian language is related to Upper Sorbian and Polish. The Sorbian museum in Cottbus and a museum in Żary record the region's history. Its coat of arms shows a bull, first documented in 1363 and still in use. Lignite mining shaped the region through the 19th and 20th centuries, and open-pit mines damaged or destroyed more than 100 villages, many of them Sorbian. Some exhausted pits have become artificial lakes, and the area is now called the Lusatian Lake District.
lower-saxony: Lower Saxony covers 47,614 km2 and is the second-largest German state by land area. It is the only state that has both a sea coast and mountains: the North Sea and the East Frisian Islands lie in the north-west, the North German Plain fills the northern half, and the Weser Uplands and the Harz Mountains rise to the south. The state of Bremen forms two enclaves inside it, the city of Bremen and its seaport Bremerhaven.

In the north-east lies the Lüneburg Heath, the largest heathland area of Germany. In the Middle Ages the town of Lüneburg was wealthy from salt-mining and the salt trade. West of Hamburg, the Altes Land on the Elbe is the state's largest fruit-farming area, with apples as its chief produce.

The name Saxony derives from the Saxons, a Germanic confederation of tribes. Before the late medieval period there was a single Duchy of Saxony. After the stem duchy was dissolved in the late 13th century, the term Lower Saxony came into use for the parts of it ruled by the House of Welf, to distinguish them from the Electorate of Saxony on one side and the Duchy of Westphalia on the other.

The modern state was created from parts of the British occupation zone after the Second World War. On 1 November 1946 the State of Hanover, a former kingdom that had been a province of Prussia since 1866, was merged with the three smaller free states of Brunswick, Oldenburg and Schaumburg-Lippe. Because most of the territory had belonged to the Kingdom of Hanover, the new state took over its coat of arms, a white Saxon horse on a red ground.

The first Landtag, appointed by the British administration, met on 9 December 1946 and elected the Social Democrat Hinrich Wilhelm Kopf as minister-president. He led a five-party coalition whose task was to improve food supplies and rebuild the cities and towns destroyed by Allied air raids.

Lower Saxony has about 8 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Hanover. It is divided into 37 districts and several urban districts, and its constitution describes it as a free, republican, democratic, social and environmentally sustainable state within the Federal Republic of Germany. Agriculture, especially livestock farming, has long been important to its economy. The state has four World Heritage Sites, and Northern Low Saxon and Saterland Frisian are still spoken in rural areas.
lozere: The Lozère is a landlocked department near the Massif Central, named after Mont Lozère. It borders Haute-Loire to the north-east, Ardèche to the east, Gard to the south, Aveyron to the west and Cantal to the north-west, and covers 5,167 square kilometres. Its geography is complicated, spanning four mountain ranges. In the north-west the basalt plateau of Aubrac rises between 1,000 and 1,450 metres, with a cold, humid climate. The Margeride mountains in the north and north-east are granite, with peaks between 1,000 and 1,550 metres and a colder, drier climate.

The Causses, very dry limestone plateaus, lie in the south-west. The Cévennes in the south-east include the granite Mont Lozère, at 1,702 metres the highest point in the department. The Tarn has its source on Mont Lozère and flows through the Gorges du Tarn in the Causses.

The Lozère was created in 1790, during the French Revolution, when the whole of France was divided into departments in place of the old provinces. It was formed from part of the old province of Languedoc. Its territory is nearly identical with the former province of Gévaudan. Pliny the Elder's Natural History praised the cheese of the area, naming the Lesura and Gabalis districts among those that supplied the cheeses most esteemed at Rome, though he added that its excellence was short-lived and it had to be eaten fresh.
Between 1764 and 1767 the Beast of Gévaudan, a creature believed to be a large wolf or an exotic animal, terrorised the Margeride Mountains in the former province of Gévaudan.

Mende is the prefecture and the most populous commune. It has the smallest population of any French department, and the number has been falling since the end of the 19th century as young people leave for cities such as Lyon, Marseille and Montpellier. Cattle farming, with the hardy Aubrac as the commonest breed, and tourism are the main activities, since the poor soil allows little arable farming. Forest covers a large share of the land. Part of the Cévennes National Park lies within the department, and rivers such as the Lot, Tarn and Truyère are noted for trout.
lu-bu: Lü Bu came from Jiuyuan County in Wuyuan Commandery, on the northern frontier of the Han empire, near present-day Baotou in Inner Mongolia, and was known for his martial valour in Bing Province. No description of his appearance survives in historical records, but he specialised in archery and horse-riding, had great physical strength and was nicknamed the Flying General. He owned a steed called Red Hare, and a saying of the time ran: among men, Lü Bu; among steeds, Red Hare. Ding Yuan, appointed Inspector of Bing, recruited him as a registrar and treated him with exceptional kindness.

In 190 a coalition of warlords led by Yuan Shao marched against Dong Zhuo, who had installed Emperor Xian as a puppet. Lü Bu defended Dong Zhuo, but Sun Jian drove him back, and Dong burned Luoyang and moved the capital to Chang'an. In 192 Lü Bu killed Dong Zhuo, at the instigation of Wang Yun and Shisun Rui. Dong's followers then attacked Chang'an, and Lü Bu fought a duel with Guo Si and eventually abandoned the city. He fled to Yuan Shu, who according to the Sanguozhi refused him, while the Houhanshu says Yuan treated him generously until his arrogance and plundering worried him. He then helped Yuan Shao fight Zhang Yan, but Yuan too came to distrust him.

In 194, while Cao Cao was attacking Xu Province, rebels invited Lü Bu into Yan Province, and he declared himself its governor. Cao took the territory back within two years. In 195 Lü Bu seized Xu Province from Liu Bei, who had sheltered him. When Yuan Shu declared himself emperor in early 197, Lü Bu, who had agreed to marry his daughter to Yuan's son, seized her back from the convoy and sent Yuan's envoy to Xu as a prisoner. Yuan attacked him in anger, and around late 197 or early 198 Lü Bu sided with Yuan Shu again.

In the winter of 198 Cao Cao besieged Xiapi. Lü Bu wanted to surrender, but Chen Gong and others, who had already offended Cao Cao, urged him not to. Captured and bound, he pleaded to be spared, and when Cao Cao hesitated Liu Bei reminded him what Lü Bu had done to Ding Yuan and Dong Zhuo. He was executed on 7 February 199. Chen Shou wrote that Lü Bu had the might of a tiger but lacked planning skills, and Fan Ye called him erratic and capricious. The 14th-century Romance of the Three Kingdoms portrays him as a nearly invincible warrior but an incapable leader, and adds fictional stories such as his romance with Diaochan.
lu-buwei: The main sources for Lü Buwei date from the first century BCE: Sima Qian's Shiji, and Liu Xiang's Zhan Guo Ce and Shuoyuan. Since these Han texts openly criticise both Lü Buwei and the Qin dynasty, some of their stories, such as his private thoughts and conversations, can be discounted. According to the Shiji he came from the state of Wey and became a successful travelling merchant. In Handan, the capital of Zhao, he met Yiren, a prince of Qin serving there as a hostage, and said, "This is a rare piece of merchandise that should be saved for later." The Zhan Guo Ce says he turned to politics after reckoning that establishing a ruler would bring an incalculable return.

Using bribes and machinations, Lü Buwei arranged for Yiren to return to Qin and persuaded Lady Huayang, the childless principal wife of the heir, to adopt him, making him heir apparent. She renamed him Zichu. The Shiji says Zichu became infatuated with Lady Zhao, a dancing girl of Lü's household, who bore a son, Ying Zheng, in 259 BCE. Zichu succeeded as King Zhuangxiang and made Lü Buwei chancellor and Marquis Wenxin, with a fief of 100,000 households in Luoyang. When Zhuangxiang died in 247 BCE, the 13-year-old Ying Zheng succeeded him, with Lü as regent.

Lü dominated the government and military and invited scholars from all over China to Xianyang, where they compiled the Lüshi Chunqiu, an encyclopaedic compendium of the ideas of the Hundred Schools of Thought, published in 239 BCE.

According to the Shiji, Lü Buwei, fearing that the Queen Dowager's illicit pursuits would be discovered, introduced to her a retainer, Lao Ai, disguised as a eunuch. Lao Ai was made Marquis Changxin and took control of the Qin government, and in 238 BCE he launched a revolt that was crushed. Lü Buwei, implicated, was stripped of his posts and titles and banished to Shu, and he took poison, fearing eventual execution.
