Ying Zheng then removed power from most of Lü's followers and restored it to the hereditary Qin aristocracy. Knoblock and Riegel observe that in the West Lü might be seen as a merchant-prince and patron of culture, a kind of Medici, whereas Han literati, who despised his merchant origins and considered Qin's unification of China an evil, condemned him as a parvenu and a fraud.
lu-xun: Lu Xun was born Zhou Zhangshou on 25 September 1881 in Shaoxing, Zhejiang, into a declining family of landlords and scholar-officials. In 1893 his father was found trying to bribe an examination official and lost his position; his grandfather was sentenced to beheading for the offence, a sentence commuted to imprisonment, and he was released in 1901 only after regular, expensive bribes. His father died in 1896 at the age of 35. Lu Xun's early education rested on the Confucian classics, which he later found neither useful nor interesting; he preferred folk stories and opera.

Family poverty sent him to the tuition-free Jiangnan Naval Academy in 1898, which he left after half a year, and then to the School of Mines and Railways, where he studied English and German and read Western authors. He enrolled at the Sendai Medical College in Japan in 1904 but left medicine for literature.

After holding brief teaching posts, Lu Xun joined the Ministry of Education of the new Republic of China in February 1912 and lived in Beijing from 1912 to 1926. In 1912 he helped design the Twelve Symbols national emblem. In 1918 he published Diary of a Madman, the first novel in vernacular Chinese, under the pen name Lu Xun, taking the surname from his mother. His writing in La Jeunesse after the May Fourth Movement of 1919 brought him prominence.

In Shanghai he lived by writing alone, rejecting regular teaching posts. He turned increasingly to Marxist thought and in 1930 co-founded the League of Left-Wing Writers, though other leftist writers soon accused him of being a feudal remnant and a counterrevolutionary. In 1931 he introduced the woodcuts of Käthe Kollwitz to China. When the Kuomintang passed stricter censorship laws that January, he went into hiding; weeks later it executed twenty-four writers. He died on 19 October 1936 and was buried in a mausoleum in Lu Xun Park in Shanghai, with an inscription in the calligraphy of Mao Zedong.

Lu Xun wrote novels, essays, poetry, translation and political commentary, in both vernacular and literary Chinese. His style mixes sympathetic engagement with ironic detachment, as in The True Story of Ah Q, while My Old Home and A Little Incident are direct. His early novellas often portray weak and frustrated characters who are victims of an oppressive culture, and he criticised what he called the Chinese national character. He judged the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 a failure, and later grew disappointed with the Nationalist government. He championed woodcuts, serial illustrations and cartoons. In China his legacy has been extensively interpreted by the Chinese Communist Party, although in his lifetime he kept a distance from any political organisation.
luan: Lu'an is a prefecture-level city in western Anhui province, bordering Henan to the northwest and Hubei to the southwest. It lies between the Yangtze and Huai rivers at the northern foot of the Dabie Mountains. The terrain is high in the southwest and flat in the northeast, forming three natural areas of mountains, hills and plains. The climate is humid subtropical with four distinct seasons, cold damp winters and hot humid summers, and most of the rain falls from June to August. The character 六, normally pronounced Liù, is read Lù here because of a historical literary reading.

During the Xia and Shang dynasties Liu was a country south of the Huai River. From the Western Zhou to the Spring and Autumn period several feudal states, among them Ying, Liu, Liao and Qunshu, arose in the area, and in the Warring States period they merged and became subordinate to Wu and then Chu. Under the Qin dynasty six counties belonged to Jiujiang County. The Western Han dynasty established the Liu'an Kingdom, taking the meaning "safety in the six places", and the Eastern Han established Liu'an County. In 1118, under the Song, the Lu'an Army was set up. Lu'an City and Lu'an County merged in December 1992, and the provincial-level Lu'an City was established in March 2000.

Ying Bu, a general of the late Qin and early Han, came from the area. He had been one of Xiang Yu's generals and was granted the title of King of Jiujiang. He later surrendered to Liu Bang, who named him King of Huainan, and he was killed for rebellion.

Lu'an Guapian, a green tea, is produced in the Dabie Mountains of Lu'an. It was called Luzhou Lu'an Tea in the Tang dynasty and appears in Lu Yu's Book of Tea. The Ming scientist Xu Guangqi wrote that the tea of Liu'an Prefecture was the best tea, and under the Qing it was listed as tribute. The leaf is shaped like a melon seed. Duan Qirui, a politician of the Republic of China, was a native of Liu'an County. The local economy includes iron ore metallurgy, food processing and machinery manufacturing.
luanda: Luanda lies on the northern Atlantic coast of Angola and is the country's chief seaport and its administrative, industrial and cultural centre. It has a hot, semi-arid climate, unusually dry for its tropical latitude because the cool Benguela Current keeps moisture from condensing into rain. The old city, the Baixa de Luanda, stands beside the port with narrow streets and colonial buildings, and the Cidade Alta is the newer part.

Paulo Dias de Novais founded the city on 25 January 1576 as São Paulo da Assumpção de Loanda, bringing one hundred families of settlers and four hundred soldiers. The Portuguese built the Fortaleza São Pedro da Barra in 1618 and the Fortaleza de São Miguel in 1634, and the city was their bridgehead in Angola from 1627, apart from a period of Dutch rule, as Fort Aardenburgh, that ended in 1648.

Luanda was the centre of the slave trade to Brazil until the trade was abolished in 1836. Brazilian ships were the most numerous in its port, and local merchants and warriors profited; in 1751 between 5,000 and 10,000 slaves were sold there each year. Angola's ports were opened to foreign shipping in 1844, and by 1850 Luanda was one of the most developed Portuguese cities outside Portugal, exporting palm and peanut oil, wax, copal, ivory, cotton and coffee. It grew from 61,208 inhabitants in 1940 to 475,328 in 1970.

After the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon on 25 April 1974, independence in 1975 and the start of the Angolan Civil War, most white Portuguese residents left as refugees. Migrants fleeing the war swelled the population, and slums called musseques spread far beyond the old limits. The war ended in 2002, and major reconstruction began.

Luanda is the capital and largest city of Angola and holds about a third of its population. Portuguese is the official language, and Kimbundu, Umbundu and Kikongo are also spoken. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic archbishop and the home of most of Angola's universities. Surviving monuments include the Fortress of São Miguel, the best preserved of the colonial forts, Luanda Cathedral and the Palácio de Ferro, and the National Museum of Slavery is in the city.
luang-prabang: Luang Prabang is the capital of Luang Prabang Province in north-central Laos. Its name means Royal Buddha Image and comes from the Phra Bang, a statue that symbolises Lao sovereignty. It was historically known as Xieng Thong. UNESCO designated the city a World Heritage Site in 1995 for its blend of Lao architecture, European colonial buildings and more than thirty Buddhist temples, and its protected area covers 33 of its 58 villages. Daily rituals such as the morning procession of monks accepting alms continue there.

By the 8th century the Mon had pushed north from the Chao Phraya valley and created city states, among them Muang Sua, the site of Luang Prabang. These states introduced Theravada Buddhism, brought by missionaries from Sri Lanka. The city experienced a period of Khmer suzerainty under Jayavarman VII from 1185 to 1191. In 1353 it became the capital of the kingdom of Lan Xang under its first king, Fa Ngum. In 1359 the Khmer king at Angkor gave the Phra Bang to his son-in-law Fa Ngum to give Buddhist legitimacy to his rule, and the capital took its name from the image. Vietnamese forces occupied it during Emperor Lê Thánh Tông's expedition of 1478 to 1480 against Lan Xang and Lanna.

In 1707 Lan Xang fell apart in a dynastic struggle, and Luang Prabang became the capital of the Kingdom of Luang Phrabang. When France annexed Laos, the French recognised it as the royal residence, and its ruler gradually came to be regarded as the figurehead of Laos. During the World War II it was held in turn by Vichy France, Thailand, Japan and Free France. On 8 April 1945 King Sisavang Vong declared an end to Laos' status as a French protectorate, but after Japan's surrender he assured returning Free French forces that Laos remained one.

In April and May 1946 the French used paratroops to retake Luang Prabang and Vientiane and drove the Lao Issara ministers out of the country. During the First Indochina War the Viet Minh and Pathet Lao forces tried to capture the city in 1953 and 1954, but French forces stopped them before they reached it. When Laos became independent, Sisavang Vong, king of Luang Prabang, became head of state of the Kingdom of Laos.
luapula-river: The Luapula River flows north in central Africa within the Congo River watershed. It rises in the wetlands of Lake Bangweulu in Zambia, which the Chambeshi River feeds, flows west and then north, marks the border between Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and empties into Lake Mweru. It gives its name to Zambia's Luapula Province. Below the Bangweulu swamps it passes rapids and the Mambilima Falls, and at Tangwa it has cut caves, arches and potholes in rocky hills.

The explorer David Livingstone found the swamps a mass of shifting channels and lagoons. He died exploring the area, and one of his last acts was to question Chief Chitambo about the course of the Luapula. The river is part of the longest tributary of the Congo and so, by convention, part of its source.

The Luapula Valley runs for 300 km from the Chembe Bridge to Lake Mweru and holds a larger rural population than the plateau around it. The fisheries and fertile farmland of the lower valley attracted Lunda invaders under Mwata Kazembe, whose capital is at Mwansabombwe. Arab traders and slavers from Zanzibar and Portuguese traders from Mozambique came in the 18th and 19th centuries. Livingstone visited in 1867, and Mwata Kazembe told him that the Luapula links the Chambeshi and Bangweulu with the Mweru, Luvua and Lualaba systems.

The Garanganze Mission of the Plymouth Brethren settled at Mambilima around 1892, and the London Missionary Society at Mbereshi in 1900. Kasenga became the first large town of the colonial era and prospered in the 1930s by supplying fish to Elizabethville and the Katanga Copperbelt. Before roads, people travelled by canoe between lakes Bangweulu and Mweru, and during World War I a fleet of 1,885 canoes and small boats carried matériel to Chambeshi.

The swamps cover about 2,500 square kilometres along the last 100 km of the river, and papyrus beds float in them. The main channel stays about 400 metres wide. The first bridge over the river, the Luapula Bridge on the Samfya-Serenje Road, was built in 1983, and the Chembe Bridge replaced the Chembe Ferry in 2008.
lubawa: Lubawa lies on the Sandela River in Chełmno Land, in Iława County, about 18 kilometres south-east of Iława and some 115 kilometres south-east of Gdańsk. It stands at an altitude of 145 metres. Its German name was Löbau in Westpreußen and its Old Prussian name Lūbawa. The town is a member of the Cittaslow network.

In 1214 the local Prussian landlord Surwabuno was christened by Christian of Oliva, the first Catholic bishop of Prussia, who now appears on the town's coat of arms. Lubawa was first mentioned in a papal bull of Pope Innocent III dated 18 January 1216, and a wooden castle was built soon afterwards. Within the state of the Teutonic Knights the Bishopric of Culm was created in 1243 by William of Modena, and in 1257 the town became church property and the seat of the bishops of Culm. The castle was destroyed in 1268. Between 1301 and 1326 Bishop Arnold built a new one in stone, which Lithuanian forces under Gediminas destroyed in 1330 and which was rebuilt.

After the Battle of Grunwald in 1410 the Kingdom of Poland captured the town, but it returned to the Teutonic Order when the war ended. In 1440 it joined the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation, at whose request King Casimir IV Jagiellon signed the act of incorporation of the region and town into Poland in 1454. Pro-Polish troops took the castle at the start of the Thirteen Years' War, and the Second Peace of Toruń confirmed the incorporation in 1466. A great fire razed the town in 1533. Nicolaus Copernicus visited the bishop's castle several times between 1535 and 1539, and the decision to publish his De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was made at Lubawa. In 1627 the castle became a Baroque palace of Bishop Jakub Zadzik.

Prussia annexed the town in 1772 in the First Partition of Poland. It belonged to the Duchy of Warsaw during the Napoleonic Wars, then returned to Prussia, and in 1871 became part of the German Empire. The 1890 German census counted 4,593 inhabitants, of whom 2,300 were Poles. It returned to Poland under the Treaty of Versailles.

Germany occupied the town after the invasion of 1939, and from 1939 to 1945 it kept a secret camp for Polish children and teenagers aged 10 to 17, who were subjected to forced labour, beatings and malnutrition. A monument to them stands in the town, which has been Polish since 1945. Lubawa is a centre of the furniture industry and of local tourism. Surviving landmarks include the ruins of a Gothic castle, two 15th-century towers, parts of the 14th-century city walls and the Gothic St. Anne's Church of 1330.
lubben: Lübben, also known as Lübben im Spreewald and in Lower Sorbian as Lubin (Błota), lies in the historical region of Lower Lusatia in the state of Brandenburg, eastern Germany. It stands in the Spree Forest biosphere reserve, between the Upper and Lower Spree Forest, on a trade route from Luckau to Gubin and Poznań. The suffix Błota means 'the swamps'. The town belongs to the Sorbian settlement area, and German and Lower Sorbian have equal status there. The linguist Arnošt Muka wrote in 1927 that Lubin meant a settlement of the glory-loving or peace-loving, and other suggested meanings include a deep place on the Spree.

The castle of Lubin in the March of Lusatia was first mentioned in an 1150 register of Nienburg Abbey, and the town had received privileges under Magdeburg law by 1220. From 1301 it belonged to the monks of Dobrilugk Abbey, who sold it to Duke Rudolph I of Saxe-Wittenberg in 1329. Emperor Charles IV acquired the March of Lusatia in 1367 and incorporated Lübben into the Kingdom of Bohemia. In the 15th century it became the seat of the Bohemian Vogt and of the provincial diet of Lower Lusatia.

The House of Habsburg inherited Bohemia and Lusatia in 1526, and in 1623 Ferdinand II pledged Lusatia to Elector John George I of Saxony, whose electorate acquired Lübben by the Peace of Prague of 1635. After the Napoleonic Wars it passed to the Prussian province of Brandenburg under the final act of the Congress of Vienna in 1815. One of the main escape routes of insurgents from the failed Polish November Uprising to the Great Emigration led through the town.

In the Second World War the town held the prisoner-of-war camps Oflag III-C and Oflag 8 for officers of several nations, a forced labour subcamp of the prison at Luckau and a subcamp of the Sachsenhausen concentration camp. Soviet troops of the 3rd Guards Army took Lübben on 27 April 1945.

Lübben is a town of about 14,000 people and the capital of the Dahme-Spreewald district. Its sights include Lübben Castle, on medieval foundations and rebuilt in the 17th century, the Paul Gerhardt Church of the 16th century, where the hymn writer preached, and the Romanesque St Pancras fieldstone church in Steinkirchen, built in the early 13th century and one of the oldest preserved churches in Lower Lusatia.
lubeck: Lübeck lies at the mouth of the Trave, which flows into the Bay of Lübeck at Travemünde. Its historic old town stands on an island and is the southwesternmost city on the Baltic Sea, the closest point of access to the Baltic from Hamburg. The city is in the Holsatian part of Schleswig-Holstein.

A Slavic fortification existed at Old Lübeck, near the confluence of the Schwartau and the Trave, by 819. The settlement, first recorded as Liubice in 1072, became a centre of the Obotrites before it was destroyed in 1138. In 1143 Adolf II, Count of Schauenburg and Holstein, founded a new town on the river island of Bucu. A fire destroyed it in 1157, and Henry the Lion rebuilt it in 1159 and in 1160 moved the bishopric there from Oldenburg. After Henry was outlawed in 1181, Emperor Frederick Barbarossa confirmed its privileges. Lübeck law was later adopted by more than 100 Baltic towns.

In 1226 Emperor Frederick II granted Lübeck imperial immediacy. It lay on the trade routes between the North Sea and the Baltic, and from the mid-13th century other Low German towns asked it to represent their common interests, so that it became the leading city of the Hanseatic League. The League concluded the Peace of Stralsund in 1370, when its power in the Baltic was at its height, and its last diet met in Lübeck in 1669, though it was never formally dissolved.

French troops occupied Lübeck after the Battle of Lübeck on 6 November 1806, and it was part of the First French Empire from January 1811 to December 1813. The Congress of Vienna recognised it as a sovereign free city in 1815. It lost its status as a state on 1 April 1937. A British air raid on 28 March 1942 caused a firestorm that destroyed nearly 1,500 houses and severely damaged the historic centre.

Lübeck has about 220,000 inhabitants. Its old town, designated a World Heritage Site in 1987, is Germany's most extensive. Six church towers exceed 100 metres, and St Mary's Church, built from 1265 to 1351, served as the model for most of the Brick Gothic churches in the Hanseatic sphere. The Holstentor was built from 1464 to 1478.
lublin: Lublin lies in eastern Poland on the Lublin Upland, about 153 kilometres south-east of Warsaw. The Bystrzyca river, a tributary of the Wieprz, divides the city into a western part with loess gorges and a flat eastern part. It is the largest Polish city east of the Vistula and the second-largest city of historical Lesser Poland.

Settlements existed on the site from the sixth to seventh centuries. The stronghold on Old Town Hill was probably one of the main centres of the Lendians, a Lechitic tribe. When it was destroyed in the 10th century the centre shifted north-east and, after the mid-12th century, to Castle Hill.

The Polish–Lithuanian Union of Krewo in 1385 contributed to the city's growth. Lublin lay on the route between Vilnius and Kraków, and in 1392 King Władysław II Jagiełło granted it an important trade privilege. The largest trade fairs of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth were held here, and the Sejm met in Lublin several times in the 16th century. On 26 June 1569 it proclaimed the Union of Lublin, which united Poland and Lithuania. In 1578 the city became the seat of the Crown Tribunal, the highest appeal court of the Commonwealth. A Calvinist congregation was founded, and Polish Brethren made it a centre of Unitarianism.

After the Third Partition of Poland in 1795 Lublin fell to the Austrian Empire, then to the Duchy of Warsaw, and in 1815 to Congress Poland in the Russian partition. A railway link to Warsaw built in 1877 spurred industry. German forces occupied the city in 1939 and it became part of the General Government.

Lublin is the capital of Lublin Voivodeship, created in 1999. Its Old Town, with narrow cobbled streets and a largely medieval layout, is one of Poland's national monuments. The city's institutions include the Maria Curie-Skłodowska University, the John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin and the National Museum of Lublin in the castle.
luc-en-diois: The Latin name of Luc-en-Diois, Lucus Augusti or Lucus for short, evokes a sacred wood of the Gauls, and it may be the origin of this Roman capital installed in the first century BCE at the foot of the mountains of the Diois. It shared with Vaison-la-Romaine the title of chief city of the Vocontii, an important romanised Gallic people. Tacitus calls it a municipium of the Vocontii. Lucus lay in the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis, and the Antonine Itinerary places it on a road from Vapincum, modern Gap, to Lugdunum, modern Lyon: the first stage after Mons Seleucus, between that place and Dea Vocontiorum, modern Die.

For reasons that are unknown, the capital of the Vocontii was transferred to Die around the beginning of the second century CE. The city withered little by little and by the beginning of the fourth century was merely a mansio, a station on a Roman road. At the same time a fort was installed at the top of the peak of Luc to watch the road, which had gained strategic importance since the Roman armies were fighting on the Rhine. Running between the Durance and the Rhône, it was the most practicable winter route between Milan and Cologne.

Luc-en-Diois is a commune in the Drôme department in south-eastern France, on the river Drôme. The remains of the ancient city, which are supposed to have been monumental, are partly hidden by landslide debris that stopped the river and made it spread into lakes. What can be seen includes the remains of a large temple, built on the same model as that of Vienne, and an arm of a monumental statue more than four metres high. Many inscriptions are in the museums of Die and of the Diois.
luca-giordano: Luca Giordano was born in Naples on 18 October 1634, the son of the painter Antonio Giordano. Around 1650 he was apprenticed to Jusepe de Ribera on the recommendation of the viceroy of Naples, and his early work was heavily influenced by his teacher. Like Ribera he painted many half-length figures of philosophers, of which the Crates of 1660 in the Palazzo Barberini is an impressive example. He earned the nickname Luca fa presto, Luca paints quickly, and two further epithets, the Thunderbolt and the Proteus of painting, for his speed and his skill at imitating other painters.

About 1652 he made his first journey to Rome, where he absorbed the Baroque art of Pietro da Cortona, and returned to Naples in 1653. In the late 1650s his experiments with other styles produced an exuberantly Baroque manner that brought new light and colour to Neapolitan painting.

In 1665 he joined the Neapolitan painters' confraternity and travelled to Florence and Venice, where his altarpieces for Santa Maria della Salute, including the Assumption of the Virgin of 1667, reflect Titian. In the late 1670s he began great fresco cycles, among them the Life of St Benedict at the abbey of Monte Cassino (1677 to 1678), destroyed in the Second World War, and St Bridget in Glory (1678) in Santa Brigida, Naples.

In 1682 he went to Florence. For Marchese Francesco Riccardi he decorated the library and the ceiling of the Biblioteca Riccardiana and the long gallery of the Palazzo Medici Riccardi, with a celebration of the Medici family in the centre, surrounded by allegorical figures and mythological episodes. He returned to Naples in 1686.

In 1692 Giordano went to Spain at the invitation of Charles II and stayed ten years. He decorated the vault of the imperial staircase at the Escorial with St Lawrence in Glory, painted the ceiling of the sacristy of Toledo Cathedral from early 1698, and worked at the Buen Retiro and the Royal Palace of Aranjuez. The king granted him the title of caballero. He left Madrid on 8 February 1702.

Back in Naples he continued to paint prolifically in a lighter style that prefigured the Rococo and was admired by Fragonard. His last works, among them the sacristy frescoes of Santa Brigida, were left unfinished and completed by his pupil Giuseppe Simonelli. He died in Naples in 1705, and sources differ over whether on 3 January or 12 January. He was buried in the church of Santa Brigida.
luca-signorelli: Luca Signorelli was born Luca d'Egidio di Ventura in Cortona, Tuscany. The date of his birth is uncertain, and dates between 1441 and 1445 have been proposed. His first impressions of art seem to come from Perugia. According to his relative Giorgio Vasari, his maternal uncle Lazzaro Vasari apprenticed him to Piero della Francesca. In 1472 he was painting at Arezzo and in 1474 at Città di Castello. He also painted for Lorenzo de' Medici, and decorated a wall of the Petrucci palace in Siena with the subject of the School of Pan.

By the 1490s Signorelli led a much sought-after workshop in central Italy. In Città di Castello he painted the Martyrdom of St Sebastian, which influenced the young Raphael. In 1498 he moved to the monastery of Monte Oliveto Maggiore near Siena, where he painted eight frescoes of the life of St Benedict, now much injured. He then went to Orvieto, where he signed the contract for the San Brizio chapel of the cathedral on 5 April 1499, for 200 ducats for the ceiling and 600 for the walls, with lodging and a monthly payment of wine and corn. The contract told him to consult the Masters of the Sacred Page on theology.

Fra Angelico had begun the ceiling fifty years earlier. Signorelli painted the Apocalypse and the Last Judgment, from the Preaching of Antichrist to the Resurrection of the Flesh, Paradise and Hell, and on the lower walls scenes linked to Dante's Purgatorio. His powerful nudes and foreshortening were striking, and Michelangelo is said to have borrowed some of his figures. In 1508 Pope Julius II summoned him with other artists to the Vatican, but dismissed them to make way for Raphael.

Signorelli paid great attention to anatomy, and it is said that he studied in burial grounds. His drawings in the Louvre resemble Michelangelo's method. He aimed at powerful truth rather than nobility of form, neglected colour and used sharp contrasts of light and shadow. He had a vast influence but no pupils of high repute. He entered the magistracy of Cortona in 1488 and held a leading position there by 1523. Partly paralysed in 1520, he died in Cortona on 16 October 1523 and is buried there.
lucera: Lucera stands on a flat knoll in the Tavoliere Plains, near the foot of the Daunian Mountains, in the province of Foggia in Apulia. It lies in the territory of the ancient tribe of the Daunii, and excavations show a Bronze Age village within the present city boundaries. The origin of the name is uncertain: it may come from Lucius, a mythical Daunian king, from a temple of the goddess Lux Cereris, or from Etruscan words meaning holy wood. From 1579 until 1806 Lucera was the capital of the Province of Capitanata and the County of Molise.

In 321 BCE the Roman army, deceived into thinking Lucera was besieged by the Samnites, walked into an ambush and was defeated at the Battle of the Caudine Forks. The Samnites occupied the city but were thrown out by a revolt, and Lucera sought Roman protection.

About 2,500 Romans moved there to strengthen the ties, and the city became known as a steadfast supporter of Rome. During the late Republic Pompey set up his headquarters there but left when Julius Caesar approached, and Caesar's clemency spared the city. After the war between Octavian and Mark Antony, Octavian settled many veterans on its lands, and the Roman amphitheatre dates from this Augustan period. In 663 the Eastern Roman Emperor Constans II captured the city from the Lombards and destroyed it.

In 1224 Emperor Frederick II, responding to religious uprisings in Sicily, expelled the Muslims from the island and moved many to Lucera over the next two decades. Under royal control they paid taxes and gave military service, and their numbers reached between 15,000 and 20,000. The city was called Lucaera Saracenorum as the last stronghold of Islam in Italy, and in peacetime the Muslims were mainly farmers.

The colony lasted 75 years until Christian forces under Giovanni Pippino di Barletta sacked it in 1300 with the acquiescence of Charles II of Naples. Most inhabitants were killed or, in nearly 10,000 cases, sold into slavery. The mosques were demolished and churches built in their place, and Charles II settled Christians, chiefly Burgundian and Provençal soldiers and farmers.

Lucera is the seat of the Diocese of Lucera-Troia. Its cathedral, built in 1300 on the site of the last standing medieval mosque in Italy, is among its sights together with the medieval Lucera Castle. The Roman amphitheatre, discovered in 1932, measures about 131 by 99 metres and could hold 16,000 to 18,000 spectators. Descendants of Provençal colonists still speak a Franco-Provençal dialect in the villages of Faeto and Celle di San Vito.
lucien-bonaparte: Lucien Bonaparte was born Luciano Buonaparte in Ajaccio, Corsica, on 21 May 1775, the third surviving son of Carlo Bonaparte and Letizia Ramolino. He studied at the military schools of Autun and Brienne and left the seminary of Aix-en-Provence in 1789. A staunch supporter of the Revolution from its outbreak, he became an orator at the Jacobin Club in Ajaccio under the alias Brutus Bonaparte, and was secretary to Pasquale Paoli from 1791 until he broke with him in 1793. He was briefly jailed in 1795 for his Jacobin activity and was freed through his brother's intervention.

Elected to the Council of Five Hundred for Corsica in 1798, though not old enough, Lucien voted mostly with the Neo-Jacobins, but under the influence of Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès he became one of the main plotters of the coup of 18 Brumaire. Elected president of the Council on 23 October 1799, he had pamphlets distributed on 9 November describing a false Jacobin plot, which justified moving the Council to Saint-Cloud. Next day he presided over a heated session until Napoleon entered the chamber with grenadiers, and he then arranged Napoleon's election as First Consul.

Lucien became Minister of the Interior on 25 December 1799, appointed the first prefects, and falsified the results of the constitutional referendum of February 1800. He clashed with Joseph Fouché over the Paris police, and the brothers fell out over a subversive pamphlet. He resigned in November 1800 and went as ambassador to Spain, where in March 1801 he and Manuel de Godoy signed the Treaty of Aranjuez, creating the client kingdom of Etruria. In 1804 he opposed Napoleon's plan to become emperor and to marry him to a Spanish princess, refused imperial honours and went into exile in Rome.

With the Papal States annexed to France, Lucien lived as a virtual prisoner on his Italian estates. In 1810 he tried to sail to the United States but was captured by the British frigate HMS Pomone, and he spent the next years in England, at Ludlow and later at Grimley in Worcestershire, writing a heroic poem on Charlemagne. After Napoleon's abdication in 1814 Pope Pius VII made him Prince of Canino. He rallied to his brother during the Hundred Days.

He inspired the Napoleonic reconstitution of the Académie Française in 1803, wrote a novel, La Tribu indienne, and published his Mémoires in 1836. He excavated at Frascati and Musignano, and in 1825 at the forum of Tusculum, where he found the portrait of Julius Caesar named after the site. He died at Viterbo on 29 June 1840 of stomach cancer. His son Charles Lucien became a naturalist and ornithologist.
lucius-aemilius-paullus-macedonicus: Lucius Aemilius Paullus was the son of the consul of the same name who was defeated and killed at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE, when he was still a boy. He belonged to an old patrician family connected by marriage and political interests to the Scipios. He was elected curule aedile in 193 BCE and praetor in 191 BCE, and he went to the Hispania provinces, where he campaigned against the Lusitanians between 191 and 189 BCE. He failed for several years to be elected consul, but held the office for the first time in 182 BCE, and in 181 BCE commanded against the Ingauni of Liguria.

The Third Macedonian War began in 171 BCE, when King Perseus of Macedon defeated a Roman army under the consul Publius Licinius Crassus at the Battle of Callinicus. After two years of indecisive fighting, Paullus was elected consul a second time in 168 BCE, and the Senate gave him the war. On 22 June he won the decisive Battle of Pydna, Perseus was taken prisoner, and the war ended.

In 167 BCE the Senate told him to pillage Epirus, a kingdom suspected of sympathy with Macedon, before returning to Rome. He loaded the treasures of the Macedonian royal palace on ships and then, contrary to his inclination, ordered the plunder of seventy towns, which led to the enslavement of 150,000 people. His triumph in Rome displayed the captured king and his sons, and the Senate gave him the name Macedonicus. In 164 BCE he was elected censor, and he died in office in 160 BCE after an illness.

Paullus married first Papiria Masonis, whom he divorced around 183 to 182 BCE, and had by her four children; a second marriage gave him two more sons and a daughter. He gave his two eldest sons up for adoption: one became Quintus Fabius Maximus Aemilianus, the other Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus, heir of the Scipios, who with his brother was tutored by Paullus' friend Polybius. His two younger sons died within days of his triumph in 167 BCE, at the ages of 14 and 9 according to Polybius.

Livy and Polybius both state that Paullus died relatively poor, having kept little from the Macedonian campaign. With his death the Aemilii Paulli became extinct, although his sons lived on under other names. His elder surviving son's line reached the consulship, and the younger is known as Scipio Aemilianus.
lucius-junius-brutus: Traditions about the life of Lucius Junius Brutus may have been fictional. The account comes from Livy's Ab urbe condita and concerns a time before reliable records, since almost all earlier records were destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome. According to Livy, Brutus was the son of Tarquinia, sister of the king Tarquinius Superbus, so that the king was his uncle. The king had put to death a number of the chief men of Rome, including Brutus' brother, and Brutus avoided the distrust of the king's family by feigning to be slow-witted; the Latin brutus means dullard.

According to Roman tradition, Brutus led the revolt that overthrew Tarquinius Superbus after Sextus Tarquinius, a son of the king, raped the noblewoman Lucretia, who then killed herself. Brutus is said to have seized the dagger and called for the overthrow of the Tarquin family. He summoned the people to the forum, and they voted for the deposition of the king and the banishment of his family. His first act, in Livy's account, was to make the people swear never to allow any man to be king in Rome. He and Lucretia's husband, Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, were elected the first consuls, in 509 BCE by Varro's dating.

During his consulship the king's family tried to regain the throne through a conspiracy that included Brutus' two sons and two brothers of his wife. The plot was discovered, and the conspirators were put to death. Brutus gained respect for his stoicism in watching the execution of his own sons. He then either forced Collatinus to resign or had him removed, and presided over the election of Publius Valerius Poplicola in his place.

Tarquinius tried again at the Battle of Silva Arsia, leading the forces of Tarquinii and Veii. Brutus led the Roman cavalry and was killed in single combat with the king's son Arruns Tarquinius, who died as well. The Romans claimed the victory, and the noblewomen of Rome mourned Brutus for a year. Modern historians challenge almost every part of Livy's story, and some dismiss Brutus as a figure of legend. A treaty with Carthage reported by Polybius is the main evidence of his historicity.

The politician Marcus Junius Brutus claimed descent from him and minted coins with his portrait, and Cassius is said to have enticed Marcus to join the conspiracy against Julius Caesar by referring to his ancestor. Brutus was a hero of republicanism during the Enlightenment.
lucius-verus: Lucius Verus was born Lucius Ceionius Commodus on 15 December 130, the first-born son of Avidia and Lucius Aelius Caesar, the first adopted son and heir of Emperor Hadrian. After his father died on 1 January 138, Hadrian chose Titus Aurelius Antoninus as his new heir and instructed him to adopt Lucius together with Marcus, Antoninus' nephew by marriage. Verus was educated by the grammaticus Marcus Cornelius Fronto and was reported to be an excellent student, fond of writing poetry and delivering speeches. He became quaestor in 153, a year before the legal age, and consul in 154.

Antoninus Pius died on 7 March 161, and Marcus Aurelius refused to take office unless Lucius received equal powers. The senate granted Lucius the imperium, the tribunician power and the title augustus. Dropping his name Commodus, he took Marcus's original cognomen, Verus. It was the first time Rome had been ruled by two emperors. In spite of this nominal equality Marcus held more authority, and was alone Pontifex maximus. Verus' biographer wrote that he obeyed Marcus as a lieutenant obeys a proconsul. Together they went to the camp of the praetorian guard, where the troops acclaimed them as imperatores.

In late summer or early autumn 161 Vologases IV of Parthia entered Armenia, then a Roman client state, and installed his own king, Pacorus. The governor of Cappadocia, Marcus Sedatius Severianus, led a legion into Armenia, was trapped at Elegeia by the Parthian general Chosrhoes and killed himself; his legion was massacred. Most of Verus' reign was occupied by his direction of the war that followed, which ended in a Roman victory with some territorial gains.

According to the Historia Augusta, Verus spent the years in Rome after the war keeping a troupe of actors and favourites, holding parties in a tavern built in his house and wandering the city unrecognised. Marcus Aurelius disapproved but could do little, since Verus performed his official tasks efficiently. When the Marcomanni invaded across the Danube, a war that lasted until 180, Verus fell severely ill on the return to Rome and died soon afterwards. Some authors suggest poison, which is unlikely; he may have died of the epidemic known as the Antonine Plague. Marcus grieved, and the senate declared Verus divine as Divus Verus.
lucknow: Lucknow stands on the Gomti River, which meanders through the city and divides it into the Trans-Gomti and Cis-Gomti regions. It lies in the middle of the Indus-Gangetic Plain, surrounded by rural towns and villages, among them the orchard town of Malihabad and Kakori.

According to one legend the city is named after Lakshmana, a hero of the Ramayana, who is said to have had a palace or estate there called Lakshmanapuri. The settlement was known as Lakhanpur or Lachhmanpur by the 11th century, and later as Lucknow, the anglicised form of the local Lakhnau.

From the 6th to the 4th century BCE Lucknow was part of Kosala, one of the 16 Mahajanapadas of the late Vedic period. From 1350 onwards it and parts of the Awadh region were ruled in turn by the Delhi Sultanate, the Sharqi Sultanate, the Mughal Empire, the Nawabs of Awadh, the British East India Company and the British Raj. The Nawabs of Lucknow took that name after the reign of the third Nawab, when Lucknow became their capital.

In 1856 the East India Company moved its troops to the border and annexed Awadh, alleging maladministration, and placed it under a chief commissioner. Lucknow was one of the major centres of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. It also took an active part in the independence movement. At the Congress session of 1916 Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru and Muhammad Ali Jinnah met for the first time, and the Lucknow Pact was signed.

Wajid Ali Shah, the last Nawab of Awadh, was a patron of Kathak, a classical dance form that is said to have originated in Lucknow. Under royal patronage the bawarchis and rakabdars, the chefs and royal cooks, developed the Nawabi cuisine of Awadh, with its slow dum cooking. The city's culture comes from the blending of its Hindu and Muslim rulers, and it is known for the ghararas of the Nawabs of Awadh and for chikankari embroidery.

Lucknow is the capital of the state of Uttar Pradesh and the administrative headquarters of its district and division. It had a population of 2.8 million at the census of 2011. It has been the headquarters of the Indian Army's Central Command since 1 May 1963, and it has a bench of the Allahabad High Court. Its monuments of the Nawabi era include the Bara Imambara, known for its Bhul Bhulaiya, the Chota Imambara and the Rumi Darwaza. UNESCO has named it a City of Gastronomy.
lucretia: No source of her own time survives for Lucretia or for the rape. What is known comes from Livy and from Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who wrote about five hundred years afterwards, and modern writers count her story as part of Roman mythohistory. The evidence is taken to point to a real woman named Lucretia and to an event that played a critical part in the fall of the monarchy, but the details vary with the writer. Dionysius puts the rape and her death at 508 BCE, setting it in the year of the first of the Roman fasti, and historians accept a range of about five years.

She was the daughter of the magistrate Spurius Lucretius and wife of Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus. Livy and Dionysius present the marriage as the Roman ideal and Lucretia as a model for Roman girls. During the siege of Ardea, the story goes, the king's sons and their kinsmen, including Brutus and Collatinus, disputed whose wife was the most virtuous. Riding home, they found the other women socialising, but Lucretia at home alone, working her wool.

Sextus Tarquinius, son of the last king, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, entered her room at night and raped her, in one version after threatening to kill her and a slave and claim he had found them in adultery. In Livy's account she sent for her father and her husband, each to bring a friend as witness, among them Lucius Junius Brutus. The men told her that the mind sins, not the body, and that where there was no consent there was no guilt. After exacting an oath of vengeance she stabbed herself in the heart.

Brutus swore on the bloody dagger to drive out the Tarquins. The body was shown in the Forum, the assembly of the curiae voted to end the monarchy, and Brutus and Collatinus were chosen as the first consuls. The story was retold by Ovid, by Augustine in The City of God, by Chaucer and by Shakespeare in his 1594 poem The Rape of Lucrece, and since the Renaissance her suicide has been a subject for artists including Titian, Dürer, Botticelli and Artemisia Gentileschi.
lucretia-mott: Lucretia Coffin was born on 3 January 1793 in Nantucket, Massachusetts, the second child of Anna Folger and the whaling captain Thomas Coffin. Her mother ran the family's mercantile business. At thirteen she was sent to the Nine Partners School in Dutchess County, New York, run by Quakers, where James Mott, her future husband, was a teacher. Staying on as a teacher at fifteen, she learned that male teachers were paid much more than female staff, which stirred her interest in women's rights. She married James Mott on 10 April 1811 at Pine Street Meeting in Philadelphia, and they raised six children, five of whom reached adulthood.

Recorded as a Quaker minister in 1821, Mott travelled widely as a preacher, stressing the inward light of the Divine in every person, as taught by Elias Hicks. After a visit to Virginia in 1818 she called for the immediate and unconditional emancipation of enslaved people. In 1833 she and her husband helped found the American Anti-Slavery Society, which as an organisation for men invited her only as a guest, and she led the Female Anti-Slavery Society. In 1838 a mob destroyed Pennsylvania Hall in Philadelphia, and Mott left it arm in arm with white and black women delegates. Her home, Roadside, served as a stop on the Underground Railroad.

In June 1840 she was one of six women delegates to the World's Anti-Slavery Convention in London, where the men voted to exclude the American women, partly so that women's rights would not be tied to the cause of abolition. In 1848 she and Elizabeth Cady Stanton organised the Seneca Falls Convention, and she signed its Declaration of Sentiments, though she at first opposed Stanton's resolution on the vote. At the Liberty Party's convention that June, five delegates voted for her as candidate for Vice President. She published the Discourse on Woman in 1850 and in 1866 became first president of the American Equal Rights Association.

Mott helped found the Female Medical College of Pennsylvania and Swarthmore College, raised funds for the Philadelphia School of Design for Women, and was a pacifist who opposed the War with Mexico and led the Pennsylvania Peace Society. She helped form the Free Religious Association in 1867. She died of pneumonia at Roadside on 11 November 1880 and was buried at Fair Hill Burial Ground, a Quaker cemetery. At her funeral a long silence was broken when someone asked, Who can speak? The preacher is dead. The area around her home is now known as La Mott.
lucretius: Almost nothing is known for certain about the life of Lucretius. The only sure point is that he was a friend or client of Gaius Memmius, to whom his poem is addressed. Ancient notes give conflicting hints. A passage in the Life of Virgil attributed to Aelius Donatus says that he died on the day Virgil assumed the toga virilis, but its consular dating is internally inconsistent. Saint Jerome, writing four centuries later, records his birth under the 171st Olympiad and gives his age at death as 43, which would place his birth in 99 or 98 BCE.

Jerome also says that Lucretius was driven mad by a love potion, wrote his books in intervals of insanity, which Cicero later emended, and killed himself. Scholars now accept that this report is inaccurate, and often explain it as confusion or anti-Epicurean bias. Lucretius was probably a member of the aristocratic gens Lucretia and was expensively educated in Latin, Greek, literature and philosophy.

His only known work is De rerum natura, usually translated as On the Nature of Things. Written in some 7,400 dactylic hexameters and divided into six untitled books, it sets out Epicurean physics. It covers atomism, the nature of the mind and soul, sensation and thought, the development of the world, and a range of celestial and terrestrial phenomena. Lucretius is the first writer known to have introduced Roman readers to Epicurean philosophy. In his account the universe runs on physical principles and chance, not on the intervention of the traditional Roman gods.

The poem also sketches the development of humankind, from a life like that of wild beasts through huts, fire, clothing, language, family and city-states. Lucretius proposes that weapons and tools passed from hands, nails and teeth to stones and branches, then copper and bronze, and finally iron. He is believed to be the first to put forward this succession, which was revived in the nineteenth century and linked to the three-age system formalised by C. J. Thomsen from 1834.

In February 54 BCE Cicero wrote to his brother Quintus that the poems of Lucretius showed many flashes of genius and great mastery. The poem influenced the Augustan poets, above all Virgil in the Georgics and the Aeneid, and Horace. It was almost lost in the Middle Ages and was rediscovered in 1417 in a monastery in Germany by Poggio Bracciolini.

It later played a part in the development of atomism, and Pierre Gassendi drew on it. Figures of the Enlightenment also used it in efforts to construct a new Christian humanism. Its account of nature experimenting over long ages, in which the best-adapted creatures survive, has been compared with later thought on evolution, although Lucretius did not hold that new species arose from earlier ones.
lucrezia-borgia: Lucrezia Borgia was born on 18 April 1480 at Subiaco, near Rome, the illegitimate daughter of Cardinal Rodrigo de Borgia, later Pope Alexander VI, and his mistress Vannozza dei Cattanei. Her father acknowledged her, and she had three full siblings: Cesare, Giovanni and Gioffre. She received a humanist education from intellectuals at court rather than in a convent. She was fluent in Spanish, Valenciano, Italian and French, literate in Latin and Greek, proficient in poetry and oration, and could play the lute and zither.

When Rodrigo became pope in August 1492 he called off Lucrezia's earlier engagements and arranged her marriage to Giovanni Sforza, Lord of Pesaro, with a proxy wedding in Rome on 12 June 1493, when she was 13. When the Borgias no longer needed the Sforzas, the pope sought an annulment. Giovanni at first refused and spread the rumour that the pope wanted his daughter back in Rome for himself, a rumour that endured for centuries and tainted her reputation. He finally signed a confession of impotence, and the annulment was finalised in December 1497.

On 21 July 1498 she married Alfonso of Aragon, Duke of Bisceglie, an illegitimate son of Alfonso II of Naples. In 1499 she became governor of Spoleto, a post usually reserved to cardinals, the first woman to hold such a governorship in the Papal States. Alfonso was attacked on the steps of St. Peter's on 15 July 1500 and strangled in his bed while recovering. It was widely rumoured that Cesare was responsible, and tradition has it that he had Alfonso killed after his political value waned. Lucrezia then acted as her father's private secretary, and a Venetian ambassador called her wise, discreet and generous.

Lucrezia married Alfonso I d'Este by proxy in Rome on 30 December 1501 and in person at Ferrara on 2 February 1502. She became Duchess of Ferrara in 1505. Her court became a centre for writers, musicians, poets and philosophers, among them Ludovico Ariosto, and she ruled as regent twice while her husband was on campaign. She bought marshland cheaply and invested in its reclamation, nearly doubling her annual income. She bore six children in the marriage.

She died on 24 June 1519 at Belriguardo Castle, aged 39, after giving birth to a daughter, and was buried at the convent of Corpus Domini in Ferrara. Rumours of incest, poisoning and murder have persisted, among them the tale of a hollow ring used to poison drinks, but no historical basis for them exists beyond the attacks of her enemies.
luddites: Machine-breaking in the English textile industry had precedents. Stockingers took organised action at various times from 1675, and in Lancashire new cotton-spinning machines met violent resistance in 1768 and 1779. Parliament had passed measures such as the Protection of Stocking Frames, etc. Act 1788. The Luddites took their name from Ned Ludd, an apocryphal apprentice said to have smashed two stocking frames in 1779; the name appears in their writings as early as 1811, often with the title Captain, General or King Ludd. The movement emerged during the economic crisis of the Napoleonic Wars, with high unemployment and inflation between 1810 and 1812, and began at Arnold, Nottinghamshire, on 11 March 1811.

The Luddites met at night on the moors to drill, and their main areas of operation began in Nottinghamshire in November 1811, followed by the West Riding of Yorkshire in early 1812 and Lancashire by March 1813. They chose the machines that threatened each region's trade. In the Midlands these were wide knitting frames making cheap lace; in the North West, steam-powered looms; in Yorkshire, shearing frames and gig mills. Yorkshire croppers broke cropping machines introduced by Enoch Taylor of Marsden with a hammer they called Enoch, shouting that Enoch made them and Enoch would break them.

Letters to mill owners and officials explained their aims and threatened further action. Midlands writers appealed to the Company of Framework Knitters, while North West letters more often asked for reforms such as a higher minimum wage and an end to child labour. Historians have argued that the movement was not hostile to machinery as such: Malcolm I. Thomis wrote that machinery was a conveniently exposed target, and Eric Hobsbawm called machine wrecking collective bargaining by riot.

About 12,000 troops, mostly militia and yeomanry, were used against the Luddites, more than Wellington led into Portugal in 1808, according to Hobsbawm. Four men led by George Mellor killed the mill owner William Horsfall near Huddersfield; one informed on the others and the other three were hanged. A mass trial at York in January 1813 charged over 60 men, many with no connection to the movement; 30 were acquitted, and the harsh sentences, including executions and transportation, quickly ended the movement. Lord Byron defended the Luddites in the House of Lords on 27 February 1812 and opposed the Destruction of Stocking Frames, etc. Act 1812, which made machine-breaking a capital crime.

The Pentrich Rising of 1817, led by Jeremiah Brandreth, a probable ex-Luddite, was a general uprising unrelated to machinery, but can be seen as the last major Luddite act. The Luddites are remembered in folk songs such as The Cropper Lads, and the word Luddite is now used for those who oppose new technology.
ludenscheid: Lüdenscheid lies in the Sauerland on the saddle of the watershed between the Lenne and Volme rivers, both of which empty into the Ruhr. The saddle stands at 420 metres, and the Nordhelle in the Ebbe Mountains reaches 663 metres. The hilly terrain gave the town the nickname Bergstadt, mountain town. The original settlement circles around the church built on a ledge of the slope above the saddle, and six dams in the surrounding area create reservoirs that regulate the Ruhr and supply drinking water.

The first settlement in the area is confirmed for the 9th century, and the place is first mentioned as a village in 1067. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was a member of the Hanseatic League, which it joined to market its metal goods more widely. In the Middle Ages the town became a centre of metal ore mining in the surrounding area, working the osemund iron. Hammers and wire drawers processed the ore, driven by water power in the valleys, and artisanal smitheries made finished products from it.

Since 1609 the town belonged to the Electorate of Brandenburg, later Prussia. In 1815 it became part of the new Prussian Province of Westphalia, and in 1975, with the creation of the Märkischer Kreis, it became the seat of its administration. With industrialisation the production of buttons and buckles played a large role, which the Button Museum reflects, and later aluminium, bakelite and plastics were adopted. A supporting industry making the forms for stamping, blanking, pressing and casting emerged. The aluminium framework of the first Zeppelin airship was built in the factory of Carl Berg in Lüdenscheid.

Lüdenscheid is a predominantly industrial city with small and medium-sized firms in the metal and plastics industries, whose products include parts for the car industry, fittings for electrical installations, lamps and toys. Its oldest church, the Church of the Redeemer, has a tower from the 11th century and a nave rebuilt in the early 19th century, while the water castle Neuenhof dates from the end of the 17th century. The coat of arms shows Saint Medardus as patron, above the red-and-white checked fess of the Counts of the Mark.
luderitz: Lüderitz is a town in the ǁKaras Region of southern Namibia, on one of the least hospitable coasts in Africa. It is a port developed around Robert Harbour and Shark Island. The climate is a cold desert one, with cool to mild temperatures all year and average annual rainfall of just 17 millimetres. Until Walvis Bay was incorporated in 1994 the harbour was the only suitable one on Namibia's coast, though its rock bottom is comparatively shallow.

Bartolomeu Dias named the bay Angra Pequena, Portuguese for Small Bay, and erected a stone cross on its southern peninsula. In the early 19th century whaling, seal hunting, fishing and guano harvesting made the place a trading post. The town was founded in 1883, when Heinrich Vogelsang bought Angra Pequena and surrounding land from the Nama chief Josef Frederiks II on behalf of Adolf Lüderitz, a merchant from Bremen. The German flag was hoisted on 7 August 1884. After Adolf Lüderitz failed to return from an expedition to the Orange River in 1886, the place was named Lüderitzbucht in his honour.

German authorities set up a concentration camp on Shark Island during the Herero Wars. Between 1,000 and 3,000 Africans from the Herero and Nama peoples died there through the conditions of forced labour. Their labour was used to expand the town, railway and port and on settlers' farms. The railway of 318 kilometres to Seeheim was built by inmates of the camp and completed in 1908.

After diamonds were found nearby in 1908, a rush brought sudden prosperity, and the diamond settlement of Kolmanskop was built. By 1912 Lüderitz had 1,100 inhabitants, not counting the indigenous population. South Africa took over the administration of German South West Africa in 1915 and many Germans were deported. From 1920 diamond mining moved south of the town, and Lüderitz lost its importance as a trading place.

Lüderitz had a population of 16,125 in 2023. It is known for its colonial architecture, including Art Nouveau work, with several buildings declared national monuments, among them the Felsenkirche of 1912 and the railway station of 1904. Kolmanskop, now abandoned, is a tourist destination being slowly buried by sand dunes.
ludovico-ariosto: Ludovico Ariosto was born on 8 September 1474 at Reggio nell'Emilia, where his father Niccolò Ariosto commanded the citadel. He was the eldest of ten children. He was interested in poetry from his earliest years, but his father obliged him to study law. After five years he was allowed to read the classics under Gregorio da Spoleto, until his teacher left for France and, soon after, his father died. Ariosto then had to give up his literary pursuits and care for a family whose affairs were in disarray, though he still wrote comedies in prose and some lyrical pieces.

His writings brought him to the notice of Cardinal Ippolito d'Este, who took him into his household. Ariosto later said the cardinal paid him poorly: the only reward for Orlando Furioso, which was dedicated to him, was the question where he had found so many stories. When the cardinal went to Hungary in 1518 and wished Ariosto to go with him, the poet pleaded ill health and the care of his elderly mother, and after a heated argument he was dismissed.

The cardinal's brother Alfonso, duke of Ferrara, then took him on. Ariosto had already made his name as a diplomat on two embassies to Pope Julius II in Rome, on one of which he was nearly killed on the pope's orders, because the pope was then in conflict with Alfonso. His salary of 84 crowns a year was suspended during the war and withdrawn after the peace. He was appointed governor of the Garfagnana, in the Apennines, for three years. The province was troubled by factions and bandits and the duke gave him little support, but both ruler and people were satisfied with his government.

His comedy Cassaria appeared in 1508 and I suppositi was first acted at Ferrara. Shakespeare later used it as a source for The Taming of the Shrew. The first version of Orlando Furioso, in 40 cantos, was published at Ferrara in 1516, and the third and final version, in 46 cantos, appeared on 8 September 1532. The poem describes the adventures of Charlemagne, Orlando and the Franks against the Saracens, with many side plots, and turns the chivalric tradition into satire. It is in ottava rima, and the narrator often breaks off a plot in mid-canto and takes it up much later. Goethe called it a graceful, smiling, fantastic creation. Ariosto died on 6 July 1533.
ludovico-manin: Lodovico Giovanni Manin was born on 14 May 1725, the eldest of five sons of Lodovico III Alvise and Lucrezia Maria Basadonna. He studied at the University of Bologna and boarded at the noble College of St. Xavier. On 14 September 1748 he married Elisabetta Grimani, who brought a dowry of 45,000 ducats and had been in poor health since childhood. They had no children.

At 26 he was elected captain of Vicenza, then of Verona, where he faced a flood in 1757, and then Brescia. In 1764 he became procurator de ultra of Saint Mark's Basilica. In 1769 he asked to be excused from office because of ill health and bad hearing, and in 1787 he was chosen to honour Pope Pius VI as he crossed Venetian territory.

Manin was elected Doge of Venice on 9 March 1789 on the first ballot of an electoral assembly of 41 members. The traditional ceremony required him to throw coins to the Venetians, which cost more than 458,197 lire, less than a quarter of it paid from the Republic's funds. By 1792 the once great Venetian merchant fleet had fallen to 309 merchantmen.

When Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Italy, Venice stayed neutral. On 15 April 1797 General Jean-Andoche Junot gave the Doge an ultimatum, which he refused. A secret addition to the Treaty of Leoben, signed on 17 April, gave Venice to Austria. The French fleet arrived at the Lido on 25 April, and Venetian guns sank one ship, but the Venetian fleet numbered only four galleys and seven galliots. The Doge surrendered on 12 May and left the Doge's Palace two days later.

French troops entered Piazza San Marco on 16 May 1797. Manin refused to become interim head of the municipality, withdrew from society and lived in the Palazzo Dolfin Manin. He returned the ducal insignia and the Golden Book of the Venetian families, which the new authorities hid. Some citizens insulted him for the surrender. He died on 24 October 1802 of dropsy and heart problems, asking for a funeral with the least possible pomp, and was buried in the Church of the Scalzi.
ludovico-sforza: Ludovico Maria Sforza was born in Milan on 3 August 1452, the fourth son of Francesco I Sforza and Bianca Maria Visconti. As a fourth son he was not expected to rule, but his mother still wanted him well educated. His teachers included the humanist Francesco Filelfo, and he studied Greek, Latin, theology, painting, sculpture and government.

His brother Duke Galeazzo Maria was assassinated on 26 December 1476, and was succeeded by his seven-year-old son Gian Galeazzo Maria. Ludovico opposed the regency of the duchess Bona and her councillor Cicco Simonetta. The attempt failed, and Ludovico was exiled to Pisa. He later took control of the city and sought alliances with Lorenzo de' Medici, King Ferrante of Naples and Pope Sixtus IV.

Ludovico had been betrothed to Beatrice d'Este, daughter of Ercole d'Este, when she was five. He postponed the wedding three times, having met Cecilia Gallerani, and decided to marry only after his nephew's marriage, consummated in 1490, produced the prospect of an heir. Gian Galeazzo and his wife Isabella of Aragon left for Pavia, and Gian Galeazzo was content to leave his uncle in charge. Beatrice bore a son, Ercole Massimiliano, in 1493 and quarrelled with Isabella over who should hold the title of Count of Pavia.

Gian Galeazzo died on 22 October 1494 in mysterious circumstances. Officially his death was ascribed to a long illness and an immoderate life, but Niccolò Machiavelli and Francesco Guicciardini believed Ludovico had poisoned him, which the historian Malaguzzi Valeri disputes. Ludovico succeeded with the support of the Milanese nobles. Threatened by King Alfonso II of Naples, he had called the French into Italy. When the Duke of Orléans occupied Novara and Vigevano, he considered fleeing to Spain, but his wife and some councillors persuaded him to stay. Beatrice died in childbirth on the night of 2 January 1497, and Ludovico never recovered from his grief.

The Duke of Orléans succeeded Charles VIII as Louis XII of France in 1498 and launched a second expedition against Milan, under the command of Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, a personal enemy of Ludovico. Ludovico fled and was taken prisoner to France. He was held in several places and from 1504 at the castle of Loches. After an attempt to escape in 1508 he was deprived of his books and other comforts, and he died in the dungeon on 27 May 1508.

Contemporaries called him mild and generous, and a patron of artists and writers whose court became one of the most important in Europe during the Italian Renaissance. Guicciardini named him the arbiter of Italy. His nickname il Moro, the Moor, was given when he was a child, and is thought to come from his dark complexion, hair and eyes.
ludvig-holberg: Holberg was born in Bergen on 3 December 1684, the youngest of six brothers, and his father died before he was a year old. He was educated in Copenhagen and began to study theology, settling for an attestats that gave him the right to work as a priest, and then taught himself law, history and languages. He earned his living as a tutor and as a travelling companion to noblemen, and visited cities in the Netherlands and France and lived for a time in Rome. From 1706 to 1708 he stayed in Oxford, where he was not formally admitted to the university but used its libraries and took part in Latin discussions with English students.

At the University of Copenhagen he was first an unpaid assistant, then assistant professor teaching metaphysics, later professor of rhetoric and Latin, and finally professor of history, the subject he prized most. His writings fall into three periods: mainly history from 1711 to 1718, satirical poetry and stage comedies from 1719 to 1731, and mainly philosophy from 1731 to 1750. As house dramatist of the first public theatre in Denmark, opened in Copenhagen in 1721, he wrote the comedies of 1722–1723 for the Lille Grønnegade Theatre. After the Copenhagen Fire of 1728 a wave of depression and puritanism clashed with his satire, and in 1731 he gave up comedy. His only novel, Niels Klim's Underground Travels, was published in Latin in 1741.

Holberg believed in an inner light of reason and held that education should teach students to use their senses and intellect rather than memorise books. He leaned towards deism, doubted original sin and held that science should be inductive and practical. His works on natural and common law were read by Danish law students for two hundred years, from 1736 to 1936.

Holberg never married and had no children. He lived modestly, invested his profits in property and left his estate to Sorø Academy, an institution for young noblemen, in an agreement with the king that also brought him the title of Baron of Holberg. He died on 28 January 1754, and his casket, the work of Johannes Wiedewelt, stands in Sorø Monastery Church. He is regarded as the founder of modern Danish and Norwegian literature. Statues of him stand in Copenhagen, Sorø and Bergen, and Edvard Grieg's Holberg Suite honours him.
ludvik-svoboda: Ludvík Svoboda was born on 25 November 1895 in Hroznatín, Moravia, then in Austria-Hungary. His father died when he was one year old. He attended the agricultural school at Velké Meziříčí and in 1915 had to join the Austro-Hungarian Army. He fell into Russian captivity at Tarnopol on 18 September 1915, joined the Czechoslovak Legion and fought at Zborov and Bakhmach. In 1921 he began a career in the Czechoslovak Army.

After the German occupation of 15 March 1939 Svoboda joined the underground organisation Obrana národa. In June 1939 he fled to Poland and, as the senior officer, formed a Czechoslovak unit at Kraków. After the defeat of Poland he led more than 700 officers and soldiers into the Soviet Union, where they were held in internment camps. For two years he negotiated with the Soviet authorities to keep the group together and send officers on to countries fighting Germany.

After Germany attacked the Soviet Union, he helped to prepare the agreement of 18 July 1941 that allowed a separate Czechoslovak unit. He then organised volunteers into a battalion that grew into a brigade and the 1st Czechoslovak Army Corps, the largest Czechoslovak unit abroad. In December 1943 he became a brigadier general, and on 10 September 1944 he took command of the corps.

He became defence minister in April 1945. During the crisis of February 1948 he remained in office when the other non-Communist ministers resigned and refused to use the army against the crowds, saying that the army would not march against the people. He then joined the Communist Party. Forced out of the army in 1950 under Soviet pressure, he was Deputy Prime Minister from 1950 to 1951, was imprisoned in the purges and was later released, and returned to public life at the wish of Nikita Khrushchev.

Elected president on 30 March 1968 on Alexander Dubček's recommendation, he warned the Soviet ambassador against an invasion and, when it came in August, signed an order keeping the army out of it. In Moscow he refused Leonid Brezhnev's demand for a peasant-workers' government and secured the release of Dubček. He passively witnessed the removal of reformists and helped to replace Dubček with Gustáv Husák in April 1969.

Husák never trusted him, and in 1975 an act of the Federal Assembly retired Svoboda, who had been in ill health, and Husák succeeded him. Svoboda died on 20 September 1979. He maintained to the end that his conduct before Brezhnev saved thousands of lives. Squares and streets in the Czech Republic and Slovakia still bear his name.
ludwig-erhard: Ludwig Erhard was born in Fürth, in the Kingdom of Bavaria, on 4 February 1897, the son of a Catholic clothing store owner. Polio in early childhood left him with a deformed right foot. He trained as a textile apprentice and worked in his father's draper's shop until he volunteered for the army in 1916. A shell wounded him badly on 28 September 1918, and seven operations left his left arm permanently shorter than his right.

Unable to return to draper's work, he studied economics in Nuremberg and then at the Goethe University Frankfurt, where he took his doctorate in 1925 under Franz Oppenheimer, whose opposition to monopolies influenced him. From 1928 he worked at a market research institute in Nuremberg, and he lost that post in 1942 after working on plans for a postwar peace that the Nazis had forbidden.

In 1944 Erhard wrote a study of war finance and debt consolidation that assumed Germany had already lost the war. After the war he led the expert commission on money and credit that prepared the currency reform of the western zones, and in April 1948 the Bizonal Economic Council elected him director of economics. The Deutsche Mark was introduced on 20 June 1948, and Erhard abolished the price-fixing and production controls of the military administration, a step beyond his authority.

Elected to the Bundestag in 1949 for the Christian Democratic Union, he served as Federal Minister for Economic Affairs for fourteen years and as vice-chancellor from 1957 to 1963. An economic liberal, he joined the Mont Pelerin Society in 1950. In 1957 he suffered defeats, notably over anti-cartel legislation, and the West German economy then developed into a conventional welfare state.

Parliament elected Erhard chancellor on 16 October 1963 by 279 votes to 180. His government introduced housing benefit in 1965 and established diplomatic relations with Israel that year. His support for the American role in the Vietnam War strained his coalition, and during the recession of 1966 the ministers of the Free Democratic Party resigned over the budget. He resigned on 30 November 1966, and Kurt Georg Kiesinger succeeded him. He remained in the Bundestag and died in Bonn on 5 May 1977.
ludwig-i-of-bavaria: Ludwig was born in Strasbourg on 25 August 1786, the son of Count Palatine Maximilian Joseph of Zweibrücken, who became Elector of Bavaria in 1799 and took the title of king on 1 January 1806. His godfather and namesake was Louis XVI of France. He studied at the university in Landshut and at Göttingen, and on 12 October 1810 he married Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen; the wedding was the occasion of the first Oktoberfest.

Ludwig rejected his father's alliance with Napoleon but still had to join the emperor's wars, and in 1809 he led the 1st Bavarian Division at the Battle of Abensberg. He backed the Treaty of Ried of 8 October 1813, by which Bavaria joined the Sixth Coalition. As a philhellene he lent 1.5 million florins from his private funds to the Greek War of Independence.

Ludwig succeeded his father in 1825. He moved the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität from Landshut to Munich in 1826, began the Ludwig Canal between the Main and the Danube, and joined the Zollverein in 1834; the first German railway, between Fürth and Nuremberg, opened in 1835. In 1832 his son Otto was elected king of Greece. He also commissioned neoclassical buildings, among them the Glyptothek, the Ludwigstraße, the Walhalla and the Befreiungshalle, designed by architects such as Leo von Klenze, and collected Greek and Roman sculpture and old paintings.

After the July Revolution of 1830 in France his earlier liberal policy became more repressive. The Hambacher Fest of 1832 showed discontent over high taxes and censorship, and about 1,000 political trials took place in his reign. His affair with Lola Montez ended the influence of the Ultramontanes at court but made him unpopular.

In the revolutions of 1848 Ludwig faced protests by students and the middle classes, and on 4 March a crowd assaulted the Armory. Unwilling to rule as a constitutional monarch, he abdicated on 20 March 1848 in favour of his eldest son, Maximilian. He lived another twenty years, remained a lavish patron of the arts, and died at Nice in 1868. He is buried in St. Boniface's Abbey in Munich. All living legitimate male-line members of the House of Wittelsbach descend from him.
ludwig-ii-of-bavaria: Ludwig was born on 25 August 1845 at Nymphenburg Palace, the elder son of Maximilian II of Bavaria and Marie of Prussia. He came to the throne in his 19th year when his father died, unprepared for office but popular for his youth and looks. He kept his father's ministers; his real interests were art, music and architecture, and one of his first acts was to summon Richard Wagner to court.

In the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 his government supported Austria, although he had wanted to stay neutral; Austria insisted on the alliance obligations. Bavaria was defeated and had to sign a mutual defence treaty with Prussia. Ludwig, who had little interest in military matters, left war policy to his ministers and withdrew to Berg Palace and Rose Island in Lake Starnberg. After Bavaria joined the German Empire in 1871 he withdrew largely from politics.

Ludwig first saw Wagner's Lohengrin at 15. Wagner was given an audience of an hour and three quarters on 4 May 1864. The king sponsored the premieres of Tristan und Isolde and Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg and, through his support of the Bayreuth Festival, those of the Ring cycle and Parsifal. Between 1872 and 1885 he had 209 private performances given for himself alone or with one guest in the two court theatres.

His main occupation was building castles, for which he approved every detail of architecture, decoration and furnishing. He paid from his personal fortune and his annual grant, the Zivilliste, and from 1873 also from an annual subsidy of 270,000 marks from Chancellor Bismarck, drawn from the sequestered assets of the dethroned King George V of Hanover. By 1885 he was 14 million marks in debt and had borrowed heavily from his family.

In June 1886 a government commission came to Neuschwanstein to deliver a document of deposition and take him into custody. Warned beforehand, Ludwig had the commissioners turned back from the gate at gunpoint. He was later taken into custody. On 13 June he walked with his doctor, Gudden, in the park of Berg Castle; both were found dead in shallow water near the shore at 10:30 that night. The death was ruled a suicide, a conclusion that is now questioned, and a theory of murder has circulated; the postmortem found no wounds.

His brother Otto, under medical supervision since 1883, succeeded him, with their uncle Luitpold as regent. Whether Ludwig was clinically insane remains unresolved. The castles that ruined his finances were given to Bavaria in 1923 and are now among its tourist attractions.
ludwig-iii-of-bavaria: Ludwig was born in Munich on 7 January 1845, the eldest son of Luitpold, Prince Regent of Bavaria, and Archduchess Auguste Ferdinande of Austria. In 1861 his uncle Maximilian II gave him a commission as a lieutenant, and he studied law and economics at Munich. In the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 he was wounded in the thigh at the Battle of Helmstadt, which contributed to his dislike of the military. On 20 February 1868 he married Archduchess Maria Theresia of Austria-Este, who brought him estates in Hungary and Moravia. The income allowed him to buy Leutstetten, which he expanded into one of the largest and most profitable estates in Bavaria. He was derided as Millibauer, 'dairy farmer'. The couple had 13 children.

Ludwig became regent on his father's death on 12 December 1912, for his incapacitated cousin Otto. On 4 November 1913 the legislature amended the constitution so that a regency that had lasted ten years could be ended by the regent, who then assumed the crown. The next day Ludwig III was declared king. Historians regard the amendment as a definitive step toward a modern constitutional monarchy. His reign was conservative and influenced by the encyclical Rerum novarum.

He supported the German Empire in 1914 and later claimed annexations for Bavaria, including Alsace. Accused of blind loyalty to Prussia, he became increasingly unpopular. On 2 November 1918 a constitutional reform turned the constitutional monarchy into a parliamentary monarchy. On 7 November he fled the Residenz in Munich with his family to Schloss Anif near Salzburg, the first monarch of the German Empire to be deposed, and the People's State of Bavaria was proclaimed the next day. On 12 November he issued the Anif declaration, releasing officials and soldiers from their oath to him. The word abdication never appeared, but Kurt Eisner's government treated it as one, ending 738 years of Wittelsbach rule.

After Eisner's assassination in February 1919 Ludwig fled to Hungary, Liechtenstein and Switzerland, and he returned to Bavaria in April 1920. He died at Sárvár in Hungary on 17 October 1921. Despite fears that a state funeral might revive the monarchy, he and his wife received one on 5 November 1921 in Munich, with an estimated 100,000 spectators, and were buried in the crypt of the Frauenkirche.
ludwig-uhland: Johann Ludwig Uhland was born in Tübingen on 26 April 1787 and studied law at the university there, while taking an interest in medieval literature, especially old German and French poetry.
