He took a doctorate of laws in 1810 and spent eight months in Paris continuing his studies of poetry. From 1812 to 1814 he worked as a lawyer in Stuttgart, in the bureau of the minister of justice.

Uhland began as a poet in 1807 and 1808 with ballads and lyrics for Seckendorff's Musenalmanach, and in 1815 collected his poems in Vaterländische Gedichte, which at once won a wide readership. He added fresh poems to almost every new edition. His two dramas, Ernst, Herzog von Schwaben (1818) and Ludwig der Baier (1819), are unimportant beside his poems. He belongs among the German romantic lyric poets, drawn like them to the Middle Ages, but his style has a precision, suppleness and grace that set his best writings apart.

As a scholar he is counted among the founders of Germanic and Romance philology. His works include a treatise on the Old French epic (1812), Walther von der Vogelweide, ein altdeutscher Dichter (1822), Der Mythus von Thôr (1836) and a collection of old German folk songs published in the mid-nineteenth century. Longfellow translated some of his pieces into English.

Württemberg was to receive a new constitution in 1815, replacing the old constitution of the Estates abolished in 1806, and Uhland became a prominent proponent of the old rights of the estates; the controversy ended in a compromise in 1819 under William I of Württemberg. He sat in the Landtag from 1819 until 1826 as one of the most vigorous and consistent of the Old Liberals. In 1829 he became honorary professor of German literature at Tübingen but resigned in 1833, when the post proved incompatible with his political views. In 1848 he became a member of the Frankfurt Parliament. He died in Tübingen on 13 November 1862. His poem Ich hatt' einen Kameraden is an integral part of military funerals.
ludwig-van-beethoven: Beethoven was baptised on 17 December 1770 in the Catholic parish of St. Remigius in Bonn. There is no authentic record of his birth date, though there is a consensus, with which Beethoven himself agreed, that it was 16 December. His grandfather, also named Ludwig van Beethoven, came from Mechelen and rose to be Kapellmeister at the court of the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne. His father, Johann, a tenor in the same establishment, was his first music teacher, from his fifth year, in a harsh and intensive regime.

Of seven children born to Johann, only Ludwig and two younger brothers, Karl and Johann, survived infancy. Aware of the successes of Leopold Mozart with his children, Johann tried to promote his son as a child prodigy, claiming on the posters for his first public performance in March 1778 that Ludwig was six, when he was seven. He later had other teachers, including Christian Gottlob Neefe. He found relief from a dysfunctional home with the family of Helene von Breuning.

At 21 he moved to Vienna, which became his base, and studied composition with Joseph Haydn. He gained a reputation as a virtuoso pianist and was soon patronised by Karl Alois, Prince Lichnowsky, which led to the three Piano Trios, Op. 1, in 1795, the earliest works to which he gave an opus number. He composed the Pathétique Sonata in 1798, around the time he began to experience hearing loss.

His career is conventionally divided into three periods, a division proposed as early as 1818. In the first he wrote in the classical style of Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and his First Symphony premiered in 1800. In the middle period, 1802 to 1812, he developed a distinctive style. The Third (Eroica) and Fifth Symphonies premiered in 1805 and 1808, and his opera Fidelio in 1805. The late period, 1812 to 1827, includes the Missa solemnis and the Ninth Symphony, both premiered in 1824, and the late string quartets.

After several months of illness that left him bedridden, Beethoven died on 26 March 1827, aged 56. The Ninth was the first major example of a choral symphony, and Brahms's First Symphony quotes its Ode to Joy theme. Alex Ross writes that the professional orchestra arose largely as a vehicle for performing Beethoven's symphonies and that the art of conducting emerged in his wake. His nine symphonies are the origin of the so-called curse of the ninth, a superstition that composers were doomed to die before finishing a tenth.

Bonn has a Beethoven House museum in the place of his birth and has hosted the Beethovenfest since 1845. In Vienna, the Beethoven Museum in Probusgasse is where he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament, and the Pasqualatihaus was his most enduring residence there.
ludwig-wittgenstein: Ludwig Josef Johann Wittgenstein was born on 26 April 1889 in Vienna. His father, Karl Wittgenstein, meant his sons to become captains of industry and had them educated at home; three of the five brothers later took their own lives. After the disappearance and presumed suicide of Hans in 1902, Karl allowed the two youngest sons to attend school, and in 1903 Ludwig entered the Realschule in Linz. From 1906 he studied mechanical engineering in Berlin. Wanting to study with Gottlob Frege, he followed Frege's advice and arrived unannounced at Bertrand Russell's rooms at Trinity College, Cambridge, on 18 October 1911.

After Karl's death in January 1913 he inherited one of Europe's largest fortunes and gave much of it to poets and artists. At the outbreak of the First World War he volunteered for the Austro-Hungarian Army. In 1916 he was posted to the Russian front, where he directed artillery fire from an observation post and was awarded the Military Merit Medal with Swords on the Ribbon. He finished the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus in August 1918; it appeared in German in 1921 and in English in 1922. In the 1920s he taught in Austrian village schools, where his use of corporal punishment caused controversy.

He returned to Cambridge in 1929, offered the Tractatus as his doctoral thesis, and in 1939 was elected to the chair of philosophy that G. E. Moore had resigned. He became a British subject on 12 April 1939. During the Second World War he worked as a porter at Guy's Hospital in London, and he came back to Cambridge for the last time in October 1944.

The Tractatus is concerned with the logical relationship between propositions and the world. Wittgenstein held that what can be said by propositions must be separated from what can only be shown. It influenced the Vienna Circle, although he was never a member.

His later thought, set out mainly in the Philosophical Investigations, published in 1953 after his death on 29 April 1951, rejected many assumptions of the Tractatus. He asked readers to think of language as a multiplicity of language games and argued that, in a large class of cases, the meaning of a word is its use in the language. His papers amount to an estimated 20,000 pages.
luftwaffe: Germany's air arms in the First World War were disbanded in May 1920 under the Treaty of Versailles, which banned Germany from having any air force. In the interwar period German pilots were trained secretly in the Soviet Union, at Lipetsk Air Base. After the rise of the Nazi Party the Luftwaffe was officially established on 26 February 1935, just over two weeks before Germany announced rearmament and conscription. The Condor Legion, a detachment sent to aid the Nationalist forces in the Spanish Civil War, served as a testing ground; its operations included the bombing of Guernica. By the summer of 1939 the Luftwaffe had twenty-eight wings and also ran a paratrooper force, the Fallschirmjäger.

The Luftwaffe was instrumental in the German victories in Poland in 1939 and western Europe in spring 1940. It inflicted severe damage on the infrastructure of the RAF in the Battle of Britain and devastated many British cities in the Blitz, but failed to force Britain to submit. It was very successful in 1941 against Yugoslavia, Greece and the Soviet Union. Its paratroopers took heavy losses on Crete in May 1941, with more than 4,000 killed.

From 1942 Allied bombing gradually destroyed its fighter arm. It lacked an effective air defence early in the war and had no long-range bomber, and its production fell behind: in 1940 British fighter output exceeded plans by 43 per cent while German output stood 40 per cent behind target. A shortage of trained pilots and fuel added to its losses, and after a failed last effort in January 1945 it ceased to be an effective fighting force. It had only two commanders-in-chief, Hermann Göring and, for the last two weeks, Robert Ritter von Greim.

The Luftwaffe was deeply involved in Nazi war crimes. In 1943 and 1944 aircraft production was moved to concentration camps, and as many as 90,000 camp prisoners worked in the aviation industry. Its demand for forced labour was one factor in the deportation of Hungarian Jews in 1944: of 437,000 deported between May and July, about 320,000 were gassed on arrival at Auschwitz. Luftwaffe paratroopers committed massacres on Crete, and several Luftwaffe divisions murdered hundreds of civilians in Italy. Prisoners were forced to take part in experiments for the Luftwaffe, and of about 400 in cold-water experiments, 80 to 90 were killed.
lugal-zage-si: Lugal-zage-si, of Umma, is considered the last Sumerian king before Sargon of Akkad conquered Sumer, and the only king of the third dynasty of Uruk in the Sumerian King List. His inscription on the Nippur vase names him as the son of Ukush, governor of Umma, and as priest of An and prophet of Nidaba. He began as énsi of Umma and led its final victory in a generation-long conflict with the city-state of Lagash over the fertile plain of Gu-Edin.

Lugal-zage-si pursued an expansionist policy. In the seventh year of his reign Uruk fell under him, and he annexed most of the territory of Lagash under King Urukagina, so establishing the first reliably documented kingdom to encompass all of Sumer. A lament over the destruction of Lagash says that the offence lay with Lugal-zage-si and not with Urukagina. He also invaded Kish, where he overthrew Ur-Zababa, and took Ur, Nippur and Larsa, and he made Uruk his capital. The Sumerian King List gives him a reign of 25 or 34 years.

On the Nippur vase he claims that Enlil gave him all the lands between the upper and the lower seas, that is, from the Mediterranean to the Persian Gulf. Some modern scholars regard his advance to the west as not much more than a successful raiding party, though the inscription is the first in which a Sumerian prince claimed to have reached what was, for them, the western edge of the world. Later tablets assert that Lugal-Anne-Mundu of Adab had conquered as far as the Mediterranean earlier, but records from before Sargon are too thin to say.

Sargon of Akkad defeated him and annexed his kingdom. According to later Babylonian copies of Sargon's inscriptions, Sargon tore down the walls of Uruk, captured Lugal-zage-si in battle and led him in a collar to the gate of Enlil at Nippur.
lugalbanda: Lugalbanda was a deified Sumerian king of Uruk who, according to various sources of Mesopotamian literature, was the father of Gilgamesh. The Sumerian King List names him as the second king of Uruk, gives him a reign of 1,200 years and the epithet "the Shepherd". His historicity is uncertain among scholars, and attempts to date him to the ED II period rest on an amalgam of second-millennium epic traditions and unclear archaeological observations.

He appears in Sumerian literature as early as the mid-3rd millennium, in the incomplete text Lugalbanda and Ninsuna from Abu Salabikh, which describes a romance with Ninsun. In the earliest god-lists from Fara he ranks much lower than the goddess, but later traditions down to the Seleucid period often list the two together. His worship as a god appears from the Ur III period, in tablets from Nippur, Ur, Umma and Puzrish-Dagan, and in the Old Babylonian period Sin-kashid of Uruk built a temple for Lugalbanda and Ninsun and made his daughter Niši-īnī-šu their priestess. Ur-Nammu and his son Shulgi called Lugalbanda and Ninsun their holy parents and themselves brothers of Gilgamesh.

Two Sumerian stories of the Ur III period, Lugalbanda in the Mountain Cave and Lugalbanda and the Anzu Bird, make him the hero. They belong to a series on the conflict between Enmerkar of Uruk and Ensuhkeshdanna, lord of Aratta, presumably in the Iranian highlands, and show Lugalbanda as a soldier in Enmerkar's army. Both are known only in later versions of the 18th century BCE, and the fragments do not say he succeeded Enmerkar.

In the Epic of Gilgamesh and the earlier Sumerian stories, Gilgamesh calls himself the son of Lugalbanda and Ninsun. In Gilgamesh and Huwawa he swears by the life of his mother Ninsun and his father, holy Lugalbanda. In Akkadian versions he calls Lugalbanda his personal god and presents him the oil-filled horns of the defeated Bull of Heaven. Scholars including Bendt Alster and Jennifer Larson have studied the early epic tradition around him.
luganda: Luganda, called Oluganda by its speakers, is a Bantu language of the African Great Lakes region. It is agglutinative and tonal, with subject-verb-object word order. It has at least 5.6 million first-language speakers, mainly in the Buganda region of central Uganda, including the capital Kampala, and about 5.4 million second-language speakers in towns such as Mbale, Jinja, Gulu and Mbarara, where it is used mostly in trade. As a second language in Uganda it follows English and precedes Swahili. It is also the most spoken unofficial language in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda. Lusoga, spoken in Busoga to the east of Buganda, is very closely related, with an estimated lexical similarity of 82 to 86 per cent.

Like the other Bantu languages of the Great Lakes region, Luganda is generally held to descend from Proto-Bantu, the ancestor of all Bantu languages, though its specific origins remain a matter of scholarly debate. During the 18th and 19th centuries contact with Arab traders, missionaries and colonial powers brought loanwords, mostly for things that had not existed in the country. From Arabic come ccaayi, tea, from shay, as well as eddiini, religion, and essaala, prayer; from English come essaati, shirt, and emotoka, car.

Luganda distinguishes long from short vowels and has geminate consonants, which speakers call simply doubling, as in bbiri, two. It has three tones, high, low and falling, and pitch changes meaning: Kabaka means king when all three syllables have the same pitch, but with a high first syllable it means the little one catches.

Spelling, standardised since 1947, uses the Latin alphabet with one added letter, ŋ, and the digraph ny, counted as a single letter. Letters and sounds correspond closely. Its grammar centres on nouns: adjectives, verbs, pronouns and possessives agree with a noun by class and number through prefixes. Ten classes are usually counted, plus four locative classes. Nouns also have two states, with the topic state marked by an initial vowel, as in the subject of a sentence.
luhansk: Luhansk lies in the Donets Basin, or Donbas, in eastern Ukraine, at the confluence of the Luhan and Olkhova rivers. Its name comes from the Luhan River, and a folk etymology links it to the word for meadow, referring to the river's floodplains. The city's main street is Sovetskaya Street, and its central venue for public events is Theatre Square. Several universities have their home there, including a medical university.

The population was 20,400 in 1897 and reached 505,000 in 1992. The census of 2001 recorded 49.6 per cent of inhabitants as ethnically Ukrainian and 47 per cent as Russian, with 85.3 per cent giving Russian as their native language.

The city traces its origin to a foundry set up under a decree of Catherine II in 1795-1796, building ammunition and cannon for the Black Sea Fleet. The British industrialist Charles Gascoigne is credited with founding it in 1797. The works grew during the Napoleonic and Crimean Wars. In 1882 the factory and the neighbouring settlement of Kamianyi Brid were merged as Luhansk, which received city status. In 1896 the German industrialist Gustav Hartmann founded a locomotive-building company there, operational from 1900.

The city changed hands several times in the civil war and was taken by the Red Army in January 1920. On 5 November 1935 it was renamed Voroshilovgrad after Kliment Voroshilov. The name Luhansk was restored in 1958 and replaced again in 1970, after Voroshilov's death, until 1990. German troops held the city from 14 July 1942 until the Red Army liberated it on 14 February 1943. The population rose from 72,000 to 212,000 between 1926 and 1939.

Luhansk was the administrative centre of Luhansk Oblast in independent Ukraine. In 2014 pro-Russian separatists seized the city and made it the capital of the self-proclaimed Luhansk People's Republic, and the Ukrainian regional administration moved to Sievierodonetsk. Russia claimed to annex the oblast in late 2022. Its industries have included locomotive building and metalworking, and it is twinned with Cardiff, Lublin and Saint-Étienne, among others.
luigi-cadorna: Luigi Cadorna was born in 1850 at Pallanza in Piedmont, the son of General Raffaele Cadorna. He entered the Turin Military Academy at fifteen and was commissioned as a second lieutenant of artillery in 1868. In 1870 he took part in the occupation of Rome in a force commanded by his father. As colonel of the 10th Regiment of Bersaglieri from 1892 he gained a reputation for strict discipline and harsh punishment, and he wrote a manual of infantry tactics that stressed the doctrine of the offensive. He became a lieutenant general in 1898.

Cadorna was first offered the post of chief of staff in 1908 and refused it over the question of political control in wartime. He accepted it in July 1914. When Italy entered the war on 24 May 1915 he commanded thirty-six infantry divisions of 875,000 men but only 120 modern artillery pieces. He chose to attack on the Isonzo, since the rest of the front against Austria-Hungary was judged even less suited to offence. The first battle there ended in stalemate, and ten more offensives followed. The Sixth Battle of the Isonzo, in August 1916, took Gorizia; the Eleventh, in August 1917, broke through on the Bainsizza plateau.

On 24 October 1917 an Austro-Hungarian and German army attacked at Kobarid, known in Italian as Caporetto, and by 12 November had reached the Piave. Cadorna had placed most of his troops far forward with little defence in depth, and he had been on leave for much of October. About 275,000 Italian soldiers were captured. The king and government dismissed him on 7 November, and Armando Diaz took his place. Cadorna was sent as Italy's representative to the Allied Supreme War Council at Versailles.

An inquiry into Caporetto, published in 1919, was highly critical of Cadorna. He answered with a two-volume memoir, La guerra alla fronte italiana. His reputation improved afterwards, and he was made a marshal of Italy in 1924. He died at Bordighera in 1928.

Historians remain divided. During the war he dismissed 217 officers, and about 750 Italian soldiers were executed, the highest number in any army of the war. Claims that he revived decimation alienated his troops; John Keegan describes his severity instead as the summary execution of individual stragglers. Giorgio Rochat, while criticising his little concern for his soldiers, argues that trench warfare had a terrible logic of its own, independent of Cadorna and other commanders.
luigi-carlo-farini: Luigi Carlo Farini was born on 22 October 1812 at Russi, in what is now the province of Ravenna. He studied at Bologna, interrupting his course to take part in the revolution of 1831, and practised as a physician at Russi and Ravenna. In 1843 his political opinions brought him under police suspicion and he was expelled from the Papal States. He lived in Florence and Paris and travelled about Europe as private physician to Prince Jérôme Bonaparte, returning to Italy when Pius IX began his reign with apparently liberal and nationalist tendencies.

In March 1848 Farini became secretary-general to the minister of the interior, but resigned with the whole ministry on 29 April, when Pius IX refused to let his troops fight Austria. Elected for Faenza, he served again in the Mamiani cabinet. He went into exile at Turin when a reactionary and priestly policy was instituted, became convinced that Italy could be liberated only through the House of Savoy, and wrote for Cavour's paper Il Risorgimento. His chief historical work, Lo Stato Romano dal 1815 al 1850, appeared in four volumes in 1850. He was minister of public instruction from 1851 to May 1852, and his two letters to William Ewart Gladstone, in 1856 and 1857, created a sensation.

When Francis V, duke of Modena, was expelled in 1859, Farini was sent to the city as Piedmontese commissioner. Recalled after the peace of Villafranca, he stayed, became a Modenese citizen and dictator of the state, and negotiated an alliance with Parma, Romagna and Tuscany. After the plebiscite for annexation to Piedmont, Cavour appointed him minister of the interior in June 1860, and later viceroy of Naples. After Cavour's death in 1861 he succeeded Rattazzi as premier, but illness forced him to resign on 24 March 1863. He died in poverty in 1866 at Quarto dei Mille in Genoa and was buried at Turin; in 1878 his remains were moved to Russi.
luis-carrero-blanco: Luis Carrero Blanco was born on 4 March 1904 in Santoña, in the province of Santander, the son of an army officer, Camilo Carrero Gutiérrez, and Ángeles Blanco Abascal. He entered the Spanish Naval Academy at San Fernando, Cádiz, in January 1918 and was commissioned in September 1922. After the Submarine School course of 1924 he took part in the Rif War, including the landings at Alcazarseguer and Alhucemas in 1925. In 1929 he married María del Carmen Pichot y Villa and was given command of the submarine B-5.

When the Spanish Civil War broke out Carrero Blanco was teaching submarine tactics at the Naval Warfare College in Madrid. He took refuge first in the Mexican embassy and then in the French one, crossed into France, and in July 1937 entered the Nationalist zone through San Sebastián. He served as naval liaison to the Army of the North, commanded the destroyer Huesca and the submarine General Sanjurjo, and in August 1939 became Chief of Operations of the Navy General Staff.

In May 1941 Franco appointed him, at 37, Under-Secretary of the Presidency of the Government. After the Begoña incident of 1942 he advised Franco to remove Ramón Serrano Suñer from his ministry and from the Political Junta of the Falange, which Franco did. The historian Joan Maria Thomàs calls him extremely faithful and submissive to the Caudillo. He became a vice-admiral in 1963 and an admiral in 1966, was the main drafter of the 1947 Law of Succession, and was made Deputy Prime Minister on 21 September 1967. When Juan Carlos of Bourbon was named Franco's heir in 1969, many expected an authoritarian monarchy guided by Carrero to carry Francoism on without Franco.

Franco appointed him Prime Minister on 8 June 1973. Six months later, on 20 December 1973, four members of an ETA cell killed him in Madrid with a bomb placed near the church of San Francisco de Borja on Calle de Serrano, as he returned from daily mass. His funeral at the Basilica of Saint Francis the Great was one of Franco's last public appearances, and he was buried at Mingorrubio Cemetery in El Pardo.

The assassination, followed by the overthrow of the Portuguese regime in 1974, dealt a blow to those who favoured a continuation of the regime. His successor, Carlos Arias Navarro, promised in February 1974 reforms including the right to form political associations. Historians such as Antonio Elorza describe Carrero's ideology as counter-revolutionary, anticommunist and hostile to Freemasonry, and he is considered a pure Francoist.
luis-de-camoes: Much of what is told about the poet's life is doubtful, and part of it is probably folklore, for only a few dates are documented. His family had its origins in the Kingdom of Galicia. On his father's side he descended from Vasco Pires de Camões, a Galician troubadour, warrior and fidalgo who moved to Portugal in 1370 and received offices, honours and lands from the king. Vasco's son Antão Vaz de Camões served in the Red Sea and married Dona Guiomar da Gama, a relative of Vasco da Gama.

Camões sailed east aboard the carrack São Bento, in the fleet of Fernão Álvares Cabral, which left the Tagus on 24 March 1553. A storm off the Cape of Good Hope destroyed the other three ships, and he landed at Goa in 1554. He entered the service of the viceroy Afonso de Noronha and fought against the king of Chembé. In 1555 he accompanied Manuel de Vasconcelos against the Moors in the Red Sea, and the squadron wintered at Ormuz.

In December 1567 he embarked for Mozambique on the ship of Pedro Barreto, to wait there for passage to Lisbon. Early biographers say Barreto made false promises. The chronicler Diogo do Couto found him two years later so poor that friends fed him, and Barreto embargoed his departure over a debt of two hundred cruzados, which friends paid. He reached Cascais on 7 April 1570. Contemporaries describe him as blind in his right eye, skilled at physical exercises and quick to fight.

His work falls into lyric, epic and drama. Os Lusíadas takes its title from Lusitania, the Roman name for Portugal, and tells how Vasco da Gama and the Portuguese sailed round the Cape of Good Hope and opened a new route to India. Couto recorded that Camões finished it at Mozambique and lost to theft another book, the Parnasum.

His lyrics, scattered in manuscripts, were collected after his death as the Rimas, published in 1595. They include sonnets after Petrarch, odes, elegies, eclogues from Virgil and the Italians, and redondilhas. He wrote three comedies, El-Rei Seleuco, Filodemo and Anfitriões, though the attribution of El-Rei Seleuco is disputed. Torquato Tasso, Cervantes and Goethe praised him.
luis-de-gongora: Luis de Góngora was born in Córdoba on 11 July 1561 to a noble family; his father, Francisco de Argote, was corregidor, or judge. At a time when purity of Christian lineage was needed for education or official appointments, he took the surname of his mother, Leonor de Góngora. His uncle, a prebendary of Córdoba Cathedral, renounced his post in favour of his nephew, who took deacon's orders in 1586. As a canon of the cathedral Góngora travelled on commissions to Navarre, Andalusia and Castile. Around 1605 he was ordained priest and afterwards lived in Valladolid and Madrid. In 1617, through the influence of the Duke of Lerma, he was appointed honorary chaplain to King Philip III, but did not enjoy the honour long.

Góngora did not publish his poems, though he tried in 1623, and manuscript copies circulated in songbooks and anthologies. His two best-known works are the Fábula de Polifemo y Galatea (1612), in royal octaves, which tells the love of Polyphemus, one of the Cyclopes, for the nymph Galatea from Ovid's Metamorphoses, and the Soledades (1613), written in a variety of metres. He also wrote sonnets, a poem of 79 royal octaves in praise of the Duke of Lerma in 1617, the Fábula de Píramo y Tisbe of 1618, and plays.

The style called culteranismo or Gongorismo made heavy use of Latinate and Greek neologisms and of hyperbaton, a distortion of ordinary word order. Opponents coined the name from culto and luteranismo, to present it as a heresy of true poetry. Góngora revived or popularised many obscure words that are common today, such as brillante, asunto and fragmento. His lifelong rival Francisco de Quevedo, associated with the witty, economical conceptismo, mocked his vocabulary and wrote satires on his nose and his gambling. Miguel de Cervantes counted him among the good poets.

In 1626 a severe illness that seriously impaired his memory forced Góngora to return to Córdoba, where he died the following year, poor from his efforts to win positions and lawsuits for his relatives. He was buried in a side chapel of Córdoba Cathedral. Juan López de Vicuña published an edition in 1627, and an edition by Gonzalo de Hozes appeared in 1633.

The Generation of '27 took its name from 1927, when it marked the tercentenary of his death, which official academic circles had ignored, with recitals and a plan for a new critical edition. It was the first group to try to revive baroque literature. Dámaso Alonso called Góngora a mystic of words and argued against the idea that he had separate simple and difficult styles. Rafael Alberti and García Lorca wrote on him, and Velázquez painted his portrait.
luis-federico-leloir: Leloir was born in Paris on 6 September 1906, a week after the death of his father, Federico, whom his parents had brought from Buenos Aires for treatment of an illness. The family returned to Argentina in 1908, and he grew up with eight siblings on the family property of El Tuyú, which his grandparents had bought after emigrating from the Basque Country. His grades were unspectacular, and he gave up the architectural studies he had begun in Paris. He later joined the medical faculty of the University of Buenos Aires, needed four attempts to pass his anatomy exam, and took his diploma in 1932.

In 1933 Leloir met Bernardo Houssay, who directed his doctoral thesis towards the suprarenal glands and carbohydrate metabolism; Houssay won the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1947. Leloir's thesis was judged the best of its year. In 1936 he went to the University of Cambridge to work under Sir Frederick Gowland Hopkins on enzymes. Houssay was expelled from the university for signing a petition against the Nazi regime and the military government of Pedro Pablo Ramírez, and Leloir went to the United States, where he worked with Carl Cori and Gerty Cori in St. Louis and then with David E. Green at Columbia University.

In 1945 he returned to Argentina and in 1947 began directing the Instituto de Investigaciones Bioquímicas de la Fundación Campomar, founded by the patron Jaime Campomar. The institute began in a few rooms with very little money; to separate cell contents when he could not buy a refrigerated centrifuge, Leloir and J. M. Muñoz spun a tire stuffed with salt and ice. In 1948 his team identified the sugar nucleotides central to carbohydrate metabolism. They also worked out the main steps of galactose metabolism, now called the Leloir pathway, and the cause of the genetic disorder galactosemia.

Leloir received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on 2 December 1970 and spent the prize money of $80,000 directly on research. He insisted that the discovery was his team's work. After Campomar's death in 1957 the institute sought funds from the National Institutes of Health in the United States, and in 1958 it moved into a former girls' school donated by the Argentine government. Leloir died in Buenos Aires on 2 December 1987 and is buried in La Recoleta Cemetery. The institute now bears his name as the Fundación Instituto Leloir. His friend Mario Bunge held that his legacy was to show that research at an international level was possible in a country in political strife.
luitpold-prince-regent-of-bavaria: Luitpold was born at the Residence in Würzburg on 12 March 1821, the third son of King Ludwig I of Bavaria and Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen, and a younger brother of King Maximilian II of Bavaria and King Otto of Greece. He was in line to the Bavarian throne and, since Otto had no children, heir presumptive in Greece, though the Greek constitution required Otto's heir to be Greek Orthodox. After Otto was deposed in 1862 and died in 1867, Luitpold and his descendants represented Otto's claim, which he never pursued.

He joined the Bavarian Army at fourteen and was a captain of artillery in 1835. In the revolutions of 1848 he mediated an audience of discontented citizens with his father. Under Ludwig II, whose long absences from the capital made him represent the royal house, he commanded the 3rd Royal Bavarian Division in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 and became Inspector General of the Bavarian Army in 1869. In the Franco-Prussian War he represented Bavaria in the German General Staff and handed over Ludwig's Kaiserbrief on 3 December 1870, endorsing Wilhelm I as German Emperor. He was appointed Field Marshal in 1876.

On 10 June 1886 Ludwig II was declared mentally incompetent and Luitpold named regent. After Ludwig's mysterious death a few days later, his brother Otto became king, but Otto had been under medical supervision since 1883, so Luitpold continued as regent. Some accused him of murdering his nephew, yet the affable prince became one of Bavaria's most popular rulers, and on 1 August 1886 he opened several of Ludwig's palaces to the public.

Politically he was largely passive. His governments moved away from the anti-Catholic Kulturkampf policies, a development that culminated in 1912 with the appointment of Georg von Hertling of the Centre Party, the largest group in the Landtag, as minister president, effectively parliamentarising the government. It had long been speculated that the diagnoses of Ludwig and Otto were pretexts, since Luitpold was thought to be pro-Prussian, but relations between Munich and Berlin remained cold.

Luitpold died of bronchitis in Munich on 12 December 1912 and was buried in the crypt of the Theatinerkirche. His eldest son, Ludwig, served as regent for another year; a constitutional amendment of 1913 let a regent whose regency had lasted ten years take the throne, and Ludwig deposed Otto and became Ludwig III.

The years of his regency, the Prinzregentenzeit, saw great artistic and cultural activity: Bavaria prospered under a liberal government, Munich became a cultural centre of Europe, and Schwabing became an important artists' quarter. Streets named Prinzregentenstrasse or Luitpoldstrasse, the Prinzregententheater in Munich and the Prinzregententorte, a layered chocolate cake, bear his name.
lulach: Lulach mac Gille Coemgáin was born about 1032. He was nicknamed Tairbith, the Unfortunate, and Fatuus, the Simple-minded or the Foolish. His mother Gruoch of Scotland had been married first to Gille Coemgáin, Mormaer of Moray, and she later married Macbeth, who became Lulach's stepfather. Through his mother he was also the great-grandson of either Kenneth II or Kenneth III.

Macbeth died at the Battle of Lumphanan on 15 August 1057, and his followers placed Lulach on the throne. He is the first king of Scotland of whom details of the inauguration are available: it probably took place at Scone on 8 September 1057. His nicknames suggest that he was a weak king, and he ruled for only a few months before he was assassinated and usurped by Malcolm III on 17 March 1058. It is also plausible that the nicknames are the result of negative propaganda, established as part of a smear campaign by Malcolm III.

Lulach is believed to be buried on Saint Columba's Holy Island of Iona, in or around the monastery, though the exact position of his grave is unknown. His son Máel Snechtai became Mormaer of Moray, and Óengus of Moray was the son of Lulach's daughter.

Lulach appears in fiction as a secondary character or protagonist. In Dorothy Dunnett's novel King Hereafter he is a seer, whom she uses as a mouthpiece for researched information about the real Macbeth, and he is a character in David Greig's play Dunsinane, where English soldiers hunt him as a threat to peace in Malcolm's Scotland. He also appears in Jackie French's children's novel Macbeth and Son and in Susan Fraser King's Lady MacBeth.
lumbini: Lumbini, whose name means the lovely or beautiful garden, is a Buddhist pilgrimage site in the Rupandehi District of Nepal. According to sacred texts and Buddhist commentaries, Queen Maya gave birth there to Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, about 563 BCE. In the Buddha's time it lay east of Kapilavastu and south-west of Devadaha, in the territory of Shakya, an oligarchic republic. The Sutta Nipata states that he was born in a village of the Sakyans in the Lumbineyya Janapada.

The site was not known as Lumbini until the discovery of the Ashoka Pillar. In 1896 the former Nepalese Army general Khadga Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana and Alois Anton Führer found a great stone pillar at Rupandehi, guided by the records of the Chinese monk-pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang. Its Brahmi inscription shows that Ashoka, emperor of the Maurya Empire, visited in the 3rd century BCE and identified the place as the Buddha's birthplace. He made the village of Lumbini free of taxes and subject to only an eighth share of the produce. A second inscription at the top of the pillar was made by King Ripumalla in the Saka year 1234.

Excavations at the Mayadevi Temple in 2013 revealed beneath a brick shrine of the Ashokan era an older timber structure that appears to be an ancient tree shrine. Robin Coningham argues that human activity began around 1000 BCE and that the site may have been a Buddhist monument from the 6th century BCE. Other scholars state that the excavations revealed nothing Buddhist and show only that the site predates the Buddha.

Lumbini is one of the four most sacred pilgrimage sites of the Buddha's life, with Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar. The complex is 4.8 kilometres long and 1.6 wide and has a Sacred Garden with the Mayadevi Temple, the Ashoka Pillar and the Puskarini sacred pond. A monastic zone is divided into an eastern zone for Theravada monasteries and a western zone for Mahayana and Vajrayana ones. Lumbini was made a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1997.
lund: Lund lies in the south-west of Scania, in Sweden's largest agricultural district and less than ten kilometres from the shore of the Öresund Strait. The city rises from the low-lying Höje River in the south to 86 metres above sea level in the north, and from the top of Sankt Hans Hill Copenhagen can be seen. The central part still largely keeps its medieval street layout. The main squares are Stortorget, where the city hall stands, Clemenstorget, Bantorget and Mårtenstorget, which was once a cattle market called Oxtorget.

Lund and Sigtuna are the oldest cities in present-day Sweden. Until the 1980s the city was thought to have been founded around 1020 by Sweyn I Forkbeard or Canute the Great of Denmark, but archaeological discoveries now suggest a first settlement around 990, possibly settlers moved from Uppåkra, a settlement going back to the 1st century BCE. The new site on a hill beside a ford was easier to defend. Under Canute the Great the Danish church was organised, and Lund became one of seven dioceses in 1048.

It became an archbishopric in 1103 or 1104, with a province covering Scandinavia and Greenland, and the cathedral was built about 1090 to 1145. Lund Cathedral School, founded in 1085 by Canute the Saint, is the oldest school in Scandinavia.

The Norwegian archdiocese of Nidaros became independent of Lund in 1152, and Sweden got its own archbishop in 1164, though nominally subordinate to Lund's. A first Academy of Lund, founded in the 1400s, was suppressed during the Danish Reformation in 1537. Denmark ceded the city to Sweden in the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658. Denmark recaptured it in 1676 in the Scanian War, and the very bloody Battle of Lund, fought just north of the city that year, ended in a decisive Swedish victory. Swedish control was confirmed again in 1720. The present Lund University was established in 1666.

Lund is the seat of Lund Municipality in Scania County, with 94,393 inhabitants in the town in 2023. The university and its buildings dominate much of the centre, and the city is a regional centre for high-technology industry; the packaging company Tetra Pak was founded there in 1951. Surviving medieval buildings include the cathedral, Liberiet, St. Peter's Priory and Krognoshuset. The population more than doubled in the second half of the 20th century, led by the growth of the university and of high-tech industry.
luneburg: Lüneburg lies on the river Ilmenau, about 30 kilometres from its confluence with the Elbe. The river once carried cogs bearing salt from the town to the larger Hanseatic ports nearby. The motto Mons, Pons, Fons, "hill, bridge, spring", describes how the town grew from the eighth century out of three and later four settlements: the refuge castle on the then much higher Kalkberg with its market quarter, the village of Modestorpe between the bridge and the square called Am Sande, and the saltworks with its walled settlement for the workers.

The first mention of Lüneburg in a medieval record is a deed of 13 August 956, in which Emperor Otto I granted the tax from Lüneburg to the monastery of Saint Michael. The Royal Frankish Annals of 795 already name a place called Hliuni on the Elbe, probably the castle on the Kalkberg, which was the seat of the Billunger nobles from 951. Because Lüneburg long held a monopoly on the supply of salt in northern Germany, it quickly joined the Hanseatic League. Its salt was needed to pickle the herring caught in the Baltic and off Norway, so that the fish could be eaten inland in periods of fasting.

With the decline of the Hanseatic League and the disappearance of the herring around 1560, Falsterbo in Scania replaced Lüneburg as the biggest customer for its salt, and the town rapidly grew poorer. Hardly any new houses were built afterwards, so the centre kept its historic appearance. The town passed to the Electorate of Hanover in 1708, to the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807, to the First French Empire in 1810, to the Kingdom of Hanover in 1814 and to Prussia in 1866. Heinrich Heine, whose parents lived there from 1822 to 1826, called it his "residence of boredom".

The houses between the saltworks and the Kalkberg stood above a salt dome. When mining increased after 1830, the ground sank by several metres, and houses and the church of St Lambert had to be demolished. The saltworks closed in 1980. On 17 September 1945 the Belsen Trial began in Lüneburg, in which 45 former SS men, women and kapos from the Bergen-Belsen and Auschwitz camps were tried.

Lüneburg is the capital of its district, with about 77,000 inhabitants, and is home to Leuphana University. It has used the title Hansestadt, "Hanseatic town", since 2007. The old saltworks now house the German Salt Museum, and only a little brine is still drawn for the thermal baths.
luneville: Lunéville is a commune in the Meurthe-et-Moselle department of north-eastern France, a subprefecture of the department. It lies on the river Meurthe at its confluence with the Vezouze. It was a resort in the 18th century and was known as the capital of Lorraine.

The Château de Lunéville was built early in the 18th century for Leopold, Duke of Lorraine, to replace an older palace. It was designed in the style of Versailles to satisfy Leopold's wife, Élisabeth Charlotte d'Orléans, a niece of Louis XIV, and became known as the Versailles of Lorraine. It includes a chapel designed by Germain Boffrand. Leopold and his wife were the parents of Prince Charles Alexander of Lorraine and of Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor, through whom they were grandparents of Marie Antoinette. The last duke of Lorraine, Stanislaus I, the former king of Poland, had a church and several follies built in his gardens for the amusement and education of visiting Polish and Lithuanian nobility and followers of the Enlightenment.

Visitors to his court included Voltaire, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, André Morellet and Montesquieu. After Stanislaus died in 1766, Louis XV annexed the duchy and turned the château into a barracks. The Treaty of Lunéville was signed at 61 Rue de Lorraine, one of the houses built against the château gardens, on 9 February 1801 between the French Republic and the Austrian Empire, by Joseph Bonaparte and Count Ludwig von Cobenzl. The Treaty of Frankfurt of 1871 made Lunéville a border town, attracting people from Alsace and Moselle who moved to keep their French nationality, and a period of prosperity known as the Belle Époque followed.

Lunéville faience, made from 1723 by Jacques Chambrette, became the Royal Factory of the King of Poland after Stanislaus sponsored it in 1749. The Croismare glass factory, built in 1858, became known for art deco glass after the Müller brothers settled there in 1897.

Much of the original construction of the château has survived and is open to the public, and its parterre gardens, designed by Yves Hours in 1711 and Louis de Nesle in 1724, are a public park. Lunéville faience still exists as Terres d'Est. Among those connected with the town, Émilie du Châtelet lived there for a long time and died there, and Georges de La Tour lived there for much of his career.
luoyang: Luoyang stands where the Luo River meets the Yellow River in the west of Henan province, on the central plain of China. Its name means the north, or sunny, side of the Luo. It has also been called Luoyi, Dongdu or "eastern capital" under the Tang, Xijing or "western capital" under the Song, and Shendu or "divine capital" during the rule of Wu Zetian. It was renamed Henanfu and regained its old name in 1912.

In 1036 BCE the Duke of Zhou built a settlement called Chengzhou for the remnants of the Shang nobility. Wangcheng became the capital of the Eastern Zhou in 771 BCE. Emperor Guangwu declared Luoyang the capital of the Eastern Han on 27 November 25 CE. A Roman mission sent by the king of Da Qin reached the city in 166 CE. The Yellow Turban rebellion and civil war followed, and the capital was burned on 24 September 189 CE. The next year Dong Zhuo ordered the city razed as he retreated, and the court moved to Chang'an.

Cao Pi made Luoyang his capital in 220, and the Jin dynasty succeeded him there. The Xiongnu-led Han-Zhao sacked it in 311 in the Disaster of Yongjia. In 493 Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei moved the capital from Datong to Luoyang, and the rock-cut Longmen Grottoes were begun, with more than 30,000 Buddhist statues found there. Gao Huan destroyed the city in 534. Emperor Yang of Sui founded a new Luoyang in 604.

Under the Tang it was Dongdu, with a population of around one million at its height, second only to Chang'an. Empress Wu moved the capital of her Zhou dynasty to it, and the An Lushan Rebellion damaged it. Epitaphs of the early ninth century record Nestorian Christian Sogdian women in the city. Under the Northern Song it was the Western Capital and the birthplace of Zhao Kuangyin, the founder of the dynasty.

Luoyang is a prefecture-level city of Henan, with about seven million people in its municipality. The Longmen Grottoes became a World Heritage Site in 2000, and in 2014 sites of the Grand Canal and of the Silk Roads, including the Han and Wei Luoyang city site, were added. Luoyang is known for its peonies, and has held a National Peony Fair since 1983.
lurs: The origin of the Lurs is disputed. They are believed to be of Elamite and Kassite origin, and the historian Walther Hinz described the Elamites as possible proto-Lurs. Others describe them as a mixture of Iranian tribes from Central Asia with the pre-Iranic peoples of western Iran, such as the Kassites and Gutians. The distinctive features of the Lur dialects suggest that they were Iranized from Persis rather than Media.

The term Lur is first recorded after the Islamic conquest of Iran. Early Islamic sources use Bilad al-Lur for a region between Khuzestan and Isfahan, and the name probably passed from the region to the tribes that lived there. It appears in a geographic sense in the 4th Islamic century and in an ethnic sense in the 5th.

The history of the Lurs is closely linked with the dynasties that ruled Khuzestan, Shiraz, Isfahan, Hamadan and the Zagros. The Buyid dynasty marched its forces through Lorestan in 935. The Hasanwayhid dynasty later controlled the Karkheh River and about 1009 took Shapur-Khwast, now Khorramabad. In 1042 the Seljuk Empire besieged it, when it was ruled by the Kakuyid dynasty. The tribal structure of the Lurs was unaffected by outside attempts to conquer Lorestan.

After a Luri tribal insurgency against Reza Shah, crowned in 1925, Lur lands were brought under the ordinary government of Iran, which included forcing semi-nomads to settle. The semi-nomadic way of life returned after Reza Shah was toppled in 1941, and in 1986 a sizeable part of the Lurs and Bakhtiaris still lived that way.

The Lur tribes were generally divided into two branches, Lor-e Kuchek and Lor-e Bozorg. Vladimir Minorsky listed the main groups as the Bakhtiari, the Kuhgilu, the Mamasani and the Lur proper. Many Lurs are small-scale farmers and shepherds, and Luri textiles and weaving are highly esteemed. Tribal elders keep a strong authority among the nomads, though less among settled townspeople. As among Kurds, Lur women have much greater freedom than women in other groups of the region.

Most Lurs are Shia Muslims, having converted to Islam after the Muslim conquest of Persia and adopted Shia Islam during the Safavid conversion of Iran. Historically a significant part of the Lurs, especially those of Kurdish descent, followed Yarsanism, but nearly all had become Shia by the 20th century, and a small minority are Christian. Luri is a Western Iranian language continuum spoken by about four million people in three dialects, Bakhtiari, Luristani and Southern Luri. It has been the main link between the Lur branches and has helped to consolidate Lur identity.
lusaka: Lusaka stands on the central plateau of south-central Zambia at about 1,280 metres. It lies on the boundary of the territories of two peoples, the Lenje to the north and the Soli to the south, and the main roads of the country, the Great North Road and the Great East Road, cross here. The first known village dates to about the 11th century, a settlement of round huts near the modern suburb of Olympia. In the 19th century slave traders from the coastal regions enslaved members of the Soli and Lenje communities, who moved often to evade them and left no major permanent settlements.

The modern city dates from 1905, when the British South African Company, which controlled Northern Rhodesia, built a railway to link its Copperbelt mines with Cape Town. Lusaka was a water stop on that line, named after a local Lenje chief called Lusaaka. White Afrikaner farmers settled in the area and made it a regional trading centre.

In March 1929 the Colonial Office recommended moving the capital of Northern Rhodesia from Livingstone, citing communications and health. The governor James Maxwell and David Alexander chose Lusaka for its place on the railway and at the crossroads of the two great roads, and the town planner Stanley Adshead confirmed the site in late 1930. The report confirming Lusaka as the planned capital was approved in July 1931. Building went on through the 1930s but was slowed by a shortage of funds. A report of 1938 noted that of 10,000 Africans living in the city only 1,500 were in formal housing, since Africans were permitted to live there only on temporary work permits.

Lusaka lost some status to Salisbury when it became capital of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland in 1953. After a campaign for majority rule led by Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party, Northern Rhodesia became independent as the Republic of Zambia in 1964, and Lusaka was named its capital. A large building programme followed, including government buildings, the University of Zambia and a new airport, and migration from rural areas created many unplanned settlements.

Lusaka is the capital and largest city of Zambia, with 2,204,059 inhabitants at the 2022 census, and the seat of its government. English is the official language. The city centre lies around Cairo Road, and the University of Zambia, founded in 1965, is the country's oldest and largest institution of higher learning. Its people come from all parts of Zambia, and a hybrid called Town Nyanja is widely spoken.
lusatia: Lusatia, also called Sorbia, stretches from the Bóbr and Kwisa rivers in the east to the Pulsnitz and Black Elster in the west, and lies in the German states of Saxony and Brandenburg and the Polish voivodeships of Lower Silesia and Lubusz. Its main rivers are the Spree and the Lusatian Neisse, which forms the border between Germany and Poland. It is divided into hilly Upper Lusatia in the south and flat Lower Lusatia in the north. The name comes from the Sorbian word for swamps or water-holes. Lusatia has never been a single administrative unit.

By the end of the 6th century the Slavic Lusatians had settled in what became Lower Lusatia, and the Milceni further south in Upper Lusatia. After campaigns by Henry the Fowler in 928–934 the Sorbian tribes were subdued by 963 under the margrave Gero I. On the death of Otto III in 1002 Boleslaw I the Brave of Poland took the lands, and the Peace of Bautzen of 1018 left them under Polish rule until Conrad II regained them in 1031–1032. German settlers arrived in large numbers around 1200, and in 1346 six towns formed the Lusatian League against robber barons.

Lusatia lay among the lands of the Bohemian Crown, passing to the House of Habsburg in 1526, and most of it became Protestant. By the Peace of Prague of 1635 most of it became a province of the Electorate of Saxony. At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Lower Lusatia and the north-eastern part of Upper Lusatia went to Prussia, while Löbau, Kamenz, Bautzen and Zittau stayed Saxon. Herrnhut, founded in 1722 by refugees from Moravia, began the organised Protestant missionary movement in 1732. After 1945 the Oder–Neisse line divided Lusatia between Germany and Poland.

Lusatia is the home of the Slavic Sorbs, one of Germany's officially recognised minorities, who live in Saxon Upper Lusatia and Brandenburgian Lower Lusatia, where signs are mostly bilingual. Bautzen is the historical capital of Upper Lusatia, and Cottbus is the largest city. Muskau Park, at Bad Muskau and Łęknica, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
lushnje: Lushnjë lies in west-central Albania, in the middle plains, with a hot Mediterranean summer climate. It stands in the Myzeqe region, a main provider of agricultural products to the rest of the country, where the land is used for growing crops and raising animals and olive growing is widespread. The town is about 30 kilometres from the Divjakë-Karavasta National Park, with its wetland, beaches and lagoon.

The first mention of Lushnjë comes from the Ottoman defter, or cadastral survey, of 1431–1432 for the Sanjak of Albania, which lists the place as Luşnye among the settlements of the Muzakiye nahiye. Three kilometres away lies the Savra field, where in 1385 the first battle between the Principality of Zeta and the Principality of Albania, backed by the Ottoman Empire, was fought. In the Battle of Savra, Balsha II, Lord of Lower Zeta, was killed.

From 21 to 31 January 1920 the Congress of Lushnjë met in the town, and the chieftains of Albania assembled there declared Tirana first the provisional and then the definitive capital. Ferit Vokopola, a signatory of the Albanian Declaration of Independence, was elected its secretary. Data from the 1918 census shows the population of Lushnjë split almost evenly between Muslims and Christians at the time of independence from the Ottoman Empire.

Under the Communist regime Lushnjë and Fier were the main districts of the concentration camps, which included the villages of Savër, Gradishtë, Bedat, Gjazë, Rrapëz and Plug. The city also had factories for paper, plastic and food processing in that period.

The Congress of Lushnjë Museum and the Ardenica Monastery are among its landmarks, and the town is home to a national Institute of Agricultural Research. Its people speak a Tosk dialect, and the population is mixed Orthodox and Muslim, as in most southern Albanian cities. The football club formed in 1927 took the name Kongresi i Lushnjës after a proposal by Vokopola, and its green stripes were chosen to symbolise the fields of Myzeqe.
lushunkou: Lüshunkou lies at the extreme southern tip of the Liaodong Peninsula, with the Yellow Sea to the south-east, Korea Bay to the east and the Bohai Sea to the west. Its inner natural harbour, a lake-like basin, was well sheltered and easy to fortify in the eyes of nineteenth-century planners. The name means port of smooth journeys and was given in 1371 to commemorate a Ming expedition that sailed from Penglai in Shandong and landed there to attack the remaining Yuan forces. English-language writers called it Port Arthur after Lieutenant William Arthur of the Royal Navy, who surveyed the harbour in 1860.

In the late 1880s the German company Krupp was contracted by the Qing dynasty to build fortifications around the port. During the First Sino-Japanese War, on 20 and 21 November 1894, 15,000 Japanese troops defeated 13,000 Qing soldiers and took the town. The Port Arthur massacre that followed killed between 2,600 civilians and 20,000 people, including Chinese soldiers. Japan was granted the peninsula by the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 but had to give it up under the Triple Intervention of France, Germany and Russia, which was seen in Japan as a great humiliation.

In 1898 Russia obtained a lease of the peninsula and a railway right of way linking it to the Chinese Eastern Railway, with a line from Port Arthur to Harbin. Tsar Nicholas II believed a Pacific port would strengthen Russian security and economic influence.

Japan attacked the port and the Russian fleet without a declaration of war on 9 February 1904, opening the Russo-Japanese War. The port fell on 2 January 1905 after the Siege of Port Arthur. Japan then took over the Kwantung Leased Territory and renamed the town Ryojun, and the railway became part of the South Manchurian Railway. After Japan's defeat in the Second World War the Soviet Union administered the port, which it rented from China, until 1950. Soviet troops stayed until 1955.

Chinese Lüshun City was set up on 25 November 1945. On 7 January 1960 it became Lüshunkou District, part of Dalian in Liaoning Province, which was known as Lüda until 1981. The district covers 512.15 square kilometres. Japanese-era war monuments stand on 203 Hill and Baiyu Mountain.
lutetia: Traces of Neolithic habitation, dating to about 4500 BCE, have been found along the Seine at Bercy and near the Louvre, and a larger settlement was established around the middle of the third century BCE by the Parisii, a Gallic tribe. The site was an important crossing of the Seine, where land and water trade routes met. Historians have long placed the Parisii's main settlement on the Île de la Cité, as Caesar's description of an island fortress suggests, but a large Gallic settlement found at Nanterre between 1994 and 2005 has led some to doubt this. Defenders of the island note that the Parisii burned their oppidum and that the island has been rebuilt many times.

The Parisii first agreed to submit to Caesar, but in 52 BCE they joined the revolt of Vercingetorix. Their forces were led by his lieutenant Camulogenus, who burned the oppidum and the bridges. The Romans under Titus Labienus marched south to Melun, crossed the river there, returned towards the city and decisively defeated them. Traces of Roman occupation appear at the end of the first century BCE, under Augustus. The city was laid out on the left bank from the heights of the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève down to the island, with a forum, baths, a theatre and an amphitheatre that could hold 17,000 spectators. It was not the provincial capital, which was Sens, but it grew through its position on trade routes.

In the middle of the third century the Franks and Alemanni invaded Gaul and the unfortified city was threatened. Parts of the left bank, including the baths and amphitheatre, were abandoned and their stones used for ramparts round the Île de la Cité, and the city shrank from a hundred hectares to a few small enclaves. According to legend Saint Denis brought Christianity about 250. In 357 and 358 Julian moved the Roman capital of Gaul from Trier to Paris, and his troops proclaimed him emperor in Lutetia in 360. Lutetia had gradually become Paris, the city of the Parisii, and Clovis I later made it his capital.

Lutetia's name probably comes from a Celtic root meaning swamp or marsh. The Thermes de Cluny, public baths of the late first or early second century, are the largest and best-preserved Roman remains and now form part of the Musée de Cluny. The amphitheatre was discovered in 1867-68 during the building of Rue Monge, and a coalition including Victor Hugo saved it from becoming a bus depot. Vestiges of the later civic basilica and baths can be seen in the archaeological crypt before Notre-Dame.
lutheranism: The word Lutheran began as a term of abuse. The theologian Johann Maier von Eck used it against Martin Luther at the Leipzig Debate in July 1519, following the Catholic practice of naming a heresy after its leader. The schism between Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism was formalised in the Edict of Worms of 1521 and centred on two points: the source of authority in the church and the doctrine of justification. Lutherans hold that Scripture is the final authority and that people are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, on the basis of Scripture alone. The Catholic Church, as defined at the Council of Trent, holds that authority comes from both Scripture and tradition.

Lutheran churches adhere to the Bible and the ecumenical creeds, and their doctrine is set out in the Book of Concord, published in 1580. They keep many liturgical practices and sacramental teachings of the pre-Reformation Western Church, with particular emphasis on the Eucharist, and generally recognise three sacraments: baptism, confession and the Eucharist. Good works are held to be the fruit of faith and not a cause of salvation. Music is central to worship, and Luther himself was a great proponent of it; Lutheran hymns are sometimes called chorales, and Johann Sebastian Bach composed a huge body of sacred music for the Lutheran church.

Lutheranism became the state church of many parts of northern Europe, beginning with Prussia in 1525. It spread through Scandinavia in the sixteenth century as the monarchs of Denmark-Norway and Sweden adopted it, and through Baltic-German and Swedish rule into Estonia and Latvia. Almost all of the Lithuanian nobility converted to Lutheranism or Calvinism, though Protestantism lost support there at the end of the seventeenth century. After Luther's death in 1546 the Schmalkaldic War began in 1547, and imperial forces oppressed and exiled many German Lutherans. Religious freedom was secured for them in some areas by the Peace of Passau in 1552 and the Peace of Augsburg in 1555, under the principle that the ruler's religion decided that of his subjects.

From about 1580 to 1730 a period of Lutheran Orthodoxy followed, with scholastic theology developed by Johann Gerhard and others to argue with the Jesuits. Sizable Lutheran missions arose in the nineteenth century, though schools were already part of the work begun in India in 1706 by Bartholomew Ziegenbalg. Lutherans now number about 90 million and live on every continent.
luxembourgers: Luxembourgers are a Germanic ethnic group native to Luxembourg, where they make up around half of the population. Most live in the Grand Duchy, a small landlocked country in Western Europe between Germany, France and Belgium, and are of Celtic or Gallo-Roman and Germanic, Frankish, origin. They share the culture of Luxembourg and speak Luxembourgish, a West Germanic language, which is the only native language of Luxembourgers as taught by parents, though nearly all learn French and German in school.

Like the Austrians and some aspects of the Swiss, Luxembourgers were historically considered a regional sub-group of ethnic Germans and regarded themselves as such until the collapse of the German Confederation. Luxembourg became independent, while remaining in personal union with the Netherlands, after the Treaty of London of 1839. The personal union proved short-lived and was dissolved by agreement in 1890. Under Luxembourgish law all citizens of the Grand Duchy are Luxembourgers, although a distinct Germanic ethnolinguistic identification is vocally espoused and promoted. The corresponding adjective is Luxembourgish.

There is a relatively large diaspora, in the neighbouring countries of Belgium, France and Germany, mostly because of the three Partitions of Luxembourg, which brought former territories into each of them. The largest contingent overseas lives in the United States. Others went to the medieval Kingdom of Hungary during the first phase of German eastward settlement in the 12th century, and later during the Modern Age. The Transylvanian Saxons, whose dialect is very close to Luxembourgish, and partly the Banat Swabians descend from these settlers, as do part of the ancestors of the Zipser Germans of Zips in Slovakia and their descendants in Maramureș and Bukovina in Romania.

The first Saxon settlers in Transylvania came from the Rhine-Moselle valley region, and so also from Luxembourg. They were invited in the late 12th century by King Géza II of Hungary to develop, fortify and defend southern and south-eastern Transylvania against invading peoples such as the Cumans, Pechenegs, Mongols and Tatars. In 2007 Luxembourg City shared the title of European Capital of Culture with the Romanian town of Sibiu, one of the most important historical centres of the Transylvanian Saxons.
luxembourgish: Luxembourgish belongs to the West Central German group of the High German languages and is the primary example of a Moselle Franconian language. It is closely related to Transylvanian Saxon, which the Transylvanian Saxons have spoken in central Romania since the High Middle Ages. The National Library of Luxembourg has described the Codex Mariendalensis, a poem of nearly 6,000 lines about the life of the 13th-century Yolanda of Vianden, as the earliest known text in Luxembourgish. It was discovered in 1999 at Ansembourg Castle. The language was considered a German dialect until about the Second World War, and then created its own standard form in vocabulary, grammar and spelling.

Luxembourgish has three genders and three cases, nominative, accusative and dative. The genitive survives only in a few phrases, and its work is normally done by the dative with a possessive, as in dem Mann säi Buch, literally the man his book. Like German and Dutch it is a verb-second language. Women and girls are most often referred to with the neuter pronoun hatt. It has borrowed many French words, and its newest vocabulary comes from English. Several dialects exist, grouped into North, East, South and Center forms, and mobility and mass media are leading gradually towards a standard Luxembourgish.

Luxembourgish is the national language of Luxembourg and one of its three administrative languages, with German and French. About 400,000 people speak it worldwide. It is also spoken in the Arelerland region of Belgium, where French has since nearly replaced it, and in small parts of Lorraine. Proposals for a standard spelling go back to the middle of the 19th century. The first official system, adopted on 5 June 1946, won little approval. The standard that became official on 10 October 1975 grew out of the Luxemburger Wörterbuch, published in five volumes from 1950 to 1977, and was modified in a reform of 30 July 1999.
luxor: Luxor lies about 670 km from Cairo and about 220 km north of Aswan. The ruins of the temple complexes of Karnak and Luxor stand within the modern city, and across the Nile lie the temples and tombs of the West Bank Theban Necropolis, which includes the Valley of the Kings and the Valley of the Queens. The name comes from the Arabic al-quṣūr, the palaces, perhaps equivalent to the Greek and Coptic names meaning three castles. Its ancient Egyptian name was Waset, and the Greeks called it Thebes or Diospolis.

Thebes began to grow into a thriving city in the 11th Dynasty, under Montuhotep II, who united Egypt after the First Intermediate Period. It played a major part in expelling the Hyksos from Upper Egypt, and from the 18th to the 20th Dynasty it was the political, religious and military capital of Egypt. Expeditions to Kush and to Canaan, Phoenicia and Syria brought it great wealth, and it drew Babylonians, Mitanni, Hittites, Phoenicians and Minoans. A Hittite prince even came to marry Tutankhamun's widow, Ankhesenamun. Its principal god was Amun, worshipped with his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, and linked with the sun god Ra as Amun-Ra.

In the Late Period the political centre moved to northern cities such as Bubastis, Sais and Alexandria, but Thebes stayed the religious capital until the Greek period, and the temple at Karnak was the most important in Egypt until the end of antiquity. The Assyrian emperor Ashurbanipal attacked the city, which fell into ruins and lost significance. Christian monks later set up monasteries among the monuments, including at the temple of Hatshepsut, now Deir el-Bahri. After the Muslim conquest part of Luxor Temple was converted from a church into the mosque now called the Abu Haggag Mosque. Europeans visited in growing numbers in the 18th century.

Luxor is the capital of the Luxor Governorate in Upper Egypt and is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. It has often been called an open-air museum, and it is a major destination for tourists. Its monuments, including Karnak, Luxor Temple and the Theban Necropolis, together with the temples, churches and mosques of the city, make up a layered cultural heritage.
luzon: Luzon covers 109,964.9 square kilometres, which makes it the fifteenth largest island in the world. The South China Sea lies to its west, the Philippine Sea to its east and the Luzon Strait to its north. The Cordillera Central, which holds the island's highest mountain, Mount Pulag at 2,922 metres, and the Sierra Madre enclose the Cagayan Valley, where the Cagayan River, the longest in the Philippines, flows. The name is thought to come from lusong, a Tagalog word for the large wooden mortar used to hull rice.

Fossils of Homo luzonensis from Callao Cave, from at least 50,000 to 67,000 years ago, represent an extinct archaic human species. Before 1000 CE the Tagalog, Kapampangan and Pangasinan peoples had established coastal polities, notably Maynila, Tondo and Namayan. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription, written in 900 and the oldest known Philippine document, names places around Manila Bay. These kingdoms were thalassocracies based on trade with neighbouring Asian states, and Portuguese sailors recorded the island as Luçonia.

Spanish rule began with an expedition sent by Miguel López de Legazpi, which reached Albay in 1569. After the defeat of the local Rajah Sulayman, the capital of the colony was moved from Cebu to Manila. The Philippine Revolution against Spain began in Cavite and spread across Luzon, and the First Philippine Republic was established at Malolos in Bulacan. It lost the Philippine–American War to the United States, which set up Baguio as a summer retreat.

Luzon holds Manila, the national capital, and Quezon City, the most populous city, and the economy of the island centres on Metro Manila. More than half of the people of the Philippines live in the Luzon island group. Most of its languages belong to the Philippine group of Austronesian; Tagalog, Ilocano, Central Bikol, Kapampangan and Pangasinan are the major regional ones. Roman Catholicism is the main religion.
lviv: Lviv lies on the edge of the Roztochia Upland, about 70 km east of the Polish border and 160 km north of the eastern Carpathians. Its highest point is the Vysokyi Zamok, or High Castle hill, which rises 409 m above sea level and overlooks the historic centre with its green-domed churches. The city has been known by many names, among them Lwów in Polish, Lemberg in German, Lvov in Russian and Leopolis in Latin.

In the 14th century Lviv became the heart of Red Ruthenia and Galicia, overtaking older cities such as Halych, Chełm, Belz and Przemyśl. It was the capital of the Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia from 1272 to 1340. In the wars over the succession King Casimir III of Poland captured the city in 1340 and burned the old princely castle, and Poland gained control of Lviv and its region in 1349. On 17 June 1356 Casimir moved the city to a new site and granted it Magdeburg rights, under which a council elected by the wealthy citizens decided city matters. In 1358 it became the seat of a Roman Catholic archdiocese.

After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the Habsburg monarchy annexed the region, and Lemberg became the capital of the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria. Its population grew from about 30,000 in 1772 to 196,000 by 1910, with urban poverty alongside the growth. After the First World War the city became a battleground between the Polish population and the Ukrainian Sich Riflemen, and on the night of 31 October to 1 November 1918 the Western Ukrainian People's Republic was proclaimed with Lviv as capital. In the interwar Second Polish Republic Lwów was, after Warsaw, the second cultural and academic centre, home to the Lwów School of Mathematics.

The Red Army entered Lwów on 22 September 1939, and the city became the capital of the new Lviv Oblast. After the war it remained in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, and most of the remaining Polish population was expelled to the former German territories, especially Wrocław. Since 1991 Lviv has been part of independent Ukraine.

Lviv is the largest city of western Ukraine and the administrative centre of Lviv Oblast. It has Lviv University and Lviv Polytechnic. Its historic heart has cobblestone streets and Renaissance, Baroque, Neoclassicist and Art Nouveau architecture, and is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
lycaon-of-arcadia: In Greek mythology Lycaon was the son of Pelasgus and either the Oceanid Meliboea or Deianira, daughter of an elder Lycaon. His wife was called Cyllene, an Oread nymph who gave her name to Mount Cyllenê, though she was sometimes regarded as his mother instead. Other accounts name his wife as Nonacris, after whom an Arcadian town may have been named. He had at least three daughters, Callisto, Dia and Psophis. According to the Bibliotheca of Pseudo-Apollodorus he had 50 sons, and in the list given by Pausanias almost each of them founded a city in Arcadia and became its eponym.

Although notorious for his deed, Lycaon was also remembered as a culture hero. He was believed to have founded the city of Lycosura, to have established a cult of Zeus Lycaeus and to have started the Lycaean Games, which Pausanias thought older than the Panathenaic Games. According to Gaius Julius Hyginus, he dedicated the first temple to Hermes of Cyllene. The Suda adds that he guarded the laws his father had set for the Arcadians and told his subjects that Zeus visited his home in the guise of a mortal to watch how lawful people were.

Several versions of the myth were already reported by Hesiod, and the most popular is that of Ovid in the first book of the Metamorphoses. Ovid's Lycaon doubted that his guest was a god, served him the flesh of a prisoner and tried to kill him in his sleep, whereupon Zeus brought the roof down and turned the fleeing Lycaon into a wolf. In the Bibliotheca, Zeus visited the sons disguised as a peasant, and they mixed a child's entrails into his meal. Zeus threw the table over, which explains the name of the city Trapezus, and killed Lycaon and his sons with lightning. Only the youngest, Nyctimus, survived, saved by Gaia.

Other writers vary the victim and the punishment. Pausanias has Lycaon turned into a wolf at once after sacrificing a child on the altar of Zeus, while Lycophron has all of them turned into wolves for devouring Nyctimus. In accounts attributed to Hyginus the victim is Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto, whom Zeus restores to life. Eratosthenes says Lycaon butchered his grandson, and Zeus struck his house with a thunderbolt.
lyceum-classical: The Lyceum took its name from Apollo Lyceus. It began as a sanctuary, later became a public exercise area, and had a gymnasium added afterwards. It is not known when the worship was introduced to Athens or when the site became a sanctuary. It lay outside and east of the city wall, between the Ilissus river to the south and Mount Lykabettus to the north, and it served many purposes: military training, meetings of the Athenian assembly before the Pnyx became the official meeting place, cult practices and teaching.

Philosophical debate had taken place there long before Aristotle. Prodicus of Ceos, Protagoras and Socrates came to teach and discuss, and Isocrates taught rhetoric there in the fourth century BCE. Plato's dialogue Lysis is set on a road from the Academy to the Lyceum.

In 335 BCE Athens was under Macedonian rule and Aristotle, then aged about fifty, returned from Asia. He taught in the mornings in the Lyceum and founded a school there. His followers became known as the Peripatetics because he tended to walk as he taught. His students were given historical or scientific research projects, and the school collected books and natural specimens. In 322 BCE a reaction against the Macedonians forced Aristotle to leave Athens, and he handed the school to Theophrastus. He died later that year in Chalcis.

Theophrastus headed the school for 36 years and bought land and buildings near the gymnasium in 315 BCE. The school closed for a year in 306 BCE, when foreign philosophers were required to leave Athens. Strato of Lampsacus followed Theophrastus, and Lyco of Troas was its last certain scholar before his death after 225 BCE. The Lyceum fell with the rest of Athens in 86 BCE, when Sulla attacked the city. Some scholars think it was refounded in the first century CE by Andronicus of Rhodes and continued until the Heruli and Goths sacked Athens in 267.

The library of the school passed from Theophrastus to Neleus, who took the books to Skepsis in Mysia. Some seem to have reached the library at Alexandria. Later the collection was returned to the school and, when Sulla attacked, shipped to Rome, where Andronicus of Rhodes arranged and edited Aristotle's surviving works between 73 and 20 BCE. About a fifth of the works were lost on the way.

The remains of the Lyceum were uncovered in 1996 during an excavation for a new museum in central Athens, near the junction of Rigillis and Vasilissis Sofias Streets. The first finds were a gymnasium and a wrestling area. The site was opened to the public in 2009 and is now a park.
lydia: Lydia was an Iron Age civilisation of western Anatolia, with Sardis as its capital and only city. Its early history is obscure. In the Late Bronze Age the territory belonged to a broader polity called Arzawa, whose sub-kingdoms Mira and Šeḫa, and the city-state of Apasa, the precursor of Ephesus, Lydia later absorbed. About 800 BCE the Lydian people appear to have achieved some political cohesion, but precise events cannot be determined because no contemporary written records survive. Literary accounts of two early dynasties, the house of Atys and the Heraclids, who allegedly ruled for twenty-two generations, are steeped in mythology and lack historical credibility.

Gyges, the first Lydian king whose existence is shown by contemporary records, is said in semi-mythical accounts to have overthrown the last Heraclid, Candaules, with the help of a Carian prince. His rise came amid the turmoil that followed the invasion of the Cimmerians, who around 675 BCE destroyed the kingdom of Phrygia.
