Gyges consolidated his kingdom into a military power and attacked the Ionian Greek cities of Miletus, Smyrna and Colophon. Around 662 BCE he sent Carian and Ionian soldiers to help the Egyptian king Psamtik I unite Egypt.

Under Alyattes and Croesus the kingdom grew to control all of Asia Minor west of the River Halys except Lycia. In 547 BCE Croesus besieged and captured the Persian city of Pteria in Cappadocia and enslaved its inhabitants. Cyrus the Great marched against him, the Battle of Pteria was a stalemate, and the Lydians retreated to Sardis. The kings met again at the Battle of Thymbra, which Cyrus won, and Sardis fell, so that Lydia became a satrapy of the Persian Empire. The Romans entered Sardis in 133 BCE, and Lydia became part of the province of Asia.

Herodotus wrote that the Lydians were the first people to use gold and silver coins, and the first to set up retail shops in permanent locations. The first coins were made of electrum, an alloy of gold and silver, and the most common opinion is that they were minted near the beginning of the reign of Alyattes, who reigned from about 591 to about 560 BCE. Their dating is among the most debated topics in ancient numismatics. Lydian was an Indo-European language of the Anatolian family, written in an alphabet related to Greek, and it became extinct in the 1st century BCE.
lyndon-b-johnson: Lyndon Baines Johnson was born on 27 August 1908 in a small farmhouse on the Pedernales River near Stonewall, Texas. In 1931 Representative Richard M. Kleberg appointed him his legislative secretary, which was Johnson's formal introduction to politics. In 1937 he won a special election for Texas's 10th congressional district on a New Deal platform and served in the House until 1949.

In 1948 Johnson won the Democratic primary for the Senate in a highly controversial runoff against the former governor Coke Stevenson, and then the general election. He became Democratic whip in 1951 and in January 1953 Senate Minority Leader, the most junior senator ever chosen for the post; he became majority leader in 1954. John F. Kennedy beat him for the 1960 Democratic presidential nomination, then offered him the vice presidential place on the ticket to balance it and attract Southern votes.

Kennedy was assassinated on 22 November 1963, and Johnson took the oath on Air Force One that day. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 followed, as did the Revenue Act of 1964. By early 1964 he used the name Great Society for a programme of anti-poverty measures, health care reform, education, urban renewal and environmental protection. After the violent attack on marchers at Selma on 7 March 1965, known as Bloody Sunday, he sent voting rights legislation to Congress. The Social Security Amendments of 1965 created Medicare and Medicaid.

On Vietnam, when he took office there were 16,700 American military personnel in South Vietnam, and Johnson came to support escalation, determined to prevent the spread of Communism. After reports in August 1964 of attacks on two US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin, he obtained the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on 7 August 1964, giving blanket approval for the use of force.

Johnson began his presidency with near-universal support, but his approval fell as the public grew frustrated with the Vietnam War and with domestic unrest, and a gap appeared between what he said and what was happening in the war, which came to be called the credibility gap. After disappointing results in the New Hampshire primary he withdrew his candidacy in 1968. He retired to his Texas ranch and died on 22 January 1973. Historians' judgements of him rest on his legislative achievements on one side and the failure of his Vietnam policy on the other.
lyon: Lyon lies at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône, to the northwest of the French Alps. The two rivers converge south of the historic city centre and form a peninsula, the Presqu'île, bounded by two large hills to the west and north and a large plain to the east. Place Bellecour stands on the Presqu'île. The northern hill, La Croix-Rousse, is known as the hill that works because it is traditionally home to many small silk workshops. The western hill, Fourvière, is known as the hill that prays, because it holds the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière, several convents and the Archbishop's residence. East of the Rhône a large flat area holds much of modern Lyon and most of its population.

The name evolved from the Gallic Lugdunon, through Lugdon and Luon, into the present form, Lyon, during the 13th century. The Gallic Lugdun, in Roman times Lugdunum, combines two words. The first may be the name of the Celtic god Lug, or lugon, meaning crow, the messenger of Lug, or another word lug, meaning light. The second is dunos, meaning fortress or hill. The name may thus designate the hill of Fourvière, on which the ancient city stands, and could mean hill of the god Lug, hill of the crows or shining hill. Julius Pokorny instead associates the first part with an Indo-European radical meaning dark, black or swamp.

Below the hill, in the present Saint-Vincent district, was the Gallic village of Condate, probably a hamlet of sailors or fishermen on the banks of the Saône. Condate is a Gallic word meaning confluence. In Roman times the city was called Caput Galliae, the capital of the Gauls. During the Revolution, on 12 October 1793, a decree of the Convention Nationale renamed it Commune-Affranchie, meaning Emancipated Commune, and it resumed its name in 1794 after the end of the Terror.

Lyon is the prefecture of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region and the seat of an archbishopric whose holder bears the title of Primate of the Gauls. The districts of Old Lyon, the Fourvière hill, the Presqu'île and the slopes of the Croix-Rousse are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Roman ruins near the Fourvière Basilica include the Ancient Theatre and the Odeon, and the Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls also survives.

Auguste and Louis Lumière pioneered cinema in the city in 1895. Each 8 December the Fête des lumières marks thanks to the Virgin Mary, who purportedly saved the city from a deadly plague in the Middle Ages, and residents place candles at their windows.
lysander: Little is known of Lysander's early life, and his year of birth is estimated at 454 BCE. His father Aristocritus belonged to the Spartan Heracleidae, claiming descent from Heracles without being of a royal family, and some ancient authors record that his mother was a helot or slave. According to Plutarch he grew up in poverty and showed himself obedient. In the Spartan upbringing he was matched as lover of the adolescent future king Agesilaus. He was elected in 408 BCE to Sparta's annual office of admiral.

Lysander sailed with 30 triremes and made Ephesus the main naval base of the Peloponnesian League. At Sardis he impressed Cyrus, the young son of the Persian king Darius, who began to fund Sparta's war on a large scale. He also encouraged oligarchs in the Aegean cities to organise into political clubs, promising to put them in power if Athens were defeated. After his year ended he was replaced by Callicratidas, and later returned as second-in-command to Aracus, since Spartan law did not allow an admiral to hold office twice.

With 125 to 150 ships he sailed to the Hellespont and destroyed the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami in 405 BCE, capturing most of the ships as they lay ashore. He then installed ten-man boards drawn from his oligarchic clubs in many cities, and democrats were often massacred or banished. Peace was concluded in spring 404 BCE, and Lysander sailed into the Piraeus, ordered the city's walls razed and its fleet burnt, and oversaw the assembly that replaced the democracy with the Thirty Tyrants.

In 403 BCE Thrasybulus led exiles who defeated the oligarchic forces at Munychia, and Pausanias, king of Sparta, arranged a settlement restoring democracy against Lysander's opposition. Lysander persuaded Sparta to make Agesilaus II king, but Agesilaus, resentful of his power, left him in command in the Hellespont when they campaigned against Persia in 396 BCE. Lysander helped start the Corinthian War and was killed in 395 BCE at the Battle of Haliartus, after bringing his troops too near the walls of the city. Xenophon, a contemporary, makes him a main figure of his history, while later writers such as Cornelius Nepos charge him with cruelty and perfidy.
lysias: Lysias was one of the ten Attic orators later canonised by Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus of Samothrace. Dionysius of Halicarnassus gave his birth as 459 BCE, but modern critics generally place it about 445 BCE. His father Cephalus, a native of Syracuse, settled at Athens at the invitation of Pericles. At Thurii, the newly founded colony, Lysias is said to have begun his study of rhetoric. The Athenian defeat in Sicily in 415–413 BCE strengthened an anti-Athenian faction there, and Lysias and his elder brother Polemarchus were accused of Atticizing, driven out and settled at Athens in 412 BCE.

The brothers were rich, having inherited from Cephalus. Lysias had a house in the Piraeus, near the shield factory that employed a hundred and twenty skilled slaves. In 404 BCE the Thirty Tyrants singled out resident aliens, and Lysias and Polemarchus were on a list of ten to be the first victims. Polemarchus was made to drink hemlock. Lysias escaped through a back door with the help of a large bribe and took a boat to Megara.

Probably poorer afterwards, he became a logographer, writing speeches for litigants to deliver in the law courts, and from 403 to about 380 BCE his output must have been incessant. In 403 BCE he accused Eratosthenes, one of the Thirty, his only direct contact with Athenian politics. At the Olympic festival of 388 BCE he spoke the Olympiacus, denouncing Dionysius I of Syracuse. His latest datable work belongs to 381 or 380 BCE, and he probably died soon after 380 BCE.

Thirty-four speeches survive complete, and 127 others are known from fragments or titles. Ancient critics made him the model of the plain style, close to the language of daily life, with simple vocabulary, sparing use of rhetorical figures and a simple arrangement of introduction, narrative, proofs and conclusion. He adapted each speech to the age, station and circumstances of the client who would deliver it, and was noted for concealing his art. His most important surviving speech is Against Eratosthenes.
lysimachus: Lysimachus was born about 360 BCE into a family of Thessalian stock who were citizens of Pella in Macedonia. His father Agathocles was a nobleman and an intimate friend of Philip II of Macedon, and Lysimachus was educated at the court at Pella. According to Pausanias and Justin, Alexander the Great had him thrown to a lion as punishment, because he had smuggled poison to a man condemned to a slow death. Both writers say he overcame the lion with his bare hands and then became one of Alexander's favourites. In 328 BCE he was one of Alexander's immediate bodyguards, and in 324 BCE at Susa he was given a ceremonial crown for his actions in India.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE Lysimachus was appointed governor of Thrace, where he had difficulties with the Thracian king Seuthes III. In 315 BCE he joined Cassander, Ptolemy and Seleucus against Antigonus, and in 309 BCE he founded Lysimachia on the neck connecting the Chersonese with the mainland. He took the royal title in 306 or 305 BCE. At the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE Antigonus was defeated and killed, and Lysimachus received Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor.

He then allied himself with Ptolemy and married his daughter Arsinoe II. A campaign beyond the Danube ended with his capture by the Getae king Dromichaetes, who freed him in 292 BCE in return for the Danubian lands he had taken. In 287 BCE he and Pyrrhus of Epirus drove Demetrius out of Macedonia, and in 285 BCE Lysimachus expelled Pyrrhus and took complete control of Macedonia.

His last years were troubled. In 284 BCE his wife Arsinoe II, wishing her own sons to succeed, intrigued against his eldest son Agathocles with her half-brother Ptolemy Keraunos, and they accused Agathocles of conspiring with Seleucus. Lysimachus had Agathocles put to death. The deed aroused great indignation, many cities of Asia Minor revolted and his trusted friends deserted him. Agathocles's widow and children fled to Seleucus, who invaded Lysimachus's territory in Asia Minor.

In 281 BCE Lysimachus crossed the Hellespont and was killed at the Battle of Corupedium. His body was found after some days, guarded from birds of prey by his faithful dog, and his son Alexander buried it at Lysimachia. He had married three times, to Nicaea, daughter of the regent Antipater, to the Persian princess Amastris and to Arsinoe II, who bore him three sons.
lysippus: Lysippos was born at Sicyon around 390 BCE and worked in bronze in his youth. He taught himself the art of sculpture and later became head of the school of Argos and Sicyon. According to Pliny, he produced more than 1,500 works, all of them in bronze. His pupil Chares of Lindos built the Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Since the statue no longer exists, it is debated whether its sections were cast in bronze or hammered from sheet bronze. Lysippos had three sons, Euthyktates, Boidas and Daippos, who were also sculptors and his pupils.

Lysippos succeeded the sculptor Polykleitos in contemporary reputation. He was personal sculptor to Alexander the Great, the only artist whom the conqueror saw fit to represent him. Epigrams by Posidippus and Asclepiades praise a bronze portrait of Alexander, saying fire is in the glance of the bronze. Lysippos is credited with the stock image of an inspired, godlike Alexander with tousled hair and parted lips, looking upward, known as the Lysippean gaze. One early Imperial Roman copy, found at Tivoli, is in the Louvre.

Works attributed to him include the Horses of Saint Mark, Eros Stringing the Bow, Agias, known from a marble copy at Delphi, the Oil Pourer, the Farnese Hercules and the Apoxyomenos, or Scraper, known from a Roman marble copy in the Vatican Museums. He was also known for bronze colossi from Taras: a Zeus 17 metres tall and a seated Herakles of seven metres.

Lysippos developed a more slender style than Polykleitos, which became known as the Canon of Lysippos. In his Historia Naturalis Pliny the Elder wrote that he introduced a new canon, making heads smaller than the older sculptors did and bodies more slender and dry, so that the statues looked taller. He is credited with establishing a canon of eight heads to the height of the body. Commentators noted the grace of his figures, their symmetria, or coherent balance, and his attention to the details of eyelids and toenails.

Together with Scopas and Praxiteles he is considered one of the three leading sculptors of the Classical Greek era, bringing transition into the Hellenistic period. The Victorious Youth, a bronze that resurfaced from the sea around 1972 and is now at the Getty Museum, has been associated with him by some, because its detail is consistent with his style and proportions.
lyuh-woon-hyung: Lyuh Woon-hyung, known by the art name Mongyang, was born on 25 May 1886 in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province, into the Hamyang Yeo clan. In 1907 he joined the National Debt Repayment Movement, and around then he became a Protestant and an associate of the American missionary Charles Allen Clark. In 1910 he broke with tradition by freeing the slaves of his household. He entered the Pyongyang Presbyterian Theological Seminary in 1911, and in 1914 went to China, where he studied English literature at a university in Nanjing before moving to Shanghai in 1917.

In Shanghai he founded in 1918 what became the Shanghai Korean People's Association and led the New Korean Youth League. In 1919 he took part in drawing up the February 8 Declaration of Independence in Tokyo, a precursor of the declaration that opened the March First Movement, and in efforts to send Korean delegates to the Paris Peace Conference. In April 1919 he was among the founders of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea.

In 1920 he joined the Korean Communist Party. In 1922 he attended the Congress of the Peoples of the East in Moscow, where he met Vladimir Lenin and Leon Trotsky. The Japanese authorities arrested him in Shanghai in 1929 and he served three years in prison. From 1933 he headed the newspaper Chosŏn Chungang Ilbo, and was forced out in 1936 after Korean newspapers erased the Japanese flag from pictures of the Olympic gold medallist Sohn Kee-chung. In 1944, expecting Japan's defeat, he organised a secret committee that spread across Korea.

Just before the surrender the Japanese official Endo Ryusaku made contact with him and agreed to release prisoners. The preparatory committee he founded on 17 August 1945 set up over 140 branches in north and south within the month. In October, under pressure from the United States Military Government, he stepped down from the People's Republic and formed the People's Party of Korea. When a movement to unite left and right arose in May 1946 he represented the centre-left, and was attacked from both extremes.

On 19 July 1947 he was killed in Seoul by Han Chi-geun, a 19-year-old who had fled from North Korea and belonged to the White Shirts Society, a right-wing terrorist group. His death was widely mourned. He is one of the few modern Korean politicians revered in both South and North Korea, and on 21 February 2008 South Korea awarded him the Order of Merit for National Foundation posthumously.
